THE
PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES
(OFFICIAL REPORT)
IN THE
SIXTH SESSION OF THE FIFTH PARLIAMENT OF NORTHERN IRELAND
APPOINTED TO MEET AT STORMONT ON THE TWENTY-THIRD DAY OF FEBRUARY,
IN THE SEVENTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF
HIS MAJESTY KING GEORGE VI
VOLUME XXVI.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Tuesday, 23rd February, 1943.
The Sixth Session of the Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed to
meet on 23rd February, 1943, in the
Seventh year of the Reign of King George
VI., was opened by the Governor (His
Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland) in
the Chair.
Brigadier-General H. G. Young,
C.I.E., D.S.O., acting Gentleman Usher,
of the Black Rod, was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Acting
Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Two
of the Clock, and then resumed.
Papers Presented.
Ministry of Finance:
Supplementary Estimate for Services
under the Government of Northern Ireland for the year ending 31st March,
1943. (By Act.)
Ministry of Labour:
Factories (Operations at Unfenced
Machinery, Amended Schedule) Regulations (Northern Ireland), 1942. (By Act.)
National Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions (Internees) Regulations (Northern Ireland), 1942. (By Act.)
Ministry of Home Affairs:
Inspectors' Reports for 1942 for Mental
Hospital in Northern Ireland. (By Act).
SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return of Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate, and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.
A
King's Speech
Sessional Orders
HOUSE OF COMMONS
WITNESSES.
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any persons have been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the.
same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the. utmast severity against
such offender.
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any persons hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered, That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein,
or thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS AND
RECORDS.
Ordered, That the Votes, Proceedings
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered, that a Committee of Privileges be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for the more effectual preventing Clandestine. Outlawries," was read
the First time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear His Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The people of Northern Ireland, who
have followed with pride and admiration the gallant exploits of the armed
forces of the United Nations in every
theatre of war, face the tasks which
lie ahead with renewed determination
and courage. My Ministers are COoperating to the fullest extent with His
Majesty's Government at Westminster,
inspired by the common purpose of
freeing the world from the tyranny of
an aggressive and brutal foe.
The continued happy relations between my Government and the various
branches of His Majesty's Forces, and
the cordial spirit of comradeship between the civil population and members
of the British, United States and other
Allied units in Northern Ireland,
afford me the greatest satisfaction.
Although many thousands of our
young men and women have volunteered
for the fighting services, many more are
still required, and I earnestly hope that
the call to duty will be answered to an
even fuller extent than in the past.
The Ulster Home Guard, which, I am
pleased to record, has reached a high
state of efficiency, reflecting the greatest
credit on all ranks, is also in need of
recruits, and I trust that those whose
duties permit will enrol in this Force,
which is so vitally necessary for the
protection of the Home Front.
My Ministers continue to attach the
utmost importance to all measures of
Civil Defence. I am glad to know that
the period of relief from air raids has
been occupied by the Civil Defence
Services in perfecting their organisation
and training their personnel in the light
of the lessons learned by grim experience, and I am confident that all
will be ready to meet any emergency
which may arise. I am pleased to
learn that good progress has also been
King's Speech

made with the unification of our local
fire brigades into the new National Fire
Service.
I have been gratified by the magnificent response made by the whole
agricultural community to the appeal
by my Government to increase the
production of food and flax during the
past year. Notwithstanding unfavourable weather and many other difficulties
only a very small proportion of the
harvest was lost, and the valuable
assistance rendered by members of the
Forces and by many of our people has
earned the gratitude of our farmers.
This season even greater efforts must be
made by the civilian population to save
the harvest. It is also essential that
there should be a further substantial
increase this year in our ploughed land
and a still larger proportion devoted to
barley, oats and potatoes. My Ministers
hope that at least one hundred thousand
acres of flax will be grown and that not
less than eighty per cent. of the crop
will be dam retted.
When I last addressed you certain
industries were facing a difficult period
because their normal products could
not by their nature be regarded as
essential under war-time conditions. On
the principle that it must be our aim to
use all available machinery and man

particularly in branches of the textile

ensure

Closely associated with the production

power purposes. I am glad to learn
that the scheme for providing additional

which work has been proceeding during

are now available to meet
emergency.

about the restraining effect of derating
on social developments in our area and
a proposal will be laid before you at an
early date which will alleviate the

have experienced in carrying out essential improvements owing to the operation of the derating system.
The arrangements which are being

additional Hospital and Medical
Services under emergency conditions
will, when complete, effect an increase

Among the measures which you will

making further provision for the protection and welfare of young persons
and the treatment of young offenders.

the

It is satisfactory to note that, notwithstanding the strain of war conditions, the public transport undertakings

During the past year grave outrages
have been committed by those elements
who are striving to undermine
Constitution; and all ranks of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary and the Class "B"
Special Constabulary deserve the highest
commendation for their devotion to
duty and bearing in dealing with the
situation.
My Government has been in consultation with the Imperial Authorities in
regard to the necessity for exercising
control over persons entering Northern
Ireland who were not ordinarily resident
in Northern Ireland on 1st January,
1940. A scheme came into operation
on the 1st January last whereby, with
certain exceptions, all such immigrants
who wish to reside in Northern Ireland
for more than six weeks are required to
be in possession of residence permits.
It is intended that the scheme will be
kept in operation for a reasonable time
after the war to facilitate the reinstatement in employment of demobilised men
from Northern Ireland who joined His
Majesty's Forces as volunteers.
Public interest has been aroused by
the issue of the Report on social security
by Sir William Beveridge. Whatever
improvements are effected by the
Imperial Government in connection
with the social services in Great Britain
will be carried out on a similar scale in
Northern Ireland.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God
may rest upon your deliberations.

Mr. MINFORD (in morning dress): I
beg to move:
a
That a humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland as followeth :
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament.
our
In rising to move this Address I should
like to reflect for a few moments on the
three years gone past. During this period
war of unparalleled ferocity and
savagery has raged throughout the world,
causing privation, want, starvation, and
misery to countless millions of innocent
peoples. Our enemies lashed with an
inhuman hatred and writhing under the
crippling and mortal blows dealt by our
gallant armies and those of our Allies are
now facing sure and certain defeat.
Looking at the recent brilliant victories,
we must all feel an unbounded admiration
and deep sense of real pride in the knowledge that many of our young and gallant

Ulstermen have taken their full share in
these martial events, and are to-day in
the van of those gigantic forces liberating the world from the tyranny and
cruelty of a bestial foe.
His Majesty's Government at West-
Minister, under their great leader, Mr.
Churchill, have faced with steadfast
determination and undaunted courage
the many heavy and grievous tasks of the
past years of war, and it is a source of
gratitude that our Government have
taken their full share in all responsibilities and have placed at the disposal of
Great Britain the entire resources of
Northern Ireland.
We must all feel an unbounded and
heartfelt admiration for our own Prime
Minister for his untiring and unfailing
devotion to this great cause, and we can
assure him and his several Ministers of
our most loyal co-operation and steadfast.
support in their mighty efforts for
winning the war and the re-establishment
of peace again on this earth.
The people of Northern Ireland
were delighted to welcome to their
shores the gallant men of the
British, American and other Allied
forces, and to extend to them that
hospitality and friendship which has
created a bond of comradeship which will
not be easily removed or forgotten. We
are not unmindful of the many men,
both young and old, who form our Ulster
Home Guard, and who have given to us
all a sense of deep security by their devotion to duty. Though their numbers
at present are very large many more recruits are required for their magnificent
work, and I trust that any young man
who has the time at his disposal will
enrol in this great force in order to play
his part in defending this beloved
Province.
I now come to civil defence. We are
delighted to know that the organisation
is being perfected in every way, and by
the grim experience of the terrible air
raids the personnel have now been trained
to meet any emergency that may in
future arise, and with the reorganisation
of the Fire Services we feel confident that
if called upon they will give a good
account of themselves in the event of
future action. We must not forget their
noble work in the past, and they are
deserving of our highest praise.

I am not unmindful of the great responsibility the Minister of Agriculture
has upon his shoulders, but I can assure
him that the farmers of Ulster are most
willing to co-operate with him in any
measure for the greater production of
food. At the same time I trust that he
I will see to it that the farmers and farm
workers will receive that remuneration
to which they are justly entitled. All
I ask for is parity with Great Britain,

I must say that I am deeply disappointed

given to farmers, and I trust that he will

With regard to the request in the
Gracious Speech for an increased acreage
of flax, it is my fixed opinion that a
satisfactory solution of this problem can
only be found in giving to the farmer of
Ulster a greater degree of financial
security, bearing in mind always that the
flax crop is of such a speculative and expensive nature that the farmer, whose

[Mr. Minford]
powers of speculation are very small,
hesitates to make a plunge in this
direction. Failure of this particular
crop often means financial disaster to the
farmer. To my knowledge quite a number
of wealthy speculators have experienced
much loss during the past two years in
the growing of flax. If these wealthy
organisations refuse to invest capital
in 1943 in the flax trade, how can
we
expect the farmer who has to
earn every penny by the sweat of his
brow to risk what little he has knowing
perfectly well that if he fails he alone
must suffer? Let the Government who
have made this request show their faith
by backing the flax grower against, not
only a dead loss on his flax crop, but up
to the equivalent remuneration of any
other crop he may grow.
As this flax is so urgently needed for
war purposes as well as for the continuance
of our linen trade, I feel that our Government must take immediate steps to met
this increasingly grave situation and face
up to its immediate urgency. Should it not
be within their power to make the
financial changes, I suggest that representations should be made to Great
Britain at Westminster for the necessary
authority and financial assistance if
required.
In the Gracious Speech the industrial
situation is reviewed as having faced and
overcome the critical period of change of
production to solely war-time needs. We
in Northern Ireland have great satisfaction in knowing that our machinery and
man-power are playing a good part in
the production of vital war materials. I
trust that in a short period those which
remain as yet unconverted will swell the
rising tide of war production, and will
reduce to a minimum the unemployment
figures in Northern Ireland. But we
must not overlook the fact that our
basic industries such as shipbuilding,
textile and engineering are sending out
an ever increasing flow of vital instruments of war. In passing I must pay a
high tribute to the women of Ulster
who are now engaged in the manufacture of munitions, whose dexterity
and dauntless courage have enabled
to carry out our commitments
in that great Ulster tradition
of love for King and Country. Our
Government has planned and secured, I
us
am delighted to know, an abundance of
electricity for power purposes, and also
auxiliary plants are already at work
ready to meet any emergency which may
arise.
We note that a proposal is to be laid
before us at an early date. enabling local
authorities to carry out essential improvements already, in my opinion, long overdue. Financial assistance is to be granted
by the Exchequer to provide, additional
Hospital and Medical Services for the
people. of Northern Ireland, and I trust
that the Government will be fittingly
generous in order that these said services
may be comparable with or even greater
than those existing in Great Britain, as I
consider the care of the health of the

It is with great regret that I look back
over the past year and recall the grievous
outrages perpetrated by that small section
of the community of this Province who
seem to have no regard for law and order.
The members of the Ulster Constabulary
and the "B" Force. deserve our highest
tribute for the competent manner in
which they have dealt with this problem
and for their fearless devotion to duty.
The existing scheme whereby aliens wishing to reside within Northern Ireland for
a period exceeding six weeks must have
a resident permit, will be continued after
the war, to enable our gallant men and
women demobilised after victory to be
reinstated in their employment. We all
feel very strongly that Ulster men and
women should have first preference in
all Ulster work.
I note with pleasure also that mention
is made of the supplementary grants to old
age pensions and to the provision of milk
at free or reduced rates to school children
and expectant mothers. These, in my
opinion, are worthy of all the consideration they have received. There is no
doubt that a life grown old in the faithful
service of its country is most certainly
deserving of every comfort and happiness
in the eventide of its existence.
I note in the Gracious Speech that a
Bill will be laid before Parliament
designed to strengthen the Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act. I am at the
moment unable to forecast what this
legislation will be, but I am certain that
every Member of this House is anxious to
make the law such as will enable the

of all general public amenities, and it is

these words are all too true:
Full many a flower is born to blush
unseen,
And waste its sweetness on the desert
air.
I should also like to pay a handsome
tribute to workers and managements of
the public transport undertakings in
Northern Ireland for the magnificent way
in which they have handled the greatly
increased volume of traffic which they have
been called upon to deal with, entailing
long hours and very arduous work.
Public interest has been keenly aroused
by the recent report of Sir William Beveridge for the immediate improvement of
social services in Great Britain. Our Prime
Minister has stated that Northern Ireland
will have equal participation in and full
enjoyment of any improvements adopted
by the Imperial Government, and I am
certain that every Member will welcome
its introduction to this House.
No longer must mass unemployment, with
its attendant poverty and disease, be the
national inheritance of our people and of
our children. Let us all make doubly sure
that the high ideals, for which so many of
our own flesh and blood are to-day giving
their all, are made, once and for all, a
living reality and a solid foundation laid
for the future of mankind that will stand
for all times "as rocks resist the billows
and the sky." Let us all now bend to our
tasks with a cheerful will, let us all now,
with a high unity of purpose, strive to
•
attain those prnciples incorporated in the
-Atlantic Charter, those principles which
can alone give to this country and the
world a glory and an honour never before

Mr. MIDGLEY: I regret that as I
was engaged on business this morning I
was not able to see a copy of this Speech
until a few minutes ago. I followed your
reading of it with great attention, and I
have probably learnt more by your reading of it than I would in any other way. I
have been unable to give time to the
consideration of the principles outlined
in this Speech that I might otherwise
have given, and so I rise this afternoon
as one who has not made a prepared
speech. I do not expect, therefore, to
be as constructive as I would have been
had I had some more time. Nevertheless
in the time at my disposal I have seen not
only the things that appear in the Speech.
but the things that have been left out of
it, and some of the things left out are as
important as the things that appear in
it, more important, probably.
Having said that, I would like to say
that I agree with the sentiments to such
an extent that it would appear ungracious
if I tried to suggest here this afternoon
that the good wishes and thanks that have
been expressed should not be participated
in by every other representative here.
I do join in in that spirit of appreciation,
especially where the thanks are expressed
through the medium of the King's Speech
to those who are upholding the honour
and integrity of the British Commonwealth throughout the world at the present time. I speak all the more proudly,
because I am the only representative of
a Commonwealth party here. I am
speaking for the first time in my capacity
as chairman of the Commonwealth party,
and I venture to predict that in a year
or two the Commonwealth party will be
exceedingly well heard of, and will be an
influential body of people throughout
Northern Ireland.

proud of them indeed to-day and let the
world know, as far as possible, that we in
Northern Ireland share the feeling that
they deserve the best that society can give
them for their sacrifices.
The agricultural problem has been referred to here this afternoon, and I am
not going to venture in where angels fear
to tread, or to set myself up as an agricultural expert. I do not know as much
about agriculture as I should like to know
and I do not know as much as other
Members of the House. One thing I do
know is, that fervent hope has been expressed in the King's Speech that still
greater efforts should be made this year
in order to do all that is necessary in the
interests of the foodstuffs of the country
Debate on the Address

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
and the supply of flax.
Tribute has been
paid in the speech to the efforts made last
year whereby only a slight proportion of
the total harvest was lost. I want to say
that there was a great deal of bungling
and inefficiency last year in regard to the
mobilisation of labour. I privately identified myself with a large organisation in
Belfast which had for its object the
recruitment of temporary labour on Wednesday afternoons and at week-ends in
various departments.
We mobilised
labour, got lists of names and submitted
them to the proper authority, and yet
many of these people were never called
upon to perform any task. On occasions they volunteered their services and
made arrangements to journey to a particular place, but whoever was responsible
from inside cancelled the arrangements at
the last minute. The people became disgusted and finally made up their minds
that their services were not wanted. Any
department concerned can have the full
facts from me privately in regard to this
matter. I hope that this kind of thing
will be avoided this year so that the people
may be encouraged to offer their services
and to do all they possibly can in this
magnificent work.
I see a passage in the Speech which
somewhat causes regret in my mind, as
it has come so late in the day. Right
at the bottom of the front page of the
Speech it says:
My Government has been concerned
about the restraining effect of derating
on social developments in our area, and
a proposal will be laid before you at
an early date which will alleviate the
difficulties which local authorities have
experienced in carrying out essential
improvements owing to the operation
of the derating system.
The Prime Minister will be aware of
the fact that it is many years since I first
mentioned this paradox or whatever you
like to call it. You can call it by any
name and each is nearly right. A system
grew up under the derating law which
enables some of the wealthiest firms in
Great Britain and Northern Ireland to
ride off scot free from 75 per cent. of
their derating expenses, while at the
same time those firms were making greater
profits than they had ever made in
history. I am now speaking of pre-war
days. Time and again in this House I
personally and I am sure others must
have done so too-pointed out to the
Government just exactly the strangling
effect this had with regard to local
authorities. The rateable capacity of the
municipality has been further injured by
circumstances over which they have no
control-namely through enemy actionand it is only now, after three years
of war, that the Government have
apparently given their attention to this
question of trying to improve legislation
in such a way that municipalities will
have some increased support by an
amendment of the law which granted
these firms the assistance they obtained
under the Derating Act.
I was interested to hear the Seconder
of the Address in reply, the Member for
Central Armagh, say that representations
had been made by the Government to the
Imperial authorities with the result that
soon we may expect amending legislation
which would have for its object the improvement of the position as it exists now
in regard to derating.
This is a very
interesting thing to hear-and I may return to this at a later stage. If it is
possible for this House to make representations in regard to this matter it is
also possible for the House to make representations in regard to other matters
which come specifically under the control
of the Imperial authorities. I am not
suggesting the Diplomatic Service as one,
otherwise I would have representations
made as to North Africa and the Vichy
government. I know that is outside our
purview. I am speaking more of internal
affairs.
In that connection may I say that the
very last paragraph of this Speech is
devoted to something on which I should
like to see representations made from this
House. The last paragraph is:
Public interest has been aroused by
the issue of the Report on social security
by Sir William Beveridge. Whatever
improvements are effected by the
Imperial Government in connection with
the social services in Great Britain will
be carried out on a similar scale in
Northern Ireland.
I think it is incumbent on the Government and imperative on all of us that a
feeling of absolute assurance should be
given to the community in regard to the
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
23 FEBRUARY 1943
Beveridge Report, and if we can make
representations with regard to derating to
the Imperial authorities I think we ought
to make representations to the Imperial
authorities regarding the acceptance of
the fundamental principles of the
Beveridge Report. We have nine or ten
Members in the Imperial Parliamentas a matter of fact we have 13, but only
11 normally attend-and representations
should be made through those Members.
This attitude of the Government is not
good. It is an uninspiring position for
the Government to take up. I think it
is most lamentable that the Government,
which has been holding all kinds of secret
sessions and meetings to consider whether
the machinery by which they came into
office is out of date and whether it is good
enough to keep them in office, should come
to the House and in the King's Speech
make such a hopeless, spineless declaration
as is in that paragraph, a paragraph with
no hope or inspiration for the masses of
the people; a paragraph which merely says
parrot-like that whatever improvements
are effected by the Imperial Government
in connection with social services will be
carried out on a similar scale in Northern
Ireland:
That is all right as far as it goes, but
that is not the clarion call that the people
are looking for. They expect the Government to develop some social philosophy of
their own, and on the Beveridge Report it
is time we made no mistake and displayed
no ambiguity as to where we stood. I
will proclaim where I stand. No matter
who took part in the debate in the
Imperial House-and I read every word
of it—and no matter how glorious the
personal achievement of one Cabinet
Minister in getting the Conservatives
to vote as they did that is what
he succeeded in doing in his final
great speech-as a representative of a
growing and intelligent democracy in
Northern Ireland, I am absolutely on
the side of the Beveridge Report. I am
for its acceptance from beginning to end,
not perhaps at once in its entirety, but
for the acceptance of the fundamental
principles of the Report, the carrying out
of the Report stage by stage, and as
quickly as possible. I am for the speediest
implementation of the Report with a
declaration to the men of the fighting
forces that when they come back again
after offering their all in defence of their
country they are going back to a country
where at least there is some freedom from
distress and insecurity.
Unless we have a declaration like that
from the Government the Prime Minister
can take it from me that the stock of the
Government, which has been falling for
some time past, will continue to fall
throughout the constituencies in the
Province. I have travelled through the
country a great deal recently, and from
present indications I am going to be able
to travel more in the days which lie
ahead, and wherever I have gone and
tried to get a grip on these social issues I
have found the people anxiously awaiting
a declaration from the Government in
regard to its desires and intentions. It
is not good enough for the Prime Minister
to get up and throw out the old slogans
and phrases about our reinsurance agreements with the other side.
The Prime Minister knows, unless he
wishes to misrepresent me, and I do not
think he would, that I appreciate all
these. I am in sympathy with the spirit.
of all these things and want to see the
Imperial tie maintained and developed in
strength. I want to see Northern Ireland
put in a better light in Great Britain.
than ever before. One of the disasters of
recent times unfortunately is that the
Government's supineness and the apathy
of the people in some respects are put in
a worse light than they should be. That
is no fault of mine. I want to see
Northern Ireland's reputation growing
across the water and her case put in a
way it has not been put. This old method
of simply saying you have this agreement
or that agreement and have entered into
a guarantee to maintain parity with the
other side. is all right, as I said, as far as
it goes, but it is not the message of hope
that the working classes and the masses
are looking for at the present time.
What the people want is an unequivocal
declaration from the Prime Minister and
his Cabinet that either they believe in
the Beveridge Report or they do not, and
how far they are prepared to go and to
use avenues of propaganda and publicity,
and the connection between Northern
Ireland and Great Britain, in order to
rouse the people, on both sides to a full
consciousness of their needs. A prominent
gentleman in the Fighting Services told
me. yesterday-it is important that you
should know this-that since the Imperial
Government declaration of last week there

take.
In the King's Speech I thought there

I saw an announcement in one of the

to raise domestic service out of the
ignoble rut in which it is now placed,

Nobody in Northern Ireland knows
where the Prime Minister stands in regard
to the Beveridge Report. Nobody knows
where any member of the Cabinet stands
in regard to the Beveridge Report. All
we have had is a kind of half devout, half
sanctified expression by this Member or
that Member that we like the principles,
or we like the recommendations here and
there, and whatever is decided upon across
the water will be adopted here; but there
has been no broad generous acceptance, in

Sir William Beveridge.
I should like the Prime Minister this
afternoon, for the first time since. the
Report was published, to make a comprehensive declaration as to the attitude
of the Government, apart altogether from
what may be done in the vicissitudes and
turmoil of politics across the water.
should like him to declare to-day the
attitude of the Northern Government
with regard to the whole of the principles

There are one or two other items in the
Speech which I think deserve attention,
so that the Prime Minister may declare
the policy of the Government. Educational
reform is referred to, and God knows
there is no place that needs it more than
the place we are in at the present time.
I say that with no pride; I say it with
great regret, but the statement is based
upon fact. Very often during the past 20
years, but especially during the past eight
or ten years, I have emphasised the need
for educational reform in Northern Ireland based upon the actual position that
exists. I need not weary the House this
afternoon with a recital of the facts which
I have placed before it on many occasions

in regard to the inadequacy of our higher
educational facilities in Northern Ireland.
All that is said in the King's Speech is
that
Educational reforms must take an
important place in any plans for postwar reconstruction, and it is the intention of my Ministers to ensure that our
young people will be given every opportunity to share in the developments to
which we confidently look forward after
the war.
I submit that there is nothing definite
about that at all. Anybody could make
a statement like that. That statement
has been made repeatedly and the fundamental position remains substantially unchanged. Let the Prime Minister face
up to this is he in favour of the
wide-spread development of nursery
schools; is he in favour of the public
control and financial assistance of nursery
schools? Is he in favour of the democratisation of education to the extent of compelling every section of the community
to start from a common level, and then
to work their way up, not on the basis
of privilege, power or wealth, but on the
basis of ability right through to the higher
seats of learning in the community? Is
the Prime Minister prepared to accept
the principle of the right of every person
in the community to higher education on
the basis of capacity? Is the Prime
Minister prepared to say that he is going
to break down the barriers and the
obstacles which at the present time keep
the vast majority of our people from
coming into contact at any stage of life's
journey with accessibility to higher
education? If the Prime Minister is
prepared to make a statement along those
lines, then the people of Northern Ireland
will know where they stand in regard to
educational opportunity. This paragraph
in the King's Speech is simply re-echoing
a time-worn sentiment-a vague hope held
out to our people in the days that lie
ahead. There is nothing fundamental,
definite and positive about it in the realm
of education.
I should also like to take this opportunity of saying something on the practical side. I appreciate all that has been
done in the way of milk provision. I
am glad to know that, speaking for our
own educational authority in Belfast,
more has been done now than has ever
been done in the municipal history of our
city in that direction. I think we have
established a standard here, and I hope
it is being followed by all the other local
authorities throughout Northern Ireland,
so that it may redound to their credit in
the days that lie ahead. This provision
of milk is one of the finest services that
has ever been carried out by any State
large or small.
I hate to introduce a note which may
be in the realm of speculation, or may
soar into the realm of things which would
be better untouched at the present time,
but I notice that the King's Speech refers
to industry. It says:
During the past year the output of
our shipbuilding, engineering and
textile industries has increased steadily.
It is as well that this House should
know that there is a feeling of grave
unrest throughout the city of Belfast,
and, indeed, throughout many parts of
Northern Ireland in regard to the output
of the war industries. One Belfast
morning paper, which I read every morning, came out a week or so ago with a
startling declaration in regard to production in one particular industry, the
industry to which I served my apprenticeship. I was startled to read that in
certain respects some of our local industries have a worse reputation than
any of the backward firms across the
water. Indeed, the way it was presented
that morning indicated that ours was the
worst in the whole country. I felt that,
because like the rest of us I desire to see
the best being done from the industrial
production point of view for the sake of
the reputation of this city and country.
I should like every section of the community to realise there can be ca'canny
in different ways as well as absenteeism.
Apropos of absenteeism, I am expressing
no opinion on that subject at the moment,
because I realise we have not had the
other side presented to us except in the
form of a brief statement which was made
in a interview recently. But there can
be ca'canny in other ways. I read a
document last night affecting a
large institution in Belfast in which it
was stated that the supplies of a certain
agricultural commodity were very scarce
at the present time owing to the action
of the farmers in holding them up
because they did not agree with certain
things that were being done by the Ministry of Agriculture. That is the statement I read. There may be no truth in
very

it; nevertheless, there it is. Members of

I should like a declaration or assurance

between the Ministry of this side and the

flow from this city and our industries in

That is the point I wish to emphasise here

There are one or two other points I must
refer to this.afternoon; although it may,
perhaps, be ungenerous to do so at this
stage. I have put forward one or two

should give early attention to the question

I have also stressed the point that education needs to be attended to in a more
definite way. I have expressed the hope

""
There is one point I would be intellectually dishonest if I did not mention, and
that is in regard to recruiting. I think
recruiting is mentioned in the Speech at a
very early stage, in the third paragraph.
It says: "Although many thousands of
our young men and women have volunteered for the fighting services, many more
are still required, and I earnestly hope
that the call to duty will be answered to
an even fuller extent than in the past.
I wish to re-echo that. I have actually
had the humiliating experience of addressing crowds in the city of Belfast and
Northern Ireland where young men had
the impertinence to get up and severely
criticise me for not emphasising sufficiently
the need for a second front. That ideological slogan is one some have got on the
brain at the present time. The only
second front some of them have got is a
fish and chip establishment.
When you
go to address a public gathering you are
frequently criticised and heckled by
people talking about second fronts. I
realise the significance of a second front
and the importance of it. I also realise
my own limitations and I realise that
there are better brains and better capacities at work grappling with this problem,
and that this matter must be dealt with
in the days that lie ahead with all the
speed that the authorities can command.
The point that amazes me is the
audacity of some young men criticising
and talking about a second front when
there is nothing to prevent them taking a
part in the fronts that at present exist.
Many ideological stalwarts I hear at the
present time talking about this town and
that town, this country and that country,
and the nobility and magnificence of their
effort, and that "we must do something."
But when they say "we" they always
mean somebody else and not themselves.
The armed Forces of the Crown are still
open to take recruits, I understand, and
I submit and suggest that a good many
people in Northern Ireland, especially
those who think themselves very revolutionary-they are not revolutionary ;
they are resolutionary-and who talk
about a second front and about striving
for the smashing of totalitarianism-these
people ought to have it pointed out that
the Army, the Navy and the Air Force
are still open and will welcome. them at

The PRIME MINISTER (Mr.
Andrews): In the first place I desire
very sincerely to congratulate my two
hon. Friends who moved and seconded
the Address in reply to the Gracious
Speech on the excellent way in which
they performed what is always considered
to be a very important and at the same
time difficult and delicate parliamentary
duty. They have spoken in my opinion
with great tact and judgment and good
taste and I feel sure that every Member
in this House no matter where he sits
must have been impressed
been impressed by their
earnestness and their desire to be helpful
in their remarks. In my opinion what
Northern Ireland requires more than anything else. is service of that kind.
The hon. Member for Willowfield has
spoken with moderation and with a great
deal of reasonableness, I am willing to
admit. But he began by saying that for
the first time he spoke on behalf of the
Commonwealth Party. I would remind
him that we who sit on this side of the
House have been speaking for the
Commonwealth or, in other words, the
Empire since the days of our youth.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And I am
glad to know as far as that is concerned
that the hon. Member for Willowfield has
come into line with us. Now the Gracious
Speech has referred to many matters of
outstanding importance some of which
the hon. Member for Willowfield has referred to. It begins by referring to the
gallant deeds of the forces of the United
Nations. We all pay tribute to these men
who in the front line on land, on sea, and
in the air are fighting in order to bring
the brutal forces of aggression which are
opposed to us, to justice, and to establish
on a sound foundation that freedom and
justice which every man throughout the
world is entitled to enjoy.
Then again the Gracious Speech goes on
to refer to the happy relations which exist
between His Majesty's two Governments
in the United Kingdom. That happy
relationship is of the greatest value to
Northern Ireland, and, I think, of some
value, if I may say so, to the Empire in
these grave times. Our Civil Defence and
Home Guard services are also referred
to. We members of the Government
realise the importance of the defence of
what is called the home front. The hon.
Member for Willowfield dealt at some
length with our war effort. I want to be
quite frank here to-day in that connection. I think, within the powers which
we possess our war effort is creditable to
all concerned. At the same time I do admit
and freely that it is a disadvantage to
Northern Ireland that conscription does
not apply here. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) But that is not the fault of this
Government. It is the decision of the
Imperial Government with all the facts
and circumstances before them, and it is
not for us to find fault with the course
which those have taken who are better
informed on the matter than we here. can
hope to be.
But at the same time within our voluntary services I say that our war effort is
creditable. All honour to the 30,000 of
our young men who voluntarily joined
the Forces of the Crown. All honour to
the thousands of men who are sailing
the high seas at the present time, risking
their lives to bring us a great portion of
the food and raw materials which we
require for our very existence here. All
honour to those who are working long
hours in our munition factories and doing
their best to produce the weapons of war
and the ships which it is necessary we
should possess in order to bring victory.
Then again I feel our farmers are entitled
to their meed of praise because of the
efforts which they and their farm
labourers are putting forth to give us
food here grown at home to an extent
never previously known.
not
And in the domain of finance, which
means much, our war effort should
be ignored. Over £60,000,000
has been saved in Northern Ireland and
lent to the British Exchequer and over
£20,000,000 is our contribution this year.
So I feel that it is not desirable that we
should discourage our people by being too
critical. I am in pretty close touch with
our industrial workers and I know they
resent being misrepresented as they
frequently are in connection with the
efforts which the vast majority of them
in my opinion are putting forward. And
remember it is a big change for our working population-and I include
employers and workmen in that term-to
our

[The Prime Minister]
change over from normal peace-time
avocations to war-time necessities and,
therefore, if some of them may not have
shown the adaptability which we should
desire it is not altogether to be wondered at.
Now the Gracious Speech refers to the
past, to the present and to the future,
and I propose to refer to it in that connection. I have deal with the
present.
But the Speech refers to what
we propose to do in order to help
in future and what we are doing at the
present time in a number of directions to
assist those of our people who need help
most, our old people, our widows and our
sick. Now it has been stated recently on
public platforms that the Government
here has done nothing to help our
pensioners. That statement is absolutely
and completely inaccurate as I am
prepared to show. No fewer than 38,000
direct supplementary pensions are being
paid at the present time in Northern Ireland, and in addition 11,000
wives .are beneficiaries, making a
total of 49,000 persons receiving
these supplementary pensions. The
average amount which is being paid
in direct supplementary pensions per
head is 12s a week, which added to the
10s a week, means the pensioner is receiving 22s a week. And yet we are told on
public platforms on important occasions.
that the Government have done nothing
in that connection.
Let me tell the House what the cost of
the supplementary pensions has been.
The Estimate for 1942-43 was over
£1,000,000, whilst the Estimate for 1943-
44 is no less than £1,181,000. That shows
the anxiety of the Government to help
those of our people who, as I have said,
require help most. If we had taken a
decision which was frequently urged upon
us by hon. Members opposite and given
pension increases on a flat rate we would
not have been taking anything like as
helpful a course as the course we have
taken in co-operation with the British
Government.
The hon. Member for Willowfield has
endeavoured to make a good deal of
capital, if I may say so with great respect,
out of the fact that we do not lead Great
Britain in connection with these social
service matters. There is a very old and
homely saying that everybody knows,
"the tail cannot wag the dog," but if we
can keep up with Great Britain we are
doing the best that can be expected of
us. Since this Government was established twenty-one years ago we have kept
up with them. That fact cannot be
denied. It is all very well for the hon.
Member for Willowfield to urge the expenditure of millions here, millions there,
and millions some other place it is very
easy to be all things to all men-but the
responsibility is with us to make good our
words, while he enjoys a freedom we do
not possess.
In that connection I would like to refer
to what the hon. Member has said about
the Sir William Beveridge Report. He
has said that I have not been definite
enough in what I have stated. A few
days after the Beveridge Report was
issued I accepted the responsibility of

form it left the Imperial House.
thought that that statement, definite and
precise as it was, would have satisfied

I
Remember, in this connection, that
many other claims have to be considered.
When you come to divide the national
income, you have to consider how you can
divide it best. In this connection, I
maintain that the claims of housing, of
adequate fresh water supplies to towns
and villages, of sewage disposal facilities,
of health services, must all be considered,
and the money available, whatever it may
be, must be disbursed where it is most
necessary it should be disbursed. Therefore, to ask me to-day to be foolish enough
to commit this Government definitely to
one side of the problems that lie ahead is
asking me to do something I am not prepared to do. One thing that we on this
side of the House stand for is common
honesty, and we are not going to promise,
in order to gain a temporary amount of
popularity, something that we might not
be in a position to fulfil.
Who knows what the position will be
after the war? We do not know how long
the war is going to continue. We do not
know what the state of exhaustion will be
when the war comes to an end. We do
not know how far it will be possible to

restore commercial relations between the
diferent countries of the world.
Therefore, definitely to commit ourselves, as I have been challenged
to do to-day, would be wrong, it
would be misleading, and, as I have
said, it would be gaining a temporary
popularity as a result. No, what we promise on this side of the House to do we
will perform. That course we have taken
for twenty-one years-
Mr. NIXON: Question.
The PRIME MINISTER-and it is
in the interests of our people as well as
only being common justice that we should
continue to follow that course in the
future. The Gracious Speech deals with
many other matters. The hon. Member
for Willowfield-I want to try to confine
myself to his remarks-referred to the
question of derating. Our derating
proposals do not mean that we intend to
extend derating.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I know that.
The PRIME MINISTER: When the
derating proposals were passed it meant
that our land and our farm buildings
were derated entirely. It also meant
that manufacturers, in order to help trade
and commerce, were derated to the extent
of 75 per cent. That is not what is
referred to in the Gracious Speech at all.
The effect of the derating has been that
our local authorities have lost the rates
which they had previously obtained, and
that has placed them at a considerable
difficulty. It is true they got grants in
lieu of rates, but those grants as time
has gone on have not been sufficient to
make up the loss with the result that the
local authorities, through no fault of their
own, have been unable to help many of
our social services to the extent that we
would wish them to help.
I refer in particular to blind persons,
to our health services, and to other
matters of a similar character. What
the Government now propose is that the
grants which have been given in recent
years to our local authorities should be
increased (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-so that any additional money that is
required would not be placed upon the
underated property, as it would impose a
burden which the underated property
Mr. SPEAKER'S
could not in reason be expected to bear.
That is being done with the sole object of
helping our local authorities to deal with
the services I have named in a more
generous way than has been possible in
the past. I would have thought the hon.
Member for Willowfield would be one of
the first to rise in his place and congratulate the Government on what they are
doing in this connection.
Another matter to which the hon.
Member referred was educational reform.
Of course the Gracious Speech does not
go into details; no Gracious Speech does.
It gives very little more than headings
for various reasons. The intention of the
Government in regard to education is that
every child in Northern Ireland with a
reasonable amount of ability and possessed of industry will get a chance during
his life's journey to make good. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do not think
that hon. Members opposite will expect
me to go further than that, especially in
these grave times.

would like to join with my hon. Friend

Oral Answer to Question.
ALLEGED PERSONATION IN
WEST BELFAST.
Mr. NIXON (by private notice) asked
the Attorney General if he would state
why the case against certain persons
charged with alleged personation in West
Belfast Election was twice adjourned;
whether the adjournment was at the
instance of the Crown, and the object of
such adjournment; whether the Crown
witnesses were present in court, at expense and inconvenience to themselves;
whether Mr. McCoy, K.C., ex-R.M.,
stated in his application to resign his
position as R.M. that as one of His
Majesty's Counsel the holding of the position of R.M. under the Northern Government was impossible if he were to retain
his self-respect, or words to like effect.
The ATTORNEY GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): With regard to the first
part of the hon. Member's question I am
informed as follows: Two persons were
charged with personation at the recent
West Belfast Election. They were brought
before a Magistrate on the 9th instant,
the day of the election, and were then
remanded until the 11th instant. On the
11th a necessary witness, the Returning
Officer, was unable to be present as he
was also Returning Officer for the Antrim
election which took place on that date
and in consequence the cases were adjourned on the application of the Crown
till the 18th instant. It was not possible
to warn every Crown witness in time of
this application and accordingly some of
them, though not all, attended the Court
on the 11th. On the 18th the hearing of
the first case was commenced. In the
course of his cross-examination the
Returning Officer was asked to produce a
document which was not in Court. The
Resident Magistrate, suggested a short
adjournment to enable the document to
be obtained but the officer in charge of
the second case then stated that one of
his witnesses had not turned up and as a
result both cases were then further adjourned till the 25th instant.
With regard to the second part of the
hon. Member's question, my information
on the subject is confined to the letter of
resignation dated 4th January of this
year addressed by Mr. McCoy, K.C., to
my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Home Affairs which was published in the
local Press.
In this letter Mr. McCoy states, "Circumstances that have arisen, and a
situation recently created, render it impossible for me, as one of His Majesty's
Counsel, any longer to retain both the
position and my self-respect." This
doubtless, is the passage referred to by
the hon. Member though I do not read
it as bearing the meaning conveyed by the
terms of the question.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Attorney-General's statement I am
exonerating the Attorney-General personally from any implication in the question
-was it not always the custom to take
the depositions. of Crown witnesses when
they were present and let the case be
adjourned afterwards; is it not a fact that
Crown witnesses in personation cases,
when the personators belong to a certain
colour, are the only people who are
punished when the whole thing is over;
did the Attorney-General take any steps
to ascertain if these witnesses or any
witnesses were being tampered with by
agents from Glengall Street, and did he
take any steps to ascertain who brought
these alleged personators to the place and
gave them the votes of the persons they
were to personate?
Sittings of the House.

rising this day do adjourn until Tuesday
next." (Sir Norman Stronge.)

Mr. McGURK: While I should not
like to withhold my congratulations from
the two hon. Members who have moved
and seconded the Address with such
acceptance to the House and satisfaction
to themselves, I regret that I cannot subscribe to all the laudations which they
have showered upon the Government. I
can find nothing in the King's Speech
that will bring any hope or comfort to
the constituents I have the honour to
represent in this House. Many of them
are seriously perturbed at the treatment
that is being meted out to the large
number of men who are being held in
prison without trial, and, indeed, without any charge being formulated against
them. There is no hope for these men in
the King's Speech.
I would have thought that the Government, which poses as the defenders of
liberty, would at least have put into
practice the gospel they preach so loudly.
It would only be common justice, if not
British justice, either to release these men
or put them on trial. The fact that they
have not been put on trial is sufficient
proof that there is no charge which can be
made against them. I make an appeal
to the Government-if, indeed, an appeal
from me would have any effect, which I
doubt to set these men at liberty, and
allow them once more to take their place
in the community. The British Government by its action in releasing the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh has set an
example which this Government might
well follow, and so be in keeping with
their step-by-step policy.
I should also like to refer to the unfair
treatment meted out to the minority in
this area in the making of appointments.
More emphasis, I am afraid, is laid on the
religion of the applicants than on their
suitability or their educational qualifications.
In putting my views before the
Government I look forward not without
hope to the time when these inequalities
will be removed, and when those I represent will be given the consideration to
which they are entitled, and which so
far they have been denied.
I should like to endorse what has been
so well said by the hon. Member for
Antrim regarding the part agriculturists
are playing on the home front. If the
Ministry of Agriculture would only act
more in the spirit of co-operation with
farmers much more could, I believe, be
done to increase both flax and food production. The farmers know that food is
required and they are prepared to do what
they can to produce it, but they are hampered and restricted in their operations
to such an extent by the regulations imposed by the Ministry of Agriculture that
many of them are losing heart, as they
find themselves unable to comply with all
the regulations in force.
The withdrawal, even temporarily, of
the grants given by the Ministry for
drainage and land improvement has not
helped the situation, and before it is too
late I would urge for the restoration of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson]
never been carried out with more acceptance to the House. I say that in all
sincerity. I should also like to take this
opportunity of congratulating the Prime
Minister upon the very clear statement
which he made. As he finished his speech
I was led to believe that we on this side
of the House are too backward in putting
our best goods in the window, and that
the time has arrived when, in the interests of the country as well as of the
political thought we represent, we should
adopt the now universal practice of
propaganda. I say that because I believe
that the average man in the street in
Northern Ireland does not appreciate all
that the Government has done because he
has not studied the question. Perhaps we
are to blame because we do not put
before him sufficiently clearly and sufficiently often what has been and is being
done. The Prime Minister by his strong
speech yesterday gave us a very good lead.
In spite of what the leader of the
Commonwealth Party stated the Prime
Minister made it perfectly clear to the
country, as he has done once before, that
we are prepared to adopt the Beveridge
Report in so far as it is adopted on the
other side. That is certainly as far as
we can possibly go at the present moment.
I am of opinion that 90 per cent. of that
Report will be adopted. How long we
can maintain the standard which it sets
depends entirely upon our export trade.
So far as the export trade of Northern
Ireland is concerned we are largely dependent on the cost of production-I am now
speaking to the Minister of Commerce
and Production-and that cost will be
affected by the price of electricity. In
post-war development we hope that
electricity will be universally used, and
the price of it will, therefore, affect the
cost of production very seriously and also
the decisions of manufacturers on the
other side in regard to whether or not
they will put their new plant in Northern
Ireland, England, Scotland or Wales.
If the Minister of Commerce and Production continues to expend money on
electrical development in Northern Ireland at the present time when costs are
high I feel he will find himself in the
same position as the Belfast electricity
undertaking found itself in at the end of
the last war. At that time a small deputation, of which I was a member, had
to go over to the Imperial Parliament
with their hats in their hands and beg
them to give a subsidy to enable a unit
charge to be made which would encourage
the development of electricity in this
country. I think the subsidy we received
at that time amounted to £150,000. In
view of the colossal expenditure that is
going on such a sum would be useless
now.
a
We are grateful for the fact that the
British Government is subsidising the
development of electricity at the present
time, but I feel it would be a great
mistake for the Minister to put in
second set at Ballylumford. I say that
because to do so would affect the primary
costs for the next 20 years. It would
also have, indirectly, a bearing upon all
our social services, because after the war
they will be dependent upon our income
and the state of our employment. That
as I stated in my opening remarks, will
be governed very largely by our ability
to export. In conclusion, I wish again
to congratulate the hon. Member for
Antrim and the hon. Member for Central
Armagh on their very able speeches.

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
With the permission of the House, and
having to carry my memory back perhaps
15 or 16 years, I would say that the
remarks I made were that a good man
with individual character and ability
could do more in a committee of the
Belfast Corporation than he could do up
here. In Parliament the business of the
House was almost entirely run by the
Cabinet, and Members were only given
an opportunity, broadly speaking, of saying yes or no, whereas in the Belfast
Corporation or other local authority they
could pull their full weight in shaping
the policy of the future.
Mr. NIXON: I thank the hon. and
gallant Member for making his remarks
so very plain. What he did say was that
when you came here you had to say yes
or no, and at that time he used to say
no occasionally. Latterly he says yes all
the time. In fact, I am not sure he is
not developing into a yes-man, much as
I like him. He said you would be better
in the Belfast Corporation where you
could pull your weight and do more
good. Yet with the high opinion of the
Belfast Corporation which he possessed
at that time I think I am right in saying
that he trudged through that Lobby to
give a vote to deprive the Corporation of
their powers and set up administrators
to watch them. He did that although it
is a body in which a man could do more
good than he could in this House.

I was in the Corporation and I do not
agree with the hon, and gallant Member
when he states that you would be better
in the Corporation than here. I say you
would be better here. But I say this, if
you develop into a yes-man you would be
better in the Corporation. If the
Member, for whom I have a great
regard, and he knows it, had stopped
where he was at that time he
would be much more useful here than in
the Belfast Corporation. He left it
voluntarily, and so did I, and I never
regretted it. I do not think that he did
either, but the difference is this, I stood
for retaining the Corporation and he did
not, although he has as much right to
stand for it as I had, especially when he
holds the views to which he has just given
expression, namely, that a man can do
more good and pull more weight in the
Corporation than here. I do not agree
with that at all..
However, before I close, I would like
to say we are all more than delighted
with the way in which the war is going,
notwithstanding the little set-back in
North Africa, which I believe will come
all right. I do not worry much about
the period after the war. The Prime
Minister is always telling us about beautiful houses which we are to get for the
people when the war is over, and he is
having photographs of those houses
printed in the Press. I do not need that
at all; it is only camouflage. I want the
war finished; I want Hitler and the
Germans defeated. After that we will
muddle through in some way.

We have a most scandalous unemployment problem. We have 22,000 persons
unemployed. That position must not be

ashamed at the small number of factories

have the unemployment figures for the

They fell in 1927 as low as 25,000, and

figures fell as low as 25,000 in 1927, when

are interested in the industrial side will
realise that there are difficulties. I shall
always be glad to receive any complaints.
and suggestions as to how we can assist in
this matter. It has continually occupied
our attention. It is, indeed, a very
serious matter. All I can say at the
moment is that we have hopes that the
quality of the coal will be improved in
the near future.
A point was raised by the hon. Member
for Woodvale with regard to the Red Flag
being flown on this building.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to it not
being flown.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, with regard to its not being flown. I understand
that there is an Order that on public
buildings the Union Jack only shall be
flown. I think that was the reason.
I now go on to matters which perhaps
affect my Ministry more closely. The hon.
Member for Willowfield and others raised
the question of nursery centres. This
question has been raised at my Production
Council. Both employers and trade union
representatives have pointed out quite
rightly that women who are working in
the war effort and they are working
magnificently-must be in a position to
place their children under proper care
while they are working in the factories.
I took the matter up with my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
and actually we are having a discussion
to-morrow to see what further progress
can be made. It is not altogether an easy
problem, but I think every hon. Member
will agree that those women who are willing and are skilled to do work which is
required should be given every facility
and help and not be under the constant
strain and anxiety that their children are
not being looked after.
Another point was raised by a certain
article which appeared in the Press and
which announced that production in our
shipyards was inferior and that absenteeism was worse in Northern Ireland than
any other part of the United Kingdom.
That remark, I think, was made without
due knowledge. I have seen the
Admiralty frequently, in fact practically
every time I have been in London, and I
have continually had expressions of satisfaction as to the work that is being carried
out in the shipyard. No doubt it could
be bettter, but nothing can be too good
during war. There is another statement
in the same article I would like to repudiate. I was supposed to have said that
I was satisfied with the work that had
