been carried out in our shipyard. May I
point out to the House that the Minister
of Production, whose representative I am
in Northern Ireland, has nothing to do
with the shipyard? That is an Admiralty
affair, and therefore it was not possible for
me to express an opinion one way or the
other; nor did I do so.
sooner
As far as absenteeism is concerned,
there are various reasons for it, and one
is the transport difficulty. That is constantly coming up, and continual alterations are made in the tramway and bus
services to the yards. We have made an
arrangement with the Corporation-and
they are most co-operative-to put up a
few barriers. The police have also
assisted. One of the troubles, however, is
that everybody likes to catch the last tram
or bus, and the consequence is that the
last bus or last tram will not take the
number of people wanting to go on it.
If perhaps the users of these vehicles
could just come
little bit
a
there would not be a crush or as much
difficulty in getting them to the works.
In addition, with a desire to solve this
question, we have had figures taken out
by various firms showing the different
methods used to prevent absenteeism.
Some are more successful than others. The
great bulk of the men want to be at their
work in time. If the position were eased
by not locking out a man who is half-anhour late it would create a difficulty, because a man who was a further 15 minutes
late might think he should be admitted,
and, therefore, the team work would
break down. It is really a matter for the
men themselves in co-operation with the
firm.
The question of unemployment was
raised by the hon. Member for South
Down. It is only right to point out that
there are now far more men and women
on the register as unemployed than ever
before. The percentage of unemployed
is very small. The greater number of the
men who are unemployed at the present
moment are either unskilled men or
There are
building trade operatives.
practically no skilled or semi-skilled men
left. There are a certain number of
women who could be trained who are not
on the register, but the position is, as I
have stated. So far as the unemployment register is concerned practically
all the skilled men have been taken off,
and those who are now on it are unskilled
or building operatives.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the right
hon. Gentleman would allow me to point
out to him that he has not made the position perfectly clear. He used the word
"unemployed" when he meant "employed." From the point of view of
Hansard it is necessary for me to point
this out.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The number of
unemployed is represented mostly by unskilled men and building operatives.
That is what I meant to say.
Mr. SPEAKER: It was really earlier
on that the right hon. Gentleman made
the slip. He made a statement to the
effect that there were a greater number of
unemployed on the register at the present
time, when he really meant to say that
there were a greater number of employed
on the register.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is really
what I meant to say.
It happens in this
way. The building position in Northern
Ireland is not as urgent as it was six
months or a year ago. That being so I
dare not ask any Ministry, simply for the
sake of taking men off the register to
proceed with building when it is not
really necessary. I have suggested to
three Ministries Works and Planning,
Admiralty and Air Ministry-that if they
want building carried out in Northern
Ireland now is the time to do it because
we have plenty of skilled building operatives available. The position has changed
and there is very little likelihood of these
men being employed in this country.
They are, however, required on the other
side, and my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour at some future date
will assist those who wish to go across the
water.
There is another point in regard to unemployment which I should like to clear
up. As the war goes on there are fresh
demands for different types of munitions
and different types of guns. I am glad
to say that we have passed from the
defensive to the offensive. In times of
peace fashions change, but what might
take three years to alter then may now
take place in half-an-hour. The planning of a year or two may be scrapped
and something entirely different produced.
We can do the planning, but
there is somebody else as well, namely,
the enemy. No matter how well we may
lay our plans and get our machinery tuned
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
up to produce a certain type of gun,
aeroplane or ship they may be altered.
In fact alterations are taking place every
minute and every hour of the day.
I should like all those interested and
engaged in production to realise it is not
faulty planning that has caused these
alterations; they have come about owing
to the fact that we have entered a new
stage of the war. We have got to meet
the enemy, and, if possible, beat him in
producing different types of guns and
other weapons of war.. I should like, if
I may, to pay tribute to the trade unions
and to express my gratitude to them for
the way in which they have assisted production. During the past year they have
had to give up many of their old privileges. In every case in which I have
approached them they have assisted me
to the very best of their ability. I am
most grateful to them for their assistance.
So far as production is concerned the
House will be pleased to learn that we
have reached our different targets except
in so far as aeroplane construction is
concerned. I am sure hon. Members do
do not wish me to go into details in regard to production, but the work that
Northern Ireland is doing is of the utmost
importance. The workers have carried
on magnificently. We have had some
troubles, but, of course, these are universal. Production is, however, satisfactory, and I am sure hon. Members will
be delighted to learn that in every case,
except aircraft, we have reached
targets.
our
I should like to touch on aircraft production because, unfortunately, there has
been a considerable amount of talk and
criticism. The machine which we are
construction here I will not go into
details has developed certain technical
difficulties. Various suggestions were put
forward to me by the engineering trade
union and others interested in aircraft
production. I showed their memorandum
to Sir Stafford Cripps when I was last
over in England. Whilst those suggestions are certainly important they are only
complementary to the trouble which has
arisen. The trouble is a technical one,
and on it the greatest brains in the aircraft world are engaged. I am glad to
say that that technical difficulty is being
got over, and that we are gradually
building up to our target figure.
It may also interest, the House to
know that Sir Crawford Cripps has asked
my Ministry to take over considerably more
responsibility in regard to aircraft production. The Permanent Secretary of
my Ministry will now become the
Regional Officer for the Ministry of Aircraft Production in Northern Ireland.
In addition to that, a highly-skilled
technician is being sent to my staff and
his services will be invaluable. Hon.
Members will realise that in work of this
nature, which is very technical, it is impossible for anybody, unless he has
the technical knowledge, to argue that
such a thing is right or that such a thing
is wrong. The gentleman that is coming
over has the necessary knowledge.
will be able to advise and help us; he
will be able to say where things are
wrong, and to look at matters from an
entirely impartial point of view.
Mr. NIXON: Perhaps.
He
Sir BASIL BROOKE: As soon as this
gentleman arrives, which will be very
shortly, I intend to get the representatives of the workers and the representatives of the firm together to discuss
the points which have been raised by the
workers, and which they claim have been
causing the technical difficulties and
technical faults that have manifested
themselves in this aerodrome.
I should now like to deal with the point
mentioned by the hon. Member for
Willowfield, namely, the Beveridge Report. The Prime Minister has told us
that he accepts it in principle, but that
he is not prepared to go as far as the hon.
Member would like him to go-accept
the whole Report. The simplest way I
can look at the Report, in fact the whole
post-war problem, is from the position of
the ordinary citizen. The ordinary
citizen, we will say, is in the position of
a residuary legatee. I do not know
whether any hon. Members have been
left as residuary legatees. Sometimes it
is not all they may think it is, and they
may find themselves, instead of getting
something from the dear departed,
saddled with his debts. It has not
happened to me, and I hope it has not
happened to any hon. Member.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I am at present very
near to it.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is the
position as I see it from the point of view
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
24 FEBRUARY 1943
of the ordinary citizen. He thinks he is
going to become extremely wealthy because he is like the residuary legatee, but
he does not realise that although these
vast sums are being spent every day they
really represent capital. They are not
ordinary current expenditure at all. The
residuary legatee feels that everything is
going to be lovely, that his pockets will
be filled, that he can, if he wishes, buy
a farm, improve his business, have a good
insurance taken out for his wife, and an
educational insurance for his children.
If such a person is not careful he will
find that he has spent a great deal more
than he is going to get. Hundreds of
different plans are going to be put forward after this war-agricultural, educational, electrical, and, indeed, every
other form of planning.
Whilst everybody agrees that the ideal
of the Beveridge Report is desirable, and
that it is one of the finest reports that
could be written, I do not see how any
Government could possibly commit itself
until it knows what the financial position
is going to be at the end of the war.
One of the considerations is not only
freedom from want and freedom from
fear, but the right to work. If you deprive industry, whether socially owned or
privately owned, of its means of providing work and wealth, then these magnificent schemes put forward by Sir William
Beveridge must fall to the ground for
the lack of funds. That being so, I
suggest that any man who is thinking of
after the war should get his plans in a
fluid condition, so that he can see exactly
what the position is at the end of the war.
He should then ask himself,
"Have I
enough money to do this or to do that?"
No man but a fool would say that he
would spend so many millions on this or
that when, perhaps, the money would
not be there. Whilst agreeing with the
principle, let us, as the Prime Minister
said, not commit ourselves until we know
what the position is.
Recruiting has been mentioned in the
King's Speech. Like the hon. Member
for Willowfield, who, as a matter of fact,
sat through a meeting at which I was
trying to encourage production, I heard
a fiery gentleman hold forth on a second
front. Any man, unless he knows the
conditions, who agitates for a second front
is doing a very dangerous thing. A man
who knows nothing about it, takes no
part in it, and who does not intend to
take any part in it, should not say anything about a second front. As the hon.
Member quite rightly said if that man
feels so strongly about a second front-
I refer to all those who speak about it—
he should enlist and see what a second
front is like. Many of us were at
Gallipoli and we know what landing on
beaches is like. If a man is keen on a
second front he should, instead of talking, join up. If he does he will not
be so keen on it after he has had an
hour's experience. We have talked about
democracy, and I believe that democracy
is the right shape for the future. There
may be other forms of government
that will come at the end of the
war. That will not be agreeable to all
Members on my side of the House, but
at least let us make sure that it is a
British shape. Let us make sure that it
is British manufacture and not some
foreign concoction that is being produced
by a lot of people with no political
experience.
Mr. NIXON: What does that mean?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It means we
do not want it produced by people with
no political experience, such as the British
people have.
Mr. NIXON: I hope you are not
treading on the toes of our Allies.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not treading upon anybody's toes. I want to see a
British shape and a British type of
Government. I do say that all who belong
to these islands feel as we do that everything must be sacrificed to victory. It is
up to them now to take action
to begin to shape the future. I
should like to see that not only have they
deserved that victory but earned and
earned with the sweat of their brows the
right to shape it as well.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): There were one or two

farmers generally that the hon. Member
who made such an excellent speech should

have been asked because he definitely is

of one of the best known farming families
in the whole of Ulster. Then again the

I have seldom known any hon. Member

The first point which was raised was
raised by the hon. Member who proposed
the Resolution and it was raised by the
hon. Member opposite. who sits for
Tyrone, that is, the case of land improvement. I should like to say this is purely
a temporary measure. We have had to
stop land improvement for the moment in
order to get the seed
in. Every
single man is required for that job
and in fact we have taken every single
inspector who was on land improvement
to get the stuff into the land in the next
couple of months. I assure the House
we have not deviated from this policy.
We look upon land improvement as one of
the main planks in our platform. Directly
we can get the crop in and get things
going we will put every effort into land
improvement again. I hope that assurance will satisfy the hon. Member opposite.
The next matter was raised by the hon.
Member for Willowfield. I am sorry he
has left the House. It was raised with
reference to the voluntary land workers
last year.
I would like to say that a far
better judge of that would be the hon.
Member for Antrim who spoke on this
subject and who was more than grateful
for the assistance he received. I may say
I never had hand nor part in any scheme
for which I have been so much thanked
and congratulated as I was for this voluntary workers' scheme, although I did not
merit the congratulation at all because it
was done by others who put their backs
into it and carried it through in a quite
exceptional way. In fact the success of
this scheme caused a good many of the
hitches that took place. When I say we
sent 800 to 1,000 people from Belfast as
far as Garvagh it will be seen what
difficulty there was in carrying it out.
Throughout it was a great success.
In saying that I wish to ask the House,
all Members of the House, to help me
with my voluntary scheme for this year,
because whilst Belfast turned out an enormous number of workers, a thousand a
day, I found that other towns in the
surrounding district, and some towns in
my own county-not Bangor: Bangor
was very good-but towns in the vicinity
of Bangor, certainly were not so good. I
would like all Members, particularly
country Members, to do their very best to
create these committees in the outside
towns to do just the way Belfast does and
get a radiation of service for the harvest
from Bangor, Donaghadee, Portadown
and all these places. I do not think it is
one man's part to save the harvest. I
think it is the duty of everyone. I am
sorry the hon. Member for Willowfield
was not present when I was speaking.
did not say anything hard about him
because I want his eloquence to help me.

The next point is one to my mind of
considerable seriousness and quite a break
from our usual practice. We have got to
face the fact that next year, this coming
year that we are in, we do not expect to
have the same military help as last year.
Soldiers are doing other things and,
therefore we are going to be turned more
and more back upon ourselves.

Girls?
to
Lord GLENTORAN: I will leave them
you. (Laughter.) Therefore after
consultation with the various parties interested we have come to the conclusion
that we will have to set out on a completely new scheme, and with the permission of the House-I do not often read
my speeches I will read this because it
is very important and I would not like to
say anything that might not be in
accordance with our agreement. I may
say in this matter we have had dealings
with Labour. I do not mean the Ministry
of Labour, although we have had dealings
with them, and they were most kind.
We have had dealings with Security and

The Government has therefore decided
that my Ministry will take into its employment, from the middle of July till the
end of October, a force of several thousand
men recruited from the employment exchanges, who will be paid by the Ministry
and have employment guaranteed to them
throughout this period. This force will be

available for the harvesting of flax and

That is quite a breach and a thing
never attempted here before. My Ministry
is taking over as an employer the
thousands of men who are unemployed on
the exchanges. We are grouping them

that with goodwill on all sides, and so

be a great advance on anything we have
done.

Commerce.
REGISTRAR OF BUSINESS NAMES.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the name,
salary and allowances of the Registrar of
Business Names, 50 Railway Street,
Lisburn; also whether he would request
the gentleman in question to write his
name legibly and thus save the time of
people who have to receive his
munications; and whether it is necessary
persistently to write to gentlemen who
have been dead for from 5 to 17 years in
respect to business premises which these
men never owned.
com-
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Mr. W. Abbott, a
principal officer of my Ministry, fills the
position of Registrar of Business Names,
which is only one of a number of duties
performed by him and does not carry any
special salary or allowance. The officer
actually in charge of the office at Lisburn
is Mr. McKernan, a staff officer. The
question of whether or not the signature
of either of these officers is legible is not
strictly relevant as all communications
should be addressed to the Registrar of
Business Names and not to any official
by name. This is stated in the directions
printed on the office stationery.
With regard to the final section of the
question, it is the practice of the
Registrar periodically to issue circular
letters inquiring whether any changes
have taken place in the particulars on
the register. It may happen that some
of the persons whose names are recorded
no longer carry on business. The duty
of notifying changes rests with the
owner of the business name or, in the
event of his death, his personal representative.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement, which amounts to
the proposition that it is immaterial
whether an official writes his name legibly
or otherwise, would he tell us how are
people who have the honour to get these
letters to know that they are genuine at
all if the principal part of the letter, the
signature of the person responsible, cannot even be read?
Education.
TULLYMORE SCHOOL.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry are aware
that their proposal to close Tullymore
School has aroused intense indignation
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
2 MARCH 1943
throughout the area; and whether, in
view of this the Ministry would consider
the advisability of deferring action in the
matter until such time as a new school
has been constructed.
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
The
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): On 14th
November, 1942, my Ministry.received a
memorial from local residents asking that
the Tullymore public elementary school
should not be closed until such time as the
Ballymena Regional Education Committee could provide a new school to
replace both Tullymore and Broughshane.
It was clear, however, that a considerable
time must elapse before such a school
could be built and as the Tullymore
children could attend Broughshane without inconvenience, my Ministry considered that grants should be withdrawn
from Tullymore. The Ballymena
Regional Education Committee and the
manager of the Tullymore public elementary school are in favour of the school
being closed and there will be a consequential saving in the number of teachers
required and in the cost of heating, lighting and cleaning.
My Ministry regrets, therefore, that it
cannot see its way to alter its decision in
this matter.
CIVIL RIGHTS OF TEACHERS.
7. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government propose
extending full civil rights to all teachers,
thus bringing Northern Ireland into line
with all other countries in the British
Commonwealth.
Mrs. PARKER: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister
to reply.
The answer to the hon. Member's question is in the negative.
This matter was the subject of a debate
in the House on the 27th March, 1934,
when a motion that all teachers in
Northern Ireland should be granted full
civil rights was rejected by 23 votes to 10.
It is not considered that any circumstances
have arisen since that time which would
warrant the Government modifying the
policy then confirmed by the House.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The reply indicates
that the decision was taken in 1934.
Would the hon. Member not agree that
the world has changed considerably since
1934? And in view of the fact that this
is the only part of the British Commonwealth of Nations in which the principle
does not operate, does she not think it
time that the whole question was
viewed?
re-
Mrs. PARKER: I am quite in agreement with the hon. Member when he says
that general circumstances have changed
since 1934, but in this particular connection he knows that circumstances here in
Northern Ireland are somewhat different
from those in other parts. The elementary teachers, for instance, are paid
directly by the State. That fact has a
bearing on the matter. I need not go
into the other particulars in connection
with the question.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Will the hon.
Member tell the House how it comes
about that because the State pay particular people those people should be
deprived of their elementary rights of
citizenship?
Mrs. PARKER: There are few matters
in which the teachers suffer any disability
in connection with civil rights. As the
hon. Member knows, they are not allowed
to engage in any occupation which would
interfere with their duties, and as the
schools are open to all creeds and classes
it would be difficult if the teachers were

Commerce.
REGISTRAR OF BUSINESS NAMES.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the name,
salary and allowances of the Registrar of
Business Names, 50 Railway Street,
Lisburn; also whether he would request
the gentleman in question to write his
name legibly and thus save the time of
people who have to receive his communications; and whether it is necessary
persistently to write to gentlemen who
have been dead for from 5 to 17 years in
respect to business premises which these
men never owned.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Mr. W. Abbott, a
principal officer of my Ministry, fills the
position of Registrar of Business Names,
which is only one of a number of duties
performed by him and does not carry any
special salary or allowance. The officer
actually in charge of the office at Lisburn
is Mr. McKernan, a staff officer. The
question of whether or not the signature
of either of these officers is legible is not
strictly relevant as all communications
should be addressed to the Registrar of
Business Names and not to any official
by name. This is stated in the directions
printed on the office stationery.
With regard to the final section of the
question, it is the practice of the
Registrar periodically to issue circular
letters inquiring whether any changes
have taken place in the particulars on
the register. It may happen that some
of the persons whose names are recorded
no longer carry on business. The duty
of notifying changes rests with the
owner of the business name or, in the
event of his death, his personal representative.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement, which amounts to
the proposition that it is immaterial
whether an official writes his name legibly
or otherwise, would he tell us how are
people who have the honour to get these
letters to know that they are genuine at
all if the principal part of the letter, the
signature of the person responsible, cannot even be read?

PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): On 14th

the Tullymore public elementary school
should not be closed until such time as the

It was clear, however, that a considerable

from Tullymore. The Ballymena

required and in the cost of heating, lighting and cleaning.
My Ministry regrets, therefore, that it

this matter.
CIVIL RIGHTS OF TEACHERS.
7. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government propose
extending full civil rights to all teachers,
thus bringing Northern Ireland into line
with all other countries in the British
Commonwealth.
Mrs. PARKER: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister
to reply.
The answer to the hon. Member's question is in the negative.
This matter was the subject of a debate
in the House on the 27th March, 1934,
when a motion that all teachers in
Northern Ireland should be granted full
civil rights was rejected by 23 votes to 10.
It is not considered that any circumstances
have arisen since that time which would
warrant the Government modifying the
policy then confirmed by the House.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The reply indicates
that the decision was taken in 1934.
Would the hon. Member not agree that
the world has changed considerably since
1934? And in view of the fact that this
is the only part of the British Commonwealth of Nations in which the principle
does not operate, does she not think it
time that the whole question was reviewed?
Mrs. PARKER: I am quite in agreement with the hon. Member when he says
that general circumstances have changed
since 1934, but in this particular connection he knows that circumstances here in
Northern Ireland are somewhat different
from those in other parts. The elementary teachers, for instance, are paid
directly by the State. That fact has a
bearing on the matter. I need not go
into the other particulars in connection
with the question.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Will the hon.
Member tell the House how it comes
about that because the State pay particular people those people should be
deprived of their elementary rights of
citizenship?
Mrs. PARKER: There are few matters
in which the teachers suffer any disability
in connection with civil rights. As the
hon. Member knows, they are not allowed
to engage in any occupation which would.
interfere with their duties, and as the
schools are open to all creeds and classes
it would be difficult if the teachers were
allowed to take part in political affairs.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to ask
the hon. Lady does she not think that
under existing conditions there is a temptation for some teachers who are not supposed to take part in such affairs to take
part in them surreptitiously because of
the restrictions placed upon them?

Agriculture.
GROWING OF BARLEY.
5. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether he is aware that
at Bangor on the 15th February at an
"Aid for Britain " meeting, the
Junior Whip advised "farmers not to
grow barley beyond what they would use
on their own farms "; and whether he
approves of this advice which is contrary
to the policy of the Government as expressed in the King's Speech.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
I have not read the report of the meeting to which the hon. and gallant Member refers, but in order to make the
position quite clear I would like to state
definitely that it is illegal to feed barley
suitable for milling to livestock. It cannot be repeated too often that any barley
grown by a farmer must be offered for
sale so that no farmer can grow barley
for his own requirements unless he has a
special permit from my Ministry.
All the additional barley that can be
grown is required for food purposes, and
it is therefore of the greatest importance
that barley should be grown on all soils
suitable for the purpose. The Minister
of Food has undertaken to purchase all
the 1943 barley of millable quality at
from £26 5s Od to £27 10s Od per ton.
Where the barley requires conditioning
before milling the maximum deduction to
cover this cost will be £2 10s Od per ton.
The minimum price for barley suitable
for milling will therefore be £26 5s Od
per ton and the minimum price for barley
potentially suitable for milling (i.e. after
reconditioning) is £23 15s Od. per ton.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply of the Minister of Agriculture, if I give him a copy of the Press
report of the meeting in question will he
convey to the Junior Whip that it is not
usual for members of the Government to
try to encourage farmers to break the
law?

Lord GLENTORAN: I really cannot
be expected to read all the eloquence

that is, that we want all the barley that
can possibly be grown by the farmers.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the

SEPARATE FLATS.
13. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the fact that owners of houses are, in
many cases, transforming the houses into
separate flats, and, by demanding separate
rents for the flats, securing a total
financial return for each house which is
in excess of the standard rent; whether
this method circumvents the Rent Restrictions Acts, and, if so, whether he
will take steps to amend the law so as to
prevent this abuse.
Mr. LOWRY: On behalf of my right
hon. Friend I would inform the hon.
Member that I am not aware that the
practice referred to by him is being
carried out to any great extent owing to
the restriction of building operations
generally and the scarcity of building
material.
With regard to the second part of the
question, it should not be overlooked that
the transforming of a house into separate
flats entails considerable expense for
which the landlord is entitled to a
monetary return, and accordingly the
Government could not justify introducing
legislation limiting this return to the
standard rent of the premises.
I may add that in so far as the practice
referred to by the hon. Member does exist
it is helping in a small measure to provide
additional housing accommodation.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I regard that as a
thoroughly and completely unsatisfactory
reply, and at the first available opportunity I will raise this question on the
adjournment.

WESTMINSTER.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
called to the statements made at Westminster by the Imperial Members of
Parliament for County Down and County
Derry on February 23rd, 1943, with regard to the fewness of the war factories
erected in Northern Ireland, and the fact
that a smaller proportion of war work
has been allocated here per head of the

Mr. Bevin, the British Minister of
Labour, that these problems have to be
faced and that "the way to get through
these difficulties is to have driving power
at the top"; and whether he can state
what action the Government of Northern Ireland propose to take in the
matter.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have been
asked to reply.
I have seen the report of the debate
to which the hon. Member refers, but as
he will appreciate I cannot go into details
for reasons of security. I can say, however, that no opportunity is being lost in
pressing supply departments to utilise
the capacity and labour in Northern Ireland to the full.
Mr. BROWN: Has the Government
taken into consideration the statement
made by a Member for County Down
who said it was a discredit both to the
Government at Westminster and to the
Government of Northern Ireland that
there should be so much unemployment
in Northern Ireland at present as the

factories and having received such a
small allocation of war work? Will the
Minister tell us if he has looked into the
question from that point of view? Will
steps be taken to remove that discredit,
both to the Government at Westminster
and to the Government of Northern Ireland referred to by the Member for
County Down?
Mr. THOMPSON : Can the Minister
state what active steps he has taken to
meet the difficulties referred to by Mr.
Bevin ?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: In answer to the
first hon. Gentleman, I am fully aware
of the difficulties of allocating work to the
full, as we would like to do. As I said
in my answer, I am continually pressing
that matter. It is a matter for the supply
Ministries on the other side. If I show
there are workers and factories available
it is for them to give the final decision.
With regard to the question by the
hon. Member for Ballynafeigh, I should

12. Major ROBINSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been drawn to a news item
published in the "Irish News" on the
2nd ultimo, under the heading "Vandalism in Larne Cemetery." and whether
the facts of the incident were correctly
reported.
Mr. LOWRY: I have seen the article
referred to, and on behalf of the Minister
of Home Affairs have had full enquiry
made in the matter.
The facts were not correctly reported
in the "Irish News" of the 2nd ultimo,
and the true facts are as follows:
On the afternoon of Saturday, 30th
January, or the morning of Sunday, 31st
January, 82 domes on glass wreaths in
the cemetery were smashed, and foot-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
prints clearly indicated that the damage
was caused by children-a number of
whom had been in the cemetery for some
days prior to the damage. In some cases
the protecting wires were removed and
stones thrown at the glass covers. In one
instance only was there damage to the
marble base of a wreath.
Of the 82 glass domes smashed, 43 were
in the Catholic section and 39 were in
the Protestant section of the cemetery.
The vandalism, even though committed
by children, is deplorable and the police
inquiries are being continued.
The statement in the newspaper report
that "the graves in the Protestant
section were untouched" is, as I have
said, untrue, and misleading reports of
this nature are, to say the least of it,
very regrettable.
I would like to thank the hon. and
gallant Member of the constituency for
drawing attention to this matter and
thereby enabling me to state the correct
facts.

state why Northern Ireland has not

anticipated it correctly.
Mr. GORDON: The requirements of
the munitions industries in Northern
Ireland for trainees have, so far, been
more than met by training classes which
my Ministry, with the helpful co-operation of education authorities, has established from time to time at technical
institutes, together with the facilities
available for utilising where necessary the
Government Training Centres in Great
Britain.

further demands.

R.M. and Absurd Questions.
Court Adjournment.

So said Mr. J. H. Campbell, K.C.,

when the police asked that the charges

Mr. Churchill's Illness.
THANKFULNESS FOR RECOVERY.
The PRIME MINISTER: With your
approval, and with the permission of the
House, I would like to make a short
statement..
I feel sure that I speak for every Member of this House when I express our
profound thankfulness that the Prime
Minister of the United Kingdom, Mr.
Churchill, is now convalescent. The
announcement of his illness gave us all
deep concern, and we trust that he will
soon be completely restored to health and
strength.
Mr. Churchill's great energy and his
indomitable will-power are of invaluable
service to the Empire and the United
Nations. His inspiring leadership is the
admiration of the Allies and the despair
of the Axis Powers. His example of untiring devotion is a spur to everyone to
work still harder for victory.
May he soon be in the forefront of the
battle again, in the full vigour of his
powers, and lead us to the grand climax
of our efforts the defeat of our enemies
and the triumph of our cause.
Mr. Churchill's Illness

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. NIXON: I have the greatest
possible pleasure in endorsing everything
the Prime Minister has said, and well
said, and also in congratulating the Prime
Minister on the statement he has made
with reference to Mr. Churchill, the
greatest War Leader, I think, that
Britain ever had, and the hope of the
liberty-loving people of the world. Under
his leadership Great Britain held the field
alone for a year, and I may say that this
morning I saw the picture, "One Day at
War." It was a Russian picture, and it
is an inspiration to know that, under
Mr. Churchill, we did hold the field until
mighty Russia got going.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to take
this opportunity of expressing my full
concurrence with the sentiments expressed
by the Prime Minister. When we look
back upon the darkness of the past and
at the uncertainty which prevailed at the
darkest hour in the history of humanity,
we can all very devoutly say that we have
a great deal to be thankful for in having
such an inspiring leader at such a time.
When France fell and Europe became
practically chained in the dungeons of
Totalitarianism, this country was the
one bright spark which lit up the firmament and kept hope alive in the heart of
mankind. The hopes and the inspiration
of the people at that time were
doubtedly centred in the Prime Minister
of Great Britain. His inspiring leadership was beyond the power of words to
convey. We are glad to know to-day that
he is recovering from his very serious
illness, and we would like him and his
Cabinet to know that all sections in
Northern Ireland who prize the connection with Great Britain and the British
Commonwealth send him hearty good
wishes, coupled with the profound hope
that he will be spared until victory comes
and the world is once more emancipated.

CLASS I. No. 2.
CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £300 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1943, to defray the salaries of the
Department of the Prime Minister, the
salaries of the Cabinet Secretariat and
other expenses in connection therewith,
including the expenses of the Privy
Council Office."
The
FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): A further sum of £300
is required under the heading of Cabinet
Offices, and three items are involved.
The first is the bonus payable to the Permanent Secretary of the Cabinet following
the arrangement made last autumn for
all Permanent Secretaries. It will be
remembered that Parliamentary authority
for an alteration in the basis of remunera-
93 Supplementary Estimates-

2 MARCH 1943
Cabinet Offices
tion of the heads of our departments was
given on the occasion of the passing of
the Supplementary Estimate for the
Ministry of Finance in November last.
The second item is the provision for
arrears of overtime worked by certain
messenger and typing staff attached to the
Cabinet Secretariat. It has been necessary, under
war conditions, to keep
Stormont Castle open to much later hours
than are normally worked, and the messenger staff at the castle has therefore
been called upon to do overtime work for
which overtime pay is properly payable.
The third provision covers the employment of additional staff, namely, a shorthand typist, a messenger and a cleaner.
I beg to move.

who will begrudge the messengers getting

know that what is taking place behind
the scenes can be discussed on

The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member
is trying to get round my ruling. He
cannot possibly deal with that question
on this Estimate. He will have to wait

Mr. BROWN: Then I will satisfy myself by asking what is the position of the
Civil Service generally in regard to the
bonus.
Major SINCLAIR: This question of
the bonus for the Permanent Secretary
is a rather complicated one, and goes
back into ancient history. Some time
ago the salaries of the intermediate grades
of the Civil Service were consolidated to
include the cost of living bonus, but that
was not done in the case of the Permanent
Secretaries. Perhaps, by leave of the
House, I had better read a short explanation giving the dates.
Revised consolidated salaries for the
Service generally were brought into
operation with effect from 1st October,
1936, in substitution for the consolidated
salaries which had, two and a half years
before, replaced the earlier arrangement
whereby remuneration was made up of a
basic and bonus portion. These revised
stabilised salaries were brought to the
notice of the House in a Supplementary
Estimate which was introduced in the
financial year 1936-7. In the light of
certain views expressed in the House while
that Estimate was under discussion, the
Government decided, however, that a reversion should be made in the case of
these senior officials-I mean the Permanent Secretaries, the Parliamentary
Counsel, and the Comptroller and
Auditor-General-to the levels of the
scales of salaries which had been in
existence prior to the general stabilisation,
and that these scales should be subject,
in the event of any future substantial
rise in the cost of living, to the payment
of a cost of living bonus, failing a revision of the scales themselves. The
Estimate accordingly makes provision for
payment of this bonus, including arrears
from 1st March, 1940. No cost of living
bonus was payable prior to that date.
As I said before, in answer to the hon.
Member for South Down, in the case of
the intermediate grades the cost-of-living
bonus was included in the stabilised
salaries, but in the case of the Permanent
Secretaries and certain other officials this
was not done.
Mr. BROWN: Then may I ask is the
hon. and gallant Gentleman satisfied that
all grades of the Civil Service have been
treated equally and fairly?
The CHAIRMAN: I do not think I
can allow the Financial Secretary to
answer that question. That would be
going into the question of policy, which
the hon. Member can raise when the main
Estimates come before the Committee
within the next few weeks.

CLASS I. No. 3.
GOVERNMENT HOSPITALITY.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £200 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1943, as a grant in aid of the Government
Hospitality Fund."
Major SINCLAIR: The Committee is
asked to agree to an extra sum of £200,
making a total of £550 for the year. It
is quite impossible to forecast in wartime
what the annual expenditure on Government hospitality is likely to be, as the
visits of distinguished persons must
normally be kept secret.
In the year
under review we had the honour of a visit
from Their Majesties the King and Queen
and certain expenditure was involved in
addition to that which the Prime Minister
incurred without making any call on the
Hospitality Fund. The present indication
is that there will probably be spent in
the current year a total sum of about
£500. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
CLASS II. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That a supplementary sum not exceeding £38,000 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1943, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Finance."
Major SINCLAIR: The chief reason
for this Supplementary Estimate is the
fact that there is a deficiency in the
receipts appropriated in aid amounting to
a net figure of £34,000. This deficit
arises on the agency fees paid by British
Departments for staff employed on
various works services carried out in
Northern Ireland for the Imperial Government, and amounts in the gross to
£39,000, which figure is offset by certain
surpluses amounting to £5,000, details of
which are set out on the face of the
a
Estimate. Hon. Members will readily
understand that it is difficult to estimate
so far ahead with any degree of accuracy
what the total annual amount of fees
accruing under the heading "Payments
for Works Services" will be. The fees
charged are generally 10 per cent. of the
cost of the works and when estimating for
total receipt in the year of some
£137,000 the Ministry were perhaps unduly optimistic. Although under our
wartime financial arrangements with the
Imperial Treasury the variation between.
actual and estimate is not of material consequence, it is nevertheless desirable
that the House should appreciate
to what extent the increase in our
'works staff is due to agency work. For
this reason a charge on as accurate a basis
as possible is raised in relation to the
value of the work carried out, and is
accounted for as an appropriation-in-aid.
We have now at the close of the year to
revise our figure downward by £39,000.
The only other item to which I need
refer is the £2,500 under subhead C for
postage, telegrams and telephones. This
increase is due to an expansion in the
activities of the Ministry and, to a certain
extent, to a delayed claim relating to the
year 1941-42. I beg to move.

CLASS I. No. 3.
GOVERNMENT HOSPITALITY.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £200 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1943, as a grant in aid of the Government
Hospitality Fund.”
Major SINCLAIR: The Committee is
asked to agree to an extra sum of £200,
making a total of £550 for the year. It
is quite impossible to forecast in wartime
what the annual expenditure on Government hospitality is likely to be, as the
visits of distinguished persons must
normally be kept secret.
In the year
under review we had the honour of a visit
from Their Majesties the King and Queen
and certain expenditure was involved in.
addition to that which the Prime Minister
incurred without making any call on the
Hospitality Fund. The present indication
is that there will probably be spent in
the current year a total sum of about
£500. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,

for the service of the year ending 31st

Major SINCLAIR: The chief reason

fact that there is a deficiency in the
receipts appropriated in aid amounting to
a net figure of £34,000. This deficit
arises on the agency fees paid by British
Departments for staff employed
various works services carried out in
Northern Ireland for the Imperial Government, and amounts in the gross to
£39,000, which figure is offset by certain
surpluses amounting to £5,000, details of
which are set out on the face of the
on
Estimate. Hon. Members will readily
understand that it is difficult to estimate
so far ahead with any degree of accuracy
what the total annual amount of fees
accruing under the heading "Payments
for Works Services" will be. The fees
charged are generally 10 per cent. of the
cost of the works and when estimating for
a total receipt in the year of some
£137,000 the Ministry were perhaps unduly optimistic. Although under our
wartime financial arrangements with the
Imperial Treasury the variation between.
actual and estimate is not of material consequence, it is nevertheless desirable
that the House should appreciate
to what extent the increase in our
'works staff is due to agency work. For
this reason a charge on as accurate a basis
as possible is raised in relation to the
value of the work carried out, and is
accounted for as an appropriation-in-aid.
We have now at the close of the year to
revise our figure downward by £39,000.
The only other item to which I need
refer is the £2,500 under subhead C for
postage, telegrams and telephones. This
increase is due to an expansion in the
activities of the Ministry and, to a certain
extent, to a delayed claim relating to the
year 1941-42. I beg to move.
Mr. NIXON: I am glad to see the

Supplementary Estimates-
Miscellaneous Expenses

There is none of that kind of foolery

make our protest here. It is the same old
story every time. Many of these people
are only wasting time and retarding the
war effort. Even the Minister of Commerce was constrained to admit in this
House, after three years effort by these
people, that the aircraft built in Northern
Ireland had developed technical defects.

Now I again protest against these Supplementary Estimates for jobs
jobs and
salaries,

CLASS II. No. 4.
PUBLIC WORKS AND BUILDINGS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £10,000 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1943, in respect of Public Works and
Buildings, including annuities and other
expenses in connection with drainage."
Major SINCLAIR: Under Sub-head
A, New Works, etc., there is one item
in this sub-head to which I should like to
draw the attention of the Committee,
namely, the new store at the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Stores Depot, Sprucefield. Six thousand pounds is the figure
included in the Estimate as payable this
year, but the total cost of the building is
estimated at £15,000. It was agreed to
erect this new brick building as the existing stores are totally inadequate to house
the greatly increased amount of material
required to be held during war-time. The
building will eventually replace some of
the old temporary stores at Sprucefield,
some of which are in a quite unfit condition for holding Royal Ulster Constabulary stores.
Under Sub-head E, Lower Bann Navigation, three thousand pounds is required for
docking facilities for dredging craft and
barges which are required for keeping the
Bann navigation open. The expenditure
is chiefly on a concrete wall with a lockgate in the centre across the canal, which
enables an area of the canal to be drained
and used as a dry-dock. In peace time
repairs requiring the use of a dry-dock
had to be carried out at Derry or Belfast.
Now all repairs with rare exceptions can
be carried out by our men on the spot
thus saving time and money.
The only other item is the anticipated
saving on drainage schemes under subhead F, amounting to £6,000. In the
Supplementary Estimate for Public Works
and Buildings presented last September
a sum of £28,000 was included for the
purchase, etc., of plant for hiring out to
local authorities for drainage schemes.
Of this amount it is estimated that £6,000
will be underspent at the end of the year.
I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

and Wales, on which building is to start
in April next so that the cottages there

time.
In the first place I would like to point
out that I am not for one moment suggest-

ing that the need for new houses in the

part and parcel of the scheme now being
proceeded with across the Channel. We
had a statement made in the British
House of Commons by Mr. Ernest Brown,
the Minister of Health. He announced
the Government's decision to start building 3,000 war-time cottages by April.
They were, he said, a very modest beginning, and would pave the way from which
the Government would be able to draw
some very useful lessons for the main
campaign when the war was over, when
250,000 new houses are planned.
He said that the number that would be

was to start building the first batch in
April. That is the point I want emphasised. This is a scheme that is being proceeded with next month. It is not a
post-war scheme in any shape or form. I
suggest we should keep step by step with
Great Britain in having a similar scheme
here. I see no reason why we should not
do so.
A speech was made the other day at
Donaghadee by the Minister of Agriculture, who said:
There is no country in the world that
has given a better farmers' contribution
acre by acre than our own. No country
has ploughed more than our farmers
have ploughed, and our products have
been good. Our position in the markets
of Great Britain has improved and is
likely to remain a strong plank in our
post-war platform.
Then the noble Lord went on to say
that while he admired the Ulster farmers
and their produce, he considered the best
product on the Ulster farm was the
children to whom they looked forward for
the future of the country. Emphasising
that they would never get anything without hard work the Minister went on to
say that one of the things required in the
future was better houses for the farm
labourers and for the farmers to raise
their families. They should take an
interest in such things as this, and see if
houses were to be built on their land they
would meet with their wishes. They must
make up their minds that there was
nothing too good for the farmers, and
they should see that they got the same
chance after the war as other sections of
the community, and not be praised and
flattered now and thrown on the scrap
heap after the war.
That was a splendid speech, and I agree
with everything in it. But I want to go
further and say we should keep step by
step with Great Britain in having these
cottages erected on a somewhat similar
scale to what is being done in England
and Wales next month. The Ministry of
Home Affairs have set up a Committee
to consider this matter of housing, not
only in the cities and towns, but also in
the rural areas. What the country wants
is not committees but cottages, and it
wants them now. In asking for them
now we merely ask the Government to
keep step by step with England and Wales
where they are to start the erection of
those 3,000 houses next month.
I do not suggest that this should be
done at the expense of the war effort. In
England they can get the materials and
they are going ahead with the scheme in
April, and there should be no difficulty
in our case either. That is the attitude
I take up in this matter. In my opinion
there are plenty of materials available. I
have travelled through most of Northern
Ireland and I have seen piles of
blocks of concrete and of bricks taken
from pulled down air-raid shelters and
other structures erected at the beginning
of the war but which have since been
demolished or are being demolished now.
There is enough material there to build
innumerable cottages. If you want any
further proof that there is ample material
take the statement of the Minister of
Health. He has sufficient material to
start with these 3,000 cottages in April
next, and we should also get our proportion of that material if we require any
material outside the material we have.
I say, however, we have practically all,
if not all, the material needed here.

On the question of building and the
position of builders in Northern Ireland,
I want to raise a very serious point in
connection with the new form of dumping
which has developed in the building
trade. It has hit the building trade very
seriously indeed. I am not suggesting it
could be otherwise, but I do say that
when people are being hit everyone
should be hit alike. In this particular
case, it seems the Ulster building trade
has been hit far more seriously than the
building industry across the water.
A remarkable state of affairs exists in
the Northern Ireland building industry.
In Great Britain, under a new grouping
scheme just announced, the British
Government, in effect, assumes responsibility for keeping the industry functioning
efficiently in spite of war conditions.
That has not been done here. The
Government in Great Britain will see to
it that contracts are allocated evenly
amongst different firms to ensure that each
firm's organisation is kept in being.
Northern Ireland contractors have not
only to compete amongst themselves for
Government contracts, but find themselves
undercut by cross-channel firms. The
situation appears all the more incomprehensible when it is realised that shortage
of labour is the principal handicap for
the big English contractors, who, nevertheless, are able to take on big jobs of
aerodrome construction, et
cetera, in
Ulster.
Mr. Whitham, secretary of the Belfast
Builders' Association, said in this
connection :
The British Government fully realise
the importance of maintaining the
firm's organisation intact for post-war
construction. These organisations will
be the main source of employment for
demobilised unskilled men and munition
workers immediately the war is over,
and the British Government is determined to look after them-
We apparently are not looking after
them-
The large cross-channel firms, receiving
Government work at reasonably spaced
intervals, are placed in a favourable
position for bidding for work in Ulster.
If a firm is enabled to maintain a big,
permanent organisation of key men and
material it can quote cheaper prices for
additional work. In other words, it is
a new form of dumping. Local firms
which are quite capable of doing these
big contracts find themselves squeezed
out in their own area. Our big contracting firms, as a result, are forced, in an
endeavour to keep their organisations
going, to take up smaller jobs. This,
in turn, puts the smaller firms out of
business-a sort of vicious circle.

connection with the new form of dumping
which has developed in the building
trade. It has hit the building trade very
seriously indeed. I am not suggesting it
could be otherwise, but I do say that
when people are being hit everyone
should be hit alike. In this particular
case, it seems the Ulster building trade
has been hit far more seriously than the
building industry across the water.
A remarkable state of affairs exists in
the Northern Ireland building industry.
In Great Britain, under a new grouping
scheme just announced, the British
Government, in effect, assumes responsibility for keeping the industry functioning
efficiently in spite of war conditions.
That has not been done here. The
Government in Great Britain will see to
it that contracts are allocated evenly
amongst different firms to ensure that each
firm's organisation is kept in being.
Northern Ireland contractors have not
only to compete amongst themselves for
Government contracts, but find themselves
undercut by cross-channel firms. The
situation appears all the more incomprehensible when it is realised that shortage
of labour is the principal handicap for
the big English contractors, who, nevertheless, are able to take on big jobs of
aerodrome construction, et cetera, in
Ulster.
Mr. Whitham, secretary of the Belfast
Builders' Association, said in
this
connection:
The British Government fully realise
the importance of maintaining the
firm's organisation intact for post-war
construction. These organisations will
be the main source of employment for
demobilised unskilled men and munition
workers immediately the war is over,
and the British Government is determined to look after them-
We apparently are not looking after
them-
The large cross-channel firms, receiving
Government work at reasonably spaced
intervals, are placed in a favourable
position for bidding for work in Ulster.
If a firm is enabled to maintain a big,
permanent organisation of key men and
material it can quote cheaper prices for
additional work. In other words, it is
a new form of dumping. Local firms
which are quite capable of doing these
big contracts find themselves squeezed
out in their own area. Our big contracting firms, as a result, are forced, in an
endeavour to keep their organisations
going, to take up smaller jobs. This,
in turn, puts the smaller firms out of
business-a sort of vicious circle.
One small builder, who was approached
on the matter, stated it seemed most
peculiar, in spite of the shortage of
labour in Britain which they heard so
much about, that the big firms there were
able to "muscle in " over here. The
industry in Ulster, it is stated, had been
trying to get the Northern Government
to put this vital industry on a similar
footing to that existing in England, but
so far without success. This is a matter
to which, I suggest the Government
should give their immediate attention. In
asking for this I am not asking for any
preferential treatment, I am merely asking
that we should get the same treatment as
the cross-channel firms.
We are in even a better position here
than they are in Great Britain, because
in many cases we have actually the land
bought and the foundations cut. In
some cases the men are ready to start in
the morning if the Government say
go." In England I understand they

been cut. Everything is ready to go

If he will keep step by step and line by

On the suggestion of my Ministry a

of the National Association in Great Britain. They have already made good

with a membership of more than 700
cadets and we hope that there will be

G.T.C. does not attract grants from the
services like the boys' units the Sea

that the Ministry of Education with the

as

I venture to say that promises great success to the movement. The Council have

I would just like to say before
formally moving this Estimate that I
look upon this matter of C.E.M.A. as of

agree with me I do not want to weary

Estimates-when I say that no
munity could really endure and prosper

am very hopeful indeed that this money
I am asking for will be used to very great

for war purposes, something absolutely
essential. I think that this is essential,

I wish to speak now of the £1,500 towards the development of the scheme for
the encouragement of music, art, and the
drama. I think this is much the same
kind of thing, only from a broader point
of view, as the music for the people idea
in Northern Ireland. The interesting
thing about the music for the people idea
is that it does not really reach the people.
Music is all right, and I want to see it
reach the people, but in effect under the
present system-I am not speaking of the
social system but the system by which this
scheme is operated-the music does not
reach the people. You will understand
that I have no dislike for Queen's
University; I have every admiration for
it as a university centre, but far too often
when we have concerts advertised as music
for the people they are centred in
Queen's. The people do not get to
Queen's for the music.
a
The music ought to be brought to the
people instead of the people being asked
to go to it. We want to carry the
message and inspiration of music right to
the people and get the most direct contact
we can with them. How can that be
done? I think it can be done to a very
great extent by making fuller use of the
elementary schools. We have now
system of modern elementary schools in
Belfast that is a credit to the community.
The other day I heard some visitors to
Belfast mention two or three of our
schools in the city and they said they
were a credit to the community. I agree
that architecturally they are very nice,
and as far as the amenities are concerned
they are a complete revolution from anything that has ever gone before. Facilities
exist in those schools for the presentation
of good music, and the drama if it were
required.
a

of life than is the case at present if it
were brought to the people. In saying
that I do not want to be misunderstood.
I am not casting the slightest reflection
upon those who have endeavoured to carry

lieve that if the Ministry of Education

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £10,000 be granted to his Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1943, to defray the grants in aid
of the cost of benefits and expenses of
administration and of the payment to
the Unemployment Arrears Fund."
The CHAIRMAN: There are three
votes under the Ministry of Labour, and
with the permission of the Committee I
should like all three to be taken together.
They are National Health Insurance,
Unemployment, and Employment Services. Is the Committee agreeable to
that course being adopted?
The Committee indicated assent.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Elliott): Under the
heading of National Health Insurance the Committee is being asked to vote
an additional sum of £10,000 for the
grant in aid of benefits and administration under the National Health Insurance Acts.
This is one of the years in which the
claims for sickness benefit received by
rather
approved societies have been
higher than was expected. There has
been no serious epidemic and the rise in
claims must be attributed to a variety of
factors.
a
In the first place there has been
growth in the number of persons insured
on account of the. expansion of industry
arising out of the war effort.
In the second place vitality generally
is probably below the average because. of
the lack of sunshine last summer; from
that point of view it was one of the worst
years on record.
Then, too, in certain quarters there is
no doubt that the effects of war strain
are beginning to be felt; but in addition
to these factors I feel that we must take
account of the effect of the increase in the
rate of sickness and disablement benefit
which came into force last year and which
may induce persons to claim benefit during short periods of incapacity which
they would have been inclined to ignore
when the rates were lower.
Vote 3, Unemployment, makes provision in the first place for the State
grant on contributions to the Unemployment Fund. Hon. Members will re-

The hon. Member for Woodvale asks
what is the necessity for this Supplementary Estimate. You have a Supplementary Estimate because more people
are employed; you have a Supplementary Estimate because more people
are unemployed. He is right. If there
were more people unemployed, and if we
had not made sufficient provision for them
in presenting the main Estimates, I would
have to come to this Committee and ask
for more money to meet the demands that
would be made upon the department by
the greater unemployment. I should like
to explain to the hon. Gentleman that
this is a difficult matter. There are three
contributors to the Unemployment Fund
-the employer, the workman, and the
State. When there are more people
employed the State has to pay a greater
contribution. Consequently, when more
people are in employment than we
expected we have to present a Supplementary Estimate.
Then there is what is known as a parity
payment in connection with the Unemployment Fund. When employment is
good in Great Britain they are able to pile
up a huge surplus, because they are not.
paying the money out in benefit. Their
employment is greater than ours, and we
are unable to pile up a surplus comparable
with that of Great Britain. Consequently
we must have a balance, and we come to
this Committee and ask for a contribution
to raise the balance in our fund commensurate with that of Great Britain. That
disposes of those two points.
The hon. Member for Woodvale also
referred to the number of persons who
have been transferred to work of national
importance in Northern Ireland and who
have therefore qualified for lodging

the 'phone, and I awaited his return
before dealing with the points he made.
He wanted to know why we were saving
on grants for juvenile instruction, relief
schemes, and the training of unemployed
persons. He raised those three points.
The reason why we are saving on grants
for juvenile instruction is that the number
of juveniles attending the class has been
reduced, and consequently we cannot
carry on the instruction that we gave
formerly. We had relief schemes in
operation. We allowed urban authorities
to carry out certain works. Those schemes
are gradually dropping out, but I want
to assure the hon. Member that if I find
unemployment increasing I will consult my
colleagues with a view to seeing that such
schemes are reintroduced for the purpose
of absorbing men and women in various
parts of the country if it should become
necessary to do so.
The other point was the question of
training unemployed persons. I would
just like to say to the hon. Gentleman I
know the interest he takes in it. I know
he examines it from the standpoint of a
trade union official. Consequently I will
deal with it from that standpoint. We
introduced about four years ago training
classes in the various technical institutes
throughout the country. We found that
they were most satisfactory. We selected
skilled men who had become unemployed
through a reduction in the work they
carried out. The hon. Gentleman will
understand that the building trade has
been hard hit for a number of years. We
selected a number of men in the building
trade, skilled artisans. We thought the
possibility was we could train them in the
various types of work-sheet metal work,
electrical work, engineering work, and
give them a smattering of knowledge
which they with their skilled instinct and
craftsmanship should be able to pick up
a great deal easier than a person who had
never been employed in work of that
character. We trained great numbers
and it was most disappointing. We
could not get them absorbed into industry. We did our utmost.
The hon. Gentleman will realise that
employers preferred to up-grade men in
the workshops rather than take this type
of men on. For instance let us take the
platers. The employers preferred to upgrade the plater's helper to become a
plater. They preferred to up-grade the
workers who were attending the
electricians. They selected in all the
various trades men who were employed.
If a man was employed on a particular
machine they up-graded him from
machine 3 to machine 2 and put a new
man on machine 3. So far as we are
concerned we did our utmost in order to
train as many as possible hoping that we
would be able to get them absorbed in
the engineering industry. We were not
successful. The employers preferred to
select their own trainees.
However, I would like to say to the
hon. Gentleman that we brought in a
Control of Employment Order, and that
meant that every engineering firm that
required a workman must take his workman through the employment exchange.
When we brought the order into operation
we were training a great number of girls
in the technical institutes to fit them to

perform certain work of technical

There was another point raised by the
hon. Gentleman. He asked, what training are you going to give the men who
are physically unfit at the present moment
in order that they may take up new
employment. I am in a difficulty about
that, but I can see the point raised by
the hon. Gentleman.
There are men
who might not be physically unfit, but
who have been trained in light work. For
instance we have a great number of
skilled men unemployed at the present
time. I regard, for instance, the clerk
as a skilled craftsman. Clerical work is
skilled work just as agricultural work is
skilled work, and just as a docker is a
skilled man at his job, and just as a man
may be regarded as being in an unskilled
occupation, but he has been in that occupation all his life and he is regarded as
skilled. There are quite a number of
men that look physically fit, but who
could never take up hard, arduous work,
and I do not know what training we can
give them to take up work of a different
character. The whole thing is to get the
work.
I agree with the statements made by
the two hon. Gentlemen that the work
should be brought here. I think it would
be possible for us to produce men from
our training schools who would undertake
work and carry it out expeditiously and
efficiently. Another point raised by the
hon. Member was regarding the increased
amount payable under health insurance,
and I think he answered the question he
asked me. He asked why was it done?
Was it due to the new conditions of
living? Was it due to different food
values and so on like that? That is the
answer. We have found, for instance,
if we have a bad summer the vitality
of the people during the winter season is
lower. My hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, during the course of
his speech, said that because of lack of
sunshine last summer the vitality of the
people was considerably lower, and that
resulted in a great deal more sickness than
ordinarily. Another point was raised by
the hon. Gentleman when he asked what
do you mean by a reserved category.
Well, now he stated that there were
certain women whom he knew employed
in the textile industry and they wanted
to change their category and go into the
engineering industry.
Mr. MIDGLEY: They are unemployed
now.
Mr. GORDON: They were offered employment through some friends and consequently they were anxious to get into the
engineering industry. That is a matter
that has given us trouble for a consider-
We have enable period of time.
deavoured, as far as we possibly could,
to get these women that are engaged in
the textile industry transferred to work
that would be more continuous and more
permanent than they are engaged in at
the present time. We are in a difficulty.
Often employers come to us when they
are short of orders and they think we
should retain on our list these women
until they are required. That is not fair
to the women. I do not think it is fair.
I think it is unreasonable to ask us to
do it. Whenever opportunity occurs, as
long as it is not detrimental to the industry-for instance, if a woman is a key
woman in an industry we are anxious she
should remain-but if she is unemployed,
if she is in an industry where she is
slipping in, slipping out and slipping
back again, we are always anxious to
assist her to change as far as we can the
category of her job to where there is a far
greater degree of permanence. I think
that covers the points raised by the hon.
Gentlemen, and I thank them for the help
they have given us in the discussion
of problems connected with the Ministry
of Labour.

insured population, and, consequently,
we must pay a contribution into the fund
in order to make our balance compare
with the balance of the fund in Great
Britain.
Mr. NIXON: Exactly. I have got the
Minister to the very place I want him to
be. There is no Supplementary Estimate
required in Great Britain, because the
income of their fund exceeds by a long
way the expenditure. They have a big
balance, but that balance is not increased
by a Supplementary Estimate. Although
we have a balance too, a minor balance,
proportionately in comparison with
theirs, we must do what they have not to
do, namely, vote a sum direct from the
Exchequer to the fund.
On facts there is nothing between the
Minister and myself, but there is this
question between us. Where does the
step-by-step policy come in? That is one
of the things we once had, but have not
now. To-day we have to take the step of
voting thousands of pounds to the fund
direct from the pockets of the taxpayers,
while the people in Great Britain have
not to do that. This is coming from me,
and I am as strong for our connection
with Great Britain as the Minister or
anyone else sitting over there. That is
not in dispute for a moment, but I do not
like this.
Mr. MINFORD: I do not wish to
occupy the time of the Committee for any
length, but I should like to refer to the
question of lodging allowances. I know
a man who lives within four miles of a

work at certain waterworks. There was
no conveyance from his house to that
provincial town, and he refused to go.
He was offered a lodging allowance of
24s 6d, but he could not accept as there
was no conveyance from his home, and
he could not ride a bicycle. He was
taken before a court in Belfast, and the
decision to refuse him benefit was upheld.
He then got a job as a labourer on work
of national importance some 10 or 14
miles from his own home, and is still
working there.
The point I want to make is this. In
this provincial town there were men idle
who required no lodging allowance and
who could take this boy's job. I can give
instances of men going from one provincial town to another and getting lodging
allowances while there were men unemployed there who could do the work. Is
it right to take these men from their
homes when there are men in the towns in
which they are billeted able to do the
work? I can give the explanation given
by the manager of the employment
exchange. The boy who refused work at
the waterworks is a boy and not a married
man. He is 21 years of age. I think it
is squandering money and is not good for
the people that they should be compelled
to take this allowance and leave their
homes when there are men idle in the
towns to which they are sent who could
take the work without the lodging
allowance. That is entirely wrong.
To-day we are considering a Supplementary Estimate when we are paying out
money to people who are taken from
their homes. Imagine taking a man four
miles to that particular town when there
are men eligible for the work there.
young man was prevented from drawing

UNEMPLOYMENT.

not exceeding £82,000 be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending 31st March, 1943, to defray the
contribution and parity payment to the
Unemployment Fund."-(Mr. Gordon.)
CLASS IV. No. 4.
UNEMPLOYMENT SERVICES.
Resolved, "That a supplementary sum
not exceeding £33,000 be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending 31st March, 1943, for employment
services." (Mr. Gordon.)
CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £12,620 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1943, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): There is not much to
put before the Committee in reference to
Supplementary Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lord Glentoran]
this Vote. The Committee will see that
the gross sum set out in the Vote is
approximately £44,000, which is offset
by appropriations in aid amounting to
over £31,000, leaving £12,620 as the net
sum actually required by my Ministry.
This sum of £12,620 arises from one or
two causes which I will fully explain to
the Committee.
The establishment of a milk pool in
Northern Ireland has required a considerable expansion to the staff, outdoor
and indoor, in this division of the Ministry. Under the pool arrangements every
farmer can obtain the liquid price for his
milk if he gives delivery daily and produces milk of the necessary standard of
quality. Arrangements have had to be
made for the testing and grading of all
milk in Northern Ireland. In order to
facilitate collection it has been necessary
to introduce a transport pool. This is a
very important matter because it shows
a great change in our social life. It is
some satisfaction to know that despite the
great increase in the consumption of milk
from between 14 and 15 million gallons
in 1939 to 25 million gallons in 1942, it
has been unnecessary to ration or restrict
the supply of milk in Northern Ireland,
and that during the present winter we
have been able to ease the difficulties in
Scotland by contributing as much as
24,000 gallons daily.
This Vote also makes provision for the
staffing of the potato drying factories in
Northern Ireland; five are now in production, and four nearing completion.
It has also been essential to double the
number of area tillage officers in order
to cope with the additional work which

added it became obvious that they would

I beg to move.

I am warning the noble Lord about

I am as anxious as the Minister

Lord GLENTORAN: There were two

Antrim. The first was in regard to subsidies. He very properly said that was a

The next point raised by the hon. Member

ruth of the matter is that we are getting
