AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£14,740 be granted to His Majesty for the
Supplementary Estimates-
Agricultural Services
HOUSE OF COMMONS
service of the year ending 31st March,
1943, to defray the expenses of the
Ministry of Agriculture in respect of
Agricultural Education and Research,
Improvement of Livestock, Agricultural
Development and Credit, Afforestation,
and Diseases of Animals, including sundry
grants in aid."
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
The
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): The
net total required under this vote is.
£14,740. There are two principal items,
the first of which is an amount of
£88,750 for the purchase, storage and
distribution of grass seed of low germination. In pre-war days the United
Kingdom was mainly dependent upon
Scandinavia, New Zealand and Northern
Ireland for its supplies of rye grass and
cocksfoot seed, etc. As the two former
sources of supply are now cut off, an
appeal was made to farmers in Northern
Ireland, at the request of the Imperial
authorities, to increase their crops to the
greatest possible extent. The result has
been that the quantity of seed now available is considerably in excess of require-
The matter has been discussed
with representatives of the Agricultural
Departments in Great Britain and the
Treasury, and it has been agreed that the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries will
accept responsibility for all Northern
Ireland seed with a germination of 85
per cent. or more, which is over and above
the normal surplus held by machiners at
the end of the season.
ments.
Expenditure in connection with this
seed will be borne on the vote of the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.
There is, however, a considerable quantity of seed, estimated at 2,500 tons, which
has a germination of less than 85 per cent.
and is not, therefore, suitable for use as
seed. It has been agreed with the
Treasury that this seed should be purchased from farmers at £35 10s per ton
and disposed of for feeding purposes, and
that expenditure incurred in connection
with this seed should be borne on my
Ministry's Vote.
The second large item is an increase of
£20,000 for grants for the improvement
of agricultural holdings. This is a service
which has always had the support of the
whole House and hon. Members will be
glad to learn that keenness of the farming
community to carry out schemes to improve the productivity of their land
continues undiminished. The latest
available figures show an annual increase
of 6,300 schemes completed and paid for.
These land improvement schemes are not
only of the greatest importance to the
national effort for increasing the production of food and flax, but also effect
a permanent increase in the value of the
farms.
I should like to make it clear that this
scheme has not been brought to a close.
I have, however, found it necessary to
say that no fresh applications would be
entertained from January 31st last until
further notice. It is essential that our
whole force should be employed putting
through the tillage campaign. It was
manifestly desirable that all farm efforts
should be concentrated on ploughing,
getting the crops sown and the coming
harvest. Applications for flax dams will
still be dealt with and encouraged, and the
scheme resumed in full as soon as circumstances permit.
Hon. Members will observe a new item
of £2,000 for the erection of kilns for
drying home-grown timber for egg cases.
Before the war nearly all egg cases used
in Northern Ireland were made from
imported timber, which is normally well
seasoned and thoroughly dry. Since the
war the Ministry has been largely dependent on egg cases made from home-grown
timber, which experience has shown
cannot be adequately dried except by
artificial means. Where damp cases are
used, the packing material absorbs
moisture from the timber and collapses,
resulting in heavy breakages to the
eggs. In addition, mould growth develops
rapidly in eggs packed in damp cases-a
factor which, if allowed to go unchecked,
must have a damaging effect on our postwar trade. Even more important,
however, than any financial consideration
is the waste of valuable food which is
involved when breakages occur or mould
growth develops. After a careful review.
of the problem we have reached the conclusion that kilns must be provided for
drying native timber, since it cannot be
properly dried by natural means within
a reasonable period of time. As the
utilisation of such timber for egg boxes
must be regarded as a war-time expedient,
some form of Government assistance must
be provided, if facilities for drying it are
to be established in Northern Ireland.

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£10,380 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1943, to defray the salaries and expenses
of the Ministry of Commerce."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): It will be seen from
my Ministry's Supplementary Estimate
that the main item for which additional
funds have to be provided is that of
salaries and expenses, due to an increase
in the number of authorised posts since
the main Estimates for 1942-43 were prepared. These posts have become necessary because of additions to and extensions in the scope of the control schemes
in operation last June when the main
Estimates were presented. I need refer
only to building operations, textile production, crushed stone and coal supplies,
the control of all of which has become
increasingly complex and of wider application. New controls which have become
the responsibility of my Ministry since
that date include contractors' moveable
plant, laundry, dyeing and cleaning services and footwear repairs.
These control functions have been
undertaken by my Ministry on behalf of
Imperial Departments, and recoveries of
salaries and other expenses additional to
those set out in the main Estimates for
the present year will be sought in due
course. Speaking generally, I need only
remind hon. Members that the object of
all these very necessary controls is to
ensure that priority needs are catered for
and that all essential requirements are
fully met.
Under item C, provision is made to
meet additional travelling and subsistence
expenses. This is necessary largely on
account of the increase in the number
and the scope of the controls to which I
have referred, and also owing to my
Ministry's increased activities in connection with war production. It is my view,
as I think hon. Members are aware, that,
having regard to the special position of
Northern Ireland, personal contact with
Departments on the other side is invaluable. I am convinced that more can
be achieved by a single visit than by a
whole spate of letters, and I consider that
the results gained fully justify expendi
ture under this head.
The sum under item J.1 is required to
cover the remuneration to the liabilities
adjustment officer and other expenses in
connection with cases under the Liabilities
(War-Time) Adjustment Act (N.I.),
1941.
Turning now to Vote No. 2, the token
grant of £10 is sought in consequence of
additional expenditure on the services
enumerated in the Estimate. Hon. Members will see that practically the whole of
the additional expenditure is offset by the
anticipated savings on the grant payable
to the Belfast Harbour Commissioners in
1942-43.
Item A covers an increase in wages to
the employees at Donaghadee and Ardglass Harbours and extra casual assistance required for work at Ardglass.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Item B represents the Government's contribution to

Transport and the Government has agreed

Message from British Prime Minister.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that according to their request
I wrote to the Prime Minister of Great
Britain and I have received a reply. I
wrote as follows:-
:-
Dear Prime Minister,
The Members of all parties in the
House of Commons at to-day's Sitting
have requested me to convey to you
their heartfelt relief that you are now
pronounced by the doctors to be in a
state of convalescence.
Our Prime Minister, supported by
Opposition Members, paid an adequate
tribute to your outstanding courage and
energy in the conduct of the war, and
all expressed the sincere hope that you
would be very soon completely restored
to your usual robust health.
May I express the hope that you
will take care of yourself, always remembering that we look on you as the
personification of the fighting spirit of
the British Empire, within which we
are proud to be doing all we can to
hasten the day of victory.
The Prime Minister replied:
Thank you so much for your very
kind letter of March 2 about my illness.
I am glad to say I am now feeling very
much better and hope soon to be quite
fit.
Will you please tell all those associated
with you in your letter how much
obliged I am to them for their
message.
WINSTON S. CHURCHILL.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Home Affairs.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY
CLOTHING.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper:
1. Mr. Nixon.-To ask the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if any
allowance is made to members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary to refit clothing
issued to them; and whether clothing as
issued often misfits the men to whom the
issue is made.
Mr. NIXON: In asking the question I
should like to point out that Royal Ulster
Constabulary in the question should be
Royal Ulster Special Constabulary. The
omission was mine.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): In
answer to the question as it stands, on
behalf of my right hon. Friend I have
to inform the hon. Member that no allowance of the kind referred to is payable.
Frocks and trousers are issued to the
Royal Ulster Constabulary in the
"unmade" state and a money allowance
is paid to enable members of the Force
to have the garments fitted and made
ready for wear by their own tailors. No
question of misfits,' therefore, can
arise in connection with these garments.

Greatcoats are issued in the ready-towear state. They are, however, made to
the measurements of the individual man,
and misfits, which are not numerous, are
re-made by the tailoring contractors.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Parliamentary Secretary's answer, will he
consider the matter in regard to the
Special Constabulary, which, of course,
are the only constabulary concerned
where there really is a misfit?
Mr. LOWRY: As I have indicated
already, the answer was prepared from
the point of view of the regular constabulary. Of course, I shall look into
the question.

Minister of Home Affairs whether Miss

HOLYWOOD-BELFAST BUS
SERVICE.
3. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
now in a position to state when the
Holywood to Belfast bus service will be
resumed during the morning and evening
hours; whether the conditions which
caused these restrictions have largely disappeared, and whether, in view of the
very serious inconvenience to which residents between Belfast and Holywood
have been subjected, he will now take
steps to implement the promise that the
question would be reconsidered as soon as
additional buses became available.
Mr. LOWRY: On behalf of my right
hon. Friend I would inform the hon.
Member that this matter has been considered from time to time since the hon.
Member put down a similar question in
July last.
The serious inconvenience caused to
residents of Holywood and intermediate
places caused by the suspension of these
services is fully realised, but, in view of
the necessity for rigid economy in the
consumption of petrol and rubber, it is
not possible to re-establish these services
at present.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: May I point
out to the hon. Member that at the
present moment buses are in service between certain towns which I shall not
publicly name, and those buses are conveying passengers purely for the purpose
of visiting picture houses in adjoining
towns. If that be so and I believe and
know it is, surely there is a case for giving
preference to those requiring them for
essential needs.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that you
are wasting both rubber and petrol in
allowing a large number of cars joy-riding
in Northern Ireland, and will you transfer
the petrol and rubber from that joy-riding
to the convenience of the passengers for
whom the hon. Member wishes the bus
service?
Mr. LOWRY: It is not only a question
of rubber and petrol; it is a question
of the utilisation of available buses at the
appropriate times.

Labour.
MEDICAL EXAMINATION OF
WORKERS SENT TO ENGLAND.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is a fact that people,
on being sent to England for work, have
to undergo a medical examination, and,
if so, whether a similar test is imposed
on people coming to work in Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): It is a fact that, in general,
people who are sent to work in England
have to be medically examined. The
practice arose because some of the largest
and best employers insisted upon it as one
of the conditions of the employment, for
Northern Ireland and British applicants
alike; and it has been continued and extended, because it has proved to be very
much in the interests of the workers
themselves. At every examination, some
persons are found to have physical defects
which would not only prevent them from
doing the proposed work efficiently, but
would make it highly dangerous for them
to attempt it. These defects cannot be
discovered without a medical examination
and are often unknown to the persons
themselves.
Employers here are at liberty to make a
similar condition if they think it desirable; but the responsibility for giving
this protection to persons from outside
Northern Ireland does not rest upon this
Government.
Public Security.
MORRISON SHELTERS.
6. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether he
can state how many Morrison shelters
have been refused or unavailed of in the
various areas; whether he is aware that
numbers of these shelters are lying in outside gardens and are rapidly becoming
destroyed, and, if so, whether he will
take steps to have these shelters made
available to homes containing invalids
and sick persons whose removal to communal shelters can only be made with
difficulty.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): The allocation
of free air-raid shelters, both outdoor and
indoor, is carried out by local authorities
of the areas concerned, and I am not,
therefore, in a position to supply the information asked for in the first part of
the question.
I am aware that in some cases indoor
shelters are not being taken care of as
they ought to be, and I have already
asked the local authorities concerned to
carry out an inspection of all indoor
shelters issued free, with a view to ensuring that they are being properly cared
for. Shelters which are not stored in
reasonably weatherproof accommodation
will be removed.
in
With regard to the last part of the
question, local authorities domestic
shelter areas are empowered to issue these
shelters free for the use of members of
eligible households who produce medical
evidence that they are suffering from ailments or disabilities which render them
permanently incapable of using the outdoor shelters provided. Indoor shelters
are also still available for sale to householders in domestic shelter areas who are
ineligible for free shelter.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Do I understand the right hon. Gentleman to say
that eligible householders are those with
a valuation under £29? The object of
my question is to request that consideration should be given to the question of the
privilege being extended in the case of
illness to houses outside £29 valuation
qualification.
Mr. GRANT: Does the hon. Member
mean to give them free to those people?
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Yes.
Mr. GRANT: Under the regulations
it is not within my power to do that, but
I will consider the question. I make no
promise further than to say I will consider it.

paper

The ban imposed by the Ministry of
Supply on the use of wood pulp for the
manufacture of certain types
of
has
paper
been applied to all paper mills throughout the United Kingdom in order to

Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move as

eight" be

of his name came as a great surprise to
me, and I take it that omission is intentional. I would be better pleased if
it were accidental, but if it is an intentional omission, it is an intentional
affront.
The hon. Member for Pottinger has
been a member of this Committee for the
past eighteen years, and for the past ten
years has acted as chairman.
He was
appointed in 1925 by this House as the
Labour representative on that Committee.
He has been to my own knowledge a
lynx-eyed guardian of the public purse.
He has attended the meetings of that
Committee day by day and year by year.
With the utmost exactitude he has discharged his duties. I do not say it in the
sense of throwing bouquets, but candidly
and fearlessly he has discharged his duty
as member and as chairman of that Committee with ability and industry.
Is it for the faithful discharge of public
duties for many years, first as private
member and then as chairman, that this
direct insult has been offered to the
Member for Pottinger? Has he done
anything and I appeal to any member
of the Committee who sat under him as
chairman and who sat with him as colleague as a member of that Committee
to which the least exception could be
taken ? If he has been guilty of any
fault, he has been too zealous in the discharge of his duty as a public trustee. He
represents a party. It is not my party.
Its policy is not my policy or the policy
of my party. In some essentially Irish
matters it is not a policy that I could
endorse, but that party is entitled to its
views. That party was admitted to be
entitled to representation on this Committee eighteen years ago. It is entitled
to representation to-day, and to-day, if
this Motion is carried, it is absolutely
denied representation. He is the only
member of that party who has a seat on
that Committee.
The hon. Member for Pottinger is
penalised and humiliated by this procedure. What is the reason for it? It
cannot be personal. Is it political? Is it
taken because the hon. Member for
Pottinger had the distinction in the recent West Belfast by-election of defeating the official Unionist candidate, the
nominee of the official Unionist Party?
I say that if that is so this is a most
unworthy and most vindictive proceeding.
To penalise and punish any party in this
House for daring to stand up for its
principles and views by putting such
humiliation on one of its members is inconsistent with the dignity of a responsible
Parliamentary assembly, and I utter
against it my strongest and most virile.
protest. I say it is unworthy, I say it
is vindictive, I say it is a breach of
courtesy, and I say it cuts right across
Parliamentary decencies. If this Motion
is carried I will have to consider seriously
whether or not I ought to serve on this
Committee. I now put it to the hon.
Members opposite-I put it to them as
individuals, not as a party; I put it to
them as gentlemen not as partisans that
they should allow my amendment which,
I submit, is elementary fairness to an
individual Member of this House, to be
carried.

do so because I contend that we should

I have inaugurated three war Savings
Committees in Newry, Warrenpoint and
Rostrevor, and I am still a member of

done here.
Another objection I have to this Committee is that although it has presented
report after report to this House-the
chairman was the hon. Member for Pottinger-yet the Prime Minister and the
Government never made any effort whatever to have these reports brought before
this House for discussion. These reports
are an absolute waste of money. They
are made out, yet the Government never
make any effort to bring them before this
House. The Prime Minister moves when
certain reports come forward that they be
considered, but he has never done so in
the case of the reports of the Public
Accounts Committee.
I have been in this House five years,
and I cannot remember one of these reports being brought forward for discussion here. I wonder is it because the
reports show a grievous waste of petrol
by the Minister of Home Affairs, the
Prime Minister and other prominent
personalities?
Is that the reason we are
never given an opportunity of discussing
these reports? That is wrong. We should
have an opportunity of discussing them,
and as long as this farce continues I will
not be a party to it. We should be given
an opportunity of discussing these reports.
Another point that has to be taken into
account is that we have not the same

England they have what is known
as a Select Committee on National
Expenditure.

Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: The reasons for the introduction of this Measure are briefly
these, and I propose to present the Bill
under these heads:-
First, to provide an alternative method
of trial in certain cases;
Secondly, the simplification of procedure in cases of importance, and also those
of somewhat minor importance;
Thirdly, the question of convenience
enters into the matter.
Last of all, there is a certain reduction
of expense with regard to particular cases
to which I shall draw the attention of the
House.
When first the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act was placed on the
Statute Book, the aim of persons of
criminal tendencies was probably somewhat more limited in scope than it is today. The aim then, in short, was to
make this Government of Northern Ireland impossible by flagrant and deliberate
breaches of the law in many directions.
It was somewhat narrow in scope as compared with the activities of similar people
to-day.
The criminal aims of these people to-day
are very much wider in scope, and are far
more dangerous by reason of the fact that
a world-wide war is now raging.
1922 and the troublous times about that
In
period there was no world-wide war
raging. This country, in common with
the rest of the British Empire, was not
involved in the struggle for existence
against formidable opponents in every
quarter of the globe. The position to-day
is different. These people are quite prepared to take advantage of this great
conflict in order to advance their criminal
aims, and one of those criminal aims undoubtedly is to produce not merely the
downfall of this Government, but the
downfall of the Government of the United
Kingdom, the collapse of the British
Empire if possible, and handing us over
to our enemies.
This aim is very much like the mischief
which was aimed at in the Treason Felony
Act of 1848. In order to remind hon.
Members of that I propose to cite Section
3 of that Act. It provides:

If any person whatsoever shall,

Gracious Lady the Queen, from the

or of any other of Her Majesty's

war against Her Majesty, within any
part of the United Kingdom, in order
by force or constraint to compel her to
change her measures or counsels, or in
order to put any force or constraint
upon or in order to intimidate or
overawe both Houses or either House
of Parliament, or to move or stir any
foreigner or stranger with force to invade the United Kingdom or any other
of Her Majesty's dominions or countries.
under the obeisance of Her Majesty,
and such compassings, imaginations,
inventions, devices, or intentions, or
any of them, shall express, utter, or

writing, . . . or by any overt act or deed,
every person so offending shall be guilty
of felony, and being convicted thereof
shall be liable, . to be transported
beyond the seas for the term of his or
her natural life,
It is perfectly plain from the documents that have fallen into the hands of
the authorities in the last few months
that the objects of this criminal conspiracy, widespread and formidable, are
none other than those contemplated by
Section 3 of the Treason Felony Act. In
such circumstances, therefore, it is idle to
punish these persons merely by bringing
them before two resident magistrates,
when the punishment that can be inflicted
upon them is confined to two years'
imprisonment with hard labour, and with
or without a fine of £100. In consequence it is contemplated by Clause 1 of
the Bill that Section 3 of the original
Act shall be amended.
Sub-section 1 of section 3 of the Act
of 1922 reads:
A person alleged to be guilty of an
offence against the regulations may be
tried by a court of summary jurisdiction constituted in accordance with this
section and not otherwise.
It is proposed, as hon. Members will
will observe, to substitute for the words
"and not otherwise" the words "or on
indictment." In other words, in serious
cases the offenders, instead of being dealt
with in summary fashion, may be returned for trial and tried upon indictment with all the consequences that follow
therefrom.
It is, as I have said perfectly plain that
this conspiracy has for its object the very
matters set forth in Section 3 of the
Treason Felony Act. That has been
demonstrated and proved in court more
than once within the last few months.
Indeed, all matters dealing with treason
felony are of a somewhat technical
character, and while the cases tried so
far under Section 3 of the Treason Felony
Act have been so clear that none of the
offenders had the temerity to attempt any
defence of a legal nature, that does not
free the Crown from the necessity of being
prepared and ready for any technicality
that might be raised.
Secondly, matters such as publishing,
printing and writing documents which
have for their object the encouragement
of such designs as the deprivation of His
Majesty of his crown and title, or the
levying of war against the King in this.
part of the country or elsewhere, or the
encouragement of foreigners to invade
this part of the Kingdom with forcethese things can be simplified very much
if this proposal becomes law, and will prevent any attempt to take advantage of
the countless technicalities which have
accumulated around this Statute in the
last 95 years.
When one reflects that in
1848 it was considered necessary to overhaul the law which had existed from the
year 1351, one will realise that the lapse
of another 95 years has made it necessary
to bring the machinery a bit more up to
date.
The law, as it stands, necessitates the
presence of two resident magistrates for
the disposal of cases that are of minor
importance. I give one instance, the
existence of the curfew when the curfew
does exist and it has to be imposed from
time to time, and, may be, will have to
be imposed again. In such cases two
resident magistrates have to sit to dispose
of cases, and it has occurred to many hon.
Members some of these cases are not of a
very heinous character. It may very well
be that by some misreading of the clock
or a watch being wrong some person might
inadvertently be caught out of doors.
Civil Authorities Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
Unfortunately, as the law presently
stands, it is necessary to summon two
resident magistrates to dispose of such
cases. So much for the matter of procedure and method of disposal.
The only other matter of great consequence is contained in Clause 2, where, of
course, seeing that these offences are contemplated to be disposed of by indictment,
it is of such a grave character that the
punishment must be altered accordingly.
Accordingly, it is proposed that on indictment a person shall be liable to not
less than three years penal servitude, the
minimum term on indictment, and to a
maximum of 14 years, or there may be a
fine of £500 or both. Now power may
be taken on summary conviction, and
especially in these cases which are considered to be such as may reasonably and
properly be disposed of by one resident
magistrate, to reduce the maximum
penalty of two years' imprisonment and
£100 fine, and to make these in the case
of curfew offences something that is more
in relation to the gravity of the offence
on the occasion. It may be urged here
that these heavier punishments are
serious matter and one that should be
very carefully considered. I should like
to point out to the House that the trials
will be on indictment and by jury, and
if the punishments are very much heavier
the accused person will have the protection that the jury system gives him. I
consequently beg to move.

learned Member, in introducing this Bill,

I cast my

felony under the Act of 1848 is compassing by overt act the overawing or intimidation of either House of Parliament,
and here in Northern Ireland under
authorities now sitting on the Front
Bench we had a standing army raised for
that express set purpose.
But this Bill is one of the series of Bills
called the Special Powers Acts. It is
a branch of a poisonous upas tree. I
do not think it is brought forward
genuinely in the interests of order and in
the interests of security. Rather it is
brought forward by the hon. and learned
Member who is piloting the Bill. May
I do him the honour, perhaps, of saying
he is not the father of this Bill? I think
he is only echoing his master's voice.
But the Bill will occur to many minds as
being brought forward to check the
stampede which has been recently exhibited amongst former friends and
followers of the administration, who are
in every constituency in Northern Ireland at the present moment in angry revolt. It is brought forward to steady
them. It is brought forward to whip
them in
in with imaginary fears and
chimeras and talk of treason felony,
penal servitude for fourteen years and
£500 fine, raising a cloud of horrors that
exist only in the imagination of the few.
It is an electioneering dodge, an
electioneering trick.
The first Special Powers Act was passed
21 years ago. The spokesmen of the Government at that time stated explicitly that it
was intended to confer a power of extraordinary stringency as a purely temporary emergency measure in the year
1922. We are now in 1943 and we have
the third of what was then designed as a
purely temporary measure brought forward. So we are progressing. In 1933
a second Special Powers Act was passed.
The provisions of the old Act of 1922
were made permanent law in the Six
Counties. This Bill makes a breach of
any one of the regulations an indictable
offence. At that time it was summary,
but a great variety of cases now become
punishable by indictment, punishable by
penal servitude for 14 years and fines of
£500 or both penal servitude and fine.
It gives one resident magistrate power
summary cases hitherto exercisable by
two.
in
I may say in regard to that that only
one of these resident magistrates is a
Catholic and many of these accused men
are Catholics. There was only one R.M.
of that persuasion 20 years ago and that
state of things remains to-day. In the
appointment of only one of that creed in
Belfast the Government had not really a
free hand, because they were fettered by a

pre-partition series of British appointments. The Minister of Home Affairs
appoints these R.M.s. He makes no mistake about their eligibility. He sees that
they dig with the right foot. The Minister
has their transfer in his hands. They are

to a Section which I had the privilege of

Act of 1935.
As regards trials by indictment the
Minister spoke of the security of the jury
system, the protection of the jury system.
The Crown can and will handpick the
juries. The Crown stand-by system in
party cases is notorious. The stand-by
of jurors in party cases has been the rule
without intermission since this Government began. Jury packing by Dublin
Castle existed. It was in no wise different
from the Stormont way, which is open,
unabashed and unchecked. I say here
the manipulation of the jury system in
party cases shakes confidence in the law
and reduces legal procedure in such cases
to a mockery and a snare. To render
accused person liable to 14 years' penal
servitude for a breach of any one of the
many regulations of various degrees of
gravity, shocks one's sense of justice.
any
One regulation makes it an offence to
possess a bicycle without a permit.
Another makes it an offence to hold a
meeting likely in the opinion of the Crown
to cause disaffection. Another prohibits
the wearing of uniform or badges indicating membership of any association of
which the Minister disapproves. Is this
regulation likely to be enforced against
any member of the body which is wont
to celebrate on 12th July? The Minister
himself is a prominent member of that
body. A suspect might get penal servitude under this Bill for refusing to answer
questions or committing an offence which
was not an offence at the time it was
committed, but was made an offence subsequently.
This Bill is a fitting supplement to a
savage Cromwellian code, in reality an
emergency war code. Not a single
Unionist paper in England has ever
uttered a word in its defence. Professor
J. S. Brierly, Professor of International
Law at Oxford, described the code as
abrogating the rule of law. An eminent
Ulster author, Mr. Robert Lynd, wrote in
regard to the report of the English
Council of Civil Liberties on this
code:
"It is an extremely important and even sensationally important
report, and most of those who read it and
who are neither Fascists nor. Communists
will agree that except as a temporary
measure during civil war it would be
dangerous to trust even the best executive
in the world or the best police in the
world with the all but absolute powers
enumerated here." The administration
seek to spread the impression that only by
the continuance of this code can they be
saved from elements working in the
interests of Republicanism and subversive
movements, and that the ordinary rule of
law is not adequate to deal with the situation in the Six Counties.
The Nazis use the same plea. They say
the rule of law as a safeguard to constitutional practice is an outworn convention and must be replaced by a system of
government by decree. They say the constitutional safeguards of liberty must be
abolished and dictatorial power must be
invested in the executive. That is the
Nazi plea. They say, "We are in a state
which must rapidly degenerate into
anarchy unless it is checked" and consequently what they do is they depart from
the elementary principles of law and
drive a coach through Habeas Corpus.
There is no Habeas Corpus here. They
drive a coach through Habeas Corpus and
make ducks and drakes of the ordinary
forms of criminal procedure. Your
dictators in Northern Ireland pretend
they are loyal to the British Constitution,
but the major safeguards of the British.
Constitution are permanently suspended
by them in Northern Ireland. After 20
years they bring forward this third
Special Powers Act, an admission that
they cannot govern without it. What an
admission after 20 years of despotic
arbitrary rule. Their settled policy has
been to draw a dark veil of dissension
between the majority and the minority,
and one of the weapons they employ for
this fell purpose is the Special Powers
Acts. The only kind of liberty they
understand is liberty to ride rough-shod
over their neighbours.

whelmed when studying its proposals. It

£858,000,000. It would be difficult to

utterly outside the capacity of our people
to pay under present circumstances.
Let us briefly examine the proposals.
The plan covers all citizens without upper
income limit, and is all-embracing in
scope of persons and of needs. In relation to social security four main classes
of working age, and two others are given
-(1) employees, that is, persons whose
normal occupation is employment under
contract of service; (2) others gainfully
occupied, including employers, traders,
and independent workers of all kinds; (3)
housewives, that is married women of
working age; (4) others of working age
not gainfully employed; (5) below working
age; (6) retired above working age.

within the scope of one comprehensive
scheme all the anomalies and paradoxes
that have got into social legislation. And
having done that, Mr. Arthur Greenwood
felt compelled in the British House of
Commons a few weeks ago to vote against
the British Government because of their
lukewarmness in this thing, and because
of their inaction and because of the fear
that vested interests were going to be too
strong. So far as this Report is concerned, there was little hope of getting
it brought into operation. It has been
the same in the history of social security.
Many politicians in this Government were
so opposed to the scheme of social
security that we had to go out into the
highways and byways to educate the
people. I think the Prime Minister does
not like that, but it is absolutely true.
The PRIME MINISTER: I deny that
it is true.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The man who would
deny that would deny his own existence.
I say it is true. There was a time in
Northern Ireland and Great Britain
when the majority of the people sitting
on the Front Bench in this House, and
the majority of the party to which the
Front Bench Members belong, were

social improvement, and were SO year
after year when progressive schemes of

Imperial Parliament as a result of reactionary opposition by many people in
the Conservative Party. When old-age
pensions came at 5s a week the stoutest
opposition was to be found in the ranks
of the Conservative Party, and amongst
those who opposed the 5s a week pension
were men eligible to retire from high

a year or £80 a week. Yet they were
opposing 5s a week to the poor people of
the country.

section of the community has all the
mental virtue or goodness. I do not

I know how uphill has been the battle. I

That is how it comes about that throughout the whole scheme of social services
you have these horrible abnormalities,
paradoxes and anomalies which I have

are three schemes if not more of widows'

services have been built up.

the scheme submitted by Sir William
Beveridge to give inspiration and hope
to our people and to ask our people to

the reward of our people for all the

struggles and sorrows of the present time
and the great struggle we are passing
through. That is the purpose of the
Resolution submitted here this afternoon.
We submit it to bring hope to our people.

in spirit and in truth. We believe in the

direction in which the social development
of mankind, and mankind's destiny will
win through this terrific conflict.
believe with Mr. Wallace, of America, in

PAY OF SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if an
increase of 3s 6d per week (to take effect
from the 2nd November, 1942) has been
granted to full-time and mobilised members of the Ulster Special Constabulary
stationed outside Belfast and Londonderry areas, and, if so, whether he can
give the reason for the exclusion of
Belfast and Londonderry; whether he can
state why this increase was only dated
back to 2nd November, 1942, instead of
from 1st June, 1942, as in the case of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary and Harbour
Police; and whether he is aware that another increase of 4s 6d per week has been
granted to the National Fire Service and
Civil Defence personnel, and that this
also applied to members of the Special
Police and War Reserve Police Force in
Great Britain, and whether he will consider the advisability of applying both
increases to all members of the police
forces in Northern Ireland.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): On
behalf of my right hon. Friend, I should
like to say that an increase in pay of 4s 6d
per week was granted to the
the Special
Constabulary and certain other police
auxiliaries in Great Britain with effect
from 2nd November, 1942. By virtue of
a previous award, however, the special
constable in Northern Ireland was in a
more favourable position, in the matter
of pay, than his counterpart in Great
Britain to the extent of 1s per week in
the country and 6s per week in the cities
of Belfast and Londonderry.
It was
decided, in view of the considerable increases in pay of the Special Constabulary since the outbreak of war, that
the continuance of this apparently preferential treatment for the Northern
Ireland special constable could no longer
be justified, and when the November,
in Great
1942, increase was awarded
Britain opportunity was taken to equate
the position of the two groups as far as
this could be done without actually reducing the pay of any Northern Ireland
special constable. Accordingly, an award
of 3s 6d per week was made to country
members which had the effect of placing
them in precisely the same position as
their counterparts in Great Britain, and
of leaving the city members with an advantage of ls 6d per week
British standard.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): Following the usual
precedent in bringing the Vote on
Account before the Committee, I shall
not go into explanatory details except to
point out that there is a decrease of about
£1,727,000 in the total figure for 1943-44,
shown in the second column of the Paper,
as compared with the total original and
supplementary provision for the current
year, shown in the third column.
Remarks have been made from time to
time that the Estimates mean little, because they are always followed by substantial supplementaries. I wish to point
out that the original Estimate this year
shows a reduction of over £600,000
on the original Estimate of last
year, but I am not to be taken as suggesting by that there will not be supplementaries this year. In war time particularly it is impossible to foretell what
the expenditure will be, and undoubtedly supplementaries will be brought
forward. Sometimes they will be only
token Estimates showing the House how
the money is proposed to be expended.
The reduction in the amount is entirely
due to the fact that the demands by Civil
Defence Services and for Civil Defence
purposes generally have materially diminished owing to the required standard in
supplies being gradually attained or to
the completion of the works put in hand.
I would also point out to the Committee
that the provision for the National Fire
Service is now set out in an Estimate by
itself (Class VIII, No. 3), the expenditure
in previous years having been included
under Civil Defence Service. I beg to
move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution to be reported to-morrow;
Committee to sit again to-morrow.

Order read for resuming adjourned
Debate on Question (9th March): "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Question again proposed.
Mr. LOWRY: Beyond the observations of the hon. and learned Member for
Central it does not appear to me that I
have any novel points to deal with. His
complaint appeared to be against the
introduction of trials by jury in certain
cases which will be the subject of indictment in future. He took the opportunity
of making an allegation that there is
nothing novel about, that a system of
jury-packing goes on in this country
habitually. As one with considerable
experience of that sort of course I give
that a flat denial. There is nothing of
the sort.
So far from dealing with the Amendments that this Bill proposes, he launched
forth into a discussion of the whole policy
of the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Acts. In common with every Member of
this House I deplore the necessity for the
continuance of these Acts, which it was
thought when first introduced would be
merely temporary measures. If they are
a permanent feature of our life, whose
fault is it? It is the fault largely of the
people that the hon. and learned Member
represents. The Government will be
delighted when the time comes when these
measures and this code can be brought to
an end. I should have liked to point out
to the hon. Member, had he been here,
that in a neighbouring State there is no
trial by jury. A military tribunal gives
the malefactors very short shift indeed.
And worse than all and more startling
to a lawyer than anything is the abolition
of the law of evidence as we know it. I
suggest that this House approves and
approves thoroughly of the Amendments
proposed.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 11th March, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Labour.
CLASSIFICATION OF NORTHERN
IRELAND WORKERS.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Labour whether in pursuance of the
promise he gave in the House on March 2,
1943, he can now state how many of
Northern Ireland's unemployed are (1)
skilled workers; (2) how many are semiskilled workers, and (3) how many are
unskilled; and whether he can state
precisely what is meant by the Ministry's definitions of skilled and semiskilled workers; and also whether he can
state if there is any ban against Northern
Ireland skilled workers going to jobs in
Great Britain, and, if so, whether there
is any work for them in Northern Ireland or any likelihood of such work in the
near future.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In reply to the hon. Member,
the classification adopted by my Ministry
and the Ministry of Labour and National
Service distinguishes between unskilled
workers and others, but does not distinguish between the various degrees of
skill, and it is not, therefore, possible to
sub-divide the figures further to show
skilled and semi-skilled separately.
The skilled workers include, in addition
to those belonging to the shipbuilding,
engineering and building industries, a
very large variety of occupations, including clerks, transport workers, agricultural workers, shop assistants, weavers,
winders, spinners, domestic servants,
stitchers, and many others. These
workers are skilled within their own
occupation.
On 1st February, 1943, the latest date
for which figures are available, there were
4,621 men and 3,058 women, aged 18 and
upwards, registering as wholly unemployed who fell into these various
categories which are regarded as skilled.
There is no bar against skilled workers
going to jobs in Great Britain unless they
are urgently needed here, and, even then,
consideration is given to relative urgency
and the circumstances of individual cases.
The problem of finding suitable employment for the varieties of the available
skilled labour is constantly engaging the
attention of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce and Production,
and myself.
Mr. BROWN: I wish to give notice
that I propose raising this matter on the
Adjournment.
Agriculture.
DISPOSAL OF GRASS-SEED.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that
many farmers are still experiencing
difficulties in disposing of their grass-seed,
and can he make a statement on the
matter.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): As the hon. Member
is aware, there was a very heavy surplus
of grass-seed this year. On representations being made, the British Government came to the assistance of our
farmers and agreed to buy this surplus
at fixed prices. An immense amount of
seed has already been bought under these
conditions. The hon. Member will
appreciate that the seed cannot all be
taken at once. My Ministry has already
bought over 2,000 tons for disposal otherwise than as seed.
RATES ON POTATO PROCESSING
FACTORY.

to the Newry Urban District Council will

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply. The
potato processing factory which has been
erected at Newry by my Ministry is the
property of the Ministry of Food and
being Government property is exempt
from the payment of rates. It is, how-

ever, the normal practice both of the

As I have said, however, the Newry

4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
people who occupy houses which were
certified as uninhabitable owing to damage
by enemy action have themselves to take
legal proceedings to recover any rent paid
in respect of such houses while they were
uninhabitable.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): On
behalf of my right hon. Friend I would
inform the hon. Member that by Section
36 of the Landlord and Tenant (War
Damage) Act (Northern Ireland), 1941,
provision is made whereby a tenant whose
dwelling-house has been rendered unfit
by reason of war damage before the passing of the Act, that is, 14th October,
1941, may make application to the court.
to have such modification of his rights and
liabilities as in the circumstances the
court thinks just. It is open, therefore,
to any tenant to make such application to
the court for a decision as to what modification, if any, of his rights and liabilities should be made. No doubt the court
in arriving at its decision will have regard
to the provisions of Section 13 of the Act
whereby no rent shall be payable in
respect of a dwelling-house let on a short
tenancy, if the dwelling-house has been
rendered unfit by reason of war damage
after the passing of the Act.
Mr. NIXON: Is it a fact that the only
way a tenant can make application is by
proceeding, and the point of the question
is, seeing that it has been created an
offence by the Government for the protection of people who are not very well able
to help themselves, have the Government
power or will they take power to sue for
rent improperly obtained by the landlord
in respect of the uninhabitable house?
Mr. LOWRY: It has not been made an
offence. Section 36 sets out clearly the
procedure the aggrieved tenant should
follow. It is impossible that the Government should take on them to become a
litigant on behalf of the aggrieved person.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the statement that it is impossible, does not the
Crown take up cases every day for people
aggrieved in a manner in which it is of
such a public nature that it is in the
interests of the public to protect them.
Mr. LOWRY: The Crown takes up and
pursues criminal offences.

PERSONATION AT ELECTIONS.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether in the interests of
democracy he will take steps to stop personation at elections.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
Personation at parliamentary and local
government elections is a serious and reprehensible crime which every citizen
should be ashamed to commit or encourage. As the hon. Member is aware,
the practice of personation is extremely
difficult to suppress by legislation alone.
By the Parliamentary and Local Government Elections Act (Northern Ireland),
1930, this Parliament has already sought
to strengthen the law on the subject, and
I have at present under consideration the
possibility of utilising the system of
national registration for the purpose
further reducing the evil.
I should add that the Act of 1930, to
which I have referred, does not deal with
the election of Members to sit in the
Imperial Parliament, as this subject is
beyond the powers of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, having regard to the
provisions of Section 19 (b) of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Government
deal with the matter in so far as it concerns their own Parliament? Is it not a
fact that personation can be stopped if
the Government take determined action,
and is it not also a fact that it is becoming impossible to have an election in
Northern Ireland owing to personation?
It has got to a ridiculous stage.
Mr. LOWRY: I have already said
that, in so far as this Parliament is concerned, the question in connection with
parliamentary and municipal elections is
under consideration.
Mr. NIXON: That is fair enough; we
will see what happens.
Pensions for Cabinet Ministers.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
drawn to the statement published in the
Press that it is reported that the Government intend bringing in a Bill to provide
pensions for Cabinet Ministers on their
retirement; whether he is aware that this
reported proposal has aroused a wave of
indignation throughout Northern Ireland;
whether he can state what the position is
in this respect in Great Britain, both
as regards Cabinet Minsters and Private
Members at Westminster; and whether
he can give the House an assurance that
no such highly controversial proposal as
that reported will be introduced by the
Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: (Mr.
Andrews): The position in Great Britain
in regard to the payment of pensions to
ex-holders of political offices is governed
by the Political Offices Pension Act, 1869,
and the Ministers of the Crown Act,
1937.
As regards private Members, their
position is dealt with by the House of
Commons Members' Fund Act, 1939,
under which a fund is established to be.
administered by trustees. Contributions
to this fund are deducted from the
salaries of members.
The question whether any provision
should be made for ex-Cabinet Ministers
and others in Northern Ireland is a
matter for the House of Commons itself,
and would require to be considered, in the
first place, by a Select Committee of the
House.

Mr. BEATTIE: After examining this
Bill I feel there are one or two things I
should say.
Could the Government not
have found more useful work for this
House to perform than to spend its time
discussing a Measure of this kind? It is
now being discussed for the second day.
I wonder could the Government not have
thought of discussing matters which
would be of benefit to the working-class
people of this Province, such as trying to
solve the unemployment problem, trying
to keep factories open, especially the one
which is now going to close and which
will disorganise 700 highly skilled
workers. There is no just cause for
closing this factory. It is not being
closed because there is a shortage of raw
material. There is ample raw material
at the disposal of the Ballyclare Paper
Mill to keep it going 100 per cent.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
will agree that he is going very far from
the matter. He is quite justified in suggesting other work might be done instead
of this, but it is out of order to give
details.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am coming to the
close of that part of my speech. I respect
your ruling in every way. Could the
Government not have discussed the question of
erecting new houses when
thousands of people are living under
overcrowded conditions, living in shelters,
and living in workhouses? Would it not
have been better for the Government to
have spent two days discussing such a
matter instead of this Bill? Would it
not have been better for them to say,
"We will examine the medical reports on
the health of the people in Northern
Ireland-and then let us discuss for two
days the question of devising ways and
means for the uplifting of humanity in
the Six Counties"?
There are many other things of a
similar kind which could be discussed and
which would be helpful and useful to the
people of the Six Counties, and perhaps,
those outside this area. If we had a
wise, careful and thoughtful Government
in office that would be done; but we are
now confined to a Measure known as the
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Bill,
which, in my opinion, leads us nowhere.
It is a blind alley; it is a Bill which will
receive no respect outside the Government. It is not a Bill one can visualise as
bringing peace, contentment, brotherhood, good fellowship, and a real desire
to have final victory brought to the side
of democracy against the Nazi and Fascist
tyrants who are trying to dominate the
world. The things contained in this Bill
do not appeal to anyone.
I want to say-I do so without malice
aforethought or in a deliberate attempt
to try to injure or destroy any personal
political standard of any Member of this

made as a sort of jumping-off groundthe Parliamentary Secretary tried to
convert this House to the idea that there

He said the criminal aims of these people
to-day were much wider in scope and far

collapse of the British Empire, and
handing us over to our enemies. He also

On examining that statement I am

in 1848 but later, he, as a learned King's

passed. He told us in this House what

the laws which were made in that year
could have been usefully employed many

If that is all you can do I would advise

I do not wish to see one hair of your head
destroyed, but I can assure you there is
a great deal of distrust regarding you,
and a rebellious spirit waiting to overcome each and everyone of you for the
twenty-three horrible years you have compelled the people of this country to pass
through. Not one Member of the Government can say I am a physical force man.
I do not believe in physical force. I would

made at that meeting, and that report did

This Bill is designed only on the
assumption that the present Government
will continue to be the ruling power in
this country. If the Government want to

You have men in prison now, Protestant
young men whom I know deep down in
my heart have never for one minute been
members of any illegal organisation. I fail
to find any reasonable justification for one

Road, on the Shankill Road, and in Sandy
Row that I do not believe in physical
force. I am a constitutionalist, and I
will use constitutional methods to attain
all the objects and aims I desire to fulfil.
The spirit that was shown in this House
on Tuesday against my membership of the
Public Accounts Committee, of which I
have been for long the honoured chairman
-elected not by myself but by the Members on the other side of the House-the
spirit in which that membership was terminated is not the spirit that should
prevail in this part of the world. That
is not the spirit of good government; that
is not the spirit that is going to reorganise
and bring closer together all those elements
that are likely to make this country fit for
heroes to live in. That spirit of vindictiveness carries you nowhere. On this
very day next week that great Assembly
at Westminster, which gives ear to the
least among its members, that Assembly

spirit, will know the ins and outs of the
methods employed by this Government.
I intend to use my time at Westminster

stands for. It is the political structure I

enable the more serious offences against
the Regulations to be tried before a judge
and jury with an increased power of
punishment. I have heard with astonishment the hon. Member for Pottinger say
that this measure denies all the principles
of the liberty of the subject. It does
nothing of the kind, if anything it improves the position of the subject by permitting trial on indictment. It provides,
as do the Defence (General) Regulations,
that offenders may be brought either before a court of summary jurisdiction or
Civil Authorities Bill-
Second Reading
11 MARCH 1943
before a judge and a jury. What liberty
does that infringe? If it had been the
other way round one might have expected
hon. Members to say that the liberty of
the subject was infringed by reason of the
fact that his guilt or innocence was to be
judged by a court in which a jury had no
part.
I have referred to the Defence Regulations. The majority of these relate to
offences which may be dealt with according to the circumstances, either summarily or by judge and jury. This Bill,
therefore, is introducing no new conception whatsoever in providing that, so far
as the Regulations of the Act of 1922 are
concerned, they may be dealt with in a
similar manner. In the case of the Defence Regulations one also finds that some
offences may be of a minor character and
some may be of a serious character, but
the Regulations provide that in the prosecution of offences the Director of Public
Prosecutions in England-it is the
Attorney-General here has a discretion
as to how prosecutons are to be brought.
So far as the. Regulations under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act are concerned it has been from the commencement the rule-it is a Statutory provision
-that all prosecutions thereunder must
be brought in accordance with the directions of the Attorney-General.
So when it is said that this is a new
political instrument in the hands of the
Executive, the simple reply is that that
statement, which is so lightly made, is
entirely contrary to the facts.
The
burden falls on me at the moment, of
directing prosecutions under these Regulations. I have never had the least suggestion from any other Member of the
Government as to how I should act in the
discharge of this duty and I know that
that was also the experience of my predecessors. So this charge of a new
weapon being placed in the hands of the
Executive, so easily made, turns out to be
entirely without foundation. Why it is
made at all without any attempt to sup-.
port it, if there is a case against this
measure, I do not know.
What is the background of this measure? Before I deal with the events of
last year-there is no need for me to go
back either 30 years or 95 years I should
say that this Bill does not in any way
attempt to alter or modify the law regarding treason or treason felony; it is a Bill
designed for the purpose of strengthening
the forces of law and order. The Act of
1922 was passed primarily for the preservation of law and order, and while I agree
with the hon. Member for Pottinger when
he says that what we want is to see the
housing conditions and the health of the
community made better, I must remind
him and every other hon. Member that
the first duty of any Government, the first
responsibility of any State, is to maintain
law and order. These various Regulations
provide a means of doing that in this
country.
In some cases, as I have. stated, they
cover what may be minor offences; in some
they are designed to strike at those who
willingly and of set purpose. set out by
violent means to overthrow the Constitution of the State. In some of these cases
one cannot prove or bring home a charge.
of treason or a charge of treason felony,
but, nevertheless, a serious offence may
have been committed involving the
safety and liberty of the community.

Having regard to what happened last
years, one must ask in some of these
serious cases whether, when prima facie,
an offence of that kind has been committed, the matter should be dealt with
by two resident magistrates or by
judge and jury with a greater power of
punishment. This Bill confers a discretion as to how such an offence may be
dealt with, and will enable the more
serious offences against the community
to be dealt with in what is, after all, the
older and more constitutional forum,
that is before a judge and jury.
I spoke of the background of this measure. It has always been the motto of
the republican forces in Ireland, and of
their military agents, the Irish Republican Army, to take advantage, of what
they call the opportunity afforded by
England's difficulties. During last year,
which as hon. Members will recollect
started with serious reverses for British
arms in the East, it became apparent
that the local members of the Irish Republican Army were attempting to put
that sentiment into practice. Many
documents were discovered from which
it became clear that the fate of British
arms in other parts of the world was to
be taken as the signal for a recrudescence of the campaign of violence in

I emphasise that these excerpts are
only samples of many similar documents
that came into the hands of the police.
Again I say that, if it stopped there, one
could afford to take a less serious view
Civil Authorities Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Attorney-General]
of the present position. But the matter
did not stop there. These plans or
similar plans, were brought to the point
of action. We all know that, and anyone who wants to face this problem cannot get away from this fact. Outrage
after outrage occurred, particularly during last autumn. The recipe for making
explosives was found in numerous places,
and explosives were used freely against
buildings and in public streets.
It did not end there, because, most
unfortunately, in the discharge of their
duty a number of policemen were shot,
and killed, and a considerable number
were wounded. That is the state of
affairs; a threat to the security of the
State, a threat to the safety of the
people, an attempt to create a situation
of anarchy which no Government could
afford to ignore without disregarding its
first duty. And yet, when this measure
is brought in, in an attempt to strengthen
the powers to cope with such conduct
in a constitutional and well recognised
way, we are told this is another weapon
in the hands of the Executive, and that
this is only a political stunt.
It is hoped that by enabling serious
crimes cognisable under the Regulations,
to be brought before a judge and jury,
the punishment will be made to fit the
crime, and that that will at least have
a deterring effect. But I am bound to
say that the best deterrent of all would
be if the community as a whole joined
with the police in their determination
not to tolerate. this sort of conduct any
longer. I have heard the hon. and
learned Member for Central speak on
many occasions in this House on the
subject of the. preservation of the peace
and of the powers taken by the Minister
of Home Affairs, and I have still to hear
him denounce on any occasion or in any
way whatsoever the villainy and violence
to which these Measures are directed.
I have never yet heard the hon. Member
for Pottinger get the length of denouncing the policy or methods of the Irish
Republican Army. I, personally, shall
listen to both these hon. Members more
carefully in this matter when they preface their remarks with a clear and
vigorous denunciation of this kind of
conduct.
The hon. Member for Pottinger says he
does not believe in physical violence. I
will take him at his word, and I am sure
the hon. and learned Member for Central
shares that belief. I do not suggest for
one moment that either of these hon.
Members would stoop to active support of
a campaign of violence. But I would
ask them to have the courage to prevent
a reign of violence by denouncing it.
That is not too much to ask of any hon.
Member in this House, and when we get
that denunciation, and when we get it
repeated amongst those whom the critics
of this Bill represent, we will be very
much nearer making this campaign of
violence impossible.
There is one other matter I should like
to mention on this aspect of the subject.
The hon. Member for Pottinger referred
to a police officer by name in a manner
that was intended to be derogatory of that
officer. The officer referred to was
District-Inspector Moffatt. I think it
was a cowardly attack on a gentleman who
is deserving of the best thanks of the
community. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear:)
I have some knowledge of the situation he
had to meet. I have not the time now to
give a detailed history of the efforts made
by the police to counter this campaign
which commenced a year ago. But I
know this; it is no exaggeration to say
that the efforts of the police in general
and of District-Inspector Moffatt in particular prevented a serious rising taking
place. I do not suggest it would have
been successful, but undoubtedly if it had
started, much life and property would
have been destroyed. The dumps of arms
that were found were very large. Every
arrangement had been made for their
disperal against the day when this outbreak was to take place in various parts
of the country, and it was only due to the
vigilance, and, I may say, the courage of
the police, that this nefarious design was
frustrated.
Now we are told that the Government
that is taking this very mild measure-
I think "mild" is the proper epithet for
this Bill to strengthen the arm of the
law is infringing the liberty of the
subject. The hon. Member for Pottinger
has informed us in no uncertain terms
that he proposes at Westminster to give
his opinion, as expressed here, on the
Government's action. All I can hope is
that those who listen to him will have
some knowledge of the conditions which
this part of the Empire has had to
Civil Authorities Bill
Adjournment
11 MARCH 1943
tolerate and bear during the past number
of years.
It is very easy, living in a land which
has not been disturbed by lawlessness for
many years, to say that every man ought
to be tried-and by a judge and jury in
serious cases. Every lawyer will agree
that that ought to be so as far as possible. But the first necessity is the preservation of the State, and nearly every
country in the world that I know of has
at some time or other been driven to
giving the Executive a power of internment. I only mention that subject because it was mentioned at some length by
the hon. Member for Pottinger though
the Bill has nothing to do with internment. I appreciate that those living in
Great Britain are very reluctant to take
take that step. So is this Government. But
the Imperial Government had to take it
when war broke out, and even before war
broke out, after a series of I.R.A. outrages, it had to pass special legislation in
1939 to deal with the situation. It was
able on that occasion to avoid the internment of persons against whom no charge
could be proved, although their complicity was certain, by providing that
they should be expelled from Great
Britain. We, unfortunately, are not in
the same happy position regarding that
simple remedy, but so far as this Bill is
concerned it is aimed, first and last, at
making provision so that in serious cases,
the punishment may be made fit the
crime, and, in trivial cases, that the
maximum punishment may be reduced
so that the trial can take place before
a single resident magistrate.
The hon. and learned Member for
Central, in one of his purple patches,
told the House that to justify this Bill
the Government would conjure up
horrors that existed only in the imagination of the few. No person looking objectively at the plain facts of last year could
say that that piece of oratory is anything other than an effort of the hon.
and learned Member's imagination. It
is divorced as far as possible from
actualities. I am sorry the hon. and
learned Member is not in the House, but
again I ask him, when will he speak
against this sort of thing, and when will
he denounce the murders and outrages
perpetrated by the I.R.A. They are
flourishing not on active support but on
passive support, and the sooner hon.
Members realise that and stand out
against it the better for them and the
better for the community.
I commend this Bill to the House as a
measure designed entirely for the purposes
I have stated. It is a measure which
we hope will do something to maintain
law and order, and it is a measure which
everyone who wants to assist in the preservation of law and order at the present
time should be glad to support.
Hon. Members: Hear, hear.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Home Affairs.
PETROL FOR DOG RACES.
1. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that dog-racing is taking place every
Sunday in Lurgan, and that scores of cars
are being used to convey men and dogs
to these races; and, if so, whether steps
will be taken immediately to stop this unnecessary waste of petrol and rubber.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): On behalf of
my right hon. Friend, I would inform the
hon. Member that it is a fact that dogracing does take place in Lurgan on
Sundays, and that in certain cases taxicabs are used to convey persons and dogs
to the races. While I am in entire sympathy with the hon. Member regarding
any waste of petrol and rubber at the
present time, and while I do deprecate
most strongly unnecessary journeys by
car, the matter is by no means simple.
An Order has been made for Great
Britain which restricts the hiring of
vehicles of the taxi-cab type to journeys
of not more than ten miles, except in
certain specified cases which must be
covered by signed records and declarations. A similar Order has been
approved for Northern Ireland and
should be issued shortly. So far as the
Lurgan race meeting is concerned, this
Order will clearly put a stop to any taxicabs from Belfast and other places more
than ten miles from Lurgan proceeding
there. It will not, however, prevent
taxis from taking fares to race meetings
or to any other sporting events within the
ten-mile radius referred to, and I do not
see how such a restriction could be made
effective. It is an obligation upon the
holder of a hackney cab licence to take
members of the public where they wish to
go, and it would be quite impracticable
to require drivers to demand of their
fares signed declarations as to the purpose
of every short journey. As the hon.
Member will appreciate, there would be
nothing to prevent a person who intended
to go to a greyhound meeting asking the
taxi-driver to put him down at a private
house a few yards from the entrance to
the race track.
ex-
I should also point out that in Great
Britain the Minister of Fuel and Power
provides petrol for the use of the electric
hare and has gone so far as to include
greyhound racing, together with ice rinks,
etc., as a favourite class of entertainment
by which large numbers of people are
entertained at comparatively small
penditure of motor spirit. In a recent
question asked on this same subject in the
Imperial House of Commons the Minister
of Fuel and Power made it very clear that
the enforcement of such an Order as
would put a stop to the use of taxi-cabs
for the purpose mentioned in the question
would be completely unworkable.
I share the hon. Member's hope that
the public of Northern Ireland will be
sufficiently public-spirited in future to
use petrol driven vehicles as far as
possible only for essential journeys, and
that for those who still persist in using
taxi-cabs unnecessarily I hope that the
Order which I have mentioned will
provide the necessary deterrent.

used?

hon. Friend I would refer the hon.

centres established. In doing so, my
Ministry is fortunate in having the
assistance of the Northern Ireland Branch
of the Nursery School Association.
The extent to which these facilities
will be developed will depend on the
experience gained in the running of the
first centres set up. I am satisfied, however, that in certain areas there is a
definite need for centres of this kind to
enable women to take up work in war
factories and to reduce absenteeism
amongst those already so engaged.
Fees for the Registration of Births,
Deaths and Marriages.
6. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether it is a fact that the fees
payable for the registration of births,
deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages,
viz.-one shilling for each birth and each
death, and sixpence for each Roman
Catholic marriage, have not been altered
since the initiation of the service nearly
one hundred years ago; whether he considers' these fees equitable, having regard
to the facts that money has depreciated
much in value in that period, and that
each registrar has to provide a deputy and
assistant registrar, also an office at which
he must attend on two days in each week;
whether in some cases his total remuneration is less than ten pounds per annum;
whether the Registrar-General several
years ago received a deputation on this
subject and promised that he would recommend the payment of a fee of half-acrown for registering the first twenty
births and the first twenty deaths and
each Roman Catholic marriage in each
three monthly period; whether anything
has since been heard of the matter; and
whether he will now give the subject his
consideration.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): As stated in the question, the
fees for registration of births, deaths and
marriages have not been altered since
they were first fixed, but as registration
work is usually done in dispensaries on
days when these are open for other purposes, it is not a fact that the registrar
is put to the expense of providing an
office. It is not possible to state what are
the total annual receipts of any registrar,
as these include, besides the fees mentioned by the hon. Member, sums paid
by the public for certified copies of
entries; that is, the documents popularly
Oral Answers
Beveridge Report
16 MARCH 1943
known as birth, death, or marriage
certificates. Further, during the war
period, fees are paid to registrars for the
issue of birth forms to enable ration books
to be issued on the birth of children, and
payments are also made for the collection
of the identity cards and ration books of
deceased persons. These fees are on the
same scale as in Great Britain and are
paid out of the Imperial Exchequer.
It is true that the late Registrar-
General has, in conversation with a
number of registrars, favoured an increased scale, and I am myself in sympathy with the hon. Member's proposal
that the present registration fees be reviewed. It must be remembered, however, that they are statutory payments
made by boards of guardians to dispensary medical officers, and the proposal,
therefore, is one which involves local
finance and forms part of the wider question of the duties and conditions of
appointment of officers connected with
the dispensary system.
I would suggest that this is a matter
which might appropriately be brought to
the notice of the Select Committee on
Health Services.

whether she is aware that many retired
public elementary school teachers are in

in poverty; whether it is a fact that these

grant, amounting in some cases to £650,

to be given either a lump sum grant
or a war bonus, or both.
""
""
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked to
reply to this question, as teachers' pensions are a matter for the Ministry of
Finance and not the Ministry of
Education.
There are 34 pensioners under the
public elementary teachers' superannuation schemes receiving ordinary pensions.
up to £40 per annum. This figure does
not include small pensions due to short
service occasioned by disability.
In reply to the second part of the
question, lump sum payments are made.
in respect of service from the 1st July,
1936, and the pensioners to whom I have
referred had, with the exception of three,
retired before that date, and did not
qualify for such payments. The largest
payment of a lump sum already made to
any one teacher is about £230 and not
£650 as stated in the question.
I cannot agree with the suggestion in
the concluding part of the question that
the payment of a lump sum to pensioners can be regarded as a practical
alternative to the award of a war bonus.
The payment of a war bonus to the pensioned teachers in question or to pensioned teachers in general must be
related to any general award affecting
all classes of pensioners, for example,
Police, Military, Naval, and Civil Service personnel both here and in Great
Britain, and if and when any such
scheme is introduced in Great Britain,
the Government will be prepared to
bring in a similar scheme in Northern
Ireland.

The PRIME MINISTER (Mr.

Ireland, but to the citizens of the whole
Kingdom. May I be excused if I make
a short, personal reference? In succession
I have been Minister of Labour and
Minister of Finance, and, during the last
two and a quarter years, I have been in
the key position of Prime Minister. From
all these different points of view I have
had special opportunities of studying the
problem, and, therefore, it may be
thought that I speak with some knowledge
of the subject. In addition, I had the
advantage of serving an apprenticeship of
more than five years to my family's business as a working man beside working
men, and I had the privilege of hearing
their views upon social problems and of
learning of the difficulties, and anxieties,
and sufferings which they frequently
endured, and I shall always remember
with feelings of gratitude the kindnessmany of them are now gone-they showed
to me.
I have also been associated with

most true, and most public-spirited

It is not unnatural, therefore, that I
