Mr. BROWN: This Beveridge Report,
accepted by Mr. Winston Churchill, is
one that no Member of this House dares
to get up and say he opposes it in its
entirety. I want to say in starting off
in regard to the two Gentlemen who proposed and seconded the Motion, and the
two Gentlemen who proposed
and
seconded the Amendment to the Motion,
that I do not propose for one moment to
question the sincerity of these four
Gentlemen or their keen desire to further
the welfare of the people as a whole, because by their actions in this House they
have shown that they have taken a most
practical part in every movement and
measure for the amelioration of the lot
of the people in general. But when we
come to consider this matter, I would like
to remind the House that some considerable time ago the hon. and reverend
Gentleman for the University moved a
motion in this House advocating one of
the things set out in this Report, namely,
family allowances, and I had the great
honour of seconding that motion. But
the Minister of Finance then in very
polite terms said that we were a pair of
visionaries. He did not use those words.
Nothing could be done about it.
I am very glad, as one like the hon.
Member for the University, who always
advocated family allowances, that this
Report includes a provision for family
allowances. I am also glad it makes provision for another matter, namely, that
hospitals should be entirely a matter for
the State, and that the degrading practice
of collections in the street for the maintenance of these most important institutions should be done away with. I have
denounced that time after time in this
House. It may be said that
voluntary hospital scheme worked very
well. That is untrue. For twenty years
and long before it, there never has been
a time when in these hospitals there was
sufficient accommodation for the patients
desiring admission. We know patients
had to wait for months for a bed. That
has been going on for years. Something
has got to be done to end that intolerable
condition of affairs.

I wish to deal with one or two points
regarding the Motion that has been put
before the House. Let me say to the
proposer and seconder that I am wholeheartedly behind any effort to wipe out
poverty and despair and to create a new
condition of things for the men and women
of the future. Having said that, I must
take two or three exceptions to the Report
of Sir William Beveridge, and explain to
the House the reasons why I cannot accept
the Motion that was so ably proposed
by the hon. Member for Woodvale and
seconded by the hon. Member for
Willowfield. The Motion reads:
That in the opinion of this House the
Government of Northern Ireland should
accept the Beveridge Report in its
entirety, and take steps to bring it into
operation at an early date.
I am prepared to accept the Report,
but not in its entirety. It is too early
to ask this House, before the whole Report
is examined, to accept the Report in its
entirety. I will give my reasons for that
statement. I have three reasons why I
cannot accept the Report in its entirety,
while I support the Report in every other
respect. First of all, who in this House
has spoken oftener than the hon. Member
for Woodvale in the interests of the
widows? Who has taken cases of widows
to me oftener than the hon. Member?
No person in this House. I do not object
to that. I appreciate the attitude that
the hon. Gentleman has taken up in that
respect, for I have had experience of the
terrible privations and sorrows that a
widowed mother has to undergo. That is
the reason why I can stand at this Box and
say I object to the passing of this Motion
-because the Report proposes to abolish
widows' pensions, and I for one would not
stand in this House, or in any other house,
to see the pension for the widowed mother
done away with.

I may be told, however, that there are
other conditions laid down for the widowed
mother. She is entitled to certain degrees
of benefit. The moment she becomes a
widow she is entitled to 36s a week for 13
weeks, and, if she has any children, she
is entitled to draw guardian's benefit of
24s a week until her youngest child attains
the age of 15, or if the child remains
whole-time at school, until it attains the
age of 16. Immediately the youngest child
becomes 16 she is offered training benefit
at 24s a week, while she is being trained
to undertake a new occupation. After a
woman has discharged her duty and has
struggled to rear her infant children in
decency and respectability, she is probably
50 years of age when her youngest child
becomes 16. I ask any Member of the
Opposition is it right that that woman
should be asked to undertake work of any
kind? No. She should be a charge upon
the State. The State should be proud to
discharge its duty to that widowed
mother who has discharged her duty to
her children and to the State. That is
my first reason.
There is a second reason why I cannot
support this Motion in its demand that

Group number one consists of people who
are paying for pensions at the present

65 they are entitled to a pension of 10s a
week. If they have no other means of
subsistence they can make application for
a supplementary amount. Some of them
receive up to £2 a week in addition to
the 10s.

These are all great steps forward, and,

feel that in the United Kingdom we do

than any other country in the world. We
in the North of Ireland are particularly

are enacted in Great Britain, and is
assured that, by adhering to its policy of
maintaining the social services in this part
of the United Kingdom on the same
standard as similar services in Great
Britain, the Government is promoting the
best interest of the people of Northern
Ireland."

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Civil Service.
COST-OF-LIVING BONUS.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number
of Civil Servants in receipt of cost-ofliving bonus, and the rules governing the
payment of such bonus in so far as those
rules relate to salary and service; and
whether these rules and all payments
made thereunder are in complete
mony with similar regulations and payments in Great Britain.
har-
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
In view of the amount of detail which
must be given in reply to a question of
this kind I propose with the hon. Member's permission to deal with it by way
of a written reply.
The following is the reply:
There are
eleven civil servants in
receipt of cost-of-living bonus. These
officers are all heads of Departments or
of analogous grades, and the bonus is
payable on the basis of the scheme which
applied to Civil Service salaries generally,
both here and in Great Britain, during
the years prior to the general stabilisation of Civil Service salaries. As its
name implies, the bonus varies with
fluctuations in the official cost-of-living
index figure.
The cost-of-living bonus, on the basis
of a standard cost-of-living figure of 130 is
calculated as follows:-
130% on the first £91 5s Od.
60% on the next £108 15s. Od.
45% on the excess over £200.
The bonus so calculated is subject to
the following reductions in the case of
salaries over £500:—
On salaries from £500 to £700—10%
On salaries from £700 to £800-15%
On salaries from £800 to £900-20%
On salaries from £900 to £1,000-25%
On salaries from £1,000 to £1,100-30%
and so on by increases of 5% on each
additional £100. No bonus is to raise
total remuneration above £2,000 p.a.
Bonus is subject to revision every six
months and is increased or decreased
by 1/26th (i.e., 5/130) for every
full five points by which the average of
the official cost-of-living index figure
for the preceding six months rises
above or falls below 130.
.
In the course of the discussion on the
Supplementary Estimate for the Cabinet
Offices Vote on the 2nd instant, I have
already explained the reasons for continuing to apply the cost-of-living bonus
scheme to the salaries of heads of Departments and analogous grades. Briefly
these were that in 1937, after revised
stabilised salaries had been settled for the
Service generally, it was decided in the
light of views which had been expressed
in the House that in the case of these
senior officials a reversion should be made
to the levels of the salaries which had
been in existence prior to the general
stabilisation. It followed that in these
cases the salaries should, in the event of
any future substantial rise in the cost of
living, be subject to the payment of a costof-living bonus, failing a revision of the
salary scales themselves.

MEMBERS ON PENSION RECALLED
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number
of civil servants in receipt of pensions
who have been recalled for service in
Northern Ireland; also the number of exservice temporary male civil servants who
have been retired from the Civil Service
without pensions on attaining the age limit
of 65 years, and who have not been reemployed by the Government.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The number of civil servants in receipt
of pensions who have been recalled for
service is 11.
The period in respect of which the hon.
Member requires the information asked
for in the second part of his question is
not stated; but on the assumption that
he has the war period in mind I have
ascertained that from September, 1939, to
date, two ex-service temporary male civil
servants have been retired from the Civil
Service on reaching the age of 65 years
and have not been re-employed by the
Government.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that there
were temporary civil servants discharged
on attaining the age limit before the war,
and how is it that retired civil servants
without pensions are not recalled or given
a chance to live while retired civil
servants with big pensions are recalled?
Major SINCLAIR: The object in recalling retired civil servants is to give
the Government the advantage of the experience gained by senior officers in the
Service.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a well-known
fact that the object is to facilitate
favourites in getting more money?
Major SINCLAIR: No, sir.

The law on the subject is the same in

that force. The reason is that the R.I.C.

clause does not

the discretion of any of His Majesty's

many years as to what the minimum

It has long been recognised by the
legislature that where penal servitude is
imposed it should not be imposed-in the

having regard to the nature of penal

the general laws as to punishment, and in

of the Penal Servitude Act of 1891, subsection (1) of Section 1 of which reads as

when this Section comes into operation

any period not less than three years,

""
Hon Members will notice that in this

in any enactment passed prior to the
Penal Servitude Act of 1891, which

limited in the downward direction to a

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
but there was no discretion to give a

That was the position when
this Act was passed in 1891. It so
happens that the opening words of subsection (1), which refer to
any enactment in force when this Section comes
into operation," do not cover the case of
Acts passed after 1891. But though,
where penal servitude is authorised by an

be exercised so as to impose a sentence of
three years or more, the invariable
practice, both here and in Great Britain,
is that no sentence of penal servitude is
given for less than three years whether
the Act under which it is imposed was

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Attorney-General]
the practice I have referred to would
bring about the same result irrespective
of the words now objected to. But it has
to be remembered that the legislature has
recognised that having regard to the
nature of penal servitude there should be
a minimum period, and it is well to state
this expressly.
The hon. Member spoke as if penal
servitude or a fine was the only punishment that could be inflicted. In that
connection I would refer him to subsection (2) of Section 1 of the Penal
Servitude Act of 1891 which says:
a
Where under any Act now in force or
under any future Act a court is
empowered or required to award
sentence of penal servitude, the court
may in its discretion, unless such future
Act otherwise provides, award imprisonment for any term not exceeding two
years, with or without hard labour.
So under Clause 2, in the case of any
charge dealt with on indictment, His
Majesty's judges have exactly the same
powers of punishment and the same discretion in regard to punishment as they
have with regard to any other crime in
respect of which the maximum punishment
is 14 years' penal servitude.
There is no attempt in this Measure to
take away anything from the ordinary
discretion of His Majesty's judges, and
the terms of the Act of 1891, which I
have read, explain the extent of the discretion and also explain that the words
"not less than three years, far from
pointing to any peculiar practice or
restriction, simply recognise what has
been the law and the practice in this
matter for a very long time.
""
The hon. Member also referred to the
proviso to this Clause that gives the
Minister power to lessen the maximum
punishment by Regulation in certain
cases. That is a matter to be judged of
in the light of experience, and, therefore, best dealt with by Regulation. It is
only from experience that one may say
whether such and such a Regulation is of
such a kind that one may classify it as
dealing with minor rather than major
offences.
Paragraph (a) is simply a re-enactment
of part of the Act as it is at present. It
does not vary the maximum punishment
on summary conviction, but the proviso
empowers the Minister, by reducing the
maximum punishment in some cases, to
enable such cases to be disposed of by one
resident magistrate instead of by two.

Supposing it does, will the Attorney-

into their minds, and I think that even

let it be the law, and strike out those few
words. Do not have someone trying to

General will not be armed with his books
to support his contention.

HEIFERS AND CALVES
SLAUGHTERED.

Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the number of (a) heifer calves;
(b) heifers, and (c) bull calves
slaughtered at Government abattoirs in
Northern Ireland from 1st January, 1943,
to the present date.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I regret that war-time
restrictions on the publication of production statistics prevent me from giving
the detailed figures requested by the hon.
and gallant Member.
1943 GRASS-SEED CROP.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the policy of the Government with
regard to the grass-seed crop for 1943 in
view of the difficulties which arose last
season.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am not in a
position to make an announcement at the
moment, but if the hon. and gallant
Member would repeat his question in, say,
a fortnight's time I hope to be in a
position to make a full statement. It is
clear that steps will have to be taken to
limit the crop saved as grass-seed in 1943.
Mr. BROWN: Can the noble Lord say
whether it is the intention of the Government to take over all supplies of grassseed still remaining on the farms?
Lord GLENTORAN: Yes, sir; it is.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
say how the hon. Member can put his
question in a fortnight's time when the
House will not be sitting then?
PRICE OF FLAX.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if his
Ministry has received any resolution or
representations regarding the price of flax
from the Ulster Farmer's Union, and, if
so, whether he can give the House the
particulars of same and state what
action, if any, he has taken in the matter.
Lord GLENTORAN: The answer to
the first part of the question is in the
affirmative, and to the second part in the
negative.
FARM TRACTORS ON ROADS.
18. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Finance whether he is aware
of the concessions recently announced regarding the use on the roads in Great
Britain of agricultural tractors for which
only a 5s licence is held, and whether he
is prepared to make similar concessions to
tractor owners in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): In reply to the hon. Member
I am glad to be able to announce that
with the sanction of the House it is proposed to remove the present limitations
governing the 5s rate of motor tax in its
application to vehicles of the tractor class.
In future tractors registered in the name
of a farmer will, at this low rate of duty,
be able to carry his own agricultural produce or articles required for agricultural
land without limit in point of distance.
This concession will also operate to enable
tractors registered in the name of a person
using such a vehicle primarily for agricultural purposes to carry agricultural
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
25 MARCH 1943
produce or articles required for agricultural land on behalf of a neighbouring
farmer, but this concession will not of
itself relieve the individual from compliance with the provisions of Section 15
of the Road and Rail Transport Act
(Northern Ireland), 1935.
I propose, pending the introduction of
a Finance Bill, to authorise the operation
of this tax concession as from 1st April,
and I should make it clear that the concession is purely a wartime measure
designed to stimulate the vital necessities
of tillage and food production.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister tell the
House and the country whether he will
put farmers using agricultural implements
on the roads in Northern Ireland in the
same position as farmers in Great Britain?
Education.
SECONDARY TEACHERS'
INCREMENTS.
4. Mr. DOWLING asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether it is a fact that lower
paid teachers in secondary schools have
been granted three increments and higher
paid teachers two increments, while parttime teachers in a great many cases have
received no increase whatever; and
whether she can state, under these circumstances, what steps her Ministry
proposes to take to put an end to what
appears to be a gross injustice to these
part-time teachers.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): Full-time
teachers in secondary schools have been
granted increases in remuneration, by way
of war bonus, the amounts of which are
payable by my Ministry. The first award
of war bonus was made with effect as from
1st April, 1940, and two subsequent
awards were made, one with effect as from
1st April, 1941, and the other with effect.
as from 1st July, 1942.
In granting these bonuses the Ministry
has pursued the policy adopted for
England and Wales, where war allowances
have been given only to full-time teachers.
No increases in remuneration have accordingly been granted by the Ministry to
part-time teachers in Northern Ireland.
If the English awards were extended to
'part-time teachers the Ministry would
consider a similar extension in Northern
Ireland.
I should add that the governors of the
schools may, if they wish, augment the
remuneration of any part-time teachers
employed by them out of school funds.
Entertainments Duty.
LURGAN DOG RACE MEETING.
5. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
if entertainment tax is charged on
admission money to dog race meetings at
Lurgan on Sundays, how this tax is
collected, and what assurance he has that
his Department is receiving the correct
amount.
Mr. BARBOUR: In reply to the hon.
Member, entertainments duty is payable
on charges for admission to dog race meetings held at Lurgan and is collected by
means of Government stamped tickets.
In reply to the latter part of the question, these meetings, as in the case of all
other entertainments, are subject to inspection by the entertainments duty
inspectors of the Ministry.

Eire Workers in Northern Ireland.
RESIDENCE PERMITS.
8. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of men and women from
Eire who have applied for permits to
reside over six weeks in Northern Ireland,
and the number of permits that have been
issued.
Mr. LOWRY: On behalf of my right
hon. Friend I have to state that the
Residence in Northern Ireland (Restriction) Order, 1942, made by the Secretary
of State under the Defence Regulations,
applies to all persons, with specified
exemptions, who were not resident in
Northern Ireland immediately before the
1st January, 1940.
The total number of applications for
permits under the Order up to yesterday's
date was 22,579. The numbers of men
and women from Eire included in this
total are 10,332 and 4,739 respectively.
The number of permits which have
been issued is 4,875.

men, and how many women, coming from
Eire, have been placed in employment

the outbreak of war, and how many
persons are now unemployed in Northern

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): Since the beginning of the war
2,330 persons have been brought from
Eire by my Department to do work of
urgent national importance. All these
were skilled men, many of whom (notably
bricklayers) have returned to their own
homes on completion of the work for

place Eire nationals in employment here
if there are any suitable Northern Ireland
workers available; but the hon. and
learned Member no doubt realises that
many Eire nationals came here and
obtained work of their own accord. When
such work is obtained my Department is
legally bound to issue an unemployment
book.
As the hon. and learned Member has
probably seen, it has been decided that
the figures of unemployment in Great
Britain and Northern Ireland are to
be published at quarterly intervals only.
The latest date for which figures are

In war time, however, it is inherent in

Treasury, as explained to the House in

The PRIME MINISTER: This is the
customary protest made by some of the
Members opposite when the sittings of
Parliament are adjourned for a few
weeks. I have explained that on former
occasions, and I feel it necessary that I
should repeat it to-day. We have had a
busy Session up to the present. We have
dealt with all the Supplementary
Estimates, we have passed several important measures, and the business at the
moment is exhausted. The Estimates for
the coming year are necessarily not ready
yet, and certain Bills which we propose
to introduce in a few months are being
considered at the present time. The truth
is there is no business available to bring
before the House.
The speech of the hon. Member (Mr.
Nixon) and he travelled over a very wide
field-in my opinion was very misleading.
In the first place he indicated, I think I
might put it stronger and say he definitely
stated, that Ministers' work ended when
Parliament was not sitting. He must
know that that is not so, that the work
of the Minister goes on; in fact, so far
as usefulness is concerned, it goes on at
a much greater speed. After all, in this
House we debate matters, but it is the
duty of Ministers, whether the House is
sitting or not, to apply their attention to
seeing what can be done to help the situation as it may be at that particular time.
The hon. Member spoke as if, should
the House continue to sit, we could deal
with housing schemes on a very large scale.
Members on this side of the House are just
as anxious as Members on the other side
that our people should be properly housed,
but the hon. Member knows quite well
that that is not possible to any appreciable
degree either here or in Great Britain
owing to the fact that it is the duty of us
all to put our war effort first, and to preserve such material and labour as are
available for war purposes.
The Government, however, are giving
continual attention to the post-war policy
which I outlined at this Table in July last,

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Acts of Parliament (Citation and
Effect) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I need not comment in
detail on this Bill, as the memorandum
on the front of the Bill indicates clearly
its general purpose and the reasons for its
promotion.
Clause 1 is designed to implement a
recommendation of the Statute Law
Committee for Northern Ireland to the
Acts of Parliament Bill
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
effect that the citation of statutes should
be by reference to the calendar year and
not to the regnal year in which they are
passed. The present system is cumbrous,
confusing and inconvenient.
The proposed change will facilitate reference and
make the task of finding a particular
statute easier for laymen as well as for
lawyers. In practice its advantages will
not be retrospective, but they will be felt
increasingly as times go on. The sooner,
therefore, the change is made, the better,
and I consider that its introduction during
the present emergency is proper and
justifiable. I commend the measure on
the broad ground that it is in the public
interest to simplify legislation and legislative reference as far as practical.
Clause 2 is designed to make it clear
that the principles applied to Acts of the
Parliament at Westminster by two
Imperial Acts apply also to Acts of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland. These
Acts are: The Acts of Parliament (Commencement) Act, 1793 (33 Geo. III, c. 13,
and the Acts of Parliament (Expiration)
Act, 1808 (48 Geo. III, c. 106), and their
description, as I have read it, is in itself
an excellent reason for the adoption of the
first Clause in the Bill.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

really is.

Mr. CAMPBELL: The series of questions at question time and the answers
thereto by the Minister really make one
think. Questions were put to him with
regard to Eire workers in Northern
Ireland and I listened and learned from
the answers of the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour that in this area,
which is part of Ireland, only 2,300 odd
Eire workers, male and female, have been
placed in employment, and only 295
people from Eire are in receipt of subsistence allowance of a very small amount in
addition to their wages. These figures
speak for themselves because the impression has been sedulously cast abroad, and
underlies these questions, that there has
been a high degree of infiltration of labour
from the other part of Ireland. The
figures are a proof that that statement
has no foundation,
As against these figures we find from
this area of Northern Ireland since the
start of the war something like 43,000
men and women have been placed in
employment in Great Britain. I wish
the Minister were less accommodating in
his answers to these queries because his
job, as far as his answers convey any idea
of it in this matter is like that of the
witch doctor among certain tribes in
Africa who picks out, selects or, as they
call it, smells out, haphazard defenceless
victims for the appeasement of a capricious chief. In this string of questions
and in the answers of the Minister there
was one chorus running and that was,
"Ferret out the Irish." I venture to
think that decent, sensible men in Northern Ireland, irrespective of politics, are
heartily sick of the Ministerial truckling

to this suggestion of a high degree of
infiltration into our territory. I should
have thought the Minister would have
deprecated at a time like this the putting
of questions raising these issues, sharp

deprecation was uttered. In fact the
Government, speaking through
Minister of Labour, lent a sympathetic
and even an encouraging ear to these calls

the
Shoals of men from Northern Ireland
in recent years have gone down South.
They are prospering and we are glad to
hear they are prospering there. There
is no corresponding outcry against these
people from our territory who have gone
down South to better their position. It
is a one-way cry, a cry peculiar to our
area. I stigmatise it as an unworthy
cry, a vindictive cry. These workers from
Eire are not so many. They are not here
because you wish them to be here. You
do not wish them to be here. They are

work which cannot be done without them.
They take nothing from you which is
yours. They earn their wages. They
give good value by their toil and skill.
They comport themselves well. They are
law-abiding people. They are a credit, I
say, by their good humour, good temper
and general conduct, a credit of which
any community might well be proud. Yet
some would deny them all benefit in our
social services and treat them as outlanders and aliens on Irish soil, soil which
is Irish, and will always remain Irish.
There are, I understand and believe,
400,000 people from Eire, workers, and
soldiers, in the service of the Crown.
Mr. GRANT: 400,000?
Mr. CAMPBELL: Yes, 400,000 is the
figure given from what I believe to be a
competent authority. They would welcome another 100,000. They are an asset
and the English know they are an asset,
and they are proud to have them. They
do not hamstring and handicap them by
restrictions such as are urged on the
Ministry in this House. Their outlook is
very different. They are out to win the
war and to use every honourable means to
do so. They are not out to wet-blanket

understand the equivalent figure from
Northern Ireland is 70,000. Why is this
discrimination practised? For one reason
and one reason only, because these are
Irishmen and Irish women. There is no
such discrimination against Irish workers
in Britain. It would not be tolerated for
one moment. It would not be countenanced by any responsible authority.
But anti-Irish prejudices and anti-
Irish pinpricks are congenial to small
minds, and small minds may sail small
craft in a summer sea, but they are helpless in a typhoon such as is raging over
the world to-day. It suits and will suit
small manœuvres. As I have said men
of the South have flocked in their thousands into the service of the Crown across
the Channel. They are welcomed there,
and I would say this: There has not been
one battle in this war fought on land,
fought in the air, or fought at sea, in
which Irish blood has not been shed and
mingled in one common stream with
English and Scots blood. You do not
object to soldiers from the South of Ireland, though you would hamstring their
brother workers coming from the same
locality and the same families into your
area.
If the Minister would ask men who
fought in the Battle of Britain, men who
fought at El Alamein, and men fighting
to-day at the Mareth Line-if you asked
these fighting men what they thought of
the discrimination against Irishmen-because they are Irish-they would tell you
they would have it otherwise. The outpouring of blood in battle cements men
with a bond of reason between them. But
these tactics that I complain of will not
help the war effort. They will not help
it in the long run. By administrative
discrimination of an unfair kind against
a very large section of the population of
Ireland, I submit, the Government are
doing a grievous disservice to the Allies'
cause. There is no use in appealing to
the Government as lovers of fair play,
which they are not, but I ask them to
believe this and to rest assured that this
differentiation will serve neither the
British nor Irish interest in the long run.
It is regrettable that no authoritative
voice has been raised among the
minority in the rest of Ireland against
this victimisation or suggested victimisa-

Any student of international affairs,

has been done against the Poles, who is

Therefore, I would counsel all people in

that, whether we like it or not, we are part

of Nations. The overwhelming majority

this war, and it is the bounden duty of

aggression that will be practised on us if

I want to point out this difficulty.
When we were establishing a National
Fire Service there was not a great deal

make me in the days to come, if I am

a bed of roses, trying to nationalise the

away from the people, it might be an

for the sake of giving a figure, we brought

if the enemy visited us again. So I had

Mr. NIXON: I am an Ulsterman belonging to one of the counties you helped.
to betray.
Mr. GRANT: Then he finds fault with
Englishmen being brought over to jobs.
He did not specify the particular jobs or
the Englishmen. I would point out to
the hon. Member that to my knowledge
I have never brought an Englishman into
the Civil Defence Service since I became
Minister of Public Security, but that is
not saying I would not do so. The hon.
Member does not object to it himself, but
still he offers criticisms if there are any
in the Service.
Mr. NIXON: On a point of correction. The point I laboured was that I
was safe in saying there is not an Ulsterman at the head of one Service in Northern Ireland except the Ministry of
Labour. I think that is "right, but if
there are more I will be glad to hear of
them. It is the heads I am talking
about.
Mr. GRANT: You mean on the Civil
Service side?
Mr. NIXON: The whole blooming
show.
Mr. GRANT: Is the commander of the
Fire Service not an Ulsterman?
Mr. NIXON: Of course, he is, but he
is not the head of the A.R.P. I had
him in mind. You know who he is; he
is a very favoured man.
Mr. GRANT: You do not like Englishmen; you do not like Ulstermen, and we
are not to bring them from Eire, so where
are are we to go for them?
Mr. NIXON: I do not like the Prime
Minister's relative to be put in over an
Ulsterman well qualified for the job.
Mr. GRANT: I am sure the hon.
Member will hardly believe me when I
say that in the appointment of commander of the Fire Service the Prime
Minister had no more to do with it than
had the hon. Member for Woodvale. If
I had not been satisfied I would not have
approved of the appointment. If I find
it necessary to make changes in any department I will make those changes and
abide by the consequences.
Mr. NIXON: There is no risk of the
consequences.
Mr. GRANT: Not for the hon.
Member, but there might be for me.
Mr. NIXON: Not at all.
Mr. GRANT: There was a suggestion
made this afternoon by a Member on the
other side of the House that from the
time the House closes to-day until 4th
May we should give up our salaries. The
man who made that suggestion has three
jobs. He gets paid for the three of them
and he did not say he would give up any
of them. If I gave up this job I would
have no alternative employment at the
moment.
Mr. NIXON: Stick to it as long as you
can.
Mr. GRANT: I am going to do that,
to be perfectly frank. (Laughter.) It
is my job, and I am going to do the best
I can in it. So long as I am allowed to
stay in it I will stay in it.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
War Damage Commission.
FOREMAN BUILDER'S WAGES.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether a complaint has been
made to the War Damage Commission by
Andrew Moorehead (23), foreman, Belfast, to the effect that a contractor working on war damaged houses paid
Moorehead 1s 1d per hour, while he
showed him on the accounts as receiving
substantially more than this amount;
whether he can state the amount actually
paid by the War Damage Commission to
the contractor and the amount paid by
the contractor to Moorehead; the date on
which Moorehead first reported the matter
to the War Damage Commission, and
what action, if any, the Commission took
in the matter.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): This matter is at present
the subject of police investigation. I am
informed that it was first brought to the
notice of the War Damage Commission
by Andrew Moorehead early in February,
1943, when he made certain statements
relating to the rate of wages paid to him
in 1941 and 1942 by a contractor for
work done in the repair of houses
damaged by enemy action. I understand
that the contractor's accounts, in so far
as they cover the work in question, have
not as yet been finally settled by the
Commission.
Belfast City Administrators.
ADVERTISEMENTS FOR
CONTRACTS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
Administrators of the Belfast Corporation advertise contracts in accordance
with the Standing Orders of the Corporation.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): On behalf of
my right hon. Friend I would inform the
hon. Member that while the Standing
Orders of the Belfast Corporation do not
bind the City Administrators, wherever
it is practicable to do so, the procedure
laid down by the Standing Orders in
regard to advertising for tenders is followed by them. It will be appreciated,
however, that in war-time it is not possible

placing a contract.

employees are now recruited through the

Mr. LOWRY: On behalf of my right

most suitable persons can be obtained.
Mr. NIXON: Was it not stated on

to appoint Administrators that one of its

Ministry of Public Security Employees.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether employees of the
Ministry are recruited through the labour
exchange.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): The Civil
Service staff employed in my Ministry are
recruited in accordance with the directions issued from time to time by the
Ministry of Finance for the Civil Service
as a whole.
If, however, the hon. Member has in
mind the personnel of the National Fire
Service, the answer is that candidates
sent forward by the employment exchanges, as well as any other candidates
presenting themselves, are interviewed by
or on behalf of the Fire Service commander and are admitted if considered
suitable in all respects and provided
vacancies exist.
Home Defence Forces.
SUNDAY TRAINING.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY (by private
notice) asked the Prime Minister whether
he has seen a Resolution passed by the
Newry Presbytery about the training of
the Home Defence Forces on the Sabbath;
whether he is aware that there is intense
dissatisfaction about this in all parts of
Northern Ireland; whether owing to this
he will advise whoever is responsible for
this training to arrange it in such a way
that the personnel can attend mid-day
church services, at least during the
summer months.
The PRIME MINISTER: (Mr.
Andrews); The answer to the first part
of the question is in the affirmative, and,
to the second, in the negative.
With regard to the remainder of the
question, while fully appreciating the
wish of my hon. Friend, I would remind
him that we are engaged in a life and
death struggle threatening our existence,
as well as our civil and religious liberties,
and I am opposed to taking any steps
which might embarrass the authorities
responsible for the training of the Ulster
Home Guard, which is our local defence
force.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Prime Minister's statement that he
appreciates that we are engaged in a life
and death struggle, I would ask why did
he and the Government take four men
out of the Army and appoint them to
jobs, one being a political job?
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: That does
not arise out of the question.
Mr. NIXON: It arises out of the
right hon. Gentleman's answer.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: It does
not.

MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
1943 Grass-seed Crop.
RESIDENT MAGISTRATES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-(Sir
Norman Stronge.)
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I gave notice
to the Minister of Agriculture that I
would ask a question which I raised the
last time Parliament sat. It is the question of the prices of grass-seed for the
current year. It will be remembered that
last season, 1942, presented considerable
difficulties to growers of grass-seed, and
the Government had to come to the assistance of the market and it cost the State
£80,000, which was passed in the Supplementary Estimate. The Ministry of
Agriculture have arranged for the harvesting of grass-seed in 1944 by restricting it
to pure seed, either Italian or perennial.
But nothing has yet been fixed for the
current year 1943. There is considerable
anxiety amongst the farmers as to what
is to become of this crop, whether the
farmer sows pure grass-seed or only mixed
grass-seed, and what the current prices
would be during this season. I ask the
Minister of Agriculture to give the necessary infórmation as to what is to be
done.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I am very grateful to
my hon, and gallant Friend for giving
notice of this question. I think it is a
very appropriate one to ask at the present
time, as there is a certain amount of
hesitation amongst those thinking of growing grass-seed. If I may I will read out
the arrangement so far.
A much larger crop of grass-seed was
produced in 1942 than is required for
sowing this season. As the hon. and
gallant Member is aware, the Government
has given a guarantee to farmers that a
market will be found for the 1942 crop,
and this will entail the purchase by the
Government of a very large quantity of
seed which will be in the hands of
machiners on the 1st July next. Clearly,
similar conditions must be avoided as
regards this year's crop, and this can only
be achieved by limiting the acreage of seed
to be harvested.
Discussions are proceeding with the
Imperial authorities as to the procedure
to be adopted. It has been somewhat
difficult to ascertain the estimated requirements of seed for the United Kingdom for
sowing in 1944, and the matter is further
complicated by the fact that it is not yet
known what quantity of surplus seed will
be purchased by the Government at the
1st July next.
It would now seem, however, that the
total quantity of seed required from the
1943 crop will not exceed about twothirds of the 1942 crop. Accordingly, an
announcement is being made this week to
the effect that not more than threequarters of the area of pure perennial
saved in 1942, may be harvested in 1943
and, similarly, not more than two-fifths
of the area of mixed seed. It is not proposed to impose any restriction on the
acreage of pure Italian to be harvested in
1943. The sale of seed from second year
crops of rye grass will not be permitted.
A further announcement will be made as
soon as discussions have been completed
with the Farmers' Union and the
machiners.

Resident Magistrates
13 APRIL 1943
city and at the same time retaining his
self-respect. The position of resident
magistrate is a position of great dignity.
It is a position of great importance. It
is a position that is sought after by the
legal profession, and when a legal gentleman, a K.C., states that he cannot hold
that position and at the same time retain
his self-respect, then I say something has
arisen that should be explained to the
people of Northern Ireland, who should
have respect and confidence in the decision
of the courts.
I am not going to speculate on what the
matter was that caused the resident
magistrate to resign and to make such a
statement on his resignation. That is not
for me.
That was a matter for the Government. Up to the present-I am
proud to stand at this Table and say itall classes so far as I know-they may not
be satisfied with the legislation: they may
not be satisfied with many things-have
extreme confidence in the higher courts,
and we want that confidence maintained
in all the courts. Some time ago by legislation the Government deprived the local
justices of all jurisdiction. You recollect.
that there was opposition to that at that
time. They brought in an Act of Parliament, and, so far as I can recollect, it
was laid down in that Act of Parliament
that every resident magistrate in future
would require to be a practising barrister
or K.C. or a solicitor of a certain standing, as the case may be.
I think it was put at six years for an
ordinary practitioner. I am not going
to guarantee that statement of six years,
but I think, roughly speaking, that is
about what it was. Well, that was
opposed. We all knew and felt that, after
all, a man who sat on the bench to
administer justice should be a man of
large legal experience. I always held that.
But then you have a man that has a legal
training, and that has served the city for
a great number of years tendering his
resignation, because he recently found it
inconsistent with his self-respect to hold
the position. What happened recently?
That is what we want to know?.

Mr. LOWRY: There is no mystery
shrouding the retirement of Mr. McCoy
whatsoever. Mr. McCoy resigned—and I
speak not merely as Parliamentary Secretary, but as a personal friend of Mr.
McCoy's of well over twenty years'
standing because the pay and emoluments of his office were not sufficient for
a man of his ability, and he preferred to
take his talents to a better market. There
is no other reason than that. There is
nothing sinister. Nobody attempted to
interfere with him. Nobody would
attempt to interfere with a resident
magistrate. Resident magistrates have
the same tenure as high court judges.
They are free and independent, and because Mr. McCoy sees a better future for
himself and returned to his own practice,
it is not a matter to be raised in this
House.
""
Mr. NIXON: Where does the word
recently" come in?
Mr. LOWRY: Whatever that may be
I say it relates solely to pay and emoluments and to nothing else. In regard to
recent appointments and the suggestion
that these gentlemen are not qualified by
Statute, of course that is nonsense. Dr.
Mills paid his licence duty for over 20
years-seven and twenty years as a
solicitor. For a great deal of that time
he served the Crown-and served it well
-in another capacity. He was a practising solicitor, and if there is any doubt of
that there is a place to challenge it by a
writ of quo warranto. The hon. Member
for Woodvale is quite an amateur
awyer at some profit to himself-
Mr. NIXON: And to you.
Mr. LOWRY: And to myself. It is
the only good thing I can say about the
hon. Member; he is a very good, judicious
and generous litigant, and is very good to
his counsel. But those days are past.
As to the other young gentleman who
has recently been appointed, he has been
a solicitor for 14 years. For the last three
years he served with His Majesty's Forces
as a member of the Atlantic convoy. He
returned to civil life, having been invalided out through the hardships he
endured in North Atlantic gales, and he
has been appointed a resident magistrate.
I am proud to think we have such a
gentleman in our service. I can say more
about him than that. He held a temporary appointment for a while under my
Ministry. I have read a letter from his
partner, which is on the files in my office,
that this young gentleman would be
welcome back into the partnership which
he has left. Again, I am proud to think
that we have such a gentleman in our
service.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESIONS.
West Belfast By-Election.
ATTEMPTED PERSONATION.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether he can now state what
steps he has taken or will take to bring
to justice the persons who aided, abetted
and procured Lillian H. Coleman, 41
Cooke Street, to commit the offence of
attempted personation in respect of which
she was convicted and sentenced to three
months' imprisonment; whether Cooke
Street, where Miss Coleman resides, is
in West Belfast constituency; whether the
offence was committed at Carlisle Circus,
which is miles from Cooke Street; whether
counsel for the defence gave the name of
the woman who procured Miss Coleman to
commit the offence; whether other people
in higher positions are involved; and
whether it is morally or legally right for
Miss Coleman, a young girl, to languish
in jail while the instigators of the crime
are at large.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): The police investigation
into this matter has not produced any
evidence on which criminal proceedings
could be instituted against any person for
aiding, abetting or procuring Miss
Coleman to commit the offence of attempted personation to which she pleaded
guilty at the last Belfast Commission.
I have little doubt that Miss Coleman's
action was instigated, or at least encouraged, by someone else, but I regret to say
that the police inquiries, which I am
satisfied were pursued with diligence and
impartiality, have failed to establish the
identity of any such person.
With regard to the second and third
parts of the question, Miss Coleman's
home in Cooke Street is in the constituency of South Belfast and the offence
was committed in the neighbourhood of
Carlisle Circus, a considerable distance
from Cooke Street.
The answer to the fourth part of the
question is, according to my information,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
4 MAY 1943
in the negative, and for the reasons
already given I am unable to answer the
next part of the question.
The circumstances affecting the last
part of the question have altered, as I
understand that Miss Coleman has
recently been released on compassionate
grounds.
I hope, however, that the period which
she has spent in jail will serve to impress
upon all sections of the community that
it is as reprehensible to steal another's
vote as it is to steal another's purse, and
that those who allow themselves to be
made the tool of others in this class of
crime cannot hope to avoid punishment
merely on the ground that the part they
played was subordinate.
Mr. NIXON: I thank the right hon.
Gentleman for the rebuke to personators
and also for the release of this young girl.
Is it a fact that counsel for the defence
stated that it was Mr. Harpur got her to
do it and that was published in the Press?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: That
suggestion was contained in the question
I remitted to the police for close inquiry,
but I cannot find anything to substantiate it.
Mr. NIXON: Then the report was
wrong.
ADVERTISEMENTS FOR VEHICLES
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether one of the candidates at
the West Belfast bye-election openly
advertised for and employed for payment
through an agent 200 horse-drawn vehicles
to bring voters to the polls; whether this
is corruption, and what steps, if any, he
will take in the matter.
By
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
section 7 of the Corrupt and Illegal Practices (Prevention) Act, 1853, it is provided, inter alia, that no payment or contract for payment shall, for the purpose
of promoting or procuring the election of
a candidate at any election, be made on
account of the conveyance of electors to
or from the poll, whether for the hiring of
horses or carriages or otherwise; and,
further, that any person knowingly acting
in contravention of this provision shall be
guilty of an illegal practice.
My attention has been drawn to advertisements in the Press on behalf of two
of the candidates in the recent West
Belfast election seeking horse-drawn
vehicles for the purpose of that election.
Neither of these advertisements, however, offered payment, and I have no
evidence to show that any payment or
contract of payment such as would constitute an offence under the section I have
mentioned was, in fact, made.
Mr. NIXON: With reference to the
Attorney-General's statement that advertisements appeared in the Press on behalf
of two candidates, is it a fact that only
one candidate advertised for vehicles for
hire, while the other candidate, though
he advertised for vehicles, did not advertise for them for hire. It is only the
hiring or attempted hiring that constitutes the offence of corruption and, consequently, it is only one candidate who
acted corruptly.
Post-War Planning.
DRAINAGE, SEWERAGE AND
HOUSING SCHEMES.
4. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Prime
Minister whether any plans have yet been
discussed with the Belfast Corporation
regarding improvement in post-war drainage, sewerage, town-planning, and new
housing schemes; whether the necessary
financial arrangements have been discussed regarding the carrying out of such
schemes.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The matters referred to by the hon.
Member are all part of post-war physical
planning, and, as such, are being dealt
with, both generally and in particular, by
the Planning Advisory Board and its
Area and Subject Committees on which
the Belfast Corporation are represented.
The question of financial arrangements
to be made in connection with these
matters obviously cannot be usefully considered until the various proposals in connection with them have been formulated,
but the hon. Member may rest assured
that discussions will take place with the
Corporation in due course.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman why when a question is
addressed to the Prime Minister a Parlia-
Oral Answers
Sittings of the House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
mentary Secretary representing Home
Affairs should reply to it?
Mr. NIXON: Perhaps he is Prime
Minister.
THE PLANNING ADVISORY BOARD
5. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he is now in a position
to lay before the House a full report of
the findings to date of the North of
Ireland Planning Advisory Board, and
whether an early opportunity will be given
to the House to discuss such reports.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
Except in the case of any matters which
may be considered so urgent as to require
immediate action, the Planning Advisory
Board like any other body or committee
of the kind does not formulate its findings
piecemeal, and as it has a great deal of
ground to cover it is not to be expected
that anything in the nature of a general
report will be forthcoming from it immediately.
The only matter which it has dealt with
separately and as a matter of urgency up
to date is the question of the control of
interim development, in regard to which
it has forwarded a resolution asking for
immediate action on the part of the
Government. The presentation of a Bill
at an early date is under consideration.
When the report of the Board is received an opportunity will, of course, be
given to the House to discuss it.
A BELFAST BY-PASS ROAD.
6. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he will consider the
advisability of giving a grant out of the
Road Fund to enable the Belfast City
Council to complete the by-pass road between Castlereagh Road and North Road
and thus divert part of the traffic from
other congested routes; and whether he
would be prepared to extend these grants
to other road improvement schemes
throughout Northern Ireland in order to
absorb all those who are still unemployed.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
As the hon. Member is
aware the .
income of the Road Fund is extremely
limited, and I should not be justified in
making any grant from it at the present
time other than for the purpose of maintaining existing roads, and particularly
those roads vitally necessary to the war
effort and to the distribution of essential
supplies.
I can assure the hon. Member, however,
that the by-pass road to which he refers
is with other similar propositions being
very carefully considered in connection
with the post-war planning of Northern
Ireland.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister bear
in mind that the maintenance of those
roads in a proper state of repair, both in
Belfast and in the country, is an urgent
matter for the war effort owing to the
extensive use of them by the military, and
will he see that this work is carried out
at once.
Mr. LOWRY: That matter has been,
and is being, duly attended to.
Lieut.-Col. HALL-THOMPSON: Will
the right hon. Gentleman consider the
possibility of taking this under an unemployment relief scheme and getting a
grant through that Fund in the interests
of the city and country.

Mr. NIXON: I want to get a promise
from the Prime Minister that in the meantime he will suspend what I may call
operations against the working people
ordered for exportation. To strengthen
my hands I gave the Prime Minister a
few facts which I can prove now, for the
men are here. As a matter of fact the
Chief Whip was kind enough to interview them. A man was offered work in
Mackie's, and he got a note signed by
Mr. Allen, the manager, that he wanted
him and would start him if he could get
an introduction card from the labour exchange. He took the note down to the
labour exchange, but they refused to allow
him to work. They did not stop there.
They sent him a letter, following the refusal to allow him to work, directing him
to go down for a medical inspection, and
he was to bring a sample of his urine with
him to see if he was fit to work, after
refusing to allow him to work. He went
down, and, of course, he passed, and they
stopped his benefit. The man had work
to go to. Another man was offered work
in Mackie's and he got a similar letter,
and was refused permission to start. He
was ordered to England, and his benefit
was stopped. He was told the reason he
would not be allowed to work was that
he was not an ex-service man. I know
that was what the Minister of Labour has
been telling the Prime Minister, but he
will have something bigger to explain
now.
Another man who was an ex-service
man of the last war was ordered to work
in England, and worked there for six
months. He came back, and as he did
not like the conditions he said he wanted
to work at home. He did not feel able to
go back. This was an ex-service man of
the last war. His benefit was stopped,
and he appealed. I helped him to fill up
the appeal form, which stated he was an
ex-service man, and that he had worked
in England, but did not feel able to go
back. He was brought before a court of
referees and the chairman of that court of
referees disallowed him benefit for six
weeks. The chairman himself was not an
ex-service man. He was a young man.
His name is Little, and this young man,
who should be in the army; this young
barrister of military age, a professor of
great loyalty, sat in the chair in state,
and an ex-service man of the last war
came before him and he disallowed him
benefit.
The fighting man who did fight had to
come clamouring before the
the well-paid
barrister who should fight but would not
fight, and the fighting man was disallowed benefit. Some of these men are
here now. I am not going to condemn
the Prime Minister for this state of
affairs. The Prime Minister is to state
his policy on a Motion in this House.
All I want the Prime Minister to do is
this in the meantime to suspend this
exportation of men until we see what his
policy will be. There are some people
who want to go. By all means let them
go, but do not take men from their
families, because some of them have
delicate families and delicate wives. One
man I know is living with his mother,
who is 80 years of age. There are only
the two of them in the house. The
order to him is to go or starve. There
is enough of that going on in occupied
Europe. We do not want it here. We
are part and parcel of Great Britain.
There are not many people coming over
here from Great Britain to work against
their will. As a matter of fact, there is
nobody. If they do come over it is to
good jobs. Anything that is good enough
for Great Britain, so far as I and the
people I represent are concerned, is good
enough for me.
I want the people-ex-Service men and
others to be treated properly. The ex-
Service men from Northern Ireland who
join the Army are not on the same footing
as the men in Great Britain when they
come off the Army, because the men belonging to Great Britain who joined the
Army and left it on medical or some other
grounds must by law get back the job he
had before he went into the Army.
brought forward a Motion here to put the
men of Northern Ireland on the same
footing, but you would not do it.

The PRIME MINISTER: I would
very much like to acquiesce in this, the
first request I have received, but I find
on making inquiries-the hon. Member
was good enough to give me notice of his
intention to raise the matter that it
would complicate the machinery if anything was suspended, even for a short

Therefore, much as I would like to oblige

Mr. NIXON: It is not a matter of

Question put, and agreed to.

the House of this day.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Health Services.
CONDITIONS IN MILL ROW,
ARMAGH.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
action the Armagh Rural Council have
taken in order to make the area known
as the Mill Row comply with the conditions as laid down by the Public Health
Act, and whether the report issued by
Dr. Weir has been adopted by the Rural
Council.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): With regard to the first
part of this question, I would refer the
hon. Member to the reply given by me
to a similar question on the 16th
February last.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, as a result of a communication
addressed by my Department to the
Rural District Council, consequent on a
report received from Dr. Weir, the
Ministry's Medical Inspector, I understand the Rural Council propose to put
before the County Council a proposal for
the repair and maintenance of Mill Row.
SUGGESTED COUNTY SANATORIA.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his Ministry has
received the resolution passed by Newry
Board of Guardians and since adopted by
various local authorities throughout Northern Ireland, advocating the establishment of a sanatorium for the treatment
of tuberculosis in each county in Northern Ireland, and whether his Ministry
intend to act on the suggestion.
Mr. LOWRY: The answer to the first
part of this question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the remainder of the
question, as the hon. Member is aware,
a Select Committee of this House is at
present investigating the general question
of public health services in Northern
Ireland, and, pending the consideration
of the report of that-Committee, I am not
prepared to make any statement on this
subject.
Mr. BROWN: Is the Minister prepared to transmit the resolution referred
to in the question to the Select Committee, so that it may be brought
officially to their notice for consideration?
Mr. LOWRY: The resolution is already
before the Select Committee.
Labour.
ENNISKILLEN COURTS OF
REFEREES.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is satisfied with the
conduct of the chairman of the courts of
referees in Enniskillen; whether Mr.
Winslow is conversant with the regulations in view of the large number of disallowances in that area; and whether he
will make inquiries into this matter in
the Enniskillen exchange area.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): Mr. Winslow is a solicitor with
many years experience as chairman of
courts of referees and my Ministry has no
reason to think that he is not fully conversant with the regulations.
I may
point out to the hon. Member that for the
six months ending 31st March, the last
half year for which statistics are available, the proportion of appeals disallowed
by courts of referees all over Northern
Ireland was 57.2 per cent., while the
proportion disallowed in Enniskillen was
only 55.1 per cent., so that there do not
seem to be grounds for any suggestion of
undue severity in that area.

AGRICULTURAL CONTROL ORDER.
4. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if the Agricultural Control Order is working in
harmony with the umpire's decision as to
the not-unemployed aspect of workers
who own small farms; and whether the
present emergency control order is based
on normal insurable occupation,
whether it includes any period which was
not insurable.
or
Mr. GRANT: My Ministry is not
aware of any conflict between the Control
of Employment in Agricultural Order and
the umpire's decisions on unemployment
benefit.
This Order defines an agricultural
worker as any person whose normal occupation is employment on work in agriculture.
The hon. Member will observe that
this covers all employment in agriculture,
including self-employment, whether insured or not. Thus the owner of a small
farm, or the son of a farmer who normally
helps his father in his work, comes under
the definition, although neither would
usually be insured. Therefore in deciding
whether a particular person is subject to
the conditions of the Order, my Ministry
has regard to the kind of work on which
he has been engaged.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he is aware
that the normal occupation of a person
can change in any one year. Is he also
aware that 26 weeks' work as an agricultural labourer makes a man's normal
occupation that of agricultural labourer?
Mr. GRANT: The hon. Member, I am
sure, is fully aware of the fact that
whether a man is a small farmer or the
son of a small farmer if he is working on
his own farm or with his father he is not
normally an insured person, but if he goes
to work for another small farmer he becomes a normally insured person in agriculture. If he leaves that employment,
or if there is no employment in agriculture available for him at the moment and
he is working in another occupation, he
is still registered as an agricultural worker
under the Agricultural Control Order.

Mr. GRANT: As no doubt the hon.

or known to him.

Ministerial Salaries.
Prime
7. Mr. BROWN asked the
Minister whether he can state the total
amount of the individual salaries, allowances and expenses to be paid to each
Cabinet Minister, including himself, all
Parliamentary and Assistant Parliamentary Secretaries in the new Government; also the total of all these salaries;
whether he can state how these salaries
compare in all respects with those of the
outgoing administration; and whether
any effort has been or will be made to
effect economy in the entire administration of Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Sinclair) I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
:
The answers to the first and third part
of the question are best expressed in a
tabular statement, and, as this is rather
lengthy, I propose, with the hon. Member's permission, to circulate it in the
Official Report.
The salaries, allowances, etc., shown in
this statement amount in the case of the
late Government to £22,400 per annum,
and in the case of the present Government to £21,200 per annum.
parison of these figures shows a yearly
saving of £1,200, and this despite the
fact that the Ministers of Finance and
A com-
Agriculture now draw their salaries, as
was not the case in the former
Administration.
Included in the statement is a proposed
contingencies allowance of £500 per
annum to the Prime Minister, and an
Estimate in respect of this item will be
brought before the House in due course.
As will be remembered, the late Lord
Craigavon, in addition to an official
residence, received an allowance for contingencies of office of £1,750 per annum.
This allowance was very generously forgone by the late Prime Minister, though
an official residence was never placed at
his disposal. I am suggesting that the
present Prime Minister should receive an
allowance, the reasons for which payment
will be dealt with fully on the occasion
of the Estimate to which I have referred
being presented to the House. Until
that Estimate has been passed the allowance will not be drawn. My right hon.
Friend will not, of course, receive any
additional remuneration in respect of his
services as Minister of Commerce and
Production.
As regards the latter part of the question, I can assure the hon. Member that
every possible economy in the administration of the Government will be effected.
Mr. BROWN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell us whether it is the proposal of the Prime Minister to retain the
dual offices of Prime Minister and
Minister of Commerce and Production in
a permanent manner, or does he propose
to retain them only in a temporary sense?
Mr. SPEAKER: That question will
arise in the debate later on.

War Pensions Appeal Tribunal.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government have
taken or intend to take any steps regarding the setting up in Northern Ireland of
Independent
War Pension Appeal
Tribunals on the same lines as those set
up by the Imperial Government.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The matter referred to by the
hon. Member is reserved to the Imperial
Authorities under the Government of
Ireland Act. An announcement was
made in the House of Commons at Westminster on the 6th instant that a Pension
Appeal Tribunal will be set up in Northern Ireland as soon as possible after the
Bill, which is in course of preparation,
becomes law.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Prime Minister
tell us whether the proceedings of these
tribunals will be retrospective? In other
words, will it be open to them to consider
all cases of disallowed pension claims
which have arisen prior to the setting up
of the Committee?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
had better wait until the Act is passed.
King's National Roll.
TENDERS FOR POTATO
PROCESSING FACTORIES.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether it is a fact that the
eminent engineering firm of Messrs.
Smith & Pearson (Belfast), Ltd., of
Belfast and Newry, tendered for the
erection of potato processing factories in
Moy, Portaferry, and Faughan; whether
their price was favourable; whether their
tender was not considered and the firm
was informed that it would not be opened
as they were not on the King's National
Roll; whether it is a fact that this firm
have been on the King's National Roll
since its inception and are still on it and
have still on their pay roll a number of
men disabled in the last war and have
maintained them in spite of the fact that
none of these men ever got pensions;
whether they are contractors to the War
Department since 1908; whether they
confirmed that the firm have been on the
King's National Roll since its inauguration; and whether he can explain why
Newry should suffer a loss of work
through this very unfair treatment and
unjustified discrimination.
Mr. SINCLAIR: The tender for the
fabrication and supply of structural steel
required for the potato processing
factories referred to in the hon. Member's
question was received from the firm of
Smith & Pearson (Belfast), Ltd. The
firm was not informed that their tender
would not be opened on account of their
not being on the King's National Roll.
The tender was, in fact, opened and considered, but their price was not more
favourable than the other tenders
received.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Sinclair]
My information is that the firm of
Messrs. Smith & Pearson (Belfast), Ltd.
is not on the King's National Roll, and,
as the hon. Member is doubtless aware,
preference is given to firms whose names
are on the Roll. I understand, however,
that the firm intends to make application
for enrolment. As to the number of
disabled ex-Service men employed by the
firm, I have no information. In view of
the confusion that appears to exist in the
hon. Member's mind, I wish to make it
clear that the firm of Messrs. Smith &
Pearson (Belfast), Ltd., is a separate
entity from the firm of Messrs. Smith &
Pearson, Ltd., and was, in fact, only incorporated in Northern Ireland as recently as 27th April, 1942. Thus,
though it is known that the parent firm
of Smith & Pearson, Ltd., was on the
King's National Roll until 1933, the fact
remains that the firm from whom the
tender was received is not on the Roll.
The question of the firm having been
contractors to the War Department since
1908 does not arise.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the firm of

Mr. SINCLAIR: Yes, sir.
Mr. BROWN: To remove the confusion that the Minister says exists in my

that I will raise this matter
on the

Linen Industry.
CLOSED MILLS.
13. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can make a statement as to the present position and
outlook in the linen industry in Northern
Ireland, and whether any steps have, or
will be taken for the utilisation of closed
mills and factories, including that at
Dromalane, Newry, where splendid
machinery is lying idle since 1940, either
for textile manufacture or alternative. war
work.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF COM-
MERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The rate of production in the spinning.
section of the linen industry shows a
slight improvement. So far as I can see.
there is no immediate prospect of a
marked change in this section.
This
Activity in the weaving section is still
at a comparatively high level.
activity can only be maintained if the
supply of flax and rayon yarns continues
to be supplemented by supplies of cotton
yarn. As cotton yarn production is outside
the control of my Ministry, I cannot make
any definite statement on the future
prospects of the weaving industry, but I
can assure the hon. Member that every
effort will be made to maintain the high
level of activity already achieved. All
skilled labour in the textile making-up
industry is being readily absorbed, and
additional workers are now undergoing
a course of training.
Arrangements have already been made
for a number of mills and factories which
are not fully occupied on their normal
type of production to be utilised for
alternative war work. A proposal on these
lines has been considered in connection
with the mill to which the hon. Member
specifically refers, but I regret that this
proposal did not succeed. I can readily
assure the hon. Member that every effort
will be made to ensure that available
labour and factory space in Northern
Ireland are. utilised in the industrial war
effort.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to
thank the Parliamentary Secretary for his
satisfactory reply to my question?

render them redundant.

change for you?

the chairman of the Pigs Marketing Board
was appointed by the Board in 1939 at a
salary fixed by the Board and approved
by the Ministry. The hon. Member has
raised the matter before and over a year
ago a full explanation was given by my
predecessor. Whilst it is quite true that

NORTH AFRICAN VICTORY.
Congratulations to Allied Forces.
The PRIME MINISTER: I feel sure
I am expressing the feelings of everyone
in this House when I say how thrilled we
