VOTE OF CONFIDENCE.
Prime Minister's Speech.
The PRIME MINISTER: In submitting to the House the Motion that
stands in my name, I am keenly aware
that in forming a Government at the request of His Grace the Governor, and
becoming third Prime Minister of
Northern Ireland, I am inheriting a fine.
and living tradition, and one which my
colleagues and I will endeavour with all
our strength to uphold.
I should like to pay a warm tribute to
the faithful service of my predecessors.
From the late Lord Craigavon, and from
my right hon. Friend who followed him
in the office of Prime Minister, I have
drawn inspiration for many years.
In
close association with both of them I
learned to admire their deep devotion to
Ulster, their intimate understanding of
its people, and their unyielding resolve to
uphold the cause in which they so fervently believed. The work they have
done for Ulster, the service they have so
ungrudgingly rendered, will always be remembered with gratitude. The House, I
know, will join with me in offering very
warm congratulations to my right hon.
Friend on his appointment to the high
dignity of Companion of Honour. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
As to ourselves, I notice one newspaper
describes us "just as a working team."
Perhaps we are not a very handsome lot
--but handsome is as handsome does, and
I think the description is a very good
omen and we will do our best to prove it
correct.
In choosing my Ministerial colleagues I
have sought out men who, in my judgment, are best qualified for the posts they
now hold. The office of a Cabinet Minister is not, and should not be, a life
appointment, and if in the light of
experience I deem changes necessary, I
shall not hesitate to make them at any
time.
There is a small instrument called a
prism which scientists use to split light
into its component colours. Thus one can
see one colour, and one another, but the
main light remains the same to all. I
sometimes think that the problems of
government very much resemble a prism.
That is to say, we all want much the same
thing the betterment of our country and
the prosperity, of our people-but we see
different ways of achieving it.
The two components I consider most
important for our country are the successful prosecution of the war-without
which we should have no future—and the
unity of Northern Ireland with Great
Britain. These will always be cardinal
points in the policy of all Ulster Governments, and I would appeal now to all
Ulster men and women who see the light
in the prism as we do, but who perhaps
have had various colours dazzling them of
late, to put aside all differences and rally
behind my Government for the things
which really matter. Without their help
we cannot succeed; with it we shall be
unconquerable.
Vote of Confidence
Vote of Confidence
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
Unity with Great Britain is and remains our ideal. We should not have to
repeat this so frequently but for the fact
that our neighbour Eire is constantly
attempting to brush it aside as being nonexistent and of no importance. She
asserts that it is the Border that causes
the division between Ulster and Eire.
The truth is that the Border merely
acknowledges the fundamental difference
between us. We intend our unity to be
with Britain, and not with Eire. To pretend that fundamental divergencies do not
exist between us and that there is not an
irreconcilable conflict of loyalties is not
statesmanship-it is folly. Ulster will
never allow herself to be coerced, and
while the people of Northern Ireland are
behind me I will never consent to it. I
see no reason why the relations between
Eire and ourselves should not be perfectly
cordial on this basis, provided that she
ceases to interfere in our affairs.
Eire's attitude to the war, which is not
shared by any other country of the
British Commonwealth, clearly shows how
widely our ideals differ from theirs.
Northern Ireland will, under my guidance,
continue and if possible further increase
her efforts in the prosecution of the war.
Already our co-operation with the United
Nations is not inconsiderable. Ulster
ports and harbours have proved vital in
the battle of the Atlantic; British troops
are trained here; the Royal Air Force
operates from our territory, and units of
the United States Forces are our honoured
and welcome guests. That is what I may
call our passive contribution. Our active
one is creditable also. Our men and
women have voluntarily joined the British
forces in large numbers-far larger
numbers than there is any record forboth in Irish and in English regiments, as
well as in the Navy, the Royal Air Force
and the Mercantile Marine. Many have
already given their lives. In addition we
have many thousands in the Home Guard,
civil defence, munitions, and agriculture
-and all of this is voluntary. We felt
and we feel that we could do no less. For
the Allied cause is our cause, and I
intend, with Ulster's support, which I am
sure will be behind me, to do my utmost
to increase even this very considerable
effort in the days to come.
It is because of the imperative need of
developing our war output to the fullest
possible extent that I have felt it right to
retain myself the portfolio of Commerce
and Production. As Minister of that
Department in the late Government I had
frequent and intimate discussions with
British Ministers in London, and found
them appreciative of the immense importance of Northern Ireland as a centre of
war industry. In my view, it is essential that these contacts should be maintained in order to ensure continuity of
policy and the speedy execution of new
decisions.
The House will agree, I am sure, that
this is not the time to attempt a review
of the developments in war production in
Northern Ireland following the administrative reorganisation which I have carried out stage by stage during the past
two years. In any event security considerations preclude this. Yet it would
be unfair to our industrial firms, and to
the great mass of men and women workers
if I did not indicate, however guardedly,
the general lines on which progress has
been made. In the earlier stages of the
war it was apparent that although there
was little precision engineering in Ulster,
and although our linen factories were not
easily adaptable to the production of war
weapons of the types most required, great
potentialities existed. There were-and
still are difficulties inherent in the
geographical situation of Northern
Ireland, in problems affecting raw
materials, transport, and the training of
labour for specialised war work. In spite
of these obstacles new factories have been
established and existing industrial concerns expanded to many times their
former capacity. In volume and range
of output our munitions firms have
achieved notable results, and the contribution made by the textile factories has
been invaluable.
Northern Ireland design and workmanship are playing their part in the Battle
of the Atlantic, in the Mediterranean,
and in every ocean where British men-ofwar and cargo ships are found. Vehicles
and weapons of the latest and most formidable types have gone out from Ulster
factories to smash the enemy in the Libyan
desert and the mountain fastnesses of
Tunisia. Between Northern Ireland
workshops and the devastating raids by
the R.A.F. in the heart of Germany there
is the closest connection. The deft fingers
of our women textile workers have provided Britain's air heroes with essential
Vote of Confidence
11 MAY 1943
Vote of Confidence
equipment and Britain's land forces with
battledress. Let me add also a note of
praise for the admirable way in which
our women workers have adapted themselves to the bench and the lathe, where
they are making a magnificent contribution to Ulster's industrial war effort.
It may interest the House if at this
point I refer to the unemployment situation in Northern Ireland to-day and compare it with the position two years ago.
In January, 1941, when I became
Minister of Commerce, the number of
persons registered as unemployed was
over 68,000. Since that time the unemployment figure has been steadily decreasing, and in April, 1943, it had fallen to
about 18,000. Of this number approximately 2,000 were either casual workers
or temporarily suspended. These figures
show that a large number of Northern
Ireland workers have been absorbed in
war industries.
Im-
Nevertheless I am not satisfied.
pressive though some of Northern Ireland's achievements undoubtedly areand the full story will be told in due
time-there are gaps that must be filled,
hindrances that must be removed, unused
capacity that must be made active,
labour resources that must be employed.
The Government is actively engaged in
examining all these problems, and
positive measures for enlarging the scope
and increasing the momentum of our
production offensive will be discussed with
British Ministers. I am glad to be able
to inform the House that in the near
future one or more British Ministersone of whom is Sir Stafford Cripps,
Minister of Aircraft Production-will
visit Northern Ireland to see for themselves, not only what is being done, but
how our war production can be further
extended and our available labour
utilised.
Mr. Oliver Lyttleton, Minister of Production, with whom I have had many
discussions in my capacity as Minister of
Commerce and Production, is intensely
interested in the development of our war
effort, and I received from him to-day
the following message:-
We shall do all we can to make use
of the productive capacity and resources
of Northern Ireland for the war, and
I look forward to continuing our
collaboration to this end.
Meanwhile, I would address a special
word to employers and operatives.
Government plans, however good, Government action, however vigorous, can never
produce ships, 'planes, and a vast array
of war weapons without the energetic cooperation of managements and the rankand-file workers. That co-operation, in
turn, depends upon harmony inside the
factories. In recent months the existence
of friction in some of our war industries
has impeded output-a lamentable situation at a time when the Allied forces in the
field need all the materials we can sendand need them quickly. The Government
fully recognises the services of the
workers and is in sympathy with their
aspirations. Machinery for negotiation
and arbitration has been set up with the
full agreement of the trade unions, and
the Government looks to the workers to
abide by this arrangement and support
the union representatives. The possibility
of accelerating the machinery is being
carefully examined by the Government.
One of the problems which has caused
me anxiety in the general supervision of
the industrial war effort is the temporary
dislocation caused by changes in the production programme necessitated by present and prospective needs of the fighting
Services. The standing-off of workers at
a time when everyone is being urged to
give of
of his best to the production
campaign gives rise to misunderstanding
and, indeed, a sense of frustration.
Nearly all the larger firms engaged in
munitions production have now set up, or
are in process of setting up, joint works
production committees, a development
which will bring about further COoperation between management and
workers, and will enable the workers to
reasons for
be kept informed of the
temporary reductions in the amount of
labour required. I welcome this new
arrangement. Even in the best managed
factories it is difficult to eliminate idle
time altogether, but energetic steps are
being taken to reduce this to a minimum.
At this stage of the conflict we cannot
afford idle machines or idle hands.
I am in entire agreement with the
principle of bringing the greatest amount
of work to the people, and this will be
the predominant aim of the Ministry of
Commerce and Production. At the same
time, the true criterion is what is best
At the
for the country and the Allies.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
moment there is a surplus of building
trade operatives, and I intend to do everything possible to secure work for them
on new constructional projects.
Before passing from the subject of
Ulster's war effort, I must pay tribute
to
our greatest industry-agriculture.
Having held the office of Minister of
Agriculture I can speak with first-hand
knowledge of the splendid achievements
of the farmers in increasing our food
supply and bringing more land into
cultivation for the growing of flax. Since
the outbreak of war the area under
crops in Northern Ireland has increased
by no less than 76 per cent. In this
respect the farmers have given a magnificent lead to Great Britain, where the
comparable figure is 58 per cent. Notwithstanding the much larger area under
the plough and the difficulty of obtaining
foodstuffs, the cattle population in Ulster
has increased. That is a highly
meritorious contribution to the winning
of the war. The noble Lord, who has
relinquished the post of Minister of
Agriculture, made many earnest appeals
to farmers to bring the flax-growing area
up to 100,000 acres, and I understand
that there is a good prospect of this
figure being reached.
To sum up this brief survey of our
position, I will only add that the determined policy of the Government is to
work unremittingly to secure for Northern Ireland such an additional volume of
war orders and such vital work on other
developments as will step up production
to higher levels.
So much for the main planks in our
programme. If the winning of the war
demands of the Government tireless
labour and buoyant energy, preparation
for the peace is a duty hardly less exacting. What is popularly called "physical
reconstruction" the replanning and
rebuilding of bombed areas, the rehousing
of the people and the provision of material
amenities will call for far-reaching
measures and bold action. In other
directions the Government will apply
itself to such matters as the expansion of
health services, agricultural development,
the future of the linen industry-on the
prosperity of which the livelihood of so
many workers depends-the supply of
cheap electrical power to factory and
farm, and other projects designed to
increase the economic prosperity of North-
Ireland and provide steady and
remunerative employment for its people.
ern
Immediately after the war there will
inevitably be a difficult transition period.
Large numbers of men and women will be
returning from the services to civil life,
and the factories and their workers must
be switched from war to peace production.
The process of absorbing them in suitable
occupations will present a challenge not
only to the Government and local
authorities, but to the community as a
whole. The Government will do its utmost
to solve these problems. I agree with the
view recently expressed by the Minister
of Production in Great Britain-that in
the post-war period private enterprise and
public utility corporations will both have
an important contribution to make to the
shaping of the country's economic life.
The Ulster linen industry will be confronted with the problem of regaining
former markets overseas, and the nation
will look to the agricultural community
for a much bigger supply of home-grown
food. In both cases a cheap and abundant
electricity supply will be an important
factor in keeping down production costs,
so helping industrialists and farmers to
produce at an economic figure and to hold
their own in keenly competitive markets.
It is hard now to foresee the future with
any exactness, but we must be prepared
as far as is possible for all eventualities.
In approaching the tasks that are before
us, my colleagues and I are impelled by
one desire to serve the State with all our
powers. We have unbounded faith in our
country and its stout-hearted people, and
in that faith we desire to play our part
in fashioning the better Ulster of tomorrow. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I beg to move:
That this House welcomes the formation of a Government whose policy is
to continue to maintain the existing
constitutional position of Northern Ireland, to bring the utmost vigour to the
task of assisting the war effort of the
United Kingdom, the Empire and the
Allied Nations, and to make further
preparation for dealing with the problems of the post-war period.

The position as I see it is that in a
changing world, in a world which is
changing with such tremendous rapidity,
we cannot afford in 1943 to take up the
identical attitude we adopted in 1923. The
intervening 20 years have seen tremendous changes. The world is more interdependent to-day than ever it was before.
We feel the repercussions of shocks in
one part of the world more rapidly and
We have
completely than ever before.
eliminated time and space by the development of radio and aviation, with the
result that conditions throughout the

they were a generation ago. Furthermore, events have taken place in the last
20 years, not only in distant parts of the
world, but at home, which have compelled
many of us who thought from a certain
political angle a generation ago to change
our minds.
It is easy for people to be heroic to-day
when no great issues are involved in the
political sphere, but I would ask those
who profess to be interested in international questions where they stood in 1936,
1937, 1938 and 1939 when Spain and
other countries were being forced into the
hands of the totalitarian countries as a

Britain.
Why did they remain silent?
Did they not see the significance of the
events of that time? These were some of

community. These try to lead the people

ideology than the Ulster tradition is the
right ideology. They are not serving the
people honestly and well. If we have
intelligence we will develop within the
social structure. We have already
improved almost beyond recognition and
have built up one of the finest social services in the world. We believe that in
the days to come it will develop, but
that depends upon our immunity from
attack. It depends upon our ultimate
victory in this war. Because I supremely
believe that Ulster has a great part to
play, and a great contribution to give,
because I believe that Ulster from the
traditional point of view, and from the
point of view of training, achievement
and everything else, moves in harmony
and in spirituality with the overwhelming
majority of the people of the British
Commonwealth of Nations, I want to see
Ulster resolved to play its part proudly
and do all it can to help the British
Commonwealth to win this war. Undoubtedly we are going to win the war.
not in association with people who tried
to betray and sabotage Great Britain, not
with people whose refusal to grant facilities has meant the loss of hundreds of
thousands of lives and hundreds of millions
of tons of material, but in association
with those who have been proud of their
British heritage. When we have won the
war, then as a vindication of that heritage
we can march forward in the building up
of a new and greater Commonwealth to
the end that we may establish enduring
peace.

and the Empire through the generations
that are to come.

Vote of Confidence
Vote of Confidence
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
represents have been saying the same
thing for 23 years, and yet notwithstanding this propaganda of theirs they
have only been able to return two Members to this House. That is the measure
of the success of the propaganda which
the hon. Member has directed against
Ulster Unionism. The hon. Member
asks for an election.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes.
Mr. WARNOCK: Why? I will tell
you why. Because 30,000 of our best
people, mainly our people, are away.
They could not vote now, but when they
come back we will be ready for an
election to meet any challenge that any
separatist elements put up, because the
heart of this country was never sounder
on the question of union than it is this
very day.
Mr. AGNEW: Question.
Mr. WARNOCK: The working men
of this country are very intelligent
students of affairs. I know and recognise
and admire their loyalty to their trade
unions, but they are not the men to saw
off the branch upon which they sit, and
when the time comes for the issue to be
presented to them, are they going to vote
for an organisation which, through the
public statements of its recognised
leaders, tends towards a breach of the
union with Great Britain? I know what
the answer of the working men of this
country will be. It will be given in the
same certain tone in which the Ulster
working man has always spoken when this
issue was presented to him.
Mr. AGNEW: The Battle of Scarva.
Mr. WARNOCK: No, sir, not the
Battle of Scarva, but the battle for the
polls, in which the Ulster workman has
always been on the one side. Labour in
this country could and should have a
powerful and benevolent influence in our
affairs. It will never attain to the dignity
and influence which it ought to have, and
which would be for the good of our public
representative institutions, until there is
a clear recognition that union with Great
Britain means employment, good wages
and security.
Mr. BEATTIE: And poverty.
WARNOCK: Separation from
Great Britain means loss of employment,
diminution of employment, the lowering
of wages-because that necessarily follows
when the demand for labour is less than
the supply-and a much lower measure of
social security. The Ulster working man
is an intelligent chap. He knows which
side his bread is buttered on. He has not
acquired that intelligence now, but he
had it at the last election when he returned
only two Members to voice the views
which the hon. Member for Pottinger so
forcibly expressed. But until labour in
this country can sever its political and
industrial functions, and come down
politically on the side of Ulster Unionism,
it will never exercise in this country any
real power or influence in our political
life.
The hon. Member was good enough to
give the Prime Minister a slogan. It was
a picture of the Queen of Ulster leaving
a derelict shore. Let him put it in his
pocket and keep it until the day which
he. visualises, when we will be separated
from England, because the Queen of
Ulster leaving a derelict shore will be an
apt picture for that drab day. It will
be a derelict shore, because within ten
years of our separating from Great Britain
the grass will be growing in our shipyards,
and the only employment in the textile
industry will be for oilers to keep the idle
machinery from rotting.

the back

hunters and plum pickers I never came

""
I got a copy of the "Northern Light
this morning. I think the Minister of
Labour also gets a copy. In that paper
it was stated that the right hon. Gentleat
man stated a meeting in Bangor
that the moderate drinker was the curse

a grocer, let alone a Cabinet Minister.
Does he not know that the vast majority
of the Members of this House partake of
some beverage at times? Undoubtedly
they do. I do not know what the right
hon. Member does behind closed doors.
Anything I have to do in the way of

because I must admit I am a moderate
drinker. I have to be even more
moderate now because of the cost of
drink.
Because a large percentage of working
men are fond of a certain beverage,
would the right hon. Gentleman suggest

medicine they can get. To them it is
food, drink, and thought. It eases their
mind and body, and enables them to go
down into the hold of a ship to do their
hard work. If the Minister of Labour
was picking coal out of a hold he would
be very glad of one, two, and three pints
•
of porter when he had finished his job.
Because he is a fanatic on the drink

Exchequer sees to it that he contributes

war.

I come to the ex-Minister of Labour.
Of course it was said of him that he was

I say Northern Ireland never had a

Minister. I argued many a point with

The truth is that we never had a better

Of these four ex-Ministers I have mentioned it can never be said, "Their honour
in dishonour stood and proved them
falsely true." No one will ever be able
to point the finger of scorn at them. I
am glad we are not taking farewell of

As regards the new administration, I
think the proper time and place to pass
judgment on them is to pass it when the
new Ministers individually present their
Estimates and give us an inkling of what
their policies will be. I will reserve my
opinion until then. There is one thing
that is very clear. The back benchers
have tasted blood. They have discovered
they have some power. Having tasted
blood and discovered that power things
can never be the same again. Let us
remember that. I think never again will
back benchers relapse into that inertia
which was brought about by the fact
that the bureaucratic dictatorships under
which we lived took care from behind the
scenes to queer the pitch and down any
suggestion no matter how sensible it was
that came from back benchers, for the
simple reason that they did not think of
it first. These things are gone, and the
Government should realise that no
Government can be in existence for 24
hours unless the back benchers say so. I
judge the new Government simply and
solely by the services they will give the
State-if they are going to provide new
factories and meet the problems that
exist now and will exist in the future.
I hope the new policy will not include
any subterfuges in regard to planning. I
want a complete change of policy in that
respect and I ask the Government for it.
As I have said the back benchers have
tasted blood. They have realised the
truth of what Mr. Lloyd George said.
He said in a recent book which I
was reading the other day that in his
Cabinet which won the last war every
decision had to be hammered out in full,
and that there was not a "yes-man" in
the Cabinet, which included Lord Carson,
Mr. Lloyd George went on to say: "I can
tell you they are a dangerous breed these
yes-men." I throw out the suggestion to
the Government that some consideration
should be given to the suggestions coming
from such back benchers.

The first comment I might make is that

There is a very old, outworn and discredited device, a device worthy of a
pettifogging lawyer, what our American
guests would call a shyster lawyer. It
consists of taking a sentence out of a
speech, divorcing it entirely from its
context, ignoring the time, the place, and
the circumstances which were present to

speech, and, most important of all,
ignoring an explanation that may be
given on a subsequent occasion; in other
words, it is the very old device, invent
your facts and comment on them. That
is exactly what has been done here.

We are on the slope of victory, and
victory has sometimes a way of galloping.
All those responsible from the Prime

gravely have warned us against overoptimism. Without being duly overoptimistic it is plain that this plan must
be pressed ahead, taking care always that

assisting the war effort of the United
Kingdom, the Empire and the Allied
Nations," and thus reach the day when
our plans for dealing with the post-war
period may be submitted to the test of
how they can be worked out in practice.

AYES
There is the question that the Civil
Service run the country. In other words,
that Ministers are not fit to be in the
positions they occupy. I am speaking
for myself at any rate when I say that
I think we owe a great debt of gratitude
to our civil servants in Northern Ireland.
They are men and women who have performed great service to the country under
very difficult circumstances. All I can
say is that any Minister who allows himself to be run by civil servants is, in my
opinion, not fit to be a Minister, but if
he invites and enlists the sympathy and
co-operation of members of the service he
will find it will not only be to his advantage, but to the advantage of the people
of Northern Ireland as a whole. I should
like, in conclusion, confidently to ask the
House to give the Government this Vote
of Confidence, and we will try to do
all we can to satisfy not only the interests
of the whole community but, a far harder
job, to satisfy ourselves.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Resolved, "That this House welcomes
the formation of a Government whose
policy is to continue to maintain the
existing constitutional position of Northern Ireland, to bring the utmost vigour
to the task of assisting the war effort of
the United Kingdom, the Empire and
the Allied Nations, and to make further
preparation for dealing with the problems
of the post-war period."
The Orders of the Day were read and
postponed.

Sinclair): I assume that the hon. Member
has in mind the salaries of Permanent
Secretaries and a few officers of analogous
grades.
The salary scales of these posts immediately before the stabilisation of
salaries for the Service at large in
October, 1936, were, in the case of the
Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of
Finance, on the scale £1,650-£1,900,
and, in the scale of the other officers concerned, on the scale £1,350-£1,750.
These were inclusive salaries fixed in relation to the cost-of-living figure of 55.
The scheme of stabilised salaries introduced for the Service at large with effect
from 1st October, 1936, included provision for a fixed salary of £2,200 for the
Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of
Finance and fixed salaries of £2,000 each
for the other officers concerned.
As explained in my written reply of
the 18th March last to a question by the
hon. Member, it was, however, decided
in the light of certain views expressed in
the House, to revert as from 1st April,
1937, to the level of the scales in force
prior to October, 1936, and for the
reasons which I indicated in that reply
these reduced salaries were regarded as
being subject to the payment of a cost-ofliving bonus in the event of any future
substantial rise in the cost of living. For
the purpose of any future cost-of-living
adjustments, therefore, the reduced salaries
brought into effect from 1st April, 1937,
have been treated as including a cost-ofliving bonus related to an index figure of
55, which means that the salary scale
£1,650-£1,900 is regarded as having included a cost-of-living bonus amounting
to £147 at the minimum of the scale and
£149 at the maximum; while the salary
scale £1,350-£1,750 has been treated as
including a cost-of-living bonus of £172
at the minimum of the scale and £139 at
the maximum.
The answer to the final portion of
the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative.
I admit it may appear illogical that
only in the case of these grades does
salary now fluctuate automatically with
variations in the cost of living, and I am
considering the advisability of substituting salaries which do not vary in this
way.
Central Heating.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether it is proposed to follow
the Imperial Government decision to lift
the ban on central heating, as announced
over the radio a few days ago.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): Since the ban on central heating did not apply in Northern Ireland,
except in so far as it was voluntarily
applied by Government departments, the
question does not arise.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Prime Minister
aware that many members of the Civil
Service in this building are ill, or have
been ill, through cold brought about by
the central heating being withdrawn in
the very cold weather, and when considering the matter will he recollect that
so far as the latitude of Northern Ireland
is concerned and latitude largely governs
climate-we are in the Scottish area and
not in the London area?
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes. I
understand the heating was turned on on
Monday morning, but the point to bear in
mind is that the greatest economy should
be applied. If, unfortunately, we get
these very bad breaks in the weather I
think the Ministries are entitled to turn
on the heating, but it would be wrong to
keep the heating going the whole time.

Londonderry Corporation War Bonuses.
3. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
Londonderry Corporation, while granting
a cost-of-living bonus to some of its
employees has withheld it from others
who are not school-teachers, trade
unionists, manual workers or those on the
clerical grading scheme (in the latter case
those only in receipt of salaries under
£220 per annum although granted to
teachers on salaries up to £525 per
annum), and whether he will take action
to persuade the Corporation to follow the
example of those local authorities in
Northern Ireland which operate a cost-ofliving bonus scheme on a more generous
and equitable scale.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Except in the case of
certain
officers of the Londonderry
Corporation, the Ministry's approval is
not required to the payment of war
bonuses. I have, therefore, no information as to the extent to which war bonuses
generally have been given to employees
of the Corporation. I would inform the
hon. Member that if certain employees of
the Corporation feel aggrieved by reason
of the refusal of the Corporation to grant
a war bonus they may refer the matter in
dispute to the Northern Ireland Arbitration Tribunal for decision. In these
circumstances it appears unnecessary to
take the action suggested by the hon.
Member.
Doctors' Petrol Allowances-Derry
and North Antrim.
4. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
doctors in the City and County of
Londonderry and in North Antrim are
so restricted in their allowances of petrol
that they are obliged to hire taxis when
these are available, and, when they are
not, are unable to afford their patients
sufficient attendance, whilst other classes of
the community get such liberal supplies
that there is a black market in petrol
and petrol coupons, and whether he will
make representations to the Petroleum
Officer to ensure that doctors get
sufficient petrol to enable them to perform
their duties adequately.
Mr. LOWRY: I am not aware that
doctors in the areas referred to are suffering any hardship in regard to their petrol
allowances. It is true that doctors in
common with those other members of the
community engaged on important and
essential services have, as a result of
restrictions necessarily imposed by the
Ministry of Fuel and Power, suffered a
slight curtailment of their allowances.
While this may involve great circumspection and care on their part in the
planning of their visits and the use of
public transport whenever practicable, I
am of the opinion that generally their
present allowances cannot, in the circumstances, be regarded as inadequate.
In assessing doctors' allowances, the
Petroleum Officer keeps in contact with a
Liaison Committee of the local branch of
the British Medical Association, and he
is guided in his decisions by the recommendations of that body, and by the instructions conveyed to him by the Ministry of Fuel and Power on the necessity
for restricting the consumption of petrol.
He is at all times ready to receive and
consider carefully any representations regarding allowances for the medical profession which may be submitted to him
through the medium of the Committee
referred to, or, in the case of qualified
doctors who are not members of the
British Medical Association, through their
appropriate organisations.
As regards the hon. Member's reference
to black market petrol, I am aware that
there is a black market in petrol as in
other rationed commodities, but in any
case which comes to the notice of the

a limited measure is possible.. I would
hon. Members that there is

in any way consideration of the issues

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Workmen's Compensation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): This Bill to which I am asking
the House to give a second reading
to-day is short and, I hope, non-contentious, so that I feel I need not occupy
the time of hon. Members with a
lengthy speech. The object of the Bill
is to deal, within the framework of
existing legislation, with some special
points which have become of increased
importance as a result of war conditions.
The Bill follows closely upon the lines
of an Act already passed in Great
Britain. Four sections of that Act are
not reproduced because they are concerned with a disease arising from dust
conditions in a particular branch of the
coal mining industry. It is confined to
certain areas in Great Britain, so that
these clauses are unnecessary in Northern Ireland. It is, in a sense, a disappointment to me that more far-reaching
proposals are not being brought forward,
but as hon. Members are, I am sure,
aware, the subject of workmen's compensation is one which Sir William
Beveridge has covered in his report on
the social services; and while that report,
with all its many implications, is under
consideration, I think it clear that only
a limited measure is possible.. I would
assure hon. Members that there is
nothing in the Bill which will prejudice.
in any way consideration of the issues
raised in the Beveridge Report.
Let me now turn to the provisions of
the Bill itself. Clause 1 of the Bill will
enable the earnings of a woman in war
work to be disregarded in calculating
the amount of compensation which she
is entitled to receive if her husband's
581 Workmen's Compensation Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
indeath subsequently occurs in an
dustrial accident. At present, as the
compensation payable is related to the
degree of dependency, such earnings
may reduce the amount of compensation
to be paid. A female relative acting as
housekeeper will be treated in the same
way as a wife.
The object of Clause 2 is comparatively
simple, but
but the wording has been
amplified to its present form to meet
certain criticisms raised at Westminster.
Compensation is based upon the average
weekly earnings of a workman for the 12
months previous to the accident. Under
existing law it is possible for the injured
workman to get his compensation
reassessed where a change of over 20 per
cent. in the rate of remuneration has
occurred since the accident; but this can
apply only when the variations have been
in operation for a period of 12 months.
There is, thus, always a time-lag and
there has to be a substantial variation in
wages before the compensation can be
reassessed.
The present clause, while retaining the
principle of existing law, provides for the
adjustment of the compensation whenever
the change occurs after the date of the
accident in the rates of remuneration of
the class of employment in which the
workman was employed before
accident.
the
Sub-clause (2) of the clause puts the
workman who has received an increase of
wages just before the accident on the
same footing as the workman who meets
with the accident before the increase of
wages has occurred and, who, under subsection (1) will get the benefit of the increase for the whole of the 12 month
period.
This particular Clause requires a little
bit of explanation, especially to those who
are not familiar with the working of the
Compensation Act. I should like, if I
can, to make it as clear as possible to
the Members of this House. Under the
existing law, if a man was injured and
claimed compensation his compensation
benefit was based on his previous 12
months earnings. Under the amending
law the increase in wages, even if the
increase only takes place a week before
the man met with the accident, is taken
into consideration and the 12-month
average would be based on that increase
that was given a week previous. I hope
that is perfectly clear to hon. Members.
And if the increase takes place any time
during the course of the man's incapacity
he is entitled to apply for a re-assessment
and the re-assessment in wages for that
particular industry will be applied over
the
included.
12 months period, the increase
Under existing law a juvenile, before
reaching the age of 21, can get his
weekly compensation payment increased
on the basis of his full wage-earning
capacity if he had remained uninjured.
That is to say, he can have taken into
account the wage to which he would
normally have been entitled on reaching
man's estate, instead of the boy's wage
which he was getting before the accident.
It will be agreed that in such cases a
further right of review should be given
on the basis of changes in the rates of
remuneration since the weekly payment
was increased. Sub-section (3) provides
that right.
That requires a little bit of explanation
also. If an apprentice or boy in industry
was injured and made a claim for workmen's compensation, and if he was 17
years of age, or 18 or 19, and the injury
lasted so long that he would be entitled
to claim the normal wages of the age he
was at that particular time had he not
been incapacitated. In other words, if
he had come out of his time as a journeyman he would have been entitled up to
the age of 21 to make a claim on that
basis. But if he did not make the claim
at the time he was 21 and became 22,
23 or 24 he was debarred from making it.
The amending Bill I am submitting to the
House to-day removes that disability, and
he can make the claim after 21 years of
age.
Clause 3 deals with the difficulty that
a workman who wishes to claim compensation for a scheduled industrial disease
and who requires a medical certificate
must seek the certificate of the examining
surgeon under the Act for the district in
which he has been employed. The reason
for this provision is that the examining
surgeon for the district where the man
has been employed may reasonably be
expected to have some knowledge of the
industries and the incidental diseases of
that district. In present circumstances
workmen are sometimes employed long
583 Workmen's Compensation Bill-

13 MAY 1943
Second Reading
distances from their home and hardship
may result where the workman contracts
a scheduled disease and goes home before
getting the examining surgeon's certificate. It is proposed, therefore, that in
such cases and subject to such conditions
as the Ministry may direct, the workman
may obtain a certificate from an examining surgeon for the district where he
resides or to which he has been removed
for medical treatment.
Again I should like if I may to clarify
that a little bit. We have been, as we
know very well, sending men and women
to different employment on the other side
of the Channel. If either a man or
woman contracts an industrial disease in
the particular district in which he or she
is working the present Act states that he
must get a certificate from the examining
surgeon in the district where he works.
Now we realise the hardship of that because naturally when a man or woman
away from home contracts such a disease
the first thing he would do is to get to
his own home surrounded by his own
people. This amending Act makes
provision for the doctor, the man's own
family doctor or some other examining
surgeon in the district in which he is
living at that particular time to grant a
certificate, rather than he should have to
get certificate from the surgeon in the
district in which he was employed.
Clause 4 is inserted at the request of
the Minister of Pensions. The Ministry
of Pensions naturally desire that there
shall be no delay in granting the weekly
payment to the dependants of a seaman
who has died in the ranks of the
Mercantile Marine owing to enemy action;
but in some cases subsequent inquiry
shows that the claim is for workmen's
compensation and not for pension.
such circumstances it is only right and
proper that the advances made by the
Ministry of Pensions should be recovered,
either from the employer liable to pay
compensation or, where the employer has
paid the money into the county court,
out of the money so paid.
In
That again requires a little bit of explanation. During war time there have
been a number of ships sunk with their
crews lost. At the particular time the
loss of the ship was reported it could not
have been proved definitely it was the
result of enemy action or of the ship
striking a rock or of a collision. So that
no inconvenience should be caused to the
dependants of those who were lost in the
ship the Ministry makes provision for
paying those dependants a grant, and if
subsequently it was proved that the ship
was not sunk by enemy action, then the
Ministry make it quite clear that they
have the right to reclaim the money they
paid until such times as the compensation
case was definitely cleared up.
I commend this Bill to the House and
trust that it will soon be placed upon the
Statute Book. I beg to move.

now read a Second time.'
""
Mr. BEATTIE: If I wanted to make
some cheap political kudos I could do so
to-day out of the right hon. Gentleman.
The first question I might ask him is who
made his speech. The second thing I
might say is that he had not the mentality or intelligence to make that speech
himself. But I am not so small. I do
not get down so low as to use such
methods of attack either in this House or
outside it. Instead of that I am going
to compliment the right hon. Gentleman
on providing himself with a brief
clarifying the measure which he has
asked the House to read a Second time.
I think it is all important and necessary
for responsible Ministers as well as responsible leaders, one of which I have the
honour to be at the present time, to be
very dignified.
I think the right hon. Gentleman will
agree with me in the points to which I
wish to direct his attention. He has
said this Bill will not interfere with
the Beveridge recommendation, but I
certainly think there might be a
tendency to take the basis of this Bill
upon which to build the compensation
which is placed in the Beveridge Report.
If the basis of workmen's compensation
is to be built upon the old workmen's
compensation then the principle is wrong.
Let me illustrate this point. The right
hon. Gentleman and I know what this
Bill really purports to set out. When I
said he might be in agreement with me I
am satisfied he will. The basis of the
reduction of purchasing power to the man
when he is injured places him under the
Workmen's Compensation Act in a worse
position than when he was fully employed.
It reduces his purchasing power, it
reduces his standard of living, and it
reduces the standard of his wife and
family. In other words, it is similar in
585 Workmen's Compensation Bill-- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Beattie]
character to the
the Unemployment Insurance Acts under which the workman
is the only unit of the family who receives
benefit. That one unit has to provide for
the wife and children in the home. The
loss sustained in purchasing power to that
home for a period of twelve months is
such that it places the workman at the
end of that period in a position whereby
he will grasp at the first chance of a
final settlement.
That is an unfair position to put the
workman into. That is the unhappy
position I have had to meet-that the
workman at the end of twelve months is
totally unfit to follow his employment,
and his home circumstances are such that
he has reached a state of poverty. The
employer then approaches him at that
period and offers him a lump sum in final
settlement of his claim. That man is not
in a healthy or strong position because
of the sights he witnesses in his
home, and he immediately makes up his
mind by saying, "If I had £100, £200
or £300 I might be able to open a little
shop or start a little business of some
description." That is the tragedy
associated with the basis of this workmen's compensation which is now being
improved in this House. I hope that is
not going to be the basis on which
the Beveridge compensation will be
calculated.
own
I want to say that while this Bill still
has the old foundations, there are benefits
given under it. I want to put a point to

with an accident. On what average earnings is he going to be paid for his disability? Is it going to be the labourer's
rate in the industry in which he met the

Now we come to another aspect of the
matter. Why is this done? Someone
with a lot of conceit and little brains
thought that that would be a substitute
for conscription, overlooking the fact that
thousands and thousands of men have
been refused entry into the army on the
ground that they were engaged in a

early stages of the war the recruiting
offices were in full swing there was a representative of the Ministry of Labour
there inquiring what the man was doing,
and turning down candidate after candidate for the Army, some of them unemployed. I make that statement, and I
can prove it.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is correct.
Mr. NIXON: I will give you one case.
An unemployed farm labourer was turned
down when he went to join the Armyand he tried several different regimentson the ground that he was a farm
labourer. He was not turned down on
the ground that he was working, because
he was not, nor could he get work at that
time. His name is McBurney. It was
at a time when we wanted men in the
Army. I went to the ex-Minister of
Labour, and he very kindly met my
request to let the man join up by changing his registration. He registered him
as something else. The man was in a
state of starvation, and so was his family.
I do not know where he is now, but I do
know that before he was four months in the
Army he was in the Middle East. I only
tell you that to illustrate how men were
kept out of the Army. Young fellows
who were working in Combe Barbour's
and Mackie's came to me over and over
again to get a reference for the Royal Air
Force, but they were not allowed to join.
Now they are going to be painted for all
time as shirkers, and are not going to get
any work. The thing is absolutely
ridiculous.
When I am on my feet, I may say there
have been a lot of anonymous letters in
the Press recently about Ulstermen not
joining the Army, and about all the men
who are at home who could be in the
Army. Ulstermen have joined in thousands and thousands and thousands, and
when it is said that certain men should
be in the Army, it is found on investigation that many of them were in the Army
and many of them are at work from
which they could not be spared. One day
I was on the Shankill Road and someone
drew my attention to eight young men in
civilian clothes at the corner of Hopeton
Street and said they should be in the
Army. I said, "I have not the slightest
hesitation in saying that they were in the
Army, or they are in it," because I knew
by the way their hair was brushed, and
so forth. I went across and got into conversation with them. Some of them were
soldiers in civilian clothes on leave, and
others were boys who had come through
Dunkirk and were discharged on medical
grounds.
That is what a lot of these anonymous
letters are based on. They are written
by people whose own record would not
stand investigation. That is why they
do not put their names to their letters. I
say that Ulster's war effort is magnificent,
and if the people who are talking about
the young men who should be in the
Army could investigate practically every
case I will not say it applies to every
one-they would find a substantial reason
why they are not in the Army-they are
either doing their bit at home or have
done their bit, or perhaps are serving
soldiers on leave.
Allied Victory in Tunisia.
MESSAGE OF CONGRATULATION.
Mr. SPEAKER: In view of the victory
which has been achieved in North Africa
within the past 24 hours, the House
might be interested to know of the action
I took as regards hon. Members' direction
to me on Tuesday to communicate with
General Eisenhower. I had to decide in
the first place whether it would be
possible to write, or more advisable to
cable. I came to the conclusion that
speed was the essence of this contract, and
that there was not very much point in
writing something which might not reach
North Africa for two or three weeks.
597 Allied Victory in Tunisia

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment
[Mr. Speaker]
Therefore, I thought the best thing to do
was to send a wire to the Prime Minister
of Great Britain as follows:
PRIME MINISTER,
12th May, 1943.
10 DOWNING STREET,
I have been directed by the House
of Commons to request you to transmit
to General Eisenhower the following
message:
The House of Commons of Northern
Ireland congratulate you and the forces
under your command on the magnificent victory you have all achieved.
The Members appreciate to the full the
wisdom of the strategy and tactics
employed, the marvellous valour and
courage displayed by the officers and
men of all the fighting forces, and are
confident that you have paved the way
to final victory.
H. MULHOLLAND,
Speaker.
Question, "That the House now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Fifteen
minutes after Three o'clock until
Tuesday next, pursuant to the
Resolution of the House of this
day.

MESSAGE FROM GENERAL

Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to the
House that I have received the following
communication from General Eisenhower:
On behalf of the Forces of the United
Nations under my command I thank
you sincerely for your generous message
of congratulation and appreciation. We
are proud to have here several battalions
and many individual soldiers from
Northern Ireland who, with the continued support of their people at home,
will play such an important part in
achieving final victory.
(Signed) EISENHOWER.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Shortage of Male P.E. Teachers.
1. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Education whether he is aware that
although the training of public elementary
male school teachers still continues in
England this has ceased in Northern Ireland, and that in consequence there will
soon be an acute shortage of these, and
what steps the Ministry proposes to take
in order to obviate such an undesirable
situation.
aware
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Rev. Professor Corkey): I am
that there are arrangements in England
whereby boys intending to become elementary teachers may attend a training
college for a strictly limited period before
being called up for military service. The.
situation in Northern Ireland is not, however, comparable with that which has
arisen in England. The question was
recently considered, and it was again
decided that in the national interest it
would not be advisable to resume the
training of men students at present.
Dr. LYLE: I should like to ask the
Minister if he is aware that in England
if a student qualifies for entrance to a
training college and is under the age of
17 years 9 months on October 1st he will
be permitted to continue in the training
college until March 31st, 1945, at the end
of which period arrangements are being
made for such students to sit for a special
final examination so that when he is conscripted for His Majesty's Forces he will
enter such as a fully qualified teacher if
he passes the special final examination.
I should also like to ask the Minister if
similar arrangements could not be made
in Northern Ireland and thus obviate the
very serious state of affairs which will
arise after the war, or even before the
termination of the war, when there will
be a serious shortage of public elementary
teachers in Northern Ireland.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: Yes, I am
aware of the facts which the hon. Member
has cited, but owing to the fact that in
England conscription is in force, while
in Northern Ireland it is not in force, it
is difficult to make comparable arrangements here. We realise that education is
suffering here to some extent, but not
nearly to the same extent as in England,
and we feel that as far as possible we
ought to keep in step with England in
regard to this matter.
Dr. LYLE: Is the Minister aware that
in the case of doctors appointed as house
surgeons to hospitals they are required to
give an undertaking before getting the
appointment that at the end of the period
of their appointment they will join His
Majesty's Forces? Could a similar undertaking not be exacted from students entering the training college in Northern
Ireland?

time obviate the necessity of the children
absenting themselves from school when
the school is in operation. These recommendations include the closing for vacations only when it is clear that the services
of the children are actually needed, and
the shortening of the school day for the
elder pupils for a limited time.
So far as secondary schools are concerned, as a result of a conference held
last month a circular letter is being prepared and will shortly be issued recommending that the arrangements which
were in force in 1942 should, in general,
hold good for the forthcoming harvest
season.
The granting of permission to students
attending Queen's University to help with
the harvest does not come within this
Ministry's jurisdiction.

Industrial Position.
PROVINCIAL AREAS.
4. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of his dual
post, including that of Minister of Commerce and Production, he can give an
assurance that he will take into account
the industrial position of provincial areas
of Northern Ireland when deciding on
any scheme of industrial revival and reconstruction; and whether he would agree
to the setting up of an Industrial Council
representative of industrialists and
workers in order to lay the basis of
prosperity in Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I can readily give the hon.
Member the assurance that the availability
of labour accommodation in provincial
areas is being taken into account in
negotiations which are constantly going on
between the Ministry of Commerce and
Production and Imperial Departments regarding the setting up of industries in
Northern Ireland. There is already in
existence a Production Council on which
organised labour as well as employers are
represented. This body meets regularly
under my chairmanship. Moreover, so
far as post-war planning is concerned, I
have already arranged with the Planning
Advisory Board for the establishment of
a committee to deal with questions relating to the location of industry in Northern Ireland.

Member.

Oral Answers
The Budget
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
tribunal, and whether he will arrange

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): Under the Unemployment
Assistance Act (Northern Ireland), 1934,
assistance can be given only to persons
who satisfy certain conditions, one of
which is that they must be capable of, and
available for, work. In applying this test
the Assistance Board takes into consideration in each case the reasonable opportunities for employment that have
existed for the individual; and, in the
case of elderly applicants, age is one of
the factors to which particular attention
is given; but the Board cannot be more
sympathetic than the law allows it to be.
As regards the remainder of the question, Mr. Kinnear is a Barrister-at-Law,
as well as a retired civil servant, and has
acted for a number of years as chairman
of courts of referees and appeals tribunals.
His experience and training fully qualify
him to discharge the duties of this position.

Manufacturing Company, Limited, and

Budget Statement by

sure the
Major SINCLAIR: I am
Committee will allow me to take this my
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
18 MAY 1943
earliest opportunity of paying tribute to
my predecessor in office and to assure him
that, while I admit that it is not without
pride that I find myself called upon to
deliver this Budget Speech, it is also with
sincere regret. I should have much preferred to have helped in the preparation
of the Budget-as I have done for the
last two years—but that it should have.
been delivered by my right hon. Friend
in that clear and lucid way which the
Committee knows so well. But my chief
regret is that my appearance here means
the severance of what I believe to have
been a very happy partnership in the
Ministry of Finance, during which-as
the Committee will, I know, appreciate-
I have received nothing but courtesy,
kindness, and help from my right hon.
Friend. During the last two years and
some months we have worked in the
closest harmony, and our relationships
have been of the happiest. I can only
hope that, in the interests of Northern
Ireland, I may have absorbed during that
period some of his wisdom, courtesy and
tact, some of his wide experience of men
and affairs, and that I may, therefore,
be able to discharge the duties of this
office as he himself would like to see them
discharged. That will certainly be my
wish and my endeavour.
Indeed, in view of the fact that the
recent Cabinet changes occurred only a
week or so before the delivery of this
Budget Speech, I should, I think, point
out to the Committee that the many satisfactory features, which I am able to record, are matters in which my right hon.
Friend took a personal interest, and are
due in no small measure to his wise
guidance and decisions.
In presenting his Budget of last year
my right hon. Friend ventured the hope
that the war effort of our Province would
make a whole-hearted contribution towards turning the progress of the war
from defence to attack, and it is with
feelings of profound thankfulness to
Providence, and of hope for the future,
that we
can contemplate the stirring
happenings of the past eventful year and,
in particular, of the past few weeks, and
take pride in the fact that in these
historic events Ulster sailors, soldiers,
airmen, and members of the women's
services, including our great Ulster
generals, have played such a conspicuous
part.
But I am dealing to-day with finance,
and we must go forward, and efforts must
be redoubled, on the financial front as
well as on every other front, if we are to
finish the job as quickly as possible, which
must be the wish of all of us.
I feel that the wise policy of the
Chancellor of the Exchequer in meeting
so great a part of the cost of the war
from taxation-great though the load undoubtedly is has met with general
approval. By this means our people have
avoided passing much of the burden on to
posterity, while as regards the balance of
the cost which has been met from savings
lent to the State, we have proclaimed our
faith in the financial stability and future
prosperity of the nation.
It has sometimes been suggested that
because Northern Ireland is relatively
poorer than Great Britain rates of taxation on incomes should be lower here
than in the rest of the United Kingdom.
Such a suggestion is based on a faulty
understanding of the meaning of taxable
capacity. If Northern Ireland were as
wealthy as the rest of the Kingdom, the
amount of our Imperial contribution
would be several times greater than it is,
and if we
upon
were called
to
pay
according to a population basis and
taxation were scaled to give the same
amount per head here as in Great Britain,
then indeed we would have a case to
argue, because our rates of taxation would
have to be substantially higher. But
our contribution is not based on population. It is based on our capacity to pay,
and I submit that to suggest that the
rate of income-tax in Northern Ireland
should be lower than in the rest of the
United Kingdom reveals a misunderstanding of that position. We may well ask
those who argue that direct taxes should
be lower in Northern Ireland why a man
earning £5 a week or £500 a year should
pay less towards the cost of the war because he lives in Belfast and not in
London. I think the case could better be
argued the other way, that it might be
said that the Londoner was entitled to
some relief because the cost of living in
that city is higher than in the Provinces,
a fact which many hon. Members must
have appreciated from their own experience.
I believe that those of us who are
whole-heartedly behind the British Government in prosecuting the war with the
utmost vigour will not wish to make any
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
smaller sacrifice than our fellow-citizens
across the water or, for that matter, to
see the Northern Ireland proceeds of war
taxation diverted from the purpose for
which they are raised.
I believe that taxation both direct and
indirect is more or less cheerfully borne
in the belief that the sacrifices we are
asked to bear, in common with the rest
of the people of the United Kingdom, are
part of our individual contribution to the
war and help as far as lies in our power
towards its early conclusion. There are
some who assert that part of this money,
even a small part, should be held back
and used for local Northern Ireland purposes. But surely those people ignore
how and why this large sum of money is
raised. To talk about keeping back
£50,000 or £100,000 out of our Imperial
contribution would be absurd when the
Government are asking the people through
Wings for Victory weeks, and in other
ways, to lend sixpences, shillings, halfcrowns, or what ever they can afford. It
takes a great many weekly sixpenny savings stamps, for which urgent appeals are
made, to make up even
thousand
pounds. It is in the knowledge that
every penny that can be raised is needed
for the war that we must carry on our
Government, and it is with that thought
in my mind that I hope to carry out my
duties as Minister of Finance. That does
not mean that cheeseparing should be
carried to the point where efficiency suffers
and it becomes a false economy, or that
normal peace-time services should be unduly curtailed.
a
But it does mean that the necessity to
avoid extravagance and waste is more
(Hon.
urgent now than ever before.
Members: Hear, hear.) While I am
sure the Committee will agree with that
statement, I wonder if all our people
realise how necessary it is to avoid extravagance and waste in our private expenditure as well as in our public expenditure. A number are in receipt of lower
incomes than before the war, either
through taxation, the disorganisation of
their businesses, or their employers' business, or from some other cause
unfortunately, because the breadwinner
is serving in the Forces-but there are a
vast number who are a great deal better
off. Rationing and controls have reduced
the varieties of goods and services on
-
some,
which these increased incomes can be
spent, but there are still many openings
for expenditure on unnecessary luxuries.
Such expenditure and the total war in
which we are engaged are incompatible.
We must all search our hearts to ensure
that we are cutting down our personal
expenditure to the lowest point compatible
with the relatively high standard of living
we are still able to enjoy, thanks to the
bravery and the endurance of our armed
forces and mercantile marine. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The balance of
our income should then be lent to the
State to hurry forward the end of hostilities and the return of our men and women
to their homes and their normal occupations. I hope hon. Members, as leaders
of the people in their constituencies, will
do all they can to encourage a limitation
of spending and an increase in lending.
Particular importance must, therefore,
be attached to the war savings campaign,
for savings can both bridge the gap between revenue and expenditure and limit
production to essential war-time requirements. What then can Northern Ireland
say in regard to its savings record since
the war began?

of war savings in Northern Ireland from
November, 1939, to March, 1943, is,
approximately £69,000,000, of which
over £10,000,000 represents the proceeds
of Ulster Savings Certificates received,
and advanced to the British Exchequer,
and it is satisfactory to note that
the proceeds of the sales of these certificates at £4,456,000 in the financial year
just ended, exceeded the previous year's
total by £1,418,000. These are substantial figures, and to a large extent
have
possible by
by the
strenuous and sustained efforts of a devoted band of voluntary workers to whose
contribution in this way to the prosecution of the war I now pay tribute. These
figures do not, of course, include the results of the recent successful Wings for
Victory Weeks in the cities of Belfast and
Londonderry, and in congratulating them
on those results I express the hope that
the opportunity of making a very special

Let me deal now with other matters
within our direct financial control. My

right hon. Friend mentioned last year

We have disposed entirely of

3 per cent stock. Simultaneously, we

our credit. This operation
enabled not only the extinction of the

more fully
present position will be
