We may, I think, congratulate ourselves on the partial establishment of our
Government Loans Fund borrowing on a
3 per cent. basis and we are entitled to
regard the success of this issue as a hopeful augury for the future.
In this connection, I am happy to be
able to announce that under arrangements completed during the last few days
I am able to reduce interest rates on
future Government Loan Fund lendings
in certain cases from 4 per cent to 3
per cent. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This concession operates only on new
loans which I consider to be virtually giltedged, namely those covered by the
security of local authority rates. While
this reduction in interest may not be of
widespread application during the present emergency when such borrowing is
restricted, it is, I think, an earnest of
the Government's intention to make
available to local authorities at the
lowest possible rates, money which they
will require for post-war development. As
the total of such borrowings is likely to
be far in excess of the present capital of
the Government Loans Fund, the actual
post-war rate of interest will naturally
depend on the rate at which the Government can borrow from the public for the
purpose.
Other debt repayments included the repayment of Ulster Savings Certificates to
an amount of £534,500, the cancellation
of £187,200 Northern Ireland 33 per cent.
stock, and the repayment of Exchequer
borrowings from the Government Loans
Fund for Housing, Bann Drainage, etc.,
amounting to over £158,000.
Borrowings on Treasury Bills and other
short-dated advances were entirely repaid
before the close of the year, the average
borrowing rate-after over three years of
war-remaining at about one per cent.
per annum. Last year my right hon.
Friend referred to a most satisfactory
arrangement, whereby the proceeds of
the realisation of Loans Guarantee securities in so far as they were no longer to
be applied to the original commitments,
should be utilised in extinguishing our
Unemployment Suspense Debt. We have
so applied receipts under the Loans
Guarantee Acts that the debt, which
under normal circumstances would not
have been redeemed until 1995, will probably be completely extinguished in the
course of the current financial year. In
addition, following the agreed policy of
keeping our Unemployment Fund in
parity with the British fund, we have
now built up an investment surplus in
that fund which amounts to over
£4,000,000.
Hon. Members will have observed
from the White Paper on the Loans
Guarantee Acts, recently circulated and
covering the year ended 31st March last,
that our contingent liabilities, which at
one time were outstanding at a figure of
over £11,726,000-the gross amount of
our guarantees was £21,000,000—have
now been reduced to £725,000. As this
latter sum is fully secured, and as it is
most improbable that anything can
happen to prevent its progressive repayment by the few companies concerned, we
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
our
are for the first time in a position to take
stock of the outcome of
Loans
Guarantee transactions. The actual
issues which had to be met from the
Exchequer over a period of several years
amounted to some £4,500,000, and hon.
Members will appreciate that when the
Exchequer was called upon to implement
guarantees to that extent it became entitled to the securities in the possession
of the original lenders. The realisation
of some of these securities has already
brought in approximately £2,000,000, so
that Exchequer advances have thereby
been reduced and are now some
£2,500,000. A conservative valuation of
the securities covering this suggests that
on a final wind-up a profit rather than a
loss will result, but I need not emphasise
to the Committee, which is well aware of
the circumstances, that if these advances
had proved irrecoverable the money
would nevertheless have been well spent.
Despite the unforeseen effects of the
war, with its necessary restrictions on
many forms of industrial activity, hon.
Members will have observed from the
special White Paper that virtually no
default exists on loans advanced under
the New Industries Acts. The firms
which have been assisted under these
Acts have largely adapted themselves to
and are engaged in essential war work.
I could give numerous other examples
of the soundness of our finances and
economic structure, but I think enough
has been said to indicate our security and
credit, and I propose now to review, as
briefly as possible, the revenue and expenditure figures for last year. I therefore ask the Members of the Committee
to examine the figures given on pages 2
and 3 of the White Paper, and, with
some more detail, on pages 4 and 5.
of
All our Estimates
transferred
revenue were exceeded in a greater or
less degree.
Estate Duty showed an increase of
£77,000, and Stamp Duties increased by
£47,000.
The increased Entertainments Duty
largely accounts for the exceeding of
£121,000 over the Estimate for Excise
Duties.
There is an increase, rather surprisingly,
of £87,000 on the estimate for Motor
Vehicles Duties, and a corresponding
increase in the payment to the Road
Fund.
The items of non-tax revenue,
which
include a payment of £200,000 in
interest by the Road Transport Board,
are well up to or beyond the estimates
and call for no special comment.
On the expenditure side the most noteworthy feature, arising mainly from the
fact that certain emergency services have
passed the peak of expenditure, is that
issues for supply services were some
£1,635,000 below the total provision made.
by Parliament.
An increase in expenditure on Consolidated Fund services is accounted for,
apart from the Road Fund item to which
I have already referred, by an acceleration of the final interest payment on the
redemption of Ulster 3 per cent. Stock,
and an adjustment, which is entirely a
matter of book-keeping, as between payments from capital and from revenue in
connection with issues under the Loans
Guarantee Acts.
Expenditure, 1943-1944.
I turn now to a brief outline of our
estimated revenue and expenditure position for the current year, the relevant
figures being set out in the third column
of Tables II and III on pages 4 and 5,
and Table VII on page 8 of the White
Paper.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
The provision for interest on borrowings
at £140,000 is reduced by over £100,000
as compared with last year, largely caused
by the extinction of debt to which I have
already referred. Full provision for our
various Sinking Funds is made in the
next item of £313,000.
The estimated payment of £550,000 to
the Road Fund is more or less a shot in
the dark, and must be so under the uncertain conditions which prevail to-day.
The substantial reduction to a £20,000
provision for miscellaneous services arises
from the fact that, so far as we can
reasonably foresee, no further advances
under the Loans Guarantee Acts will
require to be made. The total provision
for Consolidated Fund services is therefore £1,023,000.
SUPPLY SERVICES.
The provision in the published Estimates for Supply services representing a
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
18 MAY 1943
decrease of £1,727,000 from last year's
total is £15,545,000.
RESERVED SERVICES.
The cost of Reserved services is estimated at £2,700,000.
MISCELLANEOUS EXPENDITURE.
Other items of expenditure which
appear on page 8 are the usual provision
for payment to the Imperial Government
of the proceeds of new Land Purchase
Annuities and pre-1922 Local Loans, collected by us and shown as receipts on the
revenue side of the account, which
amount to £338,000.
an
Finally, provision is made for
adjustment in connection with the Residuary Share for 1941-42, amounting to
£308,000.
The total estimated expenditure in the
year is therefore £19,914,000.
Revenue, 1943-1944.
TRANSFERRED TAX REVENUE.
Turning to the revenue side, transferred
tax revenue is estimated to yield a total
of £2,360,000. Of this Estate Duties
are estimated at £750,000.
I intend to submit to the Committee a
proposal to reduce the rate of interest on
these duties from 4 per cent. per annum
to 3 per cent. Other concessions proposed relate to relief from certain death
duties in the case of dispositions of property to an adopted child, and vice versa
to an adopter, and to the exemption from
Corporation Duty of trade unions and
trade protection associations. In the
other direction it is proposed to amend
the law to ensure that the
that the payment
of Estate Duty shall not be prejudiced
on the cessation by death of a limited
interest. These matters, however, while
of administrative importance, are mainly
of a technical nature and very limited
application, and will, of course, be fully
considered on a Finance Bill to be presented in due course.
Revenue from Stamp Duties is estimated to provide £250,000.
I will submit to the Committee a
Resolution to increase as from the 30th
May, 1943, the scales of Entertainments
Duty to those now operative in Great
Britain, and I am budgeting, therefore,
for an increased revenue from this source
of £113,000, making a total of £690,000
from all transferred Excise Duties.
The estimate of £670,000 for Motor
Vehicle Duties must be considered in the
light of the cautionary remarks which I
have already made in this connection.
The proposed concession in the case of
agricultural tractors, already announced
in the House as a matter of urgency, will
cost £8,000 in the year.
NON-TAX REVENUE (TRANSFERRED).
I have estimated the total from all
sources of transferred non-tax revenue at
£1,383,000, this figure including the
local contribution to Education Services
and interest payments by the Road
Transport Board.
RESERVE TAX REVENUE.
The total estimated receipt of Reserved
Revenue is the striking figure of
£41,992,000.
The various changes in taxation have
been fully explained by the Chancellor
of the Exchequer, and the estimated
receipts under the various heads are set
out in the third column of Table III on
page 5.
RESERVED NON-TAX REVENUE.
Revenue from the Post Office, etc., is
estimated to produce £2,142,000.
MISCELLANEOUS RECEIPTS.
To these figures I have to add the items
appearing only on page 8, namely New
Land Purchase Annuities and Local
Loans, £338,000; Residuary Share
adjustment for 1941-42, £42,000; and
finally the estimated receipt of
£3,568,000 from the Imperial Votes of
Credit, for services arising out of the war
which are met over the "Datum Line"
as transferred services. I will refer to
this Datum Line later.
Total receipts from all sources are
therefore estimated at £51,825,000, and
deducting the estimated total expenditure of £19,914,000 I am left with a
balance of £31,911,000.
I am, therefore, happy to be able to
announce that, after allowing for a surplus of £111,000, our estimated Imperial
contribution for the year is no less a sum
than £31,800,000. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
By comparison, the contribution for
the year 1941-42 has been finally determined at £17,600,000, as compared with
an original estimate of £11,750,000, and
in view of the increased yield of revenue
last year for the United Kingdom as a
whole I am hopeful that the estimated
contribution of £21,300,000 for 1942-43
may, on final attribution, more nearly
approach thirty millions.
There is, I think, in many minds a
misunderstanding of the position with
regard to this Imperial contribution. I
hope that it may be made clearer by the
remarks I made earlier to-day and the
few I intend to add now. We must, of
course, consider this contribution in the
light of the estimated yield of almost
£3,000,000,000 raised by taxation from
the United Kingdom as a whole for
war purposes. If we study the details
of our war-time
revenue, which
make up the estimated contribution
of £31,800,000, it will be seen that
this amount is, to all intents and purposes, derived in approximately equal
proportions from Excess Profits Tax,
the various luxury duties and the wartime increase in income-tax and sur-tax.
That is, it is very largely derived from
taxes and duties which have been imposed
for the dual purpose of raising revenue
for the prosecution of the war and of curtailing unnecessary consumption of goods.
and services. That fact must not be lost
sight of, that this greatly increased
Imperial contribution is raised by war
taxation for war purposes and for nothing
else.
Having said this, I must also refer to
the obverse of the medal, the arrangement which we have with His Majesty's
Treasury to govern our war-time finance.
Put very briefly, but I hope none the less
clearly for that, a datum line has been
fixed which arbitrarily represents our
normal peace-time expenditure. The
effect of this arrangement is virtually to
stabilise our Budget. The income of the
Province from whatever source, but
ignoring certain self-balancing items, in
excess of this datum line, is regarded as
our Imperial contribution. But, on the
other hand, our expenditure over the
datum is regarded as expenditure due to
war causes and, as such, is specially recouped to our Exchequer from Imperial
Votes of Credit. Furthermore, by
arrangement with the Treasury, we may
rank as war expenditure for purposes of
payments from the Votes of Credit, expenditure on such services which may be
admitted to be below the standard operative in Great Britain, where a case can
be made out that the improvement in
these services is desirable, not from the
purely social amenity standpoint, but for
the improvement or maintenance of the
moral and general health of our people in
connection with the prosecution of the
war.
Active consideration is being given at
present to various schemes of this nature,
but I must repeat, subject to the overriding proviso that anything done in war
time must have its bearing on the war
itself. I have, however, not found it
necessary to include any provision for
their financing because, as I have already
explained, their cost will be met from
Imperial sources, and will, therefore, be
-as far as our accounts are concernedentirely self-balancing; that is to say
that, in so far as they are the subject of
Supplementary Estimates for which no
provision is made in the Budget, their
cost will be met by an increase in the
amount allowed to our Exchequer from
the Votes of Credit.
And here I should like to put on record
the fact that in war as in peace where
a reasonable case has been made out, it
has invariably been met by the Chancellor
of the Exchequer, and the officials of
H.M. Treasury with sympathy, understanding and help. It is too early to
forecast what our exact relations with the
Imperial Exchequer will be in the postwar years, but this can be said; that provided we maintain the principles of parity
in taxation our standards of social and
other services will be equally maintained.
Indeed the nature of our financial
arrangements with the Mother Country
provide that, even if in peace time the
yield of taxation in our Province is in
itself insufficient to maintain those services on similar Ines, means will be found
to make good the deficit.
In conclusion, I must point out that a
substantial part of our individual war
taxation and, consequently, of the Province's Imperial contribution is, in fact,
a loan to the Exchequer as Post Office
Savings Bank credits for income-tax or
credits for excess profits tax, the repayment of which in due course will be a
The Budget-
Debate
18 MAY 1943
charge on the British Exchequer, forming
a refund of part of the amounts for which
we now take credit as contribution. Sir,
I have every confidence that should still
further financial sacrifices be called for
from the British people as a whole, and
let us hope nothing more will be required.
of us, the people of Northern Ireland will
respond cheerfully to the call.
Mr. AGNEW: I wish to pay my
tribute to the new Minister of Finance
for his clear explanation of the finances
of Northern Ireland, and I feel that he
owes a debt of gratitude to his predecessor
for the kind way he has helped him in
bringing forward his first Budget. While
we on this side of the House view the
picture from what I might say is the
proper angle, we cannot feel as confident
as the Minister of Finance
as to the
situation in Northern Ireland. I know
the Minister himself has tried to paint a
very beautiful picture, but we who belong to the working-class movement must
say that all that has been said does not
really exist. I feel that the industrial
prosperity of Northern Ireland means
happiness for our people. We may produce a volume of figures, we may
produce various financial arrangements,
but the big issue that the Government and
the Minister of Finance have got to face
up to is, what benefit it will be to the
working people of Northern Ireland.
Does it mean we have abolished poverty,
that we have abolished want, and that
in view of what the Minister said, all is
well? The ex-Prime Minister states that
we have abolished workhouses. Well, it
seems to me that, despite financial
arrangements, the craving in Northern
Ireland is to find work for the workers of
Ulster in Northern Ireland, and when the
Minister of Finance is producing the
Budget he should be clear and concise and
give at least some semblance to the
realities of the situation which prevails
in Northern Ireland.
I am not speaking as a Member of
Parliament for the city of Belfast, but as
a Member from a provincial area. I can
see what it means to find our industries
in actual ruin and decay. I can see what
was once a happy area for the linen industry dormant and silent. Yet the
Minister of Finance comes along to this
House and gives us an excellent survey
financially, when we know beyond any
contradiction whatever that the industrial
situation in Northern Ireland is at its
lowest ebb in the provincial areas, despite
what we are told by the right hon.
Gentleman of Ulster's war effort. Seeing
that the Minister of Finance in his first
Budget speech has presented a picture of
the financial solvency of Northern Ireland, I should like him to take a trip
through Northern Ireland and see for
himself what the actual situation is industrially. I say the Government have
failed to free the people in industry from
the difficulties which face them at the
present time, and I hope that in the
course of this year the Minister will
find time to visit some of the
areas which I know, and which the
Government know, for they have been
told about them often from this side of
the House, but they have apparently forgotten them altogether. They have not
made any effort, and we have told the
same story across the floor of the House
for the last five years.
In the county of Armagh, in my own.
constituency, and in various other constituencies, what do we find? I do not
care what figures may be produced by the
Minister; I say the well-being of the
community comes first in the production
of goods and services. If the right hon.
Gentleman wishes to know the exact details let him, before presenting the
Budget in future years, visit the areas of
Northern Ireland and see for himself, and
then let him come along here and tell the
facts as he sees them. There is no use
painting a beautiful picture for a people
who in thousands are deprived of the
right to work, and who are sent away
from their own land to work simply because the Government have not heeded
the call of the industrialists of Northern
Ireland. I am not saying that just because I want to say it. I have come in
contact with men who have spent all their
lives in industrial activity in Northern
Ireland, and who to-day, despite what
they may read of the solvency of Northern Ireland according to the Minister's
Budget, detest the Northern Government
by reason of the fact that when they put.
forward concrete plans as to certain industries in which they are interested, the
Government do not want to hear them.
The Government do not seem to realise
the fact that the men who are discussing
these problems are capable of dealing with
industrial problems. I think that should
The Budget-
Resolutions
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
be one of the main
concerns of this
Government, and the Minister of Finance
may, I hope, have the time to spare to
visit the black spots in Northern Ireland
and give us a truer picture than that he
has given to-day.
Let us take the position of Northern
Ireland in relation to Great Britain. We
are told we must have equality of sacrifice. We are taxed on the same basis as
the people of Great Britain. We know
exactly the position in Great Britain
to-day. We know why this has taken
place. The Government had developed
a plan prior to the war to see what could
be done in regard to industry and the
giving of employment in a particular
area of Great Britain. The people of
Northern Ireland have got to bear the
same burden. We are told by the
Minister to-day that the cost of living in
London is higher than it is in other
places, but we in Northern Ireland have
to pay the same taxation, direct and
indirect, as those who live in Great
Britain, and I wonder if we are in a
position to do so? That is the point. I
feel that the Minister, despite the enormous amount he is going to send away
as an Imperial contribution, should try
to impress on the Imperial Government
the necessity of at least giving the people
why pay the right to ask for something
in return from an industrial point of
view.
After all, if the people of Northern
Ireland are willing to bear the same
burdens and make the same sacrifices as
those in Great Britain, in view of our
unfortunate industrial position we should
ask that as we pay we should have some
little guarantee for to-day and tomorrow, and in the post-war years. In
all good faith I would suggest that the
Minister of Finance should make that
recommendation to the British Government, namely, that as we pay something
should be done for us. The Minister
said in his statement that if in the postwar years there was a deficiency it would
be made good. We are deficient to-day
in the industrial field, and we have our
unemployment problem, and I would
suggest to the Government that they
should make the well-being and welfare
of our citizens their main concern, and
give them the right to work at home.
We may produce volumes of figures as
to our financial stability, but it is the
well-being of our people that counts in
the end.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 20th May, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
The Cabinet.
INCOME-TAX ON MINISTERS'
SALARIES
1. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
in regard to his reply giving information.
as to Cabinet Ministers' salaries, if these
salaries are tax free or subject to the
payment of income-tax by the recipients.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): The salaries paid to Cabinet
Ministers are subject to deduction of
income-tax and of any other tax on income for which the recipient may be
liable. I should add that this also
applies to the salaries of Parliamentary
Secretaries.
Mr. BROWN: Might I ask the Prime
Minister if the allowance of £500 for civil
contingencies by which the salary of the
Prime Minister is to be increased will be
subject to income-tax, or will it be free
from income-tax?
Major SINCLAIR: The question of
the allowance to the Prime Minister will
be fully discussed on the Supplementary
Estimate on which it will be introduced
to the House.
Mr. BROWN: Is the Minister of
Finance in order in refusing information?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
has raised a point of order. The Minister
of Finance is in order.
Mr. NIXON: Would it not be better
for the Prime Minister to state what
everybody knows and about which there
is no secret?
PRIME MINISTER'S PORTFOLIOS.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if he intends holding the dual positions of
Premier and Minister of Commerce and
Production so long as the present Government is in office or only temporarily.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The normal procedure will be
followed in the event of any changes being
made in the constitution of the Cabinet.
Mr. BROWN: Does the Prime Minister
think it wise to retain these two offices
in view of the widespread feeling in the
country that there should not be one man
in two jobs of such importance? In view
of the fact that we have no evidence as
yet that there is going to be a change in
regard to the provision of war factories
in Northern Ireland will the Prime
Minister, who was and still is Minister of
Commerce and Production, consider this
matter, and in view of the widespread
opinion in the country that they are of
such importance that they should be held
by two Ministers, will he make separate
appointments?
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
general view is that there have been too
many Ministries in Northern Ireland, and
should it not be the policy of the Prime
Minister not alone to abolish one but to
go further and abolish more if he can?
The PRIME MINISTER: I gave a
reason for my retention of the portfolio
of the Ministry of Commerce and Production in my speech in the debate on the
Vote of Confidence, the reason being that
certain contacts have been established
which, in my opinion, it is necessary to
maintain.
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact that in
the debate on the Vote of Confidence it
was made perfectly clear that the position
to-day is not one bit better than it was
six months ago so far as the provision
and erection of factories in Northern Ireland is concerned and so far as the employment position is concerned? Would
it not be better to have the whole question of the erection of war factories and
the provision of war work for the unemployed approached from a new angle, in
view of the fact that we have made no
progress within the last six months?
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
reply of the Prime Minister, may I say
that it is the opinion of many Members
sitting on these back benches that the
Prime Minister's action is correct?

6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
names of the Directors on the Board of
the Northern Ireland Farmers' Bacon Co.
in which the pig producers have a controlling interest, the amount received by
each of these Directors for the years
1940-41-42 and up to 30th April, 1943, in
salaries and expenses; and whether an
additional Director was appointed by the
present Pigs Marketing Board and what
reasons were given for such appointment.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): With regard to
the first part of the question, I would
refer the hon. Member to the answers
given to the hon. Member for South
Down (Mr. Brown) on 3rd and 16th June,
1942. It was then explained that the
company is a private limited company,
and that the Minister of Agriculture does
not nominate or control in any way any
member of the Board. I am sure the
hon. Member as a previous director of
the company is aware that the remuneration of the directors is fixed by the
company and is a matter over which the
Ministry has no control or influence. The
Ministry has no information which would
lead it to believe that the directors'
remuneration has been varied since the
hon. Member served as a director.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
reply of the right hon. Gentleman, may
I ask whether it is not a fact that when
he himself was a member of the Pigs
Marketing Board he was quite satisfied
that three directors nominated by the Pigs
Marketing Board and each of the two
factories in which they had a controlling
interest were sufficient, and whether he is
still of that opinion?
PIGS MARKETING. BOARD.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
names of the members of the Pigs
Marketing Board, the number of meetings of the Board held during the years
1940-41-42 and up to 30th April, 1943;
and the amounts paid to the chairman
and other members of that Board in
salary, allowances and expenses during
the periods under review.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: With regard
to the first part of the question, this
information is set out in full in Hansard
of 12th March, 1942, together with the
number of meetings held by the Board in
1941. The number of meetings held by
the Pigs Marketing Board in 1942 was
3 as compared with 7 in 1940. So far
this year there have been two meetings.
With regard to the remuneration of
the chairman, this matter is dealt with
fully in my answer to the hon. Member
for South Down on Tuesday, 11th
instant, and on many previous occasions
by my predecessor. The fees to members
of the Pigs Marketing Board have not been
altered since the hon. Member served on
that body, and the consent of the Ministry was obtained for the fees and
allowances recommended by the Board
at that time. The attendance fees are at
the rate of two guineas per meeting, with
half-a-guinea subsistence and first-class
travelling expenses.

in reply to questions, and get away from

things could and should be kept secret?

the Minister considers whether £300 a
year is not rather large remuneration to

Written Replies.
CONDITION OF GILLES ROW,
ARMAGH.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will make
inquiries as to the sanitary conditions
prevailing in Gilles Row, Armagh, under
the control of Armagh Rural Council,
and whether the Minister will have investigations carried out in this area in
order to have proper sanitary conditions
installed.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I would inform the hon.
Member that the Ministry is aware of the
conditions prevailing in Gilles Row.
Investigations which have already been
carried out by the Ministry medical inspector show that the sanitary condition
of the houses in the row is not unsatisfactory, and that the chief source of
complaint relates to the condition of the
street, which has a very uneven surface.
The Rural Council have taken the view
that the condition of the street would not
warrant their compelling the owners to
incur any expenditure on its repair, and
as they are the responsible authority on
the matter, I am not prepared to
intervene.
REFUSAL OF POLICE CERTIFI-
CATE TO UNEMPLOYED.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state why
his Department (Police Branch) have
refused to certify over 400 unemployed
persons as suitable for work on certain
jobs in Northern Ireland; whether his
Department will review these cases if
fresh evidence is brought forward to
Written Replies
Ways and Means
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
prove that they are suitable persons to
undertake work of national importance;
whether such procedure is in force in
Britain; and whether he is satisfied that
suspicion is sufficient to debar a person
from such work.
Mr. LOWRY: It has already been
explained in a reply given in this House
by my predecessor, on the 7th July last
year, that the duty of the police in these
cases is limited to reporting frankly on
any individual about whom inquiries are
made by a competent authority, and that
the onus of deciding whether a person is
suitable for employment rests with the
employing department.
The question of reviewing cases is not
one for my Department, but if fresh facts
are produced in any particular case they
will certainly be brought to the notice of
the employing department.
I have no information as to the procedure in force in Great Britain, but I
feel quite certain that adequate
machinery exists for excluding undesirable persons from vital work connected
with the war effort.
The point raised in the last paragraph
of the question is one for the employing
department, and is one concerning which
I am not prepared to offer an opinion.
ARMAGH RURAL DISTRICT
LABOURERS' COTTAGES.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Armagh Rural Council increased the
rents of labourers' cottages; whether

Resolutions reported:
(1) Estate Duty in respect of Residuary
Estates-
That (1) there may be included in any
Act of the present Session relating to
finance such provisions as to estate duty
as Parliament may determine in relation
to the residue of the estate of a deceased
person and to the inclusion of property
representing such residue in the property
that passes or is deemed to pass on the
death of a person dying before the completion of the administration of the estate;
(2) any such Act may provide that the
said provisions shall have effect and be
deemed always to have had effect in relation to a person so dying whether before
or after the commencement of the said
Act.
(2) Amendment of Law-
That it is expedient to amend the law
relating to certain duties of excise, to
death duties, and to stamp duty, and to
make further provision in connection with
finance.

Mr. NIXON: I think I am the sole
representative here at the moment of any
semblance of an Opposition, and I know
I will get fair play from Mr. Speaker,
and I also know that that is all the fair
play I will get. Anything I may happen
to say that might be calculated to weaken
the political position of the Government
will not be seen again except in Hansard.
Consequently, you may rest your souls in
patience. But I think the first and most
important thing to do is to express my
agreement with the Minister in his
tribute to the fighting Forces. I and all
I represent, though you would not think
it very many, judging by the number of
M.P.'s on this side, but they are a great
many, are all out-and out for one thing,
and that is the breaking of the German
and Italian and Japanese armies for all
time.
I may say I was thrilled by the great
and diplomatic speech of our Imperial
Prime Minister, that you all heard on the
wireless. I know that now it is
customary to express approval whether
or not, but I think the approval is more
than justified. And I would like that
more politicians would copy Mr. Churchill
particularly in his reference to our great
Ally. That is one of the most important
things, and it is something that has to be
learned, because we may criticise each
other without doing any harm and doing
good possibly, but that criticism should
never be extended beyond ourselves except
to our enemies. His policy has borne
fruit, and it is largely due to his wise
policy that we have the two greatest Allies
in the world-U.S.A. and Soviet Russia.
The Minister of Finance made a good
speech, and I want to pay a tribute to
him before I give him some of the other
stuff. That is in the matter of complaints
that are brought to the Minister. It is

He threw down his resignation and said:

There is a grant of almost 32 millions
to the Imperial Government for defence
purposes. I am one person who will vote
anything at all for defence. I will vote
for as much as we can afford, and even
far more than we can afford, but I am
entitled to ask that it be wisely spent.
You may say you have nothing to do with
the spending of the money, and that you
hand it over. I know that is right. Mr.
Speaker would rule that, but certainly,
without going too far, I think that perhaps this is an opportunity to state that
it is not being wisely spent. I am not
referring to the moneys spent on the men
who are fighting or their dependants, but
to money spent on departments that are
quite unnecessary. I do not want to
name them at the moment.

I was going to make a suggestion about
part of that 32 millions that might perhaps appeal to the House. We have a
good deal of unemployment. We have
shipyards, air factories, and various other
factories. Would it not be possible to
hand over 16 millions, roughly speaking
-I am only putting this forward as a
principle and say to the Imperial
Government: "Now, we have another 16
millions for you, but we have shipyards
and aircraft factories. What do you
want us to build? We will build it and
hand it over to you. Give us the design
and specifications for 16 millions' worth
of war material that you require and we
will produce it in our own factories. Our
own people are entitled to work. They
are not all getting work. We can retain
that money for work here and give you
the goods.
"None of our Colonies that I
know of are handing over money. Canada
is making a wonderful effort, and is
building and handing over ships and
munitions. So are Australia and New
Zealand. Every bit of the British.
Empire is doing so except one spot, and
that is not here, but it is not far away.
Could there not be something like that
done? In any case, that takes me to
the question of unemployment. Unemployment here in the fourth year of the
war is as bad as ever. I thought the
Minister of Labour would be in his place.
There must be some reason why he is not
here to give an answer he promised to a
question. The matter is really serious,
far more serious than members of the
Government who may not be in touch
with ordinary people really think.
Somebody made an order that practically
nobody will get work in Northern Ireland
unless he was in the Army or was an exsoldier. There is a person listening to
me who tried to join up and was rejected
on medical grounds. When he asked for
work, he was told he could not get it
unless he had been in the Army. His
allowance was stopped for six weeks. I
always bring my evidence with me, and I
have it with me now.
That is only one illustration. Yesterday I signed a recommendation for a
young fellow who wants to join the Air
Force, but who does not think he will get
away because he is in Mackie's, and I do
not think he will get away. He is 22
years of age, but according to the quality
of his work he is supposed to be
deserting-

Report
Ways and Means-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
was
an
of Finance. The ex-Minister
expert in the field of finance. My mind
travels back to the time when I entered
this House. We had then in the position
another great expert, the late Rt. Hon.
H. M. Pollock. After his death the
position fell into the hands of the right
hon. Member for Mid-Down, to whom a
tribute has been paid by one of the
greatest Prime Minister's Great Britain
has ever had. With your permission I
should like to have recorded in Hansard
that splendid tribute which was paid to
the ex-Prime Minister. I am going to
read the letter which was read from Mr.
Churchill, so that generations yet unborn will find in Hansard the type of
statesmen Ulster had from 1921 until
1943. This is the letter:
My Dear Mr. Andrews,—I am,
indeed, sorry that the ties which have
been so warmly established between us
in our public work should have to be
broken. After your long services to
Northern Ireland as Minister of Labour
and as Minister of Finance, you became Prime Minister in December,
1940.
That was a dark and dangerous hour.
We were alone, and had to face singlehanded the full fury of the German
attack, raining down death and destruction on our cities, and, still more
deadly, seeking to strangle our life by
cutting off the entry to our ports of the
ships which brought us our food and
the weapons we so sorely needed.
Only one great channel of entry remained open.
That channel remained
open because loyal Ulster gave us the
full use of the Northern Irish ports and
waters, and thus ensured the free working of the Clyde and the Mersey. But
for the loyalty of Northern Ireland and
its devotion to what has now become the
cause of thirty Governments or nations,
we should have been confronted with
slavery and death, and the light which
now shines so strongly throughout the
world would have been quenched.
To you fell the honour of being at the
head of the Government of Northern
Ireland not only during the supreme
crisis, but throughout the two and a
half years which have led us steadily
forward to safety and final deliverance.
I have always found you a faithful and
helpful colleague and comrade, and a
man who had no thought but to do his
duty. During your Premiership the
bonds of affection between Great Britain
and the people of Northern Ireland
have been tempered by fire, and are
now, I firmly believe, unbreakable.
You carry with you in your retirement the regard and respect of all who
have worked with you, including in a
grateful spirit.
Yours, very sincerely,
Winston S. Churchill.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That letter was written in connection
with an honour conferred upon our ex-
Prime Minister by His Gracious Majesty
the King, an honour which only three

that if we are going to stand idly by and

The statement which the Budget speech
contained was gratifying to me, as I am
sure it was to every Member of the House.
In the first place it was a pleasure to
know that the figures definitely settled
that our contribution in 1941-42 amounted
to no less a sum than £17,000,000, and
again, it has now been settled that the
contribution for 1942-43 will amount to
no less than £30,000,000, which greatly
exceeded the actual estimate. Then again
this year, after providing £111,000 as a
surplus, we are in a position to estimate
that the contribution to the British
Exchequer will be £31,800,000. No
doubt that is a conservative estimate, as
all these estimates very properly are, and
that sum may be substantially increased.
I am sure the more it is increased the
better we will be pleased, because it
makes it clear beyond doubt that financially as well as in other directions, Northern Ireland desires to play her part.
There are many other items in the
Budget statement that are particularly
gratifying to me. The old Unemployment Suspense Debt has been wiped out.
As hon. Members know, that was accumulated in the early days of this Parliament,
owing to the fact that the contributions
to the Unemployment Fund were not
sufficient to meet the outgoings, with the
result that a debt of approximately
£4,000,000 was created, and when the
Reinsurance Agreement was arranged
that debt was put in suspense, and an
arrangement was made by which it was
to be liquidated over a long period of
years. It is, indeed, gratifying that it
has been found possible to have it wiped
out completely during the past year.
Notwithstanding all that we heard over
and over again about the loss that was
going to be sustained in connection with
our Loans Guarantee arrangement, which
would be a burden that Ulster could not
afford, it is satisfactory to know that these
liabilities are being liquidated without
loss. May I say it is also particularly
gratifying to know that the Northern Ireland people are saving and lending to
such a substantial extent, and that
already during the war period
£69,000,000 has been raised in Northern
Ireland and passed on as a loan to the
British Exchequer to help to finance the
war? All these satisfactory conditions,
and others, have been brought about, in
my opinion, for three reasons. First of
all there is the increased general prosperity of our people, which cannot be
denied. In the second place there is increased taxation, and in the third place
it is due to various adjustments which
have been agreed to in connection with
our financial relations with Great Britain.
If I may say so, I have taken a considerable interest in Northern Ireland's
financial affairs since I served with the
late Mr. Pollock, whose memory we all
revere, with the late Mr. Stewart Blacker
Quin, who also was most helpful, and
others on a Committee over which the late
Sir L. Worthington Evans presided in
London. That Committee was established
to arrange what the financial arrangements
between Great Britain and Northern
Ireland would be at the time when the
Government of Ireland Act was passed, and
how the revenue raised in Northern Ireland would be apportioned as between the
amount spent here and the amount which
would be retained by the British Government for the Imperial Services. The
basis of that agreement, which has
worked out most satisfactorily, was in my
opinion absolutely fair. It was that we
would retain here such sums as
necessary in order to keep our services on
a par with similar services in Great
Britain, and that the balance would then
be retained by the British Government,
as I have already stated.

However, it was found by experience,
as time went on, that there were other
Ways and Means-
Report
20 MAY 1943
conditions that had not been thought of
at the time which would have to be provided for. It became quite apparent
early in our career as a Parliament that,
owing to the fact that we here were so
dependent on three industries-which
again are dependent far more on world
conditions than on Northern Ireland conditions at times, at any rate, our unemployment here would be in excess of that
in Great Britain, and would therefore
place upon our Unemployment Fund, and
on our Exchequer as a consequence, a
very serious liability. With the invaluable support and help of the then
Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr.
Churchill, the Reinsurance Agreement
was brought into existence, an agreement
which I have frequently said, and always
feel, is our working people's charter, because it established beyond all doubt the
principle that in connection with their
social services they were entitled to be
kept on the same plane as their fellowcitizens in Great Britain.
Then again, there were other matters
which, as time went on, had to be dealt
with. There was a danger ahead that
some day it was very apparent at one
time-our Budget would not be balanced,
because our financial affairs are very
largely controlled by what is done by the
British Treasury as regards the levying
of taxation itself. Therefore, it was felt
that as we were paying a contribution,
and a substantial one now that we are in
a position to do so, it was not unreasonable that if changes took place which
some day created here a debit balance, an
arrangement would be agreed to that that
debit balance would be made good. That
is a security for our financial position
which is well worth while.
Again, there were other changes which
became necessary. Our transport arrangements did not look well at one time, I
freely admit. It was felt that there
might be a serious situation created,
owing to our Transport Board being
burdened with an excess capital expenditure.
So an arrangement was made with
the British Chancellor by which that
capital liability of £4,000,000 would be
reduced by a sum of £2,000,000 by
means of a reduction from our contribution, spread over 15 years. Now, owing
to the exceptional conditions existing at
the present time, our Transport Board is
paying its full interest charges.
Other changes also required to be made,
and one of the most important in my
opinion has been made recently. It is
true that all those services which we took
over from Great Britain which were on a
par with what they were in Great Britain
at that time have been kept on a par. When
this Parliament came into being, certain
services were below the standard in Great
Britain, and an arrangement was made
a few months ago, I am glad to say,
which will enable us to make good the
lag and put on the British basis those
services such as health, which are at the
moment below British standards. Therefore, in congratulating my right hon.
Friend, the new Minister of Finance, on
the statement he was in a position to
place before the Committee on Tuesday, I
would like to add my sense of gratification
at the fact that our financial position in
Northern Ireland is sound almost beyond
measure.
In conclusion, I want to add that that
is to a considerable extent due to two
factors. The first is the happy relations
that exist between our Northern Ireland
Ministry of Finance and the British
Exchequer. In that connection I am entitled to add that that friendly and
helpful relationship has been largely due
to the able, painstaking, and thorough
way in which our officials here and the
officials of the British Treasury have
worked together for the betterment of the
United Kingdom.

interpretation means capacity to pay. I

that we in Ulster are in the same financial

water.

As the Members of the House know,
there was a time when we paid incometax on a valuation, but at the present
and for some years past we have been

entitled to a position of complete parity.
I repeat that it is a grave reflection upon

of a number of years we are in a position

In common with some other Members

Committee on Health Services on

position of deplorable inferiority with regard to our social services. It is imperative-I am speaking quite seriously
on this matter which is vital to the health

I will be satisfied.
Major SINCLAIR: I was coming
round to that, but what I was going to
say——
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister
kindly finish what I said?
Major SINCLAIR: I will follow the
wishes of the hon. Member and say that
his suggestion was that the £16,000,000,
which was to be kept, should be handed
to the Imperial Government in the form
of war supplies manufactured in this
country.
Mr. NIXON: That is it.
Major SINCLAIR: That was certainly
the suggestion. I should perhaps explain
that the question of the retention of any
part of the Imperial contribution is a
matter for the Imperial Government.
They collect these taxes here and they
allow to us what is called the residuary
share of reserved taxes which, together
with transferred taxation and other income, approximately equals our expenditure on the Consolidated Fund Services
and Supply Services. Consequently the
question of retention is rather on the
other foot. In any case I am afraid it is
not a practicable proposition. I should,
I think, point out that a very large part
of our contribution does in fact come to
Northern Ireland by means of contracts
placed here by the Supply Departments
of all kinds. I am not aware of the
amounts which those Supply Departments
do spend in Northern Ireland. I am
quite certain it is a very large figure, but
even if I were aware of it I do not think
it would be in the public interest to disclose it.
The hon. Member for Antrim, speaking
about the Imperial contribution, was
Ways and Means-
Report
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
rather concerned not about the present
position, but about what was going to
happen when the war is over.
He suggested that we might put money into a
sinking fund; he even suggested putting
money into a sinking fund when the war
is over. We do not know what we will
be able to do at that time, but as regards
our relations with the Imperial Government I think I can give the hon. Member
an assurance that when it comes to postwar reconstruction and finances are available for the Kingdom as a whole, Northern
Ireland will receive its due proportion.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And as a
matter of fact the Chancellor has agreed
that in many respects, as the hon.
Member for North Down has said, our
services are behind and there is a lag to
make up. To quote his own words, he
said, "Northern Ireland might confidently
rely on the Treasury always considering
such cases sympathetically as indeed the
principle of parity requires us to do."
I am aware that that does not meet the
hon. Member for North Down's point that
these social services should be improved
now and not wait until after the war, but
in my Budget speech I referred to the
datum line arrangement and to the fact
that the Treasury had agreed to allow
certain services which would improve the
health and moral of our people, to count
as war services and to be included in the
payment we receive from the Treasury
over the datum line. Therefore I was not
making any provision in my Budget for
Supplementary Estimates. I said that
active consideration was being given to
these problems and by that I did not mean
the deliberations of the Select Committee
the hon. Member referred to. I meant
that the Government itself was giving
active consideration to these problems,
and I hope proposals will be put before
the House in a very short time.
The hon. Member for North Down also
referred to our taxable capacity, and I
was glad to see he had as much difficulty
in pronouncing those two words together
as I had. (Laughter.) No one suggested that the average. was the same
as in Great Britain. The point I was
trying to make was that a man here and
a man in England with the same income
should be liable for the same amount of
tax. I cannot see any argument against
that, and that was really all I was trying
to bring out in my speech on Tuesday.
Again, on this question of improving our
services, particularly after the war, we
are interested in being able to get a
Northern Ireland here of which we will
all be proud, but we have got to think of
another side of that. We ourselves are
not going to be able to afford to spend
all the money we want here, and we do
want to share in the general pool of Great
Britain's money. I think we ought to
keep before us that if we try to hold back
anything now from the Imperial contribution-if we give Great Britain the
impression that both in work and in
money we are giving grudgingly-the
British people might very easily grudge
us money when the war is over. But if
the people here are going to play their
part absolutely up to the hilt we will get
a fair crack of the whip from the British
Treasury and the British people. I think
that is one thing we should keep in mind.
It is not perhaps the best motive for
giving, but it certainly is one. The hon.
Member for Mid Down I really think-

records of this House and stand for all

hundreds of tons of straw available for

are
no better purpose could be served than

Now in order that my position may not

help I can to bring to fruition the programme they have outlined for themselves. The programme, as far as I can

trying to bring that
bring that programme to

I know that new industries are very

Labour-I do feel that the time has come

We are prepared to give them the support they require in order to bring to
fruition the programme they have outlined. I suggest to the Prime Minister
that we ought to get to work immediately
so that these men whom we had to send
to Great Britain may be usefully employed

Report

that our people are properly housed and

Lord GLENTORAN: I should like
first of all to congratulate my right hon.
Friend on the excellent manner in which
he made his Budget statement in the
House. Like every Ulsterman, I was delighted to see the amount of money we
are able to contribute to His Majesty's
Government on the other side for the
prosecution of the war. It was a pleasure
not only for the reason that we are helping the war effort, but because it makes
clear not only in our own country but
outside that Ulster is doing well, and that
the Government is not as blameworthy,
according to speeches delivered, as it is
supposed to be. We were doing well
before the war, and we are doing well
now. I do not think that at any time
in the history of this country there was
so much liquid money in our midst. That
money is well distributed amongst every
class of people. It is quite remarkable
that in the 22 years we have had a
Government here we have actually contributed to the Exchequer ten times more
than the whole of Ireland contributed to
that Exchequer from the date of the Act
of Union to the 1920 Act. I think it can
be said for Ulster that she has played her
part in the last 22 years.
What I really rose to speak about was
that I regret, although I know the
reason, something could not have been
put into the Budget with reference to
help being given to certain industries.
We have been at war for some years.
The machine has been working overtime.
In many respects the machinery could do.
with a little renewal and repair. I notice
that has been recognised in England. I
see, for instance, that farmers are going
to get 30,000 houses for the whole of
Great Britain, and that large sums of
money are being spent on the reclamation
of land in England. I know quite well
that 30,000 houses would not be much,
but I think that the Minister of Finance
and the Government should watch very
carefully the sums now being spent in
England and Scotland on these reclamation and housing schemes.
I would particularly call the attention
of the right hon. Gentleman to the
speeches made by the Secretary for Scotland, Mr. Tom Johnston, a very able
man who thoroughly knows Scotland. As
far as I can see, Mr. Tom Johnston takes
the view that I have taken, and that is
that it is about time we did something
to help those people who have been working so hard for the nation. I know the
Prime Minister feels as I do, that it is
hard to drive and drive the farmers and
never give them anything. I myself was
not able to last the course and to be able
to do that, and I do not hold that against
my right hon. Friend who has taken my
place. I am going to help him so that
he will be able to do something that the

could not. I think there should be some

to the question of allowing 50 or 75 per
cent. of the amounts that farmers have
spent in carrying out repairs to cottages.
A little of the huge sum we collect could

I now come to the question of unemployment which is a matter dealt with in
the Budget. I want to call attention to a
statement made by the Prime Minister
last week in which he stated:
It may interest the House if at this
point I refer to the unemployment
situation in Northern Ireland to-day
and compare it with the position two
years ago. In January, 1941, when I
became Minister of Commerce, the
number of persons registered as unemployed was over 68,000. Since that
time the unemployment figure has been
steadily decreasing, and in April, 1943,
it had fallen to about 18,000.
The inference to be drawn from that
statement is that the credit for the reduction in the unemployment figure belongs
to the Prime Minister, who was then
Minister of Commerce. That is not in
accordance with the facts. In reply to
a question put by me in this House a
short time ago the then Minister of
Labour stated that since February 12,
1940, over 33,000 men and over 4,000
women had been placed in employment in
Great Britain by his Ministry.
Let me be quite frank and candid
about this matter. I never approved of
the policy of shipping people to Great
Britain; I always thought it would be
better to provide work for them at home.
I am of the opinion that both psychologically and economically the proper policy
is to have factories erected here and have
the people employed at home. In view of
the fact that over 33,000 men and 4,000
women were placed in employment in
Great Britain by the Minister of Labour
how can the Minister of Commerce claim
the credit for having brought down the
unemployment figure? That is not all.
We have lost the best Minister of
Agriculture we ever had, the noble Lord.
I deplore that fact. It should also be
remembered that he had his finger in a
good many pies in his time. He had his
finger in the pie in regard to reducing the
number of unemployed. He put on the
land in Ulster more workers than were
ever previously employed in agriculture.
We should give him credit for doing that.
He had a very difficult task to perform.
The previous Minister of Agriculture had
a comparatively simple task to perform
compared with that of the noble Lord.
The noble Lord had the task of adding to
what had already been achieved. That

HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 25th May, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Labour:
National Health Insurance (Dental
Benefit) Amendment Regulations (No. 2)
(Northern Ireland), 1943. (By Act.)
Oral Answers to Questions.
COMPENSATION FOR WAR
INJURIES.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether the Government propose to introduce legislation to
place men and women on a basis of
equality for war injuries similar to the
scheme proposed in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): Payment of compensation to persons in Northern Ireland who
have been injured by enemy action is
governed by an Act of the Imperial
Parliament-the Personal Injuries (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1939-which
applies to the United Kingdom as a
whole. Accordingly, the concession referred to by the hon. and gallant
Member regarding the equality of compensation for men and women will
automatically apply in Northern Ireland
in common with the rest of the United
Kingdom.
GOVERNMENT AND COMPANY
DIRECTORSHIPS.
5. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether it is the policy
of his Government that members of the
Government should continue to
directorships of public companies.
hold
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I am satisfied that the policy
which was pursued by the Governments
led by my two predecessors in office was
in the best interests of Northern Ireland,
and I see no grounds for departing from
the practice which has been followed for
21 years.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman state why he sees no reason
to depart from the very vicious practice
operating in Northern Ireland and which
has had to be stamped out in Great
Britain? In view of the serious position
caused by Members of the Cabinet holding
directorships, will he review the answer
he has given?
RECRUITING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
6. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state the
number of (a) men and (b) women who
have joined His Majesty's Forces in
Northern Ireland since the outbreak of
the war, and how many of these came
from Eire.
The PRIME MINISTER: As the hon.
and gallant Member was informed in
reply to a similar question on 28th April
last year, complete information is not
available as to the number of volunteers
from Northern Ireland who have joined
His Majesty's Forces since the outbreak
of war.
I am informed, however, that in
addition to the large numbers of Northern
Ireland men who were in the services and
in the Mercantile Marine before the war
as well as those Ulster men and women
who have joined the Forces in Great
Britain, the Northern Ireland recruits
who enlisted in Northern Ireland during
the period from the outbreak of war until
the 31st March last were-
(a) 27,600 men and (b) over 5,000
women.
I have no particulars of the number
of Eire citizens who have joined His
Majesty's Forces.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he is
aware from an authoritative source in
London that out of the grand total
recruited in Northern Ireland there are
20,000 citizens of Eire.
The PRIME MINISTER: No. I have
no information as to that.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman inquire into the authoritative
source, and is he aware that I have gone
into these figures in London and that the
statement has been made that 20,000 out
of the grand total are citizens of Eire!

CLASS I. No. 1.
HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £16,010 be
granted to His Majesty for the service of
the year ending the 31st March, 1944, to
complete the sum necessary to pay the
salaries and expenses of the Senate and
of the House of Commons. (Note-
£8,000 has been voted on account.)
Major SINCLAIR: The alteration in
this year's Estimate compared with last
year's is negligible, and consequently
there is nothing which, I think, requires
comment. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: With this Estimate
before me and knowing the work that this
Parliament is competent to carry out and
the value that the citizens of this area
receive, I do not think that any Member
of this House can charge me with being
irresponsible in what I am going to say.
I have designated this building many
times as a home from home, a better
home than some people who make it a
home ever had in their lives before, and
the time is now approaching when we
have to take the words of the Minister
of Finance more seriously than we have
done in the past. He has not in my
presence, but I have read it in Hansard,
advised everyone to have domestic savings
and cheese-paring in every unit of our
homes. Save, save, save. I wonder was
that lip-service or was it really a speech
trying to bring home to the have-nots
that they should do with less and leave
the haves quietly alone, because if he was
sincere in his utterances as reported in
Hansard then his first duty as Minister
of Finance is to tell the Department that
it is over-staffed and costing too much
money, and that in this Estimate we
expect to get a substantial saving. But
instead of that we have him getting up
here to-day and saying, No change, and
therefore there is nothing further to say
in regard to the amount which is being
asked.
But I want to have something to say.
I want to tell the right hon. Gentleman
and not only him, but to tell others also
that a more serious view is really being
taken of this House and its cost in
quarters that matter than has been taken
since the establishment of this Parliament. During the war we have been
deprived of much of the work that we
previously carried out. We have put
this building into what you would call
an evacuees' home, a home for refugees.
We have not given much accommodation
in this building to the Imperial servicesvery little and we have burdened the
Imperial cost of upkeep by renting very
substantial buildings outside Stormont in
the city of Belfast and not only in the
city of Belfast, but throughout the Six
Counties. All this adds to the enormous
cost of Services which should properly be
carried out in this building. From the
increased number in the various Departments requiring extra staff one would
believe there was insufficient accommodation in this building.
cent. more
The increased staffing could be explained in this way, there are 90 per
persons employed in the
Services of Northern Ireland than would
be necessary in connection with a reasonable or patriotic assembly who believed
that the first consideration should be the
finances of the people. Instead of that
the right hon. Gentleman preaches one
thing and practises another.
He can
talk as well as many other politicians
with his tongue in his cheek. He has
done that in the past, and I presume he
will do it in the new office for which he
is responsible. I want to tell him that
the cutting down of the costs of each
Department must be seriously considered
at once. That should be the first function
of a new Minister of Finance in regard
to the Houses of Parliament.
Can the right hon. Gentleman justify
all this elaborate expenditure that one
sees in this glorified House, supposed to
be composed of democratic representatives? I cannot see that any useful
Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
purpose would be served by my placing
before the right hon. Gentleman his
patriotic functions and duty. The first
item one has to consider is "Salaries and
allowances." This represents the sums
paid to Members of this House and of the
Senate. Then, "Salaries, wages and
allowances." When one looks at the
grand total and then examines the work
carried out in this House one wonders
whether anything of a similar kind
operates elsewhere in the world. I will
be told that the grades of the respective
officers have to be recognised and that
they must be paid according to their
grade.
Surely we do not need decorations in
well-paid jobs. There are too many
decorations in well-paid jobs in
jobs in this
House. During a period of war we can
do very well without them. The House
will not lose any of its prestige or dignity
by the immediate dismissal of any of the
ornaments to which I have referred. J
have watched the movement of certain
officers of this House, and to be quite
candid, I do not believe that county
family relationship should be the medium
through which a man should get a job
and then be retained in that job at great
cost to the State. Nor do I agreealthough the right hon. Gentleman will
agree that the old school tie should have
a certain amount of privilege in the
positions in this House. He knows that
the old school tie does operate very extensively in some of the key positions in
this House. It is time that we realised
that we are not old school tie people or of
supporters of the old family traditions,
but an industrial community, and we
believe that what we pay for we are
entitled to receive.
I claim that we do not receive the
service we are entitled to receive for the
amount of money we are asked to pass in
this House on this Estimate. It has been
stated by members of the newly-formed
Cabinet-it is rather a pity we cannot
get another word for it, because they do
not represent anything like a Cabinetthat the Belfast Corporation have been
carrying out their functions without fee
or reward. I wonder, when one finds
such a desire and ambition to be at the
City Hall at certain hours of the day and
to be at certain meetings when they are
taking place! There are two ways of
payment-the direct and the indirect. If
the Corporation of Belfast can administer
the city without all the paraphernalia
and all the decorations to be found in
these make-believe Houses of Parliament,
I think we should be able to do likewise.
Speaking to the members of the City
Council of Glasgow I tried to make them
realise what this Parliament costs us and
what it costs them. I had a copy of the
Estimates in Committee Room 14 at
Westminster, where the opportunity is
afforded Members like me who have the
great honour and privilege of belonging
to the Imperial House of putting my
view before them without being charged
with telling lies or of never having been
in the Army. All some people ever did
in the Army was to make latrine seats;
they never saw the front-line trenches.
That great assembly, which I had the
honour and privilege of speaking to last
week, were surprised and shocked at the
loyalty and patriotism spoken about so
often in the organ of the Unionist Party
which tries to extort from the public
purse money such as that I am now
criticising.
This Parliament meets only one-third
of the year-that is the maximum time
it sits and it could be run at less than
the public purse is asked to pay. There
is no officer in this House that I want to
decry. I have always found every one
of them fair and reasonable, and their
civility to me as has always been of a
kind that I appreciate very much, but I
want to be quite candid in my criticism
which is not of the person but of the
position. The salary attached to the
position of Chairman of Ways and Means
was reduced because my voice was raised
against it year after year. I thought a
beginning in that direction had been
made and that other reductions would
follow automatically. But no, that was
the only position interfered with.
There is the Clerk of this House at a
salary of £1,320. Everyone knows the
difference between being Clerk of this
House and Clerk to the British House,
and no one better than you, Sir Robert,
knows the difference in the amount of
work that has to be performed here and
in Great Britain. The clerkship of this
House is really a spare-time job. It could
be done in his spare time by any Member
of the House. I know that the moment
the right hon. Gentleman attempted to
Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
25 MAY 1943
interfere with any of these jobs he would
touch the old county family tradition and
the result would be that he would immediately lose his seat in the Cabinet.
The method by which seats were given in
the Cabinet can be employed to dispose
of those seats. Therefore, he will not
touch one of those jobs.
an
We have Assistant Clerk, and
£1,000 is a glorious salary to have to
help a man to carry out what I might
call a subsidiary occupation. Then we
have the Librarian. He is fully employed. But the Library is not of very
much use to hon. Members of this House
when they are away in their constituencies.
The only time they use the Library is
when the House is meeting, and it only
meets about 150 days in the year and
three hours a day. It will be found that
the total number of hours a year spent
in deliberation on behalf of the people is
very small. Next there is £276 for a
lady typist, and then the chaplains get
£150. I see the amount has been increased since the last time I reviewed
these figures. Perhaps that was for saying an additional prayer or two for the
new Cabinet. It is nearly time all these
things were reviewed in the light of
circumstances as we now see them. There
should be substantial reductions which
would effect a saving in conformity with
the statement of the right hon. Gentleman in his Budget speech.
Again, we have the Hansard staff. We
cannot employ them fully. The result
is that you bring on to the public purse a
charge which should not properly be.
borne to the extent it is borne on the
Estimate as I see it to-day. The major
portion of the work of the Hansard staff
is done outside the House. Why? Why
should you
interfere with trade union
rights of professional men who follow this
occupation as a livelihood? The Hansard
staff were appointed for this House, and
this House alone, but I find that the
greater portion of their time is spent
elsewhere doing work which professional
men should be engaged to perform. This
is due to the interference of the officious
staff of this House delegating work which
should be paid for through another
source.
It is very easy to find out the
reason for that. It is because they have
no work for Hansard; they do not want
the Hansard staff to be left idle, and
they delegate to them work at commissions for their friends who wish verbatim
reports of the proceedings to be kept for
their information. You have the assistant editor and reporters.
Then we come to the Serjeant-at-Arms.
There is only one Serjeant-at-Arms and
there are four doorkeepers. The latter
cost £720 and the Serjeant-at-Arms costs
£739 plus £200. Have we any room in
this Estimate for pensioners or any room
in it for money that could be spent in
another direction and more usefully
applied than at the present time? You
all know what the duties of the Serjeantat-Arms are, and the number of hours he
works each day. And yet you give him
a salary of £739 plus an allowance. I
understand he has also a very substantial pension. Maybe he got it from the
Army-the same Army as other people
belonged to, the Army that keeps miles
behind the trenches. I want to know
why this fee is still being maintained.
The Prime Minister might be in a position to give the Committee the information. It is said that new kings make
new laws and that new brooms sweep
clean. Here is some of the stuff that is
jammed into public funds. Is the
Minister prepared to clear it out? Perhaps he is and perhaps he is not. Again
the old county family tradition and the
old school tie come in. A revolt from
that undercurrent that is moving to such
an extent might unseat the right hon.
Gentleman from the ambitious position.
to which he has now attained.
have no hope for anything in this Estimate being cut down. All the signs are
pointing to an increase. Those who
helped to put the new rulers in will now
be seeking positions. As he is in danger
of his political life he cannot remove the
old gang.
He is depending on the old
as well as the new, and that being so I
have absolutely no hope of any startling
saving taking place in this Estimate.

being made the medium through which

news at all. It referred to the old committee room where they met and a

Prime Minister's speech. It was all political propaganda. The Empire Parliamentary Association will have to be
cleansed a little bit and not used as a

ideas throughout the Empire.
Before making my review of the Estimate I asked the doorkeepers and
attendants in the House about their
uniforms and allowances. The only
people I find who are impoverished in
this House are the underdogs-the men
who served in the Army and on the fighting fronts, the men who sacrificed their
all to go and fight, the men who came
back to this country and now find themselves opening and closing doors and
being treated in a very shabby, unkindly
and, may I say, disgraceful manner as
far as remuneration is concerned. They
got a pension for doing their bit on the
different fronts, and when brought back
here they do not get the benefit of
that pension. No, the reward is based on
a fee which is inadequate and not in
keeping with a decent standard of life.
You would think for every shilling you
give them on the cost of living you were
giving them £1. You dress them up in
clothing, and it would be far better to
give the cost in the form of wages.
Let those men who are operating as
attendants, and in other callings of that
kind, wear their own clothing. We do
not require them to be dressed up in the
manner in which we see them. I want
the money now spent on that clothing to
be spent in wages. Because they are
dressed up like that they get a clothing
allowance to the extent of £5 a year.
The thing is ridiculous. The first thing
I want you to do with these men is to
give them what they are entitled to
receive and increase their wages by 30s
to £2 10s a week. These men are not
under sufferance to you or anyone else.
They are qualified to carry out their
work. It has been stated that they open
and close the doors. If they did not do
so, you would have to open and close
them, and it would do some of you good
if you had to do so. If door opening
and closing is a job, then I demand, on
their behalf, that you give these men a
That is not
decent standard of life.
being done at present.
We are told to go step by step with
Great Britain in social services and every
other unit of the make-up of everyday
life. Here we come to the men who give
a little tone at the entrance of the House
and who are paid a wage which is the
lowest in any country in the world,
including Eire. It is nearly time you
thought of them. Give to the attendants
and porters that which they are entitled
to receive and which their counterparts
receive in Great Britain, Eire, and
throughout the Commonwealth. You will
then be doing something. You will be
starting on the lowest rung of the ladder,
and when you have thrown down the
reins of office you will be satisfied that
you have at least left some departments
in Parliament Buildings better than you
found them. I have given my opinion
on the various headings. I only want to
say that the Minister of Finance, if he is
sincere, cannot get away from the fact
that the building as a whole is overladen
at one end and too light at the other end.
If he takes something away from the overladen side and adds it to the lighter end
he will still find a very substantial saving
and perhaps have more efficient service
than this House is given at the present
time.

It is quite clear from the tone of the
House this afternoon, and from the
Estimates-
Cabinet Offices
