approach to turbulence in the House this
evening, that the ruling faction here.
since Lord Craigavon's death has been
rent by dissensions and jealousies. There
is not a man among them of the stature
or the strength sufficient to keep the
unruly, squabbling pack on the lead. The
Party has undergone a change into something new and strange. The newly
formed Party-because it is a newly
formed Party-is now an incoherent
jumble. It is disunity in everything
except its hatred of Ireland and things
Irish, and its slakeless thirst for the spoils
of office. It is a matter for great satisfaction to many that the rot and cancer
which were bound to come in this narrow,
circumscribed area have already set in
and may well prove too deep seated for
surgery. The Prime Minister has
gathered round him in his Cave of
Adullam, to borrow something familiar
from John Bright and Sir Walter Scott,
every one of the Party of the right hon.
Member for Mid Down that was in distress, and every one that was discontented; every one that was steeped to the
lips in intrigue.
The people outside are asking what will
happen? Experience of a long public
life has convinced me that nothing ever
happens and nothing will happen. The
band conductor has picked an orchestra
as motley as a troupe of nigger minstrels.
It is a make-shift, and I ask you to depend upon this, the gushing brook of
Tory reform will not last long before it
runs dry, because you will not get a
bountiful flow of fresh water into that
Tory pump by the simple process of
fitting it with a brand new handle,
borrowed for the nonce from a friend
from Willowfield.
It has been said that in English
politics two men can make a Party. Two
men for all practical purposes made the
Brooke Party, and when these two gentlement sit down side by side on the Front
Bench, each of them seeming perfectly
happy, perfectly at home at last, so sympathetic in outlook, so mutually attractive,
such congenial yoke-fellows as the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Public
Security, when they take shelter in the
same cave it will be an undivided Party,
thinking, meeting and moving in perfect
harmony. There will be no rift in the
lute, no dissension on any major point of
policy; in fact, there will be this beautiful climax in Ulster politics; you will
find:
Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one.
John Bright, the distinguished statesman, said of a queer medley in his day
that there was one difficulty, however,
about such a Party which it was impossible to remove. The Party, he said,
was like a Scotch terrier-It was SO
covered with hair that it could not be

the tail. I leave it to the Committee to
decide for themselves of the newlyformed Party sitting now on the Front

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
and learned Gentleman has described me
as living in a cave. I might describe
him as an ancient gnome sitting on an
oak, hoping that he can create

and learned Member that the troubles we
have had are purely and simply family

try to interfere with the unity of
Unionism in this Province.
Mr. CAMPBELL: A happy family.
The PRIME MINISTER : We are.
Even if we do have our little internal
troubles and they exist in other Parties,
including the Nationalist Party-it does
not make the slightest difference-we are
determined to remain part of the United
Kingdom and of nowhere else. The hon.
and learned Member has referred, as he
always does it is an annual thing-to
two speeches I made. One was in answer
to the hon. Member who represents South
Fermanagh, and the other was in answer
to threat which I had myself received.
The hon. and learned Member has just
made a statement that I had said that
99 per cent., or 97 per cent., or whatever
the figure was of Roman Catholics were
disloyal or were against the Constitution

of Ulster. Those were words used by the

by me. Then he referred to the fact I had
said I did not then employ any Roman
Catholics on my place, and he said I
boasted of that. I wonder if the hon.
and learned Member has taken the
trouble to read Hansard when that debate took place in 1932. There he would
have seen the explanation of that statement. The explanation was given again
recently by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs.
Perhaps the hon. and learned Member
does not know the circumstances under
which I made that statement. When I
happened to be the commandant of the
Special Constabulary in Co. Fermanagh
I was informed-and very accurately informed, as I believed that the Roman
Catholics whom I employed at my home
in Colebrooke-and at that time I roughly
divided the employment fifty-fifty-were
to be used for the kidnapping of my
eldest son. They were too cowardly to
attack me, too cowardly to shoot me,
though they threatened me, but in order
to try to force my hand they were to use
men who had been in my employment
and in my father's employment-some
were perhaps of later employment-in
order to kidnap that boy.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Did you believe one
word about that?
The PRIME MINISTER: I certainly
did. Perhaps the hon. and learned
Member can carry his mind back to the
time when forty loyalists were kidnapped
on the Border.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Prime
Minister say that that took place in
1932?
The PRIME MINISTER: I do not
remember the exact date. The hon. and
learned Member asked me if I believed
that. Surely the facts are quite sufficient
to make any man believe that those
things did take place at that time. Surely
the hon. and learned Member would have
taken the same precautions if he had been.
placed in the position I was in-having a
boy who was not allowed to go outside the
place, and a keeper with a shot-gun
accompanying him inside the grounds.
If the hon. and learned Member is the
natural father and kindly man I believe
him to be, he would have taken the same
precautions as I did. He would have
prevented the boy going outside the place
and got rid of every man who he was
told was implicated in this plot to kidnap
the boy.
Those are the facts. They were stated
in that speech, and they have never been
denied for 10 years. Yet the hon. and
learned Member still rakes it up. Personally I think it was a most cowardly
method of attacking me in the position I
held, because I was only doing my duty,
as I thought. Surely that attack should
have been made on me personally.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Prime
Minister think it right to shout this from
the house-tops?
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
and learned Member may not believe
these facts, but I do. Being a father

this propaganda, which has been very

Earlier in my remarks I referred to the
difficulty of relating agency fees to staff
costs. A case in point is the work we are
doing for an Imperial Department in the
removal of gates and railings; I suppose
one of the most unpopular my Ministry
has undertaken for years. This is a
branch of its activity in which the 10 per
cent. agency fee based on the value of the
metal collected does not cover the cost to
the Ministry of the staff so employed.
The Committee will, I am sure, be interested to know that approximately 3,800
tons have been collected to date. I learn
from the Ministry of Supply, which is the
Department responsible for the disposal
of the material, that 2,730 tons have
already been shipped, while 570 tons are
awaiting shipment. The balance is undergoing certain processing required prior to
the metal being shipped to Scotland to be
turned into munitions of war. To illustrate the urgency and necessity for this
sacrifice on the part of so many of our
people, I can inform the Committee that,
although shipments are being made at the
rate of 300 tons per week, the Ministry
of Supply have asked that the rate should
be stepped up to 500, and we are doing
everything we can to meet this request.
As regards the other Estimates for

the Committee have been given as much
information as it is possible to put on the
face of an Estimate, but, of course, I
will be glad to reply to any points on
which hon. Members require further
details.

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £39,530 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1944, for
the salaries and expenses of the Ministry
of Commerce. (Note-£20,000 has been
voted on account.)
The PRIME MINISTER AND
MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND
PRODUCTION (Sir Basil Brooke): The
Estimates for the Ministry of Commerce
and Production for the current year which
I now present to the Committee do not
call for detailed comment. They reflect
the activities of a Department engaged
week in and week out in expanding and
accelerating Northern Ireland's industrial
war effort. The past year has seen a
revolutionary change in the military
sphere. Our strategy has swung round
from defence to attack and the whole
war situation has been changed-and, we
hope, will be changed still more-by a
series of brilliant offensive actions. Such
a change inevitably had its repercussions
on the industrial and home fronts which
are an integral part of the war effort, but
here the changes are not so sensational.
Sometimes, indeed, they are temporarily
unfortunate for as our strategy changes,
so the types of weapons required must
also change, and a factory cannot alter
its production overnight. There is an
unavoidable period of dislocation while
the switch-round is being made, and we
have experienced this to some extent in
Northern Ireland. But apart from this,
which has been a minor problem, the
record of the various activities for which
I in my capacity as Minister of Commerce
and Production am responsible has been
one of consistent and increasing work and
of backing up the fighting men who have
the main job to do.
Hon. Members will appreciate that
interests of security prevent me from
telling him specifically the part that
Northern Ireland is playing in our offensive. On the production side we are doing
a good job, but I personally want us to
do still better. The achievement of this
aim depends not only on the management
and workers but also on the organisation
of production at the top. The form
arrived at here after much experiment in
the matter of co-ordination is very
similar to the improvements effected in
Great Britain through the adoption of the
recommendations of the Citrine Committee. Under this organisation, as hon.
Members will be aware, general responsibility is deputed to myself as Minister of
Commerce and Production, and the posts
of Regional Controller for the Ministry
of Production, the Ministry of Supply,
and the Ministry of Aircraft Production,
are entrusted to the Permanent Secretary
of the Ministry. My Production Council,
which holds regular meetings, provides a
direct link between workers and employers, Northern Ireland Government
Departments and Regional Representatives
of the Supply Departments, and has gone
far to eliminate the over-lapping and

Leaving what I might call direct war
production I should like to speak for a
moment about the achievements of our
textile industries, notably the linen trade.
Hon. Members are, of course, aware that
the industry's normal activities have
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
26 MAY 1943
declined progressively as the growing
restrictions of a war-planned economy
made themselves felt. In order to absorb
the surplus labour in our textile industries we secured the agreement of British
Ministers to the diversion of textile work
of an essential nature to Northern Ireland
and arrangements were made for alternative raw material in the form of cotton
yarn and long staple fibre for the production of utility cloth and essential household goods. The spinning section of the
trade cannot spin cotton and the activity
of this section has been restricted to the
spinning of the limited amount of flax
available and of a comparatively new raw
material, long staple fibre. Flax yarn
production has been almost entirely confined to the manufacture of Government
requirements. I need only mention
aeroplane fabric as an example to illustrate the importance of this contribution.
The spinning of long staple fibre on flax
machinery presents considerable difficulties, but spinners are devoting their
energies to the improvement of technique
and. I regard the experience which is
being gained in producing utility dress
cloths from the new material as a valuable asset to the linen industry. The
weaving section of the industry is more
happily situated as cotton yarn can be
woven on linen looms. Substantial quantities of cotton yarn have been diverted,
to Northern Ireland, and this is being
woven under the control of the Ministry
into utility cloths many of which in turn
go to
our making-up industries which
have recently been augmented by the
establishment of a number of new
factories.
This represents a considerable achievement. It is a remarkable piece of adaptation, the extent of which will be realised
when I say that the industry that in
peace-time made the finest table linen in
the world is now turning out materials
that are being made up-again by Northern Ireland firms-into essential clothing.
This includes shirts of which Northern
Ireland probably supplies some two-thirds
of the whole United Kingdom essential
requirements, industrial and domestic
overalls, rayon dresses for the utility
home market, and utility household
goods.
In connection with the household
trade I am glad to have been able to
arrange with the Board of Trade for the
resumption of production of linen towels.
to meet the shortage of these goods on the
home market. This is the first occasion
since the early days of the war that linen
has been manufactured in Northern
Ireland for sale in the United Kingdom.
Our clothing industry continues to
make its maximum contribution to war
production. It is engaged almost entirely
on the production either of utility wear
or of such varied service requirements as
army battledress, clothing for the
W.A.A.F. and A.T.S. and army shirts.
During the past year the contracts placed
in Northern Ireland by the Ministry of
Supply and the utility programme have
tended to exceed the industrial capacity.
As a result it has been necessary for the
Ministry to supervise both Government
and utility production so as to ensure that
the best possible use is made of the industry's capacity. Government demands
naturally fluctuate from time to time and
every effort is being made to maintain
continuity of production at the highest
possible level in this industry.
Notable as the achievements of the
textile industry have been, I feel, however,
that we cannot rest content with the present situation. The future requires planning also, for it is of the first importance
that at the cessation of hostilities our
linen industry with its vast production
capacity should be in the best possible
position to make its full contribution to
the revival of home and export trade.
In order that the industry may have its
plans matured to meet the contingencies
of the future, I have set up a committee
of the trade with a representative of the
Ministry to consider the problems with
which the industry is likely to be faced in
the post-war period and to advise as to
the measures which could best be taken
to ensure the maintenance and development of the industry in future years.
The committee has already embarked on
its deliberations.
Linked with the textile side of our
war effort has been the work of the flax
factories erected by the Ministry on behalf of the Ministry of Supply. These
were in full operation throughout last
season, handling in all some 6,000 acres
of the 1942 flax crop, in addition to considerable commitments carried over from
the extensive acreage grown in the previous
season. Additional processing and storage capacity has been and is being added
to the factories where local circumstances
have justified such a course. These
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
factories have played a useful part in the
war effort through the production of flax
fibre in areas where, but for the provision
of the factories, flax would not have been
grown. They have also made a substantial contribution to the supply of homesaved seed.
It is obvious that without adequate
supplies of electricity Northern Ireland
could not shoulder her full share of war
work, and I am glad to be able to inform
the House that our new electricity
generating capacity, the development of
which was undertaken under the direction
of the Ministry in order to meet any
serious emergency, has now been in use
for some months. This means that the
immediate position has been safeguarded
and that, should an emergency arise, all
essential demands of the Province will be
met. The Ministry is now actively
engaged in arranging to provide additional supplies of current to meet the present and future requirements of industry
engaged on the production of munitions
and materials essential to the prosecution
of the war.
Coal is almost equally important, and
the allocation and distribution of coal to
industry and to domestic consumers continues as an important function carried
out by the Ministry. During the past
year the registration of coal importers and
merchants, and their industrial and
domestic consumers has been put into
operation, and I am glad to say that the
allocation of available supplies has worked
satisfactorily, especially in ensuring that
the industrial war effort is not impeded
A
through any lack of fuel supplies.
reasonable quantity of coal has also found
its way into domestic coal cellars. The
frequent alteration in points of supply of
coal from Great Britain to Northern Ireland involves a constant survey of the
system of distribution within the Province, but I can assure the Committee that
supplies will be maintained at a regular
level so far as is physically possible.
Following the steps taken last year, it is
again proposed to purchase on Government account a supply of coal which will
be held in stock and released when necessary. Hon. Members will recollect that
approximately 10,000 tons were so purchased last year, and it is proposed to
make a similar purchase this year. Here
I should like to remind hon. Members of
the authoritative warning that further
military operations will constitute a heavy
drain on home supplies of fuel. I am
convinced, however, that if a further
tightening of the belt is necessary no one
will complain of the sacrifice of personal
comfort in the pursuit of final victory.
It will be my aim to mitigate inconveniences as far as possible and to ensure
that they are borne equally by all. Consumers should remember, however, that
the extra stocks of coal, which it is hoped
will be available from 1st June, must be
conserved for use next winter, and that
these are in no sense an addition to the
aggregate quantity which each consumer
can receive.
A great part of the time of the staff
continues to be occupied by the operation
of controls, which might be described
broadly as schemes devised by Imperial
Departments to conserve and ensure the
most economical use possible of materials
that are important to the war effort. One
of the most important schemes regulates
the control of bricks, sand, stone, cement,
tar and bitumen, and involves the operation of a large stone-crushing plant near
Belfast and the hiring of portable crushers
to quarry owners in certain districts. This
control has been of great value in the
carrying out of important military works
at high speed, and it ensures that the
Ministry is in a position to supplement
the output of stone at a moment's notice
should the necessity arise. Control is also
exercised over the importation and use in
Northern Ireland of plant used by contractors engaged upon civil engineering
works. The Factory and Storage Control
continues to conserve production and
storage space for essential services, bearing in mind always the particular needs
of the service making the demands and
the general balance in regard to planned
production. Further controls introduced
by the Board of Trade and operated by
the Ministry cover laundry services,
dyeing and cleaning services, and footwear
repairs.
One section of the Ministry continues
to be engaged on the control of civil
building work, the release of steel, cast
iron, timber, asbestos sheets for building
and non-building purposes. We frequently hear mention of the desirability
of making an immediate start on postwar constructional schemes particularly if
Estimates-

the right type of labour happens to be

this section of the Ministry always takes

blind our eyes to the fact that all schemes
of construction involve withdrawal from

It is in that light that I would ask hon.
Members to judge the standards which
we are forced to adopt in the application

Further work carried out by the

-Consumer rationing, including arrangements for the award of additional clothing coupons to manual workers in the

Price
I now come to the question of salvage,
the yield of which has declined inevitably
after 3 years of war. This makes it all
the more essential that the work of recovery by local authorities and voluntary
bodies should be maintained at maximum
pressure. To achieve this end, I have
recently set up a Directorate of Salvage in
Northern Ireland whose function will be
the co-ordination of existing efforts with
a view to securing the greatest possible
yield from all sources.
I have dealt in some detail with what
represent the war-time developments in
the Ministry, and I do not propose to take
up the time of hon. Members by dealing
exhaustively with the well-established
statutory functions of the Ministry which
cover Harbours, Canals, Fisheries, Mines
and Quarries, Weights and Measures and
Administration of Companies, Industrial
Assurance and Friendly Societies, Trade
Unions and Building Societies Acts. If
any Member wishes to have information
regarding these I shall be glad to furnish
it to him.
The centre and aim of our energies is
the winning of the war on the industrial
front; and I feel I cannot submit these
Estimates to the Committee without paying a tribute to those many anonymous
workers, managements, technicians, brain
and manual workers, who are keeping on
conscientiously and tirelessly with their
vital job. I would especially acknowledge
the help which the trades unions are
giving in a job which demands considerable staying power. In the fourth year
of war we are apt to become, perhaps, a
little weary. Monotony and industrial
fatigue are insidious enemies, and here I
should like in passing to address an
appeal through the House to managements and workers on the matter of staggering holidays. I voice the opinion of
the most competent authorities when I
say that as the war goes on workers must
have adequate holidays to enable them to
maintain efficiency and to secure maximum output. The Production Council
has already considered the question of
staggering the customary Northern Ireland July holidays, and I hope when the
time comes that I will have the co-operation of employers and employees in securing this, which in itself will constitute a
valuable service to the war effort by helping to keep up an even flow of production.
I feel that this present time as well as
being a critical stage of the war is also a
point at which we can say with complete
But
confidence that we are going to win.
to be able to say that is not enough. The
question continually in my mind is
"When are we going to win?" and it is a

and woman in Ulster, for it is on them
as much as on our fighting men that the
answer depends.
is still
The enemy
powerful and he possesses immense reserves of men and material. Our men
have shown that given the weapons they
are more than a match for the enemy.
It is the people at home who must give
them the weapons.
That side of our
offensive may not have the exciting
quality of actual fighting. It means work
and more work to a point where monotony
and staleness are felt. And the
weapons with which to fight these
particular enemies are not made with
machine tools or by Act of Parliament, but are forged by a human
realisation of the close ties that bind
us all in this struggle for freedom and
life-by a sense of responsibility and
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
common interest which we want to cement
now and to carry over into the world
which will emerge after the war. The
fighting men know no respite.
no respite. The
Eighth Army fought its way across some
2,000 miles of enemy territory, and it
never stopped until with the British First
Army and our gallant Allies, the
Americans and the French, it delivered a
smashing defeat on the Axis forces in
North Africa. And that has brought us
to the beginning of the end—a glorious
beginning, but much desperate and difficult fighting lies ahead. We cannot fail
our fighting men. We must possess the
same spirit, and we must possess the same
efficiency. I would suggest for the
workers of Northern Ireland, and for all
our people, whatever their place in the
war effort may be, that the driving force
behind their efforts in the coming months
should be not only victory but victory
sooner. It is for the achievement of that
aim that I, in my capacity of Minister of
Commerce and Production, intend to
work. I beg to move.

heard any talk about a Minister of Production or anything like that. I knew
a good deal about production in Northern
Ireland in the last war, because I spent a
good part of my time down in the shipyards. Night after night I inspected
posts, and everyone was working. Men
were almost stopped on the street and
asked to take work. I never thought I
would see the day when this much advertised, efficient Government of Northern
Ireland would say to a man, when a firm
like Mackie's want workers, "No, we will
not let you work." That is what I am
seeing now.
Mr. THOMPSON: Some few weeks
ago I raised a question in this House

Ministry of Commerce
factory. He was taken down to some of
the country towns and was shown old,
derelict factories. He was so much disgusted that he put his foot on the boat
and declared he would never come back
to Belfast again to look for a factory. I
have definite evidence of that. I have
also evidence of another gentleman who
came to Belfast looking for a factory. He
was also taken to a derelict factory, but
by good chance I happened to come across
him. I was able to take him along, and

to-day has a factory in Belfast in which
are employed probably 150 employees.
As a matter of fact, he is in this House
this afternoon.
with reference to civil aviation after the
war, and I noticed when the Prime
Minister was over in England he apparently had some discussions on that matter.
I had hoped that to-day he would
have been in a position to have informed the House of the result of those
discussions, but as far as I could hearthough I am sorry I was interrupted on
one or two occasions when he was speaking-I did not hear him make any reference to that subject. He may have done
and I may not have heard it. But whilst
I am satisfied in my own mind that our
energies must, first and always, be
directed towards the war effort, and
nothing must be allowed to divert our
attention in any way from that, at the
same time there is no reason whatever
why we should not look forward into the
future.
I believe that if steps are not taken
now to look after Ulster's interests with
reference to post-war aerodromes, we will
miss the boat. I think it is a matter of
grave importance that we should be preparing plans, and that we should be looking out to see the type of aeroplane that
may be useful when this war is over. We
ought to be going into the question of
securing the ground and securing these
aerodromes which are already in existence
for commercial purposes. I would like
the Prime Minister to give us some indication that something is being done
along these lines.
Over and over again in this House I
have made reference to factories being
erected in Northern Ireland. The Prime
Minister, I think, did say something with
reference to factories having been built.
I would like to know where those factories
are. If three years ago there had been
one single skeleton factory put up in
each of the leading towns throughout
Northern Ireland, the size of the factory
being 200 to 300 square feet with a piece
of ground capable of development, and
one end of each factory left for future
extension, I venture to suggest there
would not be a single one of these factories
to-day which would not be fully occupied.
I have on three or four occasions been
asked by different people if I could point
out to them any place in Belfast, or convenient to Belfast, where they might get
a factory. I have not been able to get
them suited. I know one gentleman who
came over to Northern Ireland to look
after a place on which to start a
Mr. NIXON: When?
Mr. THOMPSON: About a year ago.
We may be, and probably will be, told
that we cannot get the necessary material.
Surely we have still available any amount
of cement, and I know we have windows
that are suitable for factories. I also
know that if it were a case of great
importance the girders and iron work
could also be procured. Therefore, there
is no reason in my opinion why we should
not start to build a number of skeleton
factories through Northern Ireland. I
am glad the Prime Minister has told us
that more facilities are going to be given
regarding coal. I understand that the
coal we are getting at the present time is
a very great improvement on what we
have been having, and for that we are
grateful to the Prime Minister.
I may say that one of the arguments
used in connection with the erection of
factories was that we have not got the
electricity. There, again, I want to say
that the fault to a great extent lay with
the Government. If we had not the
electricity at the time, we should have
been looking sufficiently far forward to
have had enough electricity for our purpose. The Government had to fall back
on the Belfast Corporation, and had it
not been for the fact that they had a
plant in Belfast which the Government
were able to pounce upon and use, even
to-day they would have been in a very
difficult position. I am glad to say that
that difficulty has been overcome.
I am sorry that the Prime Minister has
made up his mind to hold on to the dual
offices of Prime Minister and Minister of

Commerce. The admirable gentleman
who is at the head of the Ministry of

him more work to do than any three or

this gentleman has more to do than any

Minister has it within his power to clear
the air in this respect. I sincerely hope
that in the near future we will have a
number of factories erected throughout
Our Province.

Mr. MINFORD: I am sorry I was not
in the House when the Minister
Commerce made his speech, but I was in
time to hear him pay a tribute to our
glorious fighting forces. No tribute that
could be paid could possibly be too high
for these gallant men on land, sea, and
in the air. I want to see this country of
ours made fit for these heroes to come
back to after the war is won. Nothing
will be too good for these lads. I have
letters week after week from members of
my family who have been engaged in that
great hunt in the desert, and they say
there is no Government in the world that
could do too much for these gallant men.
Their only idea is to go right on until
victory is attained, and why should we
not make this a land fit for these heroes
to live in when they return.
Reference has been made to the closing
of the Ballyclare Paper Mill, which is
partly in the constituency of the right
hon. Member for Carrick, and the displacement of 700 men and women
workers. I had negotiations with the
Minister of Commerce to see what could
be done. Now we find that the place is
closed for three years. There is an opportunity for the Minister of Commerce.
You have a magnificent building with 700
skilled or semi-skilled workers available,
Why
some of them trained mechanics.
should you not give them work to do?
When you can tell the farmer that if he
does not comply with your requirements
you will take his home, surely you can
utilise a magnificent building and 700
workers as the nucleus of a factory for
war production. I want to see a stop
put to this shifting of our workers, and
factories erected in Northern Ireland
where they can be employed. The Minister
has the necessary power to start that
factory to-morrow, and why should he not
do so? There is a grand opportunity if
he likes to grasp it. He has the power
to requisition that mill and convert it
into a magnificent factory.
I see that 27,500 men have joined the
forces in Northern Ireland, as well as
5,000 of our women and girls. What is
going to be the post-war condition of
Northern Ireland? I hope all these men
and women will come back when the war
is won, as well as the 30,000 Ulster men
and women who have gone to work in
Great Britain. The Minister has allowed
that big concern in Ballyclare to close,
although I believe he is most anxious that
every man and woman in Ulster should
do his and her part in connection with
the war effort. That is the prayer of all
of us. Every man and every woman
should strain every muscle to win this
war. That is the spirit of Ulster. The
Prime Minister of Great Britain, when
writing to our Prime Minister, said that
Ulster saved the world. The opinion of
that great statesman should not altogether
be ignored. When our boys come home
from the war we should either give them
work or something to keep them.

We are going to send £32,000,000
to Great Britain. I was very much
surprised to hear the Minister of Finance
tell the House we had no power to withhold any part of that Imperial contribution, but that if we were good boys he
would do his best to see that we got some
of that money back for post-war reconstruction. I put a similar question to the
ex-Prime Minister two months ago.
asked him whether we had the power to

the opportunity was never so great as it

I am sure that every Member of this
House, as well as every man and woman
in Ulster, will support the Prime
Minister in the great undertaking he has
shouldered in order to prosecute the war
to a successful conclusion. The people
of Ulster are willing to do their share if
the Prime Minister will give them the
lead.
When our gallant men and women return from the war I want to see them
properly housed. I want to see our
housing and educational facilities at least
on a par with those in Great Britain. I
want the right hon. Gentleman, as the
Prime Minister and Leader of this
Government, to see to it that we are not
left in that parlous position the Minister
of Finance said we might be in. I look
upon Ulster
as being part of Great
Britain. We have a Parliament of our
own, and surely we are entitled to conduct some of our own affairs. Why
should we not? We pay taxes on a par
with those in Great Britain, and surely
it is only right that this Government
should keep some of the revenue in order
to put the various services in the Six
Counties on a par with those in Great
Britain. There are approximately 18,000
people still unemployed here, and an
effort should be made to requisition the
Ballyclare Paper Mill and restart it in
order to absorb at least some of these
unemployed.
I would appeal to the Prime Minister
to see to it that Ballyclare Paper Mill is
set going again. If we require paper in
Ulster and representations are made to
the Minister of Supply he should see to
it that this mill is kept going. The
workers in Great Britain have many
alternative forms of employment, but
when workers here get out of employment
they have to go on the dole or be shipped
across the water. That is not good
enough for Ulstermen. The Government
will receive the support of every hon.
Member if they accede to my request.
We are not out to criticise, but to help
the Government. At a time when we
require weapons of war of every kind and
description it is wrong to have a big concern lying idle. The building in question
could, if necessary, be extended, because
there are many acres of land around it
which could be utilised.
In his speech the Prime Minister said
he wanted to see the workers getting a
week's holiday and living under happy
and prosperous conditions. Some sections
of workers are discontented. The Ministry of Supply placed certain contracts
with firms and the workers had to accept
a wage which is not in keeping with that
earned by those on munition and other
work. The textile workers should be
treated better. I was going to speak
about the farmers, but that would be out
of place. They are the slaves. Farming is the largest industry in Ulster.
Munitions are good, but you want the
men handling the guns to receive agricultural produce. You will stop me if I
refer to the Prime Minister. The policy
of this Government should be to give the
Ulster farmers and the workers on the
land-
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member
can raise that question when the Agricultural Estimates come forward.
Mr. MINFORD: I only mentioned
that matter, because I had already referred
to munitions of war, and I thought food
was a very good weapon. The Germans
said they had to give up in Tunisia because they had no food for two days. I
hope they will have to go without food
for two months. The textile, munition
and agricultural workers are determined
to play their part in helping to win the
war. We have a "Wings for Victory"
week in the country, and I can assure
hon. Members that it has been taken up
with more enthusiasm than was displayed
in Belfast.
All the people require is a lead from
the Prime Minister. Let him put up
munition factories. If he does that he
will not only be helping to win the war,
but he will give those that are struggling
a chance. These people do not want the
dole. They do not like standing in
queues. They are ashamed to do that.
Why should men and women have to
stand in a queue in order to get a few
shillings when there is a splendid buildin which work could be carried on? The
right hon. Gentleman should cross to
Great Britain and tell the authorities
there what I have told him to-day. There'
is no question of lack of steel, iron,
cement or bricks. They are all there. It
is a magnificent building.
If we are
given the tools, we will help to finish the
job.

Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): The presentation of the Estimates by my right
hon. Friend the Prime Minister has been
received in general in a spirit of friendly
criticism, and on his behalf I thank the
House for the reception which they have
been given. There were one or two points
raised by hon. Members to which I should
like to refer very shortly. The hon.
Member for Woodvale, perhaps not unnaturally, mentioned the fact of the
present unemployment. Whilst one regrets
that there is any unemployment in
Northern Ireland, one can appreciate the
fact that, especially in war time when you
have constant changes taking place, new
products being required, new methods
being adopted, new machinery taking its
proper place, there must always be times
when employment does not and cannot go
at an equal speed with production. This
time lag, which is unfortunate, but which
is inevitable, must always take place, and
especially at times like these. However,
the hon. Member may rest assured that
my right hon. Friend is taking every possible step in order to bring the present
unemployment to an end as quickly as
possible.
The hon. Member also mentioned the
question of electricity. He suggested
that the firm of Messrs. Kennedy & Duncan got something in the neighbourhood
of £30,000-I think that is the amount
he mentioned-and that their fees were
based upon the electrical output of the
Province.
Mr. NIXON: No.
Mr. MAGINESS: I beg your pardon.
Mr. NIXON: What I said was that
their fees were based on the money spent
on the installations about which they had
given advice.
Mr. MAGINESS: I can tell the hon.
Member that the basis on which this firm
is paid is founded on the normal professional practice. Again, he mentioned
the Ministry of Food, and suggested that
the Ministry of Commerce had been at
one time agents for that Ministry. He
said that this practice had been changed
and that the Ministry of Food were now
operating directly. What in fact happened was that some officers of the
Ministry of Commerce were transferred to
the Ministry of Food, but were still paid
by the Ministry of Commerce, who were
later reimbursed by the Ministry of Food,
but the Ministry of Commerce had no
control over the various controls established by the Ministry of Food. It was
thought more advisable that the Ministry
of Food should pay these officers directly.
Mr. NIXON: I do not wish to interrupt the Parliamentary Secretary, but I
wish the matter to be made clear. I
stated that I saw a letter from the
Ministry of Commerce to the effect that
the Minister had resigned his agency of
the Ministry of Food. I want to know
whether that is right or wrong.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I
can explain the point to the hon.
Member. The Ministry never acted as
agents in the normal way; they only acted
in the capacity of agents in that they
paid certain members of the staff to suit
the convenience of the Ministry of Food.
On the Estimate being presented I think
the hon. Member criticised me for having
that charge on my Vote and yet he was
not allowed to discuss it. It was better
that the Ministry of Food should pay
their own people without having to do so
through a Board in Northern Ireland
which had nothing to do with regard to
the deciding of policy.
Mr. NIXON: The letter I saw was in
reply to one from the Belfast Food Committee. It was not a complaint about
who paid; it was a complaint about something that was going on. The reply was
that the Minister had resigned his agency.
I think I am right in stating that.
Mr. MAGINESS: Those were the main
points outlined by the hon. Member for
Woodvale. The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh raised a point about civil aviation after the war. I can assure him
that so far as this is concerned the Prime
Minister is fully alive to the position, and
he has not lost sight of the fact that
Northern Ireland will be directly concerned in any post-war aviation schemes.
He has placed the position of Northern
Ireland before the Secretary of State for
Air. Of course the hon. Member will
understand that civil post-war aviation is
only in the initial stage at the present
time.
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
26 MAY 1943
Mr. THOMPSON : I cannot accept
that at all. It is not right to say that
civil aviation is only in the initial stages
at the present time. It is one of the
most developed concerns in the world
to-day. I have not got a reasonable
answer to the question I asked.
Mr. MAGINESS: I said that post-war
civil aviation-
Mr. THOMPSON: It is civil aviation
I am referring to.
Mr. MAGINESS- -and the plans for
it are in the initial stage at the present
time. The hon. Member can rest assured
that the position of Northern Ireland has
been taken up by the Prime Minister and
placed before the competent authorities
on the other side, and that that position
will be kept constantly before them in
the future.
The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh also
queried the fact that there had been any
new factories built in Northern Ireland.
I do not suppose for a moment that he
would expect me to tell him the position
of any new factories in Northern Ireland.
He went on to suggest that there should
be skeleton factories built throughout the
different parts of the Province, and that
these factories having been built we
should look for work for them and for
labour by which that work might be
effected. A factory can only be built for
a specific and essential purpose, and it
would not be practicable at the present
time to build a skeleton factory merely
in the hope or in the possibility that some
work would come along. One does not
build a factory merely for any purpose.
One builds a factory for a specific purpose and according to the nature of that
purpose.
The hon. Member also mentioned the
fact that some persons had been shown
derelict factories on their visits to Northern Ireland, and that as a result they
had become disgusted and had gone back
to Great Britain with a very poor opinion
of this Province. I am informed that
since the establishment of the Factory
and Storage Control, which took place
about two years ago, there has been no
instance of an industrialist who wished to
establish a manufactory in Northern Ireland failing to secure existing factory
premises reasonably suited to his purpose.
If that be so, and I have no doubt of the
facts as supplied to me, then I think there
is no cause for complaint so far as this
Ministry is concerned. If every person
who wished to start an undertaking in
Northern Ireland has managed to secure
existing factory premises reasonably suitable and no one has turned away, I think
that so far as the Factory and Storage
Control end of the business is concerned
the Ministry has played its full part.
The hon. Member for Antrim mentioned the closing of the Ballyclare Paper
Mill, and I rather gathered from him
that he was under the impression that as
a result of the closing of that mill the
workers formerly employed there had
since remained unemployed. I can assure
the hon. Member that a very large percentage of the workers formerly employed
in the Ballyclare Paper Mill have now
been absorbed into other employment,
and that those who are left are immobile.
The Ministry are taking every possible
step to secure work for those who are
still unemployed, but again I would
impress upon the hon. Member that
roughly about 90 per cent. of the workers
formerly employed in Ballyclare Paper
Mill have since found employment.
The mill was closed owing to the stoppage of further supplies of wood pulp for
the manufacture of the kind of paper
that was produced there. The hon.
Member may rest assured that so far as
he could at that time the Minister of
Production, consistent with the national
effort, did all he could to keep up the
supply of wood pulp for that particular
factory, but it was a question of priorities
-it was a question of war production
coming first. The shipping which would
bring the wood pulp to this country could
be diverted to other and more useful
purposes, and as a consequence of that
lack of wood pulp that particular factory
had to close down. It is not so simple
to use that factory for other purposes as
the hon. Member would seem to think. I
rather gathered from him that he was
under the impression that any vacant
factory could be quite easily diverted to
produce another and different product.
He must realise that the matter is not as
simple as all that. You have to consider
the existing machinery in the factory;
you have to consider storage capacity, new
machinery, and all the hundred and one
factors which must be taken into con-
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Maginess]
sideration before you
can use for a
different purpose a factory established for
a particular purpose.
I think those are the main items mentioned by the hon. Members, and on the
Minister's behalf I would like again to
thank them for the spirit in which the
Estimates were received. The criticisms
were all meant to be helpful and constructive, and I know that all hon.
Members as well as my right hon. Friend
are only too anxious to do anything in
their power to further the war effort in
Northern Ireland, an effort in which the
Ministry are particularly engaged at the
present time.
Mr. MINFORD: I thank the Parliamentary Secretary for his reply. He
said that I probably did not understand
about the machinery in the Ballyclare
mill, but surely he could travel to Carrickfergus, where a mill was closed. The
machinery was shipped to England and
new machinery immediately brought back
in order to help the war effort. In the
Ballyclare mill we have the turbine and
all the electrical equipment. In 1940 I
raised the question of getting tools for
a firm in Belfast. That particular firm
was obliged to go over to Great Britain
and procure for itself the tools. You will
remember that I suggested that the Committee of Supply which had been set up
in Ulster was only a farce.
I also suggested that the Minister of Commerce
should be Minister of Commerce and
Production.
In regard to wood pulp, the hon. and
learned Gentleman said that we must give
way to the priorities of war. I know
that, but surely in Ballyclare we have a
building with all the electrical equipment,
engines, and turbines, the very things
you want to make munitions of war.
What we want is a few thousand
pounds' worth of tools. When the firm
I referred to was able to get direct all it
wanted, surely it is not beyond the bounds
of possibility that we should be able to
get in Great Britain all the machinery
required to equip this mill and give 700
people the work they desire. As regards
the question of wood pulp, Northern
Ireland needs paper. I am not going to
criticise the Minister in that respect,
because I think he did all he possibly
could with the powers that be to get the
mill kept going; but I say when Britain
is seeking for men to make munitions, it
is wrong that such a building, containing
engines and machinery, should remain
idle when a war is on. The mill should
be kept going as a priority factory.
The Parliamentary Secretary said that
about 90 per cent. of the workers employed at Ballyclare Mill were now
employed. I do not think that is an
accurate statement, because I have some
of these men in my employment. About
three weeks ago I went to the exchange
and I found that there was a double staff
engaged in dealing with the unemployed.
The Ministry of Labour will, I am sure,
agree with me in that. A few of the
girls have gone to the Barn Mill at
Carrickfergus, but a large number of the
people hitherto working in that mill are
still unemployed. The Minister of Commerce should take immediate steps to see
that this magnificent building, with its
turbines and electrical devices, is put to
some use. It is no
mere ramshackle
building. There are 18,000 people unemployed in Northern Ireland, plus these
700 Ballyclare people. The Minister
should take steps to see what can be done
in this respect. This is a building that
could easily be converted to war work,
and it is wrong that we should not make
some effort to get a munition factory in
Northern Ireland.
This mill is adjacent to rail, and only
a few miles from the sea. It is in a very
prosperous part of the country. Ballyclare is a town with good housing.
Everything is there, and all we want is
for the Minister to tell the powers that be
that machinery is wanted so that 700
workers can be re-employed. They are
anxious to work. I still say that the
statement that 90 per cent. of these people
are now employed is wrong.
As regards the question of coal supplies,
I might mention that two merchants in
my constituency sent letters to the Coal
Controller in Belfast and got no reply.
They asked me to bring the matter up
in Parliament. I saw the Prime Minister about it, and I told him that when I
went to the building in Linenhall Street
I was able to get the difficulties complained of by the merchants settled in
ten minutes. I came away perfectly satis-
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
26 MAY 1943
fied that there was not much wrong, but
when a firm sends a letter, as one of these
firms did, on the 15th February, they
expect to get an answer before this.
People in the country districts have
complained that they have been deprived
of their small allocations of coal supplies.
These people have neither gas nor
electricity to depend on, and I think the
Minister should see
that those people
entitled even to small supplies receive
their allocations. There were towns
and villages where there was no coal
supplied for one week. I was told by an
official when I showed him a letter about
the matter that that would never occur
again. Again, I would ask the Minister
to see that this big concern in Ballyclare
is utilised for doing useful war work, and
that instead of people drawing the dole
they may be enabled to make munitions
of war in order to bring victory.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In the
various speeches that have been made a
few points have been raised. One question raised by the hon. Member for
Ballynafeigh related to the matter of overloading the Permanent Secretary of the
Ministry with work. I think the Permanent Secretary is an extremely
capable civil servant, and he is being
asked to perform more than he is
humanly or physically able to do. That
is a point to which there was no reply by
the Parliamentary Secretary.
Another point raised by the same hon.
Member was in connection with civil
aviation after the war. I hope that this
matter will not be lost sight of, and that
the facilities available in Northern Ireland will be placed at the disposal of the
proper authorities. No doubt arrangements for civil air services will have to
be worked out by the different units in
Great Britain and the Empire and the
Allied Nations, as well as those nations
on the Continent which will be allowed
to engage in aviation after the war. The
crossing of the Atlantic now seems to be
a matter of only nine or ten hours instead of a day.
When civil aviation and the matter of
landing grounds were discussed by the
Imperial Government some time before
the war the relative importance of Northern Ireland was left out, but a site
near the River Shannon in Eire, which
we
is a neutral country, was selected as a
landing ground, We in Northern Ireland have facilities for landing close to
sea and on land, and there should be no
mistake made this time. It should be seen
that Northern Ireland, in connection with
these landing grounds, gets the preference
instead of a neutral country. That point
must be strenuously stressed-that
should be part of the link. Even the
Minister of Commerce and Production
does not know exactly what part we will
play, but we should be one of the links
where 'planes come down. I hope I shall
not live to see another war, but if that
does happen there should be landing
grounds in Northern Ireland, which is
part of the United Kingdom, and can be
relied upon to support the Mother
country-
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON-and not in
a neutral country. At this point I
should like the Prime Minister and
Minister of Commerce to make the position very plain to the authorities on the
other side of the water. That is the
reason I got up to speak on this matter,
because I think the reply we got was just
rather passive-I would not say ineffectual, but rather passing the matter
It is one of the things for postwar reconstruction. We will be one of
the vital links in the Atlantic service.
over.
There was another point, and that is
this. In the speech of the Minister of
Commerce and Production he said he was
not satisfied with the present condition
of unemployment. I am very glad to
hear him say that, because I do not think
there is anybody in Northern Ireland who
is or has been happy for a long time upon
this question of unemployment. I recall
that not very many weeks ago the right
hon. Gentleman the Minister of Public
Security was speaking as a private
Member for Willowfield and pointed out
to the Government that there were
then 38,000 workers who had been sent to
England to take up employment, there were
18,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland,
and there were in addition 15,000
importees from Eire. I would recall to
the Prime Minister that when that speech
was made he, as Minister of Commerce,
said "Hear, hear" several times. So I
hoped that in his speech to-day when he
said he was not satisfied with unemploy-
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
ment he would hold out hopes that, first,
further production and work would be
brought to Northern Ireland. I hope
that the shifting of people to England
away from their own homes to work will
be brought to an end, and that unemployment here will be brought to an end by
providing vital work for the people in the
place where they can best work and that
is near their own homes.
That was largely what brought about
the change in the Administration and I
assure the Prime Minister he will get
every assistance from every Member of
this House in solving this problem. It is
good to hear that he is not happy because
that is exactly what everybody else is
unhappy about. I do hope we will see
further development in the unemployment
situation. Nobody expects the Administration, however composed, to absorb
what is called the hard core of unemployment.
But the people who are not the
hard core-I do not know what they are
called technically-should be brought into
employment and further work be made
available.
Yesterday I raised the question of how
many people had enlisted in Northern
Ireland. I was informed of the figure,
27,000, a figure which to my mind could
be improved. After all we have very
many fighting men in Northern Ireland
who are not fighting and who, I think,
should be. The Prime Minister said he
was unable to give me the figures of the
people who came up from the South and
enlisted in His Majesty's Forces and in
spite of neutrality supported the war
effort. When I opened my paper this
morning I saw the figures were given
there, and I may say with complete
accuracy. The point I am trying to make
is this, that our effort in obtaining
and doing war work is not enough.
What Northern Ireland requires is a
further fighting effort. Is it right that
we here in Northern Ireland should as it
were rely on others to do the fighting
while we content ourselves with production? All honour to those 27,600 men
and the others who are now serving in the
services, and who were serving in the
services before the war started, in the
merchant navy. All honour to them and
to the 5,000 women who have joined to
replace the men. But in my opinion and
in the opinion of very many others
Northern Ireland should do a very great
deal more in going forth, might I say, to
battle.
When I read in the papers and know
of my own knowledge, having been for
years in the King's uniform, that the
Northern Ireland regiments have lost
their territorial identity, and when I hear
a
very high ranking officer making
speeches in Belfast and stating that such
regiments as the Royal Ulster Rifles, the
Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers and the
Royal Irish Fusiliers have over 50 per
cent. of the men in the ranks from
England, it seems to me time Northern
Ireland should make a further effort to
fill these ranks. I hope the Minister will
make such effort and not be satisfied with
what we have done in the past, but go
one step further. It has been said that
what we as a Province did in the last war
should be a central rallying point and incentive on which we can found an esprit de
corps. We had a Division in the last war
and in this war we have no Division. I have
in my own head absolutely accurate figures
given in the Imperial House of Commons.
They are these: During the period
August, 1914, to the 11th November,
1918, over 70,000 men joined His
Majesty's Forces from that part of Ulster
now known as Northern Ireland, and of
this 46,000 came from the city of Belfast
alone. We had then something to be
proud of. Is our fighting effort to-day
one on which we can look with absolute
pride? I am certain of this, that the
people, numbering 27,600, who have gone
from Northern Ireland are looking over
their shoulders to see when their comrades are coming to back them up. It
is to this part of the war effort in my
opinion, and in the opinion of many
others, that we should look, and if we are
denied conscription and told we cannot
have it, then we can and should intensify
our voluntary effort.
Mr. THOMPSON: I want to say
another word or two about civil aviation.
Any person who takes this matter
seriously, or who has been reading the
different technical journals and other
sources of information, must see that if
Ulster does not move, and move pretty
soon, to take some step in regard to airports and other things, we will lose our
great opportunity when this war is over.
There are other people who in the very
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
26 MAY 1943
near future will probably make off with
the agreement in their pockets, while we
are standing up thinking. I give that
word of warning. The question of factories has been raised by the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Commerce and Production. It has
alarmed me. If that is the attitude going
to be adopted by the Government, that
they are going to wait to build their factories until such time as suitable people
turn up, then God help Ulster. That is
all I can say. The very idea of waiting!
Why, you surely have your cage before
you start looking for your bird. I want
also to say that nine business men out
of ten who want a factory to-day, want a
square building without many columns
inside, and a piece of ground around it,
with a sufficient supply of electricity and
water to meet all their requirements.
That is practically all they require. Over
in England and Scotland, what did you
see even before the war? There were factories here, factories there, and factories
yonder, all to be let or sold. If a man
wants a factory he comes along and looks
at it, and nine men out of ten select a
factory in the district in which they want
to be. Yet the Government turn round
and say in this House, "We are going to
wait until somebody turns up." Well, it
is a pity of Ulster.
The PRIME MINISTER: First of all,
with regard to civil aviation, which has
been raised by two or three hon. Members,
I have that matter in mind, and I
thoroughly agree with what the hon.
Member and my hon. and gallant Friend
said about it. It would appear that
Northern Ireland is an extremely suitable
place, and I have pointed out on two or
three different occasions to the Secretary
of State for Air that we have not only
excellent sea plane bases, but aerodromes
of the most modern construction. I am
hoping that this new Corporation, which
has been set up and is dealing entirely
with all civil aviation matters, will have
that information at their hand. Anyhow, I would like the House to be assured
that I am not losing sight of the matter,
and that it is of the utmost importance
to keep it before the British Government
on the other side.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: May I point
out to the Prime Minister that in the
past the choice went to what is now
known as a neutral country to the detriment of Northern Ireland, and will he
see it will not occur again?
I
The PRIME MINISTER: I agree.
hope it will not. I just want to deal
with one or two other points. With regard to the overloading of the Permanent
Secretary of my Ministry, he is one of the
hardest worked men I know, but I think
he revels in it. There is a great
advantage in his holding the three
positions that he does, because he is then
able to look in an impartial way at the
problems as they come forward. If there
were two officers in charge, or even three,
one in charge of supplies, one in charge
of A.M.P., and one in charge of Board
of Trade matters, there might be complications by overlapping and friction
between the three different officers. I
said there might be, but as this particular officer is placed he can
see the
problems and requirements of the three
different services, and he can allocate to
them in the most suitable way.
I discussed with him the position so far
as he was concerned if I retained the dual
office of Prime Minister and Minister of
Commerce and Production, and I understood from him that it would not increase
his work, and that probably the reverse
would be the case, because I knew the
different connections and links-up on the
other side, and it might be more difficult
for anybody else to take up that job with
him, although for a comparatively short
time there would be certain overloading
on the Permanent Secretary.
As to Ballyclare Paper Mills, the hon.
Member for Antrim is very keen about
matters in his constituency, and that is
only right. He knows the problem. I
took a great deal of personal care and
trouble over this matter, and really the
position was that the allocation of wood
pulp considered sufficient by the Ministry
of Supply was not considered sufficient by
the gentleman who owns Ballyclare Paper
Mills, and nothing more could be done
about it. The manager claimed he was
losing a considerable amount of money
every week he worked the mill, and therefore I suppose, being a sensible man, he
naturally closed down the mill. The position is, why should the Government not
have taken that factory over as other
factories had been taken over. The reason
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
of that was because paper is not considered one of the essential war products.
The hon. Member knows that paper is
still being pulped at Larne, though not at
Ballyclare. A considerable number of
employees at Ballyclare are now working
in other parts and turning out munitions.
I have endeavoured to find work for the
actual area at Ballyclare, but that has not
been possible up to the present. It is
noted by the Factory and Storage Control,
and if it is a suitable area, I hope we will
be able to get something established.
Mr. MINFORD: I thoroughly agree
Iwith what the Prime Minister has said.
He did everything possible to keep the
mill going. Speaking as an ordinary layman, I believe that Ballyclare is a most
suitable place for a munition factory,
because there is there some of the most

The PRIME MINISTER: I appreciate what the hon. Member has said. It
is noted, and if there is an opportunity
of using it I will do so without a moment's
hesitation. With regard to unemployment the position is and I think I have
pointed this out on various occasionsthat this is an engineers' war. There are
certain categories of workers who at the
present time are not required in the war
effort, such as builders, and it is impossible to absorb them in war work in
Northern Ireland. The men you want
are scarce, and the difficulty is to get
precision engineers and skilled men. I
am not in a position to analyse the 18,000
unemployed who are on the register, but
at some future time perhaps my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Labour will
be able to do so. That really is the
reason for the number of unemployed we
have at present. Unless the war effort
requires building you will not be able to
absorb your builders. Unless the war
requires painters you cannot absorb your
painters.
There are continual alterations in the
requirements of labour which vary from
day to day. You will at one time get a
new type of work coming in requiring one
particular type of labour, and the next
day perhaps that particular type of war
production goes down, and those men go

problems are continually facing us, and
will probably be troubling us for some

Mr. MINFORD: There is one point I
want to make clear. I do not desire it to

used to drive the machinery.

Ex-R.U.C. Constable's Pension.

Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state why the pension of Mr. R. Healy,
late R.U.C., has been curtailed while he
was employed with the R.A.F. Security
Police and now while employed as
Security Warden at a Royal Ordnance
Factory.
a
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The pension of this officer
was curtailed in accordance with the provisions of Article 19 (1) of the R.U.C.
Pensions Order, 1923 (S. R. & O., 1923,
No. 29).
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply of the Minister of Home
Affairs, would he please explain why this
constable's ex-R.I.C. pension is
is not
similarly curtailed?
Mr. LOWRY: The constable in question may thank God that the R.I.C.
pension is not controlled by the Northern
Government, or particularly the Ministry
of Finance.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Does the
Minister think it fair and just that a
man's pension should be curtailed in
Northern Ireland when the pension paid
by the Imperial Authority is not curtailed?
Mr. LOWRY: On the subject of the
fairness or otherwise of the regulations I
have no thoughts at all.
Lieut.-Colonel. GORDON: Will the
Minister consider altering the regulations.
to make them just and equitable?
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the R.I.C.
pension is controlled by the Imperial
Government and that the R.U.C. pension

R.I.C. pensioners are placed on by the
Imperial Government?
Food Control.
DIRECTION OF
PROSECUTIONS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether he is responsible for
criminal prosecutions in respect to
breaches of the law in Northern Ireland;
whether his attention has been drawn to
a question by an Imperial M.P., which
disclosed that 200 lbs. sugar, 134 lbs. of
tea, 170 tins of sardines, 20 dozen tins
soup, fruit, etc., 30 tins of biscuits and
rice to feed turkeys was hoarded by Mr.
Mackie, Whiteabbey, a director of the
firm of James Mackie & Sons; whether
other breaches of the law were disclosed
on the same occasion; and whether the
Attorney would take a statement from
Mr. Farmer, Belfast Food Controller, and
generally put the criminal law in motion.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): In Northern Ireland the
Attorney-General is responsible for the
direction of public prosecutions as distinguished from private prosecutions and
prosecutions initiated by officers of State
or Government Departments under powers
which do not require his consent or concurrence, as, for example, proceedings
directed by the Minister of Food in
respect of breaches of the Defence Regulations relating to food control.
My attention has been directed to the
question in the Imperial House
House of
Commons referred to by the hon. Member
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Attorney-General]
and to the answer thereto given by the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Food, who said:
This case was fully investigated by
my Department. After the most careful consideration it was decided that
there was no ground for a substantial
charge under the Acquisition of Food
(Excessive Quantities) Order, 1942,
from the provisions of which all rationed
foodstuffs are excluded. A warning
was, therefore, given to Mr. Mackie.
A sample of the rice to which my hon.
Friend refers was examined by the
Belfast city analyst, who reported that
it was not fit for human consumption.
Since this matter was raised in the
Imperial House I have sought and have
readily been granted by the Ministry of
Food an opportunity of perusing the documents in its possession regarding this case.
While I am not bound by the decision
arrived at by the Ministry, I think in the
circumstances it is but right that I should
say that a careful consideration of these
papers has not led me to any different
conclusion.
With regard to the last part of the hon.
Member's question, I have been unable
to find that Mr. Farmer was personally
concerned either with the search made of
Mr. Mackie's premises last September by
inspectors of the Ministry or with the investigations which
which subsequently took
place; nor have I succeeded in tracing any
report by him on the matter to his
superiors or to the police.
If, however, Mr. Farmer has any
material information in his possession and
puts it before the police it will receive due
consideration in conjunction with the other
evidence available.
Mr. NIXON: Did the Attorney-
General direct that a statement be taken
from Mr. Farmer? Is it a fact that Mr.
Farmer is willing, available and ready to
give a statement? How can the Attorney-
General get evidence in any case if he
only takes statements from the people
accused, and how is it that Mr. Mackie,
whose wife is a German, can have all these
goods stored while ordinary British subjects are prosecuted, some of them for
looking round them, and some of them for
nothing at all?
It is
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
not correct to suggest that statements were
only taken from the person implicated;
they were taken from many persons.
You could have taken
Mr. NIXON :
one from Mr. Farmer.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: So far
as Mr. Farmer is concerned, there is
nothing in the documents to suggest that
he had any part, direct or indirect, in
this matter. If Mr. Farmer has any
information in his possession every facility
will be given to him to submit a statement to the police that can be acted upon
if it is worthy of being acted upon. I may

I do

not know the hon. Member's acquaintance

School Kitchens and Canteens.
4. Dr. LYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
whether she is aware that the Board of
Education in England, after consultation
with the other interested Departments,
have announced that they are now
prepared to provide local education
authorities, free of charge, with premises
and all equipment for school kitchens and
canteens in connection with the supply of
meals to school-children; and whether
similar benefits will be extended to schools
in Northern Ireland.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I am
aware of the proposals which are referred
to in the hon. Member's Question and
which are contained in a circular letter
issued by the Board of Education to local
education authorities in England and
Wales a few days ago. My Ministry has
already taken up this important matter,
and we propose to confer on our schools
the same benefits as are being made available in Great Britain. The details are
now under consideration.
Agriculture.
SUPPLIES FOR NESTLE'S
FACTORY.
5. Mr. ELLIOTT (for Mr. Gamble)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
it is a fact that supplies of milk for
Nestlé's Milk Factory at Omagh are being
taken by road from Killyman, a distance
of 40 miles, instead of as formerly from
N
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
Irvinestown, Kesh and Enniskillen, and
other creameries within a 20 miles radius
of the factory; whether this is not a
waste of petrol and rubber; and whether
the only reason for so doing is the fact
that Killyman Creamery is now operated
by the Ministry.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The answer is,
Yes. It is a fact that substantial quantities of whole milk have recently been sent
a distance of 33 miles from Killyman to
Nestlé's condensery at Omagh. The principal reason is not, as stated by the hon.
Member, but because certain structural
alterations are being carried out at Killyman in order to enable this centre to
operate as a whole milk depot under the
control of my Ministry. The transfer of
certain quantities of whole milk from
Killyman to Omagh has considerably
facilitated the progress of the structural
work involved.
A COUNTY FERMANAGH
CONTRACT.
6. Mr. FERGUSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether George Veitch, of
Derryvran, County Fermanagh, and his
father, Andrew Veitch, drew the milk to
Florencecourt Creamery for 45 years;
whether they were discharged without
compensation; whether the milk from that
area is now being drawn to Enniskillen
by a resident of Eire named McGovern,
and whether George Veitch or his father
was ever offered the contract or given any
notice of it and who is responsible for the
giving of these contracts.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: At the introduction of the concentration scheme for
the creamery industry at the 1st October,
1942, Mr. George Veitch and Mr. Andrew
Veitch were delivering milk to Florencecourt Creamery by long cart. I am unable
to say how long they had been engaged
in this business. Florencecourt Creamery
was closed at the 1st October, 1942, and
since that date the milk from the area has
been conveyed direct to Enniskillen. In
these circumstances, it was no longer possible to continue the delivery of milk by
long cart from this area and arrangements
were made for the milk to be collected by
motor vehicle. A contract for this purpose has been made by the Ministry with
Mr. G. Rankin. The Ministry has no
Mr.
contractual relationship with
McGovern, but from inquiries made, it
appears that recently Mr. McGovern drove
Mr. Rankin's motor vehicle for a few
days.
In regard to the last part of the question, no single officer is responsible for the
placing of contracts for the cartage of
milk. They are completed by the Ministry
acting on information supplied by its
inspection staff.

on

CHAIRMAN OF THE PIGS
MARKETING BOARD.
10. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
date of the first meeting of the present
Pigs Marketing Board, the date on which
the Chairman commenced drawing his
salary of £300 per year, and the total
amount drawn by him in salary and
expenses up to the 31st March of the
present year.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The first
meeting of the present Pigs Marketing
Board was held on the 1st March, 1939.
The rest of the information sought by
the hon. Member has already been given
in answer to many questions of this type,
but if it will assist him, the following is
a summary of the position:
The Chairman served without salary
from his appointment till 30th June,
1940, and after persuasion by my Ministry
consented to continue making his services
available. A salary of £300 per annum
was attached to this office from the 1st -
July, 1940, and still continues.
The hon. Member, in his question, suggests that the Chairman receives expenses.
I would like to repeat and to emphasise
that the Chairman of the Pigs Marketing
Board receives no allowance whatever in
respect of travelling, subsistence or other
expenses.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that
reply, may I ask whether it is a fact that
this gentleman only consented to continue
Chairman of the Pigs Marketing Board
when a salary of £300 was attached to the
office?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I am afraid
I would need notice of that.
Mr. NIXON: As a matter of fact, is
it not a fact that this paying of a salary
to the Chairman of the Pigs Marketing
Board for doing nothing, seeing that it is
all done by the Government, is only an
excuse to give a certain man £300 a year
for nothing?

Ministry of Education
