ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Estimates, 1943-44.
SUPPLY-(4th Allotted Day).
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLASS V. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
The CHAIRMAN: With the consent
of the Committee I suggest that the two
Votes be taken together. Is that the
wish of the Committee?
The Committee indicated assent.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £50,522 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum that will come in course of payment
during the year ending the 31st March,
1944, for the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Education." (Note-£26,000
has been voted on account.)
Mrs. PARKER: Before formally introducing my Estimates may I refer briefly
to a change which has taken place recently at the head of my Ministry.
Although the Minister of Education sits
in another House, I do not think you will
consider it out of place if I say something
about the late Minister who did such outstanding work for Education in Northern
Ireland over a period of 18 years, over
twelve years as Parliamentary Secretary
and over five years as Minister. His
clear, sound judgment, his concise exposition of any case-qualities associated with the legal profession which he
possessed in a high degree-were an extremely valuable asset to the Ministry.
Our best wishes go to him in the high
office to which he has been appointed.
At the same time, I wish to tender our
good wishes to his successor in office. My
colleague in this House now enters another
arena-one in which I am certain that
his deep interest in Education-
Mr. NIXON: He got a call.
Mrs. PARKER- -his ability and his
kindly and courteous characteristics will
be as thoroughly appreciated as they are
in his own Ministry. However, I believe
there is a general impression that the
Ministry of Education is a calm and
sheltered backwater remote from political storms and tempests and rather remote.
from stern realities. I think this is hardly
an accurate picture: I wish it were! It
has been our constant endeavour to make
it so, and to keep an absolutely even, just
and impartial control over any conflicting
elements which may arise to disturb the
balance and harmony of our ways. Education authorities, teachers, members of
the different religious denominations,
managers, parents and pupils all look to
us to maintain this balance, and I would
like to take this opportunity of saying
that as long as I have any responsibility
it will be my most earnest aim to assist
the. Minister and the officials of the
Department in giving justice to all and
undue favour to none.
I shall now take the two Estimates on
the Order Paper together---Class V, No. 1
and No. 2. We are asking for £2,780,807
with which to carry out our activities.
That is an increase of £133,081 over last
year. Of that increase £4,834 is accounted
for by the increase in Vote 1-administration-and hon. Members will see that
we have now the services of an assistant
secretary and an inspector who have. returned to us from the Army and that we
have in the past year appointed four temporary inspectors to help in the inspection
of our schools. We have also had a considerable increase in our Estimate for postage, telegrams and telephones, as hon.
Members would naturally expect in these
days of stress and urgency, particularly
as my Ministry is not situated at the
headquarters of the administration of the
Government.
Hon. Members will not wish me to
spend too much time on a detailed explanation of each Estimate; they know, I
am sure, that I shall be glad to answer
any questions that may be put to me,
but in the meantime I propose to refer
only to what I think are the most important features.
First, perhaps I may explain how we
stand with regard to evacuation. After
the air raids on Belfast 14,000 children
from the city and 196 teachers were
evacuated to the country; last month
these numbers had fallen to 5,300 children
and 35 teachers and the return to the city
still continues. The two years that have
passed have been difficult for both classes
of teachers, those who were assigned to
the country and those who received the
evacuated children into their country
schools, and I am sure also that the
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
1 JUNE 1943
children concerned found it a very novel
experience. But I should like to say that
the Ministry of Education is very greatly
pleased at the absence of friction and
trouble during those two years; from the
educational point of view the scheme
worked very smoothly and I doubt if
there was any real loss in formal education. Gains in other directions there
certainly were, particularly to the children
themselves, and I would hope that when
this war is over, provision may be made
whereby the school-children of Belfast
may be given an opportunity of enjoying
the pleasures and amenities of the
countryside and the seaside in school
camps under conditions more free from
care than in war time. I think that has
been carried out in County Tyrone.
Last year I spoke about the employment of school-children on farm work,
and hon. Members are aware, I am sure,
that the Ministry wrote to education
authorities throughout Northern Ireland
recommending that it might be considered
a reasonable excuse for absence from
school if the child concerned was engaged
in helping in planting or harvesting
operations provided that certain definite
conditions were observed-first, that the
child was at least 12 years of age;
second, that the education authority was
satisfied that he or she was actually assisting as claimed, and, third, that the work
could not have been done without the
assistance of school-children. Hon.
Members know the rural conditions in
Northern Ireland very well, and they will
agree with me that the services of schoolchildren which were thus made available
were of great help to the farmers, and
that but for them planting and harvesting
could not have been carried out as effectively as they were. We cannot however,
ignore the fact that, in order to give this
assistance, a great many children were
kept from school when normally they
should have been at school, and that
where this was the case the assistance was
given at the expense of their education.
I want, therefore, to appeal to all
Members of Parliament from the rural
areas and through them to the education
authorities, school managers and teachers,
right down to the parents of the children
concerned to see that the greatest care is
taken that the child is not absent for
frivolous reasons, that he is not exploited
by either parent or farmer, and that the
scheme for his utilisation on farm work is
not abused. We have made certain
modifications in the scheme for the present year, but neither the Ministry of
Education nor the Ministry of Agriculture can ensure that it works as it should
-that depends almost wholly on the
people on the spot-on the farmer, on
the parent, on the teacher and on the
education authority that administers the
attendance regulations.
The elementary school pupil is not the
only school child who can give help on the
farm. The elder boys from the secondary
school and the junior technical school are
also very anxious to help, and a good deal
of agricultural work was done by them
last year at least 50,000 pupil-days were
spent by them in helping farmers. The
major portion of this time, however, was
given by pupils who were the children or
relatives of farmers themselves and the
fact remains that there were many pupils
from secondary schools whose parents and
headmasters were anxious that they should
help, but whose offer to work was ignored
by the farmer. We know, of course, that
the Ulster farmer is very conservative,
but if he could be induced to make use
of these willing boys during the harvesting
operations I believe he would be surprised
and pleased at the amount of excellent
work they can do for him; this was shown
last year in the few cases where they were
given work to do.
the Estimate for
Coming to
elementary education-sub-head A of No. 2
-hon. Members will find that we are
asking for £1,647,555, an increase of
almost £15,000 on the Estimate for last
year. The increase is accounted for under
two headings, A3, teachers' salaries,
where an additional war bonus has
been awarded, and A5, extra-statutory grants to managers of voluntary
schools. The extra-statutory grants are
a
new feature; they are to reimburse
voluntary managers for the expenditure
they have incurred by way of contributions due to the State under Part I of the
War Damage Act of 1941. In England
public elementary schools are exempt
from rates and do not appear in the
valuation lists; in Northern Ireland the
same type of school is similarly exempt
from rates, but is shown in the valuation
lists, and under the War Damage Act all
buildings that appear in the lists must
have war damage contribution paid in
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
respect of them. It would manifestly be
unfair that the voluntary manager in
Northern Ireland should have to pay contribution while his opposite number in
England does not owing to the fact that
his school is now shown in the valuation
lists and accordingly, with the consent
of the Ministry of Finance, my Ministry
is at present engaged in repaying to the
managers concerned the sums that the
provisions of the War Damage Act has
obliged them to pay.
In sub-head C higher educationthere is a considerable increase in the
Vote asked for £302,610 as against
£278,850 for last year. In the capitation grant there is an increase of almost
£10,000, due to a marked rise in the
enrolment in secondary schools-15,628
as against 14,447. This is most gratifying; it reflects the greater prosperity of
the Province and the desire of parents to
give their children the best education
they can afford. This increase in numbers, whilst most welcome from every
point of view, makes matters difficult for
the conductors of the secondary schools,
who are precluded from extending their
accommodation and who cannot secure the
additional teachers required. They have
other difficulties, too-for example, there
are difficulties of transport and difficulties
regarding the supply of text books. But
in spite of all they continue to do excellent
work, and there is little or no evidence of
a falling-off from peace-time standards.
The
The other chief increase under the head
of secondary education is about £17,000
for university bursaries, Oriental scholarships and engineering cadetships.
first two were in operation last year and I
told hon. Members that our bursars and
Oriental scholars were young men of
the highest quality who were bringing
credit to the secondary schools of Ulster.
I gave some examples to show that they
were fully equal to the best in Great
Britain, and I am glad to say that the
further reports we have had on their work
and performance have confirmed my
words. For instance, our four Oriental
scholars, two of whom have been studying
Persian and two Japanese, have done
very well, one gaining a second place and
the other a fourth place. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) These scholars have
been studying in London together with
picked young men of linguistic ability
from the secondary and public schools of
Great Britain and we are entitled to congratulate them on having done so well.
The engineering cadets appear for the
first time in the Estimates. They are
lads from the secondary and junior technical schools who are being given a special
course of at least 18 months' duration to
fit them for commissioned service in the
new corps of the Army-the R.E.M.E.
We have 81 of them; they are a fine lot,
anxious to serve their country in the best
way they can, and we are confident that
they will do well. A new course will be
started in the autumn of this year, and
the Ministry will be very pleased if the
applicants are of as good standard as the
cadets whom we have at present in
training.
If I do not spend too long on the Votes
for technical instruction-sub-heads D1
and D2, it is not because they are unimportant; the technical schools in our area
continue to do their work with the
highest efficiency and, in addition, are
making a contribution to the general war
effort of which they have a right to be
proud. And not only is this work being
done in the College of Technology in
Belfast; the schools in the provincial
towns are busy not only on their normal
technical classes but on special classes for
the Ministry of Labour, the Army, and
the Royal Air Force, and I am glad to
say that they are carrying out this work
in a most satisfactory way.
There are two other items on the Estimates on which I should like to speakthe meals and milk schemes for schools,
shown under sub-head F, and youth
welfare, which will be accounted for
under sub-head G. The Committee will
remember that last year I explained at
length the basis on which meals and milk
schemes were to be operated and I asked
for an Estimate of £28,000 for the purpose. Actually the Ministry has only
disbursed about £7,000;
£7,000; the meals
schemes have developed very slowly, except in Belfast and County Down. There
are one or two education committees who
refuse to have anything to do with them.
I am very sorry that this should be so.
Other committees say that a school meal
scheme is impracticable in the rural
areas; they say so because they see the
undoubted difficulties, of which I admit
there are many, but I say to them that

unin
these difficulties can be overcome if there

It would be most unfair and

Great Britain. In less than two years
the number of children taking dinner at

The great majority of the education

may

grants to

feature of our educational system not

The Ministry pays grants to organisations of all kinds-clubs run by voluntary
agencies, uniformed organisations such as
the Boys' Brigade and the Boy Scouts
pre-service organisations, such the
Army Cadet Force, the Sea Cadets, and
the Girls' Training Corps. No grants are
payable to the Air Training Corps, which
is financed wholly by the Air Ministry,
and which, incidentally, has a strength
of about 2,500 in Northern Ireland. The
clubs have more than doubled their
membership in the past few years; there
are now 70 of them in operation with
3,500 members of whom about 900 are
girls; the old established organisations
such as the Scouts, the Guides and the
Boys' and the Church Lads' Brigade are
all flourishing and doing a valuable work,
and the Army Cadet Force, which was
launched only a few months ago, already
has an
enrolment of 2,000 and will
certainly increase its numbers. Altogether, in all these organisations there
are now enrolled about 32,000 boys and
girls.
I am well aware that much remains to
be done towards bringing good influences
to bear on these young people during their
hours of recreation; all the same I do
think that a great deal has already been
done by public-spirited persons with the
minimum of interference, from the State.
And that, I think, is as it should be; this
movement will not grow out of Acts of
Parliament and Statutory Rules and
Orders, and the chief duty of my Ministry towards the youth movement is, as I

I am afraid that I have already spoken
at greater length than the Committee may
approve, but before ending, I must say a
few words about what is called reconstruction and post-war planning. The Ministry
of Education does not advertise and does
not get much limelight, and the introduction of these Estimates gives us one of
the few opportunities to blow our own
trumpet, but that does not mean that
we are waiting idly for events to overtake
us. Last year, when moving the Estimates, I mentioned some of the matters
which must be improved. The basis of our
scholarship schemes must be widened and
strengthened, our system of Technical
Education must be enlarged, and there
must be a greater provision of nursery
schools. These and the raising of the
school-leaving age remain our chief aims,
but there are many other reforms which
we hope to see carried out if the Ministry
of Finance is kind to us. We receive much
advice and instruction as to the building
of a new Utopia in education; everyone
who is interested in the subject, and I am
no exception to the rule, has his own particular hobby-horse which he exercises
before the public. Particularly those who
are free from responsibility immediately
indicate where those in authority have
fallen short in the ideal.
As regards Ulster education, I am
quite clear that we have good schools in
our elementary, technical and secondary
systems, and that we have advanced considerably in the past twenty years.
am equally clear, as regards the future,
that there are many directions in which
I
we must progress and improve. If we
resolve to make those improvements we
must also make up our minds that a much
larger Education Estimate will be necessary when peace comes.
The thoughts of my Ministry are
turned towards reform and improvement.
We are planning towards that end, and
we are also watching very carefully the
developments in education that are foreshadowed in Great Britain. If we are
allowed to spend on improvements in our
own system the same sums proportionately
or a little more than is necessary for the
education reforms in Great Britain, I
believe that we shall spend them wisely.
I hope that every member of this Committee will resolve with me that nothing
but the best is good enough for our Ulster
boys and girls, and that we shall not rest
content until every child here has as good
an educational chance as the child in
Great Britain. I beg to move.

The principal teacher of Strabane

-they gave him three months' notice
terminating his employment. At the

to the

commend that the parents should be again
prosecuted. I think that is a very, very
foolish way of dealing with the problem.
It seems that in some of the committees
concerned, their main concern is to prosecute. They are adding additional hardship to the parents and to the child.
Again, there is even a suggestion that a
child who has refused to go, or who has
been absent from, school should be sent
to an industrial school. In Northern
Ireland we should adopt a different principle altogether. We should endeavour,
if possible, to keep a child out of the
industrial school, because, after all, if
we send a boy or a girl to an industrial
school his future is blighted by the fact
that he or she has been kept in that
particular institution. I would like the
particular department concerned with
this matter to take a note of these things.
The development of nursery schools is
something I appreciate very much, because I believe in the development of such
schools, for there we are going to get at
the root of such troubles as the treatment
of disease. I believe that with greater
assistance in these schools we can remove
many of the disabilities which affect
school-children prior to the school-going
age. I believe it is something we should
help in every way possible, because much
is spent on the removal of disease and
sickness when a boy or girl comes to
school on the first occasion, but I believe
the time to start is before they begin
going to school. We must support this
scheme, otherwise we are going to spend
enormous sums. Therefore, I hope every
facility will be given for the promotion
of nursery schools.

not think there is any better work that

It is almost unnecessary for me to go

as any other schools. We must give the

children to another set of children, whatever may be their religion. The increase
in the amount is due to the war bonus,

has been dealt with now with regard to

of other schools.

(Rev. Robert Moore): I would like to

took the liberty of circulating to hon.
Members a few days ago. That was
following a precedent set by my predecessor, and the idea of it was to make
hon. Members more fully conversant with
the ramifications of my Ministry.
would be impossible otherwise for me to
cover the total activities of the Ministry
now, owing to the enormous developments
that have taken place since the war broke
out.

and on the second Vote there is a decrease

two Votes of £83,654. In regard to that

will remember that towards the end of

in connection with its activities in that

the course of the year it became necessary
to take over control of agricultural implements and machinery, not only tractors,
but other implements such as binders,
tractor ploughs, and so on. That involved
a considerable expenditure. Then in
connection with the supply of labour for
the farms there was also a considerable
expenditure incurred and in connection
with the whole tillage campaign there has
been a considerable increase in the county
staffs.

certain crops arrangements whereby part

The actual price has to be checked up

increase in the staff. Part of the increase
is recoverable, but the part that comes
under the head of land improvement is
not recoverable and, therefore, appears in
this Estimate. To review the agricultural
situation generally I would point out to
the Committee that the trading side of
the Ministry has grown to a tremendous
extent-
Mr. NIXON: It has.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE- -since the
war broke out, and I feel satisfied that it
has been all to the good of the general
community that that development has
taken place. It involves transactions
amounting in the total to round about
£40,000,000 per annum. But whilst that
figure is very impressive and whilst the
work connected with the marketing side
and the trading side is very important, it
still remains the basic function of my
Ministry to make every effort to get more
and still more food produced from our own
soil. And it might be of interest to the
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
Committee. if I just made a brief comparison in this connection between the production figures for the year 1939, in which
the war actually broke out, and the year
1942. Taking 1939 as the basic year the
production of wheat in '42 was four times
what it was in '39. Taking barley and
mixed corn the production in '42 was eight
times what is was in '39. The production
of oats which is far and away the largest
acreage that we have under a cereal crop,
was 63 per cent. increase on the acreage
in 1939. In regard to potatoes which
come second to oats in acreage the increase
was also 63 per cent.
In regard to flax in the year 1942 I can
put it perhaps most vividly if I say the
acreage was three and a half times what
it was in 1939. We have good grounds for
expecting that the acreage of flax in
1943 will be five times what it was in 1939.
Equating up all these figures we get a
total crop increase. in 1942 as compared
with 1939 of 76 per cent. That is impressive, and it has been achieved by a
steady increase in the acreage of ploughed
land. There was a very definite increase
in 1940-41. We stepped up the quota of
tillage in those years very abruptly. I
have to admit that in 1942 the actual increase in ploughed land was not as big
as had been expected and was not equal
to the annual increase in the previous
years. In regard to 1943 we have again
raised the quota, and it now stands at
45 per cent. of all arable land.
Before I ever had any thoughts of being
officially associated with this Ministry I
had been looking into the question of the
tillage quota, and I then came to the conclusion that it would not be possible to go
on increasing the actual tillage quota.
Since I became Minister I have gone into
the matter again, and although no
definite or final decision has been taken
on the matter, I cannot see how we can
increase this 45
cent. to
per
subany
stantial degree in 1944. Yet the fact remains that in 1944 the country will want
more and more food grown on our own
farms. We have been casting about to
see how this can be done. We have got
a line on the manner in which it can be
done indirectly through the results of
fertilisers in the year 1942. I cannot go
into details of the matter, but we
satisfied that without actually increasing
the quota of ploughed land-we cannot
are
allow it to diminish and we will notby a better and more judicious use and
application of fertilisers we can extract
from the same acreage a considerably
higher yield of crops than we have
managed to get hitherto.
In this connection, I would like to say
that it should be borne in mind that an
increasing amount of the cereals actually
produced on our farms is being, and will
be, diverted to the mills to be processed
and put into bread. The result will be
that the farmers will be more hard put
to it to maintain their livestock than they
have been even up to the present, but we
feel that a good deal of the grass lands,
not just exactly the rough hillside grazing
but the intermediate permanent grass,
could be vastly improved and carry a good
deal more stock if it was treated with
fertilisers. We are looking into all these
aspects of the situation.
I might perhaps say a word upon the
livestock situation. It is somewhat of an
amazement to us all that with the continual breaking up of the grass land we
should find to-day that the cattle population is some tens of thousands more
than it was in 1939. There is an explanation, of course, for that, and it is
not far to look for. We had a very great
increase in the production of cereal crops
and there were enormous quantities of
oaten straw, and hay, and so on. That
is really the explanation of the maintenance of the cattle population at this
very satisfactory figure.
When we come to sheep there is a considerable reduction, but it is really
relatively small. The biggest reduction
of all, and the one we all forecast and
anticipated, is in regard to the population
of pigs. The explanation there is similar.
We had pre-war built up an enormous
pig industry in Northern Ireland, but it
was largely based on imported feeding
stuffs, and as hon. Members will realise,
that source of supply has to a very large
extent been cut off. In addition to that,
barley can no longer be used as pig food,
it has to be diverted to the feeding of the
human population. As an offset against
the fall in the pig population, which
amounts to 60 per cent., we have a very
gratifying increase of four millions in the
poultry population as compared with 1939.
That is a sort of bird's eye view of the
general agricultural situation, and I
Estimates--
Ministry of Agriculture
2 JUNE 1943
should now like to say a word or two
about the harvest of 1942. I think that
not since the year 1879, though my
memory does not carry me back so far,
has there been a worse harvest than last
harvest. The harvest of 1879 is regarded
as one of the worst that ever happened.
A great deal of the crop was lost in that
year and the agricultural community was
faced with ruin. I dare say that like
myself hon. Members in the course of the
last harvest, as they went to and fro by
train or in a car, saw here and there a
field of grain only partly saved and
apparently rotting, and came to the conclusion that a great deal of our harvest
was being lost. We are, perhaps, too
ready to jump to conclusions from an inadequate number of facts on which to
base our conclusions. As a matter of
fact, it was only a negligible portion of
the harvest that was not safely gathered
in. It was a longsome task, but success
was eventually achieved.
The gathering in of the crop was due to
a number of factors. I think it was due.
in the first instance to the doggedness of
our farmers. There are no more industrious people to be found anywhere in
these islands than the North of Ireland
farmers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
They stuck it well. To assist them they
had the best supplies of agricultural
machinery that we could procure. They
were not altogether adequate but they
were certainly the best that we could do
for them in the circumstances. In addition to that we had the assistance of the
military, and we had the invaluable assistance of the Voluntary Land Service. We
have heard criticisms of these voluntary
land workers, but we all know how reluctant and how averse the ordinary
workaday farmer is to writing a letter if
he can help it. We will not even sign his
name if he can avoid it. Yet quite a
number of farmers have taken the trouble
to write in to my Ministry bearing testimony and expressing appreciation and
gratitude for the invaluable help they received from the National Fire Service and
from voluntary land workers generally,
not omitting the sometimes maligned civil
servants.
In regard to the 1943 harvest we are.
making such preparations as we can.
Hon. Members know something already
of the scheme, for the utilisation of unemployed industrial workers for the
harvest. That scheme, which is to begin
to operate some time in July, will be
continued, these men being made available in gangs wherever needed, for as long
as may be necessary. In addition to that
we are looking to the voluntary land
workers and we are trying to arrange, for
a better connection or linkage between
the smaller provincial towns and the
farming districts that we were able to
achieve last year. There are people in
nearly every one of these instances who
have not only a town connection but a
certain connection with the local farmers,
and we are trying to find that type of
individual who will be able to bring
volunteers in the towns into personal contact with individual farmers. If we could
only raise the response in the local towns
to the same level as we achieved in the
city of Belfast last year I think we would
have no reason to worry about the safety
of the coming harvest.
There is just one other matter that I
should like to refer to before I sit down.
I should like to say a word or two upon
the question of milk. There. has been a
good deal of criticism in this connection,
and perhaps some of it was justified. I
would like hon. Members to bear some.
facts in mind in this connection. Before
the war our total consumption of liquid
milk in Northern Ireland was about 14
million gallons. Last year, 1942, it was
26 million gallons.
In addition to those 26 million gallons
that were consumed by our own people
in the leanest time of all in the year, that
is mid-winter, we managed to send two
million gallons to Scotland, making a
total of 28 million gallons of milk produced in Northern Ireland that went into
liquid consumption. If something drastic
had not been done to handle the whole
milk situation and bring it under proper
management and control that would have
been an impossible achievement. Instead
of that what would have had to be done
would have been to just cut in half the
allowance of milk per head of our population. On the other hand hon. Members,
I think, will have to admit with some
appreciation that Northern Ireland is the
one part of the United Kingdom that as
yet knows nothing about milk rationing.
Mr. MINFORD: Due to the farmers.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: And thanks
to my Ministry.
Ministry of Agriculture 838
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. MINFORD: The farmers, not the
Ministry.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: In order to
achieve what has been done a milk concentration scheme was brought into operation by my Ministry. That no doubt
upset traditions in certain matters, but
it is well just to bear in mind some of
the things it has meant for the milk producers. For the first time in history
practically every milk producer in Northern Ireland to-day can command the full
liquid price for all the milk he produces
provided it is of decent quality and cleanliness. It has involved a tremendous
organisation in the way of transit and it
has also involved the setting up of depots
for collection and handling and for the
dispersal and distribution of this milk;
but the actual position from the milk
producer's point of view to-day is that
no matter how remote he may be in some
hillside miles away from anywhere, so
far as the price and return from his milk
is concerned he is in as good a position
to-day as the limited circle of farmers
who pre-war, for instance, supplied the
city of Belfast. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Hon. Members would do well to
remember that a scheme of such magnitude as this had to be carried out in a
matter of months and had to be carried
out also in face of the difficulties and
limitations associated with war, so that
whilst there are still little inequalities
perhaps and little wrinkles in the general
fabric that need to be ironed out-and
we are looking into them from day to day
and scrutinising and dealing with them
as fast as we can-I think as a Ministry
we have a right to congratulate ourselves
on this achievement.
In regard to the year 1943 I would just
like to say this further word in connection with milk. We want still more milk.
The one thing we are determined on today is to have no rationing of milk or any
limitation of its supply for the children
or for the grown-ups either. We want
to be in a position to supply every man,
woman and child in the Province with all
the milk they need. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I do not think I need
enlarge on the general agricultural posi
tion any further.

without trying to make us look ridiculous

minister at £1,800 a year.

Why the man who is really a farm

Why he should work under different conditions or different wages to what he received on the farm is a thing the right

My grievance is not so much with the

That is an attack on other workers. He

I know of men who left farms not far

joined other national work. They have

they were ashamed when it came to the

Those are his sentiments. That is what

Motion was:
That in the opinion of this House
the Government should take immediate
steps to ensure a fair and reasonable

The Motion was laudable enough. The
way he wanted to do that was to keep men

The right hon. Gentleman says that he is

As a member of the Armagh Mental

destroy the cows and compensate the

We know what tuberculosis means. It is
a scourge. A resolution was passed by

can be done. We know perfectly well if
it were a case of foot-and-mouth disease

figures-that the Ministry had sold milk
to distributors and had never got paid
for it, and that the Ministry were afraid
to go to court to get their money. That
does not happen to the farmer who does
not till his land. There is no holding
back of the big mailed fist in his case.
I was told there was £150,000 of a deficiency. I do not know, but I am sure
that the Public Accounts Committee will
divulge all this.
I am very glad to see there is no dealing
now in seeds, because the last time. I spoke
in this House on the Agricultural Estimates was in 1940. In that year, while I
was lying in my bed and not able to do
more than read, I read about this experiment, and I was interested to learn how it
turned out. Last night I turned it up
to
refresh my memory of the deal
in the magnificent barley in which we

have traded at all. Not only did they
lose £20,000, but the class of barley was
poor. Nearly three-quarters of the barley
sold to the farmers failed to grow.
I will bring you now to very recent

not very far from Glengormley, was compelled by the Ministry to plough up his
lands. When he had done that he said,
like the good fellow he is, What is the

Two grew and the other three did not

Anyone who asks in Glengormley where

practical man, because he knows as much

a
In my district there is a poor widow
woman with 60 fowls. The other day
a gentleman walked in, and he said,
"I am an inspector from the Ministry.
I heard you got a cwt. of corn for feeding
your fowl with." She said, "Yes, I got a
cwt. of corn from my brother." "Where
is it?" asked the inspector, demanding
to see it. You would not think that the
man knew corn from wheat. She showed
it to him, and he examined it. He then
took a sample away, and I suppose that
poor woman is now waiting to be prosecuted. The point is this: Who has the
authority to decide whether this cwt. of
oats is fit for milling or fit for giving to
fowl? That is one of the petty things, the
pin-pricking of every decent citizen in
Northern Ireland which is going on at
present. Not only that, but inspectors
are going round getting tillage returns
and examining the positions on maps. In
about a fortnight round comes another
gentleman to see that the other fellow has
done his job. I think that in this duplicating of officers we are going too far.
That has happened in my own area, and
I could give the names.
Mr. ELLIOTT: They are serving your

to make
a greater contribution than

on that

Many of the farmers in my area ploughed

It is going to leave the farmer in a hopeless position financially. There is not the

The

Minister knows perfectly well that the

The Ministry of Agriculture has established potato factories in Northern Ireland in order to provide both the people
and animals with food, and yet here is a

and famine. Because it is between June
and May we must dig potatoes.
The
right hon. Gentleman knows perfectly

Why should not an Ulster farmer, who

Surely to God the farmer is entitled to
the lowest price. It is said we get labour

I want my Ulster labourer's pay to be

These things must be redressed.
You
will find next year they will fix themselves. Make no mistake about it. The
farmer will not go on producing at a low

I was talking to a farmer on Sunday
afternoon. He asked, "How is farming
getting along about Stormont?" I said
I really could not say, but we are getting
the Estimates next week. He said, "The
times are very bad. There was a man

your meat with you, because I am farming
so many years and I cannot get my
meat." That is a true picture of farming. I do hope after all this Government
will take some steps to have a finger in
the pie in fixing agricultural prices once
the war is over. I say it is wrong for
this House to allow farmers to labour at
less or produce crops at a less price than
the farmers in Scotland and England. I
demand that they be paid at the lowest
in Great Britain. That is surely a simple.
demand. The same
been
plan has
adopted with milk, cattle, sheep, eggs and
poultry and pigs. Why should we here
lag behind in what I believe is the real
stand-by of the Ulster farmer? I have not
suggested the price the man outside
London gets, but what I ask you to do is
to make good the £1 2s 6d per ton, which
we get below, plus the 5s per ton in the
category of growing good sound potatoes.
Last year in August the Ministry issued
a very strong statement that any farmer
found taking potatoes of the second period
before 1st September would receive very
strenuous treatment. But it was a
rather peculiar thing. During the month
of August the people in Belfast and
Northern Ireland were starving for

paid was £9 6s 8d. I know a man
who has one of the best farms in
Northern Ireland, and these people
were most anxious to pay him more
money, but the Ministry would not
allow it. And in the previous
year while I was lying ill, because 100
tons had gone from my farm they sent
me two letters and let me off with a
caution because I had dared to take 7s 6d
per ton more than the price paid to the
grower. I want to see justice done.
Why should I not be able to sell potatoes
to a grocer without their passing through
the hands of a middleman at another £2
a ton. In my opinion the day is coming
when the farmers are going to rebel-I
do not want to see it in war-time, but
this is my opportunity to tell the House.
If they do not want potatoes grown in
Northern Ireland, let them tell the
farmer.
The right hon. Gentleman knows perfectly well the union, of which he was
president, at the present moment
are

fighting every way. I hope he will not

I said I was up at a place called Stormont

I told the man who I was, and then in

takes a man with a handle to get justice.
I am sorry to have to speak in this way,
but this is my opportunity of doing so.
Any other time I raise it in the House
I am told it is a question for the Ministry
of Food, and we could not touch it. I
am anxious to till every acre in order to
give the people at home all the food they
need, but I do feel that when the Cabinet
come to consider this they should ask, is
the Ulsterman not entitled to the same
standard of living as the man in Scotland,
or England, or Wales. All I have done
is to ask for the lowest standard.
Now the Minister said he had volunteers last year, and that even the
maligned civil servants took a part. I
stand in this House to say that had it not
been for the civil servants of Northern
Ireland I would never have got my crop
saved. I appealed to the gentleman in
charge and he sent men down. Some of
them were not much good. They did not
belong to Ulster. He asked me would I
take girls. I had 37 girls. (Laughter.)
It is no laughing matter. These girls
worked. I had 37 girls down one day,
and I say if they do as good work in the
Ministry as they did on my farm, they
are worth their pay. I expect them
again. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
had men from the Ministry, and I can
say they did their work and showed their
patriotism by coming and working on the
farms, and working hard. I have not
heard one single farmer in my whole
travels saying one unkind word about the
civil servants. Why should they? They
are only carrying out the law that we
make here. I have been 16 years
in
Parliament, and I never got a discourteous word from one member of the Civil
Service. I have been treated with
courtesy every time. That was not the
Ministry of Food. It belongs to Great
Britain and is not under our jurisdiction.
I was rather disappointed on hearing the
Prime Minister say we have no person in
charge of the Ministry of Food now at
all. I intend to raise that on another
Estimate.
I come now to the price of barley. I
have here the monthly report of the
Ministry of Agriculture. The gentleman
who writes this report certainly knows his
job. I read it through every month, and
I say he is certainly worth his money to
the House and to Ulster. For feeding
barley we get 14s 6d per cwt., and the
highest price we get is 23s 6d per cwt.
I would like to ask the Minister what is
feeding barley? Our farmers are perturbed about this, as the price for malting barley in Great Britain is 35s per
cwt. Would the Minister look into this?
He should ask the Minister of Food why
the price for our farmers is controlled at
23s 6d when the farmers in Great
Britain are allowed to get 35s. That is a
grave injustice.
Take oats. A man with a horse in
Belfast or in any other city or provincial
town is not allowed to buy from a
farmer. He has to have a ration card to
get oats. Those oats are brought from
Scotland, and they are the greatest
rubbish possible. The Scottish farmers
get a guaranteed price from the Ministry
of Food. We pay all the charges. The
price is £18 10s per ton. Will the
Minister give the farmers of Ulster the
same price? Why should I have to take
13s 8d for my oats when I see rubbish
sold at £18 10s per ton in Belfast? The
horse feeders of Northern Ireland would
be delighted to get fresh oats, even if
they have to pay that price. Last year
I was called in to see some oats, and I
thought they had painted them orange.
They were going to a distiller and had
been through some process, but as they
were not wanted they were sent back
again.
There are far too many inspectors in
Northern Ireland, and the farmers are
getting fed up. The Minister is a
farmer himself. A farmer who is compelled to plough and sow is sometimes up
against a stone wall because he cannot
get labour. I ask him if he were a work-

ing man in my constituency where he

gives him a price which will enable him
to do it. Any man knows that in 1943
14s is a ridiculously low price for oats.
It is no wonder the Minister has trouble
in getting the ground ploughed.
If a man is instructed by the Ministry
to plough a certain amount and has not
the labour, I say it is the duty of the
Ministry to take the crop, say oats, from
him, save it, and then pay the man the
value. That is only fair and reasonable.
If you compel a man to plough and sow
and he cannot get labour at the harvest
the Ministry, in my opinion, should take
over the crop and pay him the market
value. But, no, they do not say that,
they say, "You must plough ninetwentieths no matter whether you can get
the labour or not." That is what it
really amounts to. It does not matter
whether the ground is suitable, it must
be ploughed.
A neighbour of mine had three fields
ploughed and sown, but the crop was destroyed by cut-worm or grubs. He sowed
it a second time and it happened again,
and then he sowed it the third time and
again the crop was attacked. Now he is
living in terror lest an inspector should
come and tell him he must till the ground
properly. I think these are things
which should be brought to the notice of
the Minister. If the machinery is such

Mr. ELLIOTT: And there are others.
Mr. MINFORD: I come to the question of agricultural wages. No good
farmer can be satisfied with the pay his

Mr. ELLIOTT: That is the secret.
Mr. AGNEW: Higher prices.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
And a higher cost of living.
Mr. MINFORD: If you want food you

In regard to the grants for the improvement of agricultural holdings, I see that
the Minister has cut the total down by
£44,000. I would suggest that he should

In connection with the Agricultural College at Greenmount I would like
to ask the Minister if he can explain to
me why a grant has to be given.
Remember this place is well farmed. I
see the general upkeep of the institution

1, sub-head B1, of £3,001 expenses arising out of dispersal of staff and £5,710
from other receipts, making a total of

There is my opinion. There is an example of what the Minister can do. Do
not let him take a lead out of somebody's

farmers of Ulster are of a lower grade

When they go to
fight on land or' in the air or on the sea,

or taken to the law courts. A farmer's
life was not a bed of roses from 1935 to

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: My hon.

House did. It may well be that the Pigs

I as violently disagreed with the line

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Midgley): I should
like at the outset to take this the first

which I now hold. Hon. Members will
understand that for a variety of reasons
over which I have little or no control I
have not as yet succeeded in getting round
the various branches of the Civil Defence
Authority throughout the country..
great deal of my time has been taken up
with the organisation of "Wings for
Victory" meetings and demonstrations of
a similar nature, with the result that I
am trying to work as much overtime as I
possibly can to make myself familiar with
the work.
A
In the limited opportunities that have
come to me already I have found, to a
great extent at any rate, how much I am
indebted to my predecessors in office for
laying the foundations; I refer, of course,
to my right hon. and learned Friend the
Attorney-General and my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour. They did
their job very well during their time and
that has made it much easier for me.
I should like to add that in going round
I have mentioned to the various people
I have met how much I am indebted to
them for their most constructive work.
They took a keen interest in their work;
they aroused a great deal of enthusiasm,
and they inspired a great deal of effort
on behalf of Civil Defence work, and for
those things I am deeply thankful.
should like the Committee to understand
that in all I am about to say this afternoon I am guided by that feeling.

The Department's Estimates for the
year 1943-44 give clear evidence, if evidence were needed, that during the past
twelve months the war has entered into a
new phase. In the first place the Committee is being asked to vote a considerably
smaller sum of money to provide for the
various Civil Defence services in the
current year. If I might digress, I should
like to say that if hon. Members will note
the substantial reduction that has taken

Estimates-

place they would almost feel that I would

amount of the Vote will be spent is given
in somewhat greater detail than in the
two preceding years.
The reasons for these changes are not
far to seek. Our preparations to meet
enemy attack from the air have already
been pushed to a very large degree of completeness. There. is accordingly less need
for complete secrecy about the items of
expenditure as well as a substantial reduction in the amount of money falling to
be paid during the present year in respect
of the provision of shelters and other protective work; moreover, the whole attitude
of our people has ceased to be focussed
on the need for defensive measures and it
is now directed more and more every day
to attack. I should not, however, like to
give the Committee the impression that
the needs of Civil Defence have been in
any way underestimated, and I can assure
hon. Members that all necessary steps will
be taken to provide, for the civil population to the maximum possible extent the
services and assistance which they may
reasonably demand should we again be
made the subject of attack.

of
very deep debt
gratitude which we owe to the army of

happy to be able to inform the Committee that, in so far as I have been able
in the limited time at my disposal to

have no doubt that if and when the Civil
Defence machine is again tested it will be

I often wonder whether it is fully
realised how much Northern Ireland dethe
pends for these vital services upon
unpaid and purely voluntary work undertaken by thousands of willing helpers.
We in the Department usually refer to
But
them as the part-time volunteers.
the word "part-time," I know from my
own personal experience, is in many cases
a misnomer. There are men and women
in this business who are putting in as
many hours of work every day, without
any fee or reward, as would make their

They come from all walks of life, but they
could
give service for which no money
pay. To all these men and women, be

We must never forget that so long as
the enemy remains undefeated the risks
of war must be faced, and it may well be

ready to counter the enemy's attack, but
We
there is plenty of room for more.
here, in the absence of conscription, have

Civil Defence service to meet our needs.
I would, therefore, appeal most earnestly
to hon. Members to help me in encouraging all our citizens to play their part in
manning our defences, and, in particular,
in the matter of fire prevention.
Ministry of Public Security
Estimates-

3 JUNE 1943
the
A great deal has been done to defend
our cities and towns against incendiary
attacks, but I should like to see
numbers of fire guards and fire watchers
considerably increased and a great deal
more interest taken in this subject by the
ordinary citizen, whether or not he is
compelled under the Orders which have
been made to devote a part of his leisure
time to protecting the place at which he
works. I cannot impress upon the Committee sufficiently strongly the benefit of
adequate fire prevention measures and the
need for a clear perception on the part
of all our citizens as to where their duty
lies in this matter.
Our Civil Defence services are good.
But the burden of responsibility and
service is being borne too heavily on the
shoulders of the willing few. Whatever
may be the arguments for or against
applying conscription for military service
to Northern Ireland, there is no doubt
that the absence of conscription allows a
very large number of our citizens to sleep
comfortably in their beds instead of
sharing the hardships and separation
which membership of the fighting Services
entails. Many no doubt have good and
sufficient reasons-which I do not for a
moment deny-why they are not in the
fighting Services as volunteers; but is it
too much to ask that if they are unable.
to strike a blow at the enemy they will at
least play their part in protecting their
own homes, and the homes of their comrades in the Forces? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Believe me, they can in this way perform a valuable service to their country
which will be second only to the valour
of the fighting men; and they will be
joining a fellowship which has a record.
to be proud of in the dark days of warfare.
It is indeed my hope that when its
primary object has been fulfilled, and the
Axis powers overthrown, the fellowship of
civil defence will be projected into our
post-war world as an instrument to help
in solving the great problems of peace; for
those problems will only be solved by the
spirit of service and comradeship which
is so evident in those parts of the Civil
Defence, organisation with which I have so
far come in contact.
I should not like to leave the subject of
the Civil Defence Services without making
reference to the help which they have
given in war-time activities, quite apart
from their primary role. They
They have
helped in Salvage Drives, War Savings
Weeks and perhaps most important of all
in the saving of the harvest
of our
country; and the Committee. will, I am
sure, have welcomed the announcement
recently made that arrangements have been
made to provide similar help on an even
more extended scale in saving the coming
harvest. In all these matters, and many
more. too numerous to mention, the
Women's Voluntary Services and women
of the Civil Defence organisation generally
have played an outstanding part.
And in turning now to the Fire Service
I should like, of course, to say that they
have not been behind the other Civil
Defence Services in giving their assistance
in these war-time activities during their
stand-by and leisure periods. I am informed that on the whole satisfactory progress has been made during the first year's
working of the National Fire Service.
Hon. Members will no doubt be interested
to know that we have records of 888 fire
calls, received at N.F.S. stations during
the year ended 31st March last, and of
these no few than 349, or 40 per cent.,
were malicious. I should like the Committee to meditate very deeply upon that,
and to carry their meditations into the
larger activities of life and see if they
can get the moral, self-respecting, lawabiding members of the community to
stamp this pernicious thing out
altogether. The Fire Service must answer
all calls, and where life and property may
be at stake, time cannot be taken to
verify whether a call is genuine or not.
I cannot but deplore the large number of
malicious calls, which are bound to blunt
the enthusiasm of the service, quite apart
from the waste of petrol and the wear and
tear on tyres and vehicles at a time when
the conservation of these supplies is so
essential.
Many people, including some of the
local authorities, have been good enough
to write to the Ministry to express appreciation of the manner in which the
National Fire Service have tackled their
job, but I am by no means complacent on
the matter. This is a new service, it has
a long way to go before we can regard it
as being the very best that can be
achieved, and I am not going to be satisfied with anything less than the very best
in this branch of the service. I will,
however, give myself the pleasure of
P
Ministry of Public Security
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
imparting to the Committee one item of
information. In 1942 the value of property damaged by fire in Northern Ireland represents a substantial reduction
over the two previous years, leaving out
of account, of course, fires due to enemy
action. In the remainder of the United
Kingdom the losses of property through
fire damage, not due to enemy action,
have risen very steeply and are giving
cause for grave concern.
I am not going to claim any great
credit to the National Fire Service for
our favourable record during last year.
It may, I frankly admit, be due largely
to an element of good fortune, but at any
rate it is a good omen. One disquieting
factor in our experience last year was the
fact that in six fires lives were lost, the
total number of deaths due to fire during
the period being thirteen in all. I may
inform the Committee that careful inquiry by the Department showed that the
method in which the National Fire Service
answered the calls left nothing to be
desired. In all cases the deaths were the
subject of coroners' inquiry, and in no
case was criticism of the service substantiated. I should like to take this opportunity of impressing on all our people
the very serious danger of fire. A large
proportion of what I may call "lull-time"
fires are caused by carelessness on somebody's part. Fires cause an enormous
amount of damage every year. They
cause loss of life. These losses can be
greatly reduced by just that little bit of
extra care which makes the difference.
When a fire takes hold the National
Fire Service will come to the rescue as
quickly as possible and will fight the fire
with all the bravery and energy which
they have, but the services of the firemen
must always be regarded as the lesser of
two evils. It is bad to need a fireman;
it is worse still to need one and not get
him, but best of all is not to need the
fireman at all. So I would earnestly
appeal to everyone-householders, commercial concerns and industrialists-to
pay particular attention to the prevention
of fires at their establishments. Much
can be done by tidy habits and intelligent
forethought to prevent fires occurring at
all; and much can be done by structural
alterations to minimise the damage caused
by fires which do arise. The insurance
companies and the National Fire Service
are only too anxious to give their advice
and assistance.
I should like now to turn to a matter
about which there has been some little
controversy, and that is the acceptance of
recruits into our National Fire Service of
people not normally resident in Northern
Ireland. In order to place this matter in
its proper perspective I should like the
Committee to cast its mind back to the
post-raid situation when it was necessary
to embark upon a very heavy increase in
the number of whole-time firemen
employed. At that time-and indeed up
to quite recently-there was a scarcity
of suitable able-bodied man-power available for all the many and various tasks
which were proceeding in Northern Ireland in connection with the war effort as
a whole. In such circumstances men of
goodwill, who were willing to take an
oath of allegiance to His Majesty the
King, and who were suitable and of good
character, were gladly accepted for the
Auxiliary Fire Service, and later received
into the National Fire Service, even
though they had not been born and bred
in Ulster; and the Committee will, of
course, be aware that recruitment for the
fighting services is undertaken in exactly
the same spirit.

like to emphasise this: We were glad to

They were given out for the use of occupiers of the dwellings concerned, but they
are not being used. It is within my own

that, if those conditions exist, it is the

matters nearly six months ago the
position seems to be largely the same
to-day.
I have a special reason for mentioning
the question of Morrison shelters. I consider, and have always considered, that
the method whereby these shelters were
allocated-I am referring to the fact that
the shelters were given for the use of
owners of houses with a valuation of £29
and under-was wrong. I am seriously
perturbed by the fact that in some houses,
the occupiers of which are not able to
pay the necessary amount in order to
enable them to purchase a shelter, there
are invalids who would require Morrison

unable to leave their homes. I say it is
fair and reasonable to ask that some of

referred.

nearly £20,000,000, every Minister should
be in his place. That is my view. Yesterday I had to call the attention of the
Committee to the fact that there were
only seven Members present.
I was
rather annoyed when we were discussing
Estimates for agriculture totalling
£519,000-which I consider to be by far
the most important Estimates of this
Government that I had to call attention
to the fact that the Committee was taking
so little cognizance of that Department
of the Government. We have the first,
second, third and fourth arm of defence,
but I believe that agriculture is the first
arm of defence. In speaking like that I
may be getting off the beaten track.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I know you made

We have a standing arrangement with the

of physical fitness, which is the supreme
test. There is a wide margin in regard
to age, on the, young side and even up to
middle age, provided the men attain the
standard of physical fitness required. The
very fact that we have not yet been able
to get the numbers we require through
the instrumentality of the labour exchanges is proof that the eligible market
for employment is not nearly as large in

it is. The unemployment problem in
Northern Ireland is magnified. If you
eliminate certain categories of people who
are not available for this kind of service
you will find that the margin we have to
work on is very small indeed.
As I have said, we have a standing

other attractions being held out against

and women are being attracted into other

Men
Many people do not like the system of
service in the fire departments. The
principle is so many hours on and so many
off. The hours of duty are 48 hours on
and 24 off. That does not mean that
the personnel must stand on watch at
their post for 48 hours, but that they
must be available for duty for a period of
48 hours. There are many people who will
not accept that form of service if they
can get an alternative one limited to 8,
8, or 9 hours a day, with a guarantee of
overtime if they exceed 8 hours. The
reactions to the National Fire Service are
largely psychological. It is an essential
form of service.
I do not know what the future of the
fire service is going to be in this country,
whether it is going to be continued as a
national service-that time alone will tell
-or whether there is going to be some
form of nationalisation without municipal
control, or whether it will revert to municipal control as formerly. Whatever the
form of service is going to be, under a

That brings me to the points mentioned
by the hon. Member for Woodvale, and
also, I think, by the hon. Member for
North Down. I believe I can combine
the two points. With regard to the personnel itself, I said this afternoon that in
the post-raid period, when we were developing this service, there was a shortage
of man-power. I am assured by the
Minister of Labour that there was
acute man-power shortage at that time
from the war point of view. It was
essential to have a Fire Service. The
personnel had to be procured, but they
were not taken indiscriminately. That is
what I have been informed, and I have
every reason to accept the assurances
given to me that the people who were
recruited into the service were not
accepted indiscriminately.
They were subject to two considerations,
first, they had to take the oath of
allegiance and, second, they had to be
reported upon in all cases by the police.
The police made inquiries, and if the
applicants were found to be undesirable.
characters, as far as police investigations
could convey or indicate, they were not
accepted. They were only taken subject
to those considerations, they had to be
men, they had to take the oath of allegiance, and they had to be favourably
reported upon by the police.
It is no
doubt true that despite all the organisation in the world, and despite precautions.
like that, unsatisfactory persons will find
their way into all kinds of assemblies.
Unsatisfactory people have even found
their way into the House of Commons,
not only in Northern Ireland but in Great
Britain, and there are people who, from
a community point of view, would have
been much better in some other institutions which I do not want to specify here
this afternoon but will leave to the imagination of the members of the Committee.
That being so, one is bound to meet
some of those people, but I can give the
hon. Member for North Down an
assurance that if any member of the
Committee can give me in confidence proof
beyond doubt of disloyal sentiments or
seditious elements manifesting themselves.
in the National Fire Service, those elements will not be in that service very
long. That is what I want to assure the
Committee. We want a body of men and
women who believe in the integrity of our
State-it is not a question of the size of
the State, it is a question of the integrity
of the State-and who are prepared to
give public service for its maintenance.
With regard to the question of air-raid
shelters raised by the hon. Member for
North Down, I have looked into the question from the point of view of the
investigation or partial investigation
which took place in response to a query
of his about March of this year. In reply
the then Minister of Public Security indicated what the Government's policy was
in regard to the Morrison shelters. He
also dealt with the question of holding
in reserve those that had not been put
into use. In the light of the statement
made here to-day by the hon. Member
for North Down, I wish to give him an
assurance that, whilst that is the general
policy of the Ministry, I am prepared to
go into the question and look at it afresh.
I shall call for a report with regard to the
number of Morrison shelters, for example,
in the hands of local authorities, not
being put to the use for which they were
intended, and also with regard to those
supposed to be lying in disuse and deteriorating. The previous Minister indicated that such shelters would be called
in if there were any malpractices, or if
they were not being used for the purpose
for which they were provided.
I hope to call for an examination into
the whole question, with a view to seeing
that everything can be done shall be done
to get under our control the quantity of
stuff we ought to have under our control.
We will give consideration to the question
of whether the shelters should be held in
reserve, or whether a fuller use cannot be
made of the material available. Included
in the scope of our inquiry, I take it, will
be the point raised in regard to outstanding cases in which people cannot get the
shelters owing to their economic circumstances. We will consider that point also.
I think those are the main points. The

said they were due in the main to lack of

COeducation, and he asked for the

and camouflage must be discontinued.
Assertions are made by people in Northern Ireland that there are influences at
work in this community which are not
healthy. There are people who are

I can tell the Committee what occurred
in one municipality in Northern Ireland
when on a certain occasion I was in the
vicinity-I was there as a private individual, and SO from my presence
there, I will not be held accountable for
what happened-and a very serious fire
took place involving loss of life. One
would think that in a district where a
serious fire took place involving loss of
life the people would have had such a
shock to their sense of social conduct and
of charity that they would have been condoling with the people who suffered.
What actually happened was that, to
add to the troubles and worries of
the Fire Service, four or five malicious
calls were sent in by people in
the community that very afternoon.
Now that is evidence of disloyalty and
a disposition to disturb the harmony,
efficiency and efficacy of our machinery
here as a State and that is the kind of
conduct to which I wish to draw attention. As far as we can deal with it and
as representative of the Ministry as far
as I can deal with it by direct action it
will be dealt with thoroughly, efficiently,
and fairly. That is the position from our
point of view.

being done, but I know sufficient to be
able to assure the House that very much
more is being done than the average man
or woman might think. We have gallant
and scientific people and people of high
distinction in Northern Ireland working
here at the present time investigating the
phenomena relating to poison gas. They
are trying to rouse up the social conscience
and they are making experiments. They
are visiting the homes of the people inspecting the gas helmets or masks or
respirators of different types to ensure the
utmost efficiency.
They want co-operation on the part of
the civil community. A department cannot do everything for the people that
should be done. We want in the final
analysis really the co-operation of all
concerned and the goodwill of all concerned. If we get that co-operation and
goodwill I will guarantee we have, as high
a level of intelligence and as high a level
of devotion to duty and conscientious conviction as can be found elsewhere. I believe these things, harnessed to a recognition of the fact that the war is not over
and that we may have dark days ahead
and ought to be on our guard to preserve
and protect the lines at home inspired by
a belief in ultimate victory-I believe
these things will carry us through.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Staffing of Food Offices.
ARMAGH.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of temporary staff engaged by Armagh
Urban Food Office; how many were recruited through the Labour Exchange;
and the number of new Unemployment
Books issued to personnel employed.
temporarily in Armagh Urban and Rural
Food Offices.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): I am informed that the number
of temporary staff engaged by the
Armagh Urban Food Office is four, and
that all of these were obtained from the
Employment Exchange.
Two new unemployment books were
issued to persons temporarily employed in
the Urban Food Office, and six new books.
to persons temporarily employed in the
Rural Food Office.
LURGAN.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of workers recruited from the Labour
Exchange in Lurgan to fill temporary
appointments in the Urban Food Qffice;
whether it is a fact that the wife of an
official or servant of the Urban Council,
Lurgan, is employed in this Food Office;
and whether he can state the number of
unemployed taken on for work in Lurgan
Rural and Urban Food Offices.
Mr. GRANT: I should explain to the
hon. Member that the Lurgan Food Office
comprises the Lurgan urban and rural
areas and the Moira rural area.
I am informed that the Food Executive
Officer approached the Lurgan Employment Exchange when it became necessary
for him to make temporary appointments
for the writing-up of ration books. Of
the candidates submitted to him by the
Employment Exchange only two were.
found to be suitable for the work in
question, and eighteen persons having
clerical experience have been recruited
from other sources.
I am unaware whether it is a fact that
the wife of an official or servant of the
Urban Council is employed in the Food
Office. The hon. Member will appreciate
that the staff of a Food Office is part of
the staff of the Ministry of Food, and
that therefore the method by which such
staff is recruited is primarily a matter for
that Department of the Imperial Government. I understand, nevertheless, that
it is the practice of the Ministry of Food
to approach the appropriate Employment
Exchange in all cases in which temporary
clerical appointments are concerned.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that he is unaware
that the wife of a member of the Council
has been appointed on the staff of this
Food Office, would it not be within the
bounds of possibility that with his great
organisation and the assistance of the
various other Departments, and a horde
of officials, he should be able to find that
tiny bit of information?

PAYMENT OF UNEMPLOYED.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
precise wages that members of the unemployed whose services are to be utilised by
the Government in harvesting operations
will receive from the Ministry, and if
this is to be collected from the farmers,
and also the precise position as to accident
insurance and unemployment insurance,
etc.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: As has
already been made clear on several occasions in official statements, the unemployed
workers who will be taken into the employment of my Ministry for harvesting
operations will be paid at the highest of
the minimum rates of wages fixed by the
Agricultural Wages Board for Northern
Ireland. The farmer in his turn will be
required to refund to the Ministry the
rate of wages applicable to his own
particular district for the week, the day
or the hour, as the case may be.
As I informed the hon. Member on
the 20th May, the Ministry will have
exactly the same responsibilities as an
ordinary employer regarding insurance,
etc.
Mr. NIXON: Will the money paid to
the people who assist the farmers be paid
into their own hands?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: There are
two schemes. There is the voluntary land
service scheme, but the question I have
answered has been mainly in regard to
the scheme for using unemployed workers
in gangs.
In their case the money will
be paid directly into my Ministry.
Mr. NIXON: In the case of soldiers
who may help the farmers, as they did
last year, will the money be paid to them,
or will it not?

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I have been
asked by the Prime Minister to reply.
The hon. Member will, I am sure,
appreciate that shortly after the date he
mentions, the country became, engaged in
a life and death struggle with the Axis
powers, and that with the operation of
the Ministry of Food, the activities of
the Pigs Marketing Board are necessarily
curtailed.

hon. Member's question, I do not agree
with his implication and I am fully satisfied, as I explained last week, that in the

Board must be continued.

months elapsed from the time that

com-
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if there are
complaints from coal merchants as to the
allowance of coal granted for supplying
customers; whether customers are
plaining to the Ministry of Commerce and
blaming their supplier for not giving
them coal which he never got; whether
a number of householders are several
weeks without coal and are trying to
change their suppliers; whether all
merchants, including bell men, get a fair
and adequate supply of the coal available; and whether he can state why
practically none of the really good coal is
now allotted to Northern Ireland, or, if it
is so allotted, can he state the class of
society to which it is supplied.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
I propose with your permission, Mr.
Speaker, to give a comprehensive reply
covering the various points raised in the
hon. Member's question.
A regular supply of domestic coal (of
which over eighty per cent. is now
English coal) is being brought into Northern Ireland by the coal importers, who
have been instructed as to the proportions
in which this coal must be divided between merchants and bellmen. These
merchants and bellmen in turn have
complete lists of customers over whom
they should spread the supplies.
It is admitted that supplies are not as
plentiful as they were over a year agothat is a matter of production in Great
Britain-but they are better distributed
through the country. Complaints come
mostly from the small minority of
merchants and consumers who have not
taken the trouble to plan the equitable
distribution or economical use of the coal
supplied. The coal year ends on 31st
August and consumers who have already
exhausted their year's quota of coal ask
for more. Cases of real hardship
are, however, always treated sympathetically.

13. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether local
authorities generally have been requested
to make a survey of the accommodation
prevailing in their areas, and to obtain

in each dwelling, and will he state (a)
if the obtainment of this information is
obligatory upon the authorities concerned, and (b) if the Government proposes to reimburse the ratepayers for the
cost of making the survey.
Mr. LOWRY: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the remainder of the
question, in urban districts the Ministry
is accepting full responsibility for the
carrying out of the survey relating to the
structural characteristics and the condition of the houses, but as regards the
portion of the survey relating to overcrowding the Ministry has asked the
urban authorities to undertake this portion of the work at their own expense.
As the information obtained by the
survey will be of very great assistance to
urban authorities in preparing their postwar housing plans, I am of opinion that it
is not unreasonable to ask them to pay the
expense of the overcrowding survey which
I have no reason to believe will be
substantial.
Belfast-Holywood Bus Service.
14. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he is prepared in the interests of economy to recommend a restricted morning and evening bus service between Holywood and
Belfast for those engaged in work in the
East end of the city, and who are at
present compelled to duplicate train and
bus services to reach their place of employment.
Mr. LOWRY: As I informed the hon.
Member on the 16th March, provision
of a bus service between Holywood and
Belfast has been very carefully considered
both by the Ministry and the Northern
Ireland Road Transport Board, but I cannot hold out any hope of such a service
being introduced at present. If the
service would mean any economy of public
transport or of petrol or rubber, I can
assure the hon. Member that it would be
operated at once. The contrary is, however, the fact, as to cater adequately for
the traffic which would present itself the
Transport Board would have to run extra
buses as the present services are being
run to capacity. There would, therefore,
be no economy whatever in transport,
although it might mean a small personal
saving to individual members of the
travelling public.
