ORDERS OF THE DAY.
SUPPLY (7th Allotted Day).
Estimates, 1943-44.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
CLASS IV. No. 1.
Ministry of Labour.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £82,832 be.
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum that will come in course of payment
during the year ending 31st March, 1944,
to defray the salaries and certain expenses
of the Ministry of Labour."—(£42,000
has been voted on account.)
Mr. GRANT: In introducing these
Estimates, I should like to take the
opportunity of referring to the work of
my predecessor. For over 21 years he
rendered signal service, both as Parliamentary Secretary and as Minister of the
Department. I am sure Members on
both sides of the House will join with
me in this tribute to his work and worth.
As more than 95 per cent. of the money
for which I am asking the Committee is
for the social services and their administration, it is perhaps fitting that I should
deal at some length with them and review
the position generally. It is, I suppose,
a natural outcome of the war and of our
firm conviction of ultimate victory that
proposals for social security on the return
of peace should be engaging the attention
of the community. There may be room
for argument as to the precise nature of
the extensions which should be made, but
there can be none as to the desirability of
planning ahead for a scheme as complete
and all-embracing as it is possible to make
it. My Department is keeping in close
touch with the Departments in Great
Britain on the work of the preparation
and completion of the plans for introducing a social security scheme. Such a
scheme will come into force in Northern
Ireland on the same date as in Great
Britain.
We have an advantage over Great
Britain in one important respect. With
one or two minor exceptions, the unification of administration has already been
achieved in Northern Ireland in so far
as central Government machinery is concerned. When the Government of
Northern Ireland was established in 1921
it was decided that the proposed Ministry
of Labour should be responsible for all
schemes of welfare and insurance affecting
employers and workers. Administration
of the Factory and Workshops Acts, of
trade boards, of unemployment insurance
and of national health insurance was,
therefore, vested in my Department.
Until then three separate departments
had been responsible for those services in
Ireland, and to this day three separate
departments are responsible for them in
Great Britain.
Acting on the same principle of centralisation of social services, the administration of the non-contributory old age
pensions scheme was transferred to my
Ministry in 1927 from the customs and
excise department. That department still
administers the corresponding scheme in
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
Great Britain. We may well take credit
for the businesslike outlook and action of
our Government in the last twenty years
in bringing together all these schemes
under one Department. Further changes
will come, both in the scope of the services
themselves and in the machinery of their
administration, when the social security
plan takes its final form.
In the meantime, it is well to recollect
that by stages we have travelled a long
way towards the attainment of the goal
of social security, and on this occasion I
think it will not be out of place if I
pause to draw attention to our existing
social services. Let me then say a word
or two to show the steps by which we
have progressed in this matter since the
Ministry of Labour came into existence.
When the Department was set up in the
year 1921 unemployment insurance was
in its infancy. The Act of 1920 had just
come into operation, and whilst it embraced large sections of the industrial
population, it did not cover agricultural
workers and proved inadequate to cope
with the degree of unemployment which
was experienced. It was necessary to
pass amending Act after amending Act
to provide for the maintenance of large
numbers of the insured population.
I would remind hon. Members that
throughout all these years unemployment
insurance in Northern Ireland has remained on the same basis as in Great
Britain, a position which would not have
been tenable but for reinsurance agreements which it was found possible to make
with the Government of the United
Kingdom. The Unemployment Act of
1934 was a milestone on the way towards
putting provision against unemployment
on a proper basis. That was the Act
under which the Assistance Board was set
up, and which made provision not only
for persons insured under the Unemployment Insurance Acts on the exhaustion of their statutory benefit, but for all
persons insured under the Contributory
Pensions Acts in the event of their
inability to obtain employment.
In the year 1936 farm workers were
brought into unemployment insurance,
and in the year 1940 the scheme was extended to include black-coated workers
whose rate of remuneration fell between
the limits of £250 and £420 a year.
Since the inception of the scheme the rates
of benefit have progressively increased
and various extensions have been made to
the classes of dependants for whom
additional allowances can be claimed. In
the matter of unemployment assistance,
a personal needs test was submitted in
1941 for the family means test, and here
again the scale rates for assistance have
been increased from time to time.
Provision was made for the gradual
extinction of the debt existing in the Unemployment Fund, and I am happy to
say that in the Unemployment Fund we
have now a surplus of £4,500,000, a reserve which we hope will be added to
during the present year.
In the matter of health insurance, the
rates of sickness and disablement benefit
were increased by the 1941 Act, and,
whilst those rates may not be regarded as
adequate, it must be remembered that
they are based on the amount of the
contribution paid by employer and employee. The provision of medical treatment for the insured person accounts for
a considerable part of the contribution,
and the standard rates of benefit may be
increased in the cases of Approved
Societies which show a surplus on
valuation. It goes without saying that
provision of an adequate medical service
must be a cardinal point in any scheme
of health insurance and that the prevention of ill-health, through timely
medical attention, should be the aim of
any proper scheme of health insurance.
In these circumstances, I may recall
that when the Ministry of Labour took
over health insurance in the year 1922,
there were
in the
very serious gaps
system. One of the largest was the
absence of medical benefit for insured
persons, a benefit for which the dispensary system in Ireland was never a
satisfactory substitute. In the year 1930
medical benefit for insured persons was
established. Before that date the work
of the general body of medical practitioners under health insurance did not
extend beyond the examination of
persons
claiming sickness and disablement benefit
and the issue of certificates of incapacity.
The certifying doctor was not under any
obligation to give treatment, and was
entitled to charge for any treatment
given unless he was a dispensary doctor
treating a dispensary patient. A Government medical referee service was intro-
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
8 JUNE 1943
duced in 1927, so that a second medical
opinion should be available to approved
societies in cases of doubt, and, on the
introduction of medical benefit in 1930,
it was possible, through the medium of
these referees, to provide a consultation
service for health insurance practitioners
who also had the benefit of the referees'
opinion on questions of diagnosis and
treatment. There are now in Northern
Ireland over 500 medical practitioners
providing medical treatment to insured
persons, and over 470 pharmaceutical
chemists who are under contract to supply
medicines and appliances. It is worth
while reflecting that to-day in Northern
Ireland there are about 450,000 persons
entitled to medical treatment under the
National Health Insurance Scheme.
Here I must pay tribute to the magnificent work done by the Medical Benefit
Council and its various sub-committees in
assisting the Ministry in the administration of medical benefit. Since its inception the Council has worked in the closest
harmony with the Ministry, and its help.
and advice have been invaluable. I
should also like to pay a tribute to the
Dental Benefit Council which has assisted
in the administration of dental benefit.
Dental benefit is at present one of the
additional benefits given under national
health insurance, but we hope that the
day is not far distant when such additional benefits as dental benefit and
ophthalmic benefit will be universally
available as part of the comprehensive
health services which we hope to
established.
see
As regards provision for the aged,
widows and orphans, and blind persons,
the number of pensions continues to increase. There are at present over 102,000
pensions in payment. Of these 29,440
are non-contributory pensions and the
remainder are payable by virtue of insurance under the Contributory Pensions
Acts.
In the latter category there are
some 16,770 widows' pensions in payment
and these widows' pensions include allowances in respect of approximately 8,000
dependent children. Since the passing of
the original Contributory Pensions Act
in the year 1925 there have been various
improvements in the scheme.
I would draw attention to the fact that
in the year 1937 provision was made for
the contributory scheme to be extended
to enable persons who were not compulsorily insurable, particularly persons who
were self-employed, to become voluntary
contributors for pensions if their income,
in the case of men, not exceed £400 a
year and, in the case of women, £250 a
year. In the year 1940 the pensionable
age in the case of insured women and the
wives of insured men was reduced to 60
years, and that year also saw the introduction of supplementary pensions, of
which there are at present over 38,000 in
payment.
Since the inception of supplementary
pensions there has been an increase in the
rates and the average amount of supplementary pensions is now 10s 8d per week.
Supplementary pensions are awarded
having regard to the needs and resources
of the applicant and his dependants in
each case.
The amounts, therefore, vary
widely from 1s or so at one end of the
scale to 50s or more at the other.
figure of 10s 8d is the general average.
No pensioner living alone has less than
22s 6d a week, made up of his pension,
his supplementary pension and his other
resources, if any.
The
The Committee may be interested to
know that I estimate that expenditure on
the various benefits during the present
financial year will be of the following order:
-Unemployment insurance, £735,000;
unemployment assistance, £75,000; health
insurance, £1,030,000; non-contributory
pensions, £755,000; contributory pensions, £2,015,000; special voluntary
scheme pensions, £4,000; supplementary
pensions, £1,183,000, making a total of
almost £5,800,000.
Part of this sum is met by contributions and the balance by the Exchequer,
which, in addition, must keep the unemployment account in parity under the
Reinsurance Agreement. The amount
provided in the Estimates which I am
presenting to the House for all these services is around £5,000,000.
I turn now to the Employment Exchange and Factory Inspection branches
of the Ministry. As hon. Members are
aware, the total number of persons unemployed on our register at the end of
the financial year was 18,116, made up
of 13,482 men and boys and 4,634 women
and girls. This total is 3,090 less than
it was a year before, when we had many
large construction works in progress.
As
these approached completion many men
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
were paid off, so that the number of male
unemployed rose by about 5,000; but
against this there was a decline of over
8,000 in our women's register due to the
large demand for female workers in spinning, weaving, stitching and munition
industries. I want to draw the attention
of hon. Members to this part of the unemployment question because I see by the
Press that people are using the unemployment figures for propaganda purposes,
and the figures they give in their statements on this question are not correct.
Mr. NIXON: Who are the people?
Mr. GRANT: Some weeks
ago I
gave
the House a short account of the make-up
of our unemployed register, but Members
may be interested in one of the main facts
disclosed by a recent inspection of our
women's exchange in Belfast. About 60
per cent. of the women now on that
register are married and, naturally, very
few of them are able to take work far
from home. When you add the number
of those similarly restricted in employment
for other reasons, you find about 65 per
. cent. who are not available outside their
own district.
An inspection of Lurgan showed an
even higher proportion of women more or
less tied to their own neighbourhood;
there, it amounted to over 70 per cent.
It was also found in Belfast that about
one-third of the unemployed women had
signed on during the previous week, that
is prior to the figures being taken out,
and that about two-thirds of the register
is completely changed every three weeks.
It is from the rapidly altering two-thirds
of our register that the majority of
vacancies are filled. This is one of the
inevitable results of the exceptional demand for labour; workers who are easily
suited get employment almost at once,
and in the residue on our books, the proportion of the elderly and infirm and
those restricted to a particular locality
keeps on steadily rising. This naturally
increases my Ministry's difficulty in filling
vacancies. Nevertheless the number of
vacancies we filled during the financial
year was a record-85,887 in Northern
Ireland alone. This is about 14,000 more
than in the preceding year.
In addition we placed 7,466 people in
Great Britain, which is about 3,600 less
than in the previous year. The net total
of vacancies filled both at home and across
the Channel was thus 10,400 above our
previous high-water mark.
Over
While we are very glad to have been
able to put so many people in employment, I should like to point out that it
has been a much harder task than it
would have been in peacetime, even in
proportion to the larger numbers. In
former years when an Exchange
Manager usually had considerably more
persons unemployed than were wanted
at any one time, he could easily send
round enough to fill the small order he
happened to get. For the last couple of
years the Ministry has had to supply
workers, not in dozens but in hundreds
and even thousands. This has entailed
drawing on Exchanges scattered
wide areas, arranging for transport and
accommodation, payment of lodging
allowances, etc., and, in the case of
people going across the Channel, provision had also to be made for medical
examination and the issue of permits.
Unfortunately, too, when more vacancies
are offered more are refused, and 46,427
disallowances of benefit had to be imposed, mostly as a result of such refusals.
Of these, 4,565 were allowed on appeal.
I should explain that in a large proportion of the cases where benefit was
withheld there was little or no financial
loss to the applicant, because the reason
for the refusal of work was that he or
she had a more congenial job to go to and
obtained it. Nevertheless, this unpleasant but necessary work put an additional strain on our Exchanges. I might
also add that the rapid turnover of a
considerable part of the unemployed at
the Exchanges has a similar effect. When
a person claims benefit certain calculations have to be made, but once made
they do not, as a rule, require alteration.
The fact that so many persons were signing on and signing off at the Exchanges
every week entailed much more calculation and paper work than the average
number unemployed at any time would
seem to justify.
The decline in unemployment has
naturally reduced the number of those
in receipt of unemployment assistance,
which fell from 3,920 at the beginning of
1942 to 1,157 at its close, and to about
900 at present. I should mention that
these figures include evacuees from Belfast who get allowances under the scheme

for the prevention and relief of distress.
due to war conditions.
While I am on the subject of the

the Assistance Board investigated, on behalf of the Board of Trade, some 6,000
claims for the replacement of lost clothing coupons. On behalf of the Service
Departments, the Ministry of Pensions,
and the Dominion Governments it investigated over 9,000 applications from
dependants of serving men for increased
allowances owing to special needs.
renders other agency services such as payments towards loss or damage of essential
articles through enemy action, but as

The Assistance Board has also a most important and increased volume of work for
supplementary pensions, with which I
have already dealt.
It
Continued attention has been given by
our Inspectors to the safety, health, and
welfare of the workers in the factories.
One matter of this kind which I myself
regard as specially important at present
is the provision of factory canteens.
There have been difficulties in getting
materials and equipment, but some of
these difficulties have lessened and I am
considering further steps to secure that
more canteens shall be established. I
remember very well indeed how in the
past men used to find a comfortable spot
in which to enjoy a "crack" and their
mid-day "piece" and tea. In these days
of rationing, however, it is not so easy
to provide the "piece" and the tea and
sugar and the meals at home as well, and
I consider that the man and woman
engaged upon hard work ought to be able
to supplement their ration with a canteen
meal.
I am sure they will work all the
better for the addition to the ration.
The arrangements between my Department and E.N.S.A. for the provision of
workers' concerts have been continued
and developed, and regular performances
are being given in eighteen factories at
fortnightly intervals. It is the general
opinion of management of these factories
that the concerts benefit production, and
make for general as well as musical harmony in the works. I know that workers
appreciate and look forward to the performances, and although Ensa is hardpressed to meet all the many and widespread demands for entertainment I hope
it
may be found possible to extend the
factory concert service still further.
I should like to survey the work of the
Industrial Relations Branches of the
Department. Because of the fact that I
have so recently assumed office as
Minister of Labour, I am sure the Committee will not expect me at this juncture
to deal, except in a somewhat general
way, with the difficult subject of trade
disputes. It would, I suppose, be too
much to hope that relations between employers and workpeople under the varying stress and strain of war conditions
would constantly remain in good shape,
but it must be admitted that during the
past year there has been a great deal of
trouble from unofficial stoppages of work
which the country might well have been
spared.
matters
re-
While many of these disputes were
relatively small, I regret to say that a
few were extremely serious
indeed. These stoppages usually happened despite the good advice of
sponsible trade union leaders and officials
and their declared desire or intention,
together with the employers concerned,
to proceed by way of voluntary negotiation or arbitration. Of the 285 trade disputes reported to the Ministry, more than
two-thirds were settled without resort to
strike action-in many instances by
friendly negotiations under the auspices
of the Ministry of Labour. Eighty-four
awards were issued by the National
Arbitration Tribunal, to whose chairman
-the Right Honourable Mr. Justice
Brown-and members, the community is
greatly indebted for the continuance of
their valuable services. The Trade Board
machinery, also, has been working
smoothly and efficiently, and has carried
through without a hitch wage adjustments in no less than fifteen different
trades.
With the development of Northern
Ireland's production of munitions and
other war material, it became necessary
to ensure that labour, particularly skilled
labour in occupations where the supply is
limited, should be allocated to the best
advantage. The Ministry accordingly
made a Restriction of Engagement Order
which came into operation last July, and
which prohibits employers in general
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
engineering and electrical installation
undertakings from engaging workers, with
certain minor exceptions, otherwise than
through the employment exchanges.
Three labour supply inspectors with
practical experience and technical knowledge of the engineering and electrical
industries were appointed to assist the
Department in the equitable distribution
of skilled labour available. It is part of
the duty of these inspectors to maintain
contact with factories, acquaint themselves
with their type of production and its
relative importance to the war effort, and
advise the Ministry as regards the training and supply of additional labour or the
release of skilled labour more urgently
needed elsewhere.
The order has, on the whole, worked
satisfactorily. It has gone a long way
towards eliminating any tendency of
employers to "poach" workers from other
firms, either in the same or other industries, and has helped to stabilise labour
within the undertakings with beneficial
effects on the organisation of individual
firms and consequently, on production
generally.
Finally, I should like to urge our
people to do their utmost to settle their
trade disputes without strikes, and I
would ask the Press to make this appeal
as widely known as possible. In the
very nature of things there are bound to
be differences of opinion between workers
and employers about rates of remuneration and other conditions of employment;
but, even in normal times, strikes are a
bad way of settling these differences.
They are an appeal to force, not to reason.
Win or lose, they leave ill-feeling behind
them, and it was to prevent this that the
Executives of the Trade Unions and the
Employers' Associations built up negotiating machinery. Strike action means that
the workers suffer through loss of wages
and the community suffers through the
loss of production. The only one who
benefits is the enemy. Nothing would
please him better than a big strike. Our
important industries are so bound up with
the war that a wide-spread stoppage
would check production more than a
bombing raid.
Before the Order commonly known as
the "Strike Order" was issued, it was
submitted by the Imperial Minister of
Labour to the Joint Consultative Committee, which is composed of representatives of Employers' Associations and of
the Trades Union Congress. Both parties
were anxious that the existing negotiating machinery should be availed of in the
first instance, but they also agreed that in
the event of a deadlock any question in
dispute should be referred to the National
Arbitration Tribunal. They were at one
in their hope that by this means strikes
would be avoided; and it places the executives of the unions in a very embarrassing
position when they give their blessing to
the principle of an arbitration tribunal,
and their fellow members refuse to honour
the agreement.
It is sometimes contended that the
machinery of negotiation is too slow in
its working. Surely it is not beyond the
sagacity of employers and workers to
make such improvements as
may be
necessary for speeding up its operation.
So far as my Ministry is concerned, every
possible step will be taken to expedite the
work of the Arbitration Tribunal; but as
the parties have to be given a certain
amount of time to frame their case, there
must be a reasonable interval between the
reference of a dispute to the tribunal and
its hearing.
Our Prime Minister, as Minister of
Commerce and Production, has continually pressed the Imperial Departments
for a greater volume of work for Northern
Ireland, but he is placed in a very invidious position when it can be pointed
out to him that the work already given is
being interrupted by trade disputes. One
of our principal war industries is shipbuilding, and it may be that the failure
to deliver a particular escort vessel may
mean the loss of part of a convoy and of
the lives of some of our seamen-to say
nothing of the destruction of valuable
cargoes. I make this appeal with all the
earnestness at my command, and I know
that it will find a response in the hearts
of all those who realise the gravity of the
situation and the issues which are
involved in the titanic life-and-death
struggle in which we are engaged against
the forces of evil and darkness.

are not only being deprived now of our
right to claim part of the industry for
war, but there is the tragedy after the
war. With factories and machinery
scattered all over England and Scotland,
where shall we be in that race?
I think the time has come when something really must be done to have a Commission or a Committee set up to deal
with this matter-an unpaid Select Committee. I certainly would take good care
to resign from all paid Select Committees.
We should have an unpaid Select Committee to go into this matter and bring
about that co-ordination between all the
departments. Until we get that position
we will continue to be hopeless and still
more hopeless. We want to bring some
business brains to bear on the problem.
We have only one business man, and not a
single industrialist in the Cabinet. After
all, we have had this unemployment problem for over twenty years. It is no
better, comparatively speaking, than it
has ever been, when we take into consideration the change brought about by
the war. It is probably worse.
Our percentage of unemployed has always been
greater in Northern Ireland than it has
been in Great Britain. I can see no
reason whatever for that. We are part
and parcel of the Empire, and we should
be on the same basis industrially and in
every other way. No reason has ever
been advanced to me as to why our percentage of unemployment should be so
much greater than it is across
Channel. Why has it been that for over
20 years?

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): In presenting the Estimates for the Ministry of Home Affairs
I feel that I am breaking now an almost
immemorial tradition in that these
Estimates are not being presented by my
right hon. Friend and predecessor the
Member for Victoria. I gladly take this
opportunity to acknowledge the great
kindness and unvarying courtesy I experienced at his hands in the last three
years I was his Parliamentary Secretary.
I am sure that every Member of the Committee will rejoice to learn that he is now
restored to his accustomed health after a
prolonged and serious illness. The Committee, I am sure, will also acknowledge
with gratitude his fearless, determined
and impartial discharge of the duties of
his position during a period of 22 years,
many of which were very eventful years
indeed. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
With the approval of the Committee I
propose to go through the Estimates in the
order in which they are set forth on page
53 of the volume which is in the hands of
Members of the Committee. I will comment on such items as appear to require
comment for the information of the
Committee and give an explanation where
explanation is necessary, and where there
are increases over the Estimates of the
previous year. It will be noted on that
page to which I have referred that the
total increase is £116,518. I propose to
deal with the important increases in the
various classes of Votes, and to give such
explanation as is nceessary.
With regard to the Ministry of Home
Affairs itself there is a slight decrease.
I think the causes of it are sufficiently
apparent from the printed matter. There
are increases represented by normal increments to be found throughout the
Estimates. The salary of the Chief
Medical Officer, Dr. Boyd, is paid partly
by the Ministry of Labour and partly by
ourselves. It will be remembered that
he was appointed on the retirement of
Dr. M'Cloy, who was the Chief Medical
Officer, and whose death, I am sure, we
all deplore as he did not live long to
enjoy the leisure which he had so well
earned.
The
In the Home Office Division there are
normal increments, and it is not until we
come to page 56 that I feel it is necessary to enter into some explanation.
There are certain additions there in the
professional and technical staff. In respect of the Planning Consultant, Mr.
Davidge, this is the first full year.
date of his appointment was the 1st May,
1942, and in consequence his fee was
fixed for the year at 1,500 guineas. The
period overlapped, and the agreement for
the second year is 1,000 guineas and
that is subject to revision at the end of
this year, because it is then hoped that
a different method of remuneration,
according to such consultations as will be
necessary, may be arrived at.
The salaries of the Senior Architect
and his assistants are shown for the full
year. The Medical Inspector who is
shown there at £1,000 is in receipt of
£200 per annum because he acts as hospital officer in connection with the Emergency Hospital Scheme.
There is nothing calling for any comment in regard to the Roads and Transport Division. There is a substantial
reduction in the Evacuation Division because the great volume of the work has
already been discharged, and there is a
Ministry of Home Affairs 1000

consequent reduction of staff, the amount

As to the Establishment and Accounts
Division, there is additional clerical
assistance required by reason of the
Ministry's activities in acting as agent
for the Ministry of Fuel and Power in
regard to petrol rationing. There is also
another department-the Residence Permit Agency. The other matters are very
much on the lines of previous years.
I should like to say a word or two in
explanation of the substantial increase in
the cost of the Petrol Agency. As Members of the Committee will be aware by
reason of the further restrictions placed
on petrol there has been a great increase
in the number of appeals by people
who are evidently dissatisfied with the
cutting down of the allowances that have
been made. There is an increase of
almost £4,000 for the Residence Permit
Agency which was set up at the end of
last year.
The estimate only represents
a portion of the year. The staff is pretty
numerous, 27 in all, but the work is
laborious and very detailed. The applications for residence permits so far
amount to over 27,000. Some 20,000
have been dealt with so far, and many of
them give rise to inquiries which have to
be answered by the police. As I undertook on
one occasion to the hon. and
gallant Member for East Down, the
opportunity will arise at the end of six
months, which has almost elapsed, of
reviewing certain anomalies to which the
hon. and gallant Member referred.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: How many
of the applications have been refused?
Mr. LOWRY: Twenty-seven thousand
applications have been made, 20,000 have
been examined and granted, but I cannot
say off-hand the number of refusals up to
the moment. Twenty thousand of the
27,000 applications have been granted,
and some are still coming in. Some
people pretend not to have seen the
notices in the papers about the necessity
for these permits. That is the first Vote.
I presume it will be the wish of the
Committee that I should go straight
through the eight classes, so that hon.
Members can raise any of the points they
wish to raise. The next important class
is the Royal Ulster Constabulary. The
net sum of £957,735 is required for the
Royal Ulster Constabulary. Owing to
the additional duties that have fallen on
the police as the result of war-time conditions, it has been necessary from time
to time to increase the officers' strength
and to appoint additional policewomen.
and increase the clerical staff. An addition
of some £3,000 is due to this. In allowances an increase of some £9,000 arises
from making provision for a full year for
certain war-time allowances corresponding
to increases granted to the police force
in Great Britain. Provision is also made
for a new and more effective type of
weapon due to certain units of the force,
and this accounts for an increase of some
£7,000 under the heading of Arms and
Accoutrements. This sub-head also includes certain additional payments for
components ordered in previous years and
paid for as delivered. A reduction in the
number of vehicles to be purchased
accounts for the reduction in the
Transport sub-head. There will be a
smaller appropriation-in-aid accounted for
by the fact that last year's figure included certain arrears of payment for
responsible agency services performed by
the police which do not appear in the
current year's Estimate.
The year through which we have just
passed has been one of considerable
difficulty for the Constabulary Force of
both branches under the control of the
Inspector-General. In addition to the
numerous war-time measures for the enforcement of which they were responsible,
this force had to cope with increasing
activity on the part of subversive elements
in the community. Numerous outrages
have been perpetrated, and many of these
have resulted in the death or wounding
of members, and the manner in which
they faced up to these dangerous and
difficult tasks is worthy of the highest
praise. It is only by a sustained effort
and devotion to duty that the peace of
the community has been preserved.
Although it does not properly come
within this Estimate, I think it is desirable that I should tell the Committee
that after consultation, and having
obtained the approval of the Ministry of
Finance, it is proposed to make certain
alterations in the scales of pay of district
inspectors and county inspectors. I am
sure the Committee will recognise that no
people are so severely hit by war-time

The Estimate has been made

On this subject of the prisons the Committee will naturally expect to hear something of the two most regrettable and
deplorable incidents that occurred during
the course of last year.
The first one was
the escape of four convicted men from
the Belfast Prison on Friday morning,
the 15th January, 1943. When the preliminary investigation had been
ducted by the usual prison inspectors it
was felt that perhaps something more in
the way of investigation was necessary,
and I took an unprecedented step-and
it is unprecedented and I hope there will
never be a necessity for taking such a
step again as was taken in Belfast and
again in Derry-and that was to appoint
three gentlemen from outside any existing service to hold an inquiry under the
provision of the Prisons (Ireland) Act,
1877. I was fortunate in securing the
services as chairman of a gentleman who
acted as a Judge of the High Court of
India and he and two of our most experienced Crown solicitors held an inquiry which lasted several days and
involved the examination
witnesses.

Number seven is the very important one
dealing with grants to local authorities.
Hon. Members will observe the very
miscellaneous character of these grants
and the very wide range that they cover.
It may be that the Committee would like
to hear more about the things in which
increases took place. Fairly substantial
increases appear in relation to sub-head
K-vaccine lymph supply; sub-head Lchild welfare and maternity schemes, and
sub-head P-treatment of tuberculosis.
In regard to sub-head K, the increase of
rather more than 100 per cent. is due to
the extension of the scheme for diphtheria
immunisation and its wider application as
the benefits to be derived therefrom are
recognised by the public. I am glad to

In regard to sub-head L-maternity
and child welfare-the increase here is
largely accounted for by the extension of
the
scheme by the Public Health
Authority of the County Borough of
Belfast. The main items of new and
increased expenditure include the following: (1) Home helps; (2) obstetrical
flying squad; (3) feeding of expectant
mothers; (4) the dental treatment of expectant mothers; (5) increased grants to
institutions, and (6) the rearrangement
of additions to child welfare centres and
the appointment of additional health
visitors.
The idea behind the provision regarding
home helps is that if expectant mothers
experience difficulty in repairing to hospitals for treatment or confinement on
account of having a young family at home
to attend to, or if difficulty should arise
in the case of a home confinement on
account of the number of young children
to be looked after, a home help should be
supplied to overcome these difficulties.
These home helps will be paid at a rate
of 7s per day for a six-day week and will
be required to provide their own food.
The general period of attendance for each
obstetric case is to be two weeks, and it
is to be understood, of course, that
patients will be expected to contribute to
the cost of home helps according to their
means.
In regard to the obstetrical flying
squad, the duties of the squad will be to
attend special cases, where the doctor or
midwife in attendance at a confinement
consider the circumstances to be sufficiently serious to require the services of a
nurse and specialist with the necessary
medical outfit. The squad will be used
for such cases as anti-partum and postpartum hæmorrhage, obstetrical shock
and cases of a similar nature, and here
again patients availing themselves of the
services will be expected to contribute
according to their means.
With regard to the feeding of expectant
mothers, suitable types of concentrated
food will be supplied at cost price and at
less than cost price to necessitous cases,
and the scheme is now extended to the
provision of meals for mothers in the last
three months of pregnancy, as there are
many cases in which mothers are suffering
from malnutrition, and this has a direct
bearing on the large number of deaths.
from prematurity among infants. Up to
the present the dental treatment under
maternity and child welfare has related
This service has
only to the children.
now been extended to include expectant mothers.
So far as grants to institutions are concerned, the Corporation grant to the
Royal Maternity Hospital has been increased from £1,000 to £3,000 per
annum, the reason being the greatly increased work which the hospital now
carries out entirely on behalf of cases of
puerperal sepsis and puerperal pyrexia.
The annual grant to the Ulster Hospital
for Women and Children has also been
increased to assist the extension of the
ante-natal services.
Due to the extension of the Maternity
and Child Welfare Scheme in Belfast
County Borough it will be obvious that
the provision of additional child welfare
centres, with a consequent increase in the
number of health visitors, is necessary,
and the increased provision provides for
the opening of three additional child welfare centres with a corresponding increase
in the number of health visitors to ensure
the efficient carrying out of this important branch of the Maternity and
Child Welfare Service.
The increases under sub-head P relating to the treatment of tuberculosis is to
provide, at least in part, for the improved
arrangements for the treatment of tuberculosis, particularly in regard to its early
diagnosis by the use of mass miniature
radiography. The scheme recently
approved by the Ministry of Health in
regard to Britain provides, amongst other
things, for the payment of allowances to
persons who have to give up remunerative
work in order to undertake treatment,
and the increased provision in the Estimates is merely to provide for this scheme
in its initial stages, for the cost of
operation of such a scheme must of
necessity be entirely dependent upon the
extent to which its application is found
to be necessary as a result of examinations carried out by medical experts.
Whether or not it will be necessary to

The Estimate for derating grants
shows an increase of £10,000 as compared
with last year. This is accounted for
almost entirely by the net balance due to
rural authorities in respect of additional
grants which were payable to them last
year. As was explained in the Estimates
speech a year ago, the Government came
to the assistance of rural authorities
owing to the fact that the fixing of derating grants under the 1936 Derating
Act caused heavy burdens to be placed
upon un derated ratepayers in rural areas.
The result was that local authorities were
unable to carry on essential services as a
very slight additional expenditure involved an unduly increased rate. By the
Government's action a very substantial
increase in rates in rural
avoided. The Government is continuing
assistance to rural authorities during the
coming year on a similar scale to that
afforded last year.
areas was
There is just one other matter for
which provision has not been made-it
will be made later-because arrangements
had not been concluded at the time the
Estimates were printed. The Government has decided to make ex gratia grants
toward the amounts awarded by the courts
and paid by county councils in respect of
criminal injury claims arising out of
I.R.A. activities since 1st April, 1942.
The cases which the Government have in
mind are those of police officers killed or
wounded in such circumstances as would
give rise to a claim for criminal injury
being made. It is felt, and documents
that have fallen into the hands of the
police from time to time indicate—it is,
indeed, common knowledge-that many
of these outrages are committed not by the
people of the district in which the injury
is committed, but by people who are
imported from outside to carry out the
work while some living within the locality
act as "setters," the object being to
hinder identification of the actual perpetrators. It is felt that where a police
officer has been active, and, perhaps,
transferred to another district, and is
followed and murdered or maimed that
the people of the district to which he was
sent should not be saddled with the entire
amount of the compensation which is
rightly and properly payable in the case
of wounding to the man himself or to his
dependants in the case of his being
murdered.
The last Vote of all deals with the
Emergency Services. More detail has
been given this year and I think hon.
Members will be able to follow clearly the
matters to which the various sums are
applied, but, perhaps, I should say a
word or two in regard to some of them. It
will be recalled that these grants were
dealt with by some means of block Estimates and the items were not set out in
detail. In going through the Estimate I
propose to take the opportunity of giving
Members of the Committee a brief
account of the work which has and is
being done by this Ministry in connection.
with our Emergency Hospital Schemes.
Prior to and since the outbreak of war
the Government has been steadily extending and improving hospital facilities in
Northern Ireland for air-raid casualty
purposes. To this end additional beds
and bedding, together with surgical and
general equipment, have been supplied on
loan to existing hospitals. Hospital
authorities have been encouraged to carry
out structural alterations in order to provide improved facilities for casualties, and
those which have done so have received
substantial financial assistance from the
Ministry.
In addition, the Ministry has, during
the past twelve months, embarked on a
scheme for the provision of hospital hutting in the grounds of certain general
hospitals, while provision has been made for
similar hutments at fever and tuberculosis
hospitals to enable them to cope with the
increased demands which may be made upon
them as a result of evacuation or other
causes directly attributable to the war.
When the present programme is completed, the hospital accommodation in
Northern Ireland will have been increased
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
by 60 per cent. A sum of £42,000
representing the outstanding expenditure
on this work is included in the sum of
£157,000 under the heading of "Works
and Supplies." Also included in this
figure of £157,400 is the sum of £92,000,
representing the cost of equipment and
medical supplies for hospitals. Most of
this equipment has already been provided,
but no bills have yet been presented.
£50,000 of this amount, therefore, represents money which is being re-voted.
While on the subject of equipment, I
would like to take this opportunity of
acquainting hon. Members of the
generosity of the American Red Cross
Society, which allocated a quota of their
gifts of hospital equipment to Northern
Ireland. The Ministry are also indebted
to the joint war organisation of the British
Red Cross and the St. John organisation,
which have very kindly placed at the
disposal of the Emergency Hospital
Scheme two mobile Red Cross X-ray vans.
These vans are fully equipped with the
most modern X-ray appliances, and are
kept under constant supervision so as to
be available in an emergency
to any hospital requiring X-ray facilities.
Hon. Members may be surprised to find
an increase in the amount provided for
the maintenance and treatment of casualties, having regard to the fact that we
have been happily free from air raids. I
should explain that the increase is represented by the estimated cost of running
the Belfast Emergency Hospital, which
has been established by the Ministry in
the neighbourhood of Belfast. It has for
some time been considered that additional
hospital accommodation should be provided in case one of the larger Belfast
hospitals, upon which we are so dependent
for the treatment of air-raid casualties,
should be put out of action. The emergency hospital fulfils this purpose. I
should explain in this connection that
essential expenditure is included under
the sub-heading B (1) entitled "Works
and Supplies."
In order to avoid the anomaly of
having a fully equipped hospital complete
with staff, but without patients, and at
the same time considerable waiting lists
at voluntary hospitals in Belfast, the
Ministry have made an arrangement with
these hospitals whereby the emergency
hospital will undertake the treatment of
as many as possible of their waiting list
patients. Contributions towards the cost
of their treatmment are obtained, in the
case of regular subscribers, from the
transferring hospital, and, in the case of
non-subscribers, from the patients themselves. Special consideration has been
given to the fact that many of these waiting list patients are employed in essential
war industries, and that every effort
should, therefore, be made to render them
fit for work as soon as possible. The required expenditure for this purpose is
included in sub-head B (2).
I would also like to say a few words
about this Ministry's blood transfusion
service, for which a sum of £5,000 is
being provided. Prior to the war hospitals were, for the most part, dependent
on the Blood Transfusion Panel of Donors
Organisation by British Red Cross, Toc H
and similar organisations, or
on the
relatives of the patient for supplies of
blood. The existing arrangements have
now been unified into the Blood Transfusion Services Organisation by regional
resuscitation officers appointed by this
Ministry for the purpose. Large numbers
of donors have already been typed and
bled, and stocks of blood plasma have
been prepared. The transfusion fluids
are available, free of charge, to patients
for whom this Ministry accepts respon
sibility under the Emergency Hospital
Scheme, but arrangements have also been
made to make available to hospitals for
their ordinary civilian purposes supplies
of fresh blood or filtered blood plasma on
payment of a small charge. As a matter
of interest I might here mention that the
price per pint of blood is 10s. It is hoped
that the present scheme will form the
basis of a post-war blood transfusion
service.
Under the heading, Emergency
Health Services, sub-head C, provision is
being made for the net additional cost
to local authorities in reception
areas of
extending to evacuated persons in their
areas the normal health services of the
area. Provision is also made in this subhead for the cost of an Emergency Public
Health Laboratory Service which this
Ministry has established with the assistance of the authorities of Queen's University. The University has undertaken
responsibility for the satisfactory functioning of the service, which is designed to
meet the necessities which may arise out
Ministry of Home Affairs 1012
Estimates-
9 JUNE 1943
of serious epidemics of infectious disease,
which might result from movement of
the population. The scheme, which includes the provision of an emergency
laboratory at Whiteabbey and the storage
of a reserve of laboratory apparatus, provides also for the extension and employment of existing Public Health Laboratory Services, which are available for the
diagnosis of infectious disease.
The other activities with regard to the
Emergency Services deal largely with
evacuation, and the position there is that
most of the actual expenditure has been
carried out. Consequently there is a
reduction of some £14,000 compared with
last year's Estimates. Of course, the
Government has been disappointed in the
matter of the evacuation of children. It
seems to be impossible to persuade them
to remain out of the city, and as to the
numbers of people who left Belfast from
time to time the numbers now represent
merely one-eighth of what they once were.
However, if any person who desires to
evacuate children or any of the priority
classes will inquire at 37 University Road
they can get all the information necessary if there, is a desire to evacuate in
small numbers. I am very conscious that
in a Ministry that touches so many points
as this one does it is quite impossible to
touch on all points about which hon.
Members may desire to have further information, but if there is any point
which requires elaboration or elucidation
I shall do my best to furnish the necessary information.

The Food Controller here was a man

He was dismissed, and as my information

The question I put to the Attorney-

were disclosed

The Attorney-General (Mr. MacDermott): In Northern Ireland the
Attorney-General is responsible for the
direction of public prosecutions as distinguished from private prosecutions
and prosecutions initiated by officers of
State or Government Departments
under powers which do not require his
consent or concurrence as, for example,
proceedings directed by the Minister of
Food in respect of breaches of the
Defence Regulations relating to food
control.
My attention has been directed to

This case was fully investigated by

of Food (Excessive Quantities) Order,
1942, from the provisions of which
all rationed foodstuffs are excluded.
A warning was, therefore, given to
Mr. Mackie.

is a matter, in practice, which receives

Orders, and it is in the public interest
that this Ministry, rather than the police,

extensive emergency legislation. This
case under consideration was referred to

I agree with the hon. Member

had come to the conclusion that the circumstances were such as to warrant the
institution of criminal proceedings, I
know of no reason why I should not have
instituted them.
Whatever my faults may have been, I
have never heard it suggested yet that I
dealt with criminal prosecutions according to the standing or status of the person
involved, but the plain fact was that
after careful reading of the facts, I shared
the opinion of the various experienced
gentlemen who considered the matter in
London, that there was no substantial
breach of the law which could be proved
against Mr. Mackie. The policy of the
Ministry of Food, in fact the policy of all
responsible departments or persons who
have to administer the law, is not that for
every breach of the law there should be a
prosecution. There is such a thing, as I
have often heard the Member for Woodvale say, as discretion, but it is a discretion that has to be exercised not in
accordance with whether the person is of
low degree or high degree, but on the
ordinary principles of common sense, and
it did appear, so far as the rice in this
case was concerned, that under the

as soon as that rice was used
otherwise than for human consumption. But the evidence proved quite
plainly that the rice which was the subject
of consideration was unfit for human food,
and that being so, I think one would have
been straining the law by prosecuting Mr.
Mackie, or any person else, for feeding
rice to turkeys which in fact could not
be fed to human beings.

Internment Order.
Whereas it appears to me, on the recommendation of the Inspector-General
R.U.C., that for securing the preservation of the peace and the maintenance of order in Northern Ireland, it
is expedient that James Mulgrew, of

Now I, the Right Honourable Sir
Richard Dawson Bates, Minister of
Home Affairs for Northern Ireland, by
virtue of the powers vested in me by
the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922, and the
Regulations made thereunder, and of
all other powers me thereunto enabling,
do hereby order the said James Mulgrew forthwith to be interned in H.M.
Prison, Londonderry, and to be subject.
to all the rules and restrictions applicable to persons there interned, and to
be kept interned there until further
order.

presided over by a person who holds or

When James Mulgrew was interned, and

The Building Industry.
NUMBER OF WORKERS EMPLOYED
1. Mr. DOWLING asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if it is a
fact that unemployment in all sections of
the building industry within the past two
months has increased to a considerable
extent, and that every week shows a rising
tendency; and whether he can state (a)
the actual number of skilled men in each
category at present in this trade now unemployed, and the percentage of the
whole, (b) the actual number of unskilled
workers in this industry now unemployed,
and the percentage of the whole.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The publication of particulars of
unemployment by industries and occupations has been suspended in Great Britain
and Northern Ireland for security reasons.
I shall, however, be glad to discuss the
position generally with the hon. Member.
LICENSING REGULATIONS.
2. Mr. DOWLING asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that considerable unemployment is arising, due to
the insistence of a building licence being
obtained before proceeding with work
costing more than £100, and this notwithstanding the fact that in a great many
cases materials for carrying out work are
available locally; and whether in consequence, he will take the necessary steps to
encourage employers to retain their
workers in their home areas by amending
the regulations now in operation.
AND
AND
The PRIME MINISTER
MINISTER OF COMMERCE
PRODUCTION (Sir Basil Brooke): I am
The
aware that there has been in recent months
an increase in unemployment in the
building industry. This increase arises as
a result of the completion of certain large
scale building operations and not from the
effect of the control of civil building which
has been in operation since October, 1940,
and has, in fact, been relaxed to some
extent in its application since unemployment developed in the industry.
primary purpose of building control is to
conserve supplies of building materials for
work which is of vital importance to the
war effort. In most cases where £100 or
more is being spent on a building operation, materials such as timber and steel
are required. As the limited quantity of
these materials, which can be produced
in or shipped into the United Kingdom,
is needed for important war work, it would
be contrary to the national interest to
use such materials solely for the purpose
of creating employment in
in Northern
Ireland. In practice it has been the policy
of my Ministry to grant building licences
freely in those cases where only materials
in plentiful supply are required for the
work.
Mr. BROWN: Would unemployment in
the building industry not be ended tomorrow if the Prime Minister got Northern Ireland its share of the war factories
to which it is entitled, and would it not
also help the war effort?

asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.

methods of construction, standardisation

Furniture Removals by Transport Board.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if it
is a fact that the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board was originally debarred
from undertaking the work of furniture
removers; whether they are now extensively engaged in this business all over
Northern Ireland to the detriment of
traders whose livelihood is derived in
whole or in part from furniture removing; to the detriment of the war effort
and of the conveyance of war workers and
war goods and of the general public by
using petrol and vehicles for this purpose when the shortage of vehicles and
petrol is acute; and whether the Board's
vehicles are extensively engaged on this
work and are covering a lot of ground
which could be covered more economically and in less time by furniture removing traders.
Mr. LOWRY: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the negative.
With regard to the subsequent parts
the Transport Board in accordance with
their statutory powers has engaged in the
transport of furniture since the inception
of the Board and still does so. Special
types of vehicles are required for this
purpose which would not be suitable for
other purposes and I cannot see that
there could be any economy either in
vehicles or petrol if this work was confined to those peoole referred to by the
hon. Member as "furniture removing
traders."
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact that
there is a serious shortage of vehicles for
removing furniture, and would it not ease
that shortage if these legitimate furniture
removing firms were allowed to use their
vehicles and carry on their own work instead of having the Transport Board
encroaching upon and destroying it?

I am afraid that there is a tendency on

on the average or below the average. I

and perhaps better, than the pupils above

Before I ever had any thoughts of
being officially associated with this
Ministry I had been looking into the
question of the tillage quota, and I
then came to the conclusion that it
would not be possible to go on increasing the actual tillage quota. Since I
became Minister I have gone into the
matter again, and although no definite
or final decision has been taken on the
matter, I cannot see how we can increase this 45 per cent. to any substantial degree in 1944. Yet the fact remains that in 1944 the country will
want more and more food grown on our
own farms. We have been casting
about to see how this can be done. We
have got a line on the manner in which
it can be done indirectly through the
results of fertilisers in the year 1942.
I cannot go into details of the matter,
but we are satisfied that without
actually increasing the quota of
ploughed land-we cannot allow it to
diminish and we will not-by a better
and more judicious use and application
of fertilisers we can extract from the
acreage a considerably higher
yield of crops than we have managed to
get hitherto.-(Official Report, 2nd
June, 1943, Vol. 26, col. 833.)

pumps. It is not under my jurisdiction, but I will say this. I have some

Mr. MINFORD: I think the Minister
did not want to be inconsistent in the
answer he made to my question. He said
in regard to these evictions that the
country was in extremis, and the reason
he did not put the potato price on a par
with Great Britain was because if they
had done that the place would have been
flooded with potatoes. We have six or
eight factories for processing potatoes, and
we have no potatoes to process.
He says
potatoes are necessary, and he knows perfectly well that our flour is composed
partly of potatoes. If these organised
evictions are necessary, as he says, to take
the country out of extremity, and if he
says on the other hand that if he raised
the price of potatoes to an economic price,
or to a par with England, the country
would be flooded with them, that is an
argument that does not satisfy me. It is
inconsistent. If it was right to place the
English and Scottish farmers on the cost
of production, it was definitely wrong not
to give the same to the farmers of Ulster.
Why should they no do that? I cannot
understand it when he says it is freight,
for the same argument would apply to
oats. The Ministry of Food brings oats
from all parts of England and Scotland
to Belfast, and pays freight and storage
amounting to £18 10s. I only ask for
justice, nothing more, and I demand
nothing less for the Ulster farmer than
is given to the British farmer. I say we
in Ulster deserve the same treatment, and
I am going to demand that treatment. I
think he himself should know, because
his district are not growing to the same extent as they did grow. The Minister knows
perfectly well if you grow cereals year
after year it does not make for the productivity of the land. It takes a crop of
potatoes or a crop of roots to give the
ground the sunshine by working on it in
the summertime, weeding and so on,
which any farmer knows is essential. The
farmer who does not grow roots or
potatoes is looked upon as a poor type of
farmer. Yet he tells this House the
nation is in extremis and takes these
measures to evict a man on to the roadside, and two minutes before that he told
us that if the Ulster farmer got any more
for his potatoes the country would be
swamped with them. I never heard such
an argument in my life. He knows the
Farmers' Union, of which he was president in years gone by, are clamouring and
fighting regarding this thing. It will not
take very long to solve it, I can tell you.
If it were not for the £10 subsidy--that
is why there are so many growing. A
man gets £100, and it enables him to buy
his feeding stuffs and his seed. I come to

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Prison Officers' Association.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
aware
of Home Affairs whether he is
that, in response to a recent letter sent
to his Department, the Area Secretary
of the Prison Officers' Association was
informed that it had been found impossible, owing to pressure of work, to
deal with the matters that had been discussed at an official and staff side meeting
held in November, 1942; whether he is
aware that this reply has created intense
resentment among the prison staffs; and
whether he will ensure that his Departmental Assistant Secretaries give as much
attention to the staff problem as they give
to cases in which prisoners escape from
jail.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The reply to the first part
of the question is in the affirmative.
The matters which were discussed at
the meeting last November were under
review when the escapes from the prison
took place, and, in consequence of these
escapes and the extra work involved
thereby, their further consideration had
to be postponed.
The outstanding matters have, however, now been dealt with.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman inform the House in what
manner they have been dealt with, and
what are the results of those outstanding
matters ?
Mr. LOWRY: There were nine requests
in all made by this association, and without the papers before me and not saying
that I am absolutely correct, to the best
of my recollection they were all refused.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he knows the
seriousness of this refusal. Is he not
aware that the Prison Officers' Association, which is a recognised body in Great
Britain, are treated in a way different
from the way the prison officers' representatives in Northern Ireland have been
treated by this Government? In view of
the very distasteful decision which has
been arrived at in disallowing all the
claims, would the right hon. Gentleman
not think it worth while to have a joint
deputation meet him on the question, and
to have a full discussion?
Whitehouse Building Scheme.
BELFAST CORPORATION AND

2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether his Ministry has
been informed of the recent decision of
the Belfast Corporation in regard to the
building of 30 houses on a site which,
according to the Planning Commission,
should only contain 16 houses; whether
he is aware of the fact that the builder
concerned is a member of the Belfast
Corporation and had facilities for using
his influence in order that the recommendations of the Planning Commission
should be ignored; whether he is aware that
a prominent member of the Estate Agents'
Association, who is also a member of the
Corporation, gave his fullest support to
the proposal to build these 30 house, and,
in view of the fact that these vested
interests of the builders and the estate
agents have succeeded in getting approval
from the Corporation for a scheme definitely opposed to the public interest,
thereby making a farce of the work of the
Planning Commission, will he take steps
to see that the recommendations of the
Planning Commission are adhered to by
the Corporation, and that their decision
in regard to the houses in question is
annulled.
Mr. LOWRY: I am aware that in the
case referred to the Corporation have
passed certain plans which the Planning
Commission recommended should not be
passed, but I cannot for a moment
accept the implication contained in the
question that in taking this course the
Corporation or any of its members were
influenced by improper considerations.

Meals for School Children.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether, in view of the disclosure made by her that only £7,000 out
of an estimated £28,000 for the purpose
of developing school meals, had been disbursed during the past year, and that
with the exception of Belfast and County
Down very little was being done by local
authorities in Northern Ireland to provide proper facilities for the children of
the workers, she will introduce legislation
making it obligatory on these authorities
to provide suitable meals for the children
of the working classes of Northern
Ireland.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): In reply
to the hon. Member's question, my
Ministry does not consider that it would
be advisable to amend the existing legislation at present so as to compel local
education authorities to provide school
meals. The hon. Member will recollect
that this point was mentioned during the
debate on the Education Estimates a few
days ago.
The Ministry will, however, continue to
impress the importance of the matter on
those authorities who have so far shown
reluctance to put schemes into operation,
and is confident that this will have the
support of other interested parties, including parents, school managers and
teachers.
Mr. HENDERSON: In the event of
a local authority not putting into operation an Act passed by this Parliament to
feed these children, will the hon. lady Member see that the children are looked after?
Mrs. PARKER: I made it clear that
at the present moment the Ministry do
not contemplate any exercise of compul-
We are doing everything possible
to induce the education authorities to proceed in the right direction. At the present moment they are only three which
have no experimental scheme in operation
-they have no scheme of any kind-and
I hope very much we shall be able to
induce those three to reconsider their
attitude.
Mr. HENDERSON: The only way for
the hon. lady Member to induce them is
to exterminate them. (Laughter.)

trade labourers in Northern Ireland are

not to agree to the imposition of unfair

of a disagreement the labourers' unions

case heard by the National Arbitration

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The Council to which the hon.
Member refers was established at the instigation of my Ministry in November,
1941, for the purpose of dealing with
questions relating to rates of wages and
conditions of employment in the building
industry. It consists of an equal number
of representatives of the Northern Ireland
Federation of Building Trade Employers
and the National Federation of Building
Trades Operatives, and at their request is
presided over by an officer of the Department who acts as a neutral chairman.
It is the policy of both the Imperial
Minister of Labour and myself to ensuch reprecourage the formation of
sentative councils to settle questions concerning their respective industries, and it
would be improper for me to dictate the
conclusions at which they should arrive.
Where such machinery exists, it is only
in the last resort that trade disputes need
be referred to the Arbitration Tribunal
appointed under the Conditions of Employment and National Arbitration Order
(Northern Ireland), 1940.
Mr. GRANT: In reply to the hon.
Member, it is quite true there is a
differentiation between the percentage
rates in Great Britain and Northern Ireland, but it is also perfectly true that the
machinery in operation in Great Britain
has been actively engaged in this matter
for over 20 years. In Northern Ireland
this machinery has only been in operation
about 18 months. When it first came
into operation labourers were paid as low
as 7d and 8d per hour. To-day some,
I think, are getting ls 5d an hour. I
contend that if we have advanced so far
in 18 months under this tribunal by
mutual arrangement between employers
representatives and workers, it is much
better there should not be any Government interference at the moment, so that
both parties should have an opportunity
of continuing the good work they have
started.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman to reply to the
first part of my question. Does the right
hon. Gentleman agree with the principle
of a distinction between labour value in
Northern Ireland and labour value in
Great Britain of the labourer who is
carrying out the same class of work.
That is the point I would like answered.
R.U.C. Pensions.
5. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he will reconsider the enforcement of Article 19
(1) of the R.U.C. Pension Order, which
is not mandatory, and discriminates between R.U.C. and R.I.C. pensioners, and
which does not obtain in England as far
as police pensioners there are concerned.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary and
Royal Irish Constabulary Regulations regarding the suspension or abatement of
pension on re-employment in Government
service are similar.
Oral Answers
Supply
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
The ordinary Pension Regulations do
not, however, apply to the compensation
allowance granted on the disbandment of
the Royal Irish Constabulary.
In England the regulations governing
the suspension of pensions are different,
but in that country police are employed
by the local authorities. Here, however,
the police are in the direct employment of
the Central Government, and in the
matter of pension abatement they are
treated in the same manner as other
Government employees.
The administration of the article in
question has recently been the subject of
discussion between my Ministry and the
Ministry of Finance, and it has been
decided that there is no reason why the
existing procedure should not be continued, except that pensions granted on
medical grounds are to be exempt from
suspension or abatement.

without
any outside help it would be

paid at the rate of about £2 10s per

-as in all other countries we should have

The examination is a stiff one. If people

are carrying out ordinary street duty and

a policeman. They have been appointed
from the ranks of their own political
party, and to-day you have members of
the R.U.C. saluting people who know very
little about police work. This kind of
thing would not be tolerated in England.
They have special police in England, but
the members of that body have nothing to
do with the regular force in the various
counties.
There is another thing I want to bring
forward. Our police sent upwards of 600
of its members to serve in the last war,
and 150 of them never returned, having
given their lives in the battle for freedom.
What do we find in this war? We find
prohibition is laid down by the right hon.
Gentleman against any member of the
force serving with the colours.
Mr. NIXON: He has to resign..
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, he has to resign.

twelve young men made representations

I would do that. They would not care

work.
I say this has got to be changed. I

There is a reservation in regard to the

to

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: When
the hon. Member raised the question on
that statement last Tuesday, I told him
that I did not remember whether I had
had the statement before me. That was
the fact. That is why I felt that it would
have been of more assistance to the Committee if the hon. Member had told me,
even a short time before, that he was
going to raise this particular point, because I do not profess to anything exceptional in the way of powers of memory.
I deal with hundreds of cases in the course
of a year, and I must say that I could not
remember the details of that particular'
case on the spur of the moment because,
as I now find, it was over a year since. I
had had it before me.
On investigation, I find that it is quite
wrong to say that no heed was taken of
Mr. Farmer's statement on that occasion.
Mr. Farmer's statement was taken to the
police. He was interviewed concerning
it at considerable length. It was handed
to the police during a time when they
were investigating irregularities on the
part of certain members of the Food
Office staff, and also on the part of this
Mr. Brown. It received every care and
attention, and I find that a few days
afterwards it was submitted for my consideration, together with other papers
relative to the investigation at that time.
I also find that I directed the prosecution
of Mr. Brown and of a number of other
persons in respect of certain breaches of
the Food Control Regulations.
I did not direct a prosecution in respect
of the allegations in this particular statement. I came to the conclusion, a view
which was shared by the police as a result
of their investigations, that there was no
evidence in that statement which would
justify me in giving the requisite consent
to a charge of bribery, or would justify
me in raising any other charge. I may
say that if hon. Members read the statement carefully, I believe they will have
no difficulty in finding the ground for
that decision. It was quite apparent, on
the face of the. statement and it was also
quite apparent to the police, that Mr.
Brown was under the influence of drink
to a very considerable extent during the
course of the. long interview between
him and Mr. Farmer when Mr. Farmer
got the material for the statement.
And I think perhaps the background to
the statement, which is an indication of
its evidential value, is to be found in the
last paragraph: "This conversation did
not take place in quite the clear manner
set out above, as it was interposed by
various irrelevant talk and drink, and
the main subjects were brought back in
the conversation time and time again."
