Solicitors Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: This is a very brief
measure which originated in another
place, and which has been introduced at
the request of the Incorporated Law
Society of Northern Ireland. Under the
provisions of recent legislation affecting
Great Britain the time solicitors' apprentices, or articled clerks as they are called
in Great Britain, must spend in their
masters' offices has been very considerably reduced. In fact, two years spent
in the actual service of the master is sufficient to entitle an apprentice, on passing
the required examination, to be admitted
to the solicitors' profession.
The
There are a number of solicitors'
apprentices in Northern Ireland. Some
of them have already joined the armed
Forces, and others may do so in the
future. That being so the society wish
to be placed in the position of being able
to give them the same concessions as their
brethren in Great Britain enjoy.
Bill is a very short one. The public are
safeguarded by the fact that the apprentices must pass the necessary examination
before being admitted to the roll of
solicitors. National Service means service
in any of the armed Forces, and where
there is any doubt as to what constitutes
national service during the present emergency the matter may be determined by
the Lord Chief Justice. I am sure the
Measure is one which will commend itself
to the House as it will encourage recruiting and the forwarding of the present
struggle. I beg to move.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Finance Bill.
FINANCE
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF
(Major Sinclair): Clause 1 has nothing
in it which is new in principle and merely
gives continuing effect to the resolution
which increased the existing rates of
entertainments duty to the higher rates
recently introduced in Great Britain. The
reduced rate of entertainments duty referred to is, of course, that which is
applicable to "living", entertainments,
that is, where the performers are personally present and performing.
Clause 2 implements the undertaking
given in the House on the 25th March of
this
year to increase the scope of the use
to which an agricultural tractor could be
put under a 5s licence. Hitherto a farmer
could only carry on the road agricultural
produce or articles required for agricultural land from one part of his land to
another. Now there is no restriction
whatever in point of distance for the
carriage of such goods. This concession,
however, is purely a war-time one designed
to stimulate the vital necessities of tillage
and food production, and will be subject
to withdrawal at the end of the present
emergency. It does not, of course, exempt
a farmer from compliance with the
provisions of Section 15 of the Road
and Railway Transport Act (Northern Ireland), 1935, which,
as hon.
Members know, prohibits the carriage
of other person's goods except under
certain conditions. In my Budget
statement I said that the concession would
cost £8,100 in the current year, and,
while this is so, the normal annual loss of
revenue will only amount to a sum of
about £4,500. The difference in the
figures is accounted for by the fact that
not only will the loss of revenue be experienced in the current year, but there
will be in addition a partial refund of the
licences issued at the 1st January last.
Clause 3, though rather formidable in
appearance, is declaratory only and does
nothing to alter what has been a longestablished practice in the levying of
Estate Duty. Fresh legislation has, however, become necessary owing to the doubt
cast by a decision in the Court of Appeal
in Great Britain on the legality of past
and current practice in this respect. What
this Clause effects is that where a person,
who has a limited interest-that is, is a
life tenant only-in the unascertained
residue of an estate, dies, then that
limited interest will be subject to Estate
Duty. Hon. Members are aware, of
course, that the winding up of an estate
may take a matter of years, and that
there are instances where the owner of
such an interest dies before the completion of the administration of the estate.
It was held by the Court of Appeal, to
which I have referred, that until the
residue of an estate is ascertained the
beneficiaries have no title to that residue,
and no right to the income of the investments composing the residue for the time
being in the hands of the executors.
Finance Bill
Adjournment
15 JUNE 1943
While this decision was given in connection with a surtax case, it is held that it
also prejudices the position with regard
to the collection of Estate Duty. This
Clause now places the matter beyond all
doubt by deeming the limited interest in
such cases to have been an interest in
been
possession as if the residue had
ascertained immediately on the death of
the testator.
Clause 4 gives to an adopted child the
privileges in regard to legacy and
succession duties which have hitherto been
granted to children born in wedlock. In
order to prevent any abuse of this
privilege, the concession is not operative
unless the dispositions by the adopter or
by the adopted child have been made
more than three years before the date on
which the property passes.
Since 1919, interest charged on deferred
payments of death duties has been at the
rate of 4 per cent. This rate was fixed,
not only with regard to the prevailing
trend of interest rates, but also with regard to the effect which it had upon the
prevention of undue delay in the payment of death duties. In view of the low
rates of interest now current a reduction
from 4 to 3 per cent. is considered
justifiable. Clause 5 accordingly gives
effect to this.
The Stamp Duty referred to in Clause
6 is more generally known as Corporation
Duty. It is charged at the rate of 5 per
cent. per annum on the net profits arising
from any real or personal property vested
in any body of persons in such a manner
that the property does not become liable
to death duties. There are certain
exemptions to this tax, such as religious,
charitable, and educational bodies, and it
is proposed, following the practice in
Great Britain, to make exemption specific
in the case of Trade Unions and Trade
Protection Associations. Corporation
in
duty, I may say, is relatively unimportant as a source of revenue
Northern Ireland. I beg to move.

Police and Convictions against Persons
Seeking Employment.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the police have any
instructions on the question of supplying
employers with particulars of convictions
against ex-soldiers and other persons
seeking employment, and whether the
Minister would give instructions that no
information in respect of convictions
would be supplied except in exceptional
cases.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): No instructions have been
issued to the police to furnish particulars
of convictions against ex-soldiers or other
persons seeking employment. It is only
in exceptional cases in which it is in the
public interest to do so that Government
Departments and employers of labour
engaged in Government contracts
supplied with such information, and even
in these cases the police only report on
particular individuals at the specific
request of the employer or employing
department.
are

Transport Board Monthly Tickets.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that the
decision of the Northern Ireland Road
on
Transport Board to make monthly
tickets as from 1st August valid only for
one double journey per day will impose
unnecessary hardship
many war
workers, business and professional men,
Government and Local Government
officials, and many others, as it will almost
treble the cost of two such double journeys
if they will go home for lunch, and, if not,
will involve them in extra expense for
food which they could get cheaper at home
and will increase for them the cost of
living and will also result in increased demands by caterers for more food allocations without any alteration in each individual's home food rations, and will not
even result in any fewer buses being run
as people availing of the two double
journeys per day facility usually make
only short journeys in buses that are
travelling in any case on longer runs, and
whether he will take steps to have this
decision modified by continuing the concession to those genuinely travelling home
for lunch on available existing buses.
Mr. LOWRY: The withdrawal of the
concession referred to in the question was
one of the suggestions put forward by the
Northern Ireland Road Transport Board
in response to an appeal by the Ministry
on behalf of the Ministries of Supply and
of Fuel and Power to consider ways in
which economy in the consumption of
petrol and rubber could be effected.
The Board represented to the Government that by making the monthly ticket
valid for one double journey a day only
instead of two there would be a very considerable saving of buses and the Government thereupon agreed to the Board's
proposals.
I am aware that the proposals may
mean additional expense to certain members of the travelling public, but the
fixing of charges for ordinary and season
tickets of all kinds is a matter entirely
within the discretion of the Board subject
to the appeal procedure provided for in
the Road and Rail Transport Act, 1935.
This procedure is still open to any body of
persons who feel aggrieved.

Assistance for the Harvest.
3. Mr.
JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is in
a position to give the House any further
information as to military assistance at
harvest time and also as to the Ministry's
scheme for utilising unemployed workers
for harvesting work.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): As the hon.
Member will realise, it must be expected
that military assistance to farmers will
this year be on a smaller scale than heretofore, and it is probable that such help
will be confined to certain areas and for
restricted periods.
It follows, therefore, that the fullest
provision must be made for utilising all
other forms of help for saving the harvest.
At that season the number of unemployed
agricultural workers will be negligible and
the only sources of labour available will
be unemployed industrial workers, voluntary land service workers and students
and school-children.
My Ministry is preparing a scheme for
making available the services of industrial
unemployed workers in the form of gang
labour during the harvest season. This,
I may add, is in conformity with a resolution passed at a meeting of the Belfast
and district shop stewards held in Belfast
on 16th May last. Very soon advertisements will be issued giving particulars of
the scheme and advising farmers how to
proceed in order to avail themselves of it.
For the information of hon. Members
and others who may be interested, I am
glad to take this opportunity of stating
very briefly the main features of the
scheme.
In the districts where experience has
shown that the shortage of labour will
probably be most acute, labour officers
will be located and most of them are, in
fact, already at work. It will be the
duty of these officers to make contact with
farmers and to do everything possible to
secure that gang labour is provided where
it is required. It is not proposed to
supply fewer than four men and a gang
leader to any farmer. The object is to
get work cleared up as quickly as possible
on each farm, and where only one or two
men are required for longer periods these
must be obtained by the farmer from the
employment exchange. For that reason
it is not intended to include agricultural
workers in the gangs.
The industrial workers will be taken
into the employment of the Ministry
through the exchanges. They will be
guaranteed full weekly wages. They will
be required to report daily at centres in
their home towns. They will be transported to and from the farms at Government expense. They will be paid at the
highest minimum rate of agricultural
wages fixed by the Agricultural Wages
Board; for adult workers this is now 56s
per week. The men will be allowed to
work at piece rates when this can be
arranged, as, for example, at pulling flax.
The farmer will be required to sign a
form each evening agreeing to refund to
the Ministry the wages of the workers.
He will be asked to repay only at the
minimum rate
rate of agricultural wages
applicable in his district, or the actual

If the weather should turn wet after the

be

provided for the harvest. Hon. Members

It is

I may add that the Voluntary Land

Stormont Gates and Railings.
6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister

Estate.
The
MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): While the great bulk
of the railings surrounding the Stormont
Estate has already been surrendered for
the furtherance of the war effort, the
main entrance gates and the ornamental
railings flanking them have so far been.
retained. However, in view of the urgent
demand for metal in this form, it
has now been decided very reluctantly
to remove these gates and railings
in spite of their artistic merit
and their possible use for the control of
vehicular traffic. I should add that some
railings at the back of the estate have
not been removed because they form one
of the boundaries of a field, and have been
retained on agricultural grounds. In
this connection, it may interest the House
to know that up to a recent date 5,200
tons of gates and railings had been collected in Northern Ireland, of which
3,340 tons have been shipped for further
processing. Of the balance of 1,860 tons
still to be shipped, 1,040 tons have
already undergone the preliminary processing required.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): As the term of office of the
existing chairman and members of the
Assistance Board will expire on 30th
June, the reconstitution of the Board is
at present under consideration.

Mr. GRANT: In reply to the hon.
Member's question, I pointed out that if

Mr. BROWN: It may be suggested
that the war
for
may be
forgetting about the Pigs Marketing
Board, which figured in so many debates
in this House in pre-war days, and I want
to make it perfectly clear at the outset
that my Resolution is far from being unrelated to the war and that the war is in
fact the sole and simple reason
for my
action in bringing it forward. My only
apology to the House on that score is that
I did not bring it forward sooner, because
nothing is more important in the
effort than the utmost conservation of all
our resources both on the part of the
State and the individual, and the ruthless
cutting out of all unnecessary expenditure. Economy and austerity formed the
cry on every hand, and the supreme duty
of the Government is to set the people an
example in saving and retrenchment, and
I hope that the immediate abolition of
this wholly unnecessary board and all the
unnecessary expense it involves will be
one of the examples, more of which I
hope to point out later.
war
I readily recognise that some degree of
benefit was conferred on the agricultural
industry and on the public by the various
paid boards, councils and committees that
were set up by the Government to organise
and administer the numerous schemes
that were introduced for the marketing
of agricultural products, and that they
would have been even more successful but
for the bureaucratic interference of the
Ministry of Agriculture. And although
in peace-time I did not go so far as to
advocate that they should be scrapped
entirely I did repeatedly protest against
the fact that far too much money was
swallowed up in administrative costs both
by the Ministry of Agriculture and by the
multiplicity of paid boards, councils and
committees that they set up and encouraged, aided and abetted in lavishness of
every description.
Some idea of the Ministry's own lavish
administration can be gathered from the
statement in the House on 7th March,
1939, by the hon. Member for North
Derry, then the president of the
Ulster Farmers' Union and now Minister
of Agriculture when he said:
I find in this Milk Fund, which is
administered solely by the Ministry of
Agriculture, that despite scrutiny by
this House it takes a sum of £48,000
odd to collect £32,000 odd and disburse
that amount, plus the sum received
from the British Exchequer. I will
leave it to hon. Members to say if that
is economy.-(Official Reports, Vol. 22,
7th March, col. 336).
The hon. Member for North Derry
leaves it to Members to say if that was
economy. I leave it to the hon.
Member for North Derry, the Minister
of Agriculture, to say does he think the
Pigs Marketing Board necessary in the
fourth year of total war, with a chairman
getting £300 or roughly a guinea and a
half a minute? It is a significant and
remarkable fact that the Comptroller and
Auditor-General in his report for the year
1941-42, states:
Milk Fund Account.-This account
has not yet been rendered to me by the
Ministry of Agriculture.
Why are we given no explanation whatever as to why this has not been done?
I think that is a very important matter
and the Minister raised it himself in this
House some time ago.
When in 1939 the time came for the
Ministry of Agriculture to slay the chief
Frankenstein monster of their own creation, the Pigs Marketing Board, on
discovering that producer-control

Whatever justification may have existed
in peace-time for marketing boards like
the Pigs Marketing Board, absolutely
none exists to-day when all food is
strictly controlled and rationed by the
Government, and when we have a
marketing and food defence division of
the Ministry of Agriculture which cost
in salaries, wages and allowances in 1942
£101,378 8s 7d, and this on top of the
huge cost of administering the work of
the British Ministry of Food in Northern
Ireland.
All the other marketing bodies, such
as the Pig Industry Council, the Egg
Marketing Committee, Butter and Cream
Marketing Board, and a host of others
have disappeared, and why there should
be any necessity for continuing the
expense of the Pigs Marketing Board,
which both the Permanent Secretary of
the Ministry of Agriculture and the present Minister of Agriculture have, to use
their own words, put in cold storage for
the duration of the war?

administration of the Egg Marketing
Scheme in 1938-39 cost £25,202, towards

leaving £11,044 to be provided by the
taxpayers. Out of this £25,202 a sum of

really necessary?

think that it would only be fair that I

pigs and pig production before the first

We had a section of the farming industry
then which was rapidly disappearing. Why
was it on the point of dwindling to
nothing? Because the custom had grown
up in Northern Ireland for the farmers
to kill their pigs on the farm and take
them as carcases to the local market, where
they disposed of them. There they had
been in the habit of taking these pig carcases for generations. The carcases were
then in a very highly perishable condition,
as hon. Members need not be told, and
the result was that they had to be sold
no matter what the price offered was. If
it happened there was an extra supply in
any particular market on any day the
price dropped in that market.
Mr. NIXON: Birmingham.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: It had
nothing to do with Birmingham.

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The result
was that prices in the same week would
fluctuate as much as 3s to 10s per cwt. in
the one market. There was no confidence
on the part of producers, and the consequence was that the pig population was
decreasing steadily and something had to
be done. The pigs marketing scheme
was introduced. The purpose of that
scheme was to provide stability in
marketing and stability and uniformity
in prices.

And what happened?
successful was the scheme in regard to
these very points that immediately the
population of pigs in Northern Ireland
began to increase by leaps and bounds.
Before the introduction of this scheme
we had only one type of cure of bacon in
Northern Ireland, known as the roll and
ham curing industry, but with the increase in the pig population that old bacon
curing arrangement was simply unable to
cope with the number of pigs coming
forward and some new method had to be
found for dealing with them, and so a
second method of curing known as the
Wiltshire cure had to be introduced. It
was something new. There was a body of
farmers' representatives set up whose business it was to negotiate prices both for
the roll and ham cure and for the Wiltshire cure. That was a type of curing
of which there was no experience whatever in Northern Ireland. We knew
nothing about the costs. Pigs were taken
in alive. There were all sorts of by-products available from the industry into
which nobody in Northern Ireland had
any insight, and after the problem had
been played with for a time the Pigs
Marketing Board eventually decided to set
up on behalf of the producers a Wiltshire
factory.

Members to point me to any corresponding achievements by businessmen or anyone else in the same space of time.

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.—(Sir
Wilson Hungerford.)
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I should like
to ask the Minister of Home Affairs when
he intends to take the Second Reading of
the Local Government Officers (No. 2)
Bill which was presented this afternoon,
and copies of which are now in the pigeon
holes of Members in the Lobby. Down
County Council have asked me to represent to the Government that before this
Bill is given a Second Reading the previous Bill was withdrawn as it was unworkable-they and other authorities
should be consulted and their views
obtained by the Government. The matter
is not one that should be rushed. I am
bringing this matter forward because I
understand from the Whip's Office that
the Second Reading is to be taken early
in July. There is no meeting of the
Finance Committee of the Down County
Council until the 2nd of July. If the
Bill is taken early in July there will be
very little time in which to consult the
Down County Council or the other county,
rural and district councils. If what I
suggest were done it would give hon.
Members representing the various constituencies an opportunity of finding out
the feelings of their constituents in regard
to this Bill. I hope this Bill will not be
rushed, and that we will be given ample
time to consult with the various bodies
interested in the matter. I trust the
Government will accede to the request
which I am making on behalf of the Down
County Council.

is a person whose duties are mainly
administrative, professional or clerical, or
whose remuneration is over £420 a year.
Pensionable employment has been extended somewhat to what it was in the
original draft of the Bill, which referred
to pensionable employment in the United
Kingdom. It is now made to cover
'employment within or without Northern
Ireland, because when one contemplates
the termination of the war there doubtless
will be many men returning, notably
those perhaps in the medical service, who
were in pensionable employment in other
parts of the world, and it is but right that
people of that sort whether serving in
Africa, Asia, Australia, or on the sea or
in the air should be taken into account,
and that local authorities should have
power to recognise that pensionable
employment. That is really the reason
for changing or extending it to "within
or without" Northern Ireland, although
the gentleman from Groomsport wants it
confined solely and entirely to service in
Northern Ireland.
Pensionable office. is a definition that
occurs in very many of our Acts, some of
which were passed quite recently by this
House. I have gone through the objects
and scope of the Bill, and I desire to
reiterate that there is no desire to filch
away any powers the local authorities
have or take away from the officers any
protection which they enjoy. This Bill
extends the protection. It gives further
powers to local authorities to pension
them properly, and it provides for the
better and more economical working of
the local government system by enabling
local authorities to reapportion duties
amongst officers so as to achieve the best
results. As I have said, if it is the
desire of the House to make this mandatory on local authorities, the alteration
of two or three words does that with the
greatest of ease. I beg to move.

capable of speaking in his own defence
than Mr. Graham. I think it is hitting
below the belt and highly contemptible
that in his absence an attack of this nature
should be made upon this young man who
is carrying out his duty-it is an unpaid
position as hon. secretary of the Association.
The Minister in his statement made the
rather extravagant suggestion-I will not
characterise it as an untruth-that the
Bill proposes to bring into protection the
small number of officers still to be protected, and that a measure of protection
already applies to 90 per cent. of the

existing officers.
that the membership of the Association represented by Mr. Graham numbers 1,600
I assert without any hesitation that the
statement the Minister made is not in
accordance with the facts. It is perfectly
obvious that this Association represents
considerably more than the remaining 10
per cent. of the public officers in this

The Minister said that the scope of the
Bill does not touch upon the rights of any
existing officer. Not one speaker who

statement. Even the hon. and gallant

definitely upon the rights of existing
officers in this country. This has been described, according to the Minister,
another attempt to hand over officials to

zeal. It was implied that Mr. Graham
in writing this circular was acting in his

Mr. Graham was not writing in any such

I want to get away from expressions of
regret to that of approval of at least one
thing the practice that has apparently
been initiated by the Minister of Home
Affairs of issuing a memorandum in connection with proposed legislation.
sincerely hope that the experiment is one
that will be emulated and copied by
other Ministries when they are introducing new legislation. The memorandum
issued in connection with Bill No. 2
contains the statement-reference has
already been made to it-that this Bill
does not differ in any point of principle
from the Bill as it was originally
introduced. That is quite true, but it is
also true to say that the new Bill
introduces a new point of principle
which, in my opinion, is far more controversial and far more objectionable than
that contained in Bill No. 1. I wonder
why, in view of that fact, Bill No. 1 was
ever withdrawn. Is the introduction of
this new Bill intended merely to be a
means of throwing dust in the eyes of
Members of this House? Or is it the idea
of the Minister that by the repeated reintroduction of new Bills of this kind at
last Members of the House might
be
weary of the matter and let it pass?
Before I refer-I want to be as quick
as I can to one or two other of what I
consider the chief objections to the Billand personally I prefer to deal with the
principle of this Bill rather than with the
principles of Mr. Graham-might I draw
attention to the addition to which I have
referred? That is the reference to the
right of appeal by one of the aggrieved
parties. In the first Bill a dispute between a local authority and an officer was
to be determined by the Ministry of Home
Affairs whose decision was to have been
final. By this method if the local
authority and the Ministry wished to
conspire-I not suggesting they
possibly would-to get rid of an officer
that officer had no outside appeal.
am
Here in this Bill, not merely is the
decision of the Ministry to be final, but
you have the most extraordinary clause
that perhaps has ever been introduced
into any parliamentary Bill, that if the
two parties in disagreement shall agree
together in writing, then and then only
shall the matter in dispute go to arbitration. Did anyone ever hear a proposition
of that kind? Before the aggrieved party
can get the right of appeal to the common
law of the Crown he must have the assent
of the other party to the dispute. The
logical effect of this Clause added in the
new Bill makes it precisely the same in
operation as the old. If the Ministry and
the local authority together have any
umbrage against an officer, then I suggest
that officer has no right whatever of appeal
against the common decision of these two
authorities. I have said, and I repeat
because I think it should be emphasised,
that never in the history of this House, or
1321 Local Government Officers Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Thomas Bailie]
any other House, has such a clause been
put into any parliamentary Bill. I
am very much afraid that those who
framed this Bill must have had a very
slight regard for the intelligence of the
Members who constitute this House.
As regards the Bill in general, it is
represented to be innocuous and very
simple in its intentions, and surprise has
been expressed by the Ministry of Home
Affairs that it should have aroused the
indignation and antagonism of so many
people in this country-not merely local
government officers, but a considerable
body of public boards in the country. I
venture to suggest to the Minister
that the number of members of
public boards in the country opposed to
this Bill is greater than the 1,600 members of the. Local Government Officers'
Association. The logical conclusion is
that either these members of public boards
and local government officers are a parcel
of incompetent dolts or this simple Bill
is not as simple as it appears to be.
I have every regard for the intelligence and ability of the officials in
this country. I consider we are signally
fortunate in this country in having a
standard of ability amongst our local
government officers that is even greater
than that to be found in any other part
of the United Kingdom, and I say it is
an insult to the intelligence of these
officers that a Bill of this kind, which is
simply designed in the first instance to
create an avenue for the Belfast Corporation to get over their difficulties with
regard to the appointment of a town
clerk, should be used, as this Bill is used,
as an omnibus Bill for the introduction of
controversial issues that affect the whole
local government of the country.
Reference has been made to Clause 1.
This Clause stands practically as it was
in the former draft, but the word
"person" has been apparently substituted
for the word "officer," and the definition
of "officer" has been added to the fourth
Clause. In this definition "officer"
means a person whose duties are wholly
or mainly administrative, professional or
clerical. In actual fact, and it cannot be
denied, the local authority would not have
the right under the terms of this Bill to
employ an ordinary clerical office boy
without such approval. I see the. Minister shaking his head. I assert without
any question that that is the logical outcome of the Clause.
Mr. LOWRY: But not the legal outcome.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: The logical
outcome and I believe the legal, too. It
means that practically everybody in the
employment of the local authorities with
the exception of the manual workers is
included under this. It means, moreover,
that all the local authorities are to be
mere vassals without any effective authority and the whole question of appointments passes into the hands of the Ministry and into the hands of the Minister. If
the Minister says yea, it shall be yea, and
if the Minister says nay, it shall be nay.
Local authorities are being reduced to the
position of vassals and are being bereft of
every portion of responsibility and
authority. The only argument I have
ever heard in favour of this Bill is that
boards of guardians as at present formed
are in exactly the same position as is contemplated under this Bill. I do not know
whether the Minister has ever stopped to
consider the general reputation of boards
of guardians in this country.
I do not know whether he has ever
heard the suggestion that boards of
guardians should be discarded altogether.
I do not know whether he is aware-he
should be aware that the functions of
boards of guardians are very largely
nominal and upon them rests a very slight
degree of responsibility or initiative.
can imagine no greater disaster to this
country than that the ordinary local
authorities which are responsible boards,
manned by intelligent and self-sacrificing
men, should be reduced to the status of
boards of guardians. That, however, is
apparently the last word and the ideal
method of local government in the eyes of
the present Government of Northern Ireland. If it is going to be pursued may I'
respectfully suggest that in a very short
time we will be faced with the fact of our
inability to obtain competent men to fill
the positions in the public boards. That
is a supreme danger, in my opinion, and
nothing the Minister has said would change
my view of the danger of that clause. In
my opinion, it together with the whole of
the Bill should be abolished.

referred to the Local Government Act of

1934. Section 18 of that Act gives ample

with that power they should be content.
If they have not fully exercised that

of this House. It is the fault of the

Clause 2, to which reference has also been
made is notoriously unfair in that it excludes the rights of certain existing officers
appointed after the Local Government
Act of 1919, and apparently confers these

There is a further important point
raised in this much castigated circular of
the Local Government Officers' Association which points out the difference becivil
tween legislation applicable to
servants and the legislation applicable to
local government officers. The Minister
is aware that in 1925 legislation there was
given to civil servants the right to
pensions after the date of that Act and
full service at that date would count for
remuneration. I would like to hear him
tell the House to-day why local government officers should not be entitled to the
same consideration as that afforded by
that Act. There is a further point-I
wish to be brief-raised in the definition
of pensionable employment. If I am
correct in my interpretation there is no
reciprocal arrangement as between this
country and Great Britain. Whilst a
cross-Channel applicant for a public
position, say the town clerkship of
Belfast, can carry his superannuation
rights there into this country, an applicant on the other hand in Belfast for a
post across the water cannot transfer the
benefit of his service to the cross-Channel
local government. That is the fault of
the Government of Northern Ireland in
1927 when the Superannuation Bill was
passed and made applicable across the
water while no such Act was passed here.
If it had been passed here the necessity
for a Bill of this kind would not have
arisen. The non-existence of such a right
here is largely the cause of the anomalies
that exist at the present time.
There are other aspects of the Bill which
can be best discussed in the Committee
stage. For that reason I do not want to
pursue the matter in any greater detail
this afternoon, but I grasp the hope that
this Bill will never reach the Committee
stage. I would credit the Members of
this House with sufficient intelligence to
think they will have the courage to resist
a Bill of this kind which undoubtedly
does represent an encroachment upon
democracy. Democracy is a term I am
not afraid to use. I do consider that this
Bill to-day is a definite encroachment
upon the ordinary public rights and a step
towards bureaucracy. If the Minister
will take a suggestion from me just now
or if he will take it in the form of a
challenge I shall be very pleased to pass
it over.
If he will use his influence to
get the Members of his side of the House
free from the exercise of the party Whip
and leave this Bill to a free vote of the
House I have no doubt whatever that he
will quickly see what would be the actual
opinion of, at any rate, the majority of
the Members of this House in regard to
the proposals of this Bill. I say this and
I have done. This Bill was intended as
I understand in the first instance simply
to benefit the Corporation of Belfast in its
efforts to secure a first-class man.

intended to foist a man upon them.

local government officers, but to the

the undesirability of introducing a controversial measure of this kind at the
present juncture in our history.

would be well advised to consider the

There are many objectionable points in
the Bill. I cannot see very much wrong
myself with Clause 1, but as to Clause 2,

of the new Cabinet. They destroy this

Agricultural Problems.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I thank you
for allowing me to get up again when the
Minister of Agriculture is present. Some
time ago the ex-Minister of Agriculture
reported to this House that he was drawing up a scheme to use the unemployed
to assist the farmers in Northern Ireland
to gather in the harvest. Latterly, the
new Minister of Agriculture gave the
details as to how this scheme was to be
worked, and for the information of the
House and the farmers generally I would
like to say I have availed myself of men
under this scheme for getting my hay in..
When the weather was fine we were short
of labour, and we applied to the Ministry
of Labour authorities, and they provided
five unemployed men. I understand they
volunteered to do this work. I would
like to pay a tribute to this scheme, and
say that from my experience it is going
to be a great help to the farmers when
the corn harvest comes along. The five
men I had last week were most willing
and most helpful in dealing with my crop
of hay, and I am glad to say it is properly gathered in, which might not have
been the case had these men not been
available. I wish to advertise that this
scheme is in existence and working, and I
am sure it will be availed of in the future.
I know a lot of farmers who got 17 men
out of this scheme. So I would like to
say to the Minister of Agriculture and
those in the Ministry of Labour who
developed the scheme, that it is going to
be a very real help when we come to deal
with the very large crops.
Having got these men I intended to dig
my early potatoes. I would like to tell
the Minister of Agriculture that having
got these men I found there was no
market for first early potatoes in Northern
Ireland to-day. We were directed to
grow additional food, and I think we
agreed to grow potatoes-first earlies,
second earlies, and main crop. The
situation to-day is, as any farmer will
tell you, that you cannot dispose of early
potatoes. The price to-day is 15s 9d per
cwt.; in two or three days it will fall to
12s; in a week's time it will fall to 9s,
and by the end of August it will be
1349 Agricultural Problems

[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
down to 6s 6d. What a loss the farmers
are going to have by planting first earlies.
I personally stand to lose £60 or £70,
because I cannot dispose of my early
potato crop. The extraordinary thing is
that the Government will not allow people
with early potatoes to dig them before
14th June. There is a glut now, and
The
we are stuck with the first earlies.
second earlies are coming in, and once the
British Queens are on the market no one
is going to eat first earlies.
What am I to do with my crop? Leave
it in the ground to rot and lose some. £70?
The point is this. When the Government
ask farmers to do a thing and it is done
they should be able to market their crop,
and the result of the restriction on the
digging of the early crop means they cannot get rid of those first earlies. Large
quantities of them remain. What is to
become of them? I cannot sell mine.
Another point I wish to make is with
regard to the provision of spares for
tractor ploughs. I have a tractor plough
and I cannot get steel points for it. If
we are expected to plough our ground in
the autumn, how are we going to do it?
I am informed by the biggest firm
handling these ploughs in Northern Ireland that these malleable steel points are
not available because they are not being
made, and they provide you with castiron points. My land is heavy and stony,
and you require steel points. You might
as well stick a bottle, in the end as castiron points. I hope the Minister will.
investigate this shortage of steel points.
I congratulate the right hon. Gentleman on his effort to help farmers by the
provision of labour, but the other matters
I have mentioned require looking into.
When we do come to plough land for next
season, tractor ploughs and spares must be
available, because, what is the use of asking farmers to till their land if they cannot get the necessary implements to do it
properly.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Imperial Contribution.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state if reductions in this area's Imperial contributions of £21,000,000 can be made to meet
the urgent needs of public health, housing,
slum clearance and unemployment, and
whether it is a fact that the current
Budget of the Isle of Man, 60 miles from
Lancashire, provides for only a trivial income tax rate of about one-fifth to onethird of the income tax rate in Ulster;
that death duties are unknown there and
that the Isle has not made any free gift
to the British Government for the war.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair) The answer to the first part of
the question is in the negative. As I
explained in my Budget speech, no reduction of the Imperial Contribution will be
needed by reason of any steps which may
be taken for the improvement of public
health and similar services, but, as I
then also explained, there are limitations
on the development of such services which
war requirements impose. As regards the
second part, I regret I have not seen the
current Budget of the Isle of Man.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the right
hon. Gentleman take the opportunity of
seeing that Budget in due time? May I
also ask him whether the figure of
£21,000,000 is not altogether out of proportion to the financial resources of this
area?
Major SINCLAIR: The answer to the
second part of the supplementary question
is, no.
Ministerial Salaries.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether, in view of the fact that
the estimates recently adopted by the
House contained no provision for salaries
for the offices of Minister of Finance and
Minister of Agriculture, he can state by
what authority the Minister of Finance
and Minister of Agriculture are receiving
salaries for these offices without the sanction of Parliament; whether payment has
yet commenced of the increase in the
emoluments of the Prime Minister by
£500 per year, in the form of contingencies
allowance, whether this amount is subject
to income tax, and whether Parliament is
to be given any opportunity of expressing
its opinion on same; and whether he can
state how the odd shillings and pence in
the annual salaries for Cabinet offices are
arrived at, and the amounts for travelling
expenses, subsistence allowance, etc., as
well as the quantities and cost of petrol
issued to each Cabinet Minister for the
past two months, and by whom the cost
has been borne, and also the total annual
payments under all heads that the present
Prime Minister is entitled to and how
much of this is subject to income tax.
Major SINCLAIR: For the convenience of the hon. Member I have divided
his omnibus question into seven parts
which I have numbered in the order in
which they appear.
Part 1. While it is true that specific
provision has not yet been made in the
Estimates for the payment of salaries to
the Ministers of Finance and Agriculture,
statutory authority for the payment of
such salaries already exists in the Salaries
of Ministerial Offices Act, 1921, and the
Ministries Act of 1940. The House has
already been informed of the intention to
pay the salaries in question pending the
introduction of Supplementary Estimates.
Parts 2, 3 and 4. I have nothing to
add to the replies given to similar questions put on the 11th and 20th May,
1943.
Part 5. I refer the hon. Member again
to the salaries of Ministerial Offices Act,
1921, in which it is laid down that the
total sum payable to Cabinet Ministers,
apart from the Prime Minister, in respect
of their services as such shall not exceed
£2,500, and if the hon. Member will
divide this sum by six, he will find that
the odd shillings and pence to which he
refers cannot be avoided.
Part 6. The figures payable to each
Cabinet Minister in respect of travelling

Part 7. His salary of £2,850 per
annum, all of which is subject to incometax.

The Harvest-Use of Motor Lorries.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if Northern
Ireland is keeping step by step with Great
Britain in the concession made to farmers
enabling them to help one another by
lending their motor lorries at harvest time
without incurring liability to the higher
rate of tax applicable to vehicles on
ordinary haulage work.
Major SINCLAIR: I am aware that a
Clause has recently been introduced into
the Finance Bill at present under consideration by the Imperial Parliament
authorising the concession referred to in
the hon. Member's question, and the
question of following suit in Northern
Ireland is already under consideration.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Minister tell
us what consideration involving delay this
matter requires, in view of the fact that
the harvest operations have already begun? Is he not prepared to give the
House an immediate answer on this
matter which, in my opinion, requires no
consideration? As the harvest operations
are in progress it is absolutely necessary
that there should be a definite answer at
once on this question.
Major SINCLAIR: As a matter of fact
this is a most complicated subject, but no
unnecessary delay will occur in coming to
a decision.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister bear
in mind the fact that the harvest operations have been in progress for some time,
and, as this relates directly to the harvest,
may I again urge upon him the absolute
necessity for making an announcement?
Stormont Gates and Railings.

CABINET MINISTER'S PERSONAL.
VIEWS.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether this Government has
come to a decision on the question of
surrendering the Stormont Gates for the
furtherance of the war effort; whether
the Minister of Finance stated in Parliament on 22nd June, 1943, "In view of
the urgent demand for metal in this form,
it has now been decided very reluctantly
to remove these gates and railings in spite
of their artistic merit"; whether on the
29th June, 1943, the Minister of Education speaking on the subject is reported.
to have stated, "Speaking as
an individual he said the appeals have had
warm support, and he hoped the Government would be able to see their way to
save the gates. The Government would
be justified in doing so"; and whether the
Prime Minister would state whether a
Cabinet Minister is justified in expressing
views different from the declared considered view of the Government as
expressed in the House by the Minister of
Finance.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): My right hon. Friend the
Minister of Education, when speaking on
29th June, was aware that many appeals
had been made to the Government that
the Stormont entrance gates and flanking
railings should be preserved in view of
their artistic value, and gave expression
to his personal views on the matter. I
should explain that at that time the

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
Government had decided to review its
previous decision in regard to the gates,
and I am in communication with the
Minister of Supply on the subject.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
Minister of
of Education, knowing the
statement made in this House by the
Minister of Finance, got up at a private
meeting and made a personal statement
contrary to the statement made by his
colleague in this House, and as regards

knew it was under review at that time,
would it not have been correct, and proper

to have kept his mouth shut until the
Minister of Finance would have an opportunity in this House of reviewing, as he
has done, what he has already stated? Is
the Prime Minister aware that this is the
second time the Minister of Education
has done something like this? Is he
aware that on a previous occasion, when
the noble Lord was Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Education went
down to Bangor and advised the people
not to grow barley, although the noble
Lord was calling on them to grow barley,
and is it not time to put your foot on him,

Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the Prime

public statements by Ministers, is the
Cabinet already divided against itself?
Mr. BROWN: In view of the fact that
the Cabinet are unable to reach a decision,
may I ask the Prime Minister is he prepared to convene a meeting of this House
and put this matter to a vote of Members
and let Members make up the Cabinet's
mind for them?
Mr. MINFORD: May I suggest that
the loyal people of Ulster are prepared to
give ten times the amount to save Stormont gates?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
whole position is this. We are naturally
anxious to preserve the gates, but if, on
the other hand, these gates are wanted for
war purposes, then I think the war must
come first. We will take every step we
can to preserve the gates.
Mr. NIXON: Does the Prime Minister
want to preserve two Ministers who were
sacked, as well as the gates?
Mr. MINFORD: Is the Prime Minister
agreed that if he gets ten times the amount
of metal, or more, it would save the
gates?
The PRIME MINISTER: The point is
that if we get ten or twelve times the
amount of metal, and more metal is required, the gates will have to go. We
will do everything possible to save them.
War Damage Repairs.

made by a man named Moorhead in relation to war damage repairs.
The ATTORNEY - GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): As the police investigation
of this and other related matters has not
been finally concluded, no directions as to
legal proceedings have as yet been given.
Attorney-General's Instructions to
Prosecute.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether instructions issued by
him to prosecute certain persons in Northern Ireland have in all cases been
carried out.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: So far
as I am aware, my directions to prosecute
have been carried out in all cases in which
it has been possible to bring the persons
concerned before the Courts of this jurisdiction.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Attorney's statement that so far as he is
aware that in all cases where it has been
possible his instructions have been carried
out, does the Attorney demand a report
from the Inspector-General that his instructions are carried out, and is he quite
sure that the Inspector-General has sufficient respect for the Attorney-General's
authority to honour it if he thinks otherwise and can get out of it?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: My experience leads me to only one conclusion
on this matter, and that is that my directions are obeyed meticulously by the
police.
Recruiting in Northern Ireland.
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister if he can state whether it is a
fact that, as lately stated by the hon. and

gallant Member for East Down, the

42,188 persons have been placed in

Mr. NIXON: Yes. The point of
order is, I have put down a question to
the Prime Minister on the subject of
electoral reform in Northern Ireland.

reply was favourable or otherwise, both
myself and the people I represent would
have more confidence in it.
Mr. SPEAKER: So far as the point
of order is concerned, the Cabinet are, of
course, virtually in order in arranging
amongst themselves the most suitable
Member to answer any question. Beyond that I have no authority to go.
Mr. NIXON: I thank you for your

Minister, and if he is not prepared to

I do not wish any answer to be given to it.

to the ex-Minister of Agriculture and to

who were instrumental in having them
erected.

Transport.
APPEAL TRIBUNAL.
20. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
precise steps to be taken by a person or
body of persons in initiating and prosecuting an appeal under the appeal procedure
provided for in the Rail and Road Transport Act of 1935; and whether he can
state the names and remuneration of this
Appeals Tribunal, and the number of
times it has sat since the passing of the
Act that brought it into existence.
Mr. LOWRY: All applications for submission to the Transport Appeal Tribunal
must be made in the first instance to my
Ministry. The rules governing the procedure for the presentation and hearing of
appeals have been made by the tribunal
and may be obtained from the Stationery
Office, price one shilling.
The period for which the first members
of the tribunal were appointed has now
lapsed, and it has not since proved necessary to reconstitute it.
Only one formal meeting of the tribunal
has taken place.
LUNCH-TIME TRANSPORT
FACILITIES.
21. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has made
representations to the Northern Ireland
Road Transport Board regarding the
withdrawal of lunch-time travelling facilities; and whether he is in a position to
make a statement on the situation.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been in consultation with the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board, and in response to my
representations the Board have agreed
that monthly tickets shall continue to be
available for a second double journey at
mid-day, so as to enable people who have
been in the habit of returning home for
lunch to continue to do so.
In order to enable this object to be
attained, the second inward journey must
commence not later than 3-30 p.m. It
will not be possible to allow any variation
from this rule.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to
thank the Minister for the consideration
he gave to this matter, and to thank him
also for the satisfactory decision he has
announced.

Mr. MINFORD: One of the questions
put to the Prime Minister to-day was in
regard to the scrapping of the Stormont
gates. I feel that the loyalists of Ulster
look upon these gates as something very,
very dear to them, and I feel that the
loyalists of Ulster would sacrifice tenfold
more to save these gates, If he will let
me know the entire weight of these gates,
I, as one Member of this House, will give
him a guarantee to gather him ten times
as much scrap from the countryside to
save the gates. I do not want to labour
this question, but I say that these gates
should be taken only as a last resort, and
I hope the Prime Minister will see to it
that these should be the last gates to be
sacrificed to provide raw materials for the
making of munitions for our Fighting
Services. I know quite well there is
nothing too big or too good that we would
not sacrifice in this war for final victory.
We are all out to win the war, no matter
what sacrifice is demanded from us, but
I think the time has not arrived when we
should scrap the gates of Stormont for
munitions, for I believe that lying around
the country are hundreds of tons of scrap
which we could well afford to give for
munitions.
The second question I wish to raise
affects the farmers of Ulster, and it is in
regard to grass-seed. To-day business
men all over Ulster have been asked by
the grass-seed dealers to use the 1942 seed.
I recall the history of the 1942 crop, and
I am sure the hon. and noble Lord will
know exactly what the position is there.
We all know there were 6,500 tons of surplus seed, which was sold at £35 per ton,
irrespective of its quality. To-day I
understand that the Minister of Agriculture is taking over the seed cleaning mills
of the seed men of Ulster, and it is rather
strange to me, speaking as a farmer and
as one who has grown grass-seed, that the
Minister should be trying to put on the
market in 1944 the seed of 1942, when the
Ministry to-day have forbidden the
farmers of Ulster to save any more than
3-5ths of the crop which they are now
growing.
I am quite sure the Minister will bear
with me when I say there is no sane person
in Northern Ireland who would put in
1942 seed of poor germination and purity
when you have in your hand the whole
total of the 1943 crop. I feel it is very
wrong for the Ministry to be a party to
asking these cleaners to put upon the
market the 1942 seed. I remember prior
to the war when the Minister of Agriculture issued an Order prohibiting the
use of old seed by the farmers, and surely
this is a very narrow-minded policy when
the Minister to-day, in order to save a
loss on the 1942 crop, is advising the
farmers to sow the 1942 seed, and let
the Minister of Agriculture stand up to
the Ministry of Finance over the value of
the 6,500 tons of seed which cost £35 per
ton, and which was really only value for
£10 per ton. I think it is wrong to ask
the farmers to use 1942 seed which is discarded by the merchants of Ulster.
Let us in this House make up our minds
to face this loss on the 1942 seed, and
scrap it and give it for feeding, and let
the 1943 seed be used in 1944. I am
surprised such a proposal is made in this
House, and I want the Minister to make
a clear statement on the question. I had
to cut down 15 acres of the best mixed
seed, because I was not allowed to save the
seed, as I was not a seller on the market
last year. We are all out to win the war,
and I believe the farmers will play a very
important part, but I think it is definitely
wrong for the Minister to be a party to
trying to bolster up 1942 poor seed for
sowing in 1944, when you have got a 1943
crop, which is certainly a much better
crop and of greater germination than was
ever grown in Ulster before.
So much
for grass seed.
Let us take the potato question. In
the Ballymoney district there is a factory
into which are being sent stock seed
1387 Grass-seed and Early Potatoes
Fire Watchers and Holidays 1388
8 JULY 1943
potatoes at £15 a ton. This is a perfect
scandal. We know the percentage of meal
from new potatoes in July is not great,
and I know to-day that hundreds, yea
thousands of farmers in Ulster would be
willing to give £11 per ton for these
potatoes for stock seed. Yet they are
given to a potato factory, and their value
is equivalent to only £1 per ton for meal
purposes. If we in Northern Ireland are
in earnest to help the war effort, why
should we leave the farmers with the 1942
crop which cannot be marketed, and
allow it to go for £15 a ton? You can
consume every new potato in Northern
Ireland if you give the farmer a decent
price. To-day the price is 3s 6d per stone,
or 28s per cwt. Why should the Government not come along and meet their loss?
Why not do it to-day? Fifteen pounds
per ton for the food which the farmer
grows can only realise £1 per ton in feeding meal. I think it is a perfect scandal,
and I am speaking now for the farmers of
Ulster.
I think the time has come when we
should have practical common sense in the
Ministry. I am not blaming the Minister
because he has only recently assumed
office. I can prove to the Minister that
in the Ballymoney area scores of tons of
potatoes are going for food at £15 per
ton, and farmers are willing to pay £11
for them for seed. I am surprised that
these potatoes were stock seed, which were
most valuable as a seed in Ulster to-day.
I think the Minister made a mistake in
giving far too high a price for early
potatoes, and I think the sooner he
realises it the better. Why should a man
in Co. Antrim, or Co. Derry, or Co.
Armagh for that matter, be obliged to go
into the market and take £4 per ton for
old potatoes.
Potatoes are one of the
most important foods which we grow in
Ulster. I think the time has come when
the Minister should realise the importance
of stock seed potatoes and give them to
the farmers. I can give this guarantee;
that all the stock seed in Ulster could be
used and could be sold at £11 per ton,
but what does the Minister do? He puts
it into a factory, which, in my opinion,
makes it worth only £1 per ton for meal
purposes for a few paltry animals.
I think it is wrong, and I raise this
question because we are adjourning until
20th July, and it will be too late then to
save the situation. Let the farmers hold
the potatoes, and let the Minister get in
touch with the farmers. Only two weeks
ago I was surprised to hear in this House
that skimmed milk was being thrown
down the drain by the thousands of
gallons. I was amazed, because I as one
farmer would have been glad to take 300
gallons of skimmed milk at 13d a gallon,
if I could have got it. Yet the stuff is
wasted. I say it is up to the Ministry
and the farmer to save every available
ounce of food to win the war. I do not
blame the Minister, but there is something wrong when the farmers are being
asked, in fact are being compelled to put
in 1942 perennial seed into the land in
1944 when there is a sufficient crop of
1943 seed to meet every possible need.
Further, he has stopped any of the 1943
seed being sold; in other words, he is
going to allow a waste of 2-5ths of the
seed, which, in my opinion, is most vital
to the needs of the farmers of Ulster.
I hope the Minister will make a statement
to the House on this vital matter, because
it is wrong to waste such valuable food
and seed when the country demands the
very best.

Mr. GRANT: I should like to reply to
the question put by the hon. Member for
Woodvale. I have not a great deal of
information to give him, because the time
at my disposal was rather short.
general position is that, outside agriculture and the industries governed by Trade
Board Regulations, there is no statutory
provision for compelling employers to
make provision for holidays with pay for
their employees. A number of voluntary
schemes based on industrial agreements
are, however, in operation, and under the
Holidays with Pay Act (Northern Ireland)
1938, the Minister of Labour has power to
assist in the administration of such
schemes on the joint application of the
parties. If the hon. Member will furnish
me with particulars of the employers he
has in mind I will make inquiries as to
whether the workers concerned come
within the scope of holiday provisions or
agreements.
Lord GLENTORAN: I just want to
say a word about grass-seed, which is a
question of considerable importance to
farmers at the present time. I listened
with interest to the remarks of the hon.
Member for Antrim, who is greatly interested in this matter. In no way is the
1389 Grass-seed and Early Potatoes HOUSE OF COMMONS
Grass-seed and Early Potatoes 1390
[Lord Glentoran]
Ministry of Agriculture to blame for the
present position, because we must remember that we in Ulster are growers of
grassseed not only for the British Isles but for
the world. We cannot take one-tenth, or
even one-twentieth part of the grass-seed
we ourselves grow and, as I know from my
own experience, the Ministry have got to
conform to what is agreed to in Great
Britain. Last season we had 9,000 tons
of seed surplus to all requirements all over
the world. The result is that we have got
this 9,000 tons of seed on our hands, and
one of the greatest difficulties the Ministry
have to deal with is to get rid of as much
of this 9,000 tons as they can. The Ministry, in conjunction with the Ministry of
Food, have made considerable progress in
that respect by putting into feeding stuffs
a large quantity of this seed which is not
fit for germination.
Before I left the Ministry of Agriculture I put forward another suggestion
which I was very anxious to see carried
out, and it is this. There is a large
quantity of this, what might be called
third-class seed, which we want out of the
way altogether. It is a well-known fact
that for improving old grassland, or grass
that has been eaten down by dairy cows
year after year, there is nothing better
than harrowing it and sowing it with fresh
seed. It has been proved again and again
that the sowing of grassland with seed is
more beneficial than treating the soil with
nitrate or other manures. Therefore, the
problem the Ministry have had to face is,
could they use this old seed and underpercentage seed for ploughed up grassland.
There is a difficulty about that, because
there was a law passed some years ago
which did not permit seedsmen to put on
the market seed of lower than 80 per cent.
germination. Therefore, there is a great
difficulty in getting rid of this seed in this
way.
I did make the proposal, and I think it
is still under consideration by my late
Ministry that this seed that was not up
to 80 per cent. germination should be
classed as sweepings. For very many
years in England they have been selling
sweepings with which they have been
carrying out experiments on the Welsh
hills, where grass has been ploughed up
and rejuvenated. I hope it will be possible, by negotiation with the British
Government, to allow this low-class
germination seed to be sold as sweepings,
and let our farmers have it at a very
reasonable price. By that means I think
we could get rid of this old seed which is
not up to the standard quality. If that
could be done it would be a great help to
our farmers in Ulster. Furthermore, it
would greatly help the new sowing of grass
all over the world, because then they
would get new and proper seed for the
following year.
I should again like to make it perfectly
clear that in no way am I criticising the
present Minister of Agriculture. I know
he is making every effort to carry out the
policy about which I have been speaking.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: There is not
much need for me to say anything, after
what the noble Lord has said about grassseed. The hon. Member for Antrim, Í
think, was rather confused in his reference
to surplus seed. He talked about 6,500
tons that had been bought at a certain
figure, and that was probably correct.
There was a very considerable amount of
seed which was of very low germination
and was cleared right off the market, but
that is not the only surplus the trade has
got to deal with. That low grade seed
will not come on to the market as sowing
seed at all, and I can assure hon. Members and the farmers that things will be
so arranged that no seed of whatever
year's growth will be offered to the
farmers for sowing unless it gives a certain
percentage of germination and also of
purity. Nevertheless, I think the Member
for Antrim has got rather mixed up about
that low grade seed that had deteriorated
because of the hold-up in the market.
The Ministry of Agriculture, acting for
the Ministry of Supply on the other side,
and with the consent of the British Exchequer, stepped in and simply wiped that
off the slate. But that has left a certain
amount of seed which was surplus to sowing requirements, a surplus of seed of
good germination, and I am not going to
say that no 1942 seed of proper germination and purity will not be used for sowing in the 1944 season. What I do say
is that there will be no seed offered unless
it is up to the proper standard both of
purity and germination, and I think that
is really all the farmer as a rule wants.
In regard to the point about early
potatoes, I do not know that I can use-

Mr. SPEAKER: We cannot have two
Members of this House on the Floor at the
same time. There can only be one. I do
not mind which.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I am sorry.
Mr. NIXON: If the right hon. Gentleman rose on a point of order, you would
ask me to sit down, and I would do so.
If I thought the Minister was going to
make a useful statement I would sit down,
but no Minister, not even a minister of
religion, could make the statement the
right hon. Gentleman has made feasible.
I myself saw rotting field after field of
oats that the farmer had been compelled
to put in. I happen to know some of, the
farmers, and the last thing in the world
that the men I know would do is to let
their crops rot if they could get help to
save them.
Now, my object in referring to the past
is to utter a warning for the future. That
is really all that history is good for. Crops
will not be saved by holding meetings,
putting photographs in the newspaper,
and making speeches; crops will not be
saved by dressing up land girls and giving
them bits of lip-stick. Crops will only
be saved by having workers and transport to put them into the fields when
the crops are ready. I am now talking
about transport, and in this connection I
will give the Minister a hint which I
would have given him yesterday had I been
able to get to the meeting I referred to.
He could get any amount of voluntary
transport. By that, I mean that there
are plenty of people who have motor-cars
-I am not making this an excuse for
getting petrol for people who are not
entitled to it; I would not do that-and
they would be quite willing to bring a
load of voluntary workers for a day to
any place within ten, twenty, thirty, or
forty miles from Belfast. If the Minister
had the workers I believe he would get
any amount of volunteers to do that. The
man who would go with the car might not
be doing much else. I know some of
these people myself and could get him a
few cars. As I say, I do not want anybody to twist what I have said so as to
make it appear that I am trying to get
petrol that would not otherwise be released. I do not want that. Petrol must
be saved for the war. I hope the Minister
will consider this suggestion.

of considerable importance. I brought a

to see the Minister of Agriculture regarding the very serious position that exist"
in Mourne in regard to the muddle over

20 JULY 1943
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 20th July, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Papers Presented.
Ministry of Home Affairs:
Annual Report of the Government
Inspectors of Explosives for Northern
Ireland for the year 1942. (By Act.)
Ministry of Agriculture:
Sheep Dipping (Special Regulation)
(Northern Ireland) Order, 1943. (By
Act.)
Death of Mr. James F. Gamble, M.P.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to announce to
the House with the greatest regret the
death of Mr. James F. Gamble, Member
for North Tyrone. Mr. Gamble had been
a Member for many years and was very
highly respected in all quarters of the
House. We shall miss him very much.
Unfortunately a few days later Mrs.
Gamble died also, and, in view of this
fact, I think the House would wish to join
with me in a very special message of
sympathy to the family which has been
bereaved twice within such a short period.
ORAL ANSWER TO QUESTION.
Select Committee on Health Services.
Mr. STEVENSON asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government has considered the Interim Report of the Select
Committee on Health Services presented
to the House on Tuesday, the 6th July,
and, if so, can he state what action the
Government proposes to take in the
matter.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): Yes, Sir. The Government is
indebted to the Select Committee for the
promptness with which the Interim
Report has been presented to the House,
and is prepared to recommend
to
voluntary and rate-aided hospitals the
adoption of the scales of salary for

Pensions and Determination of Needs
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
. Grant): This is a Bill which it is a pleasure to introduce. I am sure that it will
commend itself to the House and that it
will be welcomed in many homes. It adds
to the classes of persons eligible for supplementary pension by including widow
pensioners with young children, and it
meets I submit reasonably-the objections which have been made that the
thrifty are penalised under the rules.
governing the schemes of unemployment
assistance, supplementary pensions and
financial assistance for the blind.
The present law restricts supplementation to old age pensioners, that is to say,
over the age of 65 or women (including widows) over the age of 60.
men
Pensions Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
Other classes are, however, admittedly in
need, and the only provision which exists
for their assistance is the poor law. It
has been decided that, pending the introduction of the Beveridge scheme, the
widow with children shall get priority of
treatment, and the Bill which I am introducing proposes that, if a widow is in
receipt of a contributory pension which
includes an allowance for children, she
shall become eligible for a supplementary
pension.
Allowances by way of addition to a
widow's pension are payable for children
under the age of 14, or between the ages
of 14 and 16 if under full time instruction
in a day school. If the child remains at
school, the allowance may continue up to
the 31st July following the 16th birthday.
There will, accordingly, come a time when
a widow with children will cease to be
eligible to draw additional allowances in
respect of them as part of her widow's
pension. But if she is, at that date, in
receipt of a supplementary pension there
will be no question of her becoming ineligible for further supplementation unless
she either ceases to be entitled to her
basic pension (for example, on remarriage) or her other resources reach the
point at which they are sufficient to meet
her needs in accordance with the scale.
There are in Northern Ireland about
4,000 widows with dependent children in
receipt of widows' pensions, and I expect
that the great majority of them will
qualify for a supplementary pension if
this Bill goes through-as I feel quite
sure it will. By the following example
hon. Members can judge for themselves
how the proposals will operate. A widow
with three children aged 13, 11 and 9,
and paying a normal rent, receives at
present a pension of 21s a week under the
contributory scheme. That is a pension
for which her husband had paid contributions, and, when we compare the position with that obtaining before the
introduction of the contributory pensions
scheme in 1926, we can realise what a
difference the assurance of having even
that 21s a week must make to the woman
bereft of her partner by the great
calamity of life.
How great the difference is can be
measured by the desire of the uninsured
to come into the scheme. In 1938 when
the voluntary pensions scheme was made
available in Northern Ireland to uninsured persons of moderate income, 18,000
availed themselves of it. It is undoubtedly a relief to a prudent and thoughtful
man to know that he has made provision
for his wife and children in the event of
his death. But 21s a week will not keep
a woman and three children, and, if she.
has no other resources, she may have to
have recourse, under the present law, to
the board of guardians. Under the proposals which I am putting before the
House the Assistance Board will, however, grant her in future a supplementary
pension if her resources are not sufficient
to meet her needs and the needs of her
dependants, as assessed in accordance with
the scale.
Let us suppose that she has no means
except her pension of 21s, and that she
is living in her own house with three
children. The Board may, in the circumstances, be able to regard her needs as
being about 40s a week. They may,
therefore, grant her a supplementary
pension of about 19s a week. The exact
figure will depend on the facts and circumstances.
The Bill also proposes to modify the
provisions governing the treatment of
capital assets for the purposes of supplementary pension, unemployment assistance and financial assistance to blind
persons.
May I remind the House that the 55,600
persons who are drawing old-age pensions
at present under the contributory scheme
receive those pensions without a means
test of any kind. It is true that the
additional 28,300 persons who are receiving non-contributory old-age pensions are
subject to a means test, but it is possible
for a married couple to have substantial
savings and still receive the full basid
non-contributory pension of 10s a week
each. The possession of capital assets
cannot, however, be treated so generously
in the case of supplementary pensions.
When the point is reached at which the
community as a whole is called on to
grant additional assistance to the pensioner for the House will remember that
the supplementary pension is paid entirely
by the Exchequer it is reasonable to
require the pensioner, in the first place,
to draw on his own capital if it is substantial. Therefore, under the existing
law, a person with more than £300 in
Pensions Bill-'
Second Reading
20 JULY 1943
savings has been required to draw on the
capital in excess of that figure before he
can become eligible for supplementation.
In calculating the capital no account,
however, is taken of money up to a total
of £375 lent to the nation during wartime and invested in war savings.
To meet the complaint that thrift is
unduly penalised it is proposed to raise
the limit at which a person becomes disentitled for supplementary pension from
£300 to £400, and at the same time to
introduce a more lenient scale of assessment. As mentioned in the explanatory
memorandum which has been circulated,
a person with £275 reckonable capital
may thus receive up to 5s a week more
in assistance or supplementary pension
under the new proposals than under the
present law. At the same time the law
relating to the treatment of superannuation payments is being modified in its
bearing on supplementary pensions.
In future, the first 10s 6d a week of
any such payment will be left out of
account instead of 7s 6d only as at present, provided that where a person has
more than one superannuation payment,
only 10s 6d a week in all will be disregarded. The extent of this concession can
be judged when I mention that a superannuation payment may be made by the
late employer or by a trade union, or
from some fund connected with the
employment.
Taking, for example, the case of a man
whose superannuation pay consists of 10s
a week from his trade union, the effect of
the change will be that he may, if he is
in need, receive up to 2s 6d a week more
in supplementary pension than under the
present law. A married man and his
wife, who are both in receipt of a contributory pension, and who have no other
resources than 10s superannuation pay
from his trade union, are entitled at present to 14s 6d a week in supplementary
pension. In future they will be entitled
to 17s, making their total resources 47s a
week. The extension of the Supplementary Pensions Scheme to cover widows
with children will provide a substantial
relief to the rates. This is one more of
the many steps which have been taken to
transfer to the State charges which
formerly were met by the Board of
Guardians.
May I remind the House that in 1908
the Old Age Pensions Scheme at age 70
was introduced; in 1926 the Contributory
Pensions Scheme was introduced; and
1934 the Unemployment Assistance
Scheme; and in 1940 the Supplementary
Pensions Scheme. As a result of these
measures the position to-day is that
90,000 old persons in Northern Ireland
have been removed entirely from the outdoor relief provisions of the poor law.

Now, under this Bill the further step
will be taken of providing some 4,000
widows with children with such supplementary pension as they may require,
having regard to their needs and
sources, and they too will be debarred
from receiving outdoor relief by an express provision in the first schedule.
There is a natural consequence to this
provision. A supplementary pension is
the sum adjudged necessary to maintain
the pensioner and his or her dependants,
having regard to the other resources, if
any, and it does not include a margin for
the maintenance of any person in the
household who is not a dependant of the
pensioner.
If, therefore, such a person is destitute
and outside the scope of the scheme of
State assistance, the boards of guardians
will still have the duty of relieving him,
and they may not reduce or refuse the
grant of outdoor relief to him on the
ground that a member of the same household is receiving unemployment assistance,
supplementary pension or financial assistance under the Blind Persons Acts.
money which the State has granted to
