The
The Bill has two provisions in regard
to blind persons. Under the present law
financial assistance granted by a council
to a blind person must be treated as means
for old-age pension purposes, and any
increase in the council's grant may,
therefore, in certain cases, result in a
corresponding decrease in the amount of
State pension. In other words, in such
cases the Exchequer benefits at the expense
of the rates and the blind person is no
better off. That is a position which I
would not attempt to defend, and in
Clause 4 (Section 1), it is proposed that
financial assistance by a council will no
longer be taken into account under the
Old Age Pensions Act.
Pensions Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
The Bill also proposes to apply the
principles of the Determination of Needs
Act to the provision of financial assistance to the blind by a council, but it
reserves certain matters for the discretion
of the council. Amongst other points in
the Bill is one providing that residence
in the Isle of Man shall be treated for
non-contributory old-age pension purposes as though it had been residence in
the United Kingdom. The provision will
be on a reciprocal basis and will come
into operation on a date to be agreed with
the Isle of Man authorities.
It is very desirable that the main provisions of the Bill should come into operation in Northern Ireland on the same
date as the corresponding provisions in
Great Britain. I expect that this will
be in the early autumn, and, as it will be
necessary to allow several weeks for the
receipt and examination of claims from
widows, I ask the co-operation of the
House in passing the Bill through its
various stages this week. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

an example of it in this Bill.

children would be taken from their
mother and put into a home or some other
institution. That was one of the tragedies
of the working-class people of those days.
I am glad to say that we were able to get
widows' pensions, not very adequate, but
sufficient to enable a widow to keep her
home together. Gradually these pensions.
for widows have been increased, and this
Bill takes them a step further.
Legislation of this kind is entirely
different from that advocated in speeches
we were hearing two or three months ago,
when the new world was depicted as a
place where no one would have any responsibility towards those amongst whom
he lived or even for the members of his
own family. A man who was born in
that perfect world lived on the dole from
the day he was born until the day he died.
The workers in East Belfast whom I represent do not want a world of that sort.
They want good work and decent wages,
and that is all they ask for. I believe
that legislation of this kind is a good
thing not only for the people we
legislating for but for the State itself,
because it has been proved, and we must
all admit, that children who are reared
in institutions are never as successful as
children who are reared in their own
are
homes by their own parents. Therefore,
I welcome this Bill most heartily on behalf of those who I represent in this
House.
I am very glad that in this measure we
are giving assistance to another type of
industrial worker, the blind, and here
again we are lending assistance in the
right direction. I thoroughly agree with
the statement of the Member for Woodvale that the blind are a class of people
for whom the State should do all it
possibly can. By that I do not mean that
they should be classed as a people apart.
We should recognise that a blind man is
in the same category as a person who has
lost a leg or an arm or some other
faculty, as a result of which he is handicapped in his work. I think it is wiser
that the State should try to make
that
handicap so that by doing a little work
the blind person is able to earn as much
as the man who has his sight. For these
reasons I believe this is a good Bill. It
is not by any means class legislation, and
1 hope every Member of this House will
see his way to support it and thus give
relief and happiness to the people whom
it is intended to benefit.

most heartily the Minister of Labour on
bringing forward this Bill, and on the
very able and clear manner in which he
presented it to this House. I welcome it
I

most cordially, because it covers issues
and matters I have repeatedly urged in
this House from time to time. The only

does not go far enough. As the noble
Lord has pointed out, it is quite wrong
to libel the workers of Ulster by suggesting that they do not want work and
that they would rather be living on the
State. The working classes want work
and they want fair wages for that work,
and as the noble Lord, who represents in
this House a large and most important
industrial constituency, has indicated, it
would be a particularly black and
villainous lie for anyone to suggest that
the working classes of this country are
idlers and desire only State support. We
have nearly 20,000 unemployed to-day in
the fourth year of total war. They want
work and they have the right to get work,
and they have also the right to such protection as is provided in this Bill. As I
have said, my great regret is that the Bill
does not go far enough. Undoubtedly
there has been extreme hardship in the
case of these widows' pensions.
I have
had complaints made to me day and daily,
year in and year out, about extreme
hardship. I am glad that something is
being done to alter the position, and I
would ask the Government to go on with
the good work and do something more,
because this Bill will not entirely meet
the situation which exists to-day.
There is another point for which I am
sorry no provision has been made in this
Bill, and that is the alleviation of the lot
of old age pensioners who find themselves
domiciled in charitable institutions.
There you have a case of very real and
very genuine hardship.
These old age
pensioners in charitable institutions are
denied any supplementary pensions
whatsoever. The people running these
institutions are dependent on support through public subscriptions
to keep these places going, but there are
so many war claims made on the public
to-day that the people who run these
institutions find it increasingly difficult
to raise the money they need by public
subscriptions. Consequently the old-age
pensioners in these institutions, who are
deprived of any supplementary pensions,
are suffering the greatest possible hardship. I suggest it is up to the Government to take their case into consideration,
and, although they can make no provision
for them in this Bill, let them bring in
a further Bill to remove this anomaly as
anomaly it undoubtedly is. A sum of
10s per week could not possibly maintain
these pensioners in these institutions, and
certainly a very great measure of hardship has fallen upon them by reason of
the fact they cannot claim any supplementary pensions. I am perfectly satisfied
that no man in this House has a keener or
more active knowledge and sympathy
with the poor than the Minister of Labour.
I know he is generally interested in the
welfare of the working classes, and I
would appeal to him very strongly to take

pensioners in institutions, because certainly there is a strong case for their being
brought within the operation of the Act
which authorises the payment of supplementary pensions. I welcome most strongly
this Bill, while regretting that it does not
go far enough, but I think it is a step
along the road to still greater social progress and social security.

Mr. NIXON: I want to bring up a

turn to go in and get their assistance.
The majority of them were very delicate
people and some were hardly able to
stand. All I want, and I do not think

arrangement by which they would be
sheltered from the weather and would be
able to sit down. It was all right last
Tuesday, and it is all right to-day, but we
are quickly coming to a time when they
might lose their lives. I do not know why

party. At all events, what I have said
will appear in Hansard. It is not the

he is not present. I did my best to get in
touch with Mr. Wellwood but did not
succeed. That was after I had discovered
that I had made a mistake.
At this stage the Minister of Home
Affairs re-entered the House.
Mr. NIXON: With Mr. Speaker's permission I will repeat what I have said.
This is a matter in regard to which I gave
notice to the Minister of Labour. That

concerned. There is nothing controversial
in what I am about to say. I tried to get
into touch with the Minister of Home

It is in regard to people going to draw

The PRIME MINISTER: If
memory serves me right when this Parliament was started the late Lord Craigavon
suggested that as a general principle the
rules and customs of the British House of
Commons should be followed by this
House. I understand that it is not the
custom when there is no business on the
Order Paper for the House to continue
sitting, and I should be the last person to
break a precedent which has existed down
through the ages. Although I sympathise
with the hon. Members who wish to raise
these points they are of extreme interest
-yet at the same time I think it would
be a great mistake to start something new
which would mean that this House would
become, in fact, a debating chamber, and
would sit when there was no business to
come before it. That being so, I suggest
to the hon. Gentlemen who wish to discuss
these matters that there is still considerable time left this afternoon, and there
may be considerable time on Thursday,
when the matters in which they are interested could be raised and discussed.

1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of

to make a statement as to the use
for harvesting purposes of agricultural
vehicles taxed at the lower rate of duty.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair) In reply to my hon. Friend, I
would point out that under the existing
law governing motor taxation a farmer
can get a licence for his lorry at a reduced
rate provided that he uses it only for his
own individual purposes. The extent of
the reduction is substantial, being represented, in relation (say) to a four-ton
lorry, by an £18 tax as compared with a
£50 tax for vehicles used for ordinary
commercial haulage work. To qualify
for this concession the agricultural vehicle
must be registered in the name of a
farmer and must be used solely by him in
connection with his own land. He is
allowed, however, without becoming liable
to the higher rate of tax, to carry
occasionally for some other farmer provided that the amount so carried is small
in relation to the total load and that he
does not carry for hire or reward.
I am glad to be able to announce today the introduction of a new concession
whereby liability to the higher rate of tax
will not arise solely by reason of the use
of agricultural vehicles on behalf of
neighbouring farmers in what I may describe as purely harvesting activities,
whether or not the owner himself gives
the service to a neighbouring farmer or
merely lends his vehicle. That is, for
purely harvesting purposes the limitation
to an occasional and partial user of an
agricultural vehicle and the prohibition
against taking payment therefor will no
longer apply.
I must make it clear, however, that if,
apart from this concession, any question
of hire or reward arises, the restrictions
laid down by the Road Transport Act of
1935 come into play, though, having regard to sub-section 5 of Section 15 of that
Act, these restrictions will not, in my
opinion, take away from the value of the
new taxation concession now to become
operative.
I should add that this new taxation
concession is intended to cover the
harvesting of crops of all kinds (including
flax).
As the matter is one affecting taxation
it will be necessary to seek the formal
sanction of Parliament in due course, but,
in the meantime, as a matter of urgency,
I propose, with the approval of the House,
pending formal submission for retrospective sanction in a Finance Bill to be
introduced later in the Session, to operate
the concession forthwith, that is, from
to-day's date, and to provide for it remaining in operation until November 30th
next.

Mr. LOWRY: I have made enquiries

District Council refused to accept the
tender of Mr. F. Connolly for the removal
of domestic refuse.
Eight tenders for the work were received by the council and the second

Mr. BROWN: I rise to resist this
Motion. If I am asked for a precedent
I will point to the action of the world's
greatest statesman, Mr. Winston Churchill,
who in the British House of Commons on
the 6th of October, 1938, when it was
proposed to adjourn the House, which was
then under the leadership of Mr. Neville
Chamberlain, registered a most emphatic
protest. If his protest had been heeded
many of the things which have happened
in the world since that time would have
been prevented. On that ocasion Mr.
Churchill-he was shouted down and
voted down, as no doubt I will be to-day
if I insist in my objection to this Motion,
but I am in good company-said that the
House should not be adjourned in times
of great crisis. After appealing to the
Government to allow the House to meet a
few days later Mr. Churchill said:
--
After all, we are passing through a
period of very rapid daily change in
Europe of the most serious character,
and it does not seem quite right that
Parliament should go away for 25 days
as if nothing was going on and we had
lost all interest in matters which affect
the whole future of this country.
It is now proposed to adjourn not for
25 days but for two months, and that at
a time when the country is passing
through a critical period in its history.
I say it is wrong. Mr. Churchill was
supported by Mr. Attlee, the then leader
of the Opposition. In addition to all this
the Member for Woodvale sent at that
time several telegrams to Mr. Chamberlain asking him for God's sake to resign.
I wish Mr. Chamberlain had resigned at
that time, because as a result of the House
being adjourned, very serious matters
followed. Mr. Chamberlain sold the
people and betrayed their interests. It
was an unfortunate thing that he did not
act on the advice of the Member for
Woodvale. If this House adjourns now
for several months we will be leaving
things in a condition of flux. Mr.
Chamberlain, at the time I refer
to, said that Cabinet Ministers would
be glad to see the House disperse instead of having to face the House. I
suggest that the position is similar to-day
here. There are many problems cropping
up on which the Government cannot face
the House, and I will tell you why. Mr.
Harold Macmillan, who supported the
appeal not to adjourn, said he was aware
of the strain on Ministers, but he continuel:
In recent years there has grown up
a dangerous tendency to treat the House
more and more as a kind of Reichstag,
meeting only to hear the orations and
to register the decrees of the Government of the day.
Mr. Churchill felt so seriously about the
matter that he forced a division. Actually
at that time the Imperial House of Commons was discussing the giving of ten
million pounds to Crecho-Slovakia, a sum
which afterwards got into the hands of
Hitler. I stated then in this House that
when the British Government could spare
ten millions for Czecho-Slovakia, they
should at least spare a little to reduce the
land annuities of the farmers in Ulster.
That was not done, but ten millions went
to Czecho-Slovakia, and Hitler got it.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil

-is that it

-hon. Members will forgive me if I

We have been told, as I said before,
about saving petrol and about winning
the war. There is more in this business
about saving petrol than appears at first
sight. A man living not far away from
where I live has two motor lorries. He is
paying his tax and is paying his driver.
He is a loyal citizen, and is complying
with all the requirements of the law. He
wanted some cement, but petrol must be
saved. He would not be given petrol to
go to Belfast for the cement, but the
cement arrived by a petrol-driven lorry of
the Transport Board. Was that saving
petrol? Was petrol saved simply because
a Transport Board lorry and not a private
lorry was used? That is what happened.
The cement was delivered some 10 miles
from the nearest depot. The driver got
a signature for the cement, and then two
days after a Transport Board van arrived
with a man with the bill for the cartage
of the six tons of cement. The man paid
the bill, which he would have done had
the driver asked him for it when he came
with the cement. Then we are told that
they are conserving petrol, yet a man was
sent by the Transport Board a distance of
eight or 10 miles, a round journey of 16
or 20 miles, to collect this money. The man
could not get a unit of petrol to take him
to the market town to do his business, but
the Transport Board could send a vehicle
to collect £2 11s 3d for the conveyance of
the cement.
There is another thing that came to my

He has interests in County Down. He

and he approached the railway company.
The railway company said that they

The railway company, finding that the

to a station from which it would be taken

did not go to the railway and say,
"We

The type of goods a man sells in a
grocer's shop requires points. When a
merchant comes to Belfast he brings his
points with him. He goes to a business
house, but although he has the necessary
points he may find it impossible to get the
goods he wants from that particular house.
He tries a second, a third, a fourth, and
it may not be until he calls at the fifth
wholesaler that he is able to get the goods
he requires. In such a case it is imperative that a business man should have
his own lorry. If the present suggestion
is carried out business men will not be
allowed to use their lorries for the purpose
of coming to Belfast.
Another matter which is going to affect
business men is the question of empties.
That is not taken into account at all.
Hon. Members would be surprised if they
heard the amount charged on empties.
Wholesale merchants charge 17s 6d for a
case, and they are willing to allow you
that sum when you return it. Gallaher's
people charge 15s, but credit you with
17s 6d when you return the empty. When
the merchants' lorries came to Belfast
they were filled with empties, and then
on the return journey they had a full
load of goods. If you ask the Transport
Board to take empties from your business place they will ask you how they
arrived, and if you say they came by rail
they will tell you they cannot take them.
On the other hand, if you ask the railway company to take them they will ask
you the same question, and if you say
they arrived by Transport Board lorries
they will refuse to take them. Talk
about being between the devil and the
deep sea! That is the way business men
are being treated to-daly. They do not
know where they are, and they will not
know where they are if the Transport
Board get a monopoly. In that event
they will have to close down their businesses.
I stand for fair play all round. I even
stand for fair play for the Transport

Question put, and agreed to.
Prices for Farm Produce.
Mr. MINFORD: I beg to move, "That
in the opinion of this House the Government should make representations to the
Imperial Authorities with regard to the
prices given for some farm produce, such
as potatoes and barley, so as to ensure
that the Northern Ireland farmers receive
the same prices for these commodities as
the farmers in Great Britain, thereby encouraging greater production for the war
effort."
I do not wish to place any blame upon
this Government, because I understand
the prices are fixed by the Ministry of
Food in Great Britain. When we are in
the midst of the greatest war in history,
I say that the farmers in Ulster should
not be treated in a different manner from
the farmers in Great Britain. I understand that there are eight areas in England and Scotland, and that Northern
Ireland comes into one of them. Why
did farmers in Northern Ireland receive
only 65s per ton for their potatoes in
September, 1942, when the farmers in
Great Britain obtained £3 more per ton?
It may be argued that the Ministry had
to transport them to England. That is
a very shallow argument.
The Minister of Food bases the price
on the cost of production. We demand
the same treatment for the farmers here.
Under the Act, 120s was paid for No. I
grade, but in Northern Ireland 70s was
paid. That is a difference of £2 10s 0d
per ton.
The Minister has appealed for
350,000 tons additional crop in the
1943-44 season. How is he going to get
it? If he goes to his Department in
Elmwood Avenue and consults his chief
in charge of the permits for artificial
manures he will be alarmed at the small
number of applications for permits.
could give the Minister the names of
scores of farmers who will not grow
potatoes in the future.
I
The right hon. Gentleman is aware
that it costs from £35 to £37 per acre to
grow potatoes. If there is a yield of six
tons to the acre that means the price
per ton is £3 5s-the farmer gets £19 10s.
and when the grant of £10 is added he
receives £29 10s. He is really £5 or £6
out of pocket. That will not encourage
farmers to grow potatoes. We are part
and parcel of Great Britain, and on behalf of the farmers of Ulster I demand
that they be paid the same price as is
given to farmers across the water.
It has been stated that labour costs
more in England and Scotland than here.
I want to see the farm labourer here put
1475 Prices for Farm Produce

22 JULY 1943
Adjournment
on the same footing as the farm labourer
in Great Britain. If the farmers in
Ulster receive the same price for their
produce as the farmers in Great Britain,
they are quite prepared to pay their
workmen the same wages. Surely this
House is not going to say that the farm
worker in Northern Ireland should not
have the same standard of living as the
farm labourers in England and Scotland.
The Prime Minister should give the House
an undertaking that he will raise this
matter with the Ministry of Food. Some
acton must be taken in the matter in order
to ensure that sufficient crops will be
sown in Ulster next year.
This year early potatoes were grown in
enormous quantities. The prices given
for the second crop are so bad that the
majority of the farmers in County Down
and County Antrim went in for the early
varieties. Thousands of tons have been
sent to the potato factories. Farmers who
grew the second early variety last season
were compelled by the Ministry of Food to
hold them for six months. That meant that
at 30th June the 1942 crop could not be
got rid of at £5 10s per ton, because this
season's crop was then being marketed.
The farmers here should get the same
price as is paid to the farmers in England and Scotland. If the Prime Minister
makes strong representations to the
Minister of Food I feel confident something will be done. We get the same
prices for our cattle, sheep, lambs, butter,
eggs, oats and wheat.
What happened last year? The Minister
of Agriculture, at that time the noble
Lord-barley was being sold here at 22s
per cwt. while the price in England was
33s-made representations to the Minister
of Food, and inside a month instructions
were given to the buyers in Belfast to pay
27s per cwt. for barley. The Ministerhe is the agent for the Ministry of Food
-should approach the authorities in
Great Britain and ask them to see to it
that the Ulster farmer is paid a price
which will cover the cost of producing it.
I know the right hon. Gentleman will get
up and say as he said before, Why do
the farmers grow such an uneconomic
crop?" They have to do it or else be
evicted. They have to till so much land;
if they do not do so they are fined and
evicted.

It is not right to compel the loyal people
of Ulster to grow a crop and then not
pay the same price for it as is paid to the
people in England and Scotland. Ulstermen should have the same standard of
living as Englishmen. I appeal to the
Minister to get the farmers a proper price
for their crops.
I notice the House is preparing for a
count. It is terribly mean to do such a
thing. If the Government do not want
to mete out justice to the farmers let them
say so. The Minister is slipping out.
Is
that the way to conduct this Parliament?
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: The
Minister is only consulting one of his
officials, and it is not right to make a
charge against him.
Mr. MINFORD: I am not sleeping.
If this House does not want to do justice
to the farmers let them say so. I did not
come in here by the back door.

"That this House at its rising this day

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
Chief Whip the reason for this hastily
hurried assembly and the reason for this
hurried adjournment to, I understand,
two days next week. Surely this Government realises at this very late hour of the
day that it is a community responsibility.
If the Chief Whip has regulated his
business in the month of August so that
this House should be gathered together,
will he tell us if at the end of Wednesday
next this House will be adjourned to the
5th October, and, if so, what has been the
main cause of this House being called
together to-day? I cannot see any good
cause or any purpose being served by the
Members all being recalled when we are
only going to deal with a Bill which is to
be presented here for First Reading today, and after that Bill has been finished
with we adjourn again.
If I am going to attend this House I
expect to be useful and serviceable to the
people in their needs and requirements,
and I feel that this method of conducting
Government business is of a kind that we
and the whole community of Northern
Ireland deplore. It is not because there
is nothing to do that the Government
must adjourn now until Tuesday next. I
can give you many, many questions touching the life of the people of Northern
Ireland, affecting their wellbeing, affecting the upbringing of their children and
affecting every unit that goes to make up
a happy and free life for the community
at large. But the Government does not
want these suggestions. They do not want
to hear anything about community life or
how the community is living. All they
want, in my opinion, is to bring us here
together so that the public will think that
this House has been called for services of
urgency and importance that cannot be
delayed, while the title of the Bill that I
have heard of, and which is to be introduced to-day, shows that it is a Bill that
has been introduced in this House not
only once or twice but at least half a
dozen times, and on each of these
occasions the Government has rejected it.
Surely there is some reason that we on
this side of the House are not aware of
why the Government has come in this
haste and hurry to pretend once again
that they are over-anxious to do some
useful service to the community. Now
if we are going to continue in that way,
I think that my past speeches have been
masterpieces in so far as the life of this
Sittings of the House

Government is concerned.
I think you
would be better and you would serve a

conscription but to satisfy the needs and

amongst the people concerned, have put a

The King's Regulations lay down that
no man or woman can be incarcerated in
a short-term prison for more than two
years and eleven months. Those regulations are for the protection of the lives of
the prisoners. The Government are keeping men in the Belfast short-term prison
for terms of from three years to 20 years,
and not only that but the supervision that
is necessary is lacking to a very great

Men on the staff have been working in
some cases seven days a week. Belfast

not been proved against the staff of the
prison.
I say openly that our prison staff are
as highly efficient in the carrying out of

find that the work here has been performed in a very efficient manner. That

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
GRANT): The hon. Member for Woodvale raised a point about old age pensioners, that is the pensioners over 70
years of age. It is perfectly true to say
that this point was raised by the hon.
Member by letter. I sent a reply to him,
but before he had had time to receive my
letter he had taken other steps in the
matter-he. has raised it in the House
this afternoon. The hon. Member is
entitled to a reply, and the answer I am
going to give will be exactly the same as
in the letter I sent him on this particular
question, which the hon. Member feels.
to be of some public interest.
Whether these pensioners are entitled
to work and at the same time continue to
receive the pension is a matter which
should be made quite clear. I cannot
give a simple answer to the question
because many of the persons to whom the
hon. Member refers may have supplementary pensions in addition to their
non-contributory pensions, and the rules
governing the treatment of earnings are
not the same under the two schemes.
Ignoring the complications which may
arise from the possession of unearned
income, and taking the straightforward
case of the person who has no means
except his pension, the Non-contributory
Pensions Act provides that he may earn
up to 10s a week, or 20s a week if he is
married, and still be able to draw a
pension at the full rate of 10s a week.
His wife, if she is 70 and satisfies the
other conditions, would also be. entitled
to a pension of 10s a week.
The rule under the supplementary pensions scheme is different. It provides
that the first 5s a week, or one-half of
the earnings, subject to a limit of 8s a
week, is to be disregarded and only the
balance of the earnings taken into
account as an available resource. The
rule does not provide, as in the case of
the basic pension, for the halving of the
earnings in the case of a married couple.
If, therefore, a pensioner takes up employment after he is granted a supplementary pension and earns £1 a week, his
supplementary pension will be reduced
by 12s. It will thus be seen that the
effect of these rules varies according to
the circumstances of each case and the
amount of the other resources which have
to be taken into account. If there are
any special cases in which the hon.
Member for Woodvale or any hon. Members are, interested I shall be very pleased
to go into them and give the information
desired.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): As I stated in my reply to

District is responsible for the performance

as

Rent Restriction (Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: The urgency of this
measure will, I think, become apparent
when I have addressed a few sentences to
the House. The Bill deals with two
limited questions arising out of what is,
of course, a huge problem. First of all,
there is profiteering in the rents of houses
or parts of houses, and the question
whether the part of a house that is let
purports to be let furnished
or unfurnished. One of the objects of the Bill
is to abolish the difference with regard to
the resumption or obtaining of possession.
of a house according to the time at which
the owner thereof became landlord. There
is an obvious anomaly in the case of a
man who becomes landlord before the first
day of May, 1940, and one who becomes
landlord after that date.
On Thursday last there was some discussion as to why this measure was so
urgent that the House should be summoned during the Recess. The subcommittee of the Cabinet began to sit towards the end of June, and as much information as possible was obtained. It
became very evident from the survey of
housing, from valuable information
furnished by various organisations, and
other sources, and from the continual
letters that reached my Department
setting forth certain matters and complaints, that the matter of profiteering
was one of extreme urgency. Consequently
the sub-committee made an interim report
to the Cabinet on this aspect of the
matter, and on one I am about to mention, namely, the difference between the
position of a man who owned a house
before the 1st day of May, 1940, and the
man who became an owner after that date.
These things were so convincing that it
seemed good to the Government to request
the Speaker to summon the House.
Before I proceed to discuss either of
these matters in detail, I may say there
can be no question that the housing
situation in Belfast, which is not satisfactory and has not been satisfactory for
a great number of years, became very
much worsened by the air-raids which
took place in April and May, 1941. Of
these two air-raids-I will not mention
the number of houses damaged or completely destroyed-the immediate result
was this that by the 31st May, 1941, my
Department was responsible for 67,800
billetees in the reception areas.
I say
nothing of other people who went out, of
their own accord and endeavoured to provide themselves with accommodation-but
by the 31st May, 67,800 people were being
looked after by my Department and were
quartered in different parts of the
country. In addition to those, there were
some 5,643 who had come from various
cities and towns across the Channel.
By the month of May, 1942, that
67,800 had fallen to 18,972. The people
had come back in a very great measure.
By May, 1943, the combined totals of the
67,800 and the 5,643 had fallen to
11,464, and by August, 1943, the total
was 10,071. From that 10,071 you may
safely deduct some 4,000 people representing cross-Channel evacuees, and that
means that of the 67,800 we started with
in May, 1941, all but 6,000 are now back
in this city, and that despite the fact that
some thousands of houses were completely
demolished and could not be repaired,
although a great job of work was done in
the matter of repairing houses partially
damaged.
It is quite clear that something in the
nature of trying to put a quart into a
pint pot was being attempted and the
results have been deplorable. In addition
to these people whose homes were demolished there is another factor to be taken
that there
into account, and that is
already was a considerable influx from
the country districts of people coming in

who have come either from Eire or from
across the Channel, I can give the figure
which shows how many of these permitted
residents are now in Belfast. It amounts
to 12,451 people. In all these circumstances-

was not very convincing, and I ventured
But a different situation has arisen

Iwill find that the Government were well

The Bill falls naturally into two
divisions. The first part of the Bill
provides that the Excessive Rent Prevention Act of 1941 shall be extended and
that a person shall have the right to apply
if he is aggrieved by reason of the amount
of rent he has to pay or has contracted to
pay in respect of a dwelling house to the
person from whom he has taken it in
accordance with the rules laid down. In
other words, one can go back to the same
Tribunal as was constituted before, consisting of a resident magistrate, aided by
two lay assessors, some 37 or 38 of whom
were appointed. They are still in office.
The machinery is there. It can be put
into operation just as soon as Parliament
has passed this Bill into law. An end can
be put to this matter straight away. I
think it is well worth while for the House
to re-assemble to stop profiteering on these
lines, and I do not suppose for a moment
that I know all or even the most glaring
cases.
The other matter with which the Bill
deals is this: By the Rent Restriction
Act, 1940, Section 8 (1) (d) it is provided
that no order or judgment for the recovery
of possession of any dwelling-house or for
the ejectment of a tenant there from shall
be made or given unlessthe dwelling-house is required by the
landlord for occupation as a residence
for himself, and the landlord, or the
husband or wife of the landlord, became the landlord before the commencement of this Act, and the landlord has,
after the commencement of this Act,
given to the tenant six months' notice
in writing that he requires possession
of the dwelling-house for occupation as
a residence for himself.
That Act commenced from the 1st May,
1940, and the position is that where a man
was landlord before that date he can by
giving six months' notice, and if he requires the house for a specific purpose, get
possession. The man who had acquired
his house in March, 1940, although living
elsewhere, can make a demand for the
house now and by going through the correct procedure can get possession of it. It
is not so in the case of a man who had
acquired the house after the 1st May,
1940. When one begins to divide the year
by arbitrary dates it is inevitable that
great hardships and anomalies will result.
That is one of the commonest complaints
brought to our notice. It does seem a
pity that the man who had acquired his
house in the month of March has the
right to demand possession of it on the
pretext that he requires it for his own
occupation, while the man who acquired
the house three months later has not the
opportunity of resuming possession of the
house and perhaps selling it at an enhanced price.
That difference in dates is purely
arbitrary and can work great hardships,
but indeed the whole code of the Rent
Restriction Acts, adopted as a temporary expedient as long ago as 1915 and
continued ever since, is full of very in-
I do not think
consistent provisions.
anybody, whether landlord or tenant, is
entirely satisfied with it. Its main purpose, however, was maintained throughout, namely the protection of the tenant.
The Government has come to the deliberate conclusion that the time has
come for a thorough and minute examination of the Rent Restriction Code. Of
course, that examination does not mean
that legislation will follow hard on its
heels, because, in accordance with the
pledge given by the late Lord Craigavon
and repeated by his successors, including
the present Prime Minister, controversial
legislation is to be avoided during this
period. I cannot imagine any subject
that can be more controversial than
something that attempts to regulate in a
large way the relations between landlord
and tenant. But that is no reason why
there should not be a most careful and
minute examination of this code.
Accordingly, with the sanction of the
Prime Minister and my Colleagues I propose to set up a thoroughly representative
Commission to examine the. Code, to
examine its working, to examine its procedure, and to study its effect, if any, on
the provision of houses for the needs of

What do we find happening in Edith

No. 9 is the same as No. 7 except that

a week

I want to tell the Minister of Home

a big enough man. He has not got the

Another excuse a Member of the Government did once blurt out was that it was
also due to lack of labour. We have an

We have it in our own midst. We have

the Government does not care a damn

The Members of this Government have

the money of the State in travelling;

with

a week. That is altogether

I do not want to take up the time of

problem is a serious problem. It is very

serious in the rural districts also. Unless

able to keep the. people in these areas. I

now when agriculture is playing such an

greatest obstacle to progress in agriculture at the present time is the fact that
we have not in the rural areas sufficient
houses to house the working people. It
is impossible to get agricultural labourers
to come out to the rural districts because
there. are not sufficient houses for them.
So that if the Government, in any scheme
they are formulating, or going to formulate, through the district councils or in
any other way, are going to help us in
the development of the agricultural industry, the best way they can do that is
to help to provide suitable houses for the
agricultural labourers.
The housing problem is the most acute
problem we have at the present time.
Whether it be for agricultural cottages,
artisan cottages, or any other houses in
the area, I say that the only fair way we
can arrive at a fair and equitable rent
that ought to be paid for these houses is
to set up some sort of independent tribunal to which these people, whether they
be landlords or house owners or tenants,
could apply to fix a rent for the houses.
I would appeal to the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs, when
he is setting up this Commission, that he

We all know the facts. What we want

The hon. Member for South Tyrone
spoke about a man in Bangor who was
paying £1 per week in rent. Did that
Member in years gone by even raise his

It is only now for reasons best known to

poor people. Time and again we read in

Street. She had a husband and two
children. One of the children was in the
Fever Hospital with diphtheria and the
other child was delicate. She took a
furnished house. What happened? A
decree for possession was given against her
by the court set up by this Parliament.
Had it not been for some kindly neighbour she would not have had any place
to go to. Then there was the case of the
woman who came out of the poorhouse
wheeling two children in a perambulator.
One of the children was dead. She went
to door after door looking for lodgings,
and after a long time some kindly person
in Donegall Pass took her in. It was
then found that one of the children was
suffocated.
These are the things that have been
happening in the last nine or ten years,
and no action was taken to provide homes
for such people. Dr. Carnworth, years
ago, said there were 3,000 slum houses
in Belfast. Did the Government take
any action? No. Did the Government
realise that there were 8,000 children
diagnosed as suffering from some form of
tuberculosis? The cause of that was
overcrowding in slums. All these things
make us wonder whether we are in a
civilised country at all. Are the men

The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER in the Chair.
Adjournment of the House.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House, at its rising this day
do adjourn until 12 noon on Thursday,
16th September, and that after the
Report of Royal Assent to Acts agreed
upon by both Houses, Mr. Speaker do
adjourn the House without Question put
until Tuesday, the 5th October, provided
always that in the event of any Bill being
returned from the Senate with Amendments, the House shall meet on
Wednesday, 15th September, and shall
transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date, and at its
rising shall adjourn until 12 noon on
Thursday, 16th September." (Sir
Norman Stronge.)
Mr. MINFORD: I rise to oppose the
adjournment of the House because I feel
that very important business came before
this House in the last Sittings and the
House was counted out. I need not
repeat what I said, but to-day I again
make a very strong protest against
adjourning the House when three motions
are before it. One, a very important
one, is with regard to the price of
potatoes. I was amazed this morning
when I heard that one of the Ministry's
chief guns in the Department of Agriculture is prepared to ship potatoes from
Great Britain to Northern Ireland rather
than give a fair price. If he gives anything near the price the English farmer
is getting he will get them. Potatoes
to-day are £3 15s a ton for Arran Victors,
25s less than in Great Britain. If we
have to apply the British order in Northern Ireland I demand on behalf of the
farmers and farm workers that we should
have the same standard of living.
You will get the proof that the farmers
are not going to respond next year if
you
go to Elmwood Avenue. I do not think
ten growers have applied for manure for
next season. The growing of the potato
crop is not profitable. Surely this House
has some jurisdiction and some authority.
I am proud of my connection with Great
Britain, but I am not going to be put on
a lower grade of living. The thing is a
scandal. The House was counted out the
last day. I warned the Prime Minister
if this was going on-counting out the
House on the same conditions as last day
-I shall have to make a very strong
Motion in this House of Commons. These
three Motions are down, and the Bill
brought in by the Minister was not half
as important as the Motion I and three
other hon. Members had in their names.
I do protest strongly that rather than
give the farmers justice and the workers
justice they are prepared to ship potatoes
from Great Britain into Northern Ireland.
That would cost £2 or £3 more plus
freight. Surely with a war on it is sheer
waste of shipping space to bring potatoes
from Great Britain to Northern Ireland
when the farmers have them lying in the
field. It is definitely wrong. We talk
about digging for victory and saving fuel,
and yet the Ministry is prepared to bring
in potatoes from England to Northern
Ireland when they know perfectly well
the price in Northern Ireland is ridiculous
-£3 15s a ton. I feel very strongly on
this matter, and I say it is definitely
wrong.

Friend the Minister of Finance, I rise
to move the Resolution.
The Excessive Rents (Prevention) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1941, provided for
the setting up of a tribunal to hear
appeals under that Act, and Section 3 of
the Act provided for the payment out of
moneys voted by Parliament of fees and

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
beg to move in Clause 2, sub-clause (1)
at the end of paragraph (a) to insert the
word "or."
This is an Amendment which I have
only handed in now, and I wish to apologise to the Minister of Home Affairs for
not having given him previous notice. I
am asking that after the word "family"
the word "or" be inserted. As I understand this Clause at the present moment,
if landlords want possession of their
houses they must not only provide alternative accommodation, but they must
satisfy the court that greater hardship is
caused by refusing to grant an order for
possession than by granting it. The
effect of my Amendment is that a person
can get possession without supplying
alternative accommodation if a greater
hardship would be caused by refusing
than by granting that permission.
I have in mind similar cases to that
referred to by the hon. Member for South
Tyrone yesterday when he drew attention
to the fact that the owner of a house in
order to undertake war work proceeded
to Scotland and let his house in Bangor.
In Scotland he and his wife and two
children lived in a house which was
blitzed. They moved to another house
which in turn was blitzed, so they returned to Northern Ireland. Since their
return they have been living in Bangor
in one room and paying £1 a week while
their house is occupied by two maiden
ladies who are paying them less for their
house than they pay for this one room. The
Member for South Tyrone emphasised the
great hardships and difficulties in which
these people find themselves. I should
like, therefore, that an exception should
be made in the case of a landlord whose
house has been blitzed and who for that
reason wants possession of a house which
he owns and which he has let.
Mr. MINFORD: I agree with what
the hon. and gallant Member has said,
but I should like to ask him and the
Minister of Home Affairs what is going
to happen to the tenant who has to go

the moment. What will happen when

are
Major ROBINSON: May I ask the
Prime Minister is it a fact that potatoes
now being shipped into Northern
Ireland, or is there a likelihood that
potatoes will be shipped into Northern
Ireland this year from Great Britain?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
hon. Member is misinformed with regard
to potatoes being shipped into Northern
Ireland. That is not so. Arrangements
1567 Shipment and Prices of Potatoes
Shipment and Prices of Potatoes 1568
1 SEPTEMBER 1943
are being made, I understand, to ship
1,000 tons of potatoes from Northern
Ireland to Great Britain. I do not want
to enter into the Notice of Motion on the
Order Paper, but I may say that negotiations regarding the price of the main
crop potatoes are still proceeding.
Mr. MINFORD: May I say that I
raised this question to-day because I feel
that the price of 75s per ton has been
fixed from to-day onwards? I would like
to know why should there be a drop of
10s per ton when we are not getting near
the cost of production. I was talking to
a prominent member of the Department
of Agriculture this morning. He is one
who can stand over any statement he
makes. The discussion arose with regard
to the terrible scarcity of potatoes some
time ago.
As a matter of fact I gave
over 50 tons to one man. It is common
knowledge that in the month of September, after the bad weather for the
harvesting of oats and wheat, and with
the prices given, there will be a tremendous scarcity. The Prime Minister, being
a practical farmer himself, knows perfectly well that the farmers are prepared
to work overtime and pay double wages
in order to supply the wants of the
people in war time.
If they are prepared to do that, surely
it is only reasonable that they should get
decent recompense? As I was saying, I
was talking to a member of the Ministry,
and he told me that if there was a scarcity
then potatoes would be shipped into
Northern Ireland. I said, Surely you
would not ship potatoes into Northern
Ireland at so much a ton plus freight.
Give the farmers a decent price for their
potatoes and they will double the wages
to their labourers." I am employing 56
men under the Ministry of Labour's
labour scheme, and I am prepared to pay
double wages if I get the cost of production. If this thing does happen I fear it
is going to damn the whole position of
potato growing in Northern Ireland.
Let us examine the position. When
the invasion of the Channel Islands took
place we were afraid of a scarcity of food,
and the Ministry of Food in order to encourage the British and Northern Ireland
farmers raised the price of potatoes to
£26 a ton. The result was that owing to
the high price and the good weather there
was an abundant crop, indeed there were
too many potatoes for home consumption.
We had to dump some of those potatoes
into factories, and they were worth only
£2 per ton. How can we expect the
farmers to continue growing at a price of
£3 15s a ton? We have the best farmers
in the world. They are farming under
tremendous climatic conditions, and they
are loyally struggling on.
I say in all sincerity that unless there
is a better price for potatoes the Prime
Minister will find that potato growing in
Ulster will go down and down. We do
not want that. We are loyal men, and
we want to give food to the men who are
fighting for us. If this low price is persisted in during the month of September
it will mean that potatoes will have to be
shipped to Northern Ireland. That information was given to me by one of the
Ministry's officials. The Ulster farmers
are entitled to a fair price for their
produce. I wonder how some hon.
Members would like to have to produce
potatoes at £3 15s Od per ton.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: The price
of potatoes is fixed by the Ministry of
Food, not by the Northern Ireland Ministry of Agriculture.
Mr. MINFORD: That old story is not
good enough for me. The Rt. Hon. Sir
Hugh O'Neill and Dr. James Little know
about the matter. At a meeting in
Whiteabbey Dr. James Little said that
the Northern Ireland Government had
everything to do with the production and
price of potatoes in so far as this country
is concerned.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: No matter
what is said we know what the law is.
The law is that the Ministry of Food fixes
all prices. The Ministry of Agriculture
here can put forward a price to the Ministry of Food, but they cannot dictate
to it.
Mr. MINFORD: Yes, provided your
statement is true.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: The statement is true. There is no doubt about
that at all.
Mr. MINFORD: Surely this Government could speak to Mr. Hudson. What
did Mr. Churchill say about agriculture
when he wrote a letter to the right hon.
Member for Mid Down three months ago?
Do you think that if he were informed
1569 Shipment and Prices of Potatoes HOUSE OF COMMONS

Adjournment
[Mr. Minford]
about what is taking place he would allow
it to continue? I appeal to the Prime
Minister to go across to Westminster and
tell the authorities there that the Ulster
farmers will never be content until they
get a decent reward for their labour. We
are entitled to the same treatment as the
people in Great Britain. The farmers
here are asking to be paid only the cost
of production.
The right hon. Gentleman should read
the reports which appeared in the
monthly journal of the Ulster Farmers'
Union. If a strike were to take place at
Short & Harland's the Minister would go
down and try to settle it, but the farmers
work away like slaves and never complain.
"Hope springs eternal in the human
breast." It is time the right hon.
Gentleman awakened from his slumber in
regard to the agricultural position.
Would the right hon. Gentleman care to
work for a wage which would not maintain him? The farmers are entitled to a
decent standard of living. The British
Ministry are building thousands
houses for the agricultural workers in
England. Not one house is being erected
in Northern Ireland, but a Bill is being
passed through Parliament which will
place greater hardship on certain people.
of
The farmers of Ulster are expected to
comply with the Tillage Order in the same
way as the farmers in Great Britain.
That being so they should receive the
same price for their produce. The
farmers here have risen to the occasion,
and the food they produce is second to
none. I would ask the right hon.
Gentleman to urge the powers that be on
the other side of the water to give the
Ulster farmers a price for their produce
which will cover the cost of production.
If the man who told me that potatoes are
going to be shipped to Northern Ireland
was telling an untruth it is not my fault;
I am only repeating what I was told.

is-

2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has made or
proposes to make representations to the
Imperial authorities for some modification of the Control of Motor Fuel (Northern Ireland) Order, 1943, which restricts
the use of private motor-cars and confines
the use of motor taxi-cabs to an inner
radius of 10 miles except in certain special
circumstances, in view of the fact that the
inner radius is 15 miles in parts of Great
Britain, and that in Northern Ireland
taxi-owners in towns on the sea coast are
left in the case of the inner radius with a
semi-circle of five miles to operate in and
those in towns on the border are similarly
affected, and whether in the event of
representations having been made in the
matter he can state the result.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
5 OCTOBER 1943
Mr. LOWRY: Representations have
been made to the Ministry of Fuel and
Power in regard to the 10-mile limit and
that Ministry is not prepared to consider
any extension of this limit. I cannot
understand the hon. Member's reference
to a 15-mile limit in Great Britain.
In Great Britain the limit for taxi-cabs
is five miles from the boundary of the area
inside which the vehicle is licensed to ply
for hire and as this area is a borough or
urban district there can be few if any
cases in which any taxi-cab can have even
the 10-mile field of operations allowed
universally in Northern Ireland.
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact that in
some areas in England the radius is 15
miles, and will the Minister endeavour to
have the same position brought about in
Northern Ireland?
Mr. LOWRY: The number of boroughs
in England with a 15-mile radius is so
small that it is not worth talking about.
Mr. MINFORD: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware of what is happening in
Northern Ireland? I have heard of a
taxi engaged to take a lady to the boat,
and when she got the length of the
Midland Railway the 10 miles expired,
and she had to change to another taxi in
order to reach the Fleetwood steamer.
Mr. BROWN: In view of the Minister's

same concession? As to his remark that

taking away of the livelihood of the taxiowners is a matter not worth talking about

in regard to this question of petrol Northern Ireland has been rather better treated
than any other part of the United
Kingdom?
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. and learned
Member is perfectly correct. When I

was obliged to change-

matter on the Adjournment.
Mr. SPEAKER: Will the hon. Member
resume his seat? He can only ask short
questions of fact, as he knows.

year

Post-War Agricultural Policy.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I beg to move:
That this House calls on the Government to make immediate representations
to the Imperial Government urging
upon them the necessity of making
known immediately their post-war plans
for agriculture, and is of opinion that
any delay in making such a declaration
of policy will have a serious effect on
agricultural production, as many agriculturalists believe that the absence of a
declared post-war policy is evidence of
the fact that agriculture will be rele-
1583 Post-War Agricultural Policy
Post-War Agricultural Policy 1584
5 OCTOBER 1943
gated to a position similar to that which
obtained after the last war.
In proposing this Resolution to-day I
do not think there is any necessity for me
to stress the importance of the agricultural industry. Many tributes have been.
paid to those engaged in it for the way
they have responded to the many calls
and demands that have been made upon
them. The increased production asked
for to help the nation in its present
struggle has been forthcoming and many
bouquets have been thrown at the agriculturist for his achievements. Bouquets are
very nice and it is well at times to give a
little appreciation, which very often goes
a long way. Bouquets alone, however, do
not pay the farmer's annuities or his
wages bill, and unless he receives an
adequate return for his labour he will no
longer be able to carry on. I know there
are many people who believe that all those
engaged in the agricultural industry today are amassing a fortune-that with
subsidies for flax, potatoes and wheat he
is literally getting money for nothing. I
think all those who think in this way
would be disillusioned if they were put on
a farm for a short time.
Subsidies as a war measure may be all
right, but I am not one of those who
believe that any industry can be run satisfactorily on subsidies for a permanency.
In this respect agriculture does not differ
from any other industry and if agriculture is to take, and it ought to take, its
rightful place in the life of the community it will only be when the tiller of
the soil is assured of an adequate return
for his labour-a return that will not
only suffice to give the farmer a fair
standard of life for himself and his family,
but one which will allow him a sufficient
margin to maintain a decent standard of
living for all those agricultural labourers
who are so necessary to the life of the
agricultural industry.
In the year 1940, some three years ago,
the British Minister of Agriculture
pledged the British Government's intentions towards farmers in assuring them of
a healthy and well-balanced agriculture
after the war. On many subsequent
occasions that assurance has been repeated
by Mr. Hudson himself and has also been
re-echoed by other spokesmen of the
Imperial Government. Further assurances were also given that during the war
steps would be taken in consultation with
the agricultural industry to evolve a suitable long-term policy which would carry
out the assurances given.
Three years
have gone past and nothing has been done;
not only that, but something like a bomb
was dropped on the whole industry when
Mr. Hudson, the Imperial Minister of
Agriculture, announced in the British
House of Commons a short time ago that
he was not even allowed to talk of a postwar agricultural policy.
A spirit of uncertainty and doubt is
growing in the minds of all agriculturists.
Here is a cutting taken from a local paper
a few days ago which speaks for itself,
and shows how disappointed and dissatisfied the Ulster farmers are feeling:
The Ulster Farmers' Union, representing potato growers throughout
Northern Ireland, expresses keen disappointment and indignation at the
announcement which has just been
made by the Ministry of Food that the
price to be paid to growers for potatoes
delivered in October is to be the same as
that paid in October a year ago.
In December, 1940, Mr. R. S.
Hudson, on behalf of his Majesty's
Government and representing all the
great political parties in the House of
Commons, gave a vital pledge to British
farmers in the following words: -"The
Government have now decided to go
further and to guarantee that the present system of fixed prices and an
assured market will be maintained for
the duration of hostilities and for at
least one year thereafter. Prices will
be subject to adjustment to the extent
of any substantial changes in production costs."
If the Government would translate
their pledged word into actual practice,
the farming community would have
fewer grounds to be sceptical of assurances given by Ministers. This failure
of the Ministry of Food to relate prices
to production costs is accepted as a
direct breach of faith with the farming
industry, and will have the effect of
creating almost complete lack of confidence in any pledges or promises which
have been made or are likely to be
made to the industry.
That is a damning indictment. It is not
my indictment; it is the indictment of
the Ulster Farmers' Union. I have been
careful to quote the statement word for

in which the

present war started. What is being done

Mr. LYONS: In making my first
address before this House I shall beg your

Great War farmers were asked to produce
to the limit of their capacity. They certainly did so. They saved the nation by
supplying food and enabling it to carry on
the struggle to a successful issue. During
that period wages were doubled and there
was general prosperity in the country, not
only among farmers, but among the whole
community.
Now I shall ask you to look at the other
side of the question. During the war
farmers had been promised support from
the Government in the post-war period.
What happened? The Government went
out of power at the first election after the
war. A Labour Government came in
pledged to secure cheap food for the industrial population. They did not care
what happened to the farmer. That was
no concern of theirs nor were the promises
of the preceding Government. The result
was that the farmers were cast on the
proverbial scrap heap, and those depending upon them likewise found themselves
floundering in poverty. Literally thousands of farmers were forced to sell out
their farms. Many of them did not have
the privilege of selling out. They were
just cast out. Those who remained were
not able to carry on and cultivate the
land. To a great extent good land was
put down to grass. Marginal land went
derelict. Unemployment was rife, and
in order to support the population the
Government were forced to adopt that illused and much abused unemployment
measure the dole. Is there any Member
of this House who is willing placidly to
permit a repetition of these occurrences
after this war?
I would remind you that agriculture is
by far the greatest single industry carried
on in Northern Ireland and, therefore,
should have pride of place in any scheme
of post-war reconstruction, mainly because it has always been found that when
agriculture is enjoying prosperity that
prosperity is reflected in the general life
of the whole community. On the other
hand if agriculture is neglected it has
likewise been found that the opposite is

business Government. The country wants
a business Government, and it has got to
get a business Government, and it will
have a business Government or know the
reason why. It will go on demanding a
business Government until we get a
business Government.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: I must
draw the hon. Member's attention to the
fact that we are dealing with the Amendment, not with the constitution of the
Government. I hope the hon. 'Member
will stick to the Amendment before the
House.
Mr. BROWN: We are dealing with
post-war planning for agriculture and
calling for the formulation of a policy.
I suggest that in formulating that policy
we would get the best policy from business
brains. That is why I am trying to urge
it. The Prime Minister talks about
wanting business brains in the Government after all the business brains are out
of it. I think it is time we had a business Government. On this matter of
planning, Field-Marshal Wavell, the new
Viceroy of India, the other day said that
in the new world there must be more pay
for certain sections in the community, and
less for others including lawyers. Now
the farmer is just as important and works
as hard as any lawyer. We have lawyers
in this House drawing from £2,500 a
year down.
These are grossly inflated
salaries, and yet the farmers are asked to
carry on even at a loss. There will have
to be a levelling up and a levelling down.
The whole Province will demand a change
in this matter of post-war planning and
everything else. They are sick to death
of this lawyer-ridden régime.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: I think
the hon. Member should speak to the
motion before the House. It would be.
more appropriate.
Mr. BROWN: With very great respect
there was every latitude shown to other
speakers——
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: The hon.
Member is starting to discuss a difficult
subject.
Mr. MINFORD: I think the hon.
Member is just drawing a comparison.
Mr. BROWN; With very great respect,
I was wanting to suggest that in postwar planning in agriculture and other
things there must be a levelling down and
levelling up. There must be none of
these grossly high salaries like that of the
£2,500 paid to the Attorney-General.
1609 Post-War Agricultural Policy
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS

Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER: The hon.
Member must not get personal.
Mr. BROWN: I say that in post-war
planning there should be some equity,
and these huge salaries must be levelled
down and the remuneration of the farmer
levelled up to bring about equity in postwar planning. That is my case, and I
am entitled to make that point. I say it
is essential for the success of post-war
planning. There must be this redistribution of wealth.
Mr. AGNEW: Hear, hear.
Mr. BROWN: There must be justice
not only in the social services, but also
for the farmer. The farmer will not be
allowed to be the milch cow for the rest
of the community and for the paying
of these huge salaries at Stormont.
Those people certainly do not work
as hard as the tillers of the soil.
That is the point I was making. Great hopes
have been held out by the Minister of
Agriculture. I do not share those hopes.
I say another feature. of post-war
planning should be a reduction in the
land annuities. That should be included
in the post-war policy for agriculture. I
have very little hope of that when I
remember that before. the war the present
Minister of Agriculture was the leader of
the opposition to a reduction of the land
annuities.
Notice taken that ten Members were
not present; House counted, and ten
Members being present-
Mr. BROWN: I say an essential part
of post-war planning for agriculture
should include a reduction of the land
annuities. But my hopes are very slight
when I remember that the. present
Minister of Agriculture voted against a
reduction of the land annuities when the
Motion was last moved in this House
calling for such a reduction. Is this
Government getting justice for the
farmers of Ulster at the present time?
I say, no. How then can they get justice
for the farmers in the post-war period?
If they cannot get justice for them now
when agriculture is so necessary, how are
they going to get it for them after the
war? I say it is due to the absence of
business brains, but I am not going to
develop that. I do say we are not getting
justice. We have the Ulster Farmers'
Union complaining that the farmers are
getting far less for their produce than
they are getting across the Channel.
On the question of agricultural housing
also we are not getting justice. Cottages
are being built for the farm workers
across the Channel, but nothing is being
done here. Nothing will be done. When
we look at all these things we cannot help
worrying about the future. Planning at
the present time is a sham and a subterfuge, a fraud and a humbug. It is time
we called upon the Government to face
the facts, because some day the farmers
are going to call the Government to
account and ask them to face up to the
facts. We have had enough of this
nonsense- -as much as we can stand. Our
patience is almost exhausted.
The question of agricultural education
has been mentioned. Surely it is not
necessary to wait until after the war to do
something about that along the lines of
one of the speakers. That is something
the Government should do, but again the
Government have no policy in this matter
or in any other matter except the policy
of "Run rabbit, run." That seems to be
their whole policy in this matter of agricultural housing and everything else.
Something will have to be done. I suggest that the only solution to this matter
is a business Government and then we will
have planning on proper business-like
lines. Until that is done I think we will
have nothing but continued chaos.
Amendment agreed to.
Resolved, "That this House is of
opinion that in justice to the farmers and
having regard to their great service to the
nation, a broad statement of policy should
be made by the Imperial Government at
the earliest possible moment and certainly
before the war ends, and that this statement should make it clear that in the
years following the war the position of
farmers should be secured against the
collapse which happened after the last
war."
Adjournment.
Resolved, "That this House do now
adjourn." (Sir Norman Stronge.)
Adjourned accordingly at ten
minutes after Four o'clock
until Tuesday next, pursuant
to the Resolution of the House
of this day.

1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of

been drawn to a statement made by Mr.

whether he can state what steps, if any,
he is taking to refute this unjust statement which might seriously injure the
Northern Ireland export cattle trade.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I do not think
that the irresponsible and inaccurate statement to which the hon. Member refers
can have any adverse effect on our cattle
export trade. I would suggest to the hon.
Member that he follow my policy of
ignoring the statement rather than give
it publicity to which it is not entitled.

should like to ask whether he or his

inform Mr. Green that when cattle
breeders who know their business want a

has informed Mr. Green that Northern
Ireland stock bulls have been exported to
many parts of the world for the improvement of stock.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the

guarantee that if he follows that policy he
will light in that seat one day?

one example of the fact that Northern

B.B.C.-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member

LAND FOR AFFORESTATION.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether in view of the increased prices being paid for land he will
approach the Ministry of Finance with a
view to having the prices paid by his
Ministry for land for afforestation purposes very materially revised.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: As the hon.
Member must be aware, the Ministry
purchases land for afforestation in accordance with what the Ministry deems to be
its economic value for that purpose. The
Ministry has had no difficulty in securing
the consent of the Ministry of Finance to
the purchase prices on that basis. Forestry
operations, as I am sure the hon. Member
will realise, must be conducted on an
economic basis and no one is compelled
or under an obligation to sell land to the
Ministry.
LAND IMPROVEMENT SCHEME.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his Ministry intends
reintroducing the grants for the improvement of agricultural lands, and, if so,
when.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: It is intended
to re-open the Ministry's land improvement scheme as from 1st November. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
WEIGHING OF MILK AT NESTLE'S
OMAGH FACTORY.
4. Mr. LYONS asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fact that milk producers supplying Messrs.
Nestlé's Milk Factory at Omagh with
milk are dissatisfied with the weights of
milk returned, as these do not correspond
with the suppliers' weights, and whether
some more satisfactory method cannot be
devised whereby the confidence of the
milk suppliers can be retained.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: My attention
has been drawn recently to certain cases
in which producers delivering milk to the
Ministry at Messrs. Nestlé's milk factory
at Omagh have expressed dissatisfaction.
with the weights of milk recorded. These
cases are under investigation.
Messrs. Nestlé's supply all churns for
delivery of milk by producers and wash
and sterilise the churns before they are
returned to the supplier. They leave a
clean empty churn when they collect a
full one. This arrangement involves a
departure from the usual creamery
practice of having the platform number
marked on the churn. Instead the
producer is required to attach to each
churn a label on which is shown his name
and platform number. In some instances
-relatively very few difficulties have
arisen where labels have become detached
or when they have not been clearly
marked as required. In all cases referred
to them by the Ministry, the firm have
shown themselves to be very meticulous
in the crediting of milk to suppliers, and.
in fact, have themselves reported adjustments in favour of producers which a
scrutiny of their records has shown to be
necessary.
I cannot agree that because the recorded
weights do not correspond with the
suppliers' claims regarding the quantity
of milk they have delivered the recorded
weights are necessarily wrong. Farmers
have rarely adequate facilities for weighing their milk accurately and, as I have
said, I am satisfied that every possible
care is taken by Messrs. Nestlé's to record
accurately the quantities of milk delivered but occasional differences of
opinion in these matters are inevitable.
In order that producers may have every
confidence in the weighing of their milk,
arrangements have been made to appoint

Investigation into Functions of
Ministries.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether a retired English civil
servant, Sir Francis Floud, recently held
an investigation into the Northern Ireland
Civil Service, whether the Minister discovered or suspected something wrong in
the Civil Service to justify this investigation, and whether he can state the cost
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): An investigation has recently
been carried out by Sir Francis Floud, a
distinguished administrator, but the hon.
Member is incorrect in thinking that this
investigation was into the Northern Ireland Civil Service as such. In fact, its
object was to examine the allocation of
functions between the different Northern
Ireland Ministries with a view to their
more equitable distribution and the prevention of over-lapping with particular
reference to the growth of agency services
on behalf of Imperial Departments. The
fee paid for the investigation was 150
guineas, plus out-of-pocket expenses, and
the decision to have it undertaken was
that of the Cabinet.

Spender?
Major SINCLAIR: The answer to all
the questions with the exception of the
last is no; in regard to the last, we have
complete confidence in Sir Wilfred
Spender.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil

concerned, from the point of view of

My hon. Friend is not alone in putting

the hon. and gallant Member for Mid
Armagh and the hon. Members for North
and Central Armagh are also not unmindful of the interests of their constituents. Unemployment in the county
has recently fallen, and I am glad to be
able to say that following recent negotiations certain interesting industrial developments may be looked for. For
at the

moment enlarge upon these.

of mentioning that a Government state-

ARMAGH APPEALS TRIBUNAL.
9. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Labour whether he
will consider the advisability of restoring
the Appeal Tribunal in Armagh, in view
of the inconvenience caused to applicants
for assistance and supplementary pensions
who have to travel to Portadown.
Mr. GRANT: In answer to the hon.
Member, I must remind him that under
the Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934,
it is a matter entirely for the Assistance
Board to determine where Appeal
Tribunals shall be held.
The Board inform me that from their
beginning in 1934 until 1940, appeals
from the Armagh, Lurgan and Portadown
districts were all held in Portadown, without any complaints about its suitability.
The introduction of the supplementary
pensions scheme in 1940 caused a temporary increase in the number of appeals,
and from June of that year, to meet the
extra pressure, tribunals were held in the
three towns mentioned. Towards the end
of 1941 the number of appeals fell off so
considerably that it was no longer possible
to justify the expense of tribunals at three
centres, and the original arrangement was
restored.
even
There are now far fewer appeals than
there were,
before the supplementary pensions scheme was introduced.
Portadown then heard about 30 appeals
a week from all three districts; now, only
from 20 to 30 appeals are received from
the same districts every month. It is
not, therefore, proposed to alter the present arrangements.

. 10. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Under Section 6 (4) of the
Summary Jurisdiction and Criminal

Minister of Home Affairs may by Order
made with the concurrence of the Minister
of Finance from time to time prescribe
the rates of scales of salaries and allowances to be paid to resident magistrates
and temporary resident magistrates appointed under the Act. An Order (S.R.
and O. 1943, No. 101) was made in
August last under the powers conferred
upon me by this Act, amending the rate
of annual increment payable to resident
magistrates. The Order did not alter the
maximum salary which remains at £1,100
per annum.
Resident magistrates receive payment of
allowances in respect of travelling expenses and subsistence for journeys undertaken on official duty at the usual Civil
Service rates, that is, first-class rail fare,
or, where they have to use their private
cars, normal mileage rates.

13. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can enumerate

Government in connection with housing

made by them.
Mr. LOWRY: The only Committee
primarily concerned with housing other
than the Cabinet Committee referred to
by the hon. Member is the Housing Committee set up by the Planning Advisory
Board.
As the result of a recommendation by
this Committee, which was endorsed by
the Board and accepted by the Government, it was decided to carry out a housing survey dealing with (a) overcrowding,
and (b) the structural condition of houses.
The survey embraces all boroughs and
towns and certain sample rural areas. In
urban areas the overcrowding part was
carried out by the local authorities and
the structural survey by technical officers
employed by my Ministry. In the rural
areas it was more economical for the
technical officers to do both parts of the
survey as each house had to be inspected
in any case by them. In urban areas,
however, while each house had to be
visited for the overcrowding survey, it was
decided not to examine technically the
structural condition of every one of a
number of identical houses, and, accordingly, it was much more economical to
employ the technically qualified persons
for the technical work only. This meant,
however, that a proportion of houses in
the urban areas were visited by two
persons.
The survey is well advanced, but is not
yet completed. Where a house has been
surveyed for both sections no further visits
will, of course, be paid, except, perhaps,
in a few cases where a special visit may be
necessary to clear up some doubtful
point.

The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move:
That a Select Committee be appointed
to consider-
(1) whether any alterations ought
to be made in the remuneration of

Parliamentary Secretaries and Assistant Parliamentary Secretaries; and

That notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Order No. 50 the
Committee consist of eight members.
That Mr. Agnew, Mr. T. Bailie, the
Rt. Hon. Şir Milne Barbour, Bart.;
