That the Committee have power to
send for persons, papers and records.
That five to be the Quorum of the
Committee.
That the Committee have leave to sit
notwithstanding any adjournment of
the House.
The Motion which I now submit to the
House is in two parts: the first raises
the question of the. remuneration of
members of the Government, and the
second is concerned with payments and
allowances made to other Members of the
House. The Motion is that a Select
Committee, consisting of the hon. Members whose names are given, should

but hon. Members will probably wish me
to review briefly the history of these
salaries and allowances.
Firstly, with regard to Ministerial
salaries. In 1921 a Select Committee of
the House made a Report which was the
basis of an Act passed in that year, viz.,
the Salaries of Ministerial Offices Act,
1921. This Act prescribed that the
salary of the Prime Minister should be
£3,200 per annum, and that other
Ministers, five in number, should each
receive £1,500 by virtue of their position
as heads of departments. Provision was
also made for the. offices of Parliamentary
Secretary, five of them receiving £1,000
each, and two receiving £600 per annum.
In order that a complete picture may
be given of the remuneration drawn by
the. Prime Minister and by the five
Ministers, it is also necessary that I should
refer to the provision made in the Estimates for the payment of £1,750 per
annum to the Prime Minister of the day
for contingencies of office. This
allowance was payable. from the 1st
April, 1926, and ceased to be drawn in
1940-41. In the case of other Ministers
the Act of 1921 provided that a sum, not
exceeding £2,500 per annum, should be
allocated annually among them by way
of additional salary to take account of
their work as Cabinet Ministers. This
sum was to be divided equally, with the
proviso that no Minister was to receive
an annual amount of more than £500.
At that time there were five Ministers,
and accordingly each received £500. In
1927 an amending Act provided that if
any of the Ministers was not in receipt of
salary, the sum of £2,500 should be
divided amongst those Ministers who did
actually receive a salary, the intention.
being to deal with the. situation under
which a Minister might elect not to draw
any remuneration. In the result, until
1940 Ministers actually received £500
each and even until quite recently this
amount has been drawn, despite the fact
that the number of Ministers was increased from five to six. In the present
administration, however, this is no longer
the case, and Ministers each receive only
one-sixth of the total of £2,500, i.e.,
about £416 instead of £500. It may be

I
oppose this Committee on the further
ground that it includes no representation
of Members of the Senate, and the reason
I do so is this: We had a Joint Committee set up on the question of transport
which included Members of this House
and Members of the Senate. I suggest,
with very great respect, that this Committee will not be in a position to know
the facts, because it is not a Joint Committee. One Minister sits in the Senate.
He does not sit here. This Committee of
Members only of this House will have no
means of knowing the work he does or
does not do. They cannot possibly know
the figure to arrive at, such as could be
arrived at if we had representatives both
of the House of Commons and of the

there are Parliamentary Secretaries.
One of these Parliamentary Secretaries
sits in the Senate and we do
not see him from one year's end
to another. Therefore, a Committee
composed of Members of the House of
Commons only cannot possibly be in a
position to deal with the position and
prepare the remuneration to be paid to
this Parliamentary Secretary. I say this
is a very gross reflection on the Senate.
This is not the first time that that has
been done, and it should be ended.
Not long ago a Committee was set up
to consider public health in Northern
Ireland, and the same thing was done.
The Senate was denied any representation

Senate representation on the Health
Services Committee, and it is wrong to
deny it representation on this Committee.
The best Committee we ever had during
my time at Stormont was the Joint Com-

to consider

I am not going to discuss salaries, because

them, except to say that I am opposed to

I oppose any increase. This Motion
mentions Assistant Parliamentary Secretaries. There are no Assistant Parliamentary Secretaries at Stormont, either in
this House or in the Senate. We are
asked to fix the salaries of people who do
not exist. Surely the Government know
more about what is going on at Stormont
than to call upon this House in all seriousness to set up a Committee to fix salaries
for people who have no existence whatever. There is not a single Assistant
Parliamentary Secretary in connection

to Ministers of this House and turns the

I also oppose the appointment of this
Committee for another reason. The
members will receive remuneration at the
rate of two guineas per day, free of
income-tax, plus first-class travelling expenses. Since the war started I have
refused to act on any Select Committee on
a paid basis. I have time and again
demanded that these Committees should
sit on an unpaid basis as in years gone
by. I object to the payment of the
members and for that reason I also object
to the appointment of the Committee.
The question has been asked, did anybody ask for this Committee? The Prime
Minister is not here. He does not wait to
see what the Members think. He aims at
being a dictator. He is not concerned in
the slightest degree with the views of the
Members of this House. If he had been
here I would have challenged him to get
up and name one single Member of this
House who asked for this Committee to
increase the salaries of the Cabinet and
Members. I have never asked for the
setting up of this Committee. I have
spoken to most of the other Members and
I could not discover one who asked for
it. This is the Prime Minister's' Committee. He proposed it and he took the
responsibility of giving the impression in
this House that the back-benchers asked
for it. I am most emphatically opposed to
it and will vote against it.
Another matter to which I should like
to draw attention is this. The impression
has been conveyed that the Prime
Minister and the Cabinet are engrossed in
work in connection with the war
and with the post-war period, yet
there is time to bring in a little
parochial matter like this. It is
very much to be regretted that a resolution of this kind should be brought in
to-day because it will have a very unsettling effect upon industry. We are
told of the vicious circle of rising expenditure and the rising cost of living, and I
repeat that any Motion of this kind will
have a very unsettling effect on our war
industry. The Government had better
not proceed with it at all.
We are told that finance is one of the
difficulties standing in the way of the
people being housed, that it is one of the
difficulties standing in the way of meals
being provided for school-children, and
that it also is one of the difficulties standing in the way of the farmers getting a
living. We have a statement published
by the Ulster Farmers'. Union last week
that farmers are not getting a living in
respect of various articles they produce.
The question of finance is another argument against the setting up of this Committee. It is very unfortunate that I
cannot go into the details of this question,
because if I could do so I would show that
the salaries of the Prime Minister and
other Cabinet Ministers are the highest in
the world in proportion to population.

Mr. LOWRY: I beg to move, "That
this House do agree with the Senate in
the said amendment." This amendment
brings the law exactly into line with what
it was under the Acts of 1920 and 1940.
When the Bill left this House paragraph
(b) was the only case where the landlord
was not asked to provide alternative
accommodation. Before the Bill left this
House, I indicated that this matter would
be taken into consideration, and that the
law would be brought back to the position
it was in from 1920 onwards; that is to
say, where, a man held a house by virtue
of his employment, as in the case of mill
owners' property. By reason of the
representations that were made by those
who have the widest possible, experience in
property of this sort, it was thought that
the law should be restored to what it had
been in 1940, and for 20 years previous.
Accordingly paragraph (a) has been reinserted. Paragraph (b) always has been
the law in the case of agricultural property, and paragraph (c) was inserted in
another place.
I do not know whether hon. Members
will remember the speech made by the
Member for South Tyrone in which he
pointed out the hardship of people who
had gone away on war work. Paragraph
(c) covers the case of an owner of property
who has let his house and gone into any
one of the armed Forces. I think it is
most reasonable that when a man in that
position returns he should not have to
provide alternative accommodation.
Paragraph (d) is the Amendment which.
covers the case of persons who go away
perhaps across the Channel to do essential
war work and may have let a house they
owned. I think again it is reasonable in
that case that such a person should be
able to obtain possession of his house
without having to provide alternative
accommodation. There is no change in
the principle of the Bill in that respect
whatsoever. That merely brings back the
law to what it has been for over 20 years.
Paragraph (c) is an extension. There are
some people who would be protected even
with the law as it stands if their valuation
is below £27. Paragraph (c) will now
give that protection to the military, naval
and Air Force owner when he returns
without regard to the limitation of £27.
In other words he can obtain possession
of a house up to a valuation of £75.
The fourth one, I think, is one that will
commend itself to the judgment of the
House. A man who went away to do
essential war work should be able to obtain
possession of the house when he comes to
resume his ordinary civilian avocations.
In the circumstances I suggest the acceptance of the Senate's Amendments by this
House.

I have known of officials in the city of
Belfast who sub-let their houses in 1941
when the bombs were falling and went
away to the country. Now they want
their houses back, and they want to put
out the tenants in the houses.
Of course,
they were on work of national importance
-they all are according to themselvesand all they will have to do now is to jog
into the Ministry of Labour, go to one
of the Assistant Secretaries, get certificates and back they walk to their houses.
If that is not what this is for, then what
is it for?
I would like to move an Amendment
if I am in order. I would move that
paragraph (d) should read this way:
(d) where the court is satisfied that
the landlord, during the period of the
present emergency, gave up possession
of the dwelling-house in consequence of
his having undertaken work of national
importance.
That is, I am eliminating the words
"certified by the Ministry of Labour to
be"; also the next paragraph, because it
is consequential. I hope the Minister
will see his way to accept that Amendment, because he is a lawyer himself. I
want to put the onus on the judge-and
he is well able to bear it, whoever he is
-of making up his mind on the evidence
before him without this certificate.
Supposing I happened to be an official
and I was looking for possession of my
house it would be up to me, with the aid
of a lawyer, to satisfy the judge by
evidence in open court given by witnesses
who could be cross-examined that I was
engaged on work of national importance.
Then the judge would sum up and say,
"Yes, I am satisfied" or "I am not satisfied.' A certificate should not be put in
as evidence when the man who writes that
certificate cannot be examined because he
is not there. I think that the Minister,
who is a lawyer, and a distinguished
lawyer at that, will not contradict me if
I say that the certificate of the highest
medical specialist will not be taken in a
case in the high court. Sometimes it may
be admitted in the lower courts in trivial
cases, but in any High Court action the
greatest medical specialist in England,
Ireland or Scotland must go into court
and give evidence so that the other side
can cross-examine him.
This Clause introduces a new element
into British law. A certificate from an
Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of
Labour is going to be taken as evidence
behind his back in a court, and he cannot
be examined on it. Where are we travelling to? I say that it is the legal profession
that should be defending that well-known
principle in British law instead of a layman like me. Where is the democracy
we are talking so much about and that we
are fighting for if the unfortunate person
in the house gets no hearing once the
certificate of the Assistant Secretary is
produced? It would not be so bad if the
Assistant Secretary had to come to court
to give evidence. Then the other side
could cross-examine him on that evidence,
but as it stands it is extremely bad.
Listen to what the paragraph at the end
says. It is worth reading for the last line.
It says:
For the purposes of paragraph (d) of
this sub-section, the production of a
certificate, issued by the Ministry of
Labour and signed by the secretary or
an assistant secretary of that Ministry,
that the person named in the certificate
was, during such period as may be mentioned therein, engaged in work of
national importance, shall be sufficient
evidence of the fact so certified.
Nothing more is wanted. The Minister
should fall in with my suggestion. The
Senate can get in an Amendment, and in
the interests of the honour of this House
we should put in the Amendment I move
and have some protection for the people.
If it is not put in, all the power I have is
to vote against the Clause. I should like
to vote against the first Clause, but I
cannot see how I can do it at the present
time.

Mr. NIXON: With the permission of
the House, the Minister spoke twice. I
will confine myself to replying to the
points made by the right hon. Gentleman.
The point is whether this Parliament
should interfere with the law of evidence
as we know it that is accepting as
evidence of the fact a certificate signed
by a secretary or Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Labour. The
point is, can that certificate be taken as
evidence in a court? The hon. and
gallant Member for Clifton missed the
point altogether. It is not a question of
whether the Ministry of Labour is the
proper authority; it is a question as to
whether the certificate of the Ministry
should be accepted as evidence of the
fact stated.
I submit that such a procedure contravenes the law of evidence as we know
it, and I am sure the Minister will not
contradict me on that point. The right
hon. Gentleman stated that nobody
would be in as good a position as the
Ministry of Labour to know whether a
man was on work of national importance.
I agree with that. In such circumstances
the Minister would have to go to court
to give the evidence just like and other
person. All the notes in the world would
not change the law in that respect.
If the person seeking possession of a
house wants to prove by an official of the
Ministry of Labour that he was engaged
on work of national importance there is
nothing whatever to prevent such a person from bringing that official to court
as a witness. He will then be examined,
cross-examined, and re-examined. That
is the point and the only point. It is
not a matter of the Minister or the Ministry being in the best position to know.
That point is not contested, but what is
contested is that a certificate from an
official of the Ministry of Labour is, by
this Clause, to be taken, and must be
taken, as evidence of the fact stated in
the absence of that official. That
violates everything we have done up to
the present. It exalts the official.
If a Member of Parliament here or elsewhere has a case in a court, he must go
to that court and prove it in evidence
in open court. He is liable to be
cross-examined, re-examined and crossexamined again on the evidence he has
already given, but the official of the
Ministry of Labour is going to be exalted
by this sub-clause. I am as sure as I
am standing here that there is no one in
Northern Ireland who would be more
surprised at such a thing than His
Majesty's judges. Did any hon. Members ever attend the High Court and see
the way everything is put before the
judge? No matter who the man is he
must come before him. What would His
Majesty's judges say at the present time
if someone put in a certificate from the
greatest professor or the highest man in
Belfast? They would ask: "Where is
He?" and would say: "Take that
away." They would not even read it.
A person went to conduct his own case
and he shoved a letter up to the judge,.
and the judge threw it at him. I think
it was the late Lord Chief Baron, but I
am not sure.
It would not be recognised as regular
in any country but here. An official of
the Ministry of Labour, if summoned as
a witness, has as much right to go to
court as anyone else. If I am summoned
as a witness, I must go and tell all I know
about it or be arrested and committed.
Why should the Ministry of Labour, or
the assistant secretary, be exalted into a
little god? Where are we getting to at
all? I say it is a most foolish and
dangerous thing, and it is not calculated
to help Ulster that any such Clause, should
be included in the Bill. What is wrong
with what I suggest? If a man wants
possession of a house and he is engaged
on work of national importance, he can
go and give evidence himself, and if he
wants corroboration by the. Ministry he
can bring the official along, just the same
as the police are brought to give evidence.
They are officials too, and sometimes
officials of the Ministry of Labour are
witnesses, but this official will be in a
privileged position. What he writes cannot be contradicted, nor can he be crossexamined on it.
I beseech the Minister to drop this, and
I beseech everyone who has the interests
of Ulster at heart, no matter what the
Member for Clifton says, to do nothing
whatever in this Parliament to interfere
with the law of evidence that has stood
for hundreds of years.
Are officials of the Ministry of Labour,
or any other Ministry for that matter,
above making mistakes? Do they ever
make a mistake! By way of illustration,

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ways and Means.
Considered in Committee.

[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
Duty on Agricultural Vehicles.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That it is expedient to amend the law
relating to the duties of excise on
licences for certain mechanically propelled vehicles registered in the names
of persons engaged in agriculture.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): The proposed Amendment to
the law relates solely to the concession
announced by me in the House on 22nd
July, 1943, which has been operative since
that date, but I think I ought to state
again very briefly just what changes in
taxation are involved. A goods vehicle,
registered in the name of a person engaged
in agriculture, and used for the conveyance of his own agricultural produce or
articles, enjoys a very considerable reduction in the duty imposed on a similar
vehicle engaged on general haulage work.
Hitherto, however, the reduced rate of
duty only applied when a vehicle was
carrying its owner's goods. If the owner
wished to use his lorry to carry for a
neighbour, in so far as he was allowed by
the Road and Rail Transport Act, 1935,
the full rate of tax would have had to be
paid.
The concession, as announced, now
allows farmers during harvest-time, but
only during harvest-time, to use their
vehicles to carry other persons' produce as
well as their own or to lend their vehicle
to a neighbouring farmer for agricultural
purposes without incurring any liability
to the higher rate of duty. The period to
be regarded as harvest-time will be defined
for each year that the concession remains
in force by an Order of the Ministry of
Finance. On the occasion of the
announcement on 22nd July criticism was
directed to the fact that the concession was
to be restricted to harvest-time, but this
limitation is, I think, reasonable, as the
concentration of work during the harvest
is far greater than at any other period in
the agricultural year, and the
urgency of need for road transport does
not arise during ploughing and other preharvest operations. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £132,280 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st

of animals, including sundry grants in

Agricultural Services 1680
Supplementary Estimates-
13 OCTOBER 1943
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The gross total set
out in this Estimate for additional services in connection with my Ministry
amounts to £204,290, but against that
there has to be set a sum of £72,010
receipts appropriated in aid. That brings
the net total to a sum of £132,280. The
largest item in this Estimate is in respect
of the purchase and storage of grass-seed.
That was seed of low germination of the
1942 crop. There was in 1942 a very substantial increase in the acreage of grassseed, and in addition the yield of the crop
was up by 25 per cent. These two factors
taken together the increased acreage and
the increased yield-meant that the trade
which normally handles this grass-seed
was simply unable to absorb it. In addition to that there was an unfavourable
harvest and the result was that partly
owing to damage in the harvest and partly
due to the delay on the part of the cleaners
taking in seed a very considerable quantity
of the crop deteriorated and became of low
germination so that it was eventually considered that this low germination seed
should not be allowed to go back to the
farmers for sowing purposes.
It was decided that as an increased
quantity of seed was necessary and the
farmers had responded to that demand it
was only right and fair that the Government should step in and ensure an outlet
for this surplus seed of low germination,
and that the Government should buy and
pass on the seed for the manufacture of
feeding stuffs. The seed was bought at
a price approximately of £35 10s per ton

I think that it is a commonplace well
within the knowledge of most Members
of the Committee, certainly it is well
within the knowledge of those who have
been engaged in the practice of the courts,
that people are brought from a distance
to perpetrate outrages. The object is to
bring in strangers so as to hinder the
police in the process of identification. Of
course, locals act as what I then called
setters, so that the local authority cannot expect to get off scot free. But it is
obviously unfair that when people are

the local authority within whose jurisdiction the outrage is committed. I think
that is a very fair proposition, and I
commend it to the favourable
sideration of the Committee. It implements the promise and undertaking which
I gave on 10th June last. I beg to move.
con-
Mr. NIXON: No one can, and no one
does, quarrel with the statement that it

There is no general quarrel with that

we are entitled to inquire if the police
precautions are adequate.
When I say
that, I am not to be taken as casting any
reflection upon the personnel of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. I have always up-.
held them, and will continue to do so.
Are the precautions adequate? The
other day one man was sent to escort a
lot of money to a factory in the city of
Belfast, and that man was shot dead.
Why were there not two men there? The
Coroner commented on that fact, but no
one is commenting on it more than the
police. Let me tell hon. Members at this
Table that the other men in that particular district were drilling in the
barrack yard. In that district the old
sergeant-major goes on, clicking heels and
marking time in the barrack yard. Men
of twenty years' service are doing that.
They were at it when this happened. I
am not bringing this up in order
reflect on any person, but it has got so
bad that someone has to bring it up.
to
No Member sitting here knows the
mind of the average policeman as well as
I do, not because of my former connection with the police. Somehow they
like me—I do not know why-and I like
them. No one does more to soothe

Any fool would know. If people do not
know they know nothing. Yet one man

That sort of thing is not wanted at all
-clicking heels and saluting and marching

Agricultural Services 1680
Supplementary Estimates-
13 OCTOBER 1943
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The gross total set
out in this Estimate for additional services in connection with my Ministry
amounts to £204,290, but against that
there has to be set a sum of £72,010
receipts appropriated in aid. That brings
the net total to a sum of £132,280. The
largest item in this Estimate is in respect
of the purchase and storage of grass-seed.
That was seed of low germination of the
1942 crop. There was in 1942 a very substantial increase in the acreage of grassseed, and in addition the yield of the crop
was up by 25 per cent. These two factors
taken together-the increased acreage and
the increased yield-meant that the trade
which normally handles this grass-seed
was simply unable to absorb it. In addition to that there was an unfavourable
harvest and the result was that partly
owing to damage in the harvest and partly
due to the delay on the part of the cleaners
taking in seed a very considerable quantity
of the crop deteriorated and became of low
germination so that it was eventually considered that this low germination seed
should not be allowed to go back to the
farmers for sowing purposes.
It was decided that as an increased
quantity of seed was necessary and the
farmers had responded to that demand it
was only right and fair that the Government should step in and ensure an outlet
for this surplus seed of low germination,
and that the Government should buy and
pass on the seed for the manufacture of
feeding stuffs. The seed was bought at
a price approximately of £35 10s per ton
and was sold to be manufactured for feeding stuffs at a price of approximately
£15 10s per ton. These transactions could
not, unfortunately, be completed within.
the financial year. Between 5,000 and
6,000 tons of seed were so purchased and
dealt with.
I think that I can safely say that
whilst farmers may criticise my Ministry.
on some matters they have appreciated,
and do appreciate, what was done for
them in this connection. In regard to
grass-seed, I may add that this year steps.
have been taken to control the acreage,
and arrangements have been made whereby my Ministry will this year be the
purchaser and subsequent seller of all
grass-seed purchased in Northern Ireland.

restore the Estimate to the figure at which
it stopped in the previous year.

What has occurred this year?
Minister of Agriculture has made an

the

for the farmers is British justice. I demand that the farmers be treated in a
proper manner. Farmers here have to
till the same amount of land as the
farmers in Great Britain, but they are,
not receiving the same remuneration.
Why should that be the case? Why
should the farmers here be receiving 50
per cent. less than the farmers in England when they have to do the same work?
Why are the farmers in Northern Ireland prevented from saving seed to sow on
their own land? They are prevented from
doing so under a penalty of £500 or six
months' imprisonment. On every notice
a farmer receives there is a notice in big
black type to the effect that failure to
comply with the order means so and so.
The farmers are entitled to justice, but
at the present time they are treated as
criminals. The time has arrived when
some person must rise in this House and
demand justice for the farmers. They
are only slaves. Why should they have
to stand for this bureaucracy? I demand
that the farmers receive justice.

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I know all

time and again with the hon. Member
over the telephone. I want to say that
the talk that has taken place this afternoon about my Ministry in the time of
my predecessor having cajoled and forced
the farmers to save this grass-seed is not
true to fact. There was no compulsion
on farmers to save the grass-seed of the
1942 crop, just as it was nonsense for the
hon. Member to say that officials from
my Ministry go down and tell him or his
neighbour: "You must put a certain
crop in that field." Nothing of the kind.
ever happened since the war began.
Mr. MINFORD: Of course, it did.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: It is not
true. It never happened. In regard to
the 1942 crop, what happened was that
a very attractive price was offered to
growers of grass-seed, and in addition to
that attractive price being offered it
turned out that they could not get their
hay saved, and they cut it down for
fodder and feeding in the ordinary way.
Practical farmers know that. The result
was that they resorted to the easier way
of saving it by cutting it and tying it
into sheaves. They saved it in that way.
When they cut it they threshed it and
took the money out of the crop. I am
in touch with the farming community
just as well as hon. Members who speak
as if from some height, and I defy anybody to say that the farmers are dissatisfied with the terms they got for the
1942 crop. They admit they got plenty
of money out of the seed and were well
satisfied.
>
I stated in this House on a previous
occasion-I forget whether it was on the
main Estimate that I would see to it
that the policy of my Ministry would be
adhered to, and that no seed would be
offered to farmers for sowing that was
not up to the standard of germination
such as is required. I repeat that.
The Member for Woodvale raised certain points about the workers for saving
the harvest. He referred to the item of
£22,500. That is fairly easily accounted
for. The arrangement, as I outlined
before to the Committee, was that these
workers should be paid at the highest
agricultural rate. in the Six Counties, but
that the farmer who employed them-he
was not their actual employer, because
my Ministry was responsible for accidents,
insurance, and so on, and the Ministry
was the real employer-but the. farmer
for whom they worked was to pay the rate
of wages current in his particular county.
That meant that my Ministry had to be
responsible for the balance. These men
had to be transported to and from the
farms. My Ministry had to find the
petrol for certain of the machinesmachines from civil defence work. Those
machines were under the control of the
local authorities, which had to be recouped for the petrol. In addition, the
drivers of these machines had to work
overtime, and the cost of that had to be
recouped. Some of the workers suffered
a certain loss in wages as their ordinary
employers released them for this service.
That loss had to be made good.
The weather came into the whole
picture, and time and again these
workers could not work at all. The
elements would not allow it. Perhaps
they had not arrived an hour on the farm
until the rain came. They had to go
back home, but they had to be paid.
The question about agency raised by
the Member for Woodvale has reference
to the Ministry of Labour, which performed certain services in connection with
the whole organisation and scheme on
behalf of my Ministry. In fact, it was
to a good extent due to the part that
the Ministry of Labour took in this.
business that the whole scheme worked
so smoothly and so highly satisfactorily
from the point of view of all concerned.
The Member for Antrim surveyed the
whole agricultural services. I have no
intention of following him in that survey.

The CHAIRMAN: If the hon. Member does not want to come to this House
no one compels him to come. There is
no conscription.
was
Mr. HENDERSON: That is the
trouble. I have kept away from this
House because I thought I could do
better service elsewhere, as there
nothing done here for the taxpayers. It
is pure, unadulterated highway robbery
that takes place in this Parliament, and

Question put, and agreed to.
CLASS VII. No. 2.
Fisheries, Harbours, and Commercial
Services.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £133,200 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1944, to defray the expenses of
the Ministry of Commerce in respect of
Fisheries, Harbours and Commercial
Services, including certain Grants in
Aid."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): The total
amount required under this Vote is
£133,200. The first item, Subhead B,
includes a grant-in-aid of £1,000 to
Belfast Harbour Commissioners in respect
of additional landing facilities and an
additional grant-in-aid to Coleraine
Harbour Commissioners for dredging work
at Coleraine Harbour.
The extension of the ferry service across
the Lagan for workers in the shipyard
necessitated the provision of additional
landing facilities. Hon. Members will be
interested to know that the Ministry of
War Transport provided a vessel which
was fitted out at the expense of the
Admiralty, and the Belfast Harbour
Commissioners have indicated their willingness to bear half the cost of the additional
landing facilities. The development of
this ferry service has the full approval of
the Production Council, and the material
help given by the Admiralty and Ministry
of War Transport will convince hon.
Members of the importance attached to
improving and supplementing transport
to the shipyard in this way.
Item C is in respect of grants under the
Civil Defence Act Northern Ireland),
1939, payable to Belfast Harbour Commissioners and Belfast Corporation. The
original Estimate was for £30,000, and
hon. Members are now asked to vote an
additional sum of £119,800. A substantial
part of the supplementary provision represents a re-vote of money provided for in
last year's Estimates, but which, because
of circumstances beyond my Ministry's
control could not be paid out before the
close of the year. The balance is for
additional grants towards the cost of
works which the Government regard as
necessary in the national interest. Hon.
Members will understand that I am
debarred by considerations of security
from going more fully into the purposes
for which the additional moneys are
required.
The Prime Minister, in presenting the
Estimates for his Ministry in June this
year, spoke of the splendid way in which
our women workers are making their contribution to victory. The women of
Northern Ireland are represented in all
the Services, and in business they are
taking the place of men who have joined
up, but it is when I visit our factories
that I realise most vividly just how selfless
is their contribution. It was in the 19th
century that someone observed that
"woman's work is never done." That
was true then, but how many times more
true to-day. There is the work at the
factory, the shopping, the house, cleaning, the making-do and mending which
my right hon. Friend, the President of the
Board of Trade, exhorts the woman of
1943 to carry out faithfully, and in some
cases there is the problem of who will look
after the chidren. It cannot be easy to
concentrate on the careful folding of a
parachute, the exact manipulation of tools,
if you are conscious of a nagging worry as
to whether you remembered to put the
fire guard in position.
The industrial nursery centre enables
the mothers of young children to enter
or return to industrial employment, and
1719 Supplementary Estimates-

13 OCTOBER 1943
Commercial Services
hon. Members are asked to vote the sum
of £10,200 for the establishment and
maintenance of such centres. The total
number of centres covered by the provision
is eight-four being for 25 children each,
1 for 40 children, and three for 50
children each. They are administered for
my Ministry by the Nursery Centres Committee of the Nursery Schools' Association
of Great Britain. At one centre provi-
Ision is made for children under two years
of age, and at another centre which has
not yet been opened special night accommodation is being prepared for the
children of workers engaged on night
shifts. The parents' contribution is 3s 6d.
a week for each day-child, which pays for
food; in the case of the residential centres
the contribution is 10s weekly.
Another new item to which I wish to
direct hon. Members' attention is subhead K.4-Industrial film exhibitions.
In Great Britain the Ministry of Supply
provides a film service to factories engaged on direct contracts for that
Ministry. The films exhibited are
specially selected, and the service is paid
for by the factory managements
concerned.
In April of this year this service was
extended to Northern Ireland for an
experimental period of
months.
two
From 1st June it was made available to
all firms engaged on contracts for the
Ministry of Supply and to establishments
working mainly or entirely for the
Admiralty or Ministry. of Aircraft Production. This was done with the full
approval of the departments concerned.
It is thought that it would be. impracticable and undesirable to insist that the
firms receiving the service in Northern
Ireland should be expected to make payment on the basis prevailing in Great
Britain, and it has been agreed that
payment should be made by the Northern
Ireland Government to the Ministry of
Supply in the form of an agreed sum
related to the number of projection units
employed. The amount which hon.
Members are asked to vote is £2,000.
Two operating units have been provided,
visiting on an average 24 factories a fortnight, and the recoupment to the Ministry of Supply will be on the basis of £100
per month for each unit.
In Northern Ireland the development
of "Works relations," of which this film
scheme forms an important part, has
been, perhaps, slow in gaining general
acceptance compared with other parts of
the United Kingdom, and there is no
doubt that the success of the Ministry of
Supply film service is performing a useful
function in bringing local managements
up to date in this respect. The effect on
worker and employer alike. of the specially chosen films exhibited is to improve
morale, increase a sense of responsibility,
arouse interest in the relation of the
worker and the factory to other aspects
of the war effort, relieve industrial
fatigue, and bring about an awareness of
progress in other parts of the Kingdom
in fields of technique and labour utilisation. It may legitimately be regarded as
a direct concern of the Northern Ireland
Government to assist in furthering a
scheme for achieving these aims, with
their effect on the general well-being of
Northern Ireland industry. I beg to
move.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the hon.
"and learned Member give me a guarantee
that they will not get a film made of this
show here, because-
The CHAIRMAN: That is not in this
Supplementary Estimate.
Mr. HENDERSON: This is to make
a film.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member
knows that he has got to stick to what is
in the Supplementary Estimate.
Mr. HENDERSON: Let me read this
from the Estimate:
The Government has decided that the
scheme operative in Great Britain for
exhibiting films in industrial establishments engaged on essential war work
should be extended to Northern Ireland.
The film service is provided by the
Ministry of Supply and the recoupment
of the expenses of that Ministry has
been arranged on the basis of £100 per
month for each of two operating units.
Payment for the service commences as
from the 1st June, 1943.
I had the honour of being in London
recently in
in connection with housing
matters, but I ask why should we be
bringing films from Great Britain? Why
should we not have films showing what
Ulster is doing for the Empire. Nothing
is being done in that connection at present. The people in Great Britain do not
Supplementary Estimates

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
know we exist. They think we are part of
Eire. I cannot understand the mentality
of this Government, and especially I cannot understand the mentality of the Prime
Minister, who would have been better to
have stayed at home instead of giving a
lecture at the Dirty Club in London. In
this respect I can congratulate the Minister
of Labour, because he encourages the
people to do more work in the war effort.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member is
getting away from the Estimate.
Mr. HENDERSON: I know you do not
want to put me out. You have practically
emptied the House already. If you put
me out there will be no opposition at all,
and you would not like that. If I were
Prime Minister I would have films of our
own made showing the people of England
and Scotland and the British Commonwealth, as well as the United Nations,
what Ulster is doing towards bringing
about the destruction of Hitlerism. Is
there any reason why these people should
not know what Ulster is doing? If the
Prime Minister spent less time at the
Dirty Club and went round telling the
people of London what Ulster is doing
there would be no call to bring films over
here. Let the Prime Minister start and
do propaganda work for his own country
and show what we are doing. It is an
insult to the industrial workers of Northern Ireland that no film is made which
would show what they are doing in the
factories and workshops. I appeal to the
right hon. Gentleman to let us know
exactly when we are going to do propaganda work in that connection.
The CHAIRMAN: That does not
arise. The hon. Member knows it is not
borne on this Vote, and therefore we
cannot discuss it.
Mr. HENDERSON: All I can say is
this, that instead of making films across
the water, they should have a film made
here and let the world see what the loyal
Ulster working men and working women
are doing to help to bring about the
finish of the war. It is not fair to the
workers that nothing is being done to
show what they are doing here.. I do not
mind if the Prime Minister gets filmed
a thousand times so long as he is getting
filmed doing something for Ulster. I
think it is a good thing to bring them

The PRIME MINISTER: I should
like to say to the hon. Gentleman that I
appreciate that point of view.
As a
matter of fact, he can rest assured that
the very point he has raised is being
dealt with. The point really of these
films is not so much what is being done
by workers in England in contradistinction with what is being done by
the workers here. The object of them is

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
No Scrap Metal for Eire.
1. Mr. THOMPSON (for Mr. Dowling)
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
can state if it is a fact that a percentage
of gates and railings taken from the
people's homes, business premises and
public parks in Northern Ireland is going
to Eire, and, if so, what is the percentage;
and whether he will make a statement
for the information of the House and those
directly affected, giving the reason for
this action.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I am glad to be able to assure
the hon. Member that no part of the
metal scrap obtained in Northern Ireland by the removal of gates and railings.
has been, or will be, sent to Eire.
Ministers' Allowances and Income-Tax.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether allowances to Ministers
for contingencies of office are free of
income tax.
Major SINCLAIR: At the present
time no allowances for contingencies of
office are drawn by Ministers. The hon.
Member's question does not, therefore,
arise.
Religious Instruction in Secondary
Schools.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether she can state the present
position in regard to religious instruction.
in secondary schools of Northern Ireland
and what changes there have been in the
matter in the last 20 years, and particularly in the last two years, and which of
these changes, if any, were affected by (a)
the present Minister of Education and
(b) his immediate predecessor in office.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): Governing
bodies and principals of schools have
always been free and, of course, are still
free under the regulations of my Ministry
to provide religious instruction for those
pupils whose parents desire them to
receive it. The position has not changed
in the last 20 years, and the latter part of
the question, therefore, does not arise.
Special Sunday Trains to Dublin.
4. Dr. DOUGAN asked the Prime
Minister whether it is a fact that special
trains have been run from Belfast to
Dublin in connection with hurling and
football matches on recent Sundays, and
if so, whether he will take steps to see
that this is stopped immediately in order
to conserve our coal supply, which is so
urgently needed for war and household
purposes.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been requested by my right hon. Friend
to reply.
The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative. With
regard to the latter part, in view of the
necessity of conserving coal supplies in
Northern Ireland, the Ministry of Commerce convened a meeting with the representatives of the three leading railway
companies in Northern Ireland. It has
been agreed that in general the standards
of passenger service in force in Great
Britain should be adopted in Northern
Ireland.
The principal points of agreement are:
(1) That no extra trains will be run in
connection with sporting events; (2) that
the gross mileage of passenger service in
summer will not exceed such mileage in
1942. This includes the normal July
holidays; (3) that in respect of other
special holiday periods the maximum mileage of a busy non-holiday period in the
corresponding month of 1942 will not be
exceeded; (4) the provisions will not
apply to trains run for Service or war
production requirements.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Uthwatt Report.
5. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether the Government
of Northern Ireland intends to adopt the
main principle of the Uthwatt Report,
which recommends "the -immediate vesting in the State of the rights of development in all land lying outside built-up
areas (subject to certain exceptions) on
payment of fair compensation, such vesting to be secured by the imposition of a
prohibition against development otherwise than with the consent of the State
accompanied by a grant of compulsory
powers of acquiring the land itself when
wanted for public purposes or approved
private development," and whether he
intends to fix an arbitrary price for compensation for land required for development at the values ruling on 31st March,
1939.
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
The
TARY OF THE MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Wilson Hungerford): I
have been asked by my right hon. Friend
to reply.
The Uthwatt Scheme for the purchase
of development rights has not yet been.
accepted in England, and no useful action
can be taken in the matter until a
decision is taken in Great Britain. If
such a scheme were adopted there it does
not necessarily follow that it would be
suitable for application to Northern Ireland, but it is, I think, quite certain that
the Government of Northern Ireland
could not introduce such a scheme here if
it did not operate in England.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I would point.
out that the Uthwatt recommendations do
not involve the fixing of an arbitrary
price for land required for public purposes, but merely the adoption of the
1939 values as the basis from which to
work in arriving at compensation. The
question of whether an arrangement of
this kind would be suited to Northern
Ireland conditions is at present being considered by the Planning Advisory Board,
and the Government will await their recommendations before taking any action
in the matter.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that reply of the Parliamentary
Secretary, when the Government comes to
consider this may I ask them to bear in
mind two facts? One is that the land in
Northern Ireland is vested in those who
purchased that land by the payment of
land annuities, and that they have certain
rights, and that no steps be taken to
deprive them of those rights over the
land by fixing arbitrary prices such as at
31st March, 1939, thereby depriving
them of certain rights over the land; and
is the Minister further aware that the
Planning Commission is reviewing this
matter, and is it not a fact that it should
be reviewed by this House instead of by
the Planning Commission?
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I can
give the hon. and gallant Member the
assurance that all relevant factors shall
be taken into consideration when the
Government take this matter up.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
Minister has already contemplated placing all land in the hands of the Minister
of Home Affairs.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: Most
certainly not.
Mr. NIXON: Most certainly yes.
The Linen Industry.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the present
position and outline the prospects in the
linen industry of Northern Ireland and
the textile industry generally.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been requested
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
For some time past the linen industry
has maintained a rate of activity which
has been comparatively high in the weaving section, and owing to shortage of
suitable material rather low in the spinning section. It is impossible to forecast
even the near future under wartime conditions, but I am hopeful that the existing
level of activity will be maintained at
least for some months ahead.
In the making-up industry there are
indications that it may be difficult to
maintain the high level of activity which
has prevailed for a considerable period,
but I am making every effort to provide
continuity of production.
Mr. BROWN: Arising out of that
reply may I ask the Parliamentary

The B.B.C. and Northern Ireland.
The following question stood on the

"To ask the Prime Minister whether he
can state if he has taken any steps to
secure justice and fair play for Northern
Ireland from the British Broadcasting
Corporation, in view of the fact that there
are daily news summaries for Scotland
and Wales and none for Northern Ireland,
and that the only mention Northern
Ireland ever receives is in the form of
caricatures, mostly of a grossly offensive
nature, fortnightly or even less frequently."
Mr. BROWN: Before asking the question I would like with your permission
and the permission of the House to
make a slight alteration. The word
"fortnightly" in last line should read
"'monthly."
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): While I deprecate the terms in
which the hon. Member has criticised some
of the programmes of the British Broadcasting Corporation, I think the House
should know that the Government have
made representations from time to time.
with a view to securing that the interests
and cultural outlook of Northern Ireland
are accurately and adequately represented
in broadcast features. I am informed
that Scotland has a bi-weekly news summary and that there is no regional news
service for Wales. The House will be
glad to know that the Corporation is
giving sympathetic consideration to the
possibility of instituting a special North-.
ern Ireland news service.
Mr. BROWN: Has the Prime Minister

would think there was absolutely no

Prime Minister give consideration to that
and have improvement along those lines?
Assistant Parliamentary Secretaries.

Major ROBINSON Arising out of

Labour.
DISCHARGED SOLDIERS AND
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state what is the
position of a soldier discharged from H.M.
Forces with regard to unemployment
benefit; whether it is necessary to write
to records of the unit from which the
soldier is discharged to see if the first
statutory conditions are fulfilled; whether
it is a fact that a soldier's contribution in
the Forces are treated in the same way as
a civilian worker, a stamp per week for
all his period of service; and whether he
will instruct all his exchange managers
to show sympathy to our discharged
soldiers who return unfit and help to place
them in suitable employment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): Subject to a few very small exceptions, soldiers are entitled under the
Unemployment Insurance Acts to receive
on discharge a credit of contributions
which gives them the same rights to receive benefit as if the period of service
with H.M. Forces had been insurable
employment. This credit is equivalent to
a stamp for each week of a soldier's period
of service.
The evidence of length of service provided by a soldier's Army discharge is
taken into account in deciding whether the
first statutory condition is satisfied and it
is only if this discharge cannot be produced that a reference to unit records
might become necessary.
I have no reason to think that any lack
of sympathy is displayed by our exchange
officials, many of whom are ex-service men
themselves, in their dealings with discharged soldiers, and I can assure the
hon. Member that no opportunity is
missed of placing these men in suitable
employment.
Mr. AGNEW: Would the Minister be
good enough to explain what the few exceptions are?
Mr. GRANT: I anticipated that the
hon. Member would ask me that question
and I have provided myself with the information. A credit of contributions in
respect of Army service is not given to
deserters, to recruits who are re-enlisted
pensioners not finally approved, in respect
of any complete week for which there has
been a complete forfeiture of ordinary
pay, but this does not operate during the
war.
MESSRS. WHITE, TOMKINS &
COURAGE, TANDRAGEE.
11. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if conditions
prevailing in White's Factory, Tandragee,
conform to regulations as laid down in the
Factory Act, and whether he is satisfied
that every precaution is taken by this firm
to safeguard the health of its workers.
Mr. GRANT: In answer to the hon.
Member's question, I may say that it has
been found that some of the conditions in
the factory occupied by Messrs. White,
Tomkins & Courage, Ltd., Tandragee, are
not in conformity with the Factories Act.
The attention of the firm has been
directed to the various matters and they
have given an undertaking to have them
put right as soon as the necessary materials
can be obtained.
The Department will satisfy itself that
the necessary steps are taken to comply
with the statutory requirements.
Mr. AGNEW: Thank you.

of Agriculture to save all the grass-seed
possible. That appeal was endorsed by
1733 Supply-Agricultural Services- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Report Stage
[Mr. Minford]
the Minister of Agriculture in Great
Britain, and the farmers responded right
loyally, with the. result that the very
good prices offered to the farmers brought
an increased supply in Northern Ireland,
together with an abundant crop. As a
result, there were 6,700 tons left on the
hands of the farmers. At that time, the
noble Lord, the Member for Bloomfield,
was Minister of Agriculture, and it was
decided that the seed cleaners should take
the responsibility.
The cleaners knew the position better
than anyone else, and they decided to
call a meeting. I attended that meeting,
at which it was decided that a deputation
should go to see the Chancellor of the
Exchequer in Great Britain in order to
make the position clear. I telephoned
the noble Lord in regard to that event,
and I must say that no man could have
found a more charitable gentleman to
Ideal with than the then Minister of
Agriculture. He sent his Permanent
Secretary over to Great Britain to interview the powers that be, but I think the
result was not too good. The seed
cleaners of Northern Ireland then asked
me to accompany them on a deputation,
and I said that I would. I got in touch
with the noble Lord, who met the seed
cleaners together with myself, and I do
not think that I am giving away any
secrets when I say that he said that
arrangements had been made to take
back all the grass-seed. At that meeting
the question of what was going to be
done with the surplus seed arose, and the
question was put forward that it should
be sold to the mills for making into cattle
food.
The farmers incurred a loss of more
than £200,000. I said that Parliament
was big enough and good enough to face
up to this loss, but when I came to the
House last Wednesday afternoon, I found
the loss they were facing up to was only
£116,000. There remained still in the
hands of the cleaners the residue of the
1942 seed, which has to be mixed with the
1943 seed. I speak from experience when
I say that no Minister should allow seed
which is two years old to be sown. The
1942 seed would germinate, but would not
have the robust growth to come to
maturity. It should be sold to the mills
for feeding purposes and the 1943 seed
left with a clean sheet.
I was told on the last day that I was
talking nonsense. I am prepared to show
the House a notice put up in all public
places in Northern Ireland warning any
farmer found saving or selling, seed of
1942 who had not already saved or sown
seed in 1942 that he would be severely
dealt with. I claim that the action of the
Ministry has thrown into the gutter
thousands of pounds' worth of the best
material for feeding stuff. It is no
wonder that I feel angry, because I had
to cut 25 acres down with the result that
I lost hundreds of pounds. And I was
only one of many thousands.
This House is perfectly willing to play
its part in the great war effort. I say to
the Minister that he should sell the 1942
seed to be made into feeding stuff and
let the farmers get a supply of 1932 seed.
I was told by merchants acting as agents
for the Ministry of Agriculture that instructions have now been given that the
1942 seed will not be mixed for sale to
Ulster farmers, but that it will be sold to
English farmers. We in Northern Ireland
take a great pride in our produce and we
supply at least three-fifths of the entire
world's supply of perennial and Italian
seed, and I feel that it is wrong for the
Minister to go to-day into the market of
Great Britain and sell the mixed seed.
We are faced with a crisis at the present time. We are looking forward to
the time when peace will be declared, and
with that time in view I want the Ulster
farmers' goods to occupy the high position
they have always held. I plead with the
Minister to discard this old seed. I am
assured by seed merchants-I am not talking of one isolated case-that there is
enough 1943 seed to sow the 1944 crop.
The Ministry of Agriculture have laid it
down that in 1944 no mixed seed must be
put on the market. In April of this year
the monthly Journal advised the farmers
to sow seed in the proportion of one part
Italian to three parts perennial. Then in
the next month's Journal is a notice by
the Ministry of Agriculture that no mixed
seed will be bought in 1944.
say it is wrong. I want to play my

Government in every way possible. I say
without fear of contradiction that Northern Ireland is the key-pin of the seed
trade for the entire world, and what, I
ask, is £100,000 compared with the good
name we have borne? I have always

an

I start now where he left off and demand

The hon. and gallant
Member said:
an
A certain civility is required from
people who sit on the Front Bench.
The Minister's answer now is that we
are going to get mixed seed. That
much is perfectly plain. That is all I
have to say.-(Official Report, 13th
October, Vol. 26, cols. 1713 and 1714.)
We do not get civility. It was an
unfortunate thing that two clergymen
were appointed as Ministers. A clergyman can speak from a pulpit where no
one can answer him back, but if the
Minister thinks back benchers are going
to be treated that way, he makes a great
mistake. He is not in church now, or in
the pulpit where no one can dare, answer
him back. Of all the blunders that were
made, the supreme blunder was in making
Ministers of two clergymen, who should
go back to their churches. I need not
put that further.
I demand civility from the right hon.
Gentleman, and other right hon. Gentlemen in this House. Back benchers are
going to get civility, or they will know
the reason why. They are not getting
civility at present. It is wrong for any
Minister to get up and state that Members
are talking nonsense. Ministers are paid
roughly £1,800 a year to come to this
House and hear what back benchers have
to say. They are not satisfied with that
salary, and now want an increase. I am
not going to discuss that; there will be
another chance to do so later when the
salaries of the Prime Minister and other
Ministers are being inquired into. I
want to make it clear that there. must
be an end to this constant discourtesy
from the Front Bench.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon.
Member has made that point, and he
should continue with the Motion before
the House.

the Minister to give an answer to the
question put by the hon. and gallant
Member for East Down. I hope he will
not evade the issue by asking another
question. The Minister has no right to

when a straightforward question is put
to him. I hope the Minister will treat
the House differently this afternoon.

The following Motion stood on the
Order Paper:
"That this House, having taken note
of the proposals of the President of the
Board of Education for the reconstruction
and development of the educational
system in Great Britain as foreshadowed
in the White Paper presented to the
Imperial Parliament in July of this
year, is of the opinion that the Government of Northern Ireland should now
declare its intention to introduce into
this area, at the earliest date possible, a
scheme providing for an educational
advance commensurate, as far as possible,
with that proposed for Great Britain."
*
Mr. RENSHAW (who was received
with general cheers): I beg to move,
"That this House having taken note of
the proposals of
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I ought to
mention to the hon. Member that it is not

Mr. RENSHAW: Thank you. As a
preliminary to what I wish to say I should
like if I may to quote from a book written
by a very prominent educationist, Professor Hadow, at one time Vice-Chancellor
of Sheffield University. I shall read the
quotation. It sets out the aims of education. He says that education should be
provided for the young people of the
community:-
First, because every one ought in
some form to earn his own living he
must necessarily receive some equipment
for this end. Secondly, because man is
"naturally a citizen" his education
should prepare him, in due gradations,
for playing his part in the political and
economic life of his country, and,
thirdly, all true education should aim
at satisfying the spiritual needs of man,
through the mysteries of religion, the
wonders of painting and music, the
beauty and depth and sympathy of
great literature. Indeed, the essential
value of a man's education may well be
Educational Advance
Educational Advance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Renshaw]
determined by what, in later life, is his
scale of spiritual values.
I consider that this matter of education
will be one of supreme importance once
victory has been won, and that that is so
is evidenced by the steps taken in the
Imperial House to prepare the way for a
reconstruction of educational policy after
the war. In July of this year the
President of the Board of Education
issued a White Paper, and that White
Paper is the basis of my Motion to-day.
It is called a White Paper, but I found
on getting it that it was a lengthy
pamphlet of 36 pages, and it lays down,
in the first instance, the outline of the
new scheme that is being suggested in
Britain. Briefly that is that there should
be nursery schools for children between
the ages of two and five. After that
children will proceed to the primary
school and will remain there till the age
of eleven. At the age of eleven a division
will be made, or, at any rate, it will be
decided at that period what line their
future education should take. Some wil!
go forward to what has hitherto been
called secondary education of the
usual academic type. Others will be
directed more along vocational lines.
There will be a parting of the ways at
that point. There will be a definite
parting of the ways according to the
scheme outlined in this White Paper.`
.
It is also suggested further that education should continue to the age of 15
instead of 14 as at present, and that as
soon as possible that age limit should be
raised to 16. Then following on that
there is to be a period of further education up to 18 years of age, either by remaining in full-time attendance at the
secondary school or by part-time day
attendance at a young people's college.
I suppose by that time the future of the
child will have been pretty well determined--whether he is going to proceed to
the university and into one of the professions. Following on that preliminary
outline of what is proposed there appears
in this paper more detailed kinds of
things. I see in the first heading it
mentions the present system. Of course
the present system referred to is the present system prevailing in Great Britain.
I should like just to refer briefly to the
system as I find it here. We have at
present in the primary schools some
schools that have been completely transferred to the various education authorities
and they are under the control of these
education authorities. They are grouped
together in small groups under school
committees, and I regret to say these
school committees have not functioned
very well up to the present. There are a
great number of schools that have not
been transferred and are operating under
what are called four-and-two committees.
Then there is a section of the community
that have retained complete control of
their schools, and who intend obviously
to retain complete control even in England if we are to judge by the statement
of the Archbishop of Liverpool a few
days ago.
In connection with these transferred
schools, so far as Belfast is concerned, a
great deal has been done to improve the
school accommodation, and splendid new
buildings have been put up, but unfortunately the war came and interrupted
that, so that the completion of the scheme
is being held up for the time being. I do
trust that the Ministry of Education here
will urge the Education Authority in
Belfast and the various local education
authorities to push on this scheme of
providing schools, because in many
country districts the school accommodation is far from satisfactory.
There is also a great deal of understaffing in this connection.
Classes are
far too big and something will have to
be done to alter that. That is foreshadowed here in this White Paper. It
is foreshadowed that the numbers in these
classes in England will be reduced, and I
hope a corresponding reduction will be
made here; that would mean, of course,
the employment of a great many more
teachers. In addition there is a lack of
equipment in many of the smaller schools
that should get attention. That is all I
should like to say under that heading
about the present necessity.
Then follows a considerable. section on
proposed reforms. It takes in detail the
various age limits, two to five, five to
eleven, eleven upwards, and so on, and
it outlines very well what is proposed to
be, done across the water. I should like
to see something on similar lines done
here, and I should like to make this
suggestion to the Minister. Do not stick

too rigidly to age limits in classifying
pupils. My experience has shown me
that you have, broadly speaking, two
types of young people to deal with. One
type is the slow developer, and he
usually goes a long way, very often much
farther than the very brilliant, precocious
youngster. That is why you find men of
eminence coming back to their old schools.
on prize days and telling the pupils that
when they were at the school they never
got a prize. They were of the slow
developing type, but they went a long
way.
The others are the quick developers.
To put a slow-developing child of seven
along with a quick-developing child of
seven is utterly wrong in my opinion.
There is too much of that rigid classification according to age. The pupils
should be classified according to attainments of ability, and I am sure that it
would effect a great improvement in our
education if something of that sort were
adopted.
The next section goes on to deal with
the very thorny subject of religious education, so that this matter of religious
education is covered by the terms of the
Motion that I have before the House.
It is evident that in England it is proposed that a great deal more attention
shall be paid in future to religious

In fact, Mr. Butler, President of the

London, appealed to religious denominations and educationists to avoid unnecessary controversy over the proposals in the

He and his colleagues welcomed interdenominational efforts to re-establish
religion's part in education "not as
political one, using politics in the broadest sense, but as one which concentrated
on achieving victory within the realm of
the spirit." With that, I will pass from.
this thorny topic of religious education.

Then follows the question of the

The next section deals with further
education, and it is not proposed in that
that the child's education should end at
fourteen, or fifteen, or sixteen, because
education never ends. We are all learning all the time. I have learnt a great
deal about low-germination grass-seed and
about the low price of potatoes since I came
into this House. (Laughter.) Rather I
should say that I have heard a great deal,
although I may not have learned very
much. It is proposed that the child's
education should continue past these
normal preliminaries. In that connection, I would refer anyone interested in
this matter of education to Sir Richard
Livingstone's book on the future of
education. That, to my mind, is the
finest contribution to the subject of
education that has been made, for many a
day. He points out the defects of our
system at the present time, and how we
shall have to get back to certain fundamental spiritual ideals in connection with
education if we are to get anywhere.
There is another section on technical,
commercial, and art education. I am not
qualified to talk very much on the technical and art sides, but I do know so far
as commercial education is concerned that
there can be a great deal done for it in
the schools.
Then there is a section dealing with
adult education and youth services, and
we come here strangely enough to the
health and physical well-being of schoolchildren and young people. I would have
thought that that would have come at the
beginning. We are dealing in the schools.
with body, mind and soul, all parts must
be looked after. We must have a properly co-ordinated system of physical
training in the schools. I do not think
that enough attention is really paid to
that matter. We have medical inspections and so on, and there are clinics.
The health of the children has been
looked after in that way. I think there
should be in connection with a group of
schools in a district a regular, properly
qualified organiser of games, one who can
really develop the young people physically.
With regard to mental development, of
course we will require a good curriculum,
and I have said all I intend to say with
regard to the soul part of it.

is,

Dr. LYLE: I rise to second this
Motion, and I should like to congratulate
the mover on his very able and comprehensive speech in support of it. It was
so comprehensive that it has left me very
little to say. I think that any money
which is likely to be spent, and which I
hope will be spent, on improving education in Northern Ireland will be well
invested and pay larger dividends than on
any money previously expended on education here. The mover of the Motion
emphasised the scarcity of secondary
schools in the city of Belfast. I am not
conversant with the scarcity in the city;
I am aware of it in the country.
I am under the impression that there are
fewer secondary day schools in Ulster now
than there were 50 or 60 years ago, when,
under the intermediate system, which, no
doubt, had its faults and defects, but also
had its virtues, there was an intermediate school in almost every village.
I do not advocate small schools; I do
not think they are as good as large schools,
schools which will hold 400 or 500 pupils,
but if we cannot have the best we must
be satisfied with the second best. There
is no doubt that had it not been for those
small intermediate schools-very often
they had only 20 or 30 pupils with one
or two teachers-very many men who in
the last 50 years have risen to eminence
in the professions would not have been in
any of the professions, because their
parents could not afford to send them to
boarding schools. Therefore, I think-1
do not know how it can be brought about
-that there should be some endeavour
made by the Government to increase the
number of secondary day schools throughout the Province.
I hope that the Government will act
be influenced by the views expressed in
some influential quarters and bring in a
scheme of universal free secondary education for the Province. Before any pupil
receives the right to free education from
the State there should be two tests unposed. The first test should be one of
intellectual capacity. The pupil should
prove to an impartial tribunal that he or
she is fit to benefit by extended secondary
education, and that that education will
be of benefit not only to the pupil but to
the community which is expected to pay
for it. The second test should be a means
one. No pupil, male or female, should,
in my opinion, be educated at the expense
of the State if the parents are in a
position to pay for the education of that
pupil. At the present time I know that
county council scholarships are awarded
to pupils whose parents are quite able to
pay for the education of the pupils concerned. I do not think that is a good or
proper system.
I do not propose to deal with the thorny
question of religious
religious instruction in
schools. The White Paper makes recommendations which, under the terms of the
Motion, we ask this Government to adopt.

Mrs. PARKER: I should like at the
outset to congratulate most heartily the
proposer of this Motion, the hon. Member
for the University, on his maiden speech.
It was an extremely thoughtful speech
and one full of suggestions which, I can
assure the hon. Member, will be considered very carefully by my Ministry.
I welcome the oppportunity which this
Motion gives me to make a statement on
the educational proposals contained in the
White Paper of July, 1943, and the applicability of these proposals to Northern
Ireland, coupled with a brief outline of
our educational position here and an indication of some of our hopes for the future.
But before doing so, let me say at once
that we accept this Motion as it is our intention to introduce into this area, at the
earliest date possible, a scheme providing
for an educational advance commensurate,
as far as possible, with that proposed for
Great Britain. The White Paper has
naturally aroused deep interest in Northern Ireland as well as in Great Britain.
Here there has been evidence of a general
desire that this Government should make
its views and intentions known as soon as
possible.
That is one reason why I welcome the
opportunity given by this Motion, for the
general public wants a definite and responsible statement as to our present position, and what steps we consider essential
in the interests of the children of this
Province. Of course I think we start off
with the statement which my Minister has
already made, that it is our sincere and
earnest aim to provide as good educational
opportunities for any child and young
person in Northern Ireland as for his
English and Scottish counterpart. That
is so clear cut and obvious an objective
that I do not want to over-emphasise it by
saying that we want to evolve something
better than the English system, although
I know that we would all prefer to lead
in this respect rather than to be led.
But I do say that we cannot take & blue
print from London and swallow it wholesale or copy it word for word.
I think I cannot make it too clear that
our educational system is by no means the
same as the educational system there. We
have our own particular problems. We
must hammer them out, devise our own
schemes, and be certain that we are planning on our own rules and principles, and
that what we produce is in harmony with
what we have already built. All this will
take time, but we do not intend to waste
time. We must see to it that detail
every
has deep and proper consideration in
order that the pieces may fit together
smoothly and easily and form a well
balanced and effective structure. The two
hon. Members who proposed and seconded
this Motion can rest assured that this is
our intention and that the machinery for
its fulfilment has been in motion for some
time. Now before I go into closer details
may I be allowed to give a very short
summary of the far-reaching White Paper
proposals for the benefit of those who
have not studied them very closely.
The White Paper starts with the child
under compulsory school age and proposes
to make it a duty of the education
authority to provide nursery schools for
these children where they are required.
Then it comes to the child of compulsory
school age-5 years over there, and 6
years over here-and it says that this
child shall go to a primary school until
he or she is about 11. The terms
elementary school and elementary educa-

These are very briefly the main proposals as they affect the child himself,
but there are many others which are no
less bold and far-reaching in their own
way. Higher education and adult education services are to be expanded; the

say, the chief matter embodied in the
White Paper is the abolition of elementary education and the substitution of
primary and secondary education, coupled

age and the introduction of compulsory
part-time education up to the age of 18.
Now, to turn to the position in Northern
Ireland, let us see how these proposals
could be carried out here. I should like
to say it becomes immediately obvious
In the first place and it is right and
proper that I should put these matters
before the House now-our schools all
over Northern Ireland are not controlled
by the same body, which can enlarge one

the whole field of accommodation conformably to the new plan, and decide that

They are controlled by education committees and voluntary managers, both
Protestant and Roman Catholic, and
there are 18 education committees and

where the majority are not controlled by

On the other hand, the problem in

Then there is the question of the young
people's colleges the, compulsory parttime education up to the age of 18.
Again in Belfast and in the larger towns.
the matter is relatively easy. We have

Apart from these purely administrative problems, there are those which I
