by any means exhaust the list.
Hon. Members may say to me, "Have
you set forth all your difficulties in order
to tell us that you are content to plod
along as you are, denying to our children
the educational advantages which are
being prepared for the child across the
water." I can answer that question
immediately with the full authority of the
Government. As I already stated at the
outset, we are determined, as far as possible, to introduce into this area a scheme
of educational reconstruction which will
be commensurate with that proposed for
Great Britain. That is quite definite and
certain, but we will not rush forward
recklessly, and foolishly, declaring that
we are preparing a slavish copy of the
White Paper. From what the mover and
seconder have already said, I take it that
they would not wish for a slavish copy of
the White Paper. This is far too important a matter for loose thinking or for
hasty promises. We must blend our
enthusiasm with realism.
For instance, there is a time lag in
educational administration in Northern
Ireland compared with Great Britain. Our
education authorities are only 20 years
old. We have no widespread scheme of
Hadow reorganisation, such as they have
been working on over there for many
years.
These are difficulties that must
have most careful examination. We have
begun our task-indeed, we have been
working on all these problems for some
time now. We have been surveying the
whole field of educational administration
in Northern Ireland; we have omitted
nothing and we have not confined ourselves to a narrow scrutiny of the White
Paper proposals.
But this is an immense task and one
which it will take a considerable time to
complete. We are at present in the
initial stage where our technical experts,
the inspectors of the various types of
schools and of the various subjects, are
conferring on the strictly educational
aspects of the problem. Other stages will
follow and follow soon. There will have
to be discussion and conference with
education authorities and managers of
schools, associations of teachers and other
bodies qualified to speak with authority
on matters of importance, Government
Departments such as the Ministry of
Home Affairs, the Ministry of Labour,
the Ministry of Agriculture, and last, but
certainly not least, the Ministry of
Finance.
There are, of course, many directions
in which advance should be made, quite
apart from the major matters of
Educational Advance
Educational Advance

secondary education for all and part-time

and accommodation can be made available.
There is the question of a great increase

of clothing and books, the reorganisation
of
our provision for the education of

Paper which will be presented to Parliament. It is too early to say when it can
be presented, but I can.promise that not.
a moment will be wasted.

After all, it is perhaps only a platitude

I hope that when these proposals are

criticised, not to make vexatious criticisms

be
determine that everything possible will be

We on this side of the House defy contradiction of that statement. The worker's
child must leave at the age of 14; the
child of one of the privileged classes can
get to Queen's University or any other
university.
Those children have that right and
opportunity, not so much by merit but
by the very fact of privilege. While

care how many White Papers you publish

ORAL ANSWER TO QUESTION.
Rent Restriction Acts and Ejectment
Proceedings.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if it is a
fact that a blind man named Edward
Kirk, of Boconnell, Lurgan, is being
evicted from his house because of a legal
difficulty which deprives him and several
others of the protection of the Rent
Restriction and kindred Acts passed by
this House for the protection of tenants;
whether he can take any action in this
matter, and, if not, whether he will introduce legislation to overcome this
difficulty.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): The person referred to in the
hon. Member's question has been in communication with me, stating that ejectment proceedings were being taken
against him by the proprietor of the house
which he occupied.
The proprietor is apparently a tenant
purchaser under the Land Purchase Acts,
and under the provisions of the Northern
Ireland Land Act, 1925, which is an Act
passed by the Imperial Parliament, any
attempted sub-letting by him without the
consent of my Ministry is declared to be
void. As no such consent has been sought
or obtained in this particular case, there
is therefore no statutory protection under
the Rent Restriction Acts.
The provision for the Ministry's consent is for the purpose of safeguarding
the security for the repayment of the
purchase money advanced under the Land
Purchase Acts, and the Ministry has
therefore no powers in the matter unless
and until it appears that such security is
being endangered. If, therefore, any
action has to be taken by the Ministry
against the proprietor to restore the
security endangered by an attempted subletting, it would have the same object as
the present proceedings, and would not
benefit the occupier.
As some other cases of a similar nature
have been brought to my notice, I have
directed the matter to be investigated
with a view to seeing whether any legislative action can be taken, and, if so,
whether it is within the competence of
our own Parliament.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
there is a flaw in the Acts designed and
passed by this House for the protection
of tenants during the war, and is it not
a further fact that that flaw and also any
other flaw can be corrected, and that legislation based on war-time necessities can
be passed irrespective of any deeds, or
titles, of sections in any previous Acts?
As the Minister knows, there is a section
that has affected a number of people, and
that is calculated to put a great number
of people on the road without house or
home. Therefore, will he take steps in
consultation with his legal advisers to
bring in such legislation as may be
necessary to give effect to what really was
the intention of the Ministry and the
House when these protection Acts were
passed?
Major SINCLAIR: In actual fact there
is not a flaw but a limitation, and, as I
have already said, this whole question was
raised some time ago with reference to
other cases of a similar nature. The
matter is now under consideration by the
legal advisers, and if anything can be
done it will be done at the earliest
possible moment.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's correction that there is not a
flaw but a limitation in the Acts, whether
it is a flaw or a limitation is it not something that was not foreseen at the time
these Acts to protect the tenants were
passed by this House?
well

be so, but I am afraid that I cannot enter
into the minds of the people who framed

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Planning (Interim Development) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): It would be idle for me to
pretend to the House that this is a simple
Bill. So far as its phraseology is concerned it is in the highest degree technical
and it presupposes, first of all, an intimate
knowledge of the Planning and Housing
Act (Northern Ireland), 1931; secondly,
it presupposes knowledge of some of the
main conclusions of the central planning
committees presided over by Lord Justice
Scott and Mr. Justice Uthwatt respectively; and, thirdly, it assumes a good
working knowledge of the leading principles and objects of good planning.
Be assured that it is no reflection on
our very accomplished Parliamentary
draughtsman when I describe the language
of this Bill as highly technical almost to
the point of repulsiveness. That is absolutely inevitable. The necessity is always
present where you are legislating for the
continuance of an existing code. One
must follow very closely the phraseology
that has already been adopted. There
are obvious conveniences in this practice.
Our own Act of 1931 and the English Act
of 1932 make use of a good many phrases,
some of which have been the subject of
judicial construction already, and therefore it is obviously for the convenience
and information of the public that terms
that have already been used should be
continued.
Perhaps it would facilitate hon.
Members if I stated at the outset the two
main objects of the Bill. These are—(1)
to extend planning control over our entire
Province, and (2) to strengthen control
over development during the interim
period, that is to say the period while
schemes are being prepared by the various
planning authorities. Just one word on
the existing position. Under the 1931
Act only three places have taken any steps
in the formulation of planning schemesthe county boroughs of Belfast and Derry
and the borough of Bangor. I immediately agree with hon. Members that so far
as the Belfast scheme is concerned it has
been quite outmoded by the great destruction in the air raids of April and May,
1941. A very little consideration, I feel,
will convince Members that all land within the Province must come within the
Bill.
I have alluded to the leading principles
of planning. To my mind these are,
first, the production of conditions calculated to secure the maximum of good
health for our entire population;
secondly, the securing of convenience and
comfort of life; thirdly, the most economic
expenditure of such moneys as may be
available for reconstruction and development, and lastly, the preservation as far
as possible of the beauty of our heritage.
Planning Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
in this Province. Of course, this is not
an exhaustive list, but it is sufficiently
long to enable me to illustrate the contention that the Bill must be comprehensive.
Somebody may say that Belfast is the
only sufferer on a great scale from enemy
action, and therefore this Bill need only
comprehend Belfast or at most the larger
urban areas. Such a theory would rob the
Bill of its usefulness. Belfast or the larger
urban areas are not the only places which
have an interest in health, convenience,
economy and the preservation of beauty.
On the perimeter of Belfast and the urban
areas, large or small, you would give the
opportunity for the creation of the very
conditions which are often against what
is required for health, convenience,
economy and the preservation of beauty.
One is only too familiar with the development that has taken place just outside the boundary of the city of Belfast,
or just outside the boundary of an urban
area. There has been little control.
Houses have been erected without any
regard for convenience or comfort. True
it is that by-laws apply in all rural areas
since the passing of the Act of 1931.
Whether they are always enforced with
the same strictness as they would be in
this city or other urban areas is a matter
of some doubt, but, at all events, we cannot have two standards of health, convenience or comfort, and two different
methods of applying such money as may
be available.
Let me give an illustration of that if I
may. I think it is recognised that one.
of the first essentials for the good health
of the population is an adequate and pure
water supply. Plans are in contemplation
with the idea of improving it. Now
planning, I would suggest, should follow
to a very great extent the lines of a water
supply scheme, and so on, because what
will happen is this: A good system of
water supply may be laid down and building and so forth done. Conforming with
that, you will have conditions arising
where there may be an adequate supply
to suitable sites for building and development, but nevertheless if people are uncontrolled they may build elsewhere, and
after a short period there is a demand
for the laying on of water which can only
be done at great additional cost.
The first object of the Bill, I said, was
to bring all land under the planning
schemes. It is proposed to do that after
the expiration of a period of three
months. The reason for giving three
months was that local planning authorities may have some time to look round
them and set about making their plans.
The position is now defined by Section 16
of the Act of 1931. The planning
authorities for Northern Ireland are the
two county boroughs, the six county
councils, and the Belfast Harbour Commissioners. A county council may delegate
its powers with respect to planning to one
of its rural councils; that is, the county
council must consent to the matter. It
may grant all such powers as may seem
good, but it can appeal to the Ministry
if the scheme is so clogged with restrictions as to make it of no value. One
may take it, however, that the planning
statutory authorities are the two county
boroughs, the six county councils, the
Belfast Harbour Commissioners, and such
other rural councils as are from time to
time entrusted with powers by their
parent county council. I have only two
such councils in my mind at the moment.
One is the Castlereagh Rural District
Council, which has been so entrusted with
powers by the Down County Council, and
the Derry No. 1 Council which has
similar powers entrusted to it by the
Derry County Council. In the urban
districts the borough or urban council is
the planning authority.
In making the schemes a very elaborate
procedure has to be gone through. It is
set forth in various sections and schedules
in the Act of 1931. If hon. Members
peruse the relevant sections, schedules
and regulations made thereunder, they
will immediately see that the procedure.
is most cumbersome, slow and dilatory.
Indeed, I venture to say that if everyone
of these planning authorities had to go
through all the procedure laid down, the
plan would not be ready at the end of
this war; it would be after the peace
after the next war that everything would
be done. Consequently, and in order that
their hands may not be tied and the
plans complicated it is essential now that
every piece of land in the Province should
be deemed to be the subject of a planning
scheme or a resolution passed to make a
planning scheme. The object is that
while planning authorities are drawing
up the plans they will not be set at naught
by ill-conceived planning and develop-
Planning Bill—
Second Reading
20 ОСТОВЕЕ 1943
ment which may nullify in a large measure
the efforts made to develop and build in a
reasonable way, and not according to the
fancy of each person, because there can
be no doubt that many of the things that
are complained of to-day as existing in
this city and other urban areas, simply
arose through the fact that there was no
regular plan or development in a way to
secure health, comfort and convenience.
That is the proposal. It is to cover a
period during which local planning
authorities are making their plans, so that
they shall not be embarrassed when they
have. their plans. made and ready to submit to all parties interested, in case some
step has been taken in the interval which
may cut across the plan and make it of
no effect. That is particularly important
where there are neighbouring authorities.
When I come to the Clauses later, I will
go through them in order.
Provision is made for the setting up of
joint committees in co-operation with
neighbouring authorities. It would be,
I think, obviously a foolish thing if, for
example, Belfast has its plan completedand I am glad to say it is in an advanced
state of preparation at the present timethe two rural councils which border on it
decided upon something quite different,
or something that would impede or not
fall in with a plan which I believe, can
be designed not merely for the good and
benefit of Belfast but for the surrounding
rural councils. Clause 1 makes that proposal. I suggest to the House that it is
an eminently satisfactory one. The first
object is to take land as though a scheme
already applied to it.
Clause 2 deals with the setting up of
a Central Planning Authority, and here
may I say that these two Committees to
which I have alluded-Lord Justice
Scott's and Mr. Justice Uthwatt's-both
stress most strongly the desirability of
this sort of control. The question is
what is the best sort of machinery to set
up for Belfast. If the House will pardon
me, I should just like to refer to Lord
Justice Scott's Committee's recommendations on this subject. It is at page 87,
paragraph 234:
During the "interim period" between
the decision to undertake a town and
country planning scheme and the time
when it is finally approved, it should be
made obligatory to obtain the consent
of the local planning authority. before
any building or other constructional
development is allowed to take place.
For this purpose the new legislation
should provide that every local
authority which has not already done
so shall be deemed to have passed a
resolution to undertake a town and
country planning scheme as from 31st
March, 1939.
We have not adopted that recommendation. The date will run for three months
from this Bill becoming law. The report
goes on:
Before granting such consent the
local planning authority should be
under an obligation to refer all such
cases to the Regional Officer of the
Central Planning Authority, in order
to ensure that the granting of consent
accords with the national interest. The
Regional Officer concerned should have
power, after consulting the Regional
Officers of other Departments concerned
to veto the proposed consent, subject to
the local planning authority or the
Regional Officers of any other Government Department concerned having the
right to require the case to be referred
to the Central Planning Authority for
a final decision.

Now that is the recommendation of the
Scott Committee. The Uthwatt Commitee refers to it in perhaps even stronger
terms. At page 57, paragraph 136, of
the report it says:
recom-
In our Interim Report we
mended the granting to the Central
Planning Authority forthwith of powers
of control over building and all other
developments throughout the whole
country by reference to national planning considerations, and we recommended that such power should continue in operation for a reasonable
period after the end of hostilities while
the broad lines of reconstruction were
being worked out. The Government
have recognised the necessity of some
such control, but have stated that they
think that any further safeguards necessary can be provided by strengthening the provisions of the Planning Acts.
and that they propose to introduce
legislation on these lines.
That, in fact, has been done in the
Town and Country Interim Development
Act, which was passed in the month of
June last. The report goes on:

In view of this decision it is unnecessary to do more than to point out that
the whole of the country should be
covered. Many important areas are not
at present covered by planning resolutions, and it appears that the most
convenient method of achieving the
object in view is to provide by legislation that areas not already covered by
operative schemes or resolutions to plan
should be deemed to be subject to such
resolutions; and we recommend accordingly.
Those three last lines I have read are
printed in a much heavier type than the
rest of what I have read to the House.
That is the recommendation of these two
committees, and I need hardly tell the
House that they have attracted the
greatest attention and, I think, general
support. There are certain things, of
course, in them not bearing on this
subject, which will be, I have no doubt,
the subject of very acute controversy. Our
own recommendation on this subject comes
from our Planning Advisory Board, and
that board is composed of representatives
of all the county councils and county
boroughs, rural authorities and urban
authorities, and various other public
bodies such as chambers of commerce and
so forth throughout Northern Ireland.
And they have unanimously recommended
and ask for legislation on the lines indicated by the Bill now before the House.
The House may remember that in reading that extract from Lord Justice Scott's
report allusion was made to how these
authorities might or would be constituted,
and it seemed good in the English Billthe Scottish has not yet been introducedto set up a somewhat different machinery
-in fact, very different. In the first
instance in February last a Ministry of
Town and Country Planning was set up.
Further the country is divided
into
regions and at the head of each region
there is a regional planning officer, and
he endeavours to co-ordinate the efforts of
the local authorities, If he does not
approve of what they are doing he can
veto it, and refer the matter to the
Ministry. We propose a somewhat
different method of approach to this question, and ancillary to the Planning
Advisory Board in August, 1942, a Planning Commission was set up.
This planning Commission consists of
the surveyor of each of our county
councils, the surveyor of the County of
the City of Belfast and Derry County
Surveyor, and also their planning consultant, because Derry City has a planning
consultant for a number of years, and no
doubt when Belfast proceeds to appoint
their consultant to aid the city surveyor
he also will be a member of that Commission. Other representatives on it are
the engineer of the Water Board, the
engineer of the Harbour Commissioners
and the engineer representative of each
of the Ministries. It will be observed
that the representatives of the public
bodies number twelve as against six
others. It seems to the Government that
these public officials are more desirable,
than to set up a number of paid officials

cent. No Bill that is brought before

ever a Cabinet

acting with the approval of the

returned three times. I do not think

But so long as I am here I am going to
exercise my rights as a Member of
Parliament. I want this Bill to go
through in such a way that the greatest
decency and comfort will be provided for
the people of the Province.
Mr. DOWLING: On the question of
planning, I think that this House is
unanimous that something must be done.
It is also necessary that there should be
a check on unwise development, both in
the city of Belfast and outside. As far
as I can judge, the matter that hon.
Members are not agreed on is the delegating of authority to a body of public
officers to act as a Commission. There is
a feeling that, having regard to the importance of the occasion, the Members of
the House should have some representation on that Commission, and there is also
a feeling that if the Committee stage of
the Bill was deferred for a matter of six
weeks there would be a great possibility
of better agreement being arrived at. It
would give an opportunity for the various
authorities to consider the measure and
of trying to get an agreed Bill which
would be to the best interests of all concerned. The Committee stage should be
deferred until such time as the general
public get to know what is in the Bill.
Mr. LOWRY (by leave of the House):
Several matters have been dealt with today. In the first place, I think that the
Bill was sufficiently long in the hands of
hon. Members to enable them to gather
the general principles. Of course, as I
said at the beginning, the technical
phraseology is by no means easy, but I
should say that over three weeks is ample
time for its perusal. Now, as to this
submission to authorities which would be
concerned, it must not be forgotten, that
the Planning Advisory Board comprises
representatives of the two county boroughs,
of every county council, of the rural
councils, and of the General Council of
Municipal Authorities, and that these
men, with one exception, are elected
representatives.
As long ago as February last the
Planning Advisory Board unanimously
asked for legislation in this form, and
the associations, one in particular, the
Association of Rural District Councils,
have approved of the principles of this
Bill, so that the suggestion made by the
noble Lord that it was prepared behindbacks is absolutely fantastic and is moonshine. The Planning Advisory Board,
comprising in the main popularly elected
representatives, have asked for this Bill,
and have asked for it in this form. Their
work has been held up through its not
having been passed earlier than this. It
has been ready for quite a long time.
The Bill is not an exact copy of the
English Act. It has been framed in a
manner which we considered suitable to
local conditions. It is a matter of
moment, and one not to be. disregarded
by any serious assembly, that the House
of Commons in Great Britain, and the
House of
of Lords, have unanimously
adopted these principles, and even some
more drastic. I could not help but
regret when the noble Lord, the Member
for Bloomfield, was speaking that, as he
is entitled to appear in another assembly,
he did not take the benefit of his wisdom
over there to a far wider stage and tell
it to his own noble. House at Westminster. If he had done that, at least
he would have created an element of
Supplementary Estimates 1830
Planning Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Lowry]
hilarity and introduced some degree of
humour into what seemed to me to be a
very solemn assembly that was taking its
work very seriously indeed.
I fear that the noble Lord did not take
the trouble to read the Bill, because it
does not do the things he suggested it
does. All it does is to give time to every
one of our planning authorities, be it
county borough council, county council,
urban council, or rural council which has
got a delegation from the county council,
and to prevent people interfering with
the plan. Why, in this very city not
so very long ago a matter took place
despite the resistance of some members of
the City Council. A building is being
erected, and the result is that the people
who live in adjoining houses will have to
use artificial light day and night. Their
air and their light are being equally
interfered with. If that sort of thing
can happen once, it can happen again if
the planning authorities are not armed
with the powers which we seek to give
to them.
It is suggested that the Bill is going to
vest the Ministry with vast powers. The
Ministry has no more powers conferred
on it by this Bill than it has had since
1931. The Member for Antrim said. he
would never give up the powers already
held of appeal here or there. Is there
any better way of keeping control than
that there should be a Minister responsible here for what he does and on which
he can be challenged? Does the hon.
Member want the people to engage in a
highly hazardous, uncertain and most
expensive adventure of lawsuits? No,
this Bill does not take away the rights
or powers of democracy. It does not
interfere with private enterprise. All
it does is to make sure that our planning
authorities-popularly elected bodieswill get a chance to make their plans
without interference.
How long will the period last? It will
last as long as each planning authority
takes to draw up its scheme. From the
moment a scheme is drawn up the land
within the area of the authority immediately passes away from the control of the
Planning Commission or Ministry, and
the quicker they do it the sooner they
will be out of any sort of control. It is
not a tightening up of the Ministry or
arming the Ministry or anybody with unlimited powers for an uncertain period.
If every planning authority behaves with
all reasonable speed the period should only
be a matter of months. In the meantime
surely it is plain to every Member that
it is not reasonable, whether through inadvertence or some other reason, that
somebody should be permitted to engage
in some building or development which is
bad for the community in general, and
would no doubt be bad for some particular persons near to where the practice
was to be carried on.
I commend the Bill. Ample time will
be given between the Second Reading and
the Committee stage for the consideration
of Amendments that any Member thinks
will make the Bill more worthy, more
easily understood and clearer and comprehensible to everybody. There is no intention of rushing the Committee stage.
Question, "That the Bill be read a
Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee, of the
Whole House for Tuesday next.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Home Affairs.
POLICE PENSIONERS AND
INSURANCE ACTS.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will give
immediate consideration to the position of
men discharged from the R.U.C. with
disability pensions, and their position as
to insurability under the Unemployment
and National Health Insurance Acts;
whether such men are in the same position
as to insurability as men of over 65;
whether he will consider amending the
law to help these men; and whether such
a system operates in Britain in relation
to men discharged from the Police Force.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): Members of the R.U.C.
are excepted from insurance under the
Unemployment and National Health Insurance Acts on the ground that the terms
of their employment are such as to secure
for them provision in respect of sickness,
disablement and unemployment which are,
on the whole, not less favourable than the
benefits conferred by the State Insurance
Acts.
When a man leaves the Force with
a pension he is not entitled to become an
insured person, and he is treated for the
purposes of the Acts relating to contributions as though he had obtained the
age of 65 years.
Members of the Police Forces in Great
Britain are in precisely the same position.
I do not consider that the time is
opportune for recommending to my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour, any
amendment of the law as it affects
members of the R.U.C.
OUTDOOR RELIEF IN ARMAGH,
AND DUNGANNON.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
weekly rate of outdoor relief paid by the
Armagh Board of Guardians and by the
Dungannon Guardians; whether he is
satisfied with the amounts paid and
whether these amounts guarantee security.
Mr. LOWRY: As the hon. Member is
no doubt aware the administration of outdoor relief is a matter entirely for the
board of guardians concerned which takes
into consideration the circumstances in
each case before authorising any payment.
I have no reason to believe that the
amounts granted in the individual cases
in the unions referred to are inadequate,
but if the hon. Member will draw my
attention to any cases which he considers
should be investigated I will deal with
the matter..
There is no "weekly rate" of outdoor
relief, each case being dealt with on its
merits.
The average payment of outdoor relief
in the Armagh and Dungannon Unious
is 8s and 88 8d per week respectively.
Mr. AGNEW: Scandalous!
ARMAGH AND DUNGANNON
LABOURERS' COTTAGES RENTS.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can explain why
the request from tenants in labourers'
cottages in Dungannon and Armagh rural
areas were refused right of inquiry into
the increases in rents; whether the
Ministry took into account before authorising increased rents the wishes of the
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
26 OCTOBER 1943
tenants; and whether it is a fact that
increased rents have been caused by the
neglect of rural councils to look after the
property and by the employment of
handymen.
Mr. LOWRY: In considering the request from the Dungannon and Armagh
Rural District Councils for authority to
increase the rents of labourers' cottages
the Ministry had before it the representations made on behalf of the tenants and
also special reports by the Ministry's inspector. All relevant circumstances were
given careful consideration and the
Ministry was satisfied that a public
inquiry was unnecessary.
The answer to the second part of the
question is in the affirmative, and with
regard to the last part of the question I
do not agree that the increased rents are
due to past neglect of the rural councils
concerned. I would remind the hon.
Member that each of these rural district
councils has in the past given special attention to repairs of cottages, and is at
present engaged in formulating an extensive scheme of repairs.
Mr. AGNEW: Is it not a fact that
certain cottages will not be increased
owing to the fact that repairs have not
been carried out?
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. Member is
quite correct. In cases where the state of
repair is such as, not to warrant an increase no increase has been sanctioned or
will be sanctioned until the cottage is
placed in a proper state of repair.
Mr. AGNEW: Will the right hon.
Gentleman give an assurance that he will
be definitely certain that the repairs will
be carried out by men competent to do
the job and not by handymen ?
L
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the right

labourers' cottages in Northern Ireland

Mr. LOWRY: I am glad to be able to

HOUSING.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
drawn to the announcement made by Mr.
Ernest Brown, British Minister of Health,
on the 1st instant, that local authorities
in Great Britain have now been given the
right to give permission for any repairs,
renovations and alterations of existing
houses up to £250 per house; that
authority has been given for the conversion of old houses, which are too big and
cumbersome for modern families, into
flats and maisonettes for two or more
families, within the limit of £250; and
the conversion of vacant mansions into
homes for three families; that local authorities may also complete houses started
before the war; that the new plan applies
not only to council houses, but also extends to private owners who wish to
repair or convert their property up to a
limit of £250 and who can now apply to
their local council for a certificate that the
work is essential to avoid danger to health
or grave deterioration of structure; and
whether the Government of Northern
Ireland are keeping in step with Great
Britain in this matter.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first five parts of the
question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I would point out to the hon.
Member that the main object of the
English scheme is to endeavour to arrange
that after the demands for war purposes
have been met, housing should have the
first call on immobile building labour. In
England there is an acute shortage of
labour in the building industry owing to
conscription, but in Northern Ireland the
labour position is very different, and the
need for an identical scheme in Northern
Ireland does not arise.
No doubt the hon. Member is aware
that local authorities in Northern Ireland
have already carried out extensive repairs
to houses damaged by enemy action and
that the Belfast Corporation alone has
repaired over 45,000 houses. My Ministry
has had the responsibility of supervising
this work on behalf of the War Damage
Commission, and I should like to emphasise that the work has been performed on
a very large scale.
With regard to the requisitioning of
houses and the conversion of large houses
into flats, as I stated in the House on the
Second Reading of the Rent Restriction

Agriculture.
FRESH FRUIT REGULATIONS.
9. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has considered the
new regulations dealing with Fresh Fruit,
etc., and the Restriction in Dealings
Order, 1943, as it applies in particular to

a
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The answer to the
first part of the hou. Member's question
is in the affirmative.. As regards the
second part the Ministry is following
generally the procedure adopted by the
Ministry of Food in dealing with applications for licences made by traders in Great

CORN CROPS IN TULLYWINNEY
AND DRUMHERRIFF.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can give any information with regard to the saving of the
corn crop on lands in Tullywinney,
Camlough; whether he has received a
complaint as to any neglect and carelessness; whether a quarter of the corn crop
consisting of 4 acres was left on the
ground through bad supervision and
handling of machinery; whether the crop
at Drumherriff was saved; whether a
similar state of affairs existed in this case;
whether he can state the cost of raising
this crop and the value of the straw and
corn.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The oat crop
on the lands at Tullywinney has now been
saved and threshed. One complaint has
been received regarding loss of crop. Of
the total area of 4 acres in Tully winney
less than one quarter of an acre was lost.
I am satisfied that the loss was due to
causes other than neglect or the bad
handling of machinery. The crop at
Drumherriff has been saved in good condition and has been threshed. There was
no loss except some shedding of grain due
to weather conditions.
I regret that as all the accounts have
not yet been received, I am unable to give
the particulars requested in the last part
of the hon. Member's question.

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I am pleased
to say that arrangements are being made
for the issue of acreage payments for land
under potatoes, flax, wheat and rye for
the 1944 season on the same basis as for
the 1943 season. These payments will be

statute acre for lands certified under

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
The
MacDermott): This Bill comes before
the House in its usual form. It proposes
that certain measures which in the
ordinary course, would expire at the end
of this year shall be continued
another year, that is, during 1944. The
measures in respect of which this extension is sought are set out in the Schedule
of the Bill. In Part I is set out the only
Imperial measure affected by the Bill,
for
that is, the Harbours, Docks and Piers
(Temporary Increase of Charges) Act,
1920. As hon. Members will recollect,
that measure was passed by the Imperial
House after the last war to enable harbours to have. their rates increased so as
to meet the increased cost which had
arisen during the war.
It has been continued here as a temporary measure ever
since. Although it is not applicable to
so many authorities as formerly, it is
still necessary to retain it on the Statute
Book for another year. The present
time is, of course, not one in which one
can very well frame a permanent
measure, having regard to the instability
of monetary values.
The second part of the Schedule contains measures of this Parliament which
it is proposed should be extended for
another year.
The first measure is the
Local Government (Emergency Powers)
Act, 1921. This measure empowers the
Ministry of Home Affairs to deal with the
case in which a local authority has refused, failed or is unable to perform all
or any of its statutory functions, by
appointing a person to exercise or perform the powers and duties in question.
The Act also enables the Ministry to
make provision for the resumption by the
local authority of its powers and duties,
and, where it has been dissolved, for its
reconstitution. In the opinion of the
Government the time has not yet arrived
when this measure can be allowed to
expire.
The next measure in this part of the
Schedule is the Local Authorities and
Jurors Book (Temporary Provision) Act,
1940. The Act provides for the postponement of local elections and the extension of the term of office of the existing members of the local authorities. It
is an emergency measure with which the
House is already familiar, and the
circumstances which made its passing
desirable are still with us.. The next
measure in this part of the Schedule is
the Housing (Temporary Accommodation) Act, 1942. This Act provides for
the temporary relaxation of certain bylaws and enactments regulating the
erection of houses and buildings for
human habitation. It was passed to
afford some relief in housing conditions
arising from the war, and particularly as
the result of enemy air raids. It is too
Appropriation (No. 2) Bill 1848
Expiring Laws Bill
26 OCTOBER 1943
That
of
soon to assume that its usefulness is
ended. It is proposed that that also shall
be continued in force for another year.
The next Act is the Agricultural Wages
(Flax Workers) Act of last year.
measure provided for the fixing
standard rates of wages for flax workers
by the Agricultural Wages Board for
Northern Ireland. The reason for the
passing of the measure is still operative,
and it is necessary it should be continued
for another year. The last Act in the
Schedule is the sale of Ice Cream
(Temporary Provision) Act of last year.
This was another war-time measure, the
principal provision of which was. to
suspend the statutory requirements that
milk fat and no other fat should be a
constituent of ice-cream sold. As hon.
Members are aware, the selling of icecream is at present prohibited by order of
the Ministry of Food. It is still necessary
to relieve vendors of ice-cream from the
obligation to make cream or milk fat an
ingredient of ice-cream. These are all
the measures it is proposed to continue in
force for another year. I beg to move.

Mr. AGNEW: The Local Government
(Emergency Powers) Act gives an opportunity for discussing in this House the
position of the Armagh Urban District
owing to the fact that for the last nine
years we have had a commissioner in

for those who had control of the destinies
of Armagh at the time of the dissolution
of that particular local government body,
I feel that the time is appropriate for the
people of Armagh to have the right to
elect their own government in so far as
local affairs are concerned. I feel, as representing the Labour Party, we have a
right to ask this House for the removal
of the commissioner, simply because the
Labour Party at the present time holds
the Armagh seat on the County Council.
We are, practically speaking, the voice of
the working-class inhabitants of the city.
I feel that the time has arrived for the
removal of the commissioner and for
giving us the right to utilise
democratic rights and form the local
government which we desire to form.
our
There may have been things done by the
late council when the Labour party were
not in any way associated with the official
representation on that council. We feel
we have a just right to ask to-day for
this, as the commissioner is a burden on
the ratepayers. The local government
body, which would be elected, would be
free from any burden on the ratepayers
as no salary would be paid to any member
of the council. So far as I recollect it is
something like £400 a year. We have
had a pretty long spell of the commissioner. When it came to pass that other
areas were subject to correction it was
very strange that instead of dissolving
the council they appointed administrators.
They did not treat us so well in Armagh.
At the same time I would appeal to the
responsible Government authority to give
due consideration to the position Armagh
is in. Labour has held the fort in
Armagh, and as the representative of the
county I feel we have a just right to ask
for this. We have the people behind us
in the claim. It is not an unjust claim.
The Government's duty is to give the
people the right to democratic election in
their council in Armagh and I would ask
them to give consideration to it.

Prices for Farm Produce.
The following Motion stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Minford :
That in the opinion of this House the
Government should make representations to the Imperial authorities with
regard to the prices given for some farm
produce (such as potatoes and barley)
so as to ensure that the Northern Ireland farmers receive the same prices for
these commodities as the farmers in
Great Britain, thereby encouraging
greater production for the war effort.
Mr. MINFORD: Although I have not
gathered together all the facts that I
should have desired I rise to move the
Motion. I was under the impression that
the other Motions on the Order Paper
would have been taken before this one,
hence the reason for my not having all the
facts gathered together, but as this Motion
has been so long on the Order Paper it
should be taken now. I am quite sure
that the matter mentioned will receive the
consideration of every hon. Member,
I should like the words "and barley"
to be deleted, as I understand the prices
for this commodity have been fixed. I
am not going to discuss what happened
when I rose in this House three weeks
ago, but I hope that a similar thing will
not take place to-day. We are at present
engaged in one of the greatest wars the
world has ever known, and we have been
asked by the Ministry of Agriculture,
who are the agents for the Ministry of
Food in Great Britain, to grow all that
it is possible to grow. Speaking as a
practical farmer and as one who represents
an agricultural constituency I cannot see
why we should be asked to obey the Tillage
Order to the same extent as those in
•
England and Scotland, and at the same
time receive such a miserable return for
our labour.
There are nine zones in Great Britain
and Northern Ireland, and Northern
Ireland is the lowest priced zone-No. 9.
The farmers in Northern Ireland and their
workers are at least entitled to the same
treatment as the farmers and workers in
Scotland and England receive. I understand that across the water something like
£3 per ton more is paid for potatoes than
here. The price in Northern Ireland is
£3 10s Od per ton, and on this figure
farmers are not able to make ends meet.
I fail to see why this House should permit
the farmers of Ulster to be harassed by
these low prices.
We were told by the Prime Minister,
Mr. Churchill, that we are the most loyal
people in the world. He also said that
we saved civilisation, because we opened
our ports to Great Britain. I believe that
if our Prime Minister would take his
courage in his hands and tell the British
Prime Minister what is in the minds of
hon. Members of this House it would be a
good thing for all concerned.
As far as I am aware the average crop
of potatoes in Northern Ireland works out
at between six and seven tons to the acre.
The authorities asked the Farmers' Union
to give costing figures. They returned
the figures of 12 respectable farmers, but
I understand some Ministry across the
water has asked for further figures. In
my opinion it takes £40 to produce one
acre of potatoes. If the Ministry's figures
are right-I have no doubt as to their
accuracy that there are 6 tons to the
acre then, at £3 10s Od per ton, that
comes to £22 15s Od. There must be
added to that the £10. If these figures
are correct they show that the farmers in
Ulster are producing potatoes at a loss of
from £6 to £7 per ton. It is not a question of whether or not the farmer will
produce potatoes. He has got to produce
them.
Some months ago the right hon. Gentleman was evicting one of the most loyal
men in Ulster because he refused to obey
the Tillage Order. The man had been
fined £45 and paid the full penalty of
British justice, but the Ministry were not
content-they took an out-farm of 29
acres from him. The man said that so
long as they left him the home farm he
did not mind, but I was shocked when this
Prices for Farm Produce 1856
Prices for Farm Produce

man's brother-in-law, Mr. Peel, who is
the chairman of the Antrim Unionist
Association, came to me and handed me
the eviction order. They evicted the man
from his home on the 13th June. If that
is the reward that farmers are to receive
for their loyalty what can we expect?
That may
not be relevant to potato
prices, but if a farmer is going to have
good husbandry he must put in potatoes,
otherwise he will not be allowed to keep
his farm. If the Ministry is going to
evict a man from his holding then I say
it is wrong that he should be compelled
to grow potatoes for which he receives
only £3 10s Od per ton. The distributor
is getting £8, plus £1 10s Od, making a
total of £9 10s Od. The farmer gets £3
10s Od per ton, plus £10 for each acre of
potatoes he grows, which gives him
approximately £5 per ton. I have told
you the price which the farmer in Great
Britain receives, but in addition to that
he gets £10 for each acre he grows. It is
perfectly true to say that the farmers in
Aberdeen and in the north of England
are receiving only £1 5s Od to £2 per
ton more than the farmers in Northern
Ireland. During war-time when we are
compelled to till our land surely we are
entitled to a decent price for what we
produce?
I am informed that the potatoes
shipped to Great Britain are being sold
for the feeding of cattle. Farmers here are
not allowed to feed their stock with them,
yet when they are shipped across the
water the British farmer can feed his
pigs with them. Is that justice? All I
ask for is justice. I attended a meeting
in the best farming district in Ulster.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Oh, no.
Mr. MINFORD: One of the best.
Mr. ELLIOTT: One of the best.
Mr. MINFORD: If the Minister had
attended that meeting he would have
heard what the farmers think. The Press
gave some publicity to what occurred.
Is the Minister aware that the. farmers
are on the point of revolution.
What
is happening throughout the country at
the present time? A man came to me
this morning and told me that he had
91 acres of bad tillage land, of which 25
acres were. termed arable by the Ministry,
but they are letting him off with four
acres less according to the quota, though
they are asking him to spread 14 tons of
slag on mountain land, despite the fact
that he told me he has manured as much
of his land as possible. I telephoned
Stormont about it, and the official told
me that he would look into it. What I
say is that somebody should be appointed
to look after these things either back
benchers or agricultural experts from
outside, the same as is done. in Great
Britain-so that we can get justice.
We have no redress in this House from
officialdom. If we do not do what we
are told, we are fined; if we do not do
it another time, we. are evicted. In the
Prime Minister's own constituency in Co.
Fermanagh there are farmers to-day who
are not paying their land annuities, and
yet they are let off. They did not obey
the Tillage Order. Yet when you come
to my constituency there is thrown on
to the roadside one of the most loyal
farmers. Is that the reward in Ulster
for loyalty? We are entitled here to the
same conditions as in Great Britain.
This afternoon I had only a minute or
two to look up facts in connection with
this Motion, but I did find this statement
by Mr. Hudson:
There are people who say that we
are cashing in on the fertility of the
soil. If I felt that I was responsible
for a policy of that kind, I would not
sleep comfortably at night. I would
think it disastrous.
I should like to ask, what is cashing in
on the fertility of the soil? If a farmer
goes on ploughing and sowing the same
land year after year, it is disastrous to
the farmer. It is not getting the food
we want at all. I would suggest to the
Minister of Agriculture that he should
go to Great Britain and tell the Minister
of Agriculture there that our farmers,
owing to the climatic conditions and the
state of the land here, could grow more
food with less tillage, because the farmer
could pick the land to till and could pay
more attention to it, which would mean
a greater increase in food. Further, if
there were more grassland there would
be more beef and more milk. I see that
Lord Woolton told 300 land girls, at a
Women's Land Army rally, that we are
running into a world shortage of food,
and in twelve months' time we shall be
fortunate if we can still have 1s 2d worth
of meat. As a practical farmer I say

are living in the wettest part of the
British Isles, and yet not a word is heard
about any such project.
I was responsible to-day for passing on
a sample of 14 tons of barley which had
to be cut with a combined harvester owing
to the climatic conditions prevailing.
When it was taken to the Port Area
Committee they said it was too damp. I
then telephoned the Ministry of Agriculture and was told that I could sell it for
feeding at £14 per ton. If the farmer
had had a grain drier-silo available he
would have saved the difference between
£14 a ton and £26 10s per ton. All I
demand for the Ulster farmer is equal
citizenship with the British farmer. I
do not think any man can say that is asking too much.
In regard to milk, I say that the milk
question in Ulster is deplorable. The
Ministry have taken over all milk in
Ulster. I will read to the Minister in

Great Britain:
Lord Woolton, Food Minister, has
invited the Central Milk Distributive
Committee to prepare a detailed draft
of a scheme it has outlined to him for
reconstruction of the milk industry.
The plan visualises the setting up of
a Milk Industry Council under an independent chairman and vice-chairman,
consisting of nominees from the
Ministries of Food, Agriculture, and
Health, the Board of Trade, and producers, distributors and manufacturers.
This council would be the statutory
buyer and seller of all liquid milk,
would fix prices between producer and
consumer, exercise the control now in
the hands of the Food Ministry, and
carry out activities which the Milk
Marketing Board now performs on behalf of the Ministry.
No man can turn a blind eye to the
milk question in Northern Ireland. Here

took out a licence in May for selling milk.
He began on 1st June to sell milk to the

said to him, "Go up and show it to the

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I wish to
ask the mover and the seconder of this
Motion to withdraw it. I think there is
every likelihood that they may when I
have explained the position. I think that
on reflection they will realise that practically the only leg that a Motion of this
kind has to stand on at the moment is
potatoes. They are the only crop of
which it can be said that there is this disparity. Since the beginning of the war
it has been the policy of my Ministry to
make constant representations and to
fight, I might also say, to get a common
level of prices for primary producers
throughout the United Kingdom.
The line of approach to that policy has
been that whatever might have been the
situation pre-war, since the outbreak of
war farmers in all parts of the United
Kingdom have been asked to do a certain
job in the national interest. It is not a
question any longer of a man being a
farmer entirely for what he can make out
of his farm. He is asked in the national
interest to do certain things, and indeed
in parts of the United Kingdom he is
actually directed to do certain things
whether he likes doing so or whether he
does not. Basing our case upon that
position, which I think is the real
Prices for Farm Produce 1864
Prices for Farm Produce
26 OCTOBER 1943
position of the farming community
throughout the United Kingdom, as they
are all doing a job of the same importance,
we have staked the claim that they deserve to be remunerated on the same
basis. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is no new thing. It has not arisen
since this Motion was tabled in this
House. It is the policy that we have
been advocating and pressing, and I
think that if Members from farming
constituencies will just reflect, they will
realise that we have actually achieved it
in regard to practically every commodity
but potatoes. We are getting the same
prices for our livestock. We are getting
the same prices for our milk. I believe
that if the figures for milk were worked
out there is at the present moment a
decimal point in our favour as compared
with Scotland.
The same applies to barley, which was
put in as an instance when this Motion
was drafted. When I read the Motion I
knew that the mover and the seconder
could not make any case in regard to
barley, as the scheme, price, and everything else are identical with those in
Great Britain. There are actually
instances where the producers in Northern Ireland are getting better prices
than producers of the same commodity in
Great Britain. Take tomatoes, apples,
and so on. Who can say that apples are
a small thing, having regard to the returns of money that our fruit growers got,
for instance last year, for their apples?
The fruit orchards were better than those
in any other part.
Up to the moment we have failed to
secure a uniform price for potatoes for
growers throughout the United Kingdom.
We readily recognise that. What did
happen at the outbreak of war and since
then I have tried to explain it as best
I could in this House on previous
occasions was that the Ministry of Food
took up the position that they wanted all
potatoes that we could encourage farmers
to grow. They wanted them for direct
consumption, and they wanted them as a
food reserve, not knowing what the
position in regard to imported human
food stuffs might be. But they drew the
line, and they continue to draw the line,,
at the Ministry of Food taking over the
whole potato crop in the United Kingdom.
They took the prices just as they stood at
the outbreak of war, and those who have
any knowledge of the potato trade know
that prices for potatoes pre-war varied
from district to district in Great Britain,
and that there was a variation as between
North of Ireland prices and prices in
other parts of the United Kingdom. Our
merchants had to have some scope in
which to trade. They were not going to
buy potatoes from the growers here in
Northern Ireland, ship them, find a
market on the other side, and pay all
transport costs for nothing. That meant.
that there was a very considerable gap
pre-war between our prices and the
prices in Great Britain.
What the Ministry of Food did as regards potato prices was to take the
situation as it then stood, and for every
statutory increase in wages and in the
cost of production to give the farmers in
Northern Ireland the same percentage increase as to the farmers in Great Britain
who were growing potatoes. The result
has been that for every increase that the
English or Scottish crop has got we have
got a similar increase in price, but the
basic gap between their prices and ours
still stands. That is the problem that we
have been grappling with. We have been
making the most urgent and persistent
representations to the authorities in
Westminster to have this basic difference
levelled up as soon as possible.
There are, I think, speaking from
memory, five different sets of prices for
potatoes in England, and there are at
least two for potatoes of the same name
and variety in Scotland. When this
Motion asks that we should make representations to have the same price for
potatoes here as in Great Britain it does
not make sense because there are so many
prices for potatoes in England and
Scotland that I do not know which price
the hon. Members are talking about.
Therefore I can assure the House that
we are making and have been making for
a considerable stretch of time the very
strongest representations possible in
regard to these prices of main crop
potatoes. We are still doing it. The
whole question is under consideration in
London at the present moment. Even
the Prime Minister has taken a hand in
the matter, and he along with my
Ministry has made very strong representations in regard to altering the whole
position. I do not see how if the Motion

HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 27th October, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
WRITTEN ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Removal of Gates and Railings.
CHERRYVALLEY PARK, BELFAST.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that a notice
was served on Mr. William Stewart, of
Cherryvalley Park, Belfast, for the removal of a gate which, if taken away,
would leave this small holder's property
lying open; whether it is a fact that this
gate prevents the reopening of an old
right of way through the property which
was closed some years ago; whether the
policy of the Ministry in this instance is
calculated to lead to trespassing and a
consequential depreciation of the holder's
and other property in the vicinity.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I am aware of the notice in
question, but do not accept the view that
Mr. Stewart's front gate prevents the reopening of a right of way. The reference.
to a right of way presumably relates to a
private passage between Mr. Stewart's
metal front gate in Cherryvalley Park and
the wooden field gate opening from
Wynard Park. The latter field gate is
padlocked and, in addition, there are two
other wooden gates across the passage
fitted with padbolts. Trespass through
Mr. Stewart's garden on to the adjoining
agricultural land is thereby precluded,
and the policy of my Ministry in this case
differs in no way from that which governs
the removal of gates throughout the
United Kingdom.
CONSIDERATION OF INDIVIDUAL
CASES.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if he is
prepared to set up an independent
tribunal to hear the appeals of persons
who feel aggrieved over the removal of
gates; whether the policy now being pursued of allowing a department which
requisitions gates to decide on appeals is
a negation of elementary justice; and
whether in view of the anomalies existing
in the present system as it operates in
Northern Ireland he will ensure that
legal guidance is made available to the
heads of the department concerned in
order to prevent further inequities.
Major SINCLAIR: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the negative.
The reference in the question to appeals
is apparently based on an incomplete
understanding of the legal position as the
powers conferred in this matter by the
Defence Regulations admit of no appeal.
As is generally known, my Ministry in
the collection of gates and railings is only
acting as agent for the Ministry of
Supply, and, therefore, follows the practice of the competent authority in Great
Britain, i.e., to give careful consideration
to representatives on the facts of individual cases. Suggestions of inequitable
treatment are examined under this procedure and no question of legal guidance
arises.
Numbers of Unemployed in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the present
total of unemployed in Northern Ireland
or alternatively the total at the last date.
for which exact figures are available, and
how many of these, or alternatively, what
proportion of these unemployed are building trade operatives or former employees
of any kind in the building and allied
trades.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The latest information available
regarding the numbers unemployed in
Northern Ireland relates to the position
at the 18th October, 1943.
The number of men aged 18 and over
then registered as wholly unemployed was
6,064; the number of women aged 18 and
over was 3,058; the figure for juveniles
was 1,251. In addition, there were on
the register at the date of the count
2,221 persons who were either temporarily
suspended from work or were normally in
casual employment. Of this figure of
2,221, 38 were juveniles.
The total number of persons aged 18
and over unemployed on the date of the
count was, therefore, 11,305.

Finance (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Major SINCLAIR: On the 22nd July
last when I first announced the concession,
and on the 13th of this month in moving
the Ways and Means Resolution on which
this Bill was brought in, I explained to
the House just what change in legislation
was proposed, but for the convenience of
hon. Members I propose, at the risk of
repeating myself, to refer again to the
details of the concession, which has been
in operation with the approval of the
House since the announcement on 22nd
July, which I have mentioned.
Goods vehicles registered in the name
of a person engaged in agriculture and
used on the roads solely by that person
for the conveyance of his own agricultural
produce or articles required for his own
land, pay a substantially lower rate of
tax compared with goods vehicles engaged
on general road haulage work. For example, a lorry exceeding 1 tons, but not
exceeding 2 tons in weight, unladen, is
normally taxed at the rate of £25 per
annum, but the reduced rate of tax applicable to the agricultural vehicle is only
£13 per annum. The reduction in tax,
however, as I have just stated, was only
operative when a vehicle was carrying its
owner's goods, and if a farmer wished to
use his lorry to carry for a neighbour, in
so far as he was allowed by the Road and
Rail Transport Act, 1935, he would have.
Under
had to pay the full rate of tax.
this Bill a farmer will now be allowed to
use his vehicle during harvest-time to
carry other persons' produce as well as his
own, or to lend his vehicle to a neighbouring farmer for agricultural purposes,
without incurring any liability to the increased rate of duty, thus facilitating the
provision of the maximum amount of
transport during the crucial period of getting in the crops. It will be noted that
the period of the concession is to be
defined in each year by an Order of the
Ministry of Finance, and, though the Bill
does not definitely state that harvest-time
is the time of year in mind, I may tell
the House again that it is the intention
to restrict the concession to that period.
I feel sure that hon. Members will agree
that it is only at such a time that the
need for transport becomes so urgent as to
require extraordinary measures, and it is
obviously only fair to the owners of
vehicles which pay the full rate of tax
that this relaxation of the restrictions on
use which qualify an agricultural vehicle
for a lower rate of tax should be limited
in point of time.
In leaving the actual determination of
the period to the Ministry of Finance
rather than to Parliament, we are only
following the precedent already established in the Finance Act, 1943, recently
passed by the Imperial Parliament. The
relevant Section of that Act reads:
Duty at a higher rate shall not become chargeable in respect of that
vehicle by reason only that, during such
periods and in such areas as may be

As is generally known, my Ministry in
the collection of gates and railings is only
acting as agent for the Ministry of
Supply, and, therefore, follows the practice of the competent authority in Great
Britain, i.e., to give careful consideration.
to representatives on the facts of individual cases. Suggestions of inequitable
treatment are examined under this procedure and no question of legal guidance
arises.
Numbers of Unemployed in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the present
total of unemployed in Northern Ireland
or alternatively the total at the last date
for which exact figures are available, and
how many of these, or alternatively, what
proportion of these unemployed are building trade operatives or former employees
of any kind in the building and allied
trades.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The latest information available
regarding the numbers unemployed in
Northern Ireland relates to the position
at the 18th October, 1943.
The number of men aged 18 and over
then registered as wholly unemployed was
6,064; the number of women aged 18 and
over was 3,058; the figure for juveniles
was 1,251. In addition, there were on
the register at the date of the count
2,221 persons who were either temporarily
suspended from work or were normally in
casual employment. Of this figure of
2,221, 38 were juveniles.
The total number of persons aged 18
and over unemployed on the date of the
count was, therefore, 11,305.

has been suspended in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland for reasons of security.

Order for Second Reading read.
Major SINCLAIR: On the 22nd July
last when I first announced the concession,
and on the 13th of this month in moving
the Ways and Means Resolution on which
this Bill was brought in, I explained to
the House just what change in legislation
was proposed, but for the convenience of
hon. Members I propose, at the risk of
repeating myself, to refer again to the
details of the concession, which has been
in operation with the approval of the
House since the announcement on 22nd
July, which I have mentioned.
Goods vehicles registered in the name
of a person engaged in agriculture and
used on the roads solely by that person
for the conveyance of his own agricultural
produce or articles required for his own
land, pay a substantially lower rate of
tax compared with goods vehicles engaged
on general road haulage work. For example, a lorry exceeding 1 tons, but not
exceeding 2 tons in weight, unladen, is
normally taxed at the rate of £25 per
annum, but the reduced rate of tax applicable to the agricultural vehicle is only
£13 per annum. The reduction in tax,
however, as I have just stated, was only
operative when a vehicle was carrying its
owner's goods, and if a farmer wished to
use his lorry to carry for a neighbour, in
so far as he was allowed by the Road and
Rail Transport Act, 1935, he would have.
Under
had to pay the full rate of tax.
this Bill a farmer will now be allowed to
use his vehicle during harvest-time to
carry other persons' produce as well as his
own, or to lend his vehicle to a neighbouring farmer for agricultural purposes,
without incurring any liability to the increased rate of duty, thus facilitating the
provision of the maximum amount of
transport during the crucial period of getting in the crops. It will be noted that
the period of the concession is to be
defined in each year by an Order of the
Ministry of Finance, and, though the Bill
does not definitely state that harvest-time
is the time of year in mind, I may tell
the House again that it is the intention
to restrict the concession to that period.
I feel sure that hon. Members will agree
that it is only at such a time that the
need for transport becomes so urgent as to
require extraordinary measures, and it is
obviously only fair to the owners of
vehicles which pay the full rate of tax
that this relaxation of the restrictions on
use which qualify an agricultural vehicle
for a lower rate of tax should be limited
in point of time.
In leaving the actual determination of
the period to the Ministry of Finance
rather than to Parliament, we are only
following the precedent already established in the Finance Act, 1943, recently
passed by the Imperial Parliament. The
relevant Section of that Act reads:
Duty at a higher rate shall not become chargeable in respect of that
vehicle by reason only that, during such
periods and in such areas as may be
Finance (No. 2) Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
specified by Order of the Treasury, it
is used whether by the person in whose
name it is registered or not for any
such purpose as is specified in the
Order.
It must be realised that the concession
is not only in respect of 1943, but the
power enabling my Ministry to make the
Orders referred to in the Bill will continue in force until such date as the
Governor in Northern Ireland may by
Order in Council determine, that is, until
the end of the present emergency.
No one will dispute the fact that it is
not possible to specify in advance of the
season just when the gathering in of crops
will begin and when it will come to an
end, and I feel that it is for the convenience of the House that such a detail
should not be made the subject of fresh
legislation each year.
In conclusion, may I remind the House
that this Bill does nothing to alter the
law relating to the taxation of tractors or
trailers, but is solely concerned with goods
vehicles as defined in Section 4 of the
First Schedule to the Finance Act (Northern Ireland), 1937. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.”
Mr. NIXON: I have no intention of

the Minister calls concessions. But the
Minister emphasised that it is the intention to restrict these concessions to harvest
time. Now, the so-called concessions are
something to assist agriculture, but why
restrict them to harvest time? Furthermore, the Minister in the course of his
speech speaks about this procedure following the Imperial Parliament in a certain
way, and a careless reader or a person
who did not think a little for himself
might imagine that we were in line with
the Imperial Parliament in the matter of
transport. We are not, because a trailer
which is a very useful thing, in England
can be used without any special licence,
but here it cannot. Before you can use a
trailer in Northern Ireland you have to
have your car licensed for that purpose,
and you have to pay an additional sum
for that privilege.
Consequently, the reference to the
Imperial Parliament though correct
enough in respect of how the trailer is
used at the present time is misleading on
the wider question of transport. I am
not saying, and I do not want to be
accused of saying, that the way
the Minister spoke was misleading.
He spoke correctly so far as he went, but
I do not see why there should not be a
step-by-step policy here. When this concession is given in harvest time, I think
it should also be given in springtime. (Hon
Members: Hear, hear.) All these restrictions on trailers and other means of

purpose, namely, to
to bolster up the
Transport Board. That was the idea at

I am not making these remarks to

this House, certainly for the country--
that the time has come to put Ulster on
the same footing with regard to trailers
as Great Britain. Trailers are things
that every person might want who has a
motor-car, or who has not a motor-car.
The time has come when we should be in
the same position as exists in Great
Britain, and it is up to the Members who
represent the people to see that we are
put in that position.

Farmers to-day are badly enough fixed

That is the lowest unemployment figure

Mr. MINFORD: I should like to pay
my tribute to the Minister of Labour for
what he has said. I had the experience
this year of taking on a number of his
men on my farm under the voluntary land
scheme, and all I can say is that the
Minister has played one man's part in
regard to agriculture this year. I would
also pay tribute to the Minister of Public
Security, who placed at the disposal of
those men conveyances to move them to
and from the farms. The Minister of
Labour helped the war effort greatly by
providing labour in order that the crops
should be saved. I think it was wrong of

which have been read out. All I can say
is that the Minister of Labour is at all

scheme a man can leave the Ministry
of Labour office and take on work. If he

Mr. NIXON : I think that the
Minister's statement or rather rebuke
shows that any person, whether he is in
this Parliament or the Imperial Parliament, who makes false statements calculated to mislead the House and public,
will in the long run do a disservice to
everyone. It may do good for a while,
but when a man gets a reputation for
that kind of thing-a deserved reputation
-no matter who he is, or whether he sits
on the Front Bench or Back Bench, you
cannot believe one word he says. He is
then a danger to everyone and to the
people he is helping. Furthermore, the
people he thinks believe him may believe
him just to oblige him; they do not like
to say:
"You are a liar." But he is insulting their intelligence and at the same
time he is displaying he has none himself.
Instead of 20,000 unemployed there are
only 11,000. That number is too many
after four years and one month of war,
and 5,000 would be too many in Northern Ireland when you consider the
number of people who are working in
Great Britain and the very large
number of men and girls we have in the
Forces. Regarding our war effort, Ulstermen are on every front the world over
and rendering a good account of themselves as usual. I hope we will do
nothing behind their backs to let them
down or fill vacancies and jobs they should
have a chance of filling when victory is
won. It is being won, thank God, at the
present time.
I may perhaps be allowed to wander a
little bit on this subject of victory.
It is a thing I am very strong on.
I know that there was a time when people
thought I was inclined to be a pessimist,
but now I have changed to the other view.
I think we will have the pleasure of celebrating victory over Germany, which is
the principal enemy, sooner than most of
us expect. When that time comes we
will be able to deal with the other enemy.
In the meantime, if anyone has anything
to
say let him say it, but let him keep to
the truth no matter where he is, whether
in the Imperial Parliament or the
Northern Ireland Parliament, because
any temporary advantage he may get by
telling lies will not last very long, no
matter whether he sits on the Front
Bench or the Back Bench.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 2nd November, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Local Authorities and Derating Grants.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs when the
Government intend to introduce the legislation promised in the King's Speech of
23rd February, 1943, to alleviate the
difficulties which local authorities have
experienced in carrying out essential improvements owing to the operation of the
derating grants.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I hope to be able to make
an
announcement respecting derating
shortly. A satisfactory agreement has
been arrived at with the Imperial
Treasury, but a few details remain to be
settled. I propose to issue a circular to
local authorities on the matter at a very
early date.
Planning.

the Association of Chambers of Commerce, etc.
Mr. LOWRY: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part of the
question, as none of the bodies mentioned
have suggested an interview, the matter
does not arise.

a conflict of interests between, say, the
.
Belfast Corporation and the rural district

similar reduction has been made in the

their full requirements of envelopes for
church purposes.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

Control
Orders-which

Aid to Russia Fund Flag Day.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether it is a fact that Mrs.
Churchill and other well disposed persons
promoted an Aid for Russia Fund;
whether a flag day in support of that fund
was promoted in Northern Ireland;
whether the Minister of Agriculture at a
luncheon in the Grand Central Hotel
criticised the flag day and objected to the
singling out of Russia for special concern;
and whether the Minister's attempt to
injure the Aid for Russia Fund had the
approval of the Cabinet.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The reply to the first and second
parts of the hon. Member's question is in
the affirmative.
In reply to the remainder, so far from
my right hon. Friend having any desire
to injure the Aid to Russia Fund, he has
on several occasions taken part in assisting
this movement.
I understand that my right hon. Friend
referred to the advisability of making a
block grant from the Central Red Cross
funds as an alternative. This, as the hon.
Member will appreciate, is a matter of
private opinion with which the Cabinet is
not concerned.
Mr. NIXON : With regard to the
latter part of the Prime Minister's reply
that a statement by a Cabinet Minister
on a matter of public policy is a matter
