STRIKE IN SIROCCO WORKS,
BELFAST.
Prime
6. Mr. NIXON asked the
Minister whether there is a strike in the
Sirocco Works, Belfast; whether all possible steps have been taken to settle that
strike; whether there is a local signed
agreement between the strikers and
management of the firm; whether such
agreement is observed by all concerned;
whether the Minister has certain statutory
powers; and whether he is prepared to
use these powers to end the strike and get
on with war production.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative.
The strike arose out of an alleged
breach of an agreement between the Northern Ireland Association of the Engineering and Allied Employers' Federation
and the Amalgamated Engineering
Union. The recognised procedure for
avoiding disputes was not followed, nor
was the dispute reported to my Ministry
before the stoppage took place.
It was, therefore, only with some difficulty that I was subsequently able to
bring the parties together in joint conference in the hope of promoting an immediate settlement, but I regret that it
was not possible to reach agreement at
that conference.
I have certain statutory powers for
dealing with trade disputes and the legal
aspects of the case have received consideration by the Law Officers.
In
pursuance
of these powers, under Article 2 (2) of the
Conditions of Employment and National
Arbitration Order, 1940, I have now
formally referred the matter for settlement by the agreed machinery of negotiation, together with the question as to
whether there was a breach of agreement
by the firm.
NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED.
7. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
called to the statement made by the hon.
Member for West Belfast in the Imperial
House with regard to the unemployed
situation in Northern Ireland; whether it
is a fact that since he took office the
situation has become worse in Northern
Ireland; whether the total number given
by the Minister of Labour on Wednesday
last includes persons disallowed and not
signing at the Labour Exchanges, or does
it include persons merely signing for
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
work; whether it is a fact that there is
poverty in Northern Ireland and that
there are large numbers of people without
any visible means of support; whether it
was stated by another hon. Member in the
Imperial House that there were between
20,000 and 25,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland; whether he is in a position
to contradict these statements; whether
it is a fact that there is industrial distress
in Mid and South Armagh and other
areas in Northern Ireland; and whether
this is caused by the Government's apathy
in dealing with the unemployed situation.
Mr. GRANT: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
My attention has been drawn to Press
reports of the statements made by the
hon. Member for Pottinger in another
place regarding the unemployment situation in Northern Ireland. As I told this
House on Wednesday last, the statements
attributed to the hon. Member are not
correct.
It is not a fact that the unemployment
situation in Northern Ireland has become
worse since the present Government took
office.
I need only point out that on the 12th
April, 1943, the number of persons aged
18 and over registered as unemployed was
16,754; on the 19th July, 16,039; and on
the 18th October, 11,305.
These figures included persons registered
for work, whether or not they were in
receipt of benefit or assistance, and show
the total number of persons aged 18 and
over seeking employment through the
medium of employment exchanges at the
dates mentioned.
As regards the question of poverty, I
might remind the hon. Member for South
Armagh that in Northern Ireland the
social insurance measures for the support
of the unemployed, the sick, the aged,
the widows and orphans are similar to
those which obtain in the rest of the
United Kingdom; and that at no time
since the Parliament of Northern Ireland
was set up has the amount of unemployment been so small as it is at present.
Mr. AGNEW: Question.
Mr. GRANT: The hon. Member knows
that it is the Government's constant endeavour to promote employment throughout the entire province, and, in view of
the steps taken and the results achieved,
any suggestion of apathy on the part of
the Government or of industrial distress
in the province is entirely out of place.
As to the statement attributed to another hon. Member in another place, the
only reference I can find in the Imperial
Hansard is for 15th April last. The
official figures of unemployment are
published at quarterly intervals for the
information of all concerned, and at the
time the statement was made the latest
published figures were for 18th January,
1943. Since then, as I have already said,
the numbers have been very substantially
reduced.
Mr. AGNEW: Do I take it that the
right hon. Gentleman is trying to convey
to the House. that there is absolutely no
poverty in Northern Ireland? In view
of the very unsatisfactory answer given, I
am going to raise this matter on the
Adjournment.
Mr. NIXON: Did the Minister on a
previous occasion, after giving the figures
of unemployment, state in this House that
he could even reduce his own figures?
If his own figures were correct, how could
he reduce them, and if he could reduce
his own figures, could he not reduce
almost anything at all except that hump
on myself and also on him? (Laughter.)
Mr. GRANT: Replying to the last
part of the question first, I have no desire.
to remove the hump I have myself. I
feel quite comfortable with it.
(Laughter.) The hon. Member can take
whatever measures he likes in that
respect. I think I did make it quite
clear in my statement of last week that I
could reduce these figures of people who
were actually employable though they are
registered as unemployed. The hon.
Member, and every other right hon.
and hon. Member, understands that
there are numbers of people signing the
unemployed register who, for many
reasons I am not going into at the
moment, are not fit for work; but still
they are registering, and as they are
doing so we have to submit those figures.
That is my reply to both the Member for
Woodvale and the statement made in
another place on Sunday last.

Housing.
the
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of
announcement on 18th October by the
British Minister of Health that local
authorities in Great Britain have been
given the right to give permission for
repairs, renovations and alterations of
houses up to £250 per house, and that
private owners may now repair or convert
their property up to a limit of £250 to
avoid danger to health or deterioration of
structure, he can state whether there has
been or will be any corresponding change
in the regulations of the Ministry of Commerce regarding supplies of material for
such purposes; whether there has been
any limit in respect of the expenditure
and materials for such work in Northern
Ireland hitherto, and what was the figure
of such limit and how long it has been
in operation, and how many prosecutions
there have been since the start of the war
for exceeding such limit; in how many
cases was authority granted for spending
more than the amount that could be spent
on such work without a licence, and what
was the largest amount ever authorised
by his Ministry in such cases, and the
circumstances in which such authorisation
was given.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Repairs, renovations and alterations of
houses will be sanctioned in Northern
Ireland to the same extent as in Great
Britain. The procedure by which repairs
and reconstruction will be authorised is
being considered in the light of the scheme.
initiated by the Ministry of Health and
the revised arrangements will be
announced at an early date.
The expenditure on such work has been
restricted by regulations since October,
1940. Regulation 56A of the Defence
(General) Regulations, 1939, which first
came into operation on 7th October, 1940,
provided that no building work which was
estimated to cost over £500 could be
carried out without licence. On 14th
April, 1941, the limit was reduced to
£100. Since the Regulation came into
operation there have been 11 prosecutions
for carrying out work to dwelling houses
without licence. Three hundred and
ninety-three licences have been issued for
repairs, etc. (including war
(including war damage.
repairs) to 624 houses. This figure does
not include war damage repairs to houses
carried out by local authorities.
The largest amount ever authorised
was £3,500 for the repair of a large house
following extensive damage. by fire.
Mr.
HENDERSON: In view of the
amount it takes to repair these houses is
the hon. and learned Gentleman prepared
to grant a subsidy to local authorities to
enable them to build houses, and will he
release materials at an early date so as to
try to relieve the terrible scandal that is
taking place owing to the want of houses?
Mr. MAGINESS: That does not come
within the province of the Ministry of
Commerce.
Mr. MINFORD: Is the hon. and
learned Gentleman aware that £3,000 per
month has been allocated for the distribution of building materials to Ulster? Is
he also aware that that £3,000 has not
been taken up while at the same time
people are being refused licences to repair

Mr. MAGINESS: That is already
covered by my answer.
Education.
LUMP SUM PAYMENTS TO
RETIRED TEACHERS.
Mr. BROWN (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Finance whether the
Government has given consideration to
the statement issued by the executive of
the Retired Teachers' Union to the
Members of Parliament and published in
the Belfast Press on 4th October, 1943,
and whether he can state what steps the
Government is prepared to take in this
connection.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I have given consideration to
the statement issued by the executive of
the Retired Teachers' Union to Members
of Parliament and published in the Belfast
Press on 4th October, 1943. The question
of lump sum payments, which is the main
issue, has, in fact, been under active consideration for many months, but as hon.
Members will, I know, appreciate the
subject is a complicated one which requires
considerable investigation, covering as it
does the whole period since this Parliament was set up. After full consideration
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
of the facts I have decided, with the
agreement of His Majesty's Treasury, to
meet the representation which has been
made by extending the existing schemes.
for the payment of lump sums, so as to
bring within their scope a large body of
existing pensioners who retired before the
introduction of a lump sum scheme in
Northern Ireland.
In order to explain the concessions
which I now propose to make it will,
perhaps, be best if I remind the House of
the scope of the existing schemes.
The
payment of lump sum was first introduced
in the year 1936, being made applicable
under a pension scheme of that year to
all teachers retiring on or after the 1st
July, 1936, the payments being calculated
in respect of service subsequent to the
1st July, 1936. In the year 1940 the
scheme was extended so as to include in
the calculation of lump sum, years of
service between 1st February, 1922, and
the 30th June, 1936, but the payment of
lump sum in respect of this additional
period was to be postponed until after the
war.
I propose to amend the existing scheme
in two ways:
-
1. The scheme will be further extended
so as to include all pensioners living at the
present date who retired with a State
pension on or after 1st February, 1922.
2.
Payment of benefits will not be
delayed until after the war, but will be
made as soon as the necessary schemes
have been approved by Parliament and
the necessary data for the calculation of
the payments has been prepared.
As a result of this concession a very
substantial number of existing pensioners
who received no lump sum on retirement
will now be so entitled. Payments of
lump sum benefit will, however, be subject
to a deduction of the amount of contributions at the rate of 1 per cent. per annum
for a period equivalent to the number of
years ranking for lump sum payment
before the 1st July, 1936. This also
applies to payments under the scheme as
it stands at present.
I should like to add two points. The
first is that no payments will be made to
the estates of pensioners who retired
before the 1st July, 1936, and who died at
any time before the present date.
Secondly, I must place on record that if
these concessions are approved by Parlia
ment they will represent the limit to
which I am able to go.
Mr. BROWN: As one who had a
Resolution on the Order Paper for
several weeks past calling for justice in
this matter, I should like to be allowed to
thank the Minister for the prompt and
careful consideration he gave to this
matter and for the concessions he has
announced. It is another example of the
outstanding efficiency with which he is
carrying on his duties generally.
Price of Main Crop Potatoes.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the hon. and
gallant Member asks his private notice
question, perhaps I ought to inform the
House that the question by the hon.
Member for South Down was in order as
he had previously given me notice that he
withdrew the Motion which appeared
upon the Order Paper in his name.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he is in a position to make any
statement with regard to the representations made to the Imperial Government
in relation to main crop potato prices in
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I am grateful
to the hon. and gallant Member for
giving me the opportunity to make
this statement. I should like to
assure the hon. and gallant Member that
the strongest possible representations have
been made to the British Government concerning the unsatisfactory price for main
crop potatoes in Northern Ireland. The
effect of the decision which has been given
and which we can do no other than accept,
is that the present price schedule will remain in force until end of December.
The British Government has undertaken
that between now and the end of the year,
there will be a statistical inquiry into the
general level of prosperity of the agricultural industry in Northern Ireland
compared with Great Britain, and with
this inquiry my
my Ministry will
will be
associated. The question of main crop
potato prices in Northern Ireland will
then be reconsidered.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
2 NOVEMBER 1943
I should make it clear that we have
informed British Ministers that in our
view present prices are not adequate to
meet the costs of the average grower, and
that unless there is an improvement in
prices there will be a substantial decrease
in the acreage planted to potatoes in
1944. We have also made it clear that in
our view when costs of production which
are largely controlled are very similar
throughout the whole of the United
Kingdom the present disparity in prices.
between Scotland and Northern Ireland
compared with England is not justified.
Hon. Members when discussing this
subject seem to be under the impression
that there is a Great Britain price. This
is not so.
Potatoes is the only important
crop or farm product for which there is
not a United Kingdom price. There are
seven different regional prices for potatoes
in the United Kingdom which are based
on the prices prevailing before the war
and to which have been added from time
to time identical sums per ton.
It is essential in considering this subject to bear in mind that it is not part of
the British Government's policy to make
the growing of each crop profitable.
Certain of the important crops in Great
Britain such as wheat and potatoes are
grown under direction-that is compulsion. As a consequence, certain crops in
certain areas may be grown at a loss. The
policy of the British Government is to
ensure the profitability of the industry as
a whole, or, put another way, to ensure
that the agricultural income is such as to
maintain a proper standard of living on
the farm and a fair margin of profit on
the farmer's activities as a whole.
The low price for main crop potatoes
is, in my view, unduly hard on Northern
Ireland, as the crop represents over 20
per cent. of our ploughed land, and is a
necessary part of the rotation on
smaller farms.
our
I think it only right to point out that
when, as I hope, the necessary adjustment
of our main crop potato prices has been
made, the question of taking the final
step in bringing our agricultural wages
into line with those of Great Britain will
arise.

TOWN CLERK OF BELFAST.
Mr. NIXON : I have pleasure in
moying the Motion standing in my name :
That in the opinion of this House the
salary of £2,500 fixed as a starting
salary for the new Town Clerk of
Belfast, with the approval of the
Minister of Home Affairs, is excessive,
having regard to the sacrifices demanded
of and burden borne by all classes of
the community.
In order to put the saddle on the right
horse at once in regard to where the
pressure to fix this outrageous salary came
from, I will read the remarks of the Lord
Mayor of Belfast when urging the Council
to recommend it. They were published
in the Belfast News-Letter of 2/9/43, and
this is what the Lord Mayor is reported
to have said:
In regard to the salary he explained
that the Committee of Six had considered £2,000 sufficient, although he
personally had not agreed. The Government were not satisfied with the replies
received at that figure, and suggested
that the salary should be increased.
Even at £2,500 the Government were
not satisfied and added a clause to the
advertisement: "The salary for the
post shall be £2,500 per annum (inclusive of emoluments), but a higher
salary may be paid to the successful
candidate if he possesses outstanding
qualifications."
It had been suggested that £2,000
a year was sufficient, but four other
officials were already receiving that
and he thought the Town Clerk should
have more.
That was the argument, but you can
take it here that if the Lord Mayor's
statement is correct-and it has not been
contradicted up to the moment-the Committee at that time, known as the Big
Six, fixed the salary at £2,000. Then the
Government intervened. They were not
satisfied with the replies received to the
£2,000 advertisement, because from the
first day they started they wanted Mr.
Dunlop to be the Town Clerk.

TOWN CLERK OF BELFAST.
Mr. NIXON : I have pleasure in
moying the Motion standing in my name :
That in the opinion of this House the
salary of £2,500 fixed as a starting
salary for the new Town Clerk of
Belfast, with the approval of the
Minister of Home Affairs, is excessive,
having regard to the sacrifices demanded
of and burden borne by all classes of
the community.
In order to put the saddle on the right
horse at once in regard to where the
pressure to fix this outrageous salary came
from, I will read the remarks of the Lord
Mayor of Belfast when urging the Council
to recommend it. They were published
in the Belfast News-Letter of 2/9/43, and
this is what the Lord Mayor is reported
to have said:
In regard to the salary he explained
that the Committee of Six had considered £2,000 sufficient, although he
personally had not agreed. The Government were not satisfied with the replies
received at that figure, and suggested
that the salary should be increased.
Even at £2,500 the Government were
not satisfied and added a clause to the
advertisement: "The salary for the
post shall be £2,500 per annum (inclusive of emoluments), but a higher
salary may be paid to the successful
candidate if he possesses outstanding
qualifications."
It had been suggested that £2,000
a year was sufficient, but four other
officials were already receiving that
and he thought the Town Clerk should.
have more.

Six, fixed the salary at £2,000. Then the
Government intervened. They were not
satisfied with the replies received to the
£2,000 advertisement, because from the

Dunlop to be the Town Clerk.

on.
It was stated here, and everybody knew

Dr. Armstrong was to get a job

hand, and they could not get him away
to America before the Attorney-General

they went ahead with the other end of it.
That part of it went on, and that statement of the Lord Mayor proved the driving force. This was not the first time in
Northern Ireland that an Act of Parliament was specially passed to put a certain
gentleman in a job over people who were
better qualified and better entitled to it.
However, I put that matter on the
reserve list for another occasion. It will
be there if it is wanted.
I have always stood, and always will
stand, against high salaries. The
Recorder of Belfast does not get £2,500 a
year, or anything like it. Yet when Mr.
Dunlop was holding this inquiry he had
to suspend it to get advice from the
Recorder of Belfast, who was then
Attorney-General. There is not a county
court judge in Northern Ireland who gets
£2,500 a year. There is not a high
officer in the Army who gets £2,500 a
year. I have no knowledge of the salaries
paid to high officers in the Navy, but I
would venture to state at this table that
the commander of one of our great
cruisers does not get £2,500 a year.
would not for half of a quarter of a
minute compare the responsibilities of the
Town Clerk of Belfast with the responsibilities of the Recorder of Belfast or
any of our county court judges. And
what about the commander of a cruiser?
He has all those lives in his hands, and
I
not alone has he the lives of his crew in
his hands, but he has in his hands the
British Empire. Yet when these men are

men came back there would be nothing
for them.
The former Town Clerk, Mr. Archer,
as any man well knows, was good for
another ten years, and certainly until
after the war, but he was not pressed to
remain on. He has retired on a pension
of over £2,000 a year, and another man

never so happy as when they are voting

majority of the members of the City
Council were persuaded by that speech of
the Lord Mayor's, and by some other
lobbyist, to pass a resolution asking for
Mr. Dunlop at that salary. I know that
when a man like Mr. Dunlop is going to

say they helped him to get it. They
want to be in a position to make him

has got the job now.
You might ask, what good will this
Motion do? I answer, it will do good. It
will say that these things cannot go on
with impunity. I want to say now-and
it should not be necessary for me to say
it-that neither to-day nor at any other
time since I came into this House have I
cared how any man voted. He has a
right to vote in any way he likes. I have
often made it plain to a man who was
hesitating that as far as I am concerned,
no matter how he voted he is only doing
something I have stood for since I came
into this House, and that is to do what
he liked in the matter of his vote on a
Motion of this kind. I think I can say
that I have never swerved either to the
right or to the left since I came here on
the 22nd May, 1929, and I do not
intend to. Generally speaking, I would
be better pleased if it were not necessary
to move any Motion, and if the Prime
Minister and Parliament were not distracted from doing what they should do,
and what the life of this Parliament was
extended for, and that is to carry on the
war effort. If they did that they would
not have much room for manœuvres.

The people cannot sacrifice their ideals all

salaries.
The Minister of Public Security had a
statement in the Press on 18th September,
1943, in which he gave very good advice
which has a bearing on this Motion. I
cut the extract out of the Telegraph, and
it reads as follows:
Those who use the country's hour of
necessity to foment industrial and
political disturbance and thus upset
our plans for the achievement of early
and complete victory should be regarded
as enemies of the people and betrayers
of the trust reposed in us by our
mighty dead.
That is a very sound statement, and I
say that those who
use the country's
distress to put men, no matter who they
may be, into jobs at outrageous salaries
are equally guilty. To-day we had a
question about strikes. I do not know
how anyone can do more to foment strikes
than by paying these big salaries, and I
cannot for the life of me see how any
Member can go into the Lobby to vote
for a man to get a starting salary of £50
a week and then get up and let workmen
go on strike for a few shillings a week.
The man who does that is fomenting
strikes.

Take some of the jobs in this place.

Mr. LOWRY: It is necessary for me
at the start of my observations to correct
the mistakes made. I could not say how
many mistakes were made, but they are
a very great number indeed, and I must
endeavour to deal with them all. In the
first place the very wording of the Motion
is wrong. It seems at first sight as
though £2,500 were the starting salary,
and that increases were contemplated.
That is not so. The salary is fixed at
£2,500 a year. Another matter I should
like to make clear is this. This salary was
determined upon by the Belfast Corporation and by nobody else, as I shall demonstrate quite clearly. The Ministry did
not fix this salary at all. I will go further. The Mover has quoted a speech
delivered by the Lord Mayor. Let me go
back in the history of the salary of the
Town Clerk as I know it from the year
1941. The truth is that in December,
1941, the post was advertised at £2,000
per annum without any protest, and the
suggestion was made on the part of the
Ministry that there was a doubt as to
whether suitable applicants would be got
at that sum. Our forebodings were perfectly correct. Suitable applicants were
not got.
Let me go back to an earlier stage when
a special committee of the Lord Mayor's
was endeavouring amongst other things,
to obtain a new Town Clerk. I do know
that in the month of November, 1941,
the then Lord Mayor, who is Lord Mayor
to-day, and his Committee asked my predecessor and myself if Mr. John Dunlop,
of our Ministry, would be prepared to
accept the post at £2,500 a year. I put the
matter before the Permanent Secretary,
who spoke to Mr. Dunlop, but Mr. Dunlop,
while appreciating the compliment, refused the offer without any hesitation.
I conveyed that information to the Lord
Mayor, by letter dated 24th November,
1941, and that letter is in the City Hall
to this day, I have no doubt. But as
long ago as 24th November, 1941, Mr.
Dunlop had clearly and emphatically refused the post at that salary.
On 2nd December, 1941, the post was
advertised, with the result I have told
you. Suitable applicants were not got.
At a later stage, after a prolonged debate
in the Corporation, which took place on
18th February, 1942, an amendment was
carried to the effect that the intending
Town Clerk should name his own price.
They settled it in this fashion that
£2,500 a year would be the salary, but
to a man of exceptional experience and
ability a higher rate might be paid.
When it was offered to a man of experience and ability, against whom no
charge whatsoever can be made, they
kept well within the limits they determined in the month of February, 1942.
It is perfectly idle for the mover and
seconder of this Motion to suggest there
was prompting or pressure on our part to
fix the salary at that amount, because it
was not done, and the records of the Corporation and the correspondence that has
gone on between my Ministry and the
Corporation demonstrate that beyond all
doubt whatsoever. The Corporation fixed
that salary, we acquiesced in it, and I
think they were very wise in the amount
they fixed. They had had experience of
what happened through advertising at too
low a rate.

On the other hand, the Corporation is

into decimals to work out the
go
grievous burden that is represented by the
difference in the salary to be paid to the
Town Clerk and the salary some people
think should be fixed. But this grievous
burden is not really the trouble with the
hon. Member for Woodvale. It is looking
round for something with which to assail
the Government, and it is a very far
fetched business on his part, because the
Belfast Corporation, in February, 1942,
were deliberately prepared to go higher
than the sum of £2,500. Yet the hon.
Member turns round at this hour and

Of course the opportunity is also taken
to assail other members of the Ministry.
The Member for Woodvale has even
dragged in one man who committed a
grave criminal offence and was punished.
For the information of the hon. Member
I can tell him that the offence was
detected within the Ministry, and the
Attorney-General was promptly informed
that the man was guilty of this serious
dereliction of duty. What the case of a
man who was merely collecting documents,
making notes, and handing them to the
inspectors at the inquiry has to do with
the salary of the Town Clerk is beyond
my comprehension. In comparison with
the salaries paid to town clerks in other
cities, the salary of £2,500 fixed for the
Town Clerk of Belfast is right and reasonable. Having regard to the responsibilities of the office it is a great deal less
than the salary of the two immediate
predecessors of the new Town Clerk.
This was the deliberate act of the
Belfast Corporation. It was not the
result of any corrupt or sinister bargain,
and, while I am glad to say that the hon.
Member for Shankill, who seconded the
Motion, had nothing but praise for the
new Town Clerk, I do regret that he, as
a member of the Corporation, should have
been a party to a proceeding which was
meant, I believe, not merely to reflect on
the Ministry, but to call in question the
upright motives of the members of the
Belfast Corporation who deliberately, and
under no pressure, decided to offer this
post to Mr. John Dunlop.
Mr. AGNEW: After listening to the
Minister of Home Affairs, and casting my
mind back to last year, I can recollect
that a particular Bill was passed through
this House known as the Belfast Corporation Bill. I remember that that Bill
contained a certain Clause under which
the powers of the Corporation were taken
away, and the Minister of Home Affairs
was given the power to appoint Administrators. I must say that this Motion,
which I support, has been a topic of discussion amongst the average citizen:
think the wording of the Motion is quite
correct, and there is no desire whatever
to cast any reflection on the person concerned. The real issue at stake is that of
the salary.
I
When we take what is known as human
values we sometimes wonder how Governments and corporations fix their estimates.
Let us take, for example, the men who
fight in the Navy, Army, and Air Force.
What is the human value placed on them?
It is very small. I am sure that in the
service of the Belfast Corporation there
are men who are competent to fill this post
and who feel that they have been overlooked, and that there is no possibility
of promotion for them.
The Minister is undoubtedly endeavouring to state a case, but it is remarkable
that in all he said he never yet gave us a
clear indication as to the powers of the
Corporation or of the Administrators,
and whether, as the hon. Member for
Woodvale said, quoting from the Press
that this figure was arrived at unanimously. After all, the Minister bears a
certain amount of responsibility by
reason of the fact that much delay took
place. Certain candidates were not
suitable or capable. I know that if the
question had been faced up to in a proper
way the Minister would not have had to
take any member of his staff to act in the
capacity of Town Clerk of Belfast.

It is all very well to try to disprove
certain statements made by the hon.
Member for Woodvale, but we, as Members of the Opposition, are entitled to
criticise, if we so desire, the Government
or any Department of the Government,
because, after all, the Minister of Home
Affairs himself has a great responsibility.
Practically all our local government institutions must await the approval of his
Department for certain things. I do not
know whether any objection was raised
by the Minister or his Department to the
amount of salary fixed. Further, we
were informed that Mr. Dunlop had
absolutely refused to accept this post, but
now we discover that despite all that has
been said Mr. Dunlop, after refusing the
post, has now been installed as Town
Clerk of Belfast. That is a very
peculiar state of affairs. We believe in
democracy, and the Minister also believes.
in it, but when he stands up in this
House and says that the Belfast Corporation agreed to this appointment he
forgets the very Act he got passed
through this House. There were strong
protests made against it.
I want to ask the Minister had the
Corporation any power to refuse to make
the appointment of Town Clerk or had
the Administrators the right to elect a
man in spite of the Corporation. Any
Bill which he pushed through this House
in opposition to the wishes of the people
of Belfast was wrong. That is what I
might call a peculiar state of legislation.
It is strange to the average citizen. I
know that some of the Ministry's officials

tendency to place civil servants in these
positions. That might be a very dangerous
development, and I hope it will not be
allowed to proceed at too great a pace.
'I want to make it clear that the present
Minister of Home Affairs did not make
the appointments in regard to post-war

new departure on the part of the Government in sanctioning the appointment of
an Ulsterman to the position of Town
Clerk of Belfast justifies the contention
I have made in this House during the
past five years, namely, that if there is an
Ulsterman fitted for the post he should
get it.
In this respect we have made
progress indeed. .

3 NOVEMBER 1943
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 3rd November, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sittings of the House.
Resolved, "That this House at its rising
this day do adjourn until Tuesday next.'
-(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Voluntary Registration of Women.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): I beg to move, "That this House
approves of the intention of the Government to institute forthwith a voluntary
registration of women not at present registering at the employment exchanges
who are willing to undertake work of
national importance in Northern Ireland,
and pledges its support to this effort of
the Government to stimulate the war effort
and to attract additional work to Northern Ireland."
As hon. Members are aware, we have
never before had so few unemployed
people signing our employment exchange
registers. This is very satisfactory from
many points of view: the increased employment benefits almost everyone, directly
or indirectly, and it shows how we are
helping in the war effort.
But it has one drawback. Up to now,
the most effective argument the Prime
Minister could use to get cross-Channel
employers to place work here was: "If
you give us the work, we can supply the
labour." This argument can still be used
to a certain extent about men, since we
have been able, so far, to meet the calls
made on us for male labour except for
some demands for types of skilled tradesmen who are in short supply. This applies
also to such further work for men as is
immediately in sight. Our reserve of
men, together with those released from
week to week as other work ends, should
be enough to provide the unskilled labour
required.
The position is different as regards \
Women. We have reached the point
where, if a cross-Channel firm says and
this question is always asked "If we
start a branch at such-and-such a place
can you let us have enough women to
staff it?" we cannot give an absolute
promise. It may seem strange to people
who do not know all the facts that we
should have several thousands of unemployed women on our registers and yet
not be sure that a new factory will be
able to obtain, say, four or five hundred
suitable workers from them.
Our
But the explanation is simple.
registered unemployed are scattered all
over Northern Ireland, while the number
of women who can be moved, without
hardship, to places outside daily travelling
distances from home is very small.
Women as a rule have more and stronger
domestic ties than men. Even the unmarried girls often have to keep house for
fathers or brothers, or look after younger
children or invalid relatives. It must be
remembered, too, that as the number of
unemployed falls, the proportion rapidly
rises of those who cannot easily be placed
at work owing to age or infirmity or other
causes. Even in Great Britain, where
there is the background of conscription
for men and women, the same difficulty
has arisen.
On the last date on which figures were
published there were 71,129 wholly unemployed on the register, and yet Mr.
Bevin had to move people from less
essential to more essential work, and
call up women in the later age groups.
Here in Northern Ireland we have
reached the point where we are
in danger of losing our best bargaining
weapon unless we can tap a. further source
of supply. There are very few districts
where we have enough competent unemployed women workers left on
registers to enable us to guarantee staff
for a new factory.
our
Yet we have no doubt that there is
still what I may call a hidden reserve of
female labour. We have found it in some
cases where we had employment to offer,
by advertising in the district or by houseto-house canvassing. It consists, for the
most part, of women who are under no
necessity to earn their own living, and
consequently do not attend the employment exchanges, but who would be competent and willing to work for the national
effort if opportunity arose.
If we are to attract more work here,
we must find out how many of these
women there are and where they are
living. We intend, therefore, to set up,
at all the employment exchanges, a
special register of unemployed women
Voluntary Registration-
Women
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
from 16 years of age upwards who are
not registering for work in the ordinary
way, but who are willing to take work in
Northern Ireland. We shall not ask
these volunteers to attend regularly at the
exchanges. All we want is to have enough
particulars about them to know the extent
to which they are available, and to be
able to get into touch with them if needed.
We shall ask them to tell us whether
they are ready to work full time: what
was their former occupation, if any;
whether they are prepared to go anywhere in Northern Ireland if suitable
accommodation can be found for them,
or whether they can only accept employment within daily travelling distance of
their own homes. They will not be bound
in any way by giving these particulars.
They will not be expected to refuse any
jobs that come to them in the ordinary
course just because they are on this
special register. Even if we are able to
offer them war work they will not be
compelled to take it. We want only
genuine, willing volunteers.
The Government will, of course, do
everything in its power to make this
scheme known. We shall have an
advertising campaign in the papers and
elsewhere, and, as it is intended not only
to assist the war effort but to benefit Northern Ireland, we are entitled to ask for
widespread co-operation. In particular,
we look for the support of local
authorities.
The Prime Minister has recently been
approached by deputations from various
local bodies to get additional industries
started in their districts. He is making
every possible effort to do so, but it is not
'unreasonable to expect local authorities
to aid him in inducing these unregistered
women and girls to give their names and
particulars to the nearest employment
exchange. We do not wish to dictate to
the authorities just how they should do
this. They will know best what they can
do to help us, and we will do our best to
help them.
I do not want to raise false hopes. We
cannot have new industries everywhere,
and the mere fact that we have a list of
potential workers in a district does not,
unfortunately, mean that a new factory
will be established there. But without
such a list there is very much less chance
of getting the factory. When we have
the lists, to which, of course, we will add
those already registering for employment,
the Ministry of Commerce will be able to
say to any prospective employer, "Here
are various towns with such-and-such
facilities in the way of buildings and
power and water supply, and here is the
available female labour for each district."
When we can say that, we will be in a
better position to get new orders than we
are at present. We shall have our goods
in the shop window, and we shall sell
more of them than if much of the stock
were hidden away.
Before I resume my seat there is one
point which I wish particularly to
emphasise to hon. Members, so that there
may be no misunderstanding. The object
of this Motion is to enable the Government to launch a scheme of voluntary
registration of women who would be
available, if required, for work in Northern Ireland, and that means in
Northern Ireland only. I appeal to all
the Members of this House, the Churches,
the Press, local authorities, voluntary
organisations-in fact, to all men and
women of good will-to give the widest
publicity and help in their power to this
scheme for the national advantage.
Question proposed.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I rise to support this
Motion submitted by the Minister of
Labour, and I do so for more than one
reason, but particularly because, as the
Minister has explained, it is going to do
something to stimulate and help us in our
war effort here in Northern Ireland. I believe that every Member of the House, irrespective of what side he may sit on, will
support any measure brought forward by
any member of the Government for the
purpose of stimulating our war effort. We
are all grateful for the good news that has
been coming to us from the various
fronts during the past number of months,
and we are grateful also for the tributes
that have been paid to
us by British
statesmen as to what has been already
done, but I think that something more
can still be done.
Until Northern Ireland puts forth its
last ounce of strength and until every per
son available has been brought into the
war effort we shall not be able to say that
we have done all that we could. Therefore,
1963 Voluntary Registration—

3 NOVEMBER 1943
Women
I think that this Motion will give an
opportunity to a good many people who
are at present outside war work to come
in and give some help in some particular
sphere of that work. I give the Motion
my whole-hearted support for that reason,
but I also look forward to the time when
we shall have many more industries in
Northern Ireland than we have at present.
I am grateful to the Prime Minister and
the Government for what they have done
in trying to bring new and fresh industries
into this part of the British Empire. I
think that if the Minister of Labour and
those associated with him in his work can
get this register compiled, and can thereby
show to the potential industry owners and
industry builders that there are a great
and sufficient number of efficient workers
available for industry, it may not only
help us now in our war effort, but it may
be of great assistance to us in our postwar problems.
If we can show that able-bodied
workers, both men and women, are available, and I do not think that better
workers can be got in any part of the
Empire than in Northern Ireland, it
would be a great inducement to people to
come over now and set up war-time
factories. For that reason I support the
motion whole-heartedly, believing that not
only for the war effort but during the
period after the war it will be of great
assistance to us in Northern Ireland.
I am glad to support the Motion, too,
because it will bring into operation a class
of the community who, up to the moment,
have not for one reason or another been
able to pull their full weight in the war
effort. If I heard the right hon. Gentleman aright the Motion is not going to oust
genuine workers from their employment in
order to find work for others who have
not before been on the labour market. I
believe there is room for all our people.
There is work for all. Because I believe
it is going to bring more work to Northern
Ireland, and we cannot have work unless
we have the workers to do it, and because
I believe that is a step in the right direction, first of all, in helping our war effort,
and secondly, in getting new industries to
Northern Ireland I give the Motion my
whole-hearted support.
Mr. NIXON: I am beginning to think
it is well that I came out to-day, otherwise.
there would be no semblance of an Opposition present. Some people say that it is
not worth their while turning up, but I
say it is. Seed sown does not appear at
once. Very often I see results from the
seed I sow. The hon. Member for South
Tyrone says that he will give this Motion
his whole-hearted support. I am sure
nobody is going to oppose it. I cannot
conceive of anybody opposing it because
I cannot see what harm it can do, but I
am glad that the hon. Member who has
sat down was able to go out of his way to
give it such support. It gives credence to
a story going round to the effect that since
changes were made at the Ministry of
Labour the work is getting so plentiful
that there must now be special registration. The ordinary channels for recruiting
labour are not sufficient, special efforts
have to be made, largely owing, no doubt,
to the changes made in that Department.
At all events if it does good, good luck to
the Minister and all concerned.
The Minister in his speech emphasised
no part so much as his warning. That is
the part he emphasised above every other
part. He called on the Press, the
Churches, and the local authorities to
advertise it properly. They do that
whether they are called on to do it or not.
That is one thing you can always rely on.
They will advertise to the fullest limit
anything that goes on on that side of the
House. If it does good all the better.
Later on there may be people complaining that there is class distincto
going be introduced into
the recruitment of labour. I am
one who was never afraid of
any
class distinction, because I met the people
on the level. I never met them any other
way, and I would not do so. I have no
complaint to make in that respect, but
something may develop.
tion
Mrs.
Take a case in point. Mrs. So-and-So,
who never worked and who never wet her
finger, in industrial work at all events,
gets a job through this scheme.
So-and-So can select her job and also
the place in which she is to work. The
Minister is giving attention to what I am
saying, and I want him to do that. I
want him to stop me if I make any statement that might perhaps be misleading
or that may be calculated to do any harm.
I want to be stopped at once if I show
that I do not understand the subject.
There are other girls on whose behalf I
have approached the Minister's officials.
Voluntary Registration-
Women
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
with success, thanks to the kindness of
those officials. These girls were compelled
to work at a certain class of work in this
city. One girl, who was 15, wanted to
leave a mill and go to a tobacco factory,
but was not allowed to do so.
I have already stated, and I do not
want to have to state it again, that any
case I bring before the officials of the
Ministry of Labour gets the utmost
sympathetic consideration consistent with
the law, rules and regulations. I need
not go over that again. But here is the
point. Cases like that will turn up again,
as the Minister knows, for the ordinary
workers are not allowed to work where
they like. If they get better jobs often
they are not allowed to take them. Supposing you have another register for
another class of people that never worked
before and they are allowed to work
where they like you can conceive complaints. I understand that if they work
they will get the same pay, they will get
their cards stamped, and they will get all
the benefits the other class of workers
get. I know that this scheme was brought
forward with the best intention, but
difficulties might develop in that direction.
What kind of argument would the
Minister put up if I came out with the
case of two or three girls of the working
classes who could improve their position
in Belfast by transferring from one works
to another, but were refused permission;
while, at the same time, Mrs. Somebody
else, who lived in a bigger house, and
never worked until she got this chance,
was allowed to work where she liked? I
can conceive a hullaballoo, but I am not
going to start it. I leave it there and
support the Motion.
I think the Minister told us that there
were over 11,000 people unemployed. I
do not know how many of those 11,000
are women, but if there is a substantial
number of women-ordinary workerssigning the unemployed register do you
want these volunteers to take the work
they should get? There is another thing
I know. There are women sent across
the water against their will and they
would come home if they could. It may
be, I do not know, that there are going
to be some new factories or industries that
will absorb all these workers and all the
volunteers as well. I sincerely hope
there may be.
The Member who spoke
before me emphasised a note that makes
us all happy and gives us confidence to
enjoy our debates here, and that is the
great success that our Forces and the
armies of the Allies are achieving in the
war. If the war were not going right
we could not be going for each other,
because we would have enough troubles
to contend with, but seeing that the war
is going all right and that we have the
weight in numbers and equipment I think
we can be happy. Although I have my
self a considerable amount of avoirdupois
I do not think I have enough votes behind
me to turn out the right hon. and hon.
Gentlemen I see in front of me. I am
left blank.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
have very much pleasure in supporting
this Motion for two reasons-first, because
I think it is our duty to make every
possible contribution to the war effort,
and secondly, because this scheme will
have a far-reaching effect not only upon
the war effort but upon what is also very
important, namely, our post-war effort
and on employment in Northern Ireland.
I think the Minister said in his remarks
-I regret I missed them that we have
got to look to the future as well as to the
present. There are certainly distinct
difficulties in inducing manufacturers to
start new industries in Northern Ireland,
having regard to transport difficulties and
having regard to the fact that these
manufacturers would probably have to
shift back to England most of the goods
manufactured here in order to find a
ready local market.
-
Therefore, we must be in a position to
offer attractions which are not available
on the other side. Some of these attractions include power, cheap electricity and
an ample water supply, and, of course,
last but not least the one thing that we
will be able to do under this Motion is to
offer ample labour. The fact that the
Ministry have these voluntary workers
registered will be a tremendous inducement to prospective manufacturers to
come over here to help us to help ourselves and to make the maximum contribution to the war effort and to the postwar industries of the Province.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I think that everybody sees the
importance of the war effort from the
1967 Voluntary Registration-
3 NOVEMBER 1943

Women
national as well as the provincial point
of view, and I am sure that men and
women-the women to start off withwill appreciate the importance to us of
having statistical information as to where
the pockets of labour exist. There are
obvious difficulties in giving chapter and
verse. as to the production position in
Ulster. We have expanded very considerably, but there are various points
which, I think, should be borne in mind.
First of all, none of the work is static.
It alters from day to day. Quite frequently a factory is running two or three
shifts every 24 hours. That work may
be closed down or diminished, or, on the
other hand, there may be a call from the
supply departments for an acceleration in
the production of that particular type of
munitions.
It means, therefore, that both the
workers and managements have got to be
in a position to adapt themselves to the
changed position. That is a usual thing
in war, and everybody must accept it,
although it is upsetting. There 18
nothing static in war. The position is
bound to change, just as the position on
the battlefield, in the air, or on the high
seas may change. Exactly the same
changes take place according to the
technical requirements which necessitate
different types of munitions. Therefore,
what does happen, in fact, is that a certain amount of labour is released from
time to time, and the endeavour of the
Ministry of Commerce must be to
absorb those men in the war effort as
soon as possible.
But as we see it from the information
which we have, the demand for labour
will increase very considerably during the
next six months. It is impossible, with
the changing things I have mentioned, to
give any guarantee as to numbers, but as
we see it we must look into the future
as far as we can-there will be a considerable demand for labour, amounting to
some thousands. That means we will
The
have to expand some way or other.
Minister of Labour has pointed out that
the great difficulty we are in now is a
shortage of women workers, who are in
demand
very great
at the present
moment. There are various new factories
which have been put up, and there. have
been expansions of old factories, and
these will require a considerable number
of women.
The House is aware that for the last
two years negotiations with Ministries on.
the other side have been extremely
arduous. Members are also aware that I
have been able to put up the argument
that as
we have a considerable labour
reserve in Northern Ireland we, therefore,
could relieve the pressure in the various
regions. There are 13 regions, of which
we are one. We are all out in the war
effort. The work is going on, and I feel
satisfied that Ulster is pulling, or is about
to pull, her full and maximum weight in
the war effort. Of course we have not got
the same measure of conscription or compulsion as exists on the other side, and,
therefore, it is much more difficult under
the arduous and tiring conditions which
our workers have to endure to get the
same effort which is made on the other
side. I should like to pay tribute to the
workers and the trade unions for the way
in which they have put aside for the time
being their efforts to improve their position and also those privileges for which
they worked so hard and so long.
So far as the present situation is concerned we must, as my right hon. Friend
has said, look to the future. The
immediate consideration is the war, but if
we can induce industries which are at
present working in the war effort to come
over here with a view to developing in the
post-war period it will help us to spread
the risk which we always suffer from in
this country. It will also help us to have
varieties of industries here, which I am
sure will be of very great value to the
country. This proposal is to facilitate
the war effort, and I am quite convinced,
from what I know of the loyal men and
women in this country, that they will be
only too anxious to be given the opportunity of coming into the war effort.
The hon. Member, who represents the
Opposition, was nervous for fear that
those who are brought in under the
scheme might compete with the women
who were already on the register. I can
give him the assurance that that is not
the case. The women who are at present
on the register will be given preference,
and those women who will register under
the voluntary scheme and who come into
industry will be under the same conditions
as those already working.
As I have said, from my experience
and from talking with many women, and
indeed men, in this country who are not at
present involved in the war effort or not
Voluntary Registration
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
to a great extent-I feel sure that they
will definitely welcome something of this
sort which will give them the opportunity
of doing real and valuable work for the
United Nations and also for Ulster itself.
The Minister of Labour has explained
that it will be impossible to get everybody
registered in a short time. He has explained, I think, that one of the main
considerations in getting factories in this
country is the knowledge that we have
available labour in certain areas-people
who are willing to work. It will enable
me, when I go to the other side, to explain to Ministers that in a certain area
there is a certain number of people
available.
But it must be borne in mind that there
are other considerations. Even though
there may be a considerable reserve of
labour in one particular area, if transport
facilities are bad and power facilities are
bad or other requisites for production are
not there, it will obviously be impossible
to start a factory in that particular area.
The most important thing, however, is
the human element, and if we have got
the workers in an area we can get over the
physical element. I would point out to
the House that it has been the policy of
this Government and the last Government,
as well, to do all they can to help the
workers. The Government have, as far
as we have been able, done that, and
therefore I do not think it is too much
to ask the people of this country when we
have succeeded in that task, which was
by no means an easy one, to assist us by
registering and showing their willingness
to co-operate and help in the war effort.
I therefore confidently invite the House
to agree to the Motion.

MEALS
FOR
SCHOOL-CHILDREN.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether it is a fact that all schoolchildren in Great Britain now receive
meals in school; whether she can state
how the position in this respect in Northern Ireland compares with that across the
Channel; the number of schools in Northern Ireland where (a) meals and milk are
provided, (b) where meals only are provided, (c) where milk only is provided,
and (d) where neither meals nor milk are
provided; and whether she can state the
full terms of the offer made recently by
the Ministry of free equipment, etc., and
the number of education authorities who
have availed themselves of this offer.
Mrs. PARKER: I understand from a
circular issued by the Board of Education
in May last to local education authorities
that the Government's objective will not
be reached until school meals are available
for 75 per cent. of the children. It would,
therefore, seem to follow that it is not a
fact that all school-children in Great
Britain at present receive school meals.
I regret that I am not in a position to
state the number of school-children in
Great Britain who are supplied with meals
and it is not, therefore, possible to make
a comparison with Northern Ireland.
The number of public elementary schools.
in Northern Ireland coming within the
schemes of local education authorities is
as follows:-

The full terms of the offer of the
Ministry for the supply of free equipment,
etc., are so very exhaustive that I have
arranged for the hon. Member to be
supplied with copies of the Ministry's
Circular R.1943/2 and S.1943/21 containing the details of the offer.
The number of local education authorities who have so far availed themselves
of the offer is 9.
Mr. BROWN: May I take it from the
hon. Lady's reply that her Ministry are
not satisfied with the position under which
the pupils at 1,277 schools are not receiving milk or meals at the present time,
although Mrs. Roosevelt on her recent
visit to England said that she found that
in every school meals were being provided?
Mrs. PARKER: With regard to the
observation of the hon. Member, I have,
of course, given him direct information on
the subject as far as it is possible to do
so in regard to the provision of meals in
England. As to the question of whether
my Ministry are satisfied, the hon.
Member is absolutely correct in deducing
that we are not satisfied, but we are doing
our very best to encourage the local education authorities to bring in these schemes.
A considerable number of these authorities are having experimental schemes,
some are considering the matter, while
others have brought the meals and milk
schemes into force. We shall not rest
satisfied until we find that every area in
Northern Ireland has adopted a scheme.
Mr. BROWN: I am very much obliged
to the hon. Lady for her reply. I hope
that she will continue to press
matter.
this
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the Parliamentary Secretary state that where local

Act into operation she will compel them
to do so?
Mrs. PARKER: I think we had better

Accommodation for Civil Service Staffs.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state how many
premises have been requisitioned or otherwise taken over in Northern Ireland for
the accommodation of civil servants since
the beginning of the war and how many
of these were dwelling-houses or capable
of providing dwelling-house accommodation; and whether he can given an assurance that no more dwelling-houses or
premises suitable for dwelling-house
accommodation will be taken over.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): The figures sought by the hon."
Member cannot be extracted without expenditure of labour to an extent that in
present circumstances I do not consider to
be justified.
Since the outbreak of war there has
been a large increase in accommodation
required by many Departments in connection with the discharge of war-time
services and also for the purpose of dispersal of staff and valuable records.
Ordinarily, office accommodation, both in
Belfast and provincial towns, has in
general been found inadequate to meet
the demands, while urgency and shortage
of materials have been factors in most
cases precluding the erection of new structures. It has consequently been found
impossible to avoid the acquisition of a
number of dwelling-houses for office use,
and in the national interest it may again
be found essential to do so. Therefore,
with the best will in the world I cannot
give the hon. Member the assurance asked
for in the final clause of his question.
I can, however, assure him that the
general policy of my Ministry is not to
take over dwelling-houses if suitable office
accommodation is available. Apart from
the present need to retain dwelling-houses
as such, they are usually found unsuitable for office use without extensive and
expensive adaptations.
I might add that my remarks refer
only to premises for the choice of which
my Ministry is directly responsible. The
hon. Member will appreciate that the

Ministry acts as agent for a number of
service and civil departments, and generally the choice of premises to be acquired
remains primarily with the principal
Department concerned.

6. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can give any indication when his statement on the industrialisation of County Armagh will be
made as the workers are anxious to
hear it.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
I would refer the hon. Member to the
answer given to the question put by him
on 12th October last. In that reply the
Prime Minister took the opportunity of
mentioning that a Government statement
on certain aspects of employment throughout Northern Ireland would shortly be
made. That statement was given last
Wednesday by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour.
Mr. AGNEW: Is it not a fact that the
question I put refers to County Armagh?
I do not think the reply covers that.
Mr. MAGINESS: The answer given
on the 12th October referred to unemployment generally including County
Armagh.

REPAIRS AND RECONSTRUCTION.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether in view of his statement in the House on 2nd instant that
repairs, renovations and alterations of
houses will be sanctioned in Northern
Ireland to the same extent as in Great
Britain and that the procedure by
which repairs and reconstruction will be
authorised here is being considered in the
light of the scheme initiated by the
British Ministry of Health and that the
revised arrangements will be announced
at an early date he can now state what
are the revised arrangements.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The position with regard to the repair of
dwelling-houses has now been considered
in the light of the scheme recently
initiated by the Ministry of Health, and
it has been decided that certification by
local authorities is not necessary in this
area.
same
All applications from building owners
for licences to carry out repair work to
dwelling-houses will, however, be given
exactly the
treatment as that
accorded in Great Britain and consultations will take place between the Ministry of Home Affairs, the local authority
and the Ministry of Commerce and
Production before any application for a
licence to carry out work within the
limits of the Ministry of Health scheme is
refused.
Mr. BROWN: May I be allowed to
ask the Parliamentary Secretary for a
clarification of the point, namely, whether
private owners will be able to carry out
repairs to houses at a cost of £250 as is
the case across the Channel?
Mr. MAGINESS: That point is
covered in my reply to the effect that the
same treatment as in Great Britain will
be given here.
EXPERIMENTAL HOUSES.
13. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
Department have received an offer from
the Member for Ballynafeigh to erect two
experimental houses, and whether he has
approved of their design and authorised
their erection.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
The Ministry has indicated that it
would support an application for the
release of the necessary materials to
enable the system of construction which
the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh has
suggested to be tried, but such promise
is subject to certain conditions, amongst
others that the houses will be built
strictly in accordance with plans and specifications to be deposited with the Ministry
and that the Corporation are satisfied as
to compliance with by-laws and the suitability of the site.
The plans and specifications only
reached the Ministry on Saturday last
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 NOVEMBER 1943
and they are still being examined.
Accordingly the design has not up to the
moment been approved.
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the Minister
state if he is prepared to allow others to
erect these experimental houses?
Mr. LOWRY: The Ministry is prepared
to allow five other firms or persons to
undertake the erection of houses for the
information of local authorities, builders
generally and the Ministry.
Mr. HENDERSON: Does the Minister
not think it would be better if the State
would have houses designed and erected
that would be fit for human habitation
and not allow people who have no practical knowledge of houses to do so?
Mr. LOWRY: I entirely agree with
the hon. Member. It would have been
much better if our Department had done
it, but I would have had to satisfy the
local authorities on that point.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the question, if the Member for Ballynafeigh or
any other individual is prepared to build.
two experimental houses at his own expense and his own risk why should the
Ministry or any other one that never
did anything for a house in their lives,
not even put a sash cord in, stand in the
way?
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister who
told us it would have been better if his
Department had designed and erected
houses tell us why his Department did
not do it?
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. Member for
South Down is one of the most vigorous
defenders against what he imagines to be
inroads on democracy and he would be
the first to raise a complaint if we interfered with the housing authorities of
Northern Ireland.

Minister whether he can state if any

news summary given by the B.B.C. every

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil

POULTRY TRADE.
9. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can make a statement concerning anticipated changes in
the poultry trade; whether complete
agreement was reached with all sections
of the trade, and whether it is his intention to give the House full details of
the scheme before it is put into operation.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): At the request of
the Minister of Food my Ministry has
held discussions with representatives of
the poultry trade in Northern Ireland to
consider proposals for the more equitable
distribution of supplies. At these discussions all sections of the trade-producers, collectors, shippers and retailers
--
-were unanimous in requesting that a
scheme of control should be introduced at
the earliest opportunity. Agreement in
principle was eventually reached on all
essential issues except for a slight
difference of opinion on the question of
the producer's price for poultry sold on
the farm. I am satisfied that the control
proposals are desirable in the national
interest and in the interests of our consumers who in the past have had difficulty
in securing their share of supplies at controlled prices.
The Order giving effect to the revised
arrangements will be made by the
Minister of Food who is Minister of Food
in Northern Ireland, and the Order will
not, therefore, come before the House.
I may add for the information of the
hon. Member that the proposals envisage
the licensing of a limited number of
packers who were regularly engaged in
the shipping trade prior to the war and
whose premises are suitable for the
purpose. Such packers will be directed
by the Ministry, acting for the Minister
of Food, to consign dead poultry to buying groups established by poultry retailers
in five of the largest urban areas in Great
Britain. It is also proposed to issue a
separate class of licence to collectors
authorising them to purchase live poultry

FLAX GRADING.
10. Mr. LYONS asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it is a fact that there
exists at the moment a deliberate grading
down of flax, as instanced at Omagh and
other grading centres, and whether this is
done at the instigation of his Ministry
with a view to recovering from flax
growers the acreage payments for flax.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I feel sure
the hon. Member does not
mean the
implication which the question seems to
convey. My Ministry has nothing whatever to do with the grading of flax, and
therefore could not be guilty of such a
breach of faith.
The flax grown by our farmers is purchased by the. Ministry of Supply and
graded by officials appointed by that
Ministry without consultation with my
Ministry in any way whatever.
I am
equally certain that the Minister of
Supply would not be a party to down
grading flax in order to recover the
acreage payments. I have no hesitation.
whatever in repudiating such a slur on
the Ministry of Supply as strongly as I
would repudiate it on behalf of my own
Ministry. I know that at the opening of
this season strict instructions were sent
by the Ministry of Supply to the Flax
Administrator in Northern Ireland that
there was to be no alteration in the
standards of grading, and in particular
that there must be no down grading.
I am aware that there is considerable
dissatisfaction with the grading of flax,
the standards for which should not be
varied from year to year, and I have
accordingly asked the Ministry of Supply
to allow the Flax Controller to cross to
Northern Ireland to discuss the matter
with my department.
Mr. MINFORD: What evidence has
the Minister to enable him to state that
he repudiates the statement made by the
hon. Member? Are the farmers and
millowners all fools?
TUBERCULIN TESTED HERDS.
11. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
number of tuberculin tested herds of
cows at present in Northern Ireland, and
how this number compares with that for
each year since the introduction of Grade
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 NOVEMBER 1943
"A" milk from T.T. herds; and whether
he can give a list of the areas in Northern
Ireland where Grade "A" milk is at present obtainable, and those where it is not
obtainable.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: At present
there. are 50 Grade "A" herds in
Northern Ireland.
Tuberculin tested herds were started in
1928 with 12 herds. Progress was made
every year up to 1934, when there were
61 herds, and from 1934, when Grade
"A" milk was introduced, the number of
herds has been between 50 and 60.
Grade "A" herds are distributed as
follows throughout Northern Ireland: -
Antrim 11, Down 26, Armagh 2, Fermanagh 1, Londonderry 6, Tyrone 4.
Milk is obtainable from these herds in
the districts in which they exist.
If the hon. Member wishes more
detailed information as to the location of
the herds and the distribution of the milk
from them, I shall be pleased to supply
him with that information.
Mr. MINFORD: Why was there a
decrease in 1943?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: That may be
a matter of opinion, and the hon. Member's opinion and mine might be different.
Mr. MINFORD: Why was there a
decrease? That is a simple question that
is entitled to an answer.
Home Affairs.
DISPENSARY DOCTOR FOR
RICHHILL.
12. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will reconsider
the appointment of a Dispensary Doctor
in Richhill; whether he will agree to make
this appointment permanent; and
whether he can state if it is a fact that
the Dispensary Doctor in Armagh under
the Armagh Union was made permanent
and sanctioned by him.
The MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS: This matter has already
been raised with the Ministry by the hon.
Members for Central and Mid Armagh,
to whom I have explained that on the
23rd November, 1942, the Ministry on
the urgent representations of the Medical
Personnel (Priority) Committee, issued a
circular to local authorities to the effect
that the Ministry would not in future be
prepared to fill vacancies in medical
appointments off a permanent basis unless
it could be shown that a suitable medical
officer could not be obtained on a temporary basis.
Since the issue of that circular no permanent appointments of dispensary
medical officers have been made in
Armagh Union or elsewhere.
No valid reason has been advanced in
favour of exceptional treatment for the
particular appointment referred to by
the hon. Member.
Mr. WARNOCK: Can the Minister
say whether this principle applies in
regard to all appointments to which men
of military age are available until the
return of those who are serving in the
forces ?
Mr. LOWRY: In such appointments
which require the sanction of the Ministry
that principle is being applied.
Of
course, as the hon. and learned Member
knows, there are many appointments to
which it does not apply.
Mr. NIXON: Why was that principle
not applied to the appointment of the
Town Clerk of Belfast?

asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his attention has been called to a
statement made by a Member of this
House "that there were 5,000 to 10,000
people anxious to go to Great Britain to
give their skill and services in the interests
of victory, but they are prevented from
moving outside the shores of the Six
Counties," and whether he can state how
many applications from people desirous
to go to employment in Great Britain
have been refused.
Mr. LOWRY: I have seen the statement referred to and in regard to it can
only say that obstacles are not placed in
the way of suitable people who are willing
to undertake work of national importance.

IMPORTED BRICKS.
15. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of bricks imported into Northern
Ireland since the beginning of the war
and the total cost of such bricks; whether
the brickyards in Northern Ireland are in
full production; whether imported bricks
have been extensively used on a recent
Government contract in Co. Down;
whether Ulster-made bricks were available; whether the Government will put
the Ulster brickyards into full production
at once and store the bricks so as to be
ready to proceed with a building programme at the earliest possible moment.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
I propose to deal seriatim with the
points embodied in the hon. Member's
question:
1. The total number of bricks imported
into Northern Ireland since the outbreak
of war up to October, 1942, when imports
ceased, except for two small delayed
cargoes, is approximately 34,060,000, the
total cost ex works being approximately
£110,695.
2. The brickyards in Northern Ireland
are not at present in full production.
3. No Government contract in County
