Major SINCLAIR: I hope that the hon.
Members who are interested in this
Resolution have found the memorandum
which I have had circulated with the
Order Paper helpful, and have not been
dismayed at its length. On account of the
detailed explanation of the various parts
of the Resolution given in the memorandum, I propose to confine my remarks
this afternoon to certain aspects only of
the matters under consideration.
As to Part A, the returns of the
guarantees given under the Loans
Guarantee Acts which are laid before
Parliament reveal that the Government
has had to assume direct liabilities to the
extent of £4,545,000. Of this large sum,
however, only £70,000 is regarded as a
loss finally determined. Of the balance,
£2,127,000 has been recovered and substantial securities are held in respect of
the remaining £2,348,000. The money
to meet this amount has, of course, been
found long ago, and any sums now
1989 Financial Provisions [Money]- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Major Sinclair]
obtained through the realisation of the
securities I have just referred to should
be regarded as revenue and, therefore,
paid over to the British Exchequer as
part of our Imperial Contribution.
There are good reasons, however, for
regarding moneys so received as properly
applicable to our own capital purposes,
and last year the Treasury agreed that
such windfalls might be used instead to
pay off our Unemployment Suspense Debt.
This year they have agreed to extend the
principle further, and to allow such
moneys as remain in hand after extinguishing the Unemployment Suspense
Debt to be used for the purpose of paying off other Exchequer debts, realising
that by so doing the Imperial Contribution will receive an annual and regular
increment as opposed to a distortionate
inflation in one or two years. The Unemployment Suspense Debt has not yet
been completely discharged, but we feel
justified in hoping that ultimately we will
have substantially more in hand than the
amount required for that purpose. Just
what that surplus will be, however, and
when it will materialise I am not prepared
to forecast.
A glance at our Exchequer accounts
will show the scope that we have for the
utilisation of this money, though I should
emphasise that our debt position is by no
means a burdensome one. Apart from
borrowings by means of stock and Ulster
Savings Certificates, there is an item of
some £2,500,000 borrowed from the
Government Loans Fund for capital expenditure, which is being repaid to the
Loans Fund by annuities which are voted
each year in the Estimates. If, therefore, for example, we were eventually
placed in the position to repay part of
this capital sum to the Government Loans
Fund, the Exchequer would be relieved
to the extent of the corresponding annual
payments, extending over a considerable
period of years, and the Imperial Contribution correspondingly benefited.
Here I must stress that these windfalls
may not be used for new capital expenditure, nor do they exempt us from
the necessity of seeing that we do not
exceed in any particular comparable
standards in Great Britain.
Part B of the Resolution calls for little
further comment, except to point out that
the additional expenditure which is envisaged will not rank for Government
grant, and will have to be repaid entirely
to the Exchequer by the industry. This
is, I feel, only just, as the increased
generating capacity aimed at is more of
the nature of normal expansion for everyday purposes rather than an enlargement
of standby supplies. In this connection,
however, I think it is proper to add that
the Treasury, while not countenancing
any assistance to the new programme have
agreed that that portion of the expenditure which was nugatory in the
original programme should attract a 100
per cent. grant instead of the 50 per cent.
payable in respect of the rest of the outlay. This has meant an increase of
£125,000 in the Treasury's subvention to
the earlier scheme.
Part C simply empowers the Exchequer
to pay a premium to the Government
Loans Fund in the event of the premature repayment to that fund or
variation on the repayment terms of any
Exchequer debt. Hon. Members will recall my observations in this connection
on Part A of the Resolution.
Part D provides for the retention in
office of the present Comptroller and
Auditor-General for a further year, and I
feel sure that the House will agree with
me that we are fortunate in that this extension of his services is possible.

I do not think that the need for better
housing is more clamant anywhere than
in Northern Ireland, because since. 1931
there has been little building in this

thought to the problem, but I suggest

this affects two or three Departments,

and intentions are. There has been a
feeling recently of great optimism about
the war.
I think it is inevitably moving
to a climax. I remember this day

I had no more idea than the man in the

within a week. It may be that this war
may end just as suddenly as the last. It

ends and finds our Departments unready
in regard to this question of housing.
Are the Government ready?
I want to ask for information on a
number of matters in regard to which I
am not quite satisfied. First of all, have
steps been taken to decide on the location of the first thousand houses? Has
any arrangement been made whereby the
land for those. houses can be secured and
vested immediately? I cannot myself see

very large number of houses. I do not
know why that decision cannot be made.
now. I do not suggest that we should

or places at which these houses are going
to be put. That is the first question I
want to ask the. Minister. If that has
not been done, I think he ought to explain
to the House the reasons why it has not
been done. We have now been four years
This is no new problem.
at war.
The Ministry-I do not say the Minister

for their building operations?
If they

These are matters in which foresight is

Minister is not able to give us a review

I want to come to another point, and

pre-fabrication." When I heard the

to an extraordinary extent, and it has
three or four meanings. You can have

our system has taken place which I am

as much as 10 to 25 per cent. Under this
system the houses, while having an
external dissimilarity and variation in

and living rooms are all of the same

the floors, wall coverings and joists
which are factory made are set in sections
and can be fitted up.
There is, I understand, a great deal of
possible economy in this direction, and I

his brightest young men over to Sweden
to investigate the possibilities of such a

doubt that this matter has been considered, but I would ask for a serious
consideration of the possibilities I have
indicated. I cannot speak with authority,

what I call partial pre-fabrication.

Mr. HENDERSON: I gave the right
hon. Gentleman notice that I would raise
a question about the stoppage of the
importation of beer and stout. I referred
to the matter last Tuesday. It is very
serious and affects some thousands of barmen, and is due to the action of the Eire
Government. There are people who earn
their living by having public houses, and
their premises have been closed since the
impartation of beer and stout was stopped
by the Eire Government. There are tens
of thousands of troops anxious to partake
of this beverage. I do not care if I never
saw it, but you can picture the position
of a dock labourer. I had occasion to go
into a place in Station Street on Saturday
and I was approached by at least 1,000
men who asked what was going to be done
in this matter. Take a dock labourer
who is engaged in taking coal out of the
hold of a ship. It takes something to
wash the coal dust down, and he cannot
do it with water. Water would be of
no use to wash that dust down to its
proper place. Members will not deny
that a bottle of stout or ale is both food
and drink, it is everything to a dock
labourer. These. men cannot get it.
The situation is so serious that it
means the closing down of premises. Is
it right to let de Valera close down our
public-houses? The Free State publichouses are open. We have Canadian,
American, and over-seas troops here,
and whether we like it or not, as long as
the world goes on there will be men who
will partake of these beverages. At
present they cannot get them, and they
are looking for them. You are going to
do these bar-men out of work. Thousands of small traders are in desperation.
I got a letter this morning from Larne
appealing to me to do something. The
writer does not know where to turn.
The Minister should see if it is possible to get some of this beverage, imported from Great Britain or to have it
manufactured in Northern Ireland. In
view of the fact that this is the beverage
of the working people, I think the time
has come for this Government, if they
want a new industry, to get a proper
brewery started so that they cannot be
held up to ransom by certain people.
Is it not a terrible. thing that an Ulster
man has to drink a beverage made by
people we do not like?
The matter is really serious. There are
even Members in this House who like this
beverage. I contend that the Prime
Minister has a right to say whether he
agrees that the proper thing is being done
to keep these houses closed. Personally,
I do not care whether I see the beverage
from one year's end to the other, but I
say in fairness to the war workers who are
anxious to partake of it that they are
entitled to get it. I should like the Prime
Minister to state whether he has made
any representation to the British Government to see if something can be done to
keep these houses open for the people who
want them open.
I am sure the Prime
Minister will agree this is a serious
matter.

Public Security.
AIR-RAID CASUALTIES IN PERCY
STREET, BELFAST.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
number of persons killed in the air-raid
shelter in Percy Street; the number of
persons injured in the same shelter on the
same occasion; what is being done to help
the dependants of the killed and what
pensions or allowances are being or will
be paid to the injured.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Midgley): It is not
customary for security reasons-nor indeed
is it always practicable-to publish information regarding the precise number of
casualties arising from each particular incident caused by enemy attack. I am not,
therefore, in a position to answer the
first part of the hon. Member's question.
Provisions for persons injured, and the
dependants of persons killed by war
injuries, is made in the Personal Injuries
(Civilians) Scheme administered by the
Ministry of Pensions. That Ministry is,
of course, a United Kingdom department,
but the Assistance Board in Northern
Ireland acts as its agent for the award and
payment of initial allowances. Persons
concerned may also obtain advice and
assistance in prosecuting their claims at
the Welfare Offices of the Civil Defence
Authority.
Mr. NIXON : With regard to the
Minister's statement that security would
be imperilled if he gave the information
asked for in the question, would he explain what the effect on security would
be? In regard to this particular shelter
is the Minister aware that it went down
and killed these people because of faulty
construction? Is he aware that the
Ministry of Public Security is the supreme
authority and therefore responsible for
the faulty construction? Under the circumstances will the people concerned who
apparently are too numerous to be mentioned publicly get proper consideration?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I have gone into this
question at considerable length and with
the utmost thoroughness. I wish, in
reply to the point raised by the hon.
Member, to say right away that his conclusions are completely wrong. The
shelter was not defective. It was, as far
as the experts could possibly find out, just
as good as any other shelter of that particular type. That was the predominant
type of shelter used at that particular
time, but in the light of events it was
changed. Because the type of shelter was
changed it is not to be presumed that the
shelter was defective through bad workmanship or bad material. In the light of
the knowledge then prevailing the shelter
was quite all right, but owing to the
weight of the enemy attack, and the
nature of the attack, it was found better
subsequently to adopt a different type.
What happened in Belfast happened in
practically every other centre in the
United Kingdom, that is, the authorities.
had to be guided by the course of events.
It would be just as logical to allege, because a certain type of tank was not as
effective at a particular period of the
war as a later type, that it was defective
or faulty, or that it was imperfect, through
negligence on the part of the authorities.
That is the answer to that part of the
supplementary question.
In regard to the question of security,
apart altogether from the fact that when
a general attack is made on any locality
it is extremely difficult to segregate the
casualties occurring at one particular
point where a number of incidents take
place, it is also imperative that as far as
possible we should not broadcast all the
information in a most meticulous way so

The PRIME MINISTER: I can
answer the hon. Gentleman in a very few
words. As regards the. firm of Kennedy
& Donkin, I am afraid he and I must
agree to differ. In my opinion, and in
the opinion of some of the best electrical
experts in England, this firm is as good
a firm as can be got. The hon. Member
may have a different opinion, and he is
entitled to it. I think the Government
at that time were justified in going to
what they considered was the best electrical opinion they could obtain. The
hon. Member on a previous occasion
attacked the Government because this
station was put up, and because there was
difficulty over water. Let me say there
was admittedly difficulty over water, but
that was quite the smallest consideration.
There were so many other advantages
in putting the station there, even though
there was
no water, and this was a
problem which could easily be settled by
having a condenser put in at relatively
small cost compared with the cost of other
things. There were other advantages
which could not be overlooked, such as
deep water, freedom from immediate
attack, and so forth. These things were
known when this position was settled on,
and water has now been found. I also
want to remind the hon. Gentleman when
he criticised the Government for putting
up this station, the then Government of
the day, after considering this most
carefully, realised that unless there was a
dispersal of electricity this country would
not get any work for Northern Ireland
people.
When I had the honour of putting the
case that more industries, more war work,
should come to this country, that was one
of the main arguments used across the
water against sending war work here:
that, unfortunately, at that time we had
all our eggs in one basket and one bomb
might destroy the whole thing. Machine
tools could not be sent over here if there
was any risk of those machine tools being
destroyed or damaged, and until I, as the
representative of the Government on the
production side, could give an assurance
that we had done everything to disperse
electricity and to make sure that in the
event of an incident happening and one
particular generating station being put
out of action another would be available
immediately, I could not argue the case
for Ulster. I hope that answers the hon.
Gentleman's argument.

The American authorities, I understand, from information received, would
not allow their coloured troops to go into

with conditions that have existed since

which the Prime Minister promised would

nothing but talk. I hope the Prime
Minister, as a result of his many visits

Government that he can spend 40 millions
at least on housing. The Prime Minister
and Minister of Home Affairs must
realise that 60,000 houses are needed.
Land will have to be drained and sewered
and water provided for the houses erected.
There is no use in erecting houses and
putting in dry privies that have existed
since the days when Adam and Eve were
in the Garden of Eden.
I understand that through the efforts
of certain people we are going to get a
water supply for County Down. It took
the war to get that. Now that Down is

that every village in the county will be
provided with a proper sanitary system.
Every house built should be erected
adjacent to a water supply. Let us have
no more of the appalling system that has

Houses are needed
and must be got. The Government will

Tens of thousands of houses are needed.
Many families of eight to ten are living.
in one room, and disease is prevalent. I

a

I could take you to

Until you
house the people under sanitary conditions with all modern appliances in the

built in Great Britain during the war and

right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home

The people who strongly opposed any

and comfortable homes to which they are

How can we have a prosperous Northern

Those of us who remember what the last

suitable home. Unless the Government

Statement by Minister of Finance.
Major SINCLAIR: As practically
everyone who has taken part in this debate
has referred to finance as it affects our
housing problem, it is, I think, advisable
that I should say something on the
subject. In order to make the position
clear to the House, I must refer to our
financial relationships in general, because
housing finance is only part of the whole.
The matter falls naturally into two parts;
the finance of whatever may be undertaken during the war; and of that which
must be postponed until the post-war
period; anything in the nature of an extensive housing programme falls into the
latter category.
We read of an Imperial Contribution
of £32,000,000, and without stopping to
think how that money is raised, or for
what purpose, we say, "Why can we not
keep back a million or so and spend it
here in Ulster and improve our local
conditions?" Unfortunately responsible
people, including, I regret to say,
Members of this House, have fostered this
belief, which makes it all the harder for
the man in the street to understand why
it cannot be done. The operation of our
war-time financial arrangements has been
explained to the House in successive
Housing

Budget statements, and I do not want to
go over that ground again. However, in
order to tell the House why we cannot
embark on a substantial housing programme now with some of the money
which forms our contribution, I must explain the source of these contributions,
which are so much larger than anything
in our pre-war experience.
Our pre-war expenditure and income.
lay somewhere between £12,000,000 and
£13,000,000, and there was a small credit
balance which went to the Imperial Exchequer to pay in part-a very small part,
I am afraid-for the many services to
which our British connection entitled us.
The great bulk of that income was
reserved revenue, that is, revenue for
which the rate is fixed by the British
Government and collected by that Government. When the United Kingdom was
plunged into war that Government decided to increase the rates of these taxes,
and to introduce some new ones, the
proceeds of the increases and of the new taxes
to be used for financing the war.
—
That is where our swollen contribution
comes from, and it would not be playing
fair with the British Government, and,
what is more, it would not be playing
fair with our own taxpayers, who bear
these heavy burdens comparatively cheerfully because of the war necessity it
would not be playing fair if that money
raised for one particular purpose were to
be used for any other. In my opinion it
would be much the same as if I were to
ask an hon. Member for a subscription
to a hospital, and, having extracted it,
were then to spend it on entertaining my
friends. Just as I would never do the
second, so I can never countenance the
first, however much I might like to do so
in the local interest.
It was recognised by His Majesty's
Treasury that Ulster's peace-time expenditure might be enlarged from causes over
which we had no control and arising
directly from the war, and it was agreed
that such expenditure should be met by
payments from the Treasury Votes of
Credit to our Northern Ireland Exchequer. In effect, these payments reduce
the net amount which the Imperial Exchequer receives from Northern Ireland
for the general prosecution of the war all
over the world, and the higher these payments are the less we so contribute. It
follows, therefore, that anything we spend
above our peace-time datum level must be
connected with the war, and it is on that
argument, and that argument alone, that
we can proceed with the building of
houses while war conditions prevail.
It is that argument which I used in
London; that the shortage of houses here
was such that the morale of our people
was suffering, that men and women who
either had to travel long distances to and
from their work, or who lived under
greatly overcrowded conditions, could not
be expected to give-and, indeed, would
not be physically capable of giving their
best in their work, whatever it might be.
The Treasury readily saw the force of
that argument and, after discussion,
agreed to the payment of a subsidy equal
to the highest subsidy which has, so far,
been granted anywhere in Great Britain.
The limiting factor to the number of
houses which can be built in war time
in spite of all that has been, and no
doubt will be said to the contrary, is that
of materials.

So far in referring to the Government's

subsidy, this deficiency should be met by
an increased call on the taxpayer, rather
than by one on the ratepayer of the area
concerned.
If this war has taught us anythingand I sometimes wonder if it has-it must
surely have taught us the value of comradeship; that the members of a community should be willing and ready to
help each other. Surely the ratepayers
in any particular area should cheerfully
shoulder some slight additional burden to
help their fellows to better housing conditions, or is all we hear in this House
and outside it just lip service and cant?
The idea that the Government should
always be expected to pull the chestnuts
out of the fire is based on the fallacious
assumption that the Exchequer is a bottomless purse, a gigantic widow's cruse.
The Exchequer gets its income from you
and me, either as direct or indirect taxpayers, or both, and what it can do is
limited by the amount of that income.
That might be brought home to those who
control our local authorities, and the
public in general, if any increase in subsidy were made conditional, for example,
on a rise in the tobacco or tea duties.
I now come to the second part, a postwar housing programme. Much of what
I have said about the war-time situation
applies with equal force to the post-war
period, but much of it does not. As hon.
Members are aware, when the Northern
Ireland Parliament was set up, or rather
shortly after, it was agreed that given
the existence of common standards of
taxation in both areas, social servicesusing these words in their strict senseshould be maintained in Northern Ireland
on exactly the same basis as in the rest of
the United Kingdom, but that, in determining the basis of other services, due
regard should be had to conditions generally in the Province.
Since 1922-and the process has been
greatly accelerated during the war-the
standard of living and, consequently, the
cost of living has been raised in the Province, and it is recognised that certain
services, which were perhaps adequate 20
years ago, must now in equity be brought
up to the Great Britain level, or more
nearly approach it. By "now" in this
connection I mean, of course, after the
war. This underlying principle has been
stressed by both the Treasury and my
Ministry in conversations which have
taken place about our post-war relations,
and just last week in pursuing our negotiations about the housing situation we
were authorised by His Majesty's Treasury
to make the following statement:—
As soon as the national resources can
be transferred from war to reconstruction a very big housing programme will
be set in motion to meet urgent needs
arising in all parts of the United
Kingdom. Northern Ireland will take
its share of this programme, and the
Government of Northern Ireland will
ensure that due weight is given to the
shortage of houses for the working-class
population of the Province.
Until that time is reached, it is pre
mature to discuss the financial basis of
the post-war housing programme. It is,
however, agreed between the Imperial
authorities and the Government of
Northern Ireland that while Northern
Ireland does not claim preferential
treatment over the rest of the United
Kingdom, it follows from the principle
of parity of services that the Imperial
authorities will give sympathetic consideration to the case for special measures as regards any service in which
Northern Ireland has leeway to make
up in order to attain equality of
standard with the United Kingdom.

2109 Workmen's Compensation Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 17th November, 1943.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sittings of the House.
Resolved, "That this House at its

next." (Sir Norman Stronge.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Workmen's Compensation (Temporary
Increases) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): The effects of this Bill are shown
in the memorandum, which I hope all
hon. Members have seen. I should like,
however, to begin what I have to say by
running over the main points even more
briefly. The maximum rate of Compensation for a single man or woman is
to be raised by 5s a week after the first
thirteen weeks. The increase in the case
of a man and wife is to be 5s per week
for the first thirteen weeks and 10s a
week afterwards. The maximum rate is
increased by Is for each of the first two
children, and 2s each for the others.
Instead of a child's allowance stopping
at age fifteen, it may be continued while
he remains at school until the end of the
July after he becomes sixteen. There is
to be an addition of £100 to the total
amount payable where death results from
an accident.
I have put these proposals as simply
and fairly as I can. I do not think that
anyone here will object to their being
adopted. Similar proposals have been
agreed to by the interested parties on the
other side of the water; and on this particular subject of workmen's compensation I have never heard anyone suggest
that we should not keep in step with
Great Britain. No objection has been
raised there to these improvements.
There has been a good deal of discussion,
but no real opposition to what is in the
Bill: the objections were based on what
is not in the Bill. Some critics thought
that more concessions should have been
made.
Anyhow, I will not detain you by talking about what is not in the Bill. As
you will see from Clause 4, it is only a
temporary measure. It is not to run
beyond the end of 1946; and we hope
that, long before that time, it will be
replaced by a new comprehensive system.
of workmen's compensation. In the
meanwhile, it does not prejudice full consideration of the suggestions in the
Beveridge Report. Indeed, the amounts
proposed in this Bill will bring workmen's
compensation closer than it now stands to
the amounts put forward in that Report.
That, however, is not why this Bill is
being introduced, nor is its chief intention to cover increased cost of living.
Additional sums for that purpose were
granted by an Act passed in August,
1940, and the rise in the cost of living
since that date has been only about eight
per cent.
The main reason for the proposed
changes lies in the rise in the general
level of wages during the past four years.
I think I can explain clearly and shortly
how that comes about. Before the war,
the maximum weekly payment in disablement cases was 30s. Our Act of 1940
gave an extra 5s, bringing the maximum
up to 35s. Allowances were also given
for children, subject to a total weekly
compensation payment of seven-eighths of
the pre-accident earnings. In July last
we had another Act which enabled compensation to be reckoned not on what the
workman was earning at the time of the
accident which might be years ago but
on what he would have earned if the rate
of wages now had been in force then.
This, as was intended, produced increases
for a number of cases; but where the
average earnings (calculated, as I have
said on present standards) exceeded £3
the man came up against the 35s bar.
Whether he had been earning £3 or £5 a
week he would still get exactly the same
amount thirty-five shillings a week.
In these circumstances it was felt that
it would be right to make a further concession. Consequently this Bill proposes
to raise the barrier in the case of a married
man by 5s a week from the commencement and 10s a week after the end of 13
weeks. In the case of a single man the
barrier is to be raised by 5s a week at the
end of 13 weeks. The latter proposal has
been criticised on the grounds that the
Milk Bill-
Second Reading
17 NOVEMBER 1943
increase ought to be given at the commencement of compensation payment. One
great difficulty in the way of doing so is
that, even now, he can get more than is
proposed under the Beveridge scheme for
the first 13 weeks, that is, 35s a week as
against 24s in the Beveridge Report. I
am sure no one will ask me to justify the
increase in respect of children. When the
bread-winner is laid aside their lot is
hard. Nor do I think I need say anything about the increases in the maximum
lump-sum payments: they follow naturally
from the other rises.
The whole subject of workmen's compensation is very difficult and complicated. Its code has been built up by
years of law making and decisions of
courts. When the Parliamentary draftsman has to fit a new bit into the jig-saw
puzzle he has to use the technical language that has been tried out and defined
in actions. It is his business to keep the
meaning right. I am a layman and I
have been trying to make the meaning of
this Bill clear. On the object of the Bill
I have no doubts. I believe it will do
good and will be acceptable to all. I,
therefore, beg to move, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Milk Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): As in the case of
the Bill, which has just been before the
House a memorandum was circulated to
hon. Members explanatory of this
measure. That memorandum was intended to give .hon. Members a sort of
background against which to consider the
proposals contained in this Bill. Having
regard to the fact that that memorandum
has been circulated to, and I hope read by,
hon. Members I do not propose to take
up the time of the House in going over
the same ground again, but I might make
one or two general comments by way of
introduction. We are all agreed, I think,
that milk is one of the most vital foods
we have, vital for the maintenance of the
life of any community, especially a community living under the conditions of our
modern civilisation. It is particularly
important in the case of young children
and growing boys and girls.
As
Partly owing to increased financial means
and partly because of a certain amount
of educational work that has been done,
the consumption of milk has increased.
very much since the outbreak of war.
the memorandum, I think, sets out, prewar our consumption in Northern Ireland
was about 15,000,000 gallons per annum,
and to-day that figure is round about
29,000,000 gallons. That has meant that
we have had to go farther afield to find
the necessary supply for large concentrations of population such as we find in
Belfast.
That difficulty has been got
over mainly by means of a milk scheme
that was brought into operation in Northern Ireland over a year ago. That was
a scheme intended to make a fuller supply
available for our own people and also to
help us at the same time to relieve the
stringency in certain centres across
channel.
This scheme has been in operation over
12 months, and it amounts to this, that
every milk producer in Northern Ireland.
is a virtual supplier of the liquid milk
market. Under that scheme he gets the
same basic price for his milk even if his
farm is situated in one of the remotest
districts of the Province as the producers
living in a zone round about Belfast.
As
a consequence of this arrangement we
have been able to secure an abundant
supply. The quantity problem has been
solved.
That brings us to the other side of the
problem, the quality side. I think that
without boasting we can claim that in
the matter of the general standard of
quality for liquid milk in Northern Ireland we are considerably in advance of
England. To some extent this has been
due to the Measures already on the
Statute Book. There was an Act passed
in 1934 and there have been additional
Measures passed since then up to the
outbreak of war. Taking those Acts
together the legal position is that in so
far as providing milk for the liquid
market is concerned only producers who
hold a licence to produce Grade "A,"
Grade "B," or Grade "C" quality of
milk can sell milk for the liquid market.
All other milk has to go for manufacturing purposes, and by that limitation it
has been sought to safeguard the clean-
Ll

liness and the general quality of milk
going into liquid consumption.
I
In this Bill we propose to go a step
beyond that. In the first Clause we are

power to schedule certain consuming
areas and to provide that within such a

of milk shall be permitted to be sold.
The first of the three grades that we propose to prescribe within such a scheduled
area is Grade "A," and I do not know
that I need take up the time of hon.
Members by explaining what Grade "A"
milk is. I think that the regulations
that apply to the production of Grade
"A" milk are fairly well known.
should say, perhaps, that Grade "A"
milk can only be produced by herds, the
cows in which have been inspected twice
annually by a qualified veterinary surgeon of my Ministry, and, in addition,
have passed what is known as the double
intra-dermal tuberculin test. They are
herds from which any reacting animals
have been removed. There are other
conditions in regard to the housing of
the animals and their general care and
treatment and the conditions under
which they are milked. The milk is
cooled until eventually it is put into

Grade "A" milk, which is the first grade
that we propose shall be sold in one of
these scheduled areas.
The second quality of milk that we
propose as being saleable in such an area
is Grade "B" milk from a single herd.
We will not allow even Grade "B" milk
from separate herds to be bulked
mixed. It will only be milk from a
single Grade
Grade "B" herd. Generally
speaking the conditions which
or
govern
the production of Grade "B" milk are
identical with those relating to Grade
"A" except in this respect, that the cows
are not subjected to the tuberculin test,
but they are clinically examined by a
veterinary inspector from my Ministry.
The third grade or quality of milk
that we propose to prescribe to be sold in
such a scheduled area will be heat-treated
or pasteurised milk. I do not think that
I need enlarge on these grades further.
Pasteurised milk, of course, means milk
that has been subjected to a recognised
form of treatment and that has been
thereafter immediately cooled under proper supervision to a prescribed temperature.
The only other point about Clause 1
of the Bill is that the first area that we
propose to schedule as a consuming area
will be the city of Belfast. In the light
of the experience that we gain in that
area and in accordance with the facilities
at our disposal for the treatment of milk
we shall schedule other areas later on.
Clause 1 simply asks for powers to enable
my Ministry to take those steps.
We come now to Clause 2 of the Bill.
Hon. Members will remember that I
have already said that as the law stands,
only three grades "A," "B," and "C"
go into liquid consumption. There is a
vast volume of milk that is not produced
by any of those licensed herds, and this
Clause asks for powers to enable my
Ministry to bring those other herds all
over the Six Counties under a system of

In connection with the issue of these
milk licences my Ministry, of course, asks

and to make regulations, which will be
subject to the approval of the House, in
connection with those licences. The cows
in the herds will have to be subject to

Ministry, the premises of the licence

Dr. LYLE: I wish to congratulate the
Minister of Agriculture on this Bill, but
my congratulations will be somewhat
modified by the fact that while this is
certainly a step in the right direction it
is a very small step, the step of a timid,
weakly child just beginning to learn to
walk. The strange thing about the Bill
is that the word "pasteurisation" is
never mentioned from one end to the
other, although it deals entirely with
pasteurisation. I certainly think that
the Bill will do a certain amount of good,
especially in regard to pasteurisation of
ungraded milk. A good deal of ungraded
milk is as good as Grade C, but there is
a proportion of it which is no better than
liquid filth.
A good many years ago I was called in
to see a patient. When I arrived I found
the patient was in an advanced stage of
typhoid fever. He was delirious and had
a temperature of 105. For some reason
or other I had to look under the bed, and
instead of the usual bedroom utensils I
found a milk pan, a round, shallow milk
pan full of milk. When I made inquiries.
as to what it was for-I thought it was
being used as a charm as some country
people believe in them-I found it was
milk maturing for churning. As Medical
Officer of Health for the district, as well
as the medical attendant of the people
concerned, I ordered them to throw out
the milk. They lost a basinful.
I do not say that that is a common
thing; I know it is not; but there are
still cases, not as bad as that one, of gross
contamination of ungraded milk. In such
a case pasteurisation is a step in advance,
as is also the provision that the byres and
cows producing this milk will have to be
examined. It is also a step in the right
direction to pasteurise Grade C Milk, but
it passes my comprehension why they do.
not pasteurise all milk used for human
consumption. Strange to relate, in the
Memorandum which has been issued by
the Ministry of Agriculture, the necessity
for the pasteurisation of all milk is clearly
proved, not merely the pasteurisation of
Grades C and D.
In the Memorandum there is a quotation from the report of the Committee
appointed by
by the Medical Research
Council at the request of the Ministry of
Health in England-the Committee was
presided over by Lord Dawson of Pennin regard to pasteurisation. The report,
which was made in September, 1942,
says:
Whether carried out by the "holder"
method or by the "high temperature
short-time" process it destroys tubercle
bacilli without causing any material
change in the nutritive qualities of the
milk.
The following are the words that I wish
to emphasise :
If all milk for human consumption
were pasteurised in licensed plants
under adequate supervision, it is no
exaggeration to say that tuberculosis of
bovine origin would be eliminated.
Could any stronger proof be produced of
the necessity for the pasteurisation of all
milk used for human consumption?
I will not touch the humanitarian side
of the question; I will not talk about the
deplorable deaths from bovine tuberculosis. There are Members of this
House who have had friends who died
from that entirely and completely incurable disease-tubercular meningitis.
One of the saddest duties a doctor can
undertake is to look after one of these
cases, and to see the person slowly-unfortunately very often it is a very slow
process-fade away and die and have to
acknowledge to the parents that the case
is absolutely hopeless and that he can do
nothing. These cases are always due to
bovine tuberculosis, and they would be
completely stopped if all milk were
pasteurised. If all milk were pasteurised
diseases of the bones, joints, glands would
disappear; and a very large proportion-
I will not say what proportion, but it is
a very large one-of the cripples of this
country would not be so afflicted if it were
not for the infection they get through
drinking milk.
I think there is no excuse whatever for
the Ministry stopping at Grade C and
Grade D, and leaving out Grades A and
In refusing or neglecting to pasteurise Grades A and B the Ministry are
giving a certificate of purity to the consumers of Belfast. I say that is a criminal thing to do because people will drink
this milk and think it is quite safe.
Furthermore, a certain number of people
who are drinking Grade A at the present

time-it is comparatively safe-will
change to Grade B because they are both

The Minister of Agriculture will probably tell us that he is acting on the advice of his experts. Who are his experts?
The Ministry of Agriculture is in charge
of a very important part of public health
administration in Northern Ireland.
They also deal with the diseases of horses,
cows, pigs, and asses, but they have no
medical men to advise them; they are
dependent for advice as to human diseases
on horse doctors, cow doctors, and
doctors. If the right hon. Gentleman
were ill would he call in a veterinary surgeon to attend to him? If he would not
why use his veterinary staff as experts in
matters which concern the health of
human beings? It is not as if the Minisass
try of Agriculture could not secure the
advice of a doctor.
If they wish to economise and will not
pay for such advice-we were told yesterday they can pay the sum of £100,000
in commission to a consultant on electrical matters-they might practice the form
of economy carried out by the Ministry
of Home Affairs. When my good friend
and that very capable official, Dr. John
M'Cloy, died, instead of filling his position, as they should have done, they, in
an unwonted fit of economy, asked the
principal Medical Officer of the Minis
try of Labour to take over his work.
Dr. Boyd is one of the cleverest and best
qualified medical men in the North of
Ireland.
If I may say so, that particular Ministry is the only one of the five
Ministries connected with public health
in Northern Ireland at which no stone
can be thrown. It always does its health
duties in a satisfactory manner, which
cannot be said about any of the other
four.
Instead of appointing a Principal
Medical Officer the Ministry of Home
Affairs put this extra burden upon the
shoulders of the principal Medical Officer
in the Ministry of Labour, possibly
shortening that man's life by doing so,
because he probably had enough to do
already. Could not the Minister of
Agriculture follow the example of the
Minister of Home Affairs and put an
extra burden on Dr. James Boyd's
shoulders? Probably he will die a year
or two sooner as a result, but at least he
will have the satisfaction of knowing that
his name will go down in history as the
only Civil Servant who ever died from
over-work. (Laughter). I would like
to read an extract from the British Medical Journal of August 7 in connection
with Grade "B" milk.
Accredited milk is produced under
conditions that do not ensure its safety
-that is Grade B milk-for the consumer, even in respect of tuberculosis.
The animals in the herd are submitted
to a clinical inspection by a Veterinary
Surgeon four times a year; but experience has shown the veterinary inspector
can no more diagnose early tuberculosis of the udder by palpation than a
doctor can diagnose early tuberculosis
of the lung by auscultation.
I always knew that was the case, but
apparently the experts in the Ministry

of Agriculture did not recognise that
fact. They profess to be able to diagnose tuberculosis in a B herd in time to
prevent gross contamination of the milk.
As a matter of fact it is weeks and months
from the time that the udder becomes
affected until they could possibly diagnose
it.
Accredited milk is found to contain
tubercle baccilli almost as often as
ungraded milk. The term accredited
is a misnomer and conveys to the
general public a suggestion of safety
which the milk that bears the name is
far from possessing.
So much for Grade B milk. Grade A,
T.T. milk, is not free from tuberculosis,
and, of course, it may contain all the

safe, although I grant you it is comparatively safe. Again, I have more than

Dr. LYLE: A back number.

The child on raw milk is very fit.
Chilblains are practically eliminated.
Dr. E. Sprawson has shown that teeth
are less likely to decay owing to better
dentine formation. Our experience
shows that tubercle is not the result of

Lord Moynihan wrote and expressed

boys were given a pint of raw milk daily

during the previous five years, amongst
the same number of delicate children who
got pasteurised milk, 14 cases occurred.
While the tubercle germ is killed, the
beneficial ones are also destroyed.

Then there is an important point that

It should be understood that bovine

glands and bones. This type does not
spread from person to person. If investigation is made these cases are very
rare. Human tuberculosis is the pulmonary type, or tuberculosis of the
lung. This type spreads from person
to person, and is the type which is
spreading. It is not got from drinking
milk.
That is the point that has been overlooked-the distinction between bovine

being so, we came to the conclusion that
the only way to deal with milk in bulk
was by pasteurisation. I am not one of
those who say that that is the finest thing
that can be done. Personally I have

as much about milk as I thought he did
when he set out. After all, the standard
that is set up in the Food and Drugs Act
is a purely arbitrary one. I know of no
reason under heaven why the figure 3
should have been settled upon as the
standard of butter fat in milk, because
those of us who have experience know
how it does fluctuate below and above
that standard as the milk actually comes
from the cow. But for the purposes of
the administration of that Act the law
simply says the standard is three per
cent., and certain tests are provided, and
if the butter fat falls below three per
cent. the law presumes that the milk has
been tampered with. But it is not proved
at all. It is not necessarily proved that
the milk has been tampered with.
All
that is proved is that it is not up to the
three per cent. standard of butter fat,
and as the law stands the producer is
liable to be fined.
In the administration of a Clause of
this kind we in the Ministry have tests,
and we would resort to ways and means
of our own, having regard to our experience over a long number of years,
whereby we could be satisfied that a
particular case was no exception, that it

temperature of the producer's byre, but

The Minister of Finance sometimes

for an official being started with a salary

saving finance when he is dealing with

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Home Affairs.
CHRISTMAS AMENITIES FOR
SERVICE HOSPITAL PATIENTS.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
a circular letter has been sent out by his
Ministry to the various Boards of
Guardians authorising them to spend an
extra sixpence per head to provide
Christmas amenities for any Service
patients in the Board's hospitals at
Christmas, and, if so, whether he thinks
sixpence per head is sufficient to give
Service men and women the Christmas
amenities to which their service entitles
them.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The circular to which the
hon. Member refers was drafted in
Whitehall, and was issued at the request
of an Imperial Department for which my
Ministry is agent.
The term "Christmas amenities
refers to the external (or decorative)
rather than the internal (or gastronomic)
side of Christmas cheer. Consequently,
no part of the sixpence has to be set aside
for turkeys and plum puddings-the cost
of which is authorised by the late Irish
Poor Law Commissioners and the practice
is observed by my Ministry. The entire
sum referred to is, therefore, available
for providing Service patients with false
noses, paper hats, holly and mistletoe.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that this was done
by Whitehall, is Local Government not
one of the services that are absolutely
and completely under the control of the
Government of Northern Ireland, and are
these infirmaries and hospitals not under
the control of the Government of Northern Ireland? Why is it that everything
that is unpopular is put on to the
Imperial Government and everything that
is popular to the Northern Government?
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. Member is
completely in error. Emergency hospital
services are under
control of the
Ministry of Health.
the
Mr. NIXON : If the
emergency
hospitals are under the control of the
Ministry of Health, why do you interfere
with them, putting on 6d to entertain at
Christmas? That is not what you did for
the Town Clerk of Belfast.

4. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he has received a letter
from Councillor F. J. Lavery, J.P.,
F.A.I., 93 High Street, Belfast, stating
that prior to the outbreak of war the
Castlereagh Rural District passed plans
for the erection of eight semi-detached
cottages situated at Church Road, Lower
Castlereagh, Belfast; that four of these
were completed comprising kitchenette,
scullery, three bedrooms and gardens,
front and rere, and that with a view to
providing necessary housing for homeless
families he (Mr. Lavery) is prepared to
proceed with the erection of four semidetached cottages subject to licence being
issued and the essential building materials
made available; and whether he can state
if this will be done.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part, my
Ministry is prepared to recómmend the
release of materials for the building of
six pairs of experimental houses with the
object of testing new methods or new
materials to be used, with a view to
obtaining cheaper and more rapidly constructed houses.
Apart from this, the limited supplies
of essential materials that can be released
must be devoted, in general, to local
authority schemes designed to provide
houses letting at relatively low rents. No
material can be released for houses to be

3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state when it is
proposed to introduce the necessary legislation to implement the concessions recently announced by him in respect of
the claims set forth in the manifesto of
the Retired Teachers' Union of the 4th
October last; whether he has seen and
considered a further statement issued by
the union calling attention to certain injustices that these concessions have not
removed; and whether he will again review the whole position with a view to
removing the remaining grievances of
retired teachers in view of the very strong
case made out for such further review in
this latest statement.
Major SINCLAIR: The recently
announced concessions to teacher pensioners will be brought into effect by
amending teachers' superannuation
schemes made under the provisions of the
Education Act of 1923, and laid before
Parliament for approval. In addition,
legislation is necessary to amend the
Superannuation (Teaching Services) Act,
1941, so as to release the contributions

Labour.
INSURANCE OF R.U.C.
PENSIONERS.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if exmembers of the R.U.C., who are not
ex-members of the R.I.C., are liable to pay
contributions for stamping cards when
employed in insurable work; and, if so,
whether he can state what benefits if
any they receive for such contributions.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): Leaving out of account the rare
case in which an ex-member of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is insured at the
date of his retirement by virtue of earlier
employment, the position on retirement
from the force depends on whether a
allowance has been
superannuation
granted in respect of service in it.
If a superannuation allowance has been
granted, the ex-member of the constabulary cannot become insured. He pays
no contributions, the employer's share
only being paid in respect of him if he
takes up employment, and he cannot
qualify for benefits. If, however, he has
not been granted a superannuation allowance, contributions are payable in the
ordinary way if he takes up insurable
employment, and he can qualify for full
benefits.
Mr. NIXON: Can the Minister tell us
-if he cannot tell us now will he tell us
some other time-why the police on port
duty at Bangor are paying insurance and
what will they be able to get out of it?

however, not be submitted to fill posi-

GRADING OF FLAX.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been called to the fact that at the last
meeting of the Mourne Branch of the
Ulster Farmers' Union a deputation of
farmers who had flax in the market the
previous day, attended and reported that
the grading of flax was such that some of
them had no option but to take their
flax home again, and demanded that the
Ministry of Agriculture be asked to hold
an inquiry into the way flax was graded;
whether the Ministry has confidence in
the grading staff, as the staff did not
depend on their own judgment, but consulted the umpire before announcing
their decision in each lot; and whether
it is a fact that when a dispute arose
between a grader and a farmer there
was nobody to appeal to, as the appeal
judge had already interfered in
general grading.
the
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I would refer the
hon. Member to the answer I gave to the
hon. Member for North Tyrone on
November 9th. All I can usefully add
is that since that date the grading of flax
has given general satisfaction. Steps
have been and are being taken which
will, I hope, maintain and indeed enhance the confidence of our farmers in
the equity of the grading standards and
the adherence by the graders to the
standards laid down and the procedure
for appeal.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, may I ask
whether he is aware of the fact that a
great improvement has taken place in the
grading of flax since the matter was
raised by the hon. Member for North
Tyrone in this House?

us why he has allowed this matter of the

the Resolution which was passed unanimously by this House a considerable time
ago, and which was moved by me calling
for an improvement on the grading of
flax?

Mr. BROWN: I think this matter
of electricity, in view of the
of the facts
which have been brought to light,
is one that calls for inquiry by a
Select Committee of this House, or otherwise as may be decided. The facts show
that the consultant has got some. £40,000
in fees, and is now being paid 2,500
guineas per annum. I have received
further information on this matter from
some members of the Belfast Corporation
that places it in a still more serious
light. I am told that the. Belfast Coraccount
poration has just received an
amounting to £6,000, and this is only an
interim account, and that account is for
the Corporation's share for the carting
of coal alone. That, according to
my information, would not have arisen
at all if the station had been built
elsewhere than it was built. That is only
one aspect of the matter, and it shows
there has been extravagance, and we
should obviate that in future by having
it investigated with a view to preventing
a repetition of this extravagance.
It is a well known fact that the Electricity Board of Northern Ireland gets
its electricity supply in bulk from the
Belfast Corporation. Therefore, every
bit of this extravagance in the case of

Committee

it was, in fact, less than the usual percentage rate paid to consultant engineers.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): In the first place I think it is
only right that I should congratulate
the hon. Member for Carrick on the very
fine effort he has made. If I may say
So, the whole standard of this debate
has been extremely high and most illuminating, and the criticism has been of a
most valuable character. We have had
points of view expressed by various
Members, and Members of the Government have expressed their point of view
as well. I should like to say in the first
place that as a Government we have
realised the extreme importance of this
very important question. We are aware
only too acutely of the difficulties which
exist not only in Belfast but in the
country as well, and I hope hon. Members when they criticise the Government
will appreciate the fact that we were
doing everything that could be done to
solve a very difficult problem. The
criticism that nothing has been done is
entirely unfounded.
It is not a question of whether there
is a problem; it is a question of how and
when it can be solved. The problem
divides itself into two parts; first, what
can be done during war time, and second,
what can be done in peace. During war
time we are restricted by very exceptional conditions. We cannot in any
way weaken the war effort. That is the
first essential. Then we are faced with
a shortage of materials. Even if we had
all the supplies of materials, money, and
labour, which we have not got, we still
would not be able to carry out a programme such as we are asked to do. We
are part of the United Kingdom. That
is a point which I think every hon. Member agrees with and therefore whatever
we do we must operate to the general interest. We have been rationed in other
matters, and we must be rationed in
materials as well. Though there
appears to be an ample supply of
materials I am assured from inquiries
in the highest sources that the materials
necessary are very limited indeed especially in regard to certain articles.
Some hon. Members have suggested
that part of our Imperial Contribution.
might be used on a housing scheme. In
my view the finanical arrangements which
were made by my predecessor and the late.
Mr. Pollock with the Imperial Treasury
are so valuable that it would be a bad
thing for Ulster if we did anything that
would jeopardise that position. My hon.
Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary,
will give details and will answer the
criticism which has been offered in the
House, but I should like to say that as a
result of the negotiations that have been
going on for a long time, the Imperial
Government have authorised this Government to proceed immediately with the
erection of a total of 750 houses on terms
which involve the payment of a subsidy
of £390 per house.
I should like to point out that this
number is not based on an arithmetical
comparison with houses authorised in
England, Wales or Scotland. The Imperial Authorities have recognised our
special needs in a very generous manner,
and I should like to pay tribute and put
on record an expression of gratitude to the
various Ministers on the other side who

Now, let me say something about our
plans for the post-war period. We have
two aspects to consider and two problems
to solve. We have, first of all, the question of the development and improvement
in housing which the public rightly
expect. Unfortunately we have to make
up our shortages, a leeway which is a

First of all, how we are to carry out the

houses, and, secondly, how we can make

and learned Member for St. Anne's that

Mr. right hon. Friend, the Minister of

that statement indicated that it would be

United Kingdom.
In my view it is now incumbent upon
our local authorities to carry out their

There are
obvious difficulties in the financial sphere,
but it should be possible to evolve a plan
which will enable us to go ahead with
post-war reconstruction at the earliest
•
possible moment. The time for recriminations is passed; the Government knows
the problem to be faced and it is doing
all it can to solve it. The day for satisfying all our needs and wishes has not
arrived yet, but we should do what we can
at once and make every preparation possible for our post-war reconstruction programme.
If we do that then instead of
having to wait for years, as we did after
the last war, we shall be able to give our
men and women a decent housing scheme
in a matter of months.

are

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Wilson Hungerford):
This debate has been productive. of a
great many suggestions, many of them of
very great interest, and if the Ministry
ever could have had any doubts as to the
urgency of the housing problem and the
deep interest in it taken by the Members
on both sides of the House, such doubts
would have been dispelled. The Ministry, of course, has never had any such
doubts and, as ever, it has been receptive.
of all suggestions made to it.
I feel, however, that I must point out
that a great many of the suggestions have
been founded on a misunderstanding of
various facts.
I propose to deal with
some of these facts in particular, but
before doing so, I would refer to explanation of our financial relations with the
Imperial Treasury which has been given
to the House by my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, and I would
remark that if hon. Members will consider this statement of the position they
will, I feel sure, understand why the
problem of making arrangements for the
provision of houses in war time. is not one
which my Department can deal with by
a stroke of the pen.
It is not reasonable to expect that we
should have the advantages of the financial resources of the United Kingdom
without its being necessary for us to
arrange that what we do about housing
here will not cause difficulty and embarrassment to the authorities on the other
side who, of course, have their housing
problem just as we have ours. It is for
this reason that we cannot always say at
a moment's notice exactly what provision
for war-time housing we propose to make.
I have, of course, the most complete
understanding and the fullest sympathy
with the desire of hon. Members to know
what is going to be done, but inopportune
pressure upon the Government can, in
the circumstances that exist, place it in
a very difficult position; and, while I
welcome the expression of the views of the
House, for which this debate has given
an opportunity, I am sorry my hon.
Friend, the Member for South Down, did
not find it possible to see his way to postpone the opening of the debate, as I had
asked him, for a few more days, so that

the Government were hopeful that these

the immediate future. Had it been possible to postpone the debate a little longer
much of the time of the House might
have been saved and Members might have
had a clearer understanding of the posi
tion, as we would then have been in a

position to tell them, as the

feel sure the House will realise that this

Mr. BROWN: Will the hon. Gentleman tell the House where they are going
to be built, in the city, or in the provincial areas also?
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I am
sure my hon. Friend realises the position
in Belfast. He sees it every day he is

This offer is being communicated to the

into bricks and mortar will not be long in

I should now like to deal with some
points raised in the Debate and also
correct certain statements that have been
made. One of these was in relation to
the number of houses built during the
war in Scotland. It was suggested that
the figure given by my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Home Affairs of 1,000
houses was a gross under-estimate and
that point was elaborated to some extent
by the hon. Member for Antrim. I do
not know whether the hon. Member who
raised this point thought my right hon.
Friend was for some obscure reason
deliberately misleading the House, or
whether he thought that my Department
had not taken the trouble to keep itself
informed of war time building operations
on the other side. Whatever the
planation may be, I should like to say
that we are, and have been, fully aware
of the building that has been carried out
in Scotland and that the statement of
my
exright hon. Friend was perfectly
accurate.
The number of new houses provided
under the interim building programme
authorised by the Government in Scotland is, in fact, 1,000 houses, 800 in
urban areas and 200 in rural areas. But
we have been well aware, and in fact my
right hon. Friend has specifically stated
that a large number of houses, the construction of which had been commenced
before the war began, had been completed, and he was also aware, of course,
that a number of emergency houses had
been completed for war workers. In
fact, of these houses the number started
pre-war in Scotland and at present in
hands, is about 3,800, but all that number have not been completed. The number of emergency houses for war workers
is 600.
It will be seen therefore that to quote
a figure of four thousand to five thousand
houses as the Scottish war-time programme is totally misleading, though,
as I have pointed out, it is not entirely
incorrect to say that something like that
number of new houses have come into
use in Scotland since the war.
As a
debating point, the hon. Member concerned may consider it of some value, but
I can only say that figures of this kind
are not of the slightest value from the
point of view of making our case with
the Imperial authorities. For this purpose it is necessary that our figure should
not only be accurate but that they should
be comparable, but the figure given by
the hon. Member for Armagh as the
housing requirements for the. Province
would appear to bear no sort or kind of
relation to the facts whatever. The
hon. Member informed us that no fewer
than 300,000 houses are needed at the
present time. As the total number of
houses at present in the whole of Northern Ireland is only something like
320,000 the hon. Member's suggestion,
therefore, amounts to saying that practically all the houses in Northern Ireland at present need to be rebuilt.
I would be the last to suggest that our
housing conditions are satisfactory, but
I would be very sorry indeed to think
that they were anything like as bad as
that and certainly I should be very sorry
to use such a figure in any serious discussion with the Imperial authorities.
On the other hand, the hon. Member for
Bloomfield seemed to suggest that the
solution to the problem lies not in providing new houses but in repairing existing houses. I say that this is what he
seemed to imply for I can hardly believe
that it was a serious suggestion on his
part. He must, I am sure, realise that
such appalling conditions as obtain here
in the matter of over-crowding can
hardly be met by putting existing houses
into repair.

facilities, adequate ventilation and air
space, and all other similar conditions
without which it would be impossible to
make any estimate of housing requirements over which the Ministry would be
in a position to stand in making a case
for due allocation of finance and materials.
The hon. Member for St. Anne's
raised the question of constructional
methods used in other countries. I can
give him the assurance that the Ministry
has not overlooked these possibilities. The
Ministry's technical officers have kept
closely in touch with the expert Committee that has been exploring this question on the other side, and I may say
that the Ministry's chief architect is very
familiar from personal experience and investigation on the spot with housing
methods, not only in America and on the
Continent of Europe, but in Russia and
many other parts of the world. In prefabrication, unquestionably, much can be
done in the way of standardisation of
internal fittings, but up to the present
no material solution to the housing
problem has been found on those lines.
The House is, however, aware that the
possibilities of new methods of construction have by no means been ruled out,
and that the Government is, in fact, with
the co-operation of the Belfast Corporation, facilitating the carrying out of
experiments in this matter.
The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh
spoke at some length about his efforts in
this direction, and I think the House may
have inferred from what he said that he
had experienced something in the nature
of obstruction either from the Government or from the Corporation. Any
such suggestion is without foundation,
and indeed I do not think that the hon.
Housing
Housing
23 NOVEMBER 1943
Member intended to make any such suggestion. So far as my Department is
concerned, his plans were dealt with
within six days of their receipt in the
office, and I think no reasonable person
could expect that the examination of
plans and drawings involving
new
methods of construction could be dealt
.with more expeditiously than this.
I do not wish in any way to detract
from the efforts of the hon. Member to
contribute to the solution of the housing
problem, but I think I must point out
that there is no question, as some hon.
Members have suggested, of the Government having contended that there were
insuperable difficulties in the way of
building houses, even when materials were.
available, and that the Member for Ballynafeigh has demonstrated that this is not
so. Everyone knows that anybody who
can obtain materials at the present time
can, without the slightest difficulty, build
houses and can, moreover, dispose of
them at a profit, whatever they cost. No
credit whatever, therefore, is due to
persons, merely because materials having
been given them, they have built houses.
The value. of the suggestion of the hon.
Member was that he felt he had discovered a method of construction which
would enable houses to be built more
expeditiously, or more cheaply than by
existing methods, and it was on these
grounds, and on these grounds alone,
that the Government expressed its
willingness to arrange for an allocation
of materials. Whether or not these hopes
of the hon. Member will be realised is a
matter which only the future can determine, but I am sure his experiments carry
with them the good wishes of the House.
The hon. Member for Woodvale raised
the question of bricks. He quoted an
order made by the Ministry of Commerce
upon the subject, and that is, of course,
the concern of the Ministry of Commerce.,
and not my Department. I have no
doubt that the order is fully justified, and
I would only remark that when large
scale building operations are undertaken
here, it is essential that the bricks used
should be of a quality that will wear well
and will be satisfactory in use. It is a
matter of common knowledge that extremely unsatisfactory bricks have been
produced from time to time in certain
areas
in Northern Ireland, and my
Ministry, as the Department responsible
for housing, is certainly most deeply concerned to secure that materials of this
kind will not be used in future housing
schemes, and any measure that the
Ministry of Commerce may be able to
undertake towards securing a proper
standard of quality in materials will certainly have the whole-hearted support of
my Department.
In regard to local authorities throughout the Province, they may rest assured
that as part of the post-war planning
programme materials and finances will be
allocated to Northern Ireland which will
enable them to provide large numbers of
It is
houses throughout the Province.
difficult to say exactly, of course, what
numbers of houses will be comprised in
this programme in individual areas, but
it is recognised that our housing conditions are extremely unsatisfactory and
local authorities can safely count upon it
being made possible for them to meet the
deficiency in housing to a very substantial
extent, even during the years immediately following the war, when we must
expect post-war difficulties to exist. The
Minister of Home Affairs has rightly
pointed out that until more definite information, both as to finances and
materials are in their possession, local
authorities cannot be expected actually to
purchase or earmark definitely sites for
housing, but it is most necessary that
they should give immediate consideration
to the general problem of where their
houses can best be put so that the needs
of their localities can be most conveniently met and the fullest advantage
can be taken of existing services such as
water, electric light, sewers, etc.
These are matters which local authorities should take into consideration at the
earliest possible moment, and as they are
matters directly concerned with planning,
local authorities should proceed with the
skeleton plans of their areas with the
utmost despatch. It may in individual
cases be possible for local authorities to
arrive at fairly definite decisions as to
location of the first part of their housing
programme, and where this is possible,
the Government will be prepared to
afford them all the encouragement and
assistance possible in the matter of acquiring sites, should such seem to be a desirable procedure, but it is most necessary
that they should realise the importance.
of considering at the earliest possible
moment, the question of the general loca-

object of the hon. and gallant Member is

propose later on will be in conformity

gallant Member.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): As I understand the
object of the hon. and gallant Member is
to so alter the Clause that it would be
open to the Ministry to substitute a joint.
committee for a particular local authority,

beyond doubt I have no hesitation in

propose later on will be in conformity
with the underlying idea of the hon. and
gallant Member.

Mr. MINFORD: I would like to support the Amendment. I think it is

Mr. LOWRY: It is somewhat difficult
to deal with words that are really consequential on an Amendment before the
hon. and learned Member for St. Anne's
has dealt with the substantive Amendment and until I have replied giving
reasons why it is not possible to accept
this. Might I say here that the apprehensions that have been expressed by the
hon. and gallant Member for East Down,
the hon. and learned Member for
St. Anne's and the hon. Member for
Antrim are unfounded? This merely
deals with interim development. It is
but a transitory provision and the rights
of owners cannot be interfered with
substantially until the scheme comes
out.
Under the Act of 1931 all the
necessary procedure there laid down will
form ample protection for owners so far
as planning is concerned.
The clause as it stands is intended only
as interim development procedure, and
the sole and only purpose is to prevent
development being carried out during
the interim period which will interfere
with the final plan. The only person or
authority that is concerned or that know
anything about interference with the
planning scheme is the planning authority, and, accordingly, there is no justification from the planning point of view
for giving anyone but the planning
authority notice of these applications.
Apart from this the whole objection
which has been put up is that it does
cause some interference and delay to
persons who have legitimate reasons for
wishing to develop during the interim
period.
It is, therefore, undesirable to add
further to the difficulties and delays, and
if one were to consider all the elaborate
planning set forth in the Schedules to
the Act of 1931 I firmly believe that we
should never arrive at the time when the
plan would be ready for submission and
when the rights and the wrongs, it may
be, of the people were thoroughly crystallised and recognised, and it would add
such cumbersome procedure to this
matter that it would really hold up interim planning completely. I think
that the Amendment has been brought
forward perhaps without due consideration of the procedure that is already laid
down for the protection of owners in the
Schedules to the principal Act of 1931.
I would be prepared to elaborate the
matter further if desired on the principal Amendment to be moved by my hon.
and learned Friend.

up there.

2 (Interim development
(1) The following provisions of this
section shall have effect in relation to
Planning Bill-
Committee
24 NOVEMBER 1943
orders made by the Ministry after the
passing of this Act under section four
of the principal Act (which relates to
the development of estates pending the
coming into operation of planning
schemes); and any such order is in this
Act referred to as an "interim development order."
(2) An interim development order
may itself permit the development of
land either unconditionally or subject
to such conditions as may be prescribed
in the order or may empower any local
authority specified in the order, and
acting with the approval of the
Planning Commission, to permit the
development of land in accordance with
the provisions of this section; and any
such authority, acting as aforesaid, is
in this Act referred to as an "interim
development authority."
*
(4) An interim development may, by
a notice of postponement served in the
prescribed manner on the applicant,
postpone the consideration of any
interim development application either
generally or during such period as may
be specified in the notice, unless the
applicant shows to their satisfaction
that the proposed development would
be carried out immediately if the
application were granted:
Provided that-
*
*
*
*
*
*
(b) if with respect to any interim
development application it appears
to the Ministry that there are exceptional reasons requiring the
immediate determination thereof,
the Ministry may, without prejudice to its power to require the
application to be referred to the
Ministry for decision in accordance with the subsequent provisions of this Act, give directions
requiring the interim development
authority to determine the application, and, where a notice of
postponement has been served with
respect thereto, may by order
cancel the notice.
(5) An interim development application shall be deemed to be refused at
the expiration of two months from the
date of the receipt thereof unless within that period-
*
*
*
and any such application of which the
consideration has been so postponed for
any period shall be deemed to be
refused at the expiration of two months
from the end of that period unless
within those two months notice has
been given to the applicant as aforesaid or its consideration has again been
postponed by virtue of a further notice
of postponement:
Provided that-
*

(ii) where a notice of postponement
served with respect to any application is cancelled by an order made
by the Ministry or in proceedings
instituted before a court of summary jurisdiction. under this
section, this sub-section shall have
effect in relation to the application
as if for the reference therein to
the date of the receipt of the
application there were substituted
a reference to the date of the order
of the Ministry, or, as the case
may be, to the date of the final
determination of the proceedings.
(6) An applicant who is aggrieved by
the refusal of the interim development
authority to consent to his application,
or by any conditions imposed by them,
may within twenty-eight days from the
date on which he received notice of the
decision of the authority, or such
longer period as the Ministry may
allow appeal to the Ministry, and the
Ministry, after taking into consideration any offer of compensation made by
the local authority, may dismiss or
allow the appeal, either unconditionally
or subject to such conditions as the
Ministry thinks proper to impose; but
the Ministry, before deciding any such
appeal, shall, if either the appellant or
the interim development authority so
desire, afford to them an opportunity
of appearing before and being heard by
a person appointed by the Ministry for
the purpose.
