The purpose of this amendment is to
bring our provisions for the making of
interim development orders into line
with those in England. Slight differences
exist which create complications.
short, section 4 of our principal Act restricts interim development orders to
giving permission to build. That is the sole
purpose of that section, and experience
in England has shown that it ought to be
wider. It really amounts to the. embodiment of sections 1 and 2 of the English
Act of 1932. One is bound to admit
that the experience of town planning over
here has been somewhat limited. No
great advantage was taken of the Town
Planning Act of 1931. On the other
hand, the English Act of 1932 was worked
for a very considerable number of years,
and from the experiencé garnered there
it has seemed good to the Ministry that
this is a better way of approaching the
matter.

councils seems to me to be quite wrong.
It is quite an inconsistent proceeding.

meaning of that is this.

Mr. NIXON: I think that perhaps
what the Clause leads to is this. A person makes application for development,
and it is refused. It is not necessary to
notify him that it is refused. It is
deemed to be refused after a silence of
several months. That is a thing a lot of
people are well accustomed to in regard
to one particular Department of the
Government. They never get an answer
at all, and then it is deemed that their
request has been refused. For instance,
I have a communication to that Ministry
from the wife of a soldier who has no
house. She got no answer, and it is
deemed to be refused.
The Minister was speaking very logically, because he said that if a person who
is going to build has not the necessary
finance and wants an advance from a
bank, or from a friend, or a building
society, and if he wants someone to
guarantee him he has to produce documentary evidence to that party, bank, or
building society. That is most logical,
and the Minister was on good ground
when he said that. If you want a
guarantee, you must produce your
accounts; you must show how you stand
before you can get the money. That is
logical. It has been done in every case
I know of except, for instance, in the
case of the Electricity Supply Board.
They are guaranteed, I understand, and
yet they would not submit their accounts
for audit. I am only referring to that
by way of illustration as showing that in
practice the Government depart from the
logical principle laid down here by the
Ministry of Home Affairs. That will be
useful to me again.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Dealing
with Clause 2, as a whole, which has been
debated, I would like to make a very few
remarks on the Clause as it now stands
in the Bill. The first thing is, I would
like to congratulate the Government on
having accepted the proposal put forward.
that the Planning Commission should
not be statutory should not have
statutory powers. Secondly, the principle
has been accepted as put forward by the

that the Ministry is not to be the final
judge. There is to be an appeal to some
body to be appointed, consisting of independent persons with knowledge of the
matter. I think having established these
two principles the Committee has done a
now.
There is one point I would like to speak
on. And that is there is a right of appeal
given to a court of summary jurisdiction
or petty sessions where somebody is not
satisfied. I would like the Minister to
consider whether this petty sessions court
is a suitable court for dealing with these
matters. There is in my mind a specific
instance where an estate or the trustee of
an estate lodged plans with the local
authority of rather a large nature. I
happen to know a case where plans are to
be considered and the value of the land
to which the plans apply is well over
£30,000. If these plans were lodged for
interim development and the local authority refused and the people said they were
ready to go on, the point is this is such
a body as a petty sessions court a suitable
court to give a decision on large matters
such as I have mentioned-large estates
and large development plans. I have
very little knowledge of petty sessions.
courts, but I do not think they have the
personnel for dealing with documents and
all that sort of thing. The question is
whether or not there should be an alternative acording to the valuation of the
property, the county courts or some other
body when the valuation is outside the
normal scope of the activity of a court of
summary jurisdiction. These things arise.
in my mind. It does not appear that a
court of summary jurisdiction is the best.
or most suitable court to bring valuable
estates before. I am pointing this out
for the consideration of the Minister.

CLAUSE 4 (Powers of Ministry of
Home Affairs with respect to interim
development applications).
(1) If it appears to the Ministry that
it is expedient, having regard to considerations affecting the public interest,
that any interim development application, or any class or description of such
applications, should be referred to the
Ministry for decision, the Ministry may
give directions to the interim development authority requiring that application, or applications of that class or
description, to be so referred; and any
decision of the Ministry on an application so referred to it shall be deemed
for the purposes of section five of this
Act to be a decision given by the
interim development authority, and for
all other purposes of this Act to be a
decision given by the Ministry on
appeal from the decision of the interim
development authority:
Provided that before dealing with
any application so referred to it the
Ministry shall, if either the interim
development authority or the applicant
so desire, afford to them an opportunity
of appearing before and being heard
by a person appointed by the Ministry
for the pupose.

I said in speaking earlier that many of
the Amendments that stood in my name
were put down for the purpose of discussion. That is not so with regard to
this Amendment, which is one of
substance. The Clause provides :
In any case where-
(a) an interim development application is refused or is granted
subject to conditions; or
(b) a permission for the development
of land is revoked or modified by
an order under section three of
this Act;
and the applicant or the person to
whom the permission was granted (as
the case may be) shows to the satisfaction of the local authority that he is
likely to suffer any damage or expense
by reason of the decision of the interim
development authority, then the local
authority may, if they think fit, make
a contribution, the payment of which
Planning Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
shall not be unreasonably delayed, towards the said damage or expense.
The Clause, as drafted, recognises by
reason of the refusal of an interim appli-
'cation or the modification or revocation of
permission that there is a recognition of
a title to compensation. The title to
compensation, although admitted by the
Clause, is actually not given, because
under the Bill the local authority may if
they think fit give compensation. That
is surely a completely unsatisfactory condition. If a person is injured, financially
or otherwise, by reason of the action of
the authority, then he is entitled to compensation. The right of compensation
should be given and my Amendment seeks
to achieve that purpose. I suggest the
insertion of the words:
has suffered or will suffer any damage
or expense by reason of the decision of
the interim development authority then
the local authority shall compensate
him in respect of such damage or expense, and the amount of such compensation shall be assessed, after hearing
the said person and the local authority,
by an independent person appointed by
the Ministry for this purpose.
We all know that when it is permissive
for a local authority to make contributions they will, in fact, make none, and
I would venture to say that justice demands that the right of compensation
shall be specifically given by the Clause.
The Clause seems to me to be one which
achieves nothing. I ask myself, and I
ask every Member of the Committee to
ask himself this question, if a person
is entitled to compensation why should
the right of compensation not be given?
Why should it be left in the air for a
local authority to make a payment only if
they think fit? We are not doing any
damage to the local authority by this
Amendment, because if a person makes a
claim for compensation and is not entitled
to get it then the person appointed to
determine the question will not give him
any. If he is entitled to compensation
the person appointed by the Ministry to
assess the compensation will give it.
The right to compensation should be
absolutely definite and not left contingent
on the will of a council. Everybody
knows the reluctance with which local
authorities make payments, and I do fear
that in many cases the Clause if it were
left in its present form would create injustice and that a person who was entitled
to compensation would not, in fact, get
it. I think that that is a possibility that
cannot be overlooked by any person who
knows the local authorities. If this
Clause becomes law in its present form
you will have people entitled to compensation, and whose right to compensation
is recognised by the Section, unable to
enforce that right by reason of the looseness of the wording of the Section. I
commend my Amendment to the Minister
of Home Affairs as one that might be
accepted. It will not be a big matter,
because the number of claims will not be
large in number or extent, but it does
seem wrong to leave a person who has,
in fact, a legitimate claim against a local
authority without any redress. In law
we say there is no wrong without a
remedy. If a person is wronged here he
is deliberately left without a remedy. I
consider that indefensible, and I move
my Amendment.

Mr. LOWRY: In the principal Act
there are comprehensive provisions for
compensation with regard to either the
question of property or its effects. In
the earlier Clauses of this Bill there is
provision for compensation where it
arises. In fact, between the principal
Act and this Bill every conceivable circumstance has been taken into account
whereby compensation clearly and distinctly due is provided. But the greatest
foresight cannot provide for every sort
of case that may arise, and I myself have
seen cases where the local authorities
were anxious to do something in the case
of hardship, and where perhaps a person
could not legally claim, but it could not
be done. A case has been alluded to by
the hon. Member for Woodvale where an
action was brought, but there was little
hope of its success, and a compromise was
arrived at openly and publicly, because it
was felt that, while the law was against
the person, common sense and common
decency dictated that, if possible, something should be given.
Furthermore, here is a matter which
will arise constantly in arbitration in the
question of land, as I am sure the hon.
and learned Member for St. Anne's will
agree where property is sold and the
sitting tenant gets nothing. I remember
one of the first arbitrations I ever took
part in here concerned a number of
people who were dispossessed in one of
the smallest streets in Belfast. One of
the greatest troubles was to do something
for these people, and it could not be done
because the law was against them. If
my memory serves me right—and it is
over 30 years ago now-the arbitrator
and the Corporation took the trouble of
ascertaining in advance the views of the
then Local Government Board of Ireland,
and they found that the Board would not
look too severely on a small sum of compensation being given to these people.
As we go through the untried waters
of planning, we will find that cases may
and can arise that in the principal Act
and in sub-clause (5) of this Clause may
not have been covered in all circumstances.
A case might arise where a man thinks he
has a genuine grievance and it is not
covered by any of the earlier provisions.
We want to arrive at some sort of rough
balance, and put it in the power of the
local authority to behave in a decent way,
in the same way as neighbours behave
between themselves when some injury
arises, not through the negligence of any
of them, but perhaps through the misfortune of one of them. It is reasonable
that it should be in the power of a local
authority to make some sort of compensation towards that. I am quite prepared
to consider a method of assessing what is
in a measure an ex-gratia payment.
Here is a case that might arise. Take
the case where a local authority has
power, by means of a by-law, to prevent
pig-sties being erected within a certain
distance of a house. A person may have
had a pig-sty within a short distance of
the house for some considerable time.
Suppose by that by-law that man is
injured, he has no redress. I do not say
that that is a good case in which to give
Planning Bill—
Committee
24 NOVEMBER 1943
the man a small sum of money to move
the pig-sty, but that is the sort of case
that can arise, and where it would be
proper and decent to take some steps.
At the same time I am quite ready to
consider any suggestion that may be made
with a view to the assessment of payments made in this way in a manner that
could not give rise to any possible suspicions against anyone.
Compensation in all other cases that I
can readily think of is mandatory. It
is not until one comes down to this subclause (5) that anything of an optional
nature may come into it, and I do not
agree that local authorities will not pay
money under circumstances like that.
Both professionally and since I assumed
office I have constantly had the experience
of a desire on the part of local authorities
to do the decent thing if it were legally
possible to do it, and very often I have
regretfully to tell local authorities that
they cannot behave in the way one decent
man behaves to another, because the law
does not cover that sort of thing. It is
for that reason that it is desired to place
it in the power of the local authority to
make payment under such circumstances;
but, as I have said, I am open to see
that such payment should be assessed in
a manner that will throw suspicion on
no one, either payer or payee.

sub-clause that is now under discussion.

PLATERS' HELPERS AND

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Mr. NIXON: I wish to raise a matter
on the Adjournment of which I gave
previous notice to the Minister of Labour.
It concerns a strike. I myself have only
one word for strikes, and that is to settle
them. The right time to settle them is
as soon as you can, that is in the initial
stages. There is no use in letting them
develop and there is no use in standing
on a point of principle. There is a strike.
of platers' helpers and some other sections
of workers in the Yard, and there is
another strike, but I am not talking about
the cranemen. The platers' helpers sent
a deputation here this afternoon to see
the Minister and they were accompanied
by the secretary of the Yard Production
Warnock, John Edmond
TELLER FOR THE AYES-
Mr. Warnock
Stronge, Captain Sir Charles Norman
Lockhart
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Sir Norman Stronge.
no
Committee. Their complaint is that
the Minister would not see them.
The Minister will, doubt, speak
for himself. I think the right hon.
Gentleman should have seen them.
I am afraid there is a danger of this
matter getting worse. There is not one
bit of use in always abusing the strikers.
As long as I remember, whenever there
was a strike in the city of Belfast, the
strikers, according to certain people, were
wrong. They were always in the wrong.
The
very people who entertained
Ribbentrop, shook hands with him, and
showed him everything we had, would be
the first people to say the strikers were
wrong. The people who sent every bit of
scrap down the Lagan to Germany to
make bombs, while our own men were
idle, would also say that the strikers
were wrong. I am not going to assess
who is wrong or who is right. I want the
Minister of Labour, and the Government,
to leave no stone unturned in an endeavour to settle. this strike. I think that
the secretary of the Yard Production
Committee has standing enough with the
workers for the Minister to see and negotiate with him. The Minister knows
more about the Yard than I do, because
he worked in it. Although I never
worked in the Yard, I know a lot about
the men who work in it. I meet them
all the time. They come. to see me about
one thing or another, and I never found
them to be unreasonable.
There was another big strike here
which I did my best to settle. If the.
Government had taken my advice it could
have been settled on the first day. It was
a pity it was not settled. The ultimate
end of all strikes is a settlement, and is
it not better to settle them at once? Why
does the Minister not see the secretary of
the Yard Production Committee, find out
something about it, and see what can be
done? When a deputation comes up here
representing men on strike, it is irritat-
2293 Industrial Disputes in Belfast- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Platers' Helpers and Cranemen 2294
[Mr. Nixon]
ing for them to have to go back to their
colleagues and report that they would not
be received by the Minister of Labour.
I think a meeting is being held to-night.
It is a very bad thing for these men to
have to report to the men on strike, or
contemplating strike action, that they
would not be received. I think something
should be done about the matter. Even
at this late hour I think the men should
be interviewed to see what they have to
say.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Grant): I am afraid that the hon. Member for Woodvale has got this all wrong.
The platers' helpers are not out on strike.
I know, because within the last twenty
minutes I have been in consultation with
their accredited representative and he
told me they are not on strike. Things
may be said by the hon. Member for
Woodvale with the best intentions in the
world, but they do not make it any easier
for me. I think that at this juncture I
have the right to appeal to the Members
of this House and to the community as
a whole, both employers and employees,
to give me just a bit more help than I am
getting at the present time, because I feel
I am carrying my fair share of the work
in connection with these disputes. To-day
I have had three deputations, on Friday
last I had five deputations, and I have a
very large deputation in the morning.
All these people come to tell me how to
do my job, and I think on these grounds
and on many other grounds I have the
right to the consideration of the
munity as a whole.
com-
The task is not an easy one. I am not
grumbling about it, and I am not attempting to run away from it, but I have been
approached by the trade unions and by
the Confederation of Trade Unions and
asked that I should not see any deputations unless they are accompanied by the
recognised trade union delegates. That
is the position I am taking up, and that I
intend to take up so long as I am Minister
of Labour. I do not want it to be taken
that I am standing on my dignity and that
I would refuse to see members coming up
here from the shipyards, but the men the
hon. Member for Woodvale is talking
about are not on strike.
Mr. NIXON: They are here and they
say they are. You can interview them.
Mr. GRANT: I repeat I am informed
they are not on strike.
Mr. NIXON: They say they are.
Mr. GRANT: They have not said it to
me. I am dealing with strikes that are
going on at the present time, but negotiating machinery is in operation, and I
am going to two meetings to-night dealing with these problems. I cannot do
anything more, but every Tom, Dick, and
Harry leaving the shipyards need not
expect to come up here and send in a
message saying he wishes to see me. Definitely he will not see me unless he is
accompanied by representatives of his
trade union. I try as far as I possibly
can, sometimes at great inconvenience to
myself, to fit in arrangements to see deputations. I often get only twenty minutes
or half-an-hour for lunch, but I am prepared to see these deputations so long as
they are accompanied by officials of their
trade unions. There is a strike going on
now known as the crane drivers' strike,
and I have taken action to bring about a
settlement.
No one can accuse me of saying that
the strikers are always wrong. I made a
statement in this House last week that
has not made me any more popular in
certain quarters, but I do not care two
hoots about that. I know some strikes
are brought about by the men not getting
the consideration they are entitled to, but
there are strikes which are unjustifiable.
Some people walk out without notifying
my Ministry or the employers and they
walk up to Stormont and want the
Minister of Labour who knows nothing
about it to settle the strike. All I want
to say is, I am doing everything
humanly possible to deal with all these
things, and when I am doing that I think
I am entitled to ask for the co-operation
of all respectable members of the community.
Mr. NIXON: Mr. Speaker, I know I
am not allowed-
Mr. SPEAKER: I cannot allow the
hon. Member to speak again.
Mr. NIXON: I only want to ask a
question. You can allow me to ask a
question.
Mr. SPEAKER: I know that, but I
think the hon. Member for Woodvale

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
Mr. BROWN: I should like to ask the
Prime Minister what Bills he proposes to
take to-morrow. Will the Milk Bill be
taken? We had a remarkable Division
in this House to-day in which not a single
back-bencher voted with the Government.
I am not going to discuss that matter
now. The Milk Bill is an equally controversial matter, and we wish to know
from the Prime Minister when it will be
taken. Some of the Clauses in the Bill
are going to be strenuously opposed, and
we want to know from the Prime Minister
exactly when it will be taken. Will it be
taken to-morrow or postponed until
Tuesday next? It looks as if the remaining Clauses of the Planning (Interim
Development) Bill will take up some
time.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): It is proposed to take the Planning Bill, Committee stage, to-morrow,
and if there is time, the Milk Bill.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
PRICES OF TURKEYS.
3. Mr. McGURK asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will make further
representations to the Minister of Food
to have the prices fixed for turkeys and
other fowl reviewed, as the prices quoted
are too low and in order to recoup fowl
owners for their labour and expenses it
would require an increase of at least 1/-
per lb. to make the price remunerative.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The agricultural
index number of farmers' prices for
turkeys rose from 93 in 1938 to 214 in
1942. The corresponding index
of
farmers' prices for hens and chickens rose
from 72 to 170. The general index
of all agricultural prices rose during
the same period from 85.5 to 169.
It will be observed, therefore, that the
rise in turkey and fowl prices has been
greater than in the case of agricultural
prices generally. In these circumstances
I do not consider that a special case can
be made for increasing turkey and fowl
prices, but the whole question of the
inter-relationship of prices for different.
agricultural produce is at present under
consideration, and I will bear in mind the
representations made by the hon. Member.
PAYMENT OF A CONTRACTOR'S
WORKMAN.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether
a workman named
Moorehead, engaged by a contractor repairing war damaged houses, was paid less
for his work by the contractor than the
amount which the contractor claimed
from the War Damage Commission;
whether the Attorney-General can state
the rate per hour paid by the contractor
to Moorehead and the rate per hour
claimed by the contractor from the War
Damage Commission; the total amount
paid by the said contractor to Moorehead
in respect of work done on war damaged
houses and the total amount claimed from
the War Damage Commission by the said
contractor in respect of work done by
Moorehead; also the trade union rate
fixed for work such as Moorehead had
done at that time.
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
MacDermott): This matter has been the
subject of a close investigation by the
police, which has not produced any
evidence on which criminal proceedings
against the contractor concerned could be
sustained.
The workman, Andrew Moorehead, was
employed by this contractor in 1941 and
1942 first as a handy man and later as a
slater in the repair of war-damaged
houses in Severn Street, Bracken Street
and Carlisle Street, Belfast. The repairs
in Severn Street and Bracken Street were
done by the contractor for the owners of
the houses. In Severn Street, Moorehead
was paid at a rate of 1s 1d per hour
approximately. The contractor's accounts
for this street as furnished to the owners
and passed by them to the War Damage
Commission did not mention any rate for
Moorehead in particular, but stated generally the rate for slaters as ranging from
1s Old to 1s 11d per hour. In Bracken
Street, Moorehead was paid at a rate of
1s 5d per hour approximately. The contractor's account for this street as furnished
to the owners and passed to the Commission was made out on a jobbing basis of
time and material, the contractor's profit
and overhead expenses being covered in
the prices charged which included a flat
rate of 2s 6d per hour for all tradesmen,
including slaters, and 1s 10d per hour for
labourers.
These charges were not taken by the
officials of the Commission as representing
rates actually paid, and I am satisfied
they were not intended to be so taken, as
the charge made for tradesmen slaters was
considerably in excess of the standard
rate which was 1s 11d per hour.
Carlisle Street the contractor worked for
the Belfast Corporation. Moorehead was
paid at the standard rate on this job and
no question of overclaiming arises:
In

the total of the wages paid to Moorehead
in respect of his work on war-damaged
houses, as I have no precise information
available as to the time actually worked
at the various rates; nor can I give the
total amount claimed in respect of work
done by Moorehead in view of the fact

SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
UNIFORM.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
made-up uniform is issued to the Special
Constabulary; whether it fits; whether in
the event of misfits there is any allowance
paid to the men for a refit; and whether
the quality of the material used in such
uniform is equal to the material used in
the uniform of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The uniform of the Special
Constabulary is issued to them in the
"made-up" state. It is purchased in
such a large variety of standard sizes that
normally no difficulty arises in ensuring a
good fit, but where, in the exceptional
case, standard fittings are unsuitable for
an individual, his uniform is specially
made to his own measurements. No allowance is payable for alterations.
as
The cloth used in making up Special
Constabulary uniforms is the same
that used for Royal Ulster Constabulary
uniforms except in the case of greatcoats.

The whole matter, of course,
is very

Reference has been made to compensation paid to owners of undertakings under

whether the local authority ought to be

in accordance with the terms of the Act
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: If they

not merely the loss they had suffered in
money or money's worth but to recover

country and providing better amenities
and better housing for the sections of the

to make any profit they like out of it.
That is in the interests of others.
Therefore, when one talks of compensation under this Clause, which is of a very
limited application, I agree that one must
be quite sure what one means. I think
if one speaks of compensation for consequential loss, one has to be even more
sure that one excludes from that compensation what is really loss of profit.
Once one excludes loss of profit one is
very near, if not at, the actual measure
of compensation which this Clause allows.
It seems to me that if one added profit to
the elements of compensation allowed by
this Clause, one would have little else to

under this Clause. I suggest that hon.

Mr. NIXON: The Attorney-General's
statement was very clear. It opened a
door. Nobody in
in this Committee, I
think, wants speculative compensation, or
consequential compensation for that
matter. The Clause allows compensation
equal to the expenditure incurred or, as
the case may be, to any sums reasonably
paid in discharge of any liability arising
under the contract in respect of the abandonment of the work. The Attorney-
General asks what other loss could a man
reasonably come to that is not covered by
the. Clause. Supposing a man makes a road

is not covered by the Clause, because it

be, to any sum reasonably paid by him
in discharge of any liability. It limits
the compensation to the expenditure or
the sums paid out of his pocket, but it
does not go the length of compensating
him for the damage done to his meadow.
While I say that no person wants to
give consequential compensation, no
Member either on that side. of the Committee or on this side wants a man to be
at a loss. Now, suppose there is a meadow with roads leading through it, the
meadow is destroyed as a meadow or for
other agricultural purposes. The scheme
is stopped, and all the compensation the
man gets under this Clause is what he
paid out of his pocket to the contractors
or workmen who dug or turned up the
meadow. He cannot get compensation
for his meadow under that clause. That
is all the additional compensation I can
see that he could be entitled to. You
will have to admit that. If you admit it
you will have to do something about it.
The Member for Shankill was talking
about vested interests. I have no vested
interests. I wish I had, but I have not.
I stand for fair play and justice. If you
do not stand for those, you stand for
nothing. No matter who a man is or
what he has, or how little it is, he will
squeal if he is hurt. He will squeal if you
only stand on his toe, but if you dig up
his meadow or his lawn to build houses
on it, and then stop him, he has a claim
for compensation for what he paid and
also for the damage done. At the present time there are in Northern Ireland
tribunals for fixing compensation, and I
never heard any criticism of them. If
the City Council takes the corner of a
field for a certain purpose, and the owner
does not agree to what that body would
pay, he can go before a tribunal which
will fix the compensation he should get,
and the thing goes according to law.
I am satisfied I have pointed out the
defect in this matter. It may not be
very much. Very little may arise under
it, but it is there. If the Member for
Shankill had a meadow, and in good faith
and with every reason to believe his
scheme would pass, dug the meadow up

would be read to him, and he would be

All you can get is what you are out of
pocket." He would say: "There are the

As the Bill stands if a farmer erected
out-houses or pig-sties he would immediately come under control. I propose to
alter that by having the Clause amended
to read that any repair or improvement
of such buildings as are mentioned in the
Amendment shall not be deemed to be a
development of that land, building, or
buildings, and that it shall not come
under this planning scheme. I understand that the Farmers' Union have
taken counsel's opinion on the matter,
and that as the Bill stands, to carry out
such work would bring them under
planning control. As the Clause stands
at present, if a farmer wanted to improve
his out-offices he would have to submit a
plan. Perhaps the Minister would give
his views on the matter.
Mr. LOWRY: We considered the
matter which the hon. and gallant Member has brought forward. There is a
qualification in some respects. The hon.
and gallant Member referred to a pigsty. It has not escaped his attention
that the rural councils, through their
by-laws, control that form of erection. I
should prefer the Amendment which
stands in the name of the hon. Member
for West Down, because his Amendment
covers new as well as existing agricultural buildings. If the hon. and
gallant Member withdraws his Amendment the Government will accept the
Amendment down in the name of the
hon. Member for West Down.
Amendment, by leave, withdrawn.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY: I beg to move,
in page 10, line 31, after the word " the,
to insert the words "erection or." I
will read the sub-paragraph:
...the use of land for the purpose of
agriculture, whether as arable, meadow,
pasture ground or orchard, or for the
purpose of a plantation or a wood, or
for the growth of saleable underwood,
and the use for any of those purposes
or of any building occupied together
with land so used, shall not be deemed
to be a development of that land or
building.
I hold that the Amendment which I
have moved will allow farmers to erect
or repair farm buildings without having

As I pointed out, on the Second Reading,
no repairs would be carried out if the
Clause were allowed to go through as it
stands. In a great number of cases the
plans would cost more than it would take
to carry out the repairs.

Lieut. Col. GORDON: I beg to move in
page 11, line 25, at the end to add the
words "and shall remain in force for one
year after the termination of the present
emergency." On the Second Reading the
Government were asked how long this
interim business was going to last. The
Minister in reply said, according to Hansard :
It will last as long as each planning
authority takes to draw up its scheme.
From the moment a scheme is drawn up
the land within the area of the authority immediately passes away from the
control of the Planning Commission or
Ministry, and the quicker they do it
the sooner they will be out of any sort
of control.
(Official Report, 20th October, 1943,
Vol. 26, Col. 1829).
I put this Amendment down for the
purpose of discussion. How long is this
business going to last? If we are going
to wait until each planning authority
draws up its scheme I think it will last
till kingdom come.
one.
Mr. LOWRY: The point raised by the
hon, and gallant Member is an interesting
The county councils may depute
their powers to rural councils. It would
be quite impossible to fix a date or to
state some period after the termination of
the war.
The dates will be different all
over the country. In consequence I think
it would be quite impossible to lay down
anything of that nature. It will depend

some sort of finishing clause on to these
authorities, because the difficulties would
be great. I should hope, however, that
the preliminary work of the larger and
more important local authorities will be
done even before the termination of the
war.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The point I
had in mind was exactly what the

authorities may be quick to get on with
the job and some may not. The point is
this; we do not want this thing to be
hanging over. There must be a finality
to it. If I withdraw this Amendment
perhaps the Minister will consider how
to deal with a local authority who takes
far too long with a planning scheme, or
which does not play the game, and force
it to adopt a planning scheme so that
this thing will not be hanging round our
necks for ever.
Mr. LOWRY: Even though I can
count on the support of the hon. and gallant Member for East Down if I seek
coercive powers, I am somewhat reluctant
to apply for such powers, I can assure the
hon. and gallant Member for East Down
that we will do all in our power by way

speed.

NEW CLAUSE (Power to enforce
interim development control).
(1) If, while a resolution to prepare
or adopt a planning scheme is in force
with respect to any area, any development of land within that area is carried
out after the commencement of this Act
otherwise than in accordance with the
terms of the interim development order
or of permission granted under that
order, then, subject to the provisions of
this section, the interim development
authority may, if they are satisfied that
it is necessary or expedient so to do
having regard to the provisions then
proposed to be included in the planning
scheme-
(a) where the development consists of
the erection, construction or carrying out of any building or work or
any part of a building or work,
remove or pull down the building,
work or part;
(b) where the development consists of
any use of the land or any building
thereon, by order prohibit that use
and, where necessary, reinstate the
land;
Provided that where it is reasonably
practicable, by means of alterations or
of the execution of any other works, to
bring any such building or work into
compliance with any permission granted
Planning Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
as aforesaid, the interim development
authority shall, instead of removing or
pulling down the building or work,
carry out those alterations or works so
far as appears to them to be necessary
or expedient as aforesaid.
(2) An appeal to a court of summary
jurisdiction against any action proposed
to be taken under this section shall lie
in accordance with the provisions of the
Schedule to this Act.
(3) The Ministry may give general
or special directions for controlling the
exercise by interim development authorities of their powers under this section,
and may give to any such authority
directions requiring them to exercise.
the said powers as respects any development specified in the directions in such
manner as may be so specified; and
any such directions requiring an interim.
development authority to exercise their
powers shall be enforceable, on the
application of the Ministry, by mandamus.
(4) Any expenses reasonably incurred
by an interim development authority in
taking action under this section in
respect of any development may be recovered summarily as a civil debt from
the person by whom the development
was carried out, and if that person,
having been entitled to appeal against
that action under the provisions of the
Schedule to this Act failed to do so, he
shall not be entitled in the proceedings
under this sub-section to dispute the
validity of that action.
(5) If any person uses any land or
building in a manner prohibited by an
order under this section, he shall be
guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding
fifty pounds, and if the use is continued
after the conviction he shall be guilty
of a further offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding
twenty pounds for every day on which
the use is so continued.
(6) Where permission for any development of land has been granted
(whether before or after the commencement of this Act) under Part I of the
principal Act, or under an interim development order, for a limited period
only, and that period expires before
the planning scheme comes into operation, the provisions of this section shall,
after the expiration of that period,
apply in relation to the development as
if no such permission had been granted
and as if the development had been
carried out at the expiration of the
said period the person then entitled
to possession of the land.
Brought up and read a First time.
Question proposed: "That the Clause
be read a Second time."
Lieut.-Col. GORDON : Is this the
Second Reading?
The CHAIRMAN: It is.
Lieut.-Col. GORDON: Would the
Minister of Home Affairs tell us something
about this new Clause? What is it designed for? It is lifted out of the English
Act holus-bolus.
Notice taken that 10 Members were not
present; Committee counted, and 10
Members being present-
Mr. LOWRY: The object of this Clause
is to safeguard a planning authority during the period of the preparation of a
planning scheme. It has now been
brought into the Bill at the direct request
of the Belfast Corporation. They have
pointed out that as a result of the absence
of Statutory provision of this kind the
Corporation have been obliged in the past
to go to the Chancery Court to seek a mandatory injunction in order to enforce conditions attached to development. I am
sorry that the hon. and learned Member
for St. Anne's is not in the Committee at
the moment, because in one of these cases
which was a most enjoyable and expensive
adventure he also took part. It was only
by going through a full-blown Chancery
action that the Corporation were able to
enforce the conditions.
Under the present law there is no power
during the interim period to prevent development being carried out for which permission has been refused, and the only
power that the interim development
authority has is the threat of a lawsuit at
a future date when, after the planning
scheme comes into operation, they can
demolish a structure put up without their
consent. In a great many cases that
threat is effective, as banks and building
societies are naturally unwilling to advance money for development not covered
by permission. These considerations do
not apply to all instances, and if the local
Planning Bill-
Committee
25 NOVEMBER 1943
authority have no course open to them
but to take action, after such a scheme
comes into operation results may follow
and innocent purchasers may find themselves without house or building.
This sort of thing has happened. In
fact any hon. Members who are interested
might like to know it did happen, and it
led to a great deal of trouble in the neighbourhood of Blackpool, where people had
small shops which had been started contrary to the planning scheme. Then the
owners looked about and got innocent purchasers to whom they sold these shops,
though it seems that, in fact, there was
no existing property at all. Great hardship indeed was caused, and not only were
there civil proceedings, but criminal proceedings were taken in some cases where
people were successfully prosecuted for
obtaining money by false pretences.
The deputation from the Belfast Corporation which I had the honour and
pleasure of receiving pointed out their
own difficulties arising in their own experience even in the limited fashion in
which planning has been worked in this
city since 1931. Also I think it is necessary to prevent any abuse of the nature
that was brought to light in the Blackpool proceedings. As the hon. and gallant Member for East Down has observed,
the Clause has been lifted in its entirety
from the corresponding English Bill. I
beg to move.
Lieut.-Col. GORDON: The explanation of the new Clause, which was lifted
from the English Act, is satisfactory, but
there are one or two points I am not quite
clear about. These are more or less in
connection with the Schedule. In Subclause (4) we read,
Any expenses reasonably incurred by
an interim development authority in
taking action under this section in respect of any development may be recovered summarily as a civil debt from
the person by whom the development—
The CHAIRMAN: I wonder if the hon.
and gallant Member would speak up. It
is very difficult for Hansard to hear
Members below the Gangway unless they
speak very distinctly.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I was speaking about sub-clause (4), which reads:
(4) Any expenses reasonably incurred
by an interim development authority in
taking action under this section in respect of any development may be
recovered summarily as a civil debt
from the person by whom the development was carried out, and if that
person, having been entitled to appeal
against that action under the provisions
of the Schedule to this Act failed to
do so, he shall not be entitled to the
proceedings under this sub-section to
dispute the validity of that action.
It seems to me, that under this new sub.
clause a local authority may recover from
a person costs for, let us say, the pulling
down of his house, that having been done
for him simply because he did not put in
an appeal before. a court of summary
jurisdiction. It may be that someone did
not know he had a right of appeal, and
in consequence he would have a heavy
bill of costs sent in against him by the
local authority. He would appear to
have no redress and would have to pay
the civil bill. Could the Minister clear
up this point?
Mr. LOWRY: I think the first answer
to the hon. and gallant Member is that
ignorance of the law is no excuse. Everybody is supposed to know the law, and I
cannot anticipate any great hardship
being inflicted on anyone by this subclause. People who are in possession of
property are usually pretty well advised,
and are pretty well guardians of their
own interests. I could not anticipate
any person who has the protection and is
covered by the points set forth in the
Schedule failing to take advantage of
such protection. My own experience
would certainly lead me to believe that
people in the North of Ireland are not
inclined to go to sleep when matters of
legal rights are involved. I think that is
characteristic of us. The sub-clause refers
to any expenses reasonably incurred, and,
of course, there is always some check on
what was attempted to be recovered as a
civil debt in a summary fashion, and if a
preposterous bill were put in it would be
moderated in some. fashion or other at the
time when the payment of the money was
sought to be enforced.
Question, "That the Clause be read
a Second time," put and agreed to.
Clause added to the Bill.
New SCHEDULE (Appeals from decision to exercise power to enforce interim
development control).
Planning Bill—
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
1. Not less than twenty-eight days
before taking any action under section
four of this Act, the interim development authority shall serve a notice in
the prescribed manner on the owner
and on the occupier of the building or
land in respect of which the action is
proposed to be taken and on any other
person who, in their opinion, may be
affected thereby, specifying the nature
of, and the grounds upon which they
propose to take, that action.
2. If any person served with such a
notice as aforesaid desires to dispute
any allegation contained therein, he
may, by written notice served on the
clerk of the court and on the interim
development authority within twentyeight days from the date of the service
of the original notice on him, appeal
to a court of summary jurisdiction for
the petty sessions district or place
within which the property to which the
notice relates is situated, and the interim development authority shall not
take the proposed action pending the
final determination or withdrawal of
the appeal.
3. If on any such appeal the court of
summary jurisdiction is satisfied that
the interim development authority are
entitled to take the proposed action on
the grounds specified in the notice, the
court shall dismiss the appeal and shall
by its order empower the authority
after the expiration of the said period
of twenty-eight days, to remove or pull
down the building or work, or to
execute the required alterations
works or, as the case may be, shall by
its order prohibit the building or land
from being used after the period aforesaid without the permission of the
authority or in contravention of any
conditions subject to which that permission was granted, but, if the court
is not so satisfied, it shall allow the
appeal;
or
Provided that the court by which an
order is made under this paragraph
may, if it thinks fit, direct that the
order shall, instead of taking effect
after the expiration of the said period
of twenty-eight days, take effect at such
later date as it thinks fit, being a date
not more than twenty-eight days from
the date of the order.

this new Schedule be read a Second time."

Lieut. Colonel GORDON: Arising
from the Schedule, two points occur to
me, and on them I am not quite clear.
The first is, if somebody built a house

exactly what power this court of summary jurisdiction has.
Mr. LOWRY: If the hon. and gallant
Member will look at the first sub-clause
of the new Clause we have added to the
Bill he will find it provides-
(1) If, while a resolution to prepare
or adopt a planning scheme is in force
with respect to any area, any development of land within that area is carried
out after the commencement of this
Act otherwise than in accordance with
the terms of the interim development
order or of permission granted under
that order, then, subject to the provisions of this section, the interim development authority may, if they are
satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do having regard to the
provisions then proposed to be included
in the planning scheme-
(a) where the development consists of
the erection, construction or carrying out of any building or work or
any part of a building or work,
remove or pull down the building,
work or part;
(b) where the development consists of
any use of the land or any building
thereon, by order prohibit that

It must be a positive act. The sort of
matter mentioned by the hon. and gallant
Member, the sanitary condition of a
house does not come into it. It is building or doing something in direct contravention of the Order, and the only matter
left to the court of summary jurisdiction
to decide is, was the determination of the
local authority a proper one or not in the
circumstances. In other words, has the
appellant disobeyed the planning scheme
as set forth in the new Clause.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I take it the
position is this. Someone builds a house
with bow windows, and the planning
authority says he has got to have straight
up and down windows. Under this Bill
they will have the power to tell him to
change them. He then can appeal to the
court, but the question before the court
is apparently limited to whether or not
the council or local authority had power
to make him change his windows, and not
whether it was reasonable or not, the
allegation being made that he never
should have put these windows up.
Mr. LOWRY: Of course, the aesthetic
side will not arise so much, but some man
might, so to speak, chance his arm and
start to build something without permission at all. Again, supposing he got permission to put up a dwelling-house in a
residential locality, and he proceeds, for
example, to start to build shops or a
petrol station or something entirely
different to what this Clause permits, the
only way up to the present that a local
authority could have stopped him was by
going to the Chancery Division and getting a mandatory injunction to pull the
place down. This is an easier, more
summary, and less expensive proceeding.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I agree.
Mr. BROWN: I only want to express
the hope that the debate we have had on
this measure will be as successful and
fruitful of results as the previous three
days' debate we had on housing, which
produced the decision to erect 750 houses.

We as a Ministry have not only a

duty also to the general public.
The Minister is in a very unhappy position. He has a dual duty. He has a
duty to the farmers and producers to get
the best terms possible for them. I have
every sympathy for the farmers. I think
they never really have a square deal except in war time.
The Devil was sick the Devil a monk
would be;
The Devil was well-the devil a monk
was he.
When a war is on nothing is too good
for the farmers. They were badly treated
before by Westminster and by this Government. Once war is over they are forgotten.
The Minister of Agriculture has a duty
to the farmers which duty he does, I am
sure, as well as it is possible for him to do
it. He has also a duty to the consumers
as well as to the producers. He has a
double duty, he has to serve two masters.
It is very hard to serve two masters-to
serve God and mammon. The Minister
has chosen to serve mammon. He stated
further on in his speech he did not know
how the standard of 3 per cent. butter
fats was arrived at. He went on to say:
The Ministry have tests. We have to
resort to ways and means of our own.
Only he and his experts know what these
tests are. This Committee do not. Are
they going to reduce the test of 3 per cent.
What will the mothers of Belfast think if
they get milk deficient in butter fats to
feed their infants?
As I said before the Minister has
several experts in the Ministry in the
matter of the prevention and cure of
diseases in the lower animals, but his
Ministry is entrusted with the care and
administration of a very important section
of the Public Health Acts, as it relates

as ever he wrote!

to comply with the provisions of any
regulation made by the Ministry under
the principal Act, or of any order made
or determination given by the Ministry
under this Act, shall be guilty of an
offence under the principal Act which
may be prosecuted before a court of
summary jurisdiction.
After having a good many discussions
with the Ministry and the Minister over
the amendment of this Bill I should like
to say that here, as in the Planning Bill,
I found the greatest accommodation, and
I am grateful to the Minister and his
officials for the help given to me. I believe that in this Bill we have a good Bill.
I think it is now a better Bill than when
it came into the House, and I hope it will
serve the public well. It is only a step
toward a more comprehensive Bill when
the Ministry are able to feel their way to
bring it in.
I agree with a great deal which the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Lyle)
said. I do not think the Ministry will
achieve their ultimate object by going
too far. I think they have got a difficult
constituency to deal with. I think they
would make much better progress if they
did not attempt to dragoon the farming
community. It is a good Bill and I commend it to the House and the country.
The Ministry and the Government are to
be congratulated on the step they are taking to progress towards the objective we
all desire-pure milk.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I accept the
Amendment.
Mr. HENDERSON: The statement
made by the Minister is a startling one.
He states that the test is fifty years out
of date.
The CHAIRMAN: We are dealing
with Clause 5 to which an Amendment
has been moved by the hon. and learned
Member for St. Anne's. The Government have accepted the Amendment. I
would ask the hon. Member to allow me
to put the Question to the Committee.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.
CLAUSE 6 (Short title, construction
and citation) ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
TITLE agreed to.
Bill reported with Amendments.
Ordered, That the Bill, as amended in
the Committee, be taken into consideration on Tuesday next, and be reprinted.
Message from the Senate.
The Senate have passed the Youth
Welfare Bill (Senate) to which they
desire the concurrence of the Commons.
Bill read a First time and ordered to
be read a Second time on Tuesday next
and be printed.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.

25 NOVEMBER 1943
Adjournment.
PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER IN
LONDON.
CRANE DRIVERS' STRIKE
SETTLED.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Mr. Grant.)
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
beg to ask the Prime Minister if anyone
has been appointed to superintend the
Northern Ireland Government Information Service in London.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The House will recollect that a
short time ago I announced that Sir
Lynden Macassey had been invited to fill
the appointment in connection with the
Information Services of our London
Office. I know everybody regrets that he
found himself unable to accept, and,
therefore, it was necessary for us to find
a successor.
I need hardly say that the Government
regard this work of representing the interests of Northern Ireland in London as
highly important. Our war-time industry
is closely interwoven with Great Britain,
and hon. Members will, I am sure, agree
that it is most desirable that our Public
Relations Officer in London should be
some one who is fully familiar with all
matters affecting our war production.
My colleagues and I have been giving
most careful consideration to the problem, and we have decided that Mr.
Ernest Cooper, who until only a few
weeks ago was industrial adviser to our
Ministry of Commerce, and who is now
back again in London, would be an excellent choice. I have accordingly asked
Mr. Cooper if he would be willing to act,
and I am very glad to say that he has
consented.
He will perform his duties
without remuneration, but will receive an
allowance to meet out-of-pocket expenses.
I would like to express to Mr. Cooper my
grateful thanks for undertaking the work,
and for his generous attitude in the
matter.
As no doubt most hon. Members know
already, Mr. Cooper is a man of outstanding business attainments. He was
called in to assist Lord Beaverbrook in
the Ministry of Aircraft Production, and
I myself was personally associated with
him during the period he served as Industrial Adviser in our Ministry of
Commerce. He advised me on production and industrial matters. Mr. Cooper
was instrumental in tuning up our whole
war effort here in Northern Ireland, and
I formed the highest opinion of his
capacity and judgment. He acquired an
excellent knowledge of our conditions,
and, I might add, of our peculiarities,
and he is a very good friend of Ulster.
I appreciate that some hon. Members
might have preferred that we should have
chosen an Ulsterman.
Mr. HENDERSON: What else do you
think you could do?
The PRIME MINISTER: I readily
admit the force of that view, but, at this
critical time, the field of selection is
greatly narrowed. To my mind it is most
important that the man chosen should
know all about the war effort of this
country. Therefore, in making our choice
the criterion which I applied was,
"Who
is the most suitable man to-day for the
work?" I am quite certain that Mr.
Cooper will be able to keep the general
position of Ulster well in the forefront,
and I have every confidence that he will
be an admirable ambassador for Northern
Ireland in all the activities that he will
be called upon to perform. He deserves
our thanks for his public-spirited acceptance of the post and our best wishes for
success.
Mr. NIXON : There are just a few
points I want to mention. First and
foremost I know the Minister of Labour
has good news about the strikes, and I
want to ask him for any information he
wishes to give to the House and the
Province on that subject. Perhaps the
Prime Minister would tell us what is the
order of business for next week.
With regard to his announcement that
he had great difficulty in making a selection for the office of Public Relations
Officer in England, and that after great
consideration and consultation with his
Cabinet he got Mr. Cooper persuaded to
accept the position, I think myself that
Major Henderson was a very good man.
I do not know whether he is in London or
not, but I thought he was a good man.
I am not going to criticise the Prime
Minister's appointment at all, and the
principal reason I am not going to do so
Public Relations Officer 2362
Public Relations Officer
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
is because I do not think it matters one
threepenny bit one way or the other.

Not alone do I think that, but I am
sure of it, because all that the place in
London is there for is for Members of the
Government and their friends when they
go over there. What do they do?
short time ago no less a man than the
noble Lord, the Member for Bloomfield,
gave a hint there were not any refreshments there at all. (Laughter.) I do
not know what is there, because I am not
likely ever to see it, and neither are any
of the people I represent. Mr. Cooper
addressed the Rotary Club not long ago,
and when he did that he must know all
about Ulster, top, bottom and sides, because that is what you want to know. A
man came to me and told me-and it was
the first I had heard of it-that he heard
Mr. Cooper was getting his food without
coupons. He wanted me to ask a question about it, and he tried to do something about it himself. He was told that
Mr. Cooper could not be bothered about
coupons or anything like that, and I was
not bothered about it either.
Mr. HENDERSON: How the Prime
Minister had the cheek and audacity to
insult the intelligence of the citizens.of
Northern Ireland is more than I can comprehend. Let me say right off the reel
that, while. nothing could destroy the
friendship existing between the hon.
Member for Woodvale and myself, I hold
that Ulster House has performed a useful
service, and the only regrettable thing
about it is that the Government have
not an Ulster House worthy of this great
country. We should try to realise the
magnitude of the task performed in
Ulster House. Is it not true to say that
owing to the apathy of the Prime
Minister, especially since he assumed
responsibility as the head of the Government, Ulster is practically unknown?
The present Prime. Minister, I think, was
responsible for stopping the grants when
Major-General Cooke-Collis died.
A more monstrous and iniquitous thing
I cannot think of. Here you have an
Ulster House with very competent
officials, including a very competent man
who was formerly employed by the
Belfast News-Letter. Every time I
go to
London I pay a visit to Ulster House. I
never got any hospitality there, but for
the benefit of the House I will tell you
what did happen there. On the last
occasion I visited London in connection
with town planning I called at Ulster
House, as I always do, and as it was a
cold day one of the officials asked me if
I would have, a cup of tea.
Mr. NIXON: Was there anything with
it?
Mr. HENDERSON: Unfortunately
there was not. If I had met some other
distinguished visitor from Canada,
Australia, or some other country of the
British Commonwealth, or even from
some foreign country, I should have asked
him if he had ever been at Ulster House.
He would probably have said he had not.
I would have said, "I come from
Northern Ireland, an outpost of the
British Empire, and I would like you to
pay a visit to our establishment and see
how things are done." I had the honour
to be High Sheriff of Belfast and to entertain American troops as well as members
of the Navy, Army and Air Forces, and
the highest General in the land, with
many Generals who are under him. I
had the privilege of showing them some
little Ulster hospitality. It was not
much I could give them, but I tried to do
my best. But Ulster House in London is
the only place we have got to show that
we are on the map.
The Prime Minister may speak to 30
clubs, and he may go on these periodical
jaunts to London, but Ulster House
should be supported to the fullest extent.
When I went into a post office in England
I was looked upon as a citizen of Eire. I
respect citizens of all countries. I had
the pleasure of taking twelve or fourteen
citizens from the Shankill Road to Ulster
House on
one occasion when I was
attending the English Cup final, and they
were very well received and entertained
at the expense of one of the officials,
Major Henderson. He paid the, expense
out of his own pocket because he
was not allowed to take it out of the
Hospitality Fund. When a distinguished
visitor does go to London he should be
suitably entertained at Ulster House. If
I had taken my colleagues to meet Mr.
Dulanty I am sure he would have entertained them as Irishmen. Thousands
and thousands of pounds are being spent
by the Irish Free State in London, and I
raise my
hat to them. This Government
2363 Public Relations Officer

Public Relations Officer
is so lousy-to express it in a way the
average working man will understand—
that they will spend nothing to advertise
Ulster by entertaining distinguished
visitors.
Is the Prime Minister an Ulsterman
himself? If he is, all I can say is this;
that his conduct to-day will go down in
history as reprehensible. As an Ulsterman he should be ashamed of himself.
Here we have a Province of a million and
a quarter people who have built up this
country and made it the envy of all other
countries throughout the world. It has
the largest shipyard, the largest ropeworks, the largest linen mills, and the
largest tobacco factory in the United
Kingdom, and yet the Prime Minister of
this country has the cheek and audacity
to get on his feet and say that in all
Ulster and in Great Britain there is not
an Ulsterman fit and competent to look
after our interests at Ulster House. What
is Ulster coming to? This statement will
be read with amazement by the people of
Ulster. If I were Prime Minister I could
get two dozen Ulstermen who were competent to fill the position and prepared to
give the necessary time.
Why should the Prime Minister run
about like a message boy trying to find
someone to do the job for nothing? Even
if you paid an Ulster representative in
London you would be doing Ulster a great
service, but you want to do everything
on the cheap. Has the Free State tried
to do everything on the cheap in regard
to its office in London? No. They have
a magnificent building with a Free State
flag that would cover half this floor flying
365 days in the year. Have we a flag
flying over Ulster House?
No. We have
a flag pole, but no flag. If I were Prime
Minister the flag of Ulster would fly
over Ulster House as prominently as
the flag flying over the Free State building. You cannot miss that flag. Mr.
Dulanty, the representative of the Free
State, is doing an enormous amount of
work for Ulster people, and he is an
Irishman from Southern Ireland.
Would it not have been a nice thing to
have appointed an Ulsterman, whether he
is from Northern Ireland, England,
Scotland or Wales. I say nothing about
Mr. Cooper, for I know nothing about
him. He comes from Canada, and I dare
say he has given great service to the
country for which those in authority will
be deeply grateful to him. He has my
best wishes for a happy stay in this
country. I believe he is a very clever
gentleman, but I want you to forget about
Mr. Cooper. I am not interested in Mr.
Cooper, good, bad, or indifferent. What
I am concerned about is that this appointment has been made by a Cabinet composed mostly of working men. It includes
a Member representing Duncairn, which
was represented in the Imperial Parliament by the late Lord Carson. It includes the Member for Willowfield, who
defeated the official Unionist candidate
at a by-election. Then you have the
Prime Minister, who I expect was born
in Ulster, and the Minister of Finance,
whose ancestors founded a great linen
firm. This is enough make his
ancestors turn in their graves. My
ancestors belonged to Monaghan, one of
the counties that were sold. It takes
some courage to be a Protestant and an
in
Orangeman Monaghan, but my
ancestors were never afraid to say they
were members of the British Empire and
members of a loyal organisation.

Men of Ulster are fighting our battles.

I say

and as far as I am concerned it will never

time, and if it was not for the friendships

The PRIME MINISTER: He is doing
it for nothing.
Mr. HENDERSON: He is going to
get out-of-pocket expenses.
Some
drunken corner boy might suggest things
like that, to go about the country asking
for a man wealthy enough to take on such
an important job as the representative of
Ulster at Ulster House. Much as I
admire the great work that Ulster House
is doing in London I consider the building
a disgrace to Ulster. I should like to see
in London a building that would please
the people of Ulster, a building something
like those erected by Canada, or Australia,
or some other parts of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
When the ex-Prime Minister was
honoured by the King one of the finest
messages that ever emanated from the lips
of a statesman was sent to him. If I
was Prime Minister at the time I would
have got that message printed in
pamphlet form, and I I would have
distributed it amongst all the American
soldiers, sailors and airmen. I would
have let them see what Mr. Churchill
said about Ulster when the honour was
conferred upon the right hon. Gentleman,
the Member for Mid Down, so that they
should take that message throughout the
world to show what Mr. Churchill said
about the part this Province is playing
in bringing about the destruction of
Hitlerism.
Mr. Herbert Morrison also paid him a
great compliment for which I, as an
Ulsterman, feel very proud and pleased.
But our Prime Minister had not much
respect for Ulster, because he insults the
intelligentsia and workers of the Province
by saying there is no man here fit for the
job. As I said before, I may not count
for very much, but I believe I should
have no trouble in getting a man to do
the work even for nothing but his out-ofpocket expenses. If you want to run
Ulster you will have to spend money.
Not only would I appoint a gentleman
to look after our interests, but I would
send representatives to all parts of the
United Kingdom. I would do that because we are not known, notwithstanding
the fact that Mr. Winston Churchill
made that wonderful statement.
To-day in England they think we are

has ever seen. He could not find an
Ulsterman to do an Ulsterman's job. All
I can say is, that if that is all he is able
to do, the sooner he resigns his office and
lets another Ulsterman be Prime Minister
the better. I am ashamed to sit in the
House and hear him making such a disgusting and disgraceful statement as the
statement he made, and I tell him that
everywhere I go I shall point to this
slight he has cast upon the Ulster people.
The Prime Minister has committed a
sin that will never be forgotten by all
true Ulstermen and women, and it will
come against him like a boomerang. He
has done something that is going to do
no end of injury to the Party of which
he is leader. Thank God he is not an
Independent Unionist. There is not an
Independent Unionist or loyalist would
be guilty of the crime he has committed
to-day. I would be ashamed to get up
and do what he did on this occasion. It
will be nice news to read that our Prime
Minister could not find an Ulsterman
with intelligence to go to the London
Office.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

at Messrs.
Harland &

Agriculture.
SLAUGHTER OF CALVES.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the number of calves slaughtered in
the whole of Northern Ireland since the
1st January, 1943, up to and including
the month of November.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I would point out
to the hon. Member that under the
Defence Regulations Government Departments are prohibited from furnishing
statistics. I cannot, therefore, give him
the information he requires.
If it will help the hon. Member in the
purpose for which he desires the information, I can assure him that slaughterings
of calves are not abnormal.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister
explain how it is that casualties amongst
the fighting soldiers can be published but
casualties amongst calves cannot be published in case it would help Hitler? Stop
making yourself ridiculous some time.
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the right hon.
Gentleman tell the House how it is that
our Government are allowing these calves
to be slaughtered wholesale whereas the
British Minister is appealing to farmers
to rear calves? I think the right hon.
Gentleman need not be afraid of giving
out the figures. Is it not true to say that
inside eleven months in Belfast alone
9,000 calves have been slaughtered? Do
you not think this is a terrible crime in
view of the fact that the Minister in
England is appealing to farmers to rear
their calves? Can the right hon. Gentleman not carry out the same policy in Northern Ireland instead of allowing these
calves to be slaughtered wholesale?

2. Mr. BROWN asked the. Minister of
Agriculture whether his Ministry was
consulted about and approved of the very
small and inadequate increase recently
announced in the prices of flax; whether
he intends to make representations to
secure a fairer increase, and whether he
can state if prices have yet been arranged
for next season.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I would
refer the hon. Member to the answer
given by my predecessor to this question
on October 27th, 1942, and to the hon.
Member's expression of his appreciation
of the terms then announced, which
covered the 1944 flax growing season as
well as the 1943 season.
Electricity Supply Board.
AUDIT OF ACCOUNTS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the date on
which the Northern Ireland Electricity
Supply Board was set up by the Government, and whether the accounts of the
Board have been submitted to the Public
Accounts Committee and Comptroller and
Auditor-General.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
The Electricity Board for Northern
Ireland was set up on 1st June, 1931,
under the provisions of the Electricity
(Supply) Act, Northern Ireland, 1931.
The accounts of the Board in respect of
the functions entrusted to it under the
1931 Act are audited by an auditor appointed by the Ministry of Commerce
under Section 30 of the Act.
In so far, however, as the accounts of
the Board relate to duties undertaken in
pursuance of powers delegated to the
Poard by the Ministry, namely, the
operation of the Ministry's new generating
station and of the former Larne undertaking, they fall to be audited by the

Comptroller and Auditor-General and
will be reported upon by him to the
Public Accounts Committee.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I

bring all the accounts of the whole Board
under the supervision of the Auditor-
General, so that the Public Accounts
Committee might have an opportunity of
examining them and expressing an
opinion upon them.

Mr. MAGINESS: No, sir. The

All public funds which are expended do

These moneys are not public moneys and

Mr. NIXON: Why does the Parliamentary Secretary make such an outlandish and inaccurate statement? Is the

That is a most audacious attitude to
the
take up.

General.
Mr. JOHNSTON: Is it not a fact that

TOTAL LONG-TERM BORROWINGS.
6. Mr. NIXON asked
Minister whether he can state the total
loans raised by the Electricity Supply
Board, the rate of interest paid in respect
of such loans; whether these loans or any
of them are guaranteed by the Government of Northern Ireland, and if so, the
total of such loans subject to guarantee.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Maginess]
The total long-term borrowings by the
Electricity Board are as follows:-
£1,500,000 of stock 1955/60 bearing
interest at 3 per cent.
£850,000 of guaranteed bonds bearing
interest at 3 per cent. for a period of
five years expiring on 31st March, 1944;
making a total of £2,350,000.
Both stock and bonds carry a Ministry
of Finance guarantee, but of the total of
£2,350,000 the sum of £341,366 has been
redeemed by the Electricity Board. This
leaves an outstanding balance of
£2,008,634 covered by the guarantee.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Parliamentary
Secretary still insist that though this
£3,000,000 is guaranteed by this House
and must be made good by this House, yet
this House is not entitled-or the accounts
are not entitled to be audited by the
Auditor-General ?
Education.
PURE MILK FOR PUPILS.
Mr. RENSHAW asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether she can state what
steps have been taken to ensure that the
milk being supplied to children in public
elementary schools is free from tuberculosis and other deadly germs.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): My
Ministry has drawn the attention of local
education authorities to the fact that the
production of milk and its control in Northern Ireland are vested in the Ministry
of Agriculture which is responsible for
seeing that the milk is produced under
satisfactory conditions, that it is an
essential condition, under the Milk in
Schools Scheme, that the source and
quality of the supply must in all cases be
approved by the local Medical Officer of
Health, who should in turn consult the
School Medical Officer and the local
Veterinary Officer of the Ministry of
Agriculture, and that periodical tests
should be made of the milk supplied to
the schools.
Dr. LYLE: Arising out of that reply
by the hon. Lady might I ask her if she
would consider the advisability of supplying school-children with dried milk seeing
that practically all the milk produced in
Northern Ireland is infected with tubercle
bacilli and the bacilli of other diseases?
Mrs. PARKER: I should tell the hon.
Member that we have suggested to the
local educational authorities that for
many reasons it is most desirable that
pasteurised milk should be supplied. We
also supply them with straws and I do
not think there is anything more I can
do.
ask

my right hon. Friend, the Minister of

islands, and therefore it is not right to

If that were true we would not be here
at all. We would all be dead. Therefore I do not think that statement should
go from this House. Is it not a fact that
again and again our milk has been certified as quite up to the standard of milk
throughout Great Britain?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Within the

happy indeed to show the report of the

Dr. LYLE: Is it not a fact that cannot
be disputed that the standard of milk in

7. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the

a
With regard to the second part, it is
not possible at present to authorise
scheme for houses outside Belfast, as the
limited supply of building materials does
not permit of this. It will be generally
admitted that in view of the serious

With regard to the last part of the

Gentleman aware that licences are being

NORTH DOWN WATER SUPPLY.
9. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if it is the intention of the Government to provide a water supply for
Comber, Newtownards, Conlig, Millisle,
Ballywalter and other small towns and
villages in Co. Down.
Mr. LOWRY: The provision of a public
water supply is a matter for the
appropriate sanitary authority and not
for the Government.
The question of bringing water to the
places mentioned by the hon. Member is,
however, being considered by my Department and the local authorities concerned,
and I am hopeful that the results of the

RESIDENCE PERMITS IN COUNTY
ARMAGH.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of residence permits sought by
residents of Eire living in the Armagh
Urban District, and give the figures of
overcrowding in that area created by this
influx; whether it is a fact that when the
Urban Council was in power about 400
working-class houses were required; and
whether any of his officials who have
visited Armagh recently on official
business have reported overcrowding due
to Eire residents.
Mr. LOWRY: The information sought
by the hon. Member in the first part of
the question is not readily available and
the expenditure and labour involved in
the examination of approximately 24,000
applications for the purpose of ascertaining the number of Eire people now
residing in the Armagh urban district
could not be justified.
From the information obtained from
the recent housing survey it is obvious that
there is little overcrowding in the district
because of an influx of persons from Eire,
and no officer of my Department has
reported that overcrowding has arisen
owing to that cause.
The records of my Ministry do not show
the number of working-class houses needed
when the Urban District Council was in
office.

Oral Answers
30 NOVEMBER 1943
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The reply to the first part of the question is in the negative. The Order to
which the hon. Member refers was made
by the Board of Trade and is applicable
to the whole of the United Kingdom.
