ADOPTION OF ACT.
12. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
reasons for the delay in putting into
operation the provisions of the Hairdressers' Act (Northern Ireland), 1939,
in Belfast as has been done in many cross-
Channel centres with splendid results,
thereby reducing the spreading of scabies.
and other infectious diseases now prevalent in Northern Ireland and thus
effecting a considerable saving in public
funds.
Mr. LOWRY: The Hairdressers' Act
(Northern Ireland), 1939, is an adoptive
Act, and its adoption is a matter entirely
within the discretion of local authorities.
In the circumstances the Ministry has no
power to enforce its adoption either generally or in any particular area.

MOYGASHEL FACTORY.
14. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if he is
satisfied with conditions of employment in
Messrs. Stevenson's Factory, Moygashel,
particularly in the tow department;
whether the Minister will make investigation into the working of green flax in this
concern from tank retting to the finished
article; whether any chemicals are used
in the tank retting of flax which causes
an atmosphere affecting the chests of the
workers, especially in the tow department;
whether he is satisfied with the night work
hours and whether it is a fact that girls
work 11 hours on night work.
Mr. GRANT: The conditions of employment in the factory occupied by
Stevenson & Son, Ltd., Moygashel, are
in general very satisfactory.
In the particular department to which
the hon. Member refers, known by the
firm as the flax department, no chemicals
are used in the tank retting of flax.
With regard to night employment, the
firm, under heavy pressure of work for
the supply departments, recently found
it necessary to employ a night shift, including 21 females, in the flax department. The hours of work are from 7-30
p.m. to 6-30 a.m. with two half-hour
meal breaks on each of five week nights,
making 50 hours per week. In all the
circumstances, I do not regard these hours
as unreasonable.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
the conditions of employment in the
factory to which the hon. Member's question refers do not compare very favourably with the conditions in any other
factory in Northern Ireland?
Mr. GRANT: It is perfectly true that
it is a very progressive factory in regard
to working conditions and the welfare of
the employees. A personnel manager has
recently been appointed to look after the
workers and the firm is erecting a modern
canteen where meals will be served.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.

Members: No.) If the right hon. Gentleman reads Hansard he will see that the
Parliamentary Secretary time and again.
during the course of the debate contradicted him in so far as the method of
going into the accounts is concerned. I
think it can be truthfully said that the
hon. Members on both sides of the House
who suggested that an inquiry should be
instituted were quite right. The Prime
Minister, who was responsible for this
practically bogus electricity supply scheme
being set up, handed over the baby to the
present Minister of Finance. It is to the
credit of the Prime Minister that he
asked the permission of the House for the
spending of the one million pounds, but
in this case the present Minister of
Finance, instead of coming to the House
and asking it to go outside the scope of
the original Bill-the spending of the one
million pounds-has to all intents and
purposes approved of the spending of a
further one and a half million pounds.
That system is wrong.
I suggest that in his spare time the
present Minister of Finance should consult the ex-Minister of Finance. By no
stretch of the imagination can the present
right hon. Gentleman be termed a
financial expert. Is that not quite true?
Is there any hon. Member who can say
that the Minister of Finance knows the
slightest thing about high finance? He
is bungling the whole thing. Seeing that
he is only an apprentice Minister of
Finance and knows practically nothing
about finance he should get into touch
with the ex-Minister, who is a man with
an international reputation in so far as
high finance is concerned, and get a few
tips from him.
I say that the people who are spending
this two and a half million pounds on
electrical development know nothing whatever about electricity. They are in the
hands of the Philistines, because they
have nobody but the consultant or socalled expert. Who would dream of
putting an expert in the linen trade or a
lawyer to look after such an important
matter as the development of electricity
in Northern Ireland? I believe when the
Comptroller and Auditor-General gets an
opportunity of going into these accounts
this House will hear startling revelations.
It is quite true to say that this consultant has done things without consulting
the Ministry at all. In view of the
ignorance of the Minister of Finance in
so far as high finance is concerned this
consultant treated him with the utmost
contempt. I suggest that the right hon.
Gentleman should go to the Technical
School and see if he could not learn something about electricity. A few days ago he
admitted he did not know what an amp or
a volt was. Even if he does know what an
amp or a volt is, I contend he is not clever
enough, and that the Parliamentary
Secretary is not clever enough to deal
with such an important job as the development of electricity in Northern Ireland.
As I stated previously, it has been
proved by the speeches made in this
House that this policy is wrong.
Why
did the Minister not come to the House
and tell hon. Members that he carried
out a scheme which had been brought
into being by the Prime Minister? Why
did he not tell the House that it cost the
taxpayers one million pounds, and that
he was now asking for an additional sum?
That is what ought to have been done.
Why did he not ask the House if it were
prepared to support the Ministry of
Finance in a larger scheme which would
bring current to houses throughout the
length and breadth of Northern Ireland
outside the emergency area? Why did he
not say that they were going on with a
larger scheme and that they were going
to supply current to every place in the
country where there was not so much
danger?
Why was that not done? It was always
done in the past when comprehensive
schemes were being brought in. The Bann
drainage scheme was one instance. In that
case the House gave its permission. In
this particular instance the right hon.
Gentleman gets on with the scheme and
then asks the House to give him permission to carry it out. In my opinion
the whole matter should be inquired into.
I am satisfied from what I have heard
and seen in this House that the Minister
is like clay in the potter's hands. The
liberties of this consultant have now been
curtailed; he is not going to make as
much money in the future as he did in
the past.

scheme going to cost? You could electrify
the whole of Ireland for another million

to take over the undertaking of the people

not think he is going to get the Belfast

make his scheme a paying concern.
The
whole thing is nothing but a pure unadulterated fraud, perpetrated on the

Neither the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, nor any other Member
has stated that we are justified in spending this £2,500,000. Unless there is one
hundred per cent. new industries in
Northern Ireland this cannot pay. I
challenge the Minister to deny that. The
right hon. Gentleman tried to throw dust

was going to give electricity to all the

colonised the agricultural workers and

decent houses, a picture house, a club,

from the next, there is no possibility of

In this respect it is partly cloaked up.
That is the trouble. This Parliament has
only partial powers, and it will be so
until the day comes when the rising
generation-the boys the hon. gentleman
is teaching in his clubs-will see the light

government of the people, by the people.

You are not allowed to do this or that
As a matter of fact, when a Member gets

stripped so far as the Members of this

exposed him. Between him and the
Minister they have tried to bolster up a
bad case. As far as I am concerned,

to say that I should like to see electricity
supplied to every citizen it is humanly
possible to give it to throughout Northern
Ireland.
We on this side of the House were.
pioneers in electricity. When the Minister of Finance was a youth holding on to
his mother's apron strings, we were
fighting to get electricity for the agricultural areas. We have been partly able
to secure that at considerable cost. We
would like the electricity users of
Northern Ireland to get their electricity
at a very cheap rate, but that is not going
to be so. It is going to be very dear,
and no one realises that better than the
Prime Minister, who originated the first
scheme, but who has refused to tell the
House whether we are justified in spending this extra money in view of the
uncertainty of the position. If I were
uncertain of anything, I would be very
careful.
If the Prime Minister and the Minister
of Finance, who have taken a considerable
number of jaunts to London, can tell us
that we are likely to get a hundred per
cent. new industries then I think we
would be justified in spending this money,
but not otherwise. In any case I hope and
sincerely trust that this will be the last
time that any Ministry of this Government will come here with a madcap scheme
like this. First of all they should get the
consent of the House for their policy, and
when the plans have been completed come
in for the money. The Government should
tell the House what they are going to do,
for we, who represent the taxpayers have
the right to know what the plans of any
Ministry are. When the Government get
the plans fixed up they can come back to
the House and say, "We want one million
pounds, two million pounds or three
million pounds," as the case may be. That
is how it should be done, not as has been
done in this case. I think this money
would be much better spent if the Minister
of Finance handed it over to the Minister
of Home Affairs to spend on housing the
people of Northern Ireland, who are living
in absolute hovels which are a disgrace to
any civilised State, instead of spending it
the way we are.

with reference to the spending of this

penny spent without the committee knowing all about it and thrashing out the

asked here to give consent to the spending

we do not know anything about, not even

know something about what the post-war
world is going to be like. We want to
know just what we have to plan for, and
what material we have to plan with. At
the present time our efforts should be concentrated on winning the war, and until
that is accomplished no declaration on
post-war policy is of any value whatever.
Oliver Lyttelton a few days ago said:
I think that in common fairness we
must be able to see the outlines of the
New Jerusalem before we start committing ourselves too far as to how the
New Jerusalem is to be promoted.
I think the only post-war policy that
can be indicated at the moment is
amply outlined in the words of the
Imperial Prime Minister: "Food, homes
and employment." So far as our Government is concerned they are taking steps in
all these directions.
We have heard a good deal about agriculture, and we know that our Ministry
of Agriculture is very busy not only with
plans for the present but with plans for
the future. As regards houses we have
Post-War Policy
Post-War Policy
30 NOVEMBER 1943
had ample evidence during the past week
or so that that matter, too, is receiving
attention. I am quite sure that the
Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry
of Labour are equally busy in devising
schemes that will ensure employment for
all after the war is won. Any more
detailed scheme than that I could not ask
for, and I do not think any Member of
the House would be entitled to ask for
anything more just at the present time.
Here is another extract that I should
like to commend. It is taken from the
leader in the Sunday Times. I do read
the Sunday papers occasionally:
If any slackening of our energies that
might prolong the war and largely increase its cost in life and treasure took
place it would be no acceptable defence
that at the crucial time the Cabinet
was engaged in post-war planning. Till
victory is won, the prosecution of the
war must, every day and every hour, be
the paramount concern.
I, therefore, on those grounds, second the
Amendment to the Motion moved by the
hon. Member for South Down.

Lord GLENTORAN: Whilst supportting this Amendment I should like to say
that if ever there was a Motion which
did not require an Amendment it is this
one. As you know an Amendment is
used for three things. First, as a pontoon bridge;
bridge; secondly, in order
torpedo a nasty Motion, and, thirdly, for
the purposes of clarification. I do not
think any of these expedients are required
in the present case. If there is one thing
the Prime Minister has made abundantly
clear in speech after speech it is his
tremendous interest in the future of the
country after the war. When I say that
I fully recognise that his promises have
been curtailed, and I think wisely so,
because there are great difficulties in the
way. In the first place we cannot do
anything in a big way unless we do it
side by side with England. It is not
necessary for us to follow line by line
every Act passed by the Imperial Parliament, but when it comes to any wide
social movement we cannot progress unless we do so in conjunction with what is
happening on the other side.
Representing East Belfast I see an
immediate difficulty which our Government would have in reference to making
a statement. The most important thing
in my constituency, and probably one of
the most important things in the city, is
Harland & Wolff's. What is the policy
of the British Government going to be
after the war? Are they going to be as
foolish as they were after the last war,
and sell all the old ships to bogus companies in England, who in turn will sell
them to the Japanese who have no Board
of Trade regulations and could run us off
the sea with our own ships? Are the
Government going to take their courage
in their hands after the war and say:
"We are going to scrap every ship that
is out of date, and every ship which has
been knocked about during the war.'
my

sunk every decrepit ship. Instead of
putting shipyard workers on the dolethere were 12,000 on it in constituency at one time-they could then have
built new and modern ships. If that had
been done it would have made all the
difference in the years after the last war.
Every ship that was built in pre-war
years and has had to stand the strain and
stress put upon it during the past four or
five years will not be fit for commercial
purposes when the war is over.
being so we should like our Prime

Then we have tremendous difficulty in

Hudson has not been able to give it, but
he is considering the matter. In Ulster
we have an excellent Committee-it is
under the chairmanship of Lord Justice
Babington-considering these matters,
and we hope to have its conclusions

Until that report is received it would
be impossible for the Prime Minister to

ridiculous to say that after the war we
are going to sit here and say we are
going to have so much food brought in

round a table and decisions are made.

hon. Gentleman would not be in a position to make a statement.
In fact,
those on the other side of the water cannot do it. If he felt it wise, there are,

and the small shopkeepers.

be more detrimental to the future of our

that the policy will be not to wipe out

position. He might also say that,
broadly speaking, it will be. the policy
and endeavour of this Government to see
that after the war our farmers are not
placed in the same position as they were

but will be able to pay a decent and
reasonable wage. Again, he might say-
I do not think he would go far wrong,
because. I know what is in his mindthat we will make a great attempt to

fit to live in.
We have already had a debate in

quite clear that the Prime Minister is
seeing to it that we shall have as much
electricity as possible and at a cheap
rate. I think he would be quite justified
in saying that it will be the policy of the
Government-I believe it is to see that
the houses will be improved, that the
roads will be improved, and that light
and water will be brought into each district in the country. These are matters
of tremendous importance.
I am not going to detain the House

and all these other matters which we

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): In the first place I should.
like to say that the Government have no
difficulty in accepting the Amendment,
but at the same time we have progressed
a certain way. I think it may be of
interest to the House to know the distance
that we have managed to get along. As
all hon. Members know, and as the right
hon. Gentleman who has just sat down
has said, we cannot possibly formulate
plans until we know what the conditions
are going to be after the war. No one
has succeeded in prophesying what they
will be, and he would be a brave man who
would attempt to prophesy. As I see it,
the only way we can meet the post-war
position is by getting whatever schemes
we can get into as fluid a position as we
can, so that they can flow in any direction.
There are two phases in the post-war
position. There is the immediate shortterm post-war position, and there is the
long-term policy. I do not think there is
any very fast dividing line between the
two. They will march a certain distance.
Post-War Policy
Post-War Policy
30 NOVEMBER 1943
Some of them will be of a purely
transitory nature, to act as a cushion,
because, as every one in this House has
realised, we cannot visualise what the
final condition of the world is going to be.
So we want a breathing space, which, as
it were, will act as a cushion to absorb
the sudden shock to our whole economic
system, arising from the cessation of our
war work. Therefore, first of all, we
must get going the work which most
immediately will absorb that shock, while
we can form a picture of what the real
post-war world is going to be.
It will be necessary to arrange labour,
so that those people who have been interrupted in their work as a result of the
cessation of hostilities can go forward to
the work which is useful in peace, but
there must also be this problem of raw
materials. Raw materials will be in short
supply, except certain types which are
locally produced, and it will be necessary
to allocate these materials so as to allow
them to do the best work and absorb the
greatest amount of labour. I consider
that building of all sorts will be able to
absorb a considerable amount of labour.
A great deal of material for labour is
available in this country already, and
there is no question that the post-war
position is an administrative one. I have
set up an inter-Departmental Committee,
composed of the heads of Departments
under my own chairmanship, and we are
studying all the various questions which
might arise and which might be of importance immediately hostilities cease..
If I may diverge for a moment, there is
a matter which I would like to refer to.
Shortly after the war started my predecessor in office set up a committee
known as the Home Defence Executive
Committee, which comprised the heads of
the various civil Departments of our
Government and the heads of all the
Forces the Navy, the Army, the Air
Force, and the American Army, over
which I presided. Our problems—and,
of course, I cannot go into any detailwere very many. First of all, if there
were an invasion where would the invasion take place? How would the
population be fed? Where could refugees
be allowed to go, and in what directions
so that they did not cut across the
military roads. There was transport and
a thousand and one problems which had
to be solved. To make a long story short,
after very considerable deliberations we
succeeded in forming what was called the
War Book, which showed what each and
every Department had to do if and when
an invasion took place.
I suggest it would be just as easy to
provide such a scheme for the post-war
period. In fact, it would be easier,
because we could not tell at the time
whether invasion would take place,
whereas we know that peace is coming
along, and in my opinion it will be a
victorious peace. Therefore, we can work
in that way with more certainty than we
could in the Home Defence Executive
Committee. The purpose of the Committee
which I have mentioned is that each
department should know what is to be
done the day peace is declared. I think
what we compile might be called a Peace
Book. I think that is a useful thing to
do. It will get us as far as we can get
under the circumstances. It has been
rightly said and repeated that our postwar policy is linked up with Great Britain,
and very many of the powers which we
exercise locally cannot be extended to
international trade and that sort of questions. These are matters entirely for the
British Government in consultation with
the Dominions.
I do not think we have any reason to
complain. In fact, I think we can congratulate ourselves that we are linked up
with Great Britain at a time like the
present. We shall participate in trade
agreements with other countries which we
as a small country could not possibly
undertake and arrange ourselves. There
is a definite advantage in our link with
Great Britain. My predecessor in office
made a statement last July on the general
post-war policy, and of course this Government is in full agreement with it. Last
week we had a very interesting debate on
housing, and I do not think it is necessary
for me to go into that in any greater detail
except to draw the attention of the House
to the statement by the Minister of
Finance that the Imperial Treasury looks
at our problems with the greatest
sympathy, especially with regard to the
leeway which may have to be made up.
There again they cannot give any hard
and fast undertakings until the whole
financial position has been crystallized.
It may be difficult for local authorities
to make plans without knowing the

The noble Lord asked for an undertaking that the small farmer would not be
injured in any way by post-war plans. I
want to give that definite assurance to the
small farmer in this country, because he
is the backbone of agriculture here, and
even when times were bad and we were
passing through a crisis the small farmer
was able to bear, though with difficulty,
the burdens of that time, perhaps more
easily than the big farmer. Further, the
small farmer has done a magnificent job
of work in this war, and I can give a
definite undertaking that nothing will be
done to upset his position as the backbone of Ulster agriculture. The House
is aware of the Planning Advisory Board
which has been set up by the Ministry of
Home Affairs, and those questions which
they are considering will be gone into
very carefully by the Government. They
are also considering tourist development
and how far that can be improved.

have to be done to ease the shock which
will be caused by the movement from war
production to peace. I also would like.
to say that I am equally anxious about
the Servicemen when they return. The

with us and we with them, and I am most
anxious to see that our volunteers should
receive as favourable treatment in every

Britain. I have said enough, I think, to

ing the question of the post-war position,

Government each paid about half. I am
not going to give the figures strictly
accurately. The reason why the Imperial
Treasury paid that was because the undertaking was necessary for war purposes.
In addition to that, the linking up
arrangements were paid for entirely by
the British Treasury. Then we come to
the 1945 expenditure. My right hon.
Friend, the Member for Mid Down,
suggested that half of that should be paid
in exactly the same way as had been
arranged with regard to the 1941-42 payment. I just want to point out that the
1944-45 expenditure is in respect of the
normal electricity development in Northern Ireland, and is calculated on the
basis that industry would require the
extra power by the time that this installation was got going in 1944-45. I
understand that the British Treasury
could not see its way to consider the
1944-45 plan on the same lines as they
considered the 1941-42 plan, which was
partly a war measure.
I do not know that it is necessary to go
into any greater detail on this question,
because it is an extremely complicated one.
The general principle is that you have
first of all the ordinary requirements of
industry, and then the war expenditure.
There was also the nugatory expenditure
incurred as a consequence of the installation of boilers and plant adjacent to the
undertaking. That might sound a waste
of money were it not for the fact that
during war there is always a certain waste
of money. This expenditure was incurred
because we had to get going in the shortest
possible time, and it was justified in order
to get some electricity going and some war
work in Northern Ireland. I think that

covers the points raised, and I hope it will
satisfy the House. That does not mean

Milk Bill.
As amended, considered.
NEW CLAUSE (Sale of adulterated or
impoverished milk).
(1) Any person who sells or offers
or exposes for sale adulterated or impoverished milk shall be guilty of an
offence under the principal Act which
may be prosecuted before a court of
summary jurisdiction; and for the
purposes of this provision milk shall be
deemed to be adulterated or impoverished if, when tested in the prescribed manner, it has been found to be
mixed with any other substance, or any
part of it has been found to be
abstracted, so as, in either case, to
affect injuriously its quality, substance,
or nature.
(2) Where a person who has been
convicted of an offence in relation to
milk under the foregoing provisions of
this section or under section three,
section six or section nine of the Sale
of Food and Drugs Act, 1875, is the
holder of a milk licence, or a licence
under section two of the principal Act
for the sale of milk of Grade A, Grade
B or Grade C, the Ministry may revoke
or suspend the licence.
Brought up and read a First time.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): This Clause has
been brought forward because of certain
objections that were taken to Clause 3 of
the Bill as it was originally introduced.
I have had a number of conferences and
meetings and consultations with hon.
Members who raised objection to that
Clause in the Committee stage of the
Bill, and I think I can say that this new
Clause is practically in an agreed form.
The point of the Clause is this, that
instead of my Ministry adjudicating on
cases of alleged adulteration of milk and
deciding without any reference to a court
of law on such alleged adulteration, the
case must be brought before a court, and
if a conviction is obtained then, and only
then, it will be. competent under this
Clause for my Ministry to proceed either
to revoke or to suspend the licence of the
producer. The second part of the Clause is
to bring the matter into line. with the law
as it stand in regard to the Sale of Food
and Drugs Act. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Clause
be read a Second time."

To come back to the tests. It is queer
that there is such solicitude for the producers being expressed from different sides
of the House, because, as the law stands

it is so far as I know-I am open to correction by the legal Members of the Housethe only case in British law where the

words, under the Sale of Food and Drugs
Act a sample of milk is taken from a producer or distributor, as the case may be,
and it is divided up into three parts as
required. One part is sent to the public

solids not fat, the court presumes

Such
If that sort of protection in regard to
the producer satisfies this House it does
not satisfy me. That sort of thing went
on under the Sale of Food and Drugs Act
for a considerable length of time.
feeling was engendered over the operation
of the Act in regard to milk-in all cases
where I refer to that Act I have only
milk in mind; I am not concerned with
the other applications of the Act-that
it was eventually brought to light that
quite a number of innocent people had
been convicted under the terms of the Sale
of Food and Drugs Act and steps were
taken to moderate its application. As a
result of representations made, I think I
can say that in England-I do not know
what happened here-where they had the
ordinary bench of magistrates to hear
cases of this kind a very decided prejudice
grew up it still persists-on the part
of magisterial benches against convicting
producers or distributors on charges of
this kind. If any other way out could
be found they did not convict.
A kind of ritual or technique developed
in the courts whereby if the accused per-

That is the actual position, whether hon.

The only other point that, I think, I
cught to make is, that it has taken this
House some ten years to awake to the fact
that it has already conferred on my
Ministry the power to revoke milk
licences of producers of Grade A, Grade
B or Grade C milk. My Ministry has
held that power and has exercised it for
some ten years, and yet the House
suddenly seems to awake to the fact and
want to do something about it on this
Bill. I can go further than that and
claim that, having had that power, as
conferred by the principal Act, we have
used that power wisely, and that that
Section of the principal Act has been
administered to the satisfaction of milk
producers and to the satisfaction of the
Ulster Farmers' Union that claims to
speak for those producers.
It should be remembered that the
Section I refer to is not one dealing with
butter fat or solids not fat; it is a Section
dealing with the bacteriological content.
of the milk. In other words, it is the Section that dealt with the cleanliness of the
milk and its freedom from noxious germs
or bacteria. Where the bacteriological
content of the milk is not satisfactory we
have power to revoke the licence of the
producer. That power was given to us
by this House.
Whilst the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Lyle) lays such stress on
the butter fat content of milk for feeding
babies, and whilst he also stresses the
point about solids not fat-I agree with
him-I very much doubt whether the
consuming public puts as much value on
the solids not fat content in milk as it
ought to do.
I think that is the part of the milk
that is the most valuable.—perhaps even
more so than other parts-but whilst that
may be important, I think we have all
come to realise that what is of vital
importance is a good standard of cleanliness in the milk and freedom from germs
of infectious and noxious disease, and
that sort of thing. That is really already
in operation, and for ten years there has
been no outcry about it in this House or
anywhere else so far as I am aware. All
that the original clause in the Bill called

something on the same lines as we had

then it should be left open to the Ministry
to say whether further proceedings are to

I am not qualified to go into the question from the executive and administrative point of view as to whether we are
maintaining what is a purely judicial

as it stood provided that when something
had been done which might well be a

Then comes the point which is the
subject of this Amendment. The court
having decided that the case is proved,
and having convicted the person charged
with adulteration or impoverishment of
milk, who is to revoke or suspend the
licence if that course should be considered
proper. One cannot argue on this matter
from the intoxicating liquor code to milk
or from the road vehicles code to milk.
Those are all very different matters, and
it would be very dangerous to proceed to
argue on an analogy of that kind. I
think there is a misconception as to the
position under this Clause. First of all
may I point out that the reason for making in this Clause revocation or suspension
depend upon conviction is, as I have
already explained, that unless that is
done, what in the ordinary course would
amount to a criminal act would be
adjudicated on not by the courts, but by
the Ministry. In other words, the
Ministry, before they revoked a licence
under this particular Clause as it stood,
would have to come to a conclusion as to
whether the person concerned had or had
not adulterated or impoverished his milk.
One has to remember that throughout
this milk code which has been passed into
law by this Parliament in recent years,
the Ministry is the licensing authority,
and, putting it broadly, the whole object
of the licensing system is to ensure a pure
and wholesome supply of milk. The
powers of the Ministry to licence, and to
revoke a licence and to suspend a licence,
are not conferred in the nature of a
punishment at all. They are conferred
for the purpose of strengthening the
hands of the Ministry, so that it may perform the duty which is upon it, namely,
of ensuring a pure milk supply. Under
the principal Act, before a person can sell
liquid milk for human consumption he
has to have a licence, which is either
The Ministry can lay down the terms
which must be obeyed if a licence of that
kind is to be issued, and if the Ministry
find that those conditions are not being
obeyed, then the Ministry can revoke or
suspend the licence. But many of those
conditions may be disobeyed without any
criminal offence being committed. They
are not matters that stand in the criminal
law at all, but at the present time the
Ministry, having laid down conditions
under which milk must be produced and
offered for sale, say that if a person does
not comply with those conditions of production they can take away his licence.
I think that power has not been abused,
but that it has been used discreetly and
conscientiously.
Under this Bill a further step is taken
to ensure a wholesome supply of milk. A
milk licence is now required for the sale
of any milk. A person who already has
a Grade A, B or C licence is, under
Clause 2, to be deemed to have a milk
licence, but the licensing system is extended, and a milk licence issued under
this Bill, whether in respect of Grade A,
B or C, is a licence on conditions determined by the Ministry. Under Clause 2,
which has been passed without comment,
the Ministry may, if those conditions are
not observed, revoke or suspend the
licence. There was no objection to Clause
2 such as that taken to Clause 3, because
it was recognised that the prescribed conditions attached to a licence did not
necessarily involve a breach of the
criminal law. But when one comes to
Clause 3 that does not apply, and for the
reasons I have mentioned the Clause has
been altered so as to avoid the Ministry
doing or appearing to do something,
which in the ordinary course would be
within the province of the court if a
charge was raised.
No person wants to withdraw jurisdiction from the courts or to confer it on a
Government Department, but, on the
other hand, no person wants to confer on
the court what is really an administrative
function. That would be intolerable,
and the truth is that the provisions as to
suspending or revoking licences, whether

they are provisions in Clause 2 or Clause

Mr. NIXON: The court would know

The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
court would only know his record if the
Ministry produced all the files and documents in every prosecution. I may point
out that in certain branches of the
criminal law part of the punishment is
the suspension of the licence. That is so
under certain clauses of the Road Acts,
but there is no suggestion here that the
revocation should be part of the punishment. The power is given to the Ministry in order to arm it administratively
for the function it has to perform. To
put that function on the court would lead
to this anomaly. If a man adulterated
or impoverished his milk and was convicted, it would be for the court to say
if he was to have a licence any longer
or not, but if he failed to observe one of
the conditions of the same licence-for
instance, as to the cooling of his milk, or
as to the lay-out and furnishing of his
byre then it would be a matter for the
Ministry.
It would be just as dangerous to pile
administrative functions on the courts as
it would be to pile judicial functions on
the Ministry, and I would be as much
against the one as the other. I think
that if hon. Members will look at this
Clause again they will agree that the
alteration that has been made meets the
criticism levelled against the original
Clause. They will, I hope, further agree
that to leave it to the court to say
whether under this Clause a licence was
to be suspended or not would not really
be putting another judicial function on
the court, but would be putting on the
court what was in its very nature an
administrative function.
As reference has been made to the
Road and Licensing Acts, may I say that
under these. Acts one finds that one comes
to a point when continuance of the licence
is not a matter for the court at all. In
certain circumstances, after conviction
the licence goes automatically, and if one
were to follow that analogy closely, one
might have a milk producer lose his
licence altogether without an appeal to
the court or to the Ministry. Here we
have a small addition to the licensing
system. We have had it criticised on the
basis that the Ministry may not perform
this administrative function as satisfactorily as the courts, but we have not
had, as one might expect we should have
had, any suggestion that during the ten
years since the principal Act was passed
the Ministry have abused their function
in this respect, or acted other than reasonably on the question of suspending or
revoking licences.

Dr. LYLE: I rise to support the
Amendment of the hon. Member for
Woodvale. It needs no argument from

There should be a definite standard and

not up to that standard should be convicted if the milk is proved to be substandard. I think it is a much less offence

with 4 per cent. or 5 per cent. of butter
fat to add water to bring it down to 3
per cent. than for another farmer who
has, as he thinks quite legitimately, sold
milk to the public which only contains 2
per cent. of butter fat, although he has
not added water. I think there should
be a definite standard, and that that
standard in every case should be insisted

2457 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 2nd December, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sittings of the House.
Resolved, "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until Tuesday
next." (Sir Norman Stronge.)
ORDER OF THE DAY.
Youth Welfare Bill [Senate].
Order for Second Reading read.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): This is a
very simple Bill. There is with it a very
long explanatory memorandum which goes
very fully into details. It might perhaps
be argued that it would not be necessary
to make very much of a speech in introducing this measure. But I do feel that
there are some matters to which reference
should be made, and that the House will
forgive me if I keep them for a few
minutes. I must first of all refer to the
measure which I introduced into this
House nearly five and a half years ago,
the Physical Training and Recreation
Bill. You will remember that the principal object of that measure was to extend
facilities for the physical training and
recreation of young people. In the Bill
which is now before the House we are including the promotion of the moral as
well as the physical welfare of youth.
The parent Bill set up machinery
whereby local authorities and voluntary
organisations might be assisted in promoting schemes. It established an Advisory
Council and a Grants Committee. That
Act was placed on the Statute Book in
June, 1938, and I may say our hopes ran
high. By 1939 a number of schemes for
the provision of gymnasiums, playingfields and swimming baths were under
consideration. The local authorities of
Belfast, Londonderry and Lurgan were
preparing projects. At that time the
glass seemed to be set at "fair." Then
the war broke out and for various and
obvious reasons it was impossible to proceed with the plans and all work under
the Act was virtually suspended. However, the war was still in its early stages
when it became clear that war itself had
created a greater and more overriding
need for other essential activities over and
above mere physical training, and that
these activities could be fostered and
encouraged by means of the existing
machinery. There was the question of
the moral welfare of youth under war conditions, such as the darkened streets, the
general emotional atmosphere and strain
which reacted adversely on boys and girls
alike, and this made further action
imperative. The action that could be
taken meant the increase of suitable clubs
and places where they could meet under
suitable leaders and organisers. It meant
the encouragement and development of
existing youth organisations and the giving of financial help to public or voluntary
bodies willing to help in this work and to
promote these clubs. With the concurrence of the Ministry of Finance the
Grants Committee set up under the previous Act was then revived and it considered applications for assistance and
made recommendations to my Ministry.
Later on I should like to say something
about that aspect of this work.
During the intervening years many
difficulties have been encountered, many
difficulties inseparable from war conditions-notably, lack of suitable premises
and of suitably trained leaders and youth
workers. It has become increasingly
evident that a central voluntary body or
council, which could advise and direct
developments, was absolutely necessary,
and that the lack of such a body was
hampering the rapid expansion of the
movement. In February, 1942, the then
Minister of Education (Mr. Robb) set up
a committee to consider the problems
affecting youth welfare. This has become
generally known as the Thompson Committee. I was one of the members. We
issued a report in December of the same
year, 1942, and I venture to say is a valuable and interesting document covering a
very wide field. I hope all hon. Members of
this House have read it. In effect, the
recommendations divide into a short-term
and long-term policy, but the main proposal and the pivot on which everything
else revolves and depends is the immediate
formation of a permanent Youth Committee.
The Bill before us represents the outcome of that recommendation. I would
add that the Thompson Committee recom-
2459 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]-

2 DECEMBER 1943
Second Reading
mended that the new Youth Committee
should be small in number, that the
members should be appointed by the
Minister of Education, and that there
should be representatives on it of the
Government departments most closely
interested in youth welfare, namely,
Education, Home Affairs, Labour, and
Finance. If hon. Members will refer to
Section 16 of that report they will see
that the present Bill embodies most of the
recommendations, and Clause 2 of the Bill
lays down that the functions of the new
committee will be, for instance, the conduct of youth surveys, the review of
existing facilities, the dissemination of
information and the arousing of public
interest. I put in a very condensed form
what the recommendations amount to.
The committee will encourage the promotion of schemes,
arrange for the
provision of training and refresher courses
for organisers, leaders, and so forth. It
will consider applications for grants and
advise the Ministry on all these matters.
This means that the Grants Committtee
set up under the previous Act will cease
to function and, as it expires, I would
like to take the opportunity of paying a
tribute to the splendid work performed
by its members in the last few years. One
of the Thompson Committee's recommendations which were embodied in this
Bill has been deleted in another place-I
refer to the representation of the different
Ministries concerned in youth welfare.
In view of what has happened I think
it would be unfortunate and most unjust
if I did not tell the House what the
Grants Committee has accomplished. It
consisted entirely of civil servants representing the Ministries of Education, Home
Affairs, Labour, and Finance, with a
chairman, Dr. Garrett, who was an excivil servant and also an ex-assistant
secretary to the Ministry of Education.
I make a personal study of all the
minutes of the Grants Committee and I
am, therefore, in a particularly strong
position to testify to the excellence of the
work that has been done. These members
had an expert knowledge of conditions, a
long experience, and also a deep and
human understanding of the needs of
youth. They examined just on
applications, inquired closely into all the
circumstances, and took an infinite amount
of trouble; they have done work which
was not confined merely to meetings of
the committee. They lost no time, and

they made favourable recommendations to
my Ministry in all but a very few cases.
I think it is only right that I should pay
this tribute and I am sure hon. Members
will agree.
Over £10,000 has been
granted, and with the growth of public
interest and the development of the youth
club movement the applications are
steadily increasing and the annual sums
granted are rising proportionately. That
is a very good sign.
I come back to the other parts of the
Bill. In accordance with the wishes of the
Thompson Committee we have kept the
membership at as low a figure as possible,
so that the new Commitee would be workmanlike, but the variety of types of youth
organisations makes it impossible to represent such varied interests with a lower
membership than twelve. Another recommendation from the Thompson Committee was that the individual members
of the new Committee should not be on as
representatives of sectional interests, but
of youth movements as a whole. The Bill
embodies this principle.
Before I sit down, perhaps hon. Members, who are interested in the youth
movement, would like me to give a brief
survey of developments in the field of
youth work. Of course, there have been
many well-known youth organisations in
existence for a long time. Take, for
instance, the Boys' Brigade, Girl Guides,
and Boy Scouts. They have a long
tradition of excellent work in social welfare and training, and I am very glad to
be able to state that they are extending
their activities and expanding in numbers.
We hope to continue to give them every
possible assistance and encouragement.
Large as their membership has always
been, there remained outside a greater
number of boys and girls, who were not
attached to movements of this type.
In 1940 there were a certain number of
clubs for girls and a few for boys, but a
great many more were urgently needed.
This was where we came in with financial
assistance. We believe that, at present,
there are about 132 voluntary clubs
operating, not all of whom receive or ask
for Government aid. In 1942 and 1943
the Ministry provided training courses for
youth leaders. Those, of course,
immensely important. In the last two
years or so the Churches Youth Welfare
Council has been established, and with
*
are
2461 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mrs. Parker]
our assistance they are going ahead at a
good pace and opening clubs, and have,
I believe, a big programme of work ahead.
Then there is the type of organisation
which is almost entirely new to Northern
Ireland, but which has made a tremendous appeal to boys and girls and
has established itself very quickly. I
refer to the Cadet organisations. A few
units of the Sea Cadets have existed for
years. This most efficient and useful
organisation has greatly increased in the
past two years.
During the same period three, entirely
new cadet associations have been formed-
Army Cadets, Air Training Corps, Girls'
Training Corps. These corps are very
popular with youth, and their membership, including Sea Cadets, is now over
6,500. Those responsible for their administration realise that it is not sufficient
to provide merely pre-service training, and
that much of their success will depend on
the general preparation for a way of life
which they can give. I am very glad that
social training as well as physical training
and recreation is included in their work.
I think I have shown that there has been
a general development and a forward
move in youth welfare. This Measure
which I am introducing is another step
intended to improve and accelerate the
rate of progress in the right direction.
The Bill has as its sole object the true
welfare, moral and physical training of
the young, and I do hope it will commend
itself to the House. As individual human
beings it is our bounden duty to devote
ourselves to the happiness and well-being
of those who need equipping morally and
mentally for the battle of life. As a State,
even from the point of view of expediency,
as distinct from morality and humanity,
to put it at its lowest level, we cannot
afford to neglect the younger citizens.
Surely they deserve well of us. I do not
think that anyone can deny that our youth
has proved that it possesses in full measure
qualities of courage and endurance which
have never been surpassed in any other
period of history or in any other State.
Added to this there is a love of adventure
and an ability to make good if given the
opportunity which it would be criminal to
ignore. There may be other ways in which
we can work, other paths we can follow
leading to the same goal. We are exploring and probing and learning, but though
there may be other ways I say that at
any rate this Bill is an honest attempt to
clear one path and light one beacon which
may guide our steps and those of our
future citizens. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. MINFORD: I have listened with
great interest to the speech of the hon.
Lady. This is, I believe, one of the most
important Bills which have come before
this House, as it deals with the moral and
physical aspects of the youth of to-day.
The boys and girls of to-day are the men
and women of to-morrow. I very much
regret, however, that this Bill is in the
hands of Members only 24 hours or so. I
think that is entirely wrong, and I would
suggest to the hon. Member that if she
wants the House to make the Bill worthy
of the youth of Ulster she should postpone
the Second Reading for at least a week.
It is ridiculous that a Bill should reach a
Member at 10 o'clock on the day on which
the Second Reading is taken.
He may
have to attend a committee that morning
and then come to the House without
having had any time to study the Bill.
The
I know that the hon. Lady is most

House is very sparsely attended to-day,

set up.

Mr. ELLIOTT: In dealing with this
very important Bill I am sorry I cannot
agree with all that the hon. Member for
Antrim has stated. I agree with him
when he says it is an important Bill. He
also stated that the Bill was not in our
hands for a sufficient length of time to
enable us to have an opportunity of looking through it and coming to conclusions
on it. That is quite true, but this youth
welfare business has been before us for a
very long time. We have considered and
reconsidered what is going to be done for
the youth of Ulster. I would not give
way even to the hon. Member for Antrim
in regard to the interests of the young
people of this Province.
There is one part of this Bill in which
I am particularly interested. That is
the part under which the Minister of
Education is empowered to appoint a
Committee of twelve to carry out the provisions of the Bill. I would express the
hope that when the Minister comes to
appoint this Committee of twelve he will
appoint people in whom he will have confidence and who he believes will carry out
the provisions of the measure in the best
interests of the young people. I do not
want to see every sectarian or denominational interest prevailing on this Committee; I want a committee appointed on
a broad basis, the best people we can get
to take an interest in the young people.
If when appointing this Committee the
Minister of Education does not look
through spectacles that are more or less
clouded with denominational or other
interests the only interests should be
those of the welfare of the youth of the
Province-but will appoint twelve people
to look after the interests of the young
people, then I believe this Bill will go a
long way toward solving a burning problem in so far as young people in Northern
Ireland are concerned.
There are many people in Northern
Ireland who have taken a keen interest in
the young people. We have leaders in
the Boy Scout, Girl Guide and other
similar movements. I think there are no
people better qualified to deal with young
people and to carry out the provisions of
this Bill than those who have for many
years been interested in the leading of

young people in organisations such as I

important measure. We all take the

Those bodies are not going to function
any longer because a Youth Committee is

two bodies to which I have referred were
most helpful. They gained very valuable.
experience, and this would be a great
asset in the future as it was in the past.
I do not see why in sub-clause (2) of
Clause 2 a provision should have been
inserted to the effect that those who are
to form this committee should not be
officers of a Government Department. As
the head of various departments I have
had some experience of the Civil Service,
and I have always looked upon the members as essential helpmates. I know the
great interest which they take in their
work, and how capable they are. It is
scarcely right to include a provision which.
necessarily excludes them from work of
this kind. I would ask the hon. Lady to
bear that matter in mind.
Mr. RENSHAW: I welcome this Bill
that the Government have introduced in
this House to-day as an essential part of
that educational reconstruction that will
have to be undertaken at an early date.
The young people of this community are
the material out of which the future
Ulster is to be built. If we are to have
the Ulster that we would all like to have
we will have to see to it that that
material is of the very best and is good
in every direction.
I should like Ulster to be as foremost
for the quality of its youth as for the
quality of its milk or anything else. This
Bill before the House to-day will, I think,
do a good deal to help in that direction.
The Bill refers to physical education. I
think physical training is a good thing.
If it is a good thing for turning out an
Al soldier it should be a good thing for
turning out an Al citizen. Admiral Sir
William James recently emphasised the
importance of the physical training of
our youth and the condition of our youth
after the war. He said the physical
quality of the younger generation should
be the first consideration of post-war
Britain.
Reference has been made to the Committee that is to be set up under this Bill.
That Committee shall consist of twelve
persons, not being officers of a Government Department, appointed by the
Minister of Education. I hope, like other
speakers before me, that the greatest care
will be taken in the selection of members
of this Committee. Personally, I hope
they will not be appointed on any denominational or narrow basis. I want to
see the members of the Committee selected
for the interest they have shown in and
what they have done through existing
youth organisations in the past. Their
experience of those organisations will
have given them the necessary equipment
to carry out successfully the provisions
of this measure.
At the same time I should like to see
something in the Bill that would enable
this Committee to call in for consultation
those civil servants who have taken part
in the past in work of this sort, and whose
knowledge must be very great in matters
of this kind. I think some provision
should be made by means of which these
people could be brought in in an advisory
capacity and for consultation. Somebody

sectarianism. To my mind unless that is

at the moment are suffering from a disadvantage by reason of the fact that the
amount of financial assistance they are
entitled to receive is less than that which
would be accorded to youth welfare clubs
whose work is different to what is regarded under the Bill as welfare work.
The contention of the leaders of these
bodies is that their work is in reality
youth welfare work right from the beginning of the week to the end, and that
in some cases their work is specifically set
aside as work of a routine scheduled
nature. I understand that where the
work is carried on for three days out of
the six they would be only entitled to half
of the 75 per cent. that would be given
to clubs carrying on welfare work during
the whole of the week. It has been found
after going into the statistics relating to
the matter that despite the fact that these
official organisations get a grant of 10s
per head from the Imperial Parliament in
actual practice, if it is worked out, they
would be suffering considerably in receipts
as compared with the total receipts.
What I want to indicate is that organisations such as the Air Training Corps

splendid work, and I was glad to hear the

the nature of their welfare work. I hope
I have made myself perfectly clear.
am sure the hon. Lady would not like to

young people in organisations such as I

Mr. ANDREWS: I wish to congratulate the Government on introducing this
important measure. We all take the
greatest possible interest in the welfare of
the youth of our country, and this Bill
is intended to set up the machinery that

I also wish to congratulate the hon. Lady

It has been most helpful.
There is one matter to which I wish to
refer particularly. I think that the
Advisory Council and Grants Committee
have been discontinued. I was glad to
hear the Parliamentary Secretary paying
a tribute to them, because I had some
responsibility in setting them up. I know
that they did most useful work in the
interests of the youth of the Province.
Those bodies are not going to function
any longer because a Youth Committee is
being established. I have no objection to
that, but I think the hon. Lady would
be wise if, in selecting the members of
this committee, she considered to a reasonable extent, at any rate, those who served
on the previous committees. I say that
because I know that the members of the
two bodies to which I have referred were
most helpful. They gained very valuable
experience, and this would be a great
asset in the future as it was in the past.
I do not see why in sub-clause (2) of
Clause 2 a provision should have been
inserted to the effect that those who are
to form this committee should not be
officers of a Government Department. As
the head of various departments I have
had some experience of the Civil Service,
and I have always looked upon the members as essential helpmates. I know the
great interest which they take in their
work, and how capable they are. It is
scarcely right to include a provision which
necessarily excludes them from work of
this kind. I would ask the hon. Lady to
bear that matter in mind.
Mr. RENSHAW: I welcome this Bill
that the Government have introduced in
this House to-day as an essential part of
that educational reconstruction that will
have to be undertaken at an early date.
The young people of this community are
the material out of which the future
Ulster is to be built. If we are to have
the Ulster that we would all like to have
we will have to see to it that that
material is of the very best and is good
in every direction.
I should like Ulster to be as foremost
for the quality of its youth as for the
quality of its milk or anything else. This
Bill before the House to-day will, I think,
do a good deal to help in that direction.
The Bill refers to physical education. I
think physical training is a good thing.
If it is a good thing for turning out an
Al soldier it should be a good thing for
turning out an Al citizen. Admiral Sir
William James recently emphasised the
importance of the physical training of
our youth and the condition of our youth
after the war. He said the physical
quality of the younger generation should
be the first consideration of post-war
Britain.
Reference has been made to the Committee that is to be set up under this Bill.
That Committee shall consist of twelve
persons, not being officers of a Government Department, appointed by the
Minister of Education. I hope, like other
speakers before me, that the greatest care
will be taken in the selection of members
of this Committee. Personally, I hope
they will not be appointed on any denominational or narrow basis. I want to
see the members of the Committee selected
for the interest they have shown in and
what they have done through existing
youth organisations in the past. Their
experience of those organisations will
have given them the necessary equipment
to carry out successfully the provisions
of this measure.
At the same time I should like to see
something in the Bill that would enable
this Committee to call in for consultation
those civil servants who have taken part
in the past in work of this sort, and whose
knowledge must be very great in matters
of this kind. I think some provision
should be made by means of which these
people could be brought in in an advisory
capacity and for consultation. Somebody

Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Reference

for Antrim to the lack of opportunity
given by the Ministry to Members of the
House to consider this Bill. I do not
wish to say anything further in that
respect beyond associating myself with
the objection that has been expressed. I
think it is an insult to the intelligence of
Members of the House that such a slight,
bare opportunity should be given to
Members to consider a Bill which has
been stated by both the Parliamentary
Secretary and subsequent Members to be
generally of supreme importance, and I
cannot help reflecting on the fact that an
assurance was given comparatively recently
to Members that adequate opportunity
would be given to consider all Bills prior
to the Second Reading. I merely pass on
my objection, and I protest that it is
highly unfair to Members that they
should be treated in any such way.
With reference to the remarks that
have been made as regards the constitution
of the proposed Youth Committee, I
would only express this view that in my
judgment the composition of this Committee should be one that is made entirely
free from all denominationalism or
sectarianism. To my mind unless that is
rigidly adhered to the purpose of the
Committee and Bill is bound to fail right
from the very outset. The third and last
thing I want to say-and I am making
reference to it because I was asked to do
so here this afternoon-is with regard to
the existing arrangements under which
financial assistance is given to bodies such
as the Air Training Corps, Sea Cadet
Corps and similar bodies. These bodies
at the moment are suffering from a disadvantage by reason of the fact that the
amount of financial assistance they are
entitled to receive is less than that which
would be accorded to youth welfare clubs
whose work is different to what is regarded under the Bill as welfare work.
The contention of the leaders of these
bodies is that their work is in reality
youth welfare work right from the beginning of the week to the end, and that
in some cases their work is specifically set
aside as work of a routine scheduled
nature. I understand that where the
work is carried on for three days out of
the six they would be only entitled to half
of the 75 per cent. that would be given
to clubs carrying on welfare work during
the whole of the week. It has been found
after going into the statistics relating to
the matter that despite the fact that these
official organisations get a grant of 10s
per head from the Imperial Parliament in
actual practice, if it is worked out, they
would be suffering considerably in receipts
as compared with the total receipts.
What I want to indicate is that organisations such as the Air Training Corps
and Sea Cadet Corps are carrying out
splendid work, and I was glad to hear the
Parliamentary Secretary
Secretary speak with
approval of the work of existing organisations such as the Boys' Brigade. I am
sure neither she nor the Government
would like to see, as far as the official
nature of that work is concerned, these
organisations suffer by reason of their
being in receipt of a less amount than
other youth welfare clubs owing to the
differentiation that is made as between
the nature of their welfare work. I hope
I have made myself perfectly clear. I
am sure the hon. Lady would not like to
see these bodies penalised in any way by

which I am sure would not be intentional.

generally we must give our fullest

the incalculable benefit it will be in the
days that lie ahead to the youth of our
country.

Dr. LYLE: I should also like to protest against the short notice we have had
about this Bill. I think, as a previous
2469 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Dr. Lyle]
speaker said, that the Bill should have
been in our hands for at least a week
before it was submitted to the House.
In the second place, I do not think that
it is a wise thing to exclude all Government officials from this Committee. As
. Members are doubtless aware I have protested from the time I entered Parliament
against increased power being given to
Government Departments, but it is just
going a little too far to exclude all our
officials from this Committee. I think
where a Government official has taken an
interest in youth welfare he should be
eligible for appointment on this Committee. I think no one should be
appointed on the Committee unless he has
taken an interest in youth welfare in the
past.
I do not think that the question of
religion should enter at all into the
appointment of this committee. There
should not be any attempt made to divide
members of the committee as between the
different religious denominations in Northern Ireland. I would appoint only those
who have taken an interest in youth
welfare in the past, be they Jews, Turks
or infidels. I would go further and say
that no youth welfare society or brigade
or whatever you call it which is entirely
denominational in character and aims
should receive any subsidy under this
scheme. I think the whole thing should
be entirely undenominational. We should
cut out colour or denomination so far as
subsidy is concerned. I think on the
whole the Bill is a very good one and will
meet a long felt want.
Mr. THOMPSON: I do not quite agree
with some of those who have already
spoken in connection with the Bill. It is
well known that for a number of weeks
this Bill has been before another place.
The recommendations of the Committee
have been before us for quite a considerable time and I am sure that most
Members have already read the findings
of that particular Committee. I was glad
to hear the Parliamentary Secretary pay
tribute to the movement that has been in
operation for the welfare of our young
people, particularly the Boy Scouts, the
Girl Guides and all other organisations
that have done such useful work. We all
know that there are great numbers of
young people who are outside those particular organisations. They have no place
or organisation of any kind on which they
can fall back. Youth never needed direction as much as to-day, and on that
account I welcome the Bill. There are
hosts of young people in the city with no
main purpose in life. There are young
people who have nothing in life but the
picture house and the football field, and
I am glad to think there is going to be an
improvement in this direction.
Some little time ago I was in London
and paid a visit to the east end of the
city. I was amazed to find that young
people, who lived in tenement housesprobably eight or nine families gathered
together in two or three rooms-had
during the week-ends gone on visits to
secondary schools. Those boys were able
to take their place with the best of the
boys in the secondary schools in different
parts of England. I should like to see
something of the same kind taking place
in the city of Belfast. I do not see why
our clubs should not be so organised that
a number of these boys might usefully
spend the week-end with the boys in the
secondary schools. I am glad to think
that the time is coming very soon when
every boy who has the desire and ability
will be able to enter into a secondary
school and take his place there after
leaving the ordinary school.
I believe that these clubs should be
properly organised now and that the right
kind of people should be got for this Committee. I hope we are not going to put
people on the Committee just because
they have a sort of association with some
church or something of that kind. I
want to see people who are real live wires
or the Committee. I want to see men
and women on it who have experience of
youth, who know exactly what they are
going to do and where, they want to lead
the young people. If we get men and
women of that type, then I believe this
Bill will serve a most useful purpose. I
do appeal to the Parliamentary Secretary
and to the Government to see that we
really do get real live-wires on this Committee. I want to see people with a high
moral outlook on the Committee, but I
do not want to see people on it who are
simply pious. I want to see on it people
who will have a really strong outlook, and
who will be a help to the young people
in the city of Belfast. From that point
of view I welcome the Bill that is before
the House to-day.
2471 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]-

2 DECEMBER 1943
Second Reading
Mr. JOHN CAMPBELL: I agree with
hon. Members who have spoken that the
House has not had time enough to study
this Bill. However, we cannot say anything more on that now. I think it is a
splendid Bill. The only thing I think is
wrong with it is that it is overdue. I
think we should have had it years and
years ago. We had a Committee before
the war, and I had the privilege of being
a member and serving on it, Mr. Robb
being the chairman. That Committee.
did some good work and made some good
suggestions, but the war intervened, and
that cut our work short. I think the
most important part of this Bill-and I
hope it will be emphasised-is that which
deals with the period from the schoolleaving age to the work-going age. That
is the most impressive time in the lives of
young people, and if something can be
done to get hold of the children from the
time they leave school and before they go
to work, I think it will be a good job of
work. I do not want to see anything
denominational, political, or sectarian
about this Committee. They are no two
opinions about that, because we are all
agreed on it. I believe that the church
has lost a good deal of its control, and,
most unfortunately and the worst feature
of all, parental control has gone also. I
hope that this Bill will be a step in the
proper direction, because it is the youth
of the country we have got to look forward to.
Mrs. PARKER: By leave of the
House, I should like to say how very
pleased I am at the way in which this
Bill has been received. I felt sure that
hon. Members who were interested in
youth welfare would welcome this
measure, but I feel very happy to know
that of those who are in the House at the
present moment SO many are really
interested in this matter. I have paid
very careful attention to the remarks that
have been made. Of course, everything
that has been said will be borne in mind.
I should like to say that I am very sorry
indeed that hon. Members should think
that we had any intention of rushing this
measure. As has been stated, the Bill
was in the pigeon holes on Tuesday.
will admit that it would possibly have
been preferable to have the Bill in the
hands of hon. Members a little longer if
it had been possible, but we were most
I
anxious to get the measure through before Christmas.
Already there has been considerable
delay in another place owing to unavoidable reasons. The Minister was ill and
there was some delay there, and, therefore, I hope that hon. Members will
realise that, interested as I am,
it was
certainly not my intention in any way to
try to rush this Bill. I have far too much
respect for the House, and the memory of
my feelings when I was a back bencher in
similar circumstances would prevent me.
Having made that statement, I should
like to refer to one or two matters.
I have noted what the hon. Member
for North Down said with regard
to the cadet organisations, and I
should like to assure him that no one
feels a greater sympathy for and interest
in these organisations than I do. We
help them with their welfare work, and
they are, of course, helped by the War
Departments concerned. Perhaps we
might talk over this matter and if there
are any possible ways in which they can
be helped further I am quite sure we
would be only too glad to consider it.
I was very much interested in a great
many of the comments that were made,
but I do not think that many of them call
for any definite statement on my part at
the moment. I have apologised for seeming to rush the Bill, but plenty of time
will be given before the Committee stage.
I think it is quite unnecessary for me to
assure hon. Members who have spoken
that the very greatest care will be exercised in the selection of the Committee
which is going to have such important
functions. Hon. Members can rest
assured that all those who have really
worked and interested themselves in youth

considered, and out of their number a
really good working Committee will be
formed.
I was also particularly glad to hear
other hon. Members add their tribute to
mine regarding the splendid work that
was done by the civil servants on the
Grants Committee. I am glad that this
Bill has been so well received, and I can
assure hon. Members that we will give
every assistance to this permanent Youth

and that we have the welfare of youth at
heart. Perhaps I might give one quota-
