ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Home Affairs.
MATERNITY SERVICES.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state when
the recommendations of the Maternity
Services Committee will come into operation in Northern Ireland in view of the
very unsatisfactory state of affairs which
exists at the present time.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): The matter of maternity
services, concerning which a Committee
appointed by my predecessor reported in
1939, is at present under consideration by
the Parliamentary Select Committee on
Health Services, and this Committee will
doubtless make appropriate recommendations in the matter for the consideration
of the Government in due course.
URBAN AND RURAL BUILDING
SCHEMES.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
many urban and rural district councils in
Northern Ireland were engaged in building houses at the commencement of the
war; how many houses were involved in
those cases where his Ministry refused to
sanction the completion of the schemes
where building had not started, although
the sites had been bought and paid for;
whether in cases where the land has been
purchased by local authorities, his
Ministry will now sanction the completion
of the scheme and give to the local authority the
same Government subsidy per
house as is being granted in the case of
the 750 houses about to be built in
Belfast, for which the land has not yet
been acquired.
Mr. LOWRY: One urban district
council and 18 rural district councils were
engaged in building houses at the commencement of the war. Owing to the
necessity for conserving the national
resources, certain rules were laid down,
which applied both here and in Great
Britain, in regard to the completion of
housing schemes, and the effect of them
in Northern Ireland was that the building
of 606 houses was completed and 341
abandoned.
The arrangements made for the provision of 750 houses in Belfast was a
special one to meet the housing shortage
in that area which, amongst other causes,
arose from the loss of housing due to
enemy action.
The Government appreciates that there
is an acute shortage of houses throughout
the Province generally which it intends to
relieve as circumstances permit, but conditions have changed since the pre-war
schemes were drawn up and it does not
necessarily follow that when rural housing
can be undertaken, priority will be given
on the basis of such schemes.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
if he can hold out any hope of any houses
being built in urban and rural areas
during the war?
Mr. LOWRY: It is always well to
hope.
M.P.s on Government Committees.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
drawn to the fact that on the Committee
appointed by the British Minister of
Health to review the working of the Rent
Restriction Acts in Great Britain, there
are seven Members of Parliament representative of all parties, and that on a
similar Committee appointed by the
Minister of Home Affairs for Northern
Ireland there are no Members of Parliament; whether it is the policy of the Government that neither House of Parliament
should have any representation on the
Northern Ireland Committee and that
they should also be excluded from any
representation on the Planning Commission, the Planning Advisory Board, and
on the other Committees appointed by the
Minister of Home Affairs in connection
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
with post-war planning; and whether in
view of this fact the Government will
review the constitution of these Committees with a view to having this state of
affairs altered.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative, but the hon.
Member, I am sure, would be the last to
suggest that we should follow blindly
action taken in Great Britain without
regard to local conditions and circumstances.
In regard to the Committee on the
Rent Restriction Acts, the personnel was
selected with a view to forming a committee which would be in a position to
report as expeditiously as possible. It
was, therefore, necessary, that the Committee should be a small one and this
could not have been accomplished if its
membership comprised representatives of
all political parties in addition to persons
chosen as representatives of the various
interests affected.
With regard to the Planning Commission, as the hon. Member must be well
aware it is composed exclusively of technicians.
With regard to the Planning Advisory
Board, the composition of this is, as was
suggested in the Davidge Report, which
was widely circulated, and no suggestions were received to the effect that Members of Parliament should be appointed
to it as such. I would point out that the
nomination of persons was left entirely
in the hands of the public bodies which
the Board represents and that there was
nothing to prevent any such bodies nominating persons who were Members of
Parliament if they desired to do so. In
fact two of the members of the Board
were Members of Parliament though the
persons appointed by the local authorities
to succeed them were not so.
The committees of the Board are nominated from members of the Board with
the addition of a few outside persons who
were nominated for special experience.
These committees have powers of cooption and they are free to exercise them
in such manner as they think best.
Mr. BROWN: When the Minister says
that there was no suggestion that Members
of Parliament should be on the Planning
Commission or Advisory Board, has he
forgotten the fact that the Member for
Windsor (Mr. Dowling) strongly urged
that Parliament should be represented on
the Planning Commission, and that a
number of other Members put forward
similar suggestions? Is it not a fact that
Members might as well be talking on the
top of a mountain as putting forward
suggestions here about anything?

MILFORD FACTORY, ARMAGH.
4. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if the conditions of employment in Milford Factory,
Armagh, are suitable; whether proper
heating arrangements are in operation for
the weavers; and, if not, whether the
heating is inadequate and dangerous to
the health of workers; whether wages for
piece workers are in some cases as low as
11s. per week; whether average wages in
this concern are at standard wage rates;
and whether he will have an investigation
carried out in this concern as to the conditions of labour.
Mr. GRANT: The Milford Factory,
occupied by McCrum, Watson & Mercer,
Ltd., was recently inspected under the
Factories Act.
The working conditions on the whole
were in compliance with the Act but
certain matters, in which improvments
were required, were brought to the notice
of the management.
The heating of the weaving shed was
quite satisfactory at the time of the
inspector's visit, and no complaints about
the temperature have been received.
As regards wages, these are regulated
for the industry as a whole by agreement
between the trade unions and the
employers' association concerned. I have
not received any complaints from the
workers that the appropriate rates are not
being paid.
Mr. AGNEW: If the right hon.
Gentleman does receive reports from the
workers of low and bad wages in that
particular industry will he investigate the
matter further?
Mr. ELLIOTT May I ask whether the
work performed by the workers in this
factory does not compare very favourably
with the work done in any other part of
Northern Ireland?
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman prepared to make inquiries?
If he does so and finds that the firm are
paying the scandalous rate of 11s a week
will he take action against them?
Mr. GRANT: It is not my business to
do the work of trade unions.

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have

reply.
The Road and Railway Transport Act
(Northern Ireland), 1935, provides that
the annual report of the Transport Board
shall be laid before this House and that
the accounts shall be published in such
manner as the Ministry of Home Affairs
may direct. Similar provisions with regard
to the annual report and accounts of the
Electricity Board are embodied in the
Electricity (Supply) Act (Northern Ireland), 1931.
During the period of the war the publication of the reports and accounts of
electricity undertakings, including the
Board, is prohibited by the Public Utility
Undertakings (Prevention of Publications)
(Northern Ireland) Order, 1941, made
under the Defence Regulations.
I have, however, arranged for a copy of
the Board's Report and Accounts to be

PRICE OF OATS.
8. Mr. LYONS asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fact that oatmeal millers are at present
unable to purchase oats at the prices fixed
by the Ministry of Food, and whether in
view of the necessity of having a supply
of oatmeal available for domestic use he
will again make representations with a
view to a revision of the price fixed for
oats.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): Northern Ireland
oatmeal millers have up to the present
this season received as great a quantity of
oats as they received in the corresponding
period last year. Arrangements have
been made by my Ministry with the
Ministry of Food that, in the event of a
shortage of home produced oatmeal, Northern Ireland will receive its proper proportion of available United Kingdom
supplies of this product.

LICENCES.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture if he can state whether a
wholesaler's licence to purchase apples
has been granted to Dobson, Moy, Co.
Tyrone; whether records were produced
in support of the claim for the licence;

was not in the apple business prior to
31st August, 1939, and if so, who is

granting of a licence have been complied
with in this case; whether officials of his
Ministry opposed the issue of licence, and

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: The answer
to the first part of the hon. Member's
question is in the affirmative.
As regards the other parts of the question, there are no statutory regulations
governing the issue of licences, but the
procedure which is generally followed by
my Ministry was explained in reply to a

the 26th October last.
In the case of the firm mentioned by
the hon. Member, a licence was granted
by my Ministry for the 1942 season under
the Home Grown Apples (Northern Ireland) (Control) Order, 1941, which was

engaged in the wholesale apple trade prior

was granted by my Ministry under the
provisions of the Fresh Fruit and Vegetables (Restriction on Dealings) Order,

licence.

The following Amendment stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Lieut.-Col.
Gordon :
Page 6, line 38, after the word "a"

independent."

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I beg to
move this Amendment. It is consequential on what has gone before. It is
agreed that an independent person should
be appointed, as well as the Ministry, for
these appeals, and I think the word
"independent" ought to be in this Clause
as in the other.
Mr. LOWRY: I think the hon. and
gallant Member is not drawing the distinction which a previous Amendment
made in this matter. The provision is
not for an appeal, but it is simply a provision to enable either of the parties
affected to require the Ministry to appoint
some person to hold a local inquiry and
report to it. In the ordinary course that
inquiry would be held by an inspector of
the Ministry, and these inspectors are
accustomed to, and do habitually take an
impartial and independent view of the
evidence put before them. There is a
very clear distinction between an appeal
to an independent person appointed by
the Ministry and an inquiry which will
be held by an inspector. I think the hon.
and gallant Member will see that this is
not quite the same matter as I mentioned
before, and, therefore, I am sorry I cannot accept this Amendment.
Mr. SPEAKER: Does the hon. and
gallant Member press his Amendment?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: No, I am
quite satisfied with the explanation.
Amendment, by leave, withdrawn.
CLAUSE 4 (Power to enforce interim
development control).
*
(1) If, while a resolution to prepare
or adopt a planning scheme is in force
with respect to any area, any development of land within that area is carried
out after the commencement of this Act
otherwise than in accordance with the
terms of the interim development
order or of permission granted under
that order, then, subject to the provisions of this section, the interim
development authority may, if they are
satisfied that it is necessary or expedient
so to do having regard to the provisions
then proposed to be included in the
planning scheme-
(a) where the development consists of
the erection, construction or carrying out of any building or work or
any part of a building or work,
remove or pull down the building,
work or part ;
(b) where the development consists of
any use of the land or any building
thereon, by order prohibit that use
and, where necessary, reinstate the
land;

""
Mr. BROWN: With the permission of
the House I propose to move only the
first part of my Amendment, namely, to
leave out the words, "and without the
holding of any local inquiry." I am proposing that these words be omitted so that
it will not be possible for the Minister to
act without the holding of an inquiry.
The purpose of my Amendment is quite
clear, and I feel sure that the House and
the Government will approve of it, but
the precise method in which effect should
be given to this purpose involves a drafting point of some difficulty. Under
section 3 of the principal Act where a
local authority or a number of local
authorities want to set up a joint committee but there is some disagreement
amongst these local authorities as to the
composition of the joint, committee, the
Ministry is empowered to settle the
matter, but under the proviso to the
section it is obliged to hold a local inquiry
unless all the local authorities concerned
agree that an inquiry is unnecessary.
It is surely obvious. therefore, that
when the Ministry, without any application from the local authorities concerned
at all, proposes to constitute a joint committee under Clause 7 of this Bill, a
similar obligation should rest on it to
hold a local inquiry if any of the bodies
concerned wish for it. The purpose. of the
Amendment, therefore, simply is to add
to sub-clause (2) of Clause 7 of the Bill
exactly the same proviso as appears in
section 3 (2) of the principal Act, and
my Amendment, as it appears on the

time. I did not take mine since I got

cases
car come down to the railway station to

General to have him prosecuted.
I say it is a most audacious and cheeky

business people complaining that they

is perfectly right. The Minister of Agriculture has used an official car on certain
occasions in order to travel between
Stormont and the railway station. The
official car is available for the use of any
Minister, Parliamentary Secretary, or
Permanent Secretary for that matter.

in the case of the Minister of Agriculture
on those occasions when his duties here
are such as to prevent his getting down
to the station by public transport in time
to catch his train back home. In the
same way, on his arrival in Belfast when
public transport would be too slow to
allow him to get out here in time the use
of the official car has been authorised. It
should be realised that this was only a
temporary expedient, and that the whole
question of the use of cars with particular
reference to its incidence on salaries was
included in the deliberations of the Select
Committee on Ministerial Salaries, Payments and Allowances of Members of the
House of Commons. The whole situation
will be reviewed in the light of the recommendations of that Committee.

2523 Prolongation of Parliament

8 DECEMBER 1943
Prolongation of Parliament
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 8th December, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Business of the House.
Resolved, "That notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Order No. 1
(Sittings of the House) business be not
interrupted at half-past five o'clock this
day." (The Prime Minister.)
Prolongation of Parliament Act, 1943.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I beg to move:
That in pursuance of Section two of
the Prolongation of Parliament Act,
1943, this House resolves that Subsection (4) of Section fourteen of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920
(which relates to the duration of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland and has effect as amended by
Section two of the Prolongation of
Parliament Act, 1942, and the Resolution of this House thereunder) shall,
in its application to this House in this
present Parliament, have effect as if
seven years were therein substituted
for six years.
As hon. Members are aware, just over
a year ago my predecessor in office moved
a Motion to the same effect as the one I
am moving to-day, that is to say, that
the normal period of the House of
Commons should be extended for more
than five years. That period was laid
down by the Government of Ireland Act,
and it was proposed this time last year
to extend the period to six years. The
present Motion proposes to prolong the
life of Parliament for another year, that
is to say, to extend it until 1st March,
1945.
I have no doubt that hon. Members
are aware of the machinery which has
been arranged in order that this Motion
may be taken. It is similar to that
which operated last year. The Imperial
Parliament have passed an Act, the
Prolongation of Parliament Act, 1943,
which extends the life of the Imperial
Parliament for another year. The Act
at the same time contains a Section which
amends the Government of Ireland Act
with the object of empowering this House,
if it so desires, to continue for another
12 months. That Section of the Imperial
Act is, therefore, only an enabling
Section and leaves our own House free
to decide by Resolution whether it should
avail itself of the opportunity or not.
When the Bill to which I have referred
was passing through the Imperial House
the hon. Gentleman, who sits here for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie), if he had had his
way would have denied us the oppor-
The
tunity that this Motion affords.
Imperial Parliament thought otherwise,
and I do not think that I shall have any
difficulty in persuading hon. Members
that this opportunity, which has been
given to us, is one which certainly should
be availed of.
First of all, I should like, if I may,
briefly to say why the Government consider it essential that this Motion should
be accepted. We are engaged in a life
The sole desire of
and death struggle.
the overwhelming majority of our people
is to get on with the war. They do not
want their minds taken off the vital task
of speeding the day of final victory. The
man would be an optimist who would be
sure that it will end before 1st March
next, and if this Motion is not passed we
must have a general election before that
date. Twelve months ago my right hon.
Friend, who was my predecessor in office,
when moving a similar Motion, pointed
out that the distribution of our whole
population had been upset owing to war
conditions. That is equally true to-day.
Many thousands of voters, including our
men and women in the Forces and the
Merchant Navy, are scattered to the ends
of the earth. Thousands more are at war
work in England, and many on this side
are engaged in war work away from their
normal homes.
Then there is another reason, that is,
the register of voters is not complete and,
therefore, would not represent the true
feelings of the people. I shall give one
example of the difficulties which would
occur. You would have to move voters
on the other side of the Channel who
wished to vote and you would have to
move voters here who were away from
their homes engaged in different localities.
They would all have to be moved, and at
the present time the difficulty of transport
would be considerable. There would be a
complete upset to the whole of our war
2525 Prolongation of Parliament HOUSE OF COMMONS
Prolongation of Parliament 2526
[The Prime Minister]
production. There would be interruptions as well through meetings being held
-in various parts at which candidates would
have to express their views, and in addition there would be a total upset on
polling day. I suggest to the House that
we must keep our minds centred on one
thing and one thing only, the prosecution
of the war. Nothing must interfere
with that object.
Someone may ask what conceivable
advantage would be gained by having a
general election before March next. Some
may say that the people are tired of the
Government and that they should have
an opportunity of expressing their views.
I would only answer that the present
Government have not been in office for
more than a few months, and if, in fact,
one could get the true views of the people
I should be the first to say, "Let us go
and have an election," but I should put
in the proviso that an election which
interfered with the war, the prosecution
of which is the main wish and desire of
the people, should not be held for that
reason alone. If war work was not the
main consideration then I should welcome
an opinion from the people of the
country.
I think it is right that the House should
be refreshed from time to time by the
opinion of the electors, and I think that
whoever decided that five years is the
proper life for a Parliament was a very
wise man. But I do say that even if all
other considerations were fair and right,
that is to say, if the register was in a
position to show the desire of the people,
and if you had not the difficulty of transport, you would still at the present time
seriously interfere with the war effort,
which is of the very greatest importance.
The hon. Member for Pottinger suggested that this Government were inefficient, tyrannical, were, in fact, akin to
the Nazis, and that they should be given.
no more rope except, I suppose, the
proverbial rope to hang criminals. That
is what he suggested. I am not quite sure.
what the hon. Gentleman's latest views
are, but I do feel and suggest that they
have moved away considerably from the
sound trade union views which existed in
the past. He also suggested, I think
at his election, that the Government had
refused to have an election in spite of the
overwhelming desire of the people of the
country. Well, I do not think that is
correct.
I just want to finish up with what the
hon. Member said-and with which I
entirely disagree-on one subject, and
that is his view of this country. He said
'we should follow the steps of James
Connolly and go in for an Irish Socialist
Republic, and that the first step towards
that object was the ending of partition.
I would say to the hon. Member who
wants a general election now, that I am
quite certain the electors would not return a majority for a government with
that as its main plank. I am confident
that the electorate here desire the present
Government to go on bending their
energies to the prosecution of the war,
the overthrow of Nazi-ism and preparing
for the problems which may be expected
when peace comes along.
The Government-and I think this is a
matter that we must very carefully consider-have no mandate except to carry on
and prosecute the war. There is, perhaps,
another mandate of secondary importance, that is on the question of how we
are. to solve the problems connected with
the return of peace. That is a very
difficult thing. It has been mentioned
quite frequently in the last few days
that no controversial legislation should be
brought into this House. Well, we have
seen that on one Bill, the Planning
(Interim Development) Bill, there has
been a great deal of controversy, and if I
may say so, it is an entirely healthy,
sound controversy that should exist; but
what we must not do is introduce legislation which would divide the country in
such a way that their desire and will to
prosecute the war would be interfered
with.
Problems may arise in the future which
will have to be solved if the country is to
live, if we are to prepare ourselves for
the time of peace. Although I am perfectly certain that every Member of the
House will agree in principle with what
is being done, they may not and probably will not agree. with the method
which may be suggested in order to
achieve that end. That I do not call
controversial legislation. I will give this
assurance now to the House, that beyond
facing the problems of war and legislating
to render more efficient our effort towards

Prolongation of Parliament
winning the war-and further legislation
will be brought forward where it is necessary in order to establish and safeguard
our position when peace comes alongnothing else will be introduced for which
we have no mandate. We will go on
doing what we can to help in the war,
and go on trying to plan and solve the
problems which come before, us from day
to day and endeavour to place this
country in a position where it can take
advantage of peace and security when
they do arise. I beg to move.

a

support the Motion which has been proposed by the Prime Minister. I do so
not because I am under any compulsion
to do it but as a voluntary act of goodwill
and good faith, and because I believe in
the inherent justice of the Motion. I
should like in the first place to clear up
one or two misapprehensions. The statement has been made several times in the
House this afternoon that this Motion is
tantamount to extending the life of the
Government of Northern Ireland. I
should like the Members of this House to
remove any such misapprehension from
their minds. This Motion refers to the
prolongation of the life of Parliament, not
the prolongation of the life of the
Government. The intellectual forces of
the country can, if they express themselves in a constitutional fashion, change
the personnel of the Government from
time to time, but as I have said, this
Motion refers to the prolongation of
Parliament not of the present form of
Government or the personnel of the
Government.
Another misapprehension I should like
to remove is this. It was stated by the
Member for Pottinger in his opening
remarks that representations had been
made by this Government to the Imperial
Government to have provision for the prolongation of this Parliament included
within the scope of the British Act. That
is not correct. . This year the Government
of Northern Ireland decided not to make
any such representations, but to leave the
justice of their case to the common sense,
decency, and traditional fair play of the
British Government, and it succeeded
because of those principles.
The hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's, who feels most secure in his seat,
as I do in mine, challenged the right of
certain people to speak for the Labour and
trade union movement. So do I, and I
am going to submit it to a very good
test. The Member for Pottinger took it
upon himself a few weeks ago to go to
the Imperial House of Commons and claim
-I have Hansard here that he was
speaking with the united backing of the
trade union movement in Northern Ireland. He claimed that the trade union
movement had sent him there. I wish to
analyse that statement. There are 80,000
trade unionists in Northern Ireland. The
overwhelming majority of those are in
British trade unions-about 76,000 out of
80,000. There are only about 16,500 out
of that total of 80,000 affiliated to the
Northern Ireland Labour Party. In other
words, roughly one-fifth of the total trade
union movement in Northern Ireland is
associated with the Northern Ireland
Labour Party, as the trade unions in
Great Britain are affiliated to the British
Labour Party.
as I

in this country has any right to claim

or to another House or to represent a particular constituency by the trade union
movement alone. If we were to try to

became eligible. and I know

Take the question of affiliation again. Ont
of 80,000 trade unionists, mostly in

just over 16,000 are affiliated to the Northern Ireland Labour Party. How is that
affiliation brought about? I will tell you.

I give all my support to further extending the life of this Parliament.
That was the British Parliament. The
British Parliament is an older Parliament than the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. The Imperial Parliament was
returned in 1935, and this Parliament
was elected in 1938, as I have good cause
to remember, and therefore from the
point of view of age this is a more
modern Parliament than the Imperial
Parliament. But listen to this:
I give all my support to further
extending the life of this Parliament.
By extending the life of the Parliament at Westminster you are automatically extending the life of 13 Members
who represent constituencies in Northern
Ireland in the Imperial Parliament.
Therefore, if it is democratic to come to
the Parliament of Northern Ireland one
day and say, "You ought to have free
and open elections with all convenient
speed because this is Northern Ireland,
and because of the inherent corruption
and shortcomings of the people of Northern Ireland," surely the same argument
must apply to anything which affects 13
constituencies in Northern Ireland which
are represented in the Imperial Parliament unless-and I hesitate to think this
is the case the person concerned happens
to have an eye on the seat he himself re-)
presents in the Imperial Parliament, and
feels a little doubtful about the duration
of his stay in that particular seat.
Later on in his speech to-day the
Member for Pottinger said: "I only wish
the Prime Minister would read the life
of Connolly." Later on he quoted a
speech by the chairman of the Ulster
Unionist Council along the lines of "Each
for all and all for each," and then he
said those ideals were synonymous with
the ideals of Connolly. It is easy to take
a quotation from someone's work, compare it with something someone else has
said, and then say they are identical.
They may not be, and in this case they
were not. You can believe in the principle of "Each for all, and all for each,"
and not believe in Nationalism, either
economically or politically. The difference between a man who believes in the
British connection and a man like
Connolly, who stood for a complete and
out-and-out Republic, is so marked as
to bear no resemblance at all.
No Member of this House is better
acquainted-although some may be as
well acquainted-with the philosophy of
the man referred to as James Connolly
than I am myself, for I have read all his
works. I know he was an intense partisan
and a complete Nationalist, that he believed in absolute and irrevocable separation of Great Britain from Ireland, and
that he did not believe in any of the
present-day institutions of the British

British Parliament is being prolonged?
It is only being prolonged because there
is a National Government. This Government is not a National Government. It
is not even a Coalition Government. Who
said it was a Coalition Government?
Herbert Morrison. If I were a Member
of the British Parliament I would have
pulverised and paralysed the Right Hon.
Herbert Morrison. He would only be
small fry if I got to my feet to talk to
him. What right has he to say that the
Government here is a Coalition Government? In regard to some of the reforms
that have taken place here, I believe the
Member for Willowfield has had his
finger in the pie. I give him credit for
that. Although he has carried out some
reforms by no stretch of the imagination
can this Government be called a Coalition
Government?
The right hon. Member for Willowfield
-I know my friend will pardon me for
saying this because he will hit me as hard
on some other occasion when he will use
a few jawbreakers about me-won Willowfield as a Labour man. He went out as a
100 per cent. Labour man. Then he
changed from Labour to the North of
Ireland Commonwealth Labour Party.
With all respect to him, if he had carried
on with his Commonwealth Labour Party
and kept out of the present Government
I might have been along with him. We

Like the right hon. Member for Willowfield, I have fought so many elections I

If there were an election to-morrow we

would be in it both ways. Lawyers are

9 DECEMBER 1943
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 9th December, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Written Answer to Question.
COLLECTION OF SCRAP METAL
FROM LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
Mr. STEVENSON asked the Minister
of Finance whether his attention has been
drawn to the recent Press reports that
the Direction by the Ministry of Supply,
which makes it compulsory for certain local
authorities to collect scrap metal, has been
withdrawn; whether this will also apply
to local authorities in Northern Ireland;
and, if so, whether the necessity still remains to collect heavy scrap metal such
as railings and gates.
no
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): I am grateful to the hon.
Member for raising this matter. I am
aware of the decision of the Ministry of
Supply to withdraw the compulsory
Direction to collect ferrous scrap from
those local authorities which have
baling or flattening equipment. This
decision, I am informed, is due to the
gratifying fact that supplies of the types
of domestic scrap collected by local
authorities, viz., tins and light metal, are
more than sufficient for the needs of the
furnaces. Those local authorities which
operate baling equipment will, however,
continue to be subject to the Direction to
collect scrap metal of all sorts within their
districts, and it is estimated that the
tonnage arising from such sources will be
sufficient to meet the national needs for
these light materials.
One thing I would like to make clear,
and that is that the decision does not
mean that the need for heavy scrap is in
any way affected. In fact, the need for
this form of scrap is greater than ever.
Though the position in respect of one
item of salvage is so satisfactory, there
has been no diminution in the acuteness of
the position generally. So far from this
being the case, it is the intention that
the diversion of energy from the collection of tins should allow of even greater
efforts being put forth in other fields of
salvage. In evidence of this, I may say
that the Ministry of Supply has asked
that deliveries should be increased by 10
per cent.
an
A further point is that some of the
abnormal sources of supply of heavy scrap
are becoming exhausted, and the drive in
other directions calls therefore for
intensification of effort. Accordingly the
collection of railings and gates, farm
scrap, structural steel, and all other
heavy materials will continue to be
prosecuted with the utmost vigour.
Sittings of the House.
Resolved," That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until Tuesday
next." (Sir Wilson Hungerford.)

Mr. WARNOCK: I beg to move, in
page 2, after line 24, to insert the words:
"The persons first appointed shall
continue to hold office until the expiration of twelve months from the
termination of the present emergency
and shall then cease to hold office; and
thereupon the Minister of Education
shall appoint as members of the Youth
Committee twelve persons of whom not
less than six shall at the date of their
appointment be under forty years of
age.'
The Amendment, which stands in my
name, relates to the appointment of the
Youth Committee. This Bill which had
a reception universally cordial has given
rise to criticism or debate upon only one
subject, and that is the composition of
the Committee. It is, I think, the focal
2589 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]→ HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Mr. Warnock]
point of the Bill, and upon the success of
the Youth Committee the whole question
of youth welfare development will depend.
It will be obvious to every Member of
the House that at the present time there
are a very large number of young persons
who are not only interested in youth welfare, but have for many years past been
extremely active in this movement. They
are not here to-day, because they are
engaged in a sterner struggle elsewhere,
and it appears to me it would be a very
great mistake if we should now appoint a
Committee of any permanent nature while
SO many of those who are vitally
interested and who work so hard in this
endeavour are away. For that reason my
Amendment suggests that the persons
who are appointed on the Youth Committee shall only continue to hold office
for a limited period, and the period I
suggest is twelve months from the
termination of the present emergency.
That is the first part of my Amendment,
and I think the principle behind it will
commend itself to every Member of the
House.
The second part of the Amendment
relates also to the composition of the
Committee which is to be appointed at
the termination of 12 months after the
cessation of hostilities. I do not think
anyone can suggest that during the interim between the last war and the present war our elder statesmen or older
people made much of a success of that
period. The position in which we find
ourselves to-day is, I think, a condemnation of our policy during that period,
and I suggest that, when the new Committee comes to be appointed, when our
men have returned from the fighting
Forces, that Committee should consist of
at least 50 per cent. of persons who are
under 40 years of age. Perhaps you do
not realise it, but I think after a man
reaches the age of 40 he begins, perhaps
insensibly, to lose touch with youth. The
Amendment if it meets with the acceptance of the House will secure that at
least half of the members of the Committee will be persons of ripe experience
and judgment.
I should like to see on this Youth
Committee, which as I say is the focal
point in the whole business, a very large
proportion of young people. If they
succeed the Amendment will have
achieved some purpose; if they do not
succeed we will at least have given them
the opportunity of having a very substantial voice in the management of what,
after all, is their own affair. I would
venture to hope that the Amendment
will provoke a lively discussion upon this
subject which is, I think, the only part
of the Youth Welfare Bill which requires
a careful examination.
I hope hon. Members of all sections of
the House-there is only one section
present to-day-will give the Parliamentary Secretary the benefit of their views
on this subject. I think it is right,
holding the views I do, that I should
endeavour to provoke discussion on this
subject. Personally, I believe that the
Amendment, which stands in my name,
will improve the Bill and will secure
ultimately, when our boys return from
abroad, a thoroughly good Committee.
The natural objection, and one which has
some force, is the fixing arbitrarily of an
age limit.
I think it is necessary to fix
an age limit. I cannot possibly in this
connection refer to the Parliamentary
Secretary, but I think you will find
generally that the people in control of the
Ministry of Education will be persons
who are up in years if I may use that
expression.
I think it is necessary in the interests
of this committee itself that these people
should be compelled to appoint a number
of young persons. You will find in this
country at least half a dozen persons
under 40 who have been very active in
youth welfare organisation, and who are
persons not irresponsible but whose judg
ment, drive, energy, and youthful ideas
can be relied on. People under 40 are
far more receptive and have newer ideas
than those over 40. This matter of
youth welfare is not in its infancy. We
want the impact of young ideas in this
Committee. I cannot see any way of
absolutely ensuring it otherwise than by
the imposition of an arbitrary age limit.
There are plenty of people under 40, or
will be when hostilities cease, who will
have new views and new ideas and who
will be able to bring those forward in the
Committee.
I commend this Amendment to the
Committee. I hope it will promote a
lively discussion, and that by the clash of
ideas in debate we may arrive at some
solution of a problem which is, admittedly, a difficult one.

PARLIAMENTARY
SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): At the
outset I must say that my Ministry and
my Minister have the greatest sympathy
with the principle embodied in the suggestion put forward by the hon. and
learned Member for St. Anne's. First
of all, the whole Amendment is intended
to ensure that youth should get its due
representation on this Youth Committee.
The first part of the Amendment is really
directed to that end as well as the second
part.
Before I go into this matter in detail I
should like to tell the hon. and learned
Member what he probably knows already
-that the Thompson Committee recommended that a certain percentage of the
members of the new Permanent Youth
Committee should be under 40. The
Minister has every intention of carrying
out that principle as far as is humanly
possible. It is quite true, as the hon.
and learned Member stated, that there
might be much more difficulty in making
those appointments at the present time
when people who would be of the greatest
help to the committee are serving their
country in another way. That is an
accepted fact, but I want him to realise
that we are fully aware of the necessity
of bringing this impact of youth to bear.
I also want him to realise that we will
do our best to see that the outlook of
youth is brought to bear on the very
serious problems of youth welfare, but I
would suggest to him that in some ways
his Amendment is liable to defeat its
object.
I will deal with the first part of the
Amendment. It was always intended to
set a term, not a very lengthy one, on
what I might call the life of membership. Sub-clause (4) of Clause 2 states:
Persons appointed as members of the
Youth Committee shall hold office for
such terms, and upon such conditions
as to retirement, ceasing to hold office,
and re-appointment, as the Minister of
Education may from time to time prescribe.
That gives the Minister an opportunity of
using his judgment in this matter. I can
assure the hon. and learned Member that
it was never the intention to make a
very lengthy term for the life of membership of the committee. What I am afraid
of is that the Amendment might prolong
that life unduly; well over the period
which might be in the mind of the
Minister. It would prolong it very
arbitrarily, and perhaps much longer than
the hon. and learned Member would like.
We all hope and pray that the contrary
will be the case, and that the present
emergency will be over sooner than we
expect. In that event, if the Amendment
were accepted, another twelve months
would be added before there could be any
question of the committee which had been
appointed ceasing to hold office. That is
one point I should like to make. I think
it would be a great pity if we set up this
committee in such an arbitrary manner.
Then we come to the question of the
appointment of the members of the Youth
Committee. The Amendment says,
"twelve persons of whom not less than
six shall at the date of their appointment
be under forty years of age." That, too,
very arbitrary. There might be men
and women who were one or two months
over the age of 40 and who consequently
would not be eligible for membership no
matter how great their capacity to render
useful service in this direction. I am not
disagreeing with the principle that youth
must be represented and that it is necessary to have as many young people as
possible on the committee, but we must
remember that it is not always the exact
age that matters; it is the outlook of the
persons concerned.
I recognise that the hon. and learned
Member is only suggesting that six out of
the twelve should be so appointed, but I
think what I have already stated should
be borne in mind. I am going to ask
the hon. and learned Member how he proposes to carry this out. Does he propose
that the Minister should ask for birth
certificates? Does he 'realise that this
committee is going to be composed of
women as well as men? That being so
he may have great difficulty in the
matter. That is going to make the situation more difficult.
I hope that the hon. and learned
Member will realise that the principle
which he has stressed will be recognised
as fully as possible both now and later
on. I hope it may be possible to take
advantage of the services of those who
were interested in young people, but who

GORDON : I

14 DECEMBER 1943
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 14th December, 1943.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Papers Presented.
Ministry of Home Affairs:
Royal Ulster Constabulary Pay
(Amending) Order, 1943. (By Act).
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Home Affairs.
NURSES' SALARIES.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
Northern Ireland is keeping in step with
Great Britain regarding the new and
improved salaries and conditions for
nurses just announced.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Lowry): As the hon. Member is
doubtless aware, the Government
accepted the recommendation contained
in the Interim Report of the Parliamentary Select Committee on Health
Services, commending the adoption of
the Scottish or Taylor scales of nurses'
salaries by all rate-aided and voluntary
hospital authorities in Northern Ireland,
and undertook to pay such authorities
fifty per cent. of the cost of raising their
nurses' salaries to the Taylor level.
It is understood that the question of
the salaries of nurses other than hospital
nurses has engaged the attention of the
Select Committee, which committee will
doubtless make appropriate recommendations in the matter to the Government
in their forthcoming report.
URBAN AND RURAL HOUSING.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can now state
whether the Government have any intention of authorising, during the war, the
erection by local authorities in the urban
and rural areas of Northern Ireland of
dwelling houses under the same subsidy
scheme as in Belfast.
Mr. LOWRY: As I informed the hon.
Member on the 7th December the
Government appreciates that there is an
acute shortage of houses throughout the
Province generally which it intends to
relieve as circumstances permit. The
position has not changed since that date
and I have, therefore, nothing to add
to the reply I then gave.
MILK AND MEALS FOR SCHOOL
CHILDREN.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether she can supplement
the information given in the House on
the 7th instant regarding the comparative
positions in England and Wales and Northern Ireland in the matter of the provision of meals and milk in public
elementary schools with similar information under both heads as to the comparative positions in Scotland and
Northern Ireland, and, if not, whether
she will procure such information.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I regret
that I am not yet in a position to supplement the information given by me to the
hon. Member on the 7th inst. regarding
the comparative position in England and
Wales and Northern Ireland in respect
of the provision of meals and milk in
public elementary schools. I have no information as to the present position in
elementary schools in Scotland, but my
Ministry is in correspondence with the
Scottish Education Department on the
subject.
WRITTEN ANSWERS.
Poultry Control Order.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has received representations from collectors in Ballymena who are affected by the new Poultry
Control Order; whether he can define the
position of the packers under this scheme
and what licence they hold; whether it is
a fact that shippers also hold collectors'
licences which puts them in favourable
positions; whether it is a fact that egg
merchants can buy eggs in country
districts and hold also a poultry collector's
licence; whether in view of the plight of
collectors in Northern Ireland he will reconsider the whole position and the
anomalies which exist in the granting of
Written Answers
Adjournment of House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
licences; and whether he is aware that
unemployment has been created as a result of this scheme.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the
affirmative.
Two classes of licences for the sale of
poultry by wholesale are issued under the
Poultry (Control and Prices) (Northern
Ireland) Order, 1943. These licences are
specified in Paragraph 3 of the Order as
"(a) a collector's licence being a licence
for the purchase of live poultry
from producers and the sale or disposal thereof alive to licensed
packers.
(b) A packer's licence, being a licence
for the purchase of live poultry
from producers or collectors and
the sale or disposal of that poultry
after slaughter, plucked and packed
in accordance with the conditions
of the licence."
I am not aware of any anomalies with
regard to the issue of licences, nor can I
accept the suggestion that the licensing
provisions of the Order have adversely
affected the position of collectors. Packers
have always been free to engage in both
the collection and the shipping of poultry,
and the provisions with regard to a
packer's licence simply recognise the customary trade practice. Similarly, many
egg merchants have in the past engaged
in the Christmas poultry trade, and they
have been licensed for a seasonal trade
over the Christmas period. These seasonal licences will expire on January 15th.
Broadly speaking, people have been
licensed for the class of business they
carried on before the war, provided they
have, suitable premises and other facilities
for the conduct of that trade, and I see
no reason to reconsider any of the provision of the Order.
Special Constabulary, Shankill Road,
Belfast.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
name, address and place of employment
of the Station Commandant of the
Shankill Special Constabulary; the distance of the Commandant's residence
from the Shankill Road; whether petrol
coupons are supplied for the use of his
car on this duty to and from Belfast;
and whether any qualified person in
Belfast is available for this position.
Mr. LOWRY: The Sub-District Commandant of Shankill Road Special Constabulary is Mr. Robert Armstrong, who
resides at Stoneyford, Co. Antrim, a distance of about 8 miles from the Shankill
Road. He receives an allowance of
petrol from the Petroleum Officer to enable him to travel, in the course of his
private employment, over a considerable
area of South Antrim extending to
Belfast, and including frequent visits to
the, city.
As these journeys are not undertaken
on Special Constabulary duty no petrol
coupons are issued for them through
constabulary sources, but, in common
with other officers who necessarily use
motor cars, Mr. Armstrong receives an
allowance of petrol solely for official purposes within his Own Constabulary
District.
This officer has performed his Special
Constabulary duties most satisfactorily
for over twenty years, and as he would
have to travel to Belfast in any event for
private business purposes, there is no
reason why any other person should be
considered for his post.

Mr. SPEAKER: Before we proceed

years of

At the same time I can see and sympathise strongly with the views of the hon.

and recommending the setting up of a

will have power to initiate schemes.
should like to know the position in that
respect.
I
I should also like to refer to the statement issued by the Churches Welfare
Council, in which they draw attention to
a number of important points. They
stress the great importance of the
Christian basis of the work to be carried
on by the committee. I am not going
into the matter in detail, but I should
like to know the view of the Ministry of
Education on that subject. I agree that

a basis of Christianity common to all the

Hon. Members, I am sure, have got
copies of the statement, and I will not

Lord GLENTORAN: In the Committee
stage I said I thought this was one of the
most important Bills we had had before
the House for a considerable time. I am
satisfied the Bill is going to be a good
Bill. I do not think that the amendments
from the Back Benches have done any
harm; in fact, I think they have greatly
improved the Bill. There is one thing I
am glad of and that is that civil servants,
who have always played such a strenuous
and active part in everything pertaining
to the welfare of the country, are to be
allowed to take part in this movement.
Another Amendment, which is very
valuable, is one concerned with youth.
The extraordinary suspicion that old men
have about young men is always amazing
to me. They never seem to have the same
suspicion about young women. (Laughter.)
Sometimes I think it would be a good
thing if they had. (Laughter.) In any
case I always find in this House that older
Members are most suspicious about young
men. You have only to look round you
to see colonels under thirty, and young
men of twenty and twenty-one commanding submarines. This is the day of the
young man, and it is most proper that
such young men should have representation on the committee.
The real reason I got up was to express
the feeling I have about the tremendous
importance of the Bill itself. In my own
constituency there is the Ledlie Memorial
Hall which has been a magnificent training centre for the young in Ballymacarrett. This committee is going to
have a most difficult job. The failure or
success of the whole thing will depend on
the composition of this committee. It was
quite extraordinary that throughout the
excellent debates on the Bill more pressure
was not brought on the Minister to disclose the sort of people to be put on the
committee. That is a point we had not
enough information about. Success or
failure of the movement will depend on
these things. There are two ways of looking at this matter. This youth movement
may develop into a pagan movement as
happened in Germany. We have seen the
marvellous effect of the youth movement
in that country-admittedly wrongfrom the pagan point of view. On the
other hand it may endeavour to go along
the lines of the Church Lads' Brigadewhat I might call without any offence a
clerical control movement. There again I
think that would bring about failure.
Therefore, we have to have a dividing
line between physical control and spiritual
control. Leadership will be of immense.
importance.
I should like to say with great respect
to the Parliamentary Secretary that the
leaders of those voluntary associations
which have been a success the Boy
Scouts, for instance--have been quite outstanding in the youth movement. The
Boys' Brigade has been excellent. There
is another association which is not so well

There should be no dominating influence
on the Committee, but it should go forward as a unanimous and harmonious
body with only one thing in view-the
improvement of the youth of the country.
Mr. HENDERSON: May I take this
opportunity of saying how delighted I
am to see the Government taking such a
keen interest in the youth of the country?
To me it is rather a surprising thing,
because for the past 20 years the Government have neglected the youth of the
country, and had it not been for the
war-
Mr. SPEAKER: We are now on the
Third Reading and, therefore, the only
matters that can be discussed are those
contained in the Bill. The speech which
the hon. Member is making would be very
appropriate on the Second Reading, but
this is the Third Reading.
Mr. HENDERSON: I agree with the
noble Lord that we must not destroy the
thing we are trying to bring into being.
During the past number of years certain
people have taken a keen interest in the
youth of the country who had been
allowed to run wild. Many people tried
to do things for the youth of the country
which should have been performed by
the State. It would retard the whole
movement if consideration were not given
to the people who had rendered such
great service. I agree that the Government have taken a step in the right direction, and I wish to congratulate the hon.
Lady on the way she introduced this
measure. No matter what committee is
set up nothing can be done unless the
homes of these boys and girls are brightened. There are many homes in Northern Ireland to-day in which the young
people are not living in happy and prosperous conditions.
I wish to congratulate the Government
on bringing this measure forward and I
can assure them that they have the best
thanks of every citizen interested in the
welfare of our youth.
Mr. MINFORD: I agree with what
the noble Lord has stated. The committee is one of great importance, and I
should like the hon. Lady to tell us what
their duties will be and how far they can
go. There are many voluntary organisations all over Ulster which have done
great work. The question of age was
raised by the hon. and learned Member
for St. Anne's. As far as I know this
Committee will have no power of initiation. There may be districts in Belfast
or in the rural areas where no interest
will be taken in the young people. Has
this committee power to take up that
matter and see that youth is served? The
committee should have some power in
regard to initiation. The organisations
in being before the Government took up
this matter were enthusiastically received
by the great majority of the people of
Ulster.
When it comes to appointing the members of this committee the leaders in the
voluntary organisations should not be
cast aside. The people who started these
youth organisations are worthy of a
place on the committee. So far as the
Civil Service is concerned I think I was
the first Member of this House to stand
up for its members. Some say I do not
like civil servants. Some of them are
the best men in Ulster and I do not want
any bar placed on civil servants. I
want to see the appointment of 12 men
who have a good Christian outlook and
who will take care of the moral and
physical welfare of the youth of Ulster.
What are the young men of Ulster
doing to-day? If there are men under 40
who want jobs let them go to the Desert.
The place for the men under 40 is in the

fighting Forces. We do not want such
men to take charge of the youth welfare
movement. The place for them is on
the battlefield. I am disgusted when I
find men under 40 appointed to committees. We want "King's Men," to
quote the words of the late Lord
Craigavon; we do not want cowards. We
want men with energy and pluck.

to
see

The leaders of the voluntary youth
movements in Ulster have done a noble
work. I stand for men with energy, push
and go.
I want men of intelligence
appointed, men who will not guide the

Christian
loyal,
appointed. Men who set up various

dragged into the committee, men who will
not go out and fight for their country.
The place for the men under forty is in
the mountains of Italy or some other
fighting front. I hope the hon. Lady will
see to it that no one is appointed to the
committee whose place is on the battlefield.
We are engaged in the greatest war in
history. We have no conscription here,
but we have some people who have played
the coward's game. If the war were over
then I would be content if men under
forty-those who served their countrywere appointed to the committee. They
are at present fighting for Ulster. Older
people like us will soon pass away and
then these youths will take our place. I
want consideration given to those who
inaugurated voluntary organisations
irrespective of whether they are thirty,
forty or fifty. I want men appointed who
will lead the youth of Ulster in a
Christian spirit, and I want the committee to have power to start a movement in districts that are not being
catered for.
Mr. AGNEW: I cannot agree with the
last speaker in regard to the question of
the age of those who will serve on the
Youth Committee. The people who are
appointed to the committee should look
at the matter of youth welfare from the
spiritual and temporal outlook. We want
to see the boys and girls getting a better
life than we have had; we want to see
them facing the future backed up with
the proper ideals; we want to see them
taken out of the rut of what we might
call blind alley jobs, and we want to see
them given a proper outlook so that the
future of Northern Ireland will be safe
in their hands.
Those who live in towns and cities
should not forget the rural areas. Quite
a lot could be done for the young people
who live in the lonely parts of Northern
Ireland, something which will help to
keep them in the country and on the
land. We know that when young people
leave the country and go to the larger
cities and towns they face certain dangers.
The committee will have great responsibilities, and they will perform a useful
purpose if the youth of the country is
enlightened in regard to the dangers and
pitfalls which they have to face when
they go out into the world.
The members of the committee must
be imbued with the proper spirit, the
Christian one. If the youth of the country
are imbued with that spirit then we need
have no fear for them because they will
know how to face danger. I should like
those in authority when setting up the
committee to look for the best material
possible irrespective of age. Something
should be done for the boys and girls
who live in remote areas. They should
be given some instruction so that when
they go further afield they may know
what they have to face. There is no use
in passing this Bill, electing committees,
and as the years roll on to find very little
is being done. I want to see some improvement made in the lives of our young
people I want to see the boys and girls
brought up in a proper atmosphere, and
given a
what
true picture of
life
will hold for them. If the young people
are given the proper spiritual outlook
then we can rest assured that the future
of Ulster will be in capable hands.
Lieut.-Colonel PANTER: It seems to
be that there is some difference of opinion
as to the age of the members of the Committee. They should be young men with
Christian and soldierly qualities. The
noble Lord mentioned the youth movement in Germany. The youth movement
in Germany was the finest one in the
world, but, unfortunately, it was led by
the Junkers, who ran it along wrong
channels. I agree with the hon. Member
who stated that we should get men who
have fought in the Forces sailors,
soldiers and airmen. These are the kind
of men who should replace the committee

The hon. Member for South Down said

that the committee should go to fields
afar and should cover the whole of Northern Ireland. I agree with him in that.
The work should not be confined to
Belfast or other cities. The committee
should see to that. You want young,
vigorous men and you can get them when
the men come back from the war. I am
absolutely for youth being on this committee, and not persons over forty.
Mrs. PARKER: I should like to point
out to the hon. Member for South Down
and the hon. Member for Antrim that
the functions of the committee which is
being set up are very clearly defined in
the second Clause of this Bill, and it does
seem to me that it is possible the hon.
Member for South Down has not read
the Clause very carefully because he
would not have asked me any questions
on the subject if he had done so.
To deal with the point raised by the
hon. Member for Antrim about the
initiation of schemes by this committee,
I should say that it has always been an
underlying principle with my Ministry
that it would not set up State youth clubs
and State organisations. This committee
will not actually start youth clubs or
institutions of any kind, because, for one
thing, it is desirable to realise that if
the committee did so those institutions
would be set up and provided for entirely
by the State, and it is quite obvious that
there then might be a certain differentiation against voluntary associations which
are working clubs as they would receive
only a certain proportion from the State. I
think those voluntary organisations might
then be at a certain disadvantage.
would just put that forward as one of
the reasons why it is not proposed that
the new committee should actually
initiate activities. Their probable duty
will be to encourage the promotion of
schemes and to give facilities for youth
welfare in all its aspects. That is why
I need not enumerate the different ways
I
in which this committee will be able to
do a tremendous work for youth.
I must say that I have been extremely
delighted at the great interest which has
been shown by so many right hon. and
hon. Members in this House. I really do
not think that it is necessary for me to
assure right hon. and hon. Members that
we have every intention of benefiting
from the experience and the wonderful
work carried on by existing organisations.
There is no intention of refusing to
the
recognise those organisations-on
contrary, as I think I made perfectly
plain on other occasions, we hope to
benefit much by their ripe experience in
all matters connected with youth welfare.

in the youth movement as a whole. So
far as possible the interests of youth

with youth work, but it is our intention

membership of 12-but those who bore

leaders in this movement.

I need not refer to the question of age.
That has been dealt with already quite
adequately on the Committee stage and
the Report stage. I am astonished to
find that perhaps inadvertently hon.
Members have stressed and stressed again
the importance of the men who are going
to work on this Committee. I hope that
that was by inadvertence, because I think
hon. Members should realise that women
have played a great part in this movement for youth welfare, and that it is
not only boys who need help in youth but
girls, and that the problem of looking
after the girls of our nation is as great
if not greater than the problems of the
boys. So I hope that when hon. Mem-
2635 Youth Welfare Bill [Senate]

Adjournment
bers stressed the word "men" they meant
it to include the opposite sex, because I
think that no committee could function
properly unless it has the experience of
those who have been accustomed to deal
in this work with girls.
I do not think there is anything that
I can add to what has been said. I do
think it is an extremely healthy sign
that so many hon. Members in this House
have spoken on the Bill and that so many
are interested in this movement. I hope
that they will, when this Bill has become
an Act, give us further assistance and
that they will continue to show this
great interest in youth work.
I hap-
I
pened to inspect some premises the other
day connected with one of the great
cadet organisations and their welfare
work. I found that very few of the
general public had ever been there.
do not think any Member of Parliament
had been interested. That particular
unit had splendid premises and was doing
the very best work possible for those
boys with whom I was immensely impressed. I should like to see hon.
Members, who have a great responsibility
to lead the public, pay individual attention wherever they go in their country
districts-we referred to country districts
to-day-and here in Belfast. I should
like to see them going and inspecting and
encouraging and helping, and in that
way they will be doing just as much for
the work of youth welfare as I believe
we are to-day in passing this measure,
and as the Ministry of Education hopes
to do by encouraging and fostering everything connected not only with education,
but this work, which is now known to
the world in general as youth welfare
work.
Question put, and agreed to.
Ordered, That the Clerk do carry the
Bill to the Senate and acquaint them that
this House has agreed to the same, with
Amendments, to which they desire the
concurrence of the Senate.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.
Adjournment.
Resolved, "That this House do now
adjourn." (Sir Norman Stronge.)
Adjourned accordingly at Ten
minutes after Three o'clock
until Tuesday, the 25th
January, 1944, provided
always that if it appears to
the satisfaction of Mr.
Speaker, after consultation
with the Government, that
the public interest requires
that the House shall meet
at any earlier date during
the adjournment, Mr.
Speaker may give notice
that he is so satisfied and
thereupon the House shall
meet on the date and at the
time stated in such notice
and shall transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date.
